en: Homage to that Blessed One, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Self-Awakened One.
The Root Commentary on the Vibhaṅga in the Abhidhamma Piṭaka.
1. Analysis of the Aggregates (Khandhavibhaṅga) 1.

Explanation of the Suttanta Exposition (Suttantabhājanīyavaṇṇanā) The "Vision of the Four Truths" refers to the four truths taken together as the "Four Truths"; one who sees these four truths is called "one who has vision of the Four Truths."
Although both disciples and paccekabuddhas possess the vision of the Four Noble Truths, the Blessed One alone is especially worthy of praise as "the seer of the Four Noble Truths.
This is because his vision of the Four Noble Truths was not preceded by anyone else; because he attained omniscience regarding them and mastery over the ten powers;
and because it is perfectly manifest through its extension into the mental continuums of others.

He is called a *nātha* because he protects; he aspires for and prays for the welfare and happiness of those to be trained (*veneyya*), or he afflicts the calamity of the defilements residing in the mental continuums of others.

Alternatively, the meaning is that he requests various practices for their benefit, according to such passages as: "It is good, monks, for a bhikkhu from time to time to reflect upon his own perfection. He is endowed with supreme sovereignty of mind over all beings.
Or, because he rules over and surpasses others through his qualities, the Blessed One, the Supreme Lord, is called the "Protector" (*nātha*).

Having stated the reason for the necessity of listening—namely, that one should act with the thought, "Having shown reverence for the True Dhamma, I shall do so"—he speaks again, enjoining them to listen: "Listen to that, being composed.
Or, by the phrase "having delved into the method of the ancient commentaries, I shall do so," he indicates the reason for listening with careful attention.
Having stated the reason, he says, "Having shown reverence for the True Dhamma, listen to it," while enjoining them to do so.
Herein, the expression "one who sees the Four Truths" is a praise on account of the quality of seeing that which corresponds in number to the teaching divided into fourfold;
and the expression "endowed with the eighteen Buddha-qualities" is [a praise] on account of the qualities corresponding in number to the teaching divided into eighteenfold.
It should be understood as follows: By means of the aforementioned unsurpassed vision of the Four Noble Truths, the Blessed One was capable of teaching the *Dhammasaṅgaṇī* in four ways;
and by virtue of his possession of the eighteen qualities of a Buddha, he was capable of teaching the *Vibhaṅga* in eighteen ways.
This [verse] indicates the qualities that produce such capability in teaching: "He who sees the Four Truths, endowed with the Buddha-qualities..."

"...the eighteen [factors]. By this, demonstrating the non-erroneous nature of the aforementioned teaching because it was spoken by the Omniscient One, he enjoins sentient beings to undertake its study and so forth;
and by showing his own exertion in reaching the final conclusion, he arouses reverence for listening to the *Aṭṭhakathā*.
Furthermore, he demonstrates that the *Dhammasaṅgaṇī* and the *Vibhaṅga-pakaraṇa* could not have been taught by anyone other than the Omniscient One who possesses the aforementioned qualities.
By presenting [this], one generates exceptional reverence for the commentary on that [text] and elucidates the qualities—such as perfect enlightenment—of the Jewels beginning with the Buddha.
Among these, the Four Truths are indeed well-known; however, the eighteen Buddha-qualities should be understood as follows: "In the past..."
The Buddha, the Blessed One, possesses unimpeded knowledge regarding the future... [and so on] ...regarding the present... [and so on].
For the Buddha, the Blessed One, who is endowed with these three qualities, every bodily action is preceded by knowledge and follows after knowledge; every verbal action...
[and so on] ...every mental action... [and so on]. For one who is endowed with these six qualities...
For the Buddha, the Blessed One, there is no decline in zeal, no decline in the teaching of the Dhamma,
no decline in energy, no decline in concentration, no decline in wisdom, and no decline in liberation.
For the Buddha, the Blessed One, who is endowed with these twelve qualities, there is no jesting, no clamor, and nothing left unperceived.
“There is no hurrying, there is no unoccupied mind, there is no equanimity lacking clear comprehension.
In this context, “there is no frolic” means there is no activity with the intention of play. “There is no clamor” means there is no impulsive activity.
“There is no untouched” means there is nothing that has not been touched by knowledge. “There is no hurrying” means there is no hurried activity.
There is none. "There is no unapplied mind" means there is no purposeless mental activity.
"There is no equanimity without reflection" means there is no ignorant equanimity. However, in some places, instead of writing "there is no deficiency in the teaching of the Dhamma," they write:
"there is no deficiency in zeal, no deficiency in energy, no deficiency in power."

1. In the *Dhammasaṅgaṇī*, having grouped the states—beginning with the wholesome (*kusala*)—into triplets and dyads, the *Vibhaṅga* treatise was spoken in order to analyze those very same states as they are stated in the Suttas by way of the aggregates (*khandha*) and so forth.
In that context, "analysis" (*vibhaṅga*) is the analysis of the aggregates and so forth that were stated in brief.
That particular analysis which is established and predominant for a given text is called the "*Vibhaṅga-pakaraṇa*" (The Treatise of Analysis).
It is so called. "Excessive" (adhikato) means it is grasped by way of being something that ought to be stated.

In this context, within the *Khandhavibhaṅga*, which is the beginning of the *Vibhaṅga-pakaraṇa*, the passage "The five aggregates: the aggregate of form... [and so on]... the aggregate of consciousness" is known as the *Suttantabhājanīya*.
Is it not the case that the *Suttantabhājanīya* consists of only this much? True; however, by the word "iti" (thus),...

However, by means of the word *pana* (but/however), which indicates the meaning of "beginning" (*ādi*) or indicates the sense of "manner" (*pakāra*), one should understand that this entire Suttanta-bhājaniya—beginning with "the consciousness aggregate" (*viññāṇakkhandho*) and so forth—is of such a kind.

Alternatively, it points to the whole by means of a part, just as one might point to mountains or oceans [by mentioning a single peak or wave]. In that context, [it refers to] all things except for Nibbāna...

Because they encompass all phenomena (*sabbadhamma*) and because the aggregates (*khandha*) consist of fewer terms than the bases (*āyatana*) and other categories that also encompass everything, the Analysis of the Aggregates (*Khandhavibhaṅga*) is stated at the beginning.

It does not follow after that [the Analysis of the Bases], because form and the rest lack the intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*) of feeling and so forth; and it is within that intrinsic nature that the past and other time-periods constitute "heaps" (*rāsi*).

Having stated this, it should be said that because there is nothing other than that which undergoes deformation (ruppana) and so forth, the previous enumerations were intended to show that conditioned phenomena are not fully exhausted [by those categories], and not to suggest that the mere enumeration itself is absent.
However, because there is no sixth aggregate, he says "not above. For there is nothing that has escaped from phenomena possessing divisions and is devoid of pastness and so forth.
There is the sense of a "heap" (*rāsa*) for the single *nibbāna*. By the phrase "in a heap," he shows the scope of the word *khandha* together with its literal meaning (*saddattha*).
By the phrase "in qualities, in designation, and in conventional usage," he shows only the scope of the word *khandha*, not its literal meaning.
For [the word] occurs by taking all qualities such as virtue (*sīla*), both mundane and supramundane, without exception.
The word *khandha* indicates the sense of a "heap" (*rāsa*) distinguished by qualities such as virtue (*sīla*). However, some say that here the sense of "quality" (*guṇa*) is the sense of *khandha*.
But in the case of the term "wooden log" (*dārukkhandha*), the word *khandha* does not function in the sense of a conventional designation (*paññatti*);
rather, when wood possesses such breadth and length, it receives the designation "wooden log," and thus it falls under the category of a designation.

It has been stated thus. Likewise, when the term *khandha* refers to the aggregate of consciousness (*viññāṇakkhandha*) as it occurs even within a single moment of consciousness, it does not express the meaning of a conventional term (*ruḷhī-sadda*).

However, since the word *khandha* is conventionally established for a collection (*samudāya*), when it occurs in reference to a single part of that collection, it functions by virtue of that very convention;
therefore, it is said that the word *khandha* falls under the category of a conventional term.

In the phrase "rāsito guṇato," the ablative case (*nissakkavacana*) used everywhere should be understood as being employed with reference to the fact that the word *khandha* functions as the cause for the application [of the term] specifically to its object.
In order to define this meaning of "from a heap" (*rāsito*) according to the etymological sense of the word (*saddatthavasena*), he said:

"For this so-called 'meaning of aggregate' (*khandhaṭṭho*) is the meaning of a mass (*piṇḍaṭṭho*)," and so forth. Even in the sense of a "portion" (*koṭṭhāsaṭṭhe*) as the meaning of *khandha*, [it is the sixth case...].

The aggregates must be understood as such. For even Nibbāna is a sixth constituent part (*koṭṭhāsa*). Therefore, it is appropriate to say that "the meaning of aggregate (*khandha*) is the meaning of a heap (*rāsa*).

Alternatively, for those things that possess differentiation by way of the past and so forth, their status as specific constituents is spoken of by way of their respective characteristics, such as being subject to change (*ruppana*).
Thus, even though Nibbāna is devoid of differentiation, its nature as an aggregate is established by virtue of its being a constituent part.
It should be understood that it is not stated [in full].
"To this extent" means by way of a mere enumeration. It is analyzed as follows: "The four great elements... [and so on] ...are form. If one asks, "Where?
it is in eleven locations. By the word "iti," used in the sense of illustration, the entire method of analysis is shown.
And this analysis, as well as the analysis of the eye-base and so forth among the coarse and the rest, should be applied as appropriate to the eleven locations;

likewise for the aggregate of feeling and the others. However, the consciousness aggregate is analyzed within the first five of the eleven locations by way of the distinction of the six classes of consciousness, namely: "eye-consciousness... pe ... mind-consciousness."

In that context, there is no differentiation such as "mind-element" (manodhātu) and "mind-consciousness-element" (manoviññāṇadhātu). However, in order to show the point that those two are spoken of as "mind-consciousness" (manoviññāṇa), it should be understood that they are stated as "mind-element and mind-consciousness-element" in the Commentary (Aṭṭhakathā).

Having thus shown the delimitation of phenomena (dhamma-pariccheda) within the five aggregates according to the method of the Canon (Pāḷi), he said "Moreover" (apica) and so forth, in order to show it again by another way. "Therein" (ettha) means in this exposition of the aggregates (khandhaniddesa).
1. Explanation of the Description of the Aggregate of Form (Rūpakkhandhaniddesavaṇṇanā) 2.

Regarding the phrase "whatever" (*yaṃ kiñci*): here, *yaṃ* is an indefinite indication by way of generality, while *kiñci* is an indefinite indication that touches upon the distinctions of various categories.
By both together, [it refers to] whatever is past... or near, whether little or much.

Because the term "whatever" (*yaṃ kiñci*) encompasses everything that is suitable for neuter designation—whether it be of such a kind or of another kind—it would follow that it would also apply to other things suitable for neuter designation.
Seeing this over-extension (*atippasaṅga*), he said "form" (*rūpaṃ*) in order to restrict its application to the intended meaning.
[He did so] by taking the word *yaṃ* from the compound *yaṃ-kiñci* and the word *kiṃ*.
By taking the word "one" (*eka*) in the sense of illustrating a single meaning even when there is no fixed rule, it is said:
"even by two words. "And what, monks, do you call 'form'? means: you also call form "form"—for what reason do you say so?
Or alternatively, for what reason is it "form"? State that reason. Then, among these...
When the bhikkhus had become silent, the Blessed One said, “It is ‘it is disturbed’ (ruppati),” and so forth.

He says “it breaks up” (bhijjati) with reference to the dissolution of the preceding continuum, because one observes the arising of a dissimilar continuum upon the encounter with cold and other conditions.
And since dissolution is the attainment of a dissimilar state or a transformation, the meaning of “it breaks up” is that it undergoes transformation (vikāram āpajjati).

And "undergoing modification" (*vikārāpatti*) refers precisely to the arising of a dissimilar form when there is a combination of cold and so forth. However, because the immaterial aggregates (*arūpakkhandha*) undergo extremely rapid change,

just as material phenomena encounter cold and so forth during their moment of presence (*ṭhitikkhaṇa*), such that they lack the capacity to produce a subsequent continuity similar to the preceding one—
whether due to temperature or nutriment and so on— in the same way, there is an encounter with other factors [in the case of the immaterial].
There is none. Furthermore, the term *ruppaṇa* (being affected) is conventionally established in the sense of undergoing change through impact;

therefore, because non-material phenomena lack such impact and because they do not possess manifest change as material phenomena do, they are not said to "be affected" (*ruppanti*) nor are they described as having "the characteristic of being affected" (*ruppanalakkhaṇā*).
As for being affected by hunger and thirst, this occurs through the convergence of the digestive fire in the stomach.
It should be understood as "it occurs. And here, by the word *kuppati* ("it is disturbed"), he shows the formation of the term *rūpa* in the sense of the agent;

by the words *ghaṭṭīyati* ("it is struck") and *pīḷīyati* ("it is oppressed"), he shows it in the sense of the object. For the very act of being disturbed (*kopādi-kiriyā*) is the act of being affected (*ruppana-kiriyā*).
Furthermore, in order to show the meaning that this thing—whether existing as an agent or as an object—is subject to breaking apart, he says: "the meaning is 'it breaks apart' (*bhijjati*)."

It has been stated. Alternatively, the formation of the word *rūpa* in the sense of the agentive-objective (*kammakattuttha*)—as in "it is affected (*ruppati*), therefore it is form (*rūpa*)"—is explained.

For "affection" (*ruppana*) means change. For this very reason, he shows the meaning by means of the verb *bhijjati* (to break) in the sense of the agentive-objective, stating: "the meaning is 'it breaks'.
Furthermore, that which is affected and breaks is so called because it is disturbed, struck, and oppressed. Therefore...
By these words, the meaning of the term has been made clear. To the question, "In what sense?", it is stated, "In the sense of being afflicted (ruppana)," following the nature of the inquiry.

It is not merely the literal meaning that constitutes "being afflicted"; rather, since this meaning also possesses a characteristic, he said, "It is also appropriate to say that 'it is matter (rūpa) by virtue of having the characteristic of being afflicted.'"
"Having been cut" means either having been released by falling into a swoon, or having been cut by the severing of limbs and members.
Regarding the phrase "with extremely salty cold water," the state of being "extremely salty" may have been stated with reference specifically to its extreme coldness;
for that water which lasts for an eon (*kappa*) cannot be as salty as the water that destroys an eon, since it is conducive to well-being and supports the earth.
"For if that were so, the earth would dissolve. By "the great Avīci hell," the crowded Avīci hell is meant;

for this very reason, it says, "Therein... and so forth. Regarding "Pettivisaya... they do not exist," the intention is that such beings do indeed exist, since there is no restriction that they must be of this specific kind alone.
The same applies to the Kālakañjika hell and others. "Moving along while remembering" means...
He explains the meaning of the word *sarīsapa*.
Regarding the term *abhisaññūhitvā*, here the meaning is also "having made a collection. By this, it is shown that all form... [etc. ...is demonstrated;
by this he shows that the word *rūpakkhandha* functions as a coordinate compound (*samānādhikaraṇa-samāsa*). For this very reason he says: "Indeed not..."

"By way of form... [as before] ...there is. 3. "Having inserted": here the meaning is "having inserted form into the eleven bases. For it is not merely by inserting the table of contents (*mātikā*) that the table of contents is established; rather, it is form as it occurs in the treatise (*pakaraṇappatta*).
Another method... [as before] ..."has reached its reckoning right here"—by this, the instrumental case is used in the sense of the locative, namely "in the past portion."
It shows [this]. To show the manner in which it has been counted, the passage beginning with “the four great elements” was stated.
This being the case, it follows that the state of being the great elements and derived matter (*upādāyarūpa*) is the reason for the counting in the past section.
For this statement is not intended to exclude past feelings (*vedanā*) and so forth; rather, by the words “whatever form,” these are already excluded.
Because it has been excluded; nor for the purpose of excluding other modes of matter, since every mode is included therein;
nor for the purpose of excluding future and present aspects, since those are excluded by the very term "belonging to the past.
Furthermore, the meaning is that whatever is reckoned as "past" is reckoned in this way: "the four [great elements]... and matter."
If this is intended, then this would be a demonstration of a different category of enumeration, rather than a demonstration of the types enumerated within the past;

for if that were demonstrated, it would necessarily follow that what was enumerated among the past types is of that same nature by virtue of being composed of the primary and derived material elements (bhūta-upādāyarūpa).
And such a nature cannot be the reason for its being enumerated among the past, since it is precisely because it possesses that very nature [that it is so].
Because [the nature of] pleasure and so forth is included among the present and future, and because it is included among the past, therefore the former method alone is correct.
A similar meaning is also obtained in the explanations of "internal" and "external.

It is said "by way of the Suttanta method" because the Sutta teaches by way of a figurative approach (pariyāya); it is said "by way of the Abhidhamma exposition" because the Abhidhamma teaches without such a figurative approach.

It is said that because the *Niddesa* is a definitive exposition (*nicchaya*) of the *Abhidhamma*, it is called an "exposition" (*niddesa*). Regarding the phrase "Even though... and so forth, this is the intended meaning:

since it belongs to the *Suttanta-bhājaniya*, just as in passages such as "One should not review the past," where the state of being past and so forth is expressed by way of time (*addhāna*), so too here it might be demonstrated in that same manner. Even so, the *Suttanta-bhājaniya* is indeed an exposition of the *Abhidhamma*.

Because it proceeds by way of investigating and analyzing the phenomena taught in the Suttas, the state of being past and so forth is demonstrated precisely through the exposition of the Abhidhamma. Regarding the phrase "by way of extent (addhā), continuity (santati), time (samaya), and moment (khaṇa)": here, the word *addhā* refers to a period of time delimited by death and rebirth-linking; this is understood from such Suttas as, "Was I indeed in the past extent? and so on. "There are these three... [The text continues:]... "O monks, there are these three extents (*addhā*): the past extent, the future extent, and the present extent. Here, the word *addhā* is used in the sense of a long duration of time. Furthermore, the word *addhā* is used in the sense of a short duration of time, as in the passage: "Bhikkhus, when one has abandoned the five lower fetters, one is said to have 'traversed the extent' (*addhagū*) and is a non-returner, one who will attain final nibbāna there without returning from that world. In this context, the word *addhā* is used in the sense of a short duration of time. Moreover, the word *addhā* is used in the sense of a path, as in the passage: "Bhikkhus, I shall teach you the path that has been traversed (*addhagata*), the path yet to be traversed (*anaddhagata*), and the path being traversed (*gamyamāna*). In this context, the word *addhā* is used in the sense of a path. Furthermore, the word *addhā* is used in the sense of a field, as in the passage: "Bhikkhus, I shall teach you the field that has been traversed, the field yet to be traversed, and the field being traversed. In this context, the word *addhā* is used in the sense of a field.
