“Monks, there are three time periods. Which three? The past time, the future time, and the present time.

In this context, however, when "time" (*addhā*) is delimited from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramattha*), it is appropriate as being delimited by moments (*khaṇa*), according to the *Niruttipatha-sutta*.
For therein it is said: “Monks, whatever form has been born and has become manifest, the designation for it is ‘it exists’ (*atthī*).”
The state of being present belongs to that which exists; prior to and subsequent to that, it is said to be past and future respectively.

However, for the most part, the temporal period (addhā) consisting of the past and so forth as defined by death and rebirth-linking is taught in the Suttas; it is precisely this that is referred to here as "by way of time" (*addhāvasena*).
Cold is of the same nature as cold, and likewise, heat is of the same nature as heat. As for that which is cold or hot in the body...
That which has come together, proceeding by way of continuity, neither deficient nor redundant, and uniform in aspect—that is called "one season.
The singular term "season" is used because a homogeneous season does not possess an absolute singularity of nature; the same applies to nutriment.

The phrase "arising from a single cognitive series and a single impulsion" is stated with reference to the five or six sense doors. The discussion regarding continuity and time was set forth in the commentaries for the benefit of those practicing insight meditation (*vipassanā*).

The function of the cause has been completed; the function of the cause is completed while the function of the condition is not; both functions have not yet arrived; and that which is present at the moment of its own function is the present. The cause is the producer, while the condition is the supporter; their respective functions are producing and supporting.

Just as the seed has the function of producing the sprout, while the earth and so forth have the function of supporting it, so too does karma have the function of producing the resultant materiality born of past action (*kaṭattā-rūpa*).

The support for nutriment and so forth is likewise to be applied, as far as possible, to the functions of the conascent, prenascent, and postnascent conditions that act as the producers and supporters of each individual group (kalāpa) and of each arising of consciousness—
namely, karma, the immediately preceding condition, and others. Therein, the function of the cause (hetu) is to be seen at the moment of arising, and [it persists] throughout all three moments.

The function of conditionality (*paccayakicca*). The respective functions of earth and the other elements, such as supporting, and of contact and the other factors, such as touching, constitute their own function (*sakicca*).
The moment of performing that function is the "moment of its own function" (*sakiccakkhaṇa*). Alternatively, that which is together with its function is "possessing its own function" (*sakicca*);
the moment when a form or a non-form possesses its own function is the "moment of its own function," and at that moment it is present.
6. *Ettakameva* (only this much): This refers precisely to the meaning already stated by the reduplicated expression *tesaṃ tesaṃ* (of this or that), in the sense of pervasiveness.

*Aparassa aparassa* (of another and another) is an illustration of "another. By the word *pariyesatu* (let him seek), he shows that there is no reason for avoiding the name of what is undesirable through seeking.
For indeed, due to the fault of karma and the fault of mental perversion, [beings become] such as dung-eating animals and so forth.

Furthermore, madmen and others would seek it out; and Greeks and others [would not seek it] due to a perversion of view. Because the object possesses the nature of being sought after, whereas this [unpleasant object] possesses the nature of not being sought after, the meaning is that it is called "undesirable" (*aniṭṭha*) precisely because of that.

"Due to the absence of excellence" means that visible forms and so forth possess a state of abundant beauty because they are the fruit of wholesome karma in the realms of celestial and human excellence.
And "success" (sampatti) means being devoid of that [beauty]. For that very reason, it should not be sought after.
Furthermore, certain beautiful forms such as elephants and so forth, though produced by unwholesome kamma, do not become causes of happiness for those very same elephants and so forth;
therefore, in order to include them, the term "unpleasant" (akanta) was stated. For each respective being, [the object] by itself—
That which is produced by wholesome karma is a condition for pleasure, while that produced by unwholesome karma is a condition for pain.
Therefore, the desirability or undesirability of things born of karma should be understood in relation to the sentient being who performs the karma.

However, in the *Aṭṭhakathā*, it is stated only that "there is nothing produced by wholesome karma that is undesirable," but it is not stated that "[there is nothing] produced by unwholesome karma..."
"There is nothing called 'desirable'. By this, it would follow that even what is born of unwholesome karma is admitted to be beautiful and desirable to other beings.
However, they say that what is born of wholesome karma is indeed desirable to everyone.
Yet, for some animals, the human form is unpleasant, such that they flee upon merely seeing it; and humans [flee] from the form of a deity...
Seeing it, they are afraid; yet even for them, resultant consciousness arises as a wholesome result (kusalavipāka) taking that form as its object.
However, the intention is that because they lack such merit, they have no delight in it.
Just as there is an absence of the undesirable produced by wholesome karma, so too should the absence of the beautiful and desirable produced by unwholesome karma be stated.
For even elephants and the like, when born of unwholesome karma, are objects for the unwholesome resultants of human beings;
however, those born of wholesome karma that have arisen during the course of existence are objects for the wholesome resultant.

But because of being mixed with desirable objects, it can be said that a small amount of what is born of unwholesome karma will not be a cause for the arising of a large amount of unwholesome resultant.
However, since it is impossible to deceive the result (vipāka) in any case, the determination of desirable and undesirable objects by way of their result is well stated.
Therefore, following that principle, the state of being desirable or undesirable should be applied everywhere.
Why is it said that "the five strands of sensual pleasure are undesirable," when it has been stated [elsewhere] that "forms cognizable by the eye are desirable," and so forth?

Are only desirable forms and so forth called "strands of sensual pleasure" (kāmaguṇa)? [The answer is: Because the designation "strand of sensual pleasure" is applied to things similar to the strands of sensual pleasure;

and this similarity consists precisely in their being forms and so forth, not in their being desirable. Alternatively, by the term "undesirable," the state of not being a strand of sensual pleasure is indicated;

thus, forms and so forth that are dissimilar to the strands of sensual pleasure are called "strands of sensual pleasure," just as there is the usage of the word "auspicious" (siva) for what is inauspicious (asiva). Or, all [forms]—both desirable and undesirable—[are included].

Form and the other [sensory objects] are indeed "strands of sensual pleasure" (kāmaguṇā) because they serve as the basis for craving. For it is said: "Forms in the world are lovely things, pleasant things," and so forth.
However, because they are exceedingly desirable, these desirable forms and so on are called "strands of sensual pleasure" in the Suttas.
In both instances—whether referring to inferior or superior [states]—the expression "by way of unwholesome kamma" or "by way of wholesome kamma" refers to those...

Because it is analyzed by specifying [them] "of those beings" (*tesaṃ sattānaṃ*) according to the category of beings, this meaning should be understood as stated using the genitive case (*sāmivacana*) in the sense of a part-whole relationship (*avayavayoga*), as in "of this or that" (*tesaṃ tesaṃ*). It is said "by way of kamma-born" (*kammajavasena*) because among those included within the continuity of beings (*sattasantāna*), the kamma-born is distinguished.
However, if the phrase "of this or that" (*tesaṃ tesaṃ*) is used in the sense of "by this or that" (*tehi tehi*), [then it refers to the specific causes].
The term "possessive" (sāmivacana) refers either to a relationship between object and subject;
it is not only by way of kamma that visible forms and so forth are analyzed, but they are understood to be analyzed by way of all those things bound up with the faculties.

And here, since the method has been shown by means of the manifest visible forms and so forth, the distinction between inferior and superior should likewise be applied to the eye and the other faculties.
"‘The pleasant as its limit’ means that I declare the five strands of sensual pleasure to have the pleasant as their limit, serving as their boundary.
For what reason? Because they are pleasant to some and unpleasant to others; and for whomever they are pleasant, for them alone they are supreme.
Therefore, the supremacy of the strands of sensual pleasure depends upon the individual’s own inclination."
It exists, yet not by way of their own intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*).
"In this way" means according to the method stated in this sutta.

Because of the relishing and revulsion toward one and the same [object], because the very nature of the object (*ārammaṇa-sabhāva*) possesses the state of being desirable and undesirable, and because of the grasping of the undesirable as "desirable" and the grasping of the desirable as "undesirable."
And the meaning is that there is no such thing as "the desirable" and "the undesirable" separately distinguished from one another.

By the phrase "through the perversion of perception," etc., it is meant that the grasping of the desirable and the undesirable occurs with respect to other objects just as it does with respect to Nibbāna;

this is like the grasping of bitterness by those intoxicated by bile and the like, due to a perversion of perception arising from the presence of a defect in milk, sugar, and so forth. This is the point.
This shows that it was spoken with the intention (*sandhāya*) that [the world] has a pleasant limit.
"It exists analyzed" (*vibhattaṃ atthi*) means "it exists determined" (*vavatthitaṃ atthi*); or alternatively, it means "it has been analyzed and revealed by the masters of the Aṭṭhakathā.
And that [analysis] is determined and revealed by way of the person of medium capacity (*majjhimaka-satta*), and for others, by way of their perversions (*vipallāsa*).
The intention is that this [object] becomes both desirable (*iṭṭha*) and undesirable (*aniṭṭha*).

When one who has thus defined what is desirable and undesirable perceives the undesirable as desirable and so forth, it can be said that the cause is not merely a perversion of perception (*saññā-vipallāsa*), but also the state of being a cause for the arising of wholesome and unwholesome resultant states through the disturbance of the elements (*dhātu-kkhobha*), such as the occurrence of a transformation of the faculties (*indriya-vikāra*). For instance, cold water [is desirable] to those tormented by heat.
It is the cause for wholesome-resultant body-consciousness, and for unwholesome-resultant [body-consciousness] in those overcome by cold.

The touch of cotton is painful when there is a wound but pleasant when there is no wound; likewise, the stroking of soft, tender hands produces pleasure, while striking with that same hand produces pain.
Therefore, it is appropriate to define the object by way of its result.

With the words "Even though" (*kiñcāpi*) and so forth, [the author] demonstrates that even when there is a perversion of perception (*saññā-vipallāsa*), wholesome resultant consciousness arises in the seeing of the Buddha’s form and the like, while unwholesome resultant consciousness arises in the seeing of excrement and the like.
By this, he shows that the desirability or undesirability of the object is determined by that resultant consciousness.

Furthermore, the demonstration of the necessity of the result by way of the object—even while a perversion of perception exists—is made solely for the purpose of demonstrating the necessity of the object itself.

Furthermore, by the passage beginning with "also by way of the doors," it is shown that because a condition for suffering or pleasure in one door produces a resultant (vipāka) of pleasure or pain in another door, there is a determination of the object by way of the result;
and because even when the tangible object such as a jewel is identical in one and the same door, pleasure and pain arise respectively from its slow contact and its rubbing.
It is understood that the state of being desirable or undesirable is shown by way of karmic result (vipāka).

The "lower method" refers to the manner explained by taking as the object that which is established by way of the result for a middling person, beginning with the words, "disregarded by this or that being," and so forth. "Conventionally agreeable" refers to a middling person.
That which is considered and established as agreeable by way of kamma-result (vipāka) is established by its very intrinsic nature;

thus, the intention is that one does not break it precisely because it is not to be broken. However, one breaks what is taken as agreeable even by persons such as those in hell through the perversion of perception (*saññā-vipallāsa*)—namely, the disagreeableness of persons—with the words "But this or that... and so forth. This also includes the form of the *vemānika* petas.
It is said to be "inferior to the human form" because it is produced by unwholesome kamma and because it serves as a basis for suffering such as being subjected to punishment.

7. One should understand that gross material phenomena are well-apprehended by way of their resistance to the physical bases and objects, whereas subtle phenomena are difficult to apprehend due to the absence of such resistance.
By virtue of this difficulty in apprehension, they are likewise difficult to penetrate regarding their specific characteristics (lakkhaṇa).
They are to be seen. The phrase "tenfold" is stated for the purpose of showing that which was not mentioned as "distant. However, even what has been mentioned is indeed distant by way of location.

The "lower method" is the method handed down after demonstrating [matter] according to its characteristic—beginning with "the faculty of femininity... pe ... this is called near matter"—and by way of the location determined as twelve cubits. That [method] is [applied] by way of distance and proximity through characteristics and locations.
Because it was taken away after being seized together, he went along breaking it and making it mixed.
Alternatively, "breaking" means that by showing its form, he went along distinguishing it by way of characteristic (*lakkhaṇa*) and by way of location (*okāsa*).
Or else, "by way of characteristic" refers to near and far, while "by way of location" refers to making them distant or near.
It is said, "going while breaking," because it proceeds by breaking nearness and making distance,
and by breaking distance and making nearness. However, in this context— "taking each respective material form (rūpa) again and again"—
it does not break [the continuity] according to the previous method by way of characteristic, but rather by making what was distant in space into something nearby.
"O Blessed One, it is neither by making [them] distinct through spatial distance, nor by making them mixed despite spatial distance"—this is the meaning. But what does it do?
It differentiates that which is distant in space. Here, however, the meaning should not be seen as threefold according to the method stated previously;
for it does not make that which is distant in space near in terms of characteristic, nor does it make that which is near in terms of characteristic distant.
Or it is "mixed" by that [method]. Here, "breaking" (*bhedana*) should be understood as making that which is distant in terms of location become near, precisely from the standpoint of location.

Furthermore, regarding the phrase "it does not break what is distant by way of characteristic," here too it is not stated that the threefold breaking is not performed according to the method previously explained; rather, it refers to taking each instance of the near and the distant by way of their respective characteristics.

It should be understood that because there is no state of being distant or near, the non-production of a state of nearness from the very characteristic of distance is the non-differentiation of distance by way of its characteristic. This method is not like the previous method;
for here it is shown only to this extent. Furthermore, in the phrase "breaking [it]," a different kind of breaking was mentioned, whereas here the breaking is mentioned differently.
The commentary on the description of the aggregate of material form is finished.
2. Commentary on the description of the aggregate of feeling. 8.

The sensitive organs, beginning with the eye, are included within a gross or mind-made personal existence; therefore, they are designated by the term "body" (*kāya*), and [the feelings] have them as their basis.

The phrase "neither-painful-nor-pleasant bodily" is stated figuratively, not because it has the physical sensitivity (kāyapasāda) as its basis; for the eye and so forth are not the physical sensitivity of the body.

Regarding the phrase "by way of continuity and by way of moments, etc.," there is no mention here of the state of being past and so forth by way of duration (addhā) or time (samaya), because the state of being past and so forth is spoken of in reference to what is divided by pleasure and the rest. For it is not the case that pleasure alone [is defined] by way of duration.
Furthermore, by way of time (*samaya*), it is past and so forth; likewise, [feeling] is divided into bodily and mental, and so on, as painful, pleasant, and neither-painful-nor-pleasant.
Therefore, the origin of feeling deserves to be described in terms of the past and so forth by way of time-periods (*addhā-samaya*), because a collection must be delimited by those [periods].
However, only a portion of feeling is taken here; thus, by way of continuity (*santati*) and moments (*khaṇa*), [the distinction is made].
They are worthy of being delimited because, in that context, those things which are to be delimited in such a manner have been grasped.

However, within a single continuum, since there is the presence of various distinctions such as pleasure and so forth, that which delimits a single type of distinction—which has been grasped as the object to be delimited—is manifest;
it proceeds by way of the door and the object associated with that [feeling], and it proceeds through an uninterrupted conjunction with a single kind of object that produces its arising.
Because it is fit to exist as a continuity (*santati*), its grasp is made by way of its delimiting nature without referring to any other internal division.
Alternatively, since phenomena that revolve rapidly deserve delimitation precisely through their revolution, the delimitation is stated by way of the moments of the continuity.
By the phrase "situated in the past, future, and middle," he shows the method described by way of the functions of causes and conditions.
11. They are "with a burden" (sadaratha) due to their association with the fires of the defilements (*kilesaggi*). By this, he shows their grossness by way of intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*);
by the phrase "in the sense of having suffering as their result," he shows it by way of function (*kicca*) through the production of a gross result.

Results (*vipāka*) are cast forth by the momentum of karma and are bound to karma; they are effortless because they lack the activity of bodily action and so forth. Functional states (*kiriyā*) are effortful and are non-results (*avipāka*). [Results] possess results.
And because it is gross, like being pregnant, its opposite is said to be subtle and non-resultant (*avipāka*).
"In the sense of being unpleasant" means in the sense of not being sweet. By this, he shows its nature to be undesirable, as the opposite of what is pleasant (*sāta*).
"In the sense of suffering" means in the sense of being a state of pain. By this, he shows its function of tormenting those who suffer. "This which, venerable sir, is neither-painful-nor-pleasant..."

Because of the statement, “This feeling, O Sāti, was spoken of by the Blessed One as peaceful and sublime pleasure,” it is called *santa* (peaceful) because it lacks the nature of pervading [the mind] that is characteristic of the neither-painful-nor-pleasant [feeling], and because there is no possibility for the underlying tendencies (*anusaya*) of sensual lust and aversion to persist within it. It is called *paṇīta* (sublime) because it has been brought to a state of excellence, having exhausted attachment to pleasure and being something to be attained.
Furthermore, it is not something to be attained [in the same way as those lower states].

Without confusing the classes such as those belonging to the sense-sphere (*kāmāvacara*), one should apply the terms "pleasant" and "exquisite" to those of the same class—such as those associated with or dissociated from knowledge—and to those of the same sub-class.

They are "pleasant" by being the condition for the elements that have been nourished, and "painful" by being the condition for those that have been disturbed. Both arise as if they were pervading the entire body.
"It pervades" (pharati). "Intoxicating" (madayamānaṃ) means producing intoxication. "Covering" (chādayamānaṃ) means generating desire, or else it means overspreading.
It is said "as if pouring out" because, just as the body of one scorched by heat is refreshed when sprinkled with a jar of cold water, so too is it for one possessed of happiness.
"Only on the sign of unity" (ekattanimitteyeva) refers to the earth-kasiṇa and so forth.
Regarding the phrase "in a single object": it is subtle because, like feeling (*vedanā*) in the impulsion (*javana*) consciousness, it lacks the agitation found in various types of objects.

Regarding the phrase "unskilled in the intention": this is because [the text] has come down in the *Kusala-ttika* (The Triplet on the Wholesome), etc., stating: "Wholesome and unwholesome feelings are gross; indeterminate feelings are subtle.
The passage beginning with "And furthermore" (*yampi*) is commenced in order to show the distinction between different planes (*bhūmantara*).

By this method— namely, by explaining the state of grossness and subtlety in various instances through the distinction of intrinsic nature and so forth, such as "compared to sense-sphere pleasure, sense-sphere equanimity is subtle"—
he shows the principle that [the Buddha] does not contradict [his own teaching].

Since these [teachings] are spoken as a mixture of mundane and supramundane, therefore, because the inferior and the sublime have been extracted from among the exclusively sublime [states], it is exactly thus.
The meaning is that since inferiority and superiority must be extracted from what is exclusively inferior according to the possibility of their occurrence, it is thus permitted;
therefore, one should not feel remorse in extracting them in either case.
Because unwholesome states lack the subtlety found in wholesome states and so forth, and because they cannot be substituted for what has come down in the text, the "lower method" [is applied].
It is said that it was stated, "it should not be looked at. Even when speaking according to this or that specific method (*vāpana*), there is no shifting [of the sequence];
thus, it was not with reference to such shifting that it was said, "the lower method should not be looked at.

However, since the lower method has already been stated, it would be appropriate to say "this or that" by taking up the method not yet stated; therefore, [it is argued] that "the lower method should not..."
It should be understood that it is stated, “it is to be observed. Unwholesome states have great fruition and are gross due to being saturated with hatred;
likewise, wholesome states have little fruition. Unwholesome states have little fruition and are subtle due to having weak hatred; likewise, wholesome states have great fruition.

The grossness and subtlety of the sense-sphere and other realms arise from their being the basis for the attraction of the gross and the subtle. That too—referring to what is produced by meditation—[is to be understood].

It should be understood that by means of the analysis [of giving], the individual analysis of those things consisting of giving and those consisting of virtue is shown through the method of classification.
Alternatively, "that too" (*sāpi*) should be construed with "threefold" (*tividhāpi*).

The sense of "dissimilar" (*visabhāga*) is the state of belonging to different categories by way of birth and so forth. The sense of "having dissimilar functions" (*asadisa-kicca-tā*) is by way of having results such as suffering and so forth.

Alternatively, it is "unmixed" (*visaṃsaṭṭha*) by virtue of having a dissimilar nature, not by way of non-association (*asampayoga*). If that were so, then proximity (*santika*) would occur through the opposite of distance;
thus, proximity would result in the sense of being "mixed" (*saṃsaṭṭha*), yet there is no association of feeling with feeling.

Furthermore, the meaning should be understood according to the method already stated, for in the commentary on the word "proximity" (*santika*) he will say: "by way of sharing a common nature and by way of similarity."

Why was it said that "the near should not be extracted from the far"? Is it because, just as the unwholesome is extracted from the near as being "far" from the unwholesome, so too the wholesome cannot be extracted from the far as being "near" to the wholesome?
It is not impossible. For if that were the case, by treating the wholesome as "near" to the wholesome, the near would simply be extracted from the near.
If that were so, it would result in a mere statement of relative proximity; for here, distance and proximity are spoken of only in relation to one another.

Therefore, just as it is impossible to extract something from a distance by means of what is even more distant, it is likewise impossible to extract something from proximity by means of what is even more proximate, because neither "distance-furtherness" nor "proximity-proximity" is intended [as the primary sense]. Now, however, he might say:

“The wholesome [state] should not be extracted from the vicinity of the wholesome itself; rather, it should be extracted from that unwholesome state which is distant from it”—but that is not the case.

For the wholesome is never in the vicinity of the unwholesome. Or if one were to say, “That unwholesome state which is in the vicinity of the wholesome should be extracted from the wholesome as being distant from it”—that too is not the case. For in the wholesome...

There are unwholesome states which could be extracted from that [proximity]. Therefore, because the "far" mentioned here is absolutely dissimilar to the "far" [mentioned] there, it is not possible to extract "proximity" from that "far," thinking "there is no proximity in the far.
However, when "proximity" is mentioned here, the "far" is obtained right there within that very [proximity] once it is analyzed; thus he said, "But the 'far' should be extracted from 'proximity'."
From one instance of clinging to another, it is impossible to extract the near from the far.
For when it is said that "that accompanied by greed is far" and "that accompanied by hatred is near," what is near is being extracted from what is already near.
Likewise, when it is said that "that accompanied by hatred is far" and "that accompanied by greed is near," here too, [the distinction is made] from one similar state to another similar state.

Because it has been extracted, and because it is impossible to say of that which is accompanied by greed, "it is far," or of that which is accompanied by hatred, "it is near"—since there is no reason for that which is accompanied by hatred to have the status of being near—it follows that dissimilarity does not occur without grasping at difference.
Therefore, because it does not pervade what is similar, one cannot effect the extraction of the near from the far on the basis of distance. Not...
For it proceeds by pervading everything that is associated with defilements and shares the nature of the unwholesome.
However, since "likeness" (sabhāgatā) proceeds by including difference within itself, because it is a pervader of the dissimilar, it is possible to extract it from its vicinity due to its proximity.
For unwholesomeness (akusalatā) pervades all dissimilar states, such as those associated with greed and so forth. Therefore he said: "Not from afar..."
"...should be extracted from its vicinity," and so forth.
The commentary on the exposition of the aggregate of feeling (*vedanākkhandha*) is finished.
3. Commentary on the Exposition of the Aggregate of Perception (*saññākkhandha*).

17. Regarding "perception born of eye-contact": although here the name of contact is derived from its basis (*vatthu*) and perception is derived from contact, yet perception—being distinguished by contact that is itself distinguished by its basis—is also distinguished by that basis, because it has that same basis as contact does.
Therefore, it is said: "derived from its basis. Regarding "perception born of impact-contact" (*paṭigha-samphassa-jā saññā*), it is the same here as well.
Just as contact arises through the impact of the basis and the object, so too does the perception and rapture born from that;

thus it is said, "arising from the basis and the object. And here it should be understood that "contact born of resistance" (*paṭighasamphassa*) is stated by eliding the latter member of the compound, meaning either "contact born of resistance" or "contact cognizable by means of resistance."

The mental aggregates are called "designation" (*adhivacana*) because they function by depending on speech regarding the state of being cognizable, or because they are dependent on speech, or because they possess a designation as their manifestation. Contact born from that is "designation-contact" (*adhivacana-samphassa*);
or, contact itself is called "designation-contact" because it is both a designation and a contact according to the meanings stated above.

Alternatively, contact that is to be understood by means of a designation (*adhivacanaviññeyya*) is "designation-contact" (*adhivacanasamphassa*); or, those [perceptions] born from that, or in that [contact], are "born of designation-contact.

Since the aforementioned meaning is also possible in the case of contact through the five doors, perception born from that [five-door contact] is likewise called "born of designation-contact" according to that method. However, because no other kind is possible, [perception] born of mind-contact (*manosamphassajā*) is so called.
In the direct sense (*nippariyāya*), it is called "born of designation-contact" (*adhivacana-samphassaja*);
however, this [feeling born of resistance-contact] is not so called because there exists a distinct, unique mode of occurrence—this is the intended meaning.
If that were the case, then even the four aggregates, being born from the aforementioned contact, would also be "born of designation-contact."
It would be appropriate to speak [of them] as such; why then is it said that they are merely *saññā* (perception)?

Because the term "designation-contact-born" (*adhivacana-samphassa-ja*), which occurs wherever even a name acquired by the three formless aggregates functions as an expression of phenomena (*dhammābhilāpa*) due to its conventional usage, is applied specifically to that *saññā*, while the [term "designation"] itself is withdrawn.
Therefore, he said: "For the three formless aggregates," and so forth.

Alternatively, since there is another distinguished name for that which arises from contact through resistance (*paṭighasamphassajā*)—namely, "arising from contact through designation" (*adhivacanasamphassajā*)—it is fitting that this belongs only to the three [mental] aggregates (*khandha*).
However, with the intention of showing that these [three aggregates] withdraw after having given their own name to perception (*saññā*), he said:
"For the three formless aggregates," and so forth. Even after having observed with the five sense-doors, perception...

The statement "it is possible to know" is said with reference to the fact that, just as a communication (viññatti) consisting of hand gestures and the like becomes the sign for knowing another's intention when performed with that specific purpose,
so too, in the case of gazing while being impassioned, the gazing itself becomes manifest upon contact with the object of eye-consciousness as the sign for knowing the state of passion and so forth;
thus it is stated with regard to the perceptual cognition (saññā) associated with that [eye-consciousness] which likewise becomes manifest.
Thinking that, having been excited, it might become manifest through looking and so forth and thus capable of proceeding as a javana,

he said "only those having a basis of confidence" in order to dispel that apprehension. "Thinking of something else" means thinking of something other than what was previously thought or known by him.
The commentary on the exposition of the aggregate of perception is finished.
4. Commentary on the Exposition of the Aggregate of Volitional Formations (saṅkhārakkhandha). 20.
Regarding the phrase "at the lower limit," this is an ablative case construction. For therein, the primary [limit] is shown. If that is so, [then...]
Does it follow that it is not shown by the upper limit? It does not follow, because the state of being at the lower limit cannot exist without the state of having reached the upper limit.
For the lower limit is all-pervasive. In the second [instance], there is a description of the instrument;
the connection is "arrived at by means of the lower limit. Or else, regarding what was stated previously as "by the lower limit," that too—
"By way of seeing the volitional formations of striving (*padhāna-saṅkhāra*)"—this is a statement of the instrument (*karaṇa-niddesa*) by means of establishing a connection.
"The formations associated with that" refers to the forty-ninefold classification of formations; they are indeed included because they are bound up with it.
The commentary on the exposition of the aggregate of formations (*saṅkhārakkhandha-niddesa-vaṇṇanā*) is finished.
Commentary on the Miscellaneous Discourse:

The term *samuggama* is established in the sense of birth or initial arising. For, when combined with their respective conditions, the upward movement from the prior limit—namely, the previous existence—is *samuggama*;
or rather, the emergence at the point of connection, that is, at rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*), is *samuggama*.

However, it is shown precisely where the five aggregates arise in their full completion. By this method, the arising of incomplete aggregates can be understood in the cases of the one-aggregate and four-aggregate realms.

Alternatively, "arising together" (*samuggama*) refers to the simultaneous emergence or production of even those five aggregates as they have been attained; in this sense, there is the occurrence of conceptual differentiation (*vikalpa*).
It is not included. "Jāti-uṇṇā" refers to the wool of a high-bred goat born in a region of the Himalayas.
Regarding the phrase "a drop of cream of ghee," the word *bindu* (drop) should be applied here as well. "Of such color and appearance" means of such color and such shape.
Alternatively, *paṭibhāga* means resemblance; the sense is the sharing of likeness, that is, the attainment of similarity. Such is the resemblance of color.
“Of this” means of that which resembles such color.
“Heads of the continuity” (santatisīsāni) means the roots of the continuity, or the portions of the continuity. For a principal factor is called a “head” because it is a composite of many faculties;
thus, the portions such as the decad of the physical basis (vatthudasaka) consist of a collection of many material phenomena.
“They are called ‘heads’ (sīsāni),” it is said.
This is stated with reference to the completion of the count—that the five aggregates (*pañcakkhandhā*) are complete—not with reference to the completeness of each individual aggregate.
Because it is stated in terms of the sequence (*paveṇi*) originating from kamma, [it implies] the sequences born of temperature, mind, and nutriment [also persist] for this long a time.
One might say, "It exists after having transcended," and so forth; however, since that will be explained under the heading "from the preceding and the succeeding," it is not discussed here.
Furthermore, because not all successions born of karma have been stated, the emergence of the *opapātika* (spontaneously born) is shown to demonstrate what has not yet been mentioned. Thus...
[pe] ...the five aggregates become complete; this is the method by way of those with complete sense bases (*paripuṇṇāyatana*).

This has been demonstrated; however, for those sense-sphere (*kāmāvacara*) and fine-material-sphere (*rūpāvacara*) beings with incomplete sense bases, as well as for one who has lost their sense bases, the loss of the continuity-peak (*santatisīsa*) should be understood by way of these factors.
As for "in terms of before and after," this investigation does not concern the arising of the five aggregates, but rather the production of matter (*rūpa*) by them.
It should be seen. Showing that, he said, “But thus,” and so forth. By the phrase “arising neither before nor after,” he shows the cause for doubt;
for when things arise simultaneously, it is impossible to discern, as it were unshown, that “this material phenomenon first produces [the consciousness], and this one afterwards.
And here, in this investigation, rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*) serves as the basis for the consideration of priority and posteriority.

The five aggregates that have arisen and are occurring are what are grasped. And in this context, since the locative case is used in the sense of selection (*niddhāraṇa*), he says, "matter first produces matter.

Otherwise, if the locative were used in the sense of characterizing an action by another action (*bhāvena bhāvalakkhaṇatthe*), they would be saying that at the very moment matter produces matter, there is also the production of matter by karma; thus [he specifies] "both."
"It may be said": this investigation proceeds by taking both the continuity of the material and the immaterial; thus it is stated, "matter first originates matter.
Otherwise, if the investigation were conducted by taking only that which exists at the moment of rebirth-linking (paṭisandhi), there would be no origination of matter by the immaterial at all;
therefore, this is indeed an investigation into the mutual origination of preceding and succeeding moments.
“It could be said that it does not arise here. This was stated with reference to the weakness of all material phenomena at the moment of their arising;
for at that time, being devoid of the postnascent condition (*pacchājāta-paccaya*) and not supported by nutriment and so forth, it is called “weak.
As for the phrase “because it is projected by the force of kamma,” this refers even though the life-continuum (*bhavaṅga*)...

This was said with reference to this meaning: at the moment of rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*), the continuity of fruition (*vipākasantati*)—insofar as it possesses the nature of being born of karma—is, as it were, cast forth by a different karma than that which produced the preceding life-continuum (*bhavaṅga*) and is thus not yet established;
however, thereafter, within the same continuity, having obtained the conditions of immediate antecedence (*anantarapaccaya*) and prenascence (*purejātapaccaya*), it becomes established.

"It is linked in a continuous series" (*paveṇī ghaṭiyati*) means that the continuity of the bases such as the eye is linked by way of the cessation of one and the arising of another while one [base] still exists;
the meaning is that it does not proceed with interruption like the bases that serve as the support for death and rebirth-linking.
"From a factor" (*aṅgato*) means from a jhāna-factor. For the jhāna-factors, together with consciousness, are the originators of material form, and they provide supporting power to those [factors].
This is because, when the path-factors and so forth are present among them, one observes the manifestation of specific material forms.

Alternatively, the meaning is that they are not deficient in the jhāna-factors and so forth, which provide strength to those mental factors—such as volition—that function as factors and companions in the production of matter by the mind.
For it is due to being deficient in these that eye-consciousness and the other types of consciousness do not produce matter.

However, as for one who might say: "Since the co-nascent physical basis (vatthu) is 'pre-arisen' (purejāta) at the moments of its own stability and dissolution relative to the rebirth-linking consciousness (paṭisandhicitta), let it produce matter during those two moments because there is no deficiency in the conditions," [the author] says "If indeed the mind...
and so forth, in order to refute that. In this context, even during the moments of their stability and dissolution... [of those phenomena].
He grants that it cannot even be said that the "pre-arisen basis" (*vatthu-purejāta*) does not exist, yet he points out the flaw therein:
if matter were to arise at that time, then according to your own view, the rebirth-linking consciousness (*paṭisandhi-citta*) would also have to arise;

however, at that time, there is no arising of matter at all. And when there is the arising of matter, then, according to your view as well, [it must occur] during the moment of its origination (*uppādakkhaṇa*).

At the moment of rebirth-linking (paṭisandhi), there is simply a deficiency of conditions because of the absence of the "pre-arising" and "support" conditions; therefore, the meaning here is that the rebirth-linking consciousness does not produce matter.
It arises having taken up eight types of matter at the moment of its own arising. Why?
Because immaterial states arise only when they possess momentum through conditions such as "immediate" (anantara) and so forth, and when their strength is complete.
"Because it is not its object" means that for a newcomer to a village he has never visited before, [the village] is not within his range of perception.

"Because it is not well-mastered" means that he lacks mastery over it there. "Mind-originated... remain" refers to all those modes by which mind and mental factors act as conditions for mind-originated matter;
by all those [modes], at the moment of rebirth-linking, the mind and mental factors [act as conditions] for the thirty-two types of kamma-born matter.
This was stated on the grounds that conditions exist according to their possibility.

"The root of the round" refers to craving and ignorance. One should consider the non-arising [of matter] because the root of the round has been stilled; for the matter arising at the moment of death does not arise in the next existence in the same way as matter arising at earlier moments.

"Due to the absence of matter" means: because of the escape from material phenomena, there is no immaterial [matter]; and because of its abandonment through dispassion, there is nothing further to be produced.
This was said with reference to non-existence (*abhāva*). Alternatively, it means that while matter exists in the space of matter, there is the production of matter by means of material conditions;
however, immateriality is not the space for matter. Thus, the meaning is that when a certain matter exists, that very [matter] which would otherwise cause another matter to arise is absent there.
For even the preceding matter possesses the state of being a condition, as is shown by the analogy of a son's joy.
But temperature first arouses matter at the moment of the presence of the rebirth-linking consciousness;

this is the intended meaning. The statement, "This temperature indeed ceases slowly," and so forth, is said for the purpose of showing the reason for its arising at the moment of its own presence, and for the purpose of showing the time of arising for non-material phenomena.
For because it ceases slowly, it is powerful at the moment of presence.

Then it arouses matter; the intention is that while that [matter] is still persisting, because of its rapid cessation, when sixteen moments of consciousness have arisen, the consciousness immediately following rebirth-linking arouses matter again that was previously aroused by the physical temperature (*utu*).
By the statement, "While that [matter] is still persisting, sixteen moments of consciousness arise and cease," if one considers the moments of arising and cessation—

If only the moment of presence (*dharamānakkhaṇa*) is taken, it is said that "matter has a lifespan of sixteen mind-moments"; thus, by not taking the moment of arising (*uppādakkhaṇa*) but taking only the moment of cessation (*nirodhakkhaṇa*), it is said that "it has a lifespan of seventeen mind-moments.

If, however, the moment of cessation is not taken but the moment of arising is taken, it is said that "it has a lifespan of more than sixteen mind-moments. But if both the moments of arising and cessation...
At the moment of its existence, [the rebirth-linking consciousness] is not included; thus it is said to have a lifespan of "more than seventeen mind-moments.

However, because the phrase "immediately after those [moments], the rebirth-linking [consciousness]" includes the rebirth-linking itself among those that have arisen at the moment of its existence, the arising-moment is thereby included within the moment of existence. Consequently, since the cessation-moment is not included, its lifespan is exactly sixteen mind-moments.
It should be understood that what is about to be explained—or rather, what has already been grasped—is intended as the duration of sixteen mind-moments (*cittakkhaṇa*).

"The nutritive essence (*ojā*) is coarse" is said with reference to nutritive essence that possesses a physical basis (*savatthuka*). For while the nutritive essence is subtle by its own intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*), there exists a distinction between coarse and subtle in terms of its physical basis.
"And consciousness itself" is stated because of the primacy of consciousness; however, those states associated with it are also the originators of material form.
They exist. As it is said: “Roots are a condition, by way of root-condition, for those states associated with roots and for the matter originated by them,” and so forth.
Or rather, “consciousness” (citta) here includes the arising of consciousness (cittuppāda), not just a single non-existent factor like the volition of karma (kammacetanā).
If it is argued that what is originated by karma must also be originated by its associated factors, we say no; for it is not by those [associated factors]...
Because the state of having arisen has not been mentioned, and there is no mention of it because those [factors] lack the nature of being conditions for one another through any cause whatsoever.

"By way of the delimitation of duration" means by way of the delimitation of time. In that context, the intended delimitation of duration is this: "Seventeen thought-moments are the duration of matter;
the seventeenth part of matter is [the duration] of the immaterial. At the moment of rebirth-linking...
This should be understood as a mere illustration of the method;

it should not be taken as referring to the absence of non-simultaneous arising at the moment of rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*), for he himself will later explain the arising of matter even during the moments of the subsistence and dissolution of the rebirth-linking consciousness.
Furthermore, by way of showing that [the result] has reached fruition...

This demonstrates that the material and immaterial [factors] do not exist at the same time; it does not, however, intend to demonstrate their non-arising together, because that is not the purpose of the undertaking.

Nevertheless, since the fact that they do not exist at the same time is clearly illustrated by their non-arising together, the mention of "arising together" is used solely for the purpose of clarifying that point.

If this is so, then because the material and immaterial [factors] do not exist at the same time, would it not follow that the occurrence of the material factor takes place after the immaterial factor has already ceased? To this [objection]:

To prevent such a misconception, he says: "In this regard, although... and so forth. "Of the same measure" means that among material and immaterial phenomena occurring without interval, there is no material phenomenon devoid of the immaterial, nor any immaterial phenomenon devoid of the material;
this is stated with reference to the occurrence of kamma-born materiality in the five-aggregate plane, excluding the attainment of cessation which resembles Nibbāna.
"Katā" should be understood as "seen. "Pada by pada" means stepping very quickly, as if placing one's own footstep upon each preceding footprint.
"Anohāya" means not abandoning [the previous state] until the moment of death; however, at the moment of death, they cease simultaneously.
And that period during which they proceed without abandoning one another is delimited by rebirth-linking and death, at most.
"Of these, 'addhā' (time/extent). It should be understood that by the word "evam" (thus), both the minimum extent of time previously mentioned and this [present] one are included.

Regarding "from simultaneous arising and non-simultaneous cessation": having taken both of these together, it should be understood that a single mode of viewing has been stated for both the material and immaterial [phenomena], namely, "from simultaneous arising and non-simultaneous cessation.
The same applies to those that follow. "Excluding that which is born of the final karma..."
They say it was stated [in that way] because there is no "cessation at different times" (nānānirodha), since [the mind-element] ceases simultaneously with the death-consciousness (cuticitta).

However, for that [mind-element], there is also no "arising at the same time" (ekuppāda), because in the preceding section on the sixteen [mental states], arising is mentioned only at the moment of dissolution (bhaṅgakkhaṇa) of the last one.
If, however, something lacks both "arising at the same time" and "cessation at different times," that should be excluded. This applies to all [states] of the mind.

It should be understood that it is said, "excluding the final kamma-born [materiality]," because at the moment of dissolution, while the final kamma-born materiality has already arisen, once the subsequent consciousnesses have occurred, there is no further arising of kamma-born materiality;
thus, at that time, there is nothing to be excluded and nothing to be included. However, prior to that, there is a continuity of forty-eight types of kamma-born materiality.
Regarding the phrase "it exists" (*atthi*): there, that which has arisen at the moment of arising (*uppādakkhaṇa*) of the mind ceases at the moment of arising of another;
thus, by taking this as "simultaneous arising and separate cessation" (*ekuppāda-nānānirodha*), the construction should be understood as follows:

having excluded those material phenomena (*rūpa*) that arise during the moments of presence (*ṭhiti*) and dissolution (*bhaṅga*), they are to be known as such through simultaneous arising and separate cessation. For that material phenomenon [is simultaneous] with the immaterial (*arūpa*), and the immaterial...

"By that, [it is shown] as 'arising together and ceasing separately. In this context, the statement "forty-eight born of kamma" was made by treating the connection as a continuous succession, like a chain;
otherwise, the statement would have had to be "forty-nine born of kamma. "Arising separately... pe ...
should be illustrated by the final kamma-born"—this was stated because it is well-illustrated by that. For by this method...
It is possible that even prior to that, matter arisen at the moment of the dissolution of one consciousness ceases precisely at the moment of the dissolution of another;
thus, it can be understood that matter does not arise without the corresponding mental state, and the mental state does not cease without the corresponding matter.
However, in both cases, matter arisen at the moment of the presence (sthitikkhaṇa) of one consciousness [ceases] at the moment of the presence of another.
Furthermore, the non-material phenomenon (arūpa) that arises at the moment of its own duration and ceases at that very moment of duration is not included [in the previous categories];

it should be understood that this falls under the inclusion expressed by "neither from different arising nor from different cessation," because here the illustration is shown of what has arisen at the moment of duration, whereas that which has not been shown [is implied].
For the demonstration of "neither different arising nor different cessation" and so forth is by means of the material form belonging to the fourfold continuity (catusantatika-rūpa).
"By way of this, there is the demonstration of the method. Even for one who has entered the womb and remains among the eighty types of materiality born of karma, death exists;
therefore, by way of those very factors, the final [case] has also been applied. Why might they be called "immortal"?
Because the occurrence of the six bases is exactly like that of the karma which produces them, as well as the life-continuum (*bhavaṅga*) and so forth, which have those bases as their support.
"It should be understood that they would continue to function. For there is no cause by which some [mental states] among those born of karma would continue to function while others would not.
Therefore, it is said that "they would be immortal" because of the non-deficiency of the life-formations, such as vitality, heat, and consciousness.

The intention behind stating, "That which has arisen at the moment of arising ceases at the moment of arising of another; that which has arisen at the moment of presence ceases at the moment of presence of another;
that which has arisen at the moment of dissolution ceases at the moment of dissolution of another," is that this was said because it is found in the Aṭṭhakathā.
However, his own [personal] intention is that what arises at the moment of arising ceases at the moment of cessation.
This demonstrates that what has arisen at the moment of presence ceases at the moment of dissolution, and what has arisen at the moment of arising [ceases] at the moment of presence.
And having established it thus, it is stated in the *Addhānapariccheda*: "But that ceases together with the seventeenth consciousness.
Why does this not contradict the canonical text? Because even for materiality produced by the four causes, there is an equal duration of life (*samānāyukatā*).

The intended meaning is that [matter] must come to be. However, as these [authorities] have joined [the arguments], there is simply no such thing as matter having simultaneous arising and cessation, nor simultaneous non-arising and cessation.

Furthermore, regarding the statement by these [authorities] that matter has a lifespan of seventeen thought-moments (*cittakkhaṇa*), and the statement in the *Aṭṭhakathā* that it has a lifespan of sixteen thought-moments plus one-third more—
In the *Paṭiccasamuppādavibhaṅga-aṭṭhakathā*, in order to show that rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*) with a present object occurs immediately after death with a past object, it says:
"At this point, eleven thought-moments (*cittakkhaṇa*) have passed; likewise, fifteen thought-moments have passed.
Then, within the life-span of five remaining thought-moments—or even a single thought-moment—rebirth-linking consciousness arises upon that very same object."
This contradicts the fact that material phenomena have a lifespan of sixteen mind-moments, as demonstrated by the statement, "It arises.

For it is impossible to say that "matter enters the range of the senses at the very moment of its own subsistence. If that were the case, eleven or fifteen mind-moments would not have passed for the matter;
rather, more than eleven or fifteen mind-moments would have elapsed. Therefore, even in the case of the five sense-doors...
It would be logical to say that only matter which has reached the state of stability (ṭhiti) strikes the sensitive organ (pasāda);

however, in the case of the mind-door (manodvāra), it must be admitted that [the object] enters the range of the sense-field even during its moment of arising (uppādakkhaṇa). For nothing among past objects and so forth fails to enter the range of the mind-door.
And regarding the mind-door, it is stated thus: "Eleven consciousness-moments have passed, and then [it occurs] during the remaining five consciousness-moments of its life-span."

Furthermore, as for the moment of the mind’s persistence (*ṭhitikkhaṇa*) mentioned here, it must be investigated whether it exists or does not exist. For in the *Cittayamaka*, only this much is stated: "That which has arisen (*uppanna*) is that which is arising (*uppajjamāna*)? At the moment of dissolution (*bhaṅgakkhaṇe*), it has arisen, but it is not arising. It is not stated: "At the moment of persistence and at the moment of dissolution. Likewise: "That which is not arising is not arisen? [The answer is: "At the moment of dissolution, it is not arising, but it has not arisen. It is not stated: "At the moment of persistence and at the moment of dissolution. Therefore, the moment of persistence is not included there. Consequently, it should be understood that the moment of persistence does not exist. Thus, the statement "the moment of persistence exists" is merely a conventional expression. However, the moment of arising (*uppādakkhaṇa*) and the moment of dissolution (*bhaṅgakkhaṇa*) do exist. This is because they are established by way of their respective characteristics. For the characteristic of arising is established by the very fact of its occurrence; likewise, the characteristic of dissolution is established by the very fact of its occurrence. But the characteristic of persistence is not established by the very fact of its occurrence. Why? Because it is established by the non-occurrence of the characteristic of dissolution. For when the characteristic of dissolution occurs, the characteristic of persistence does not occur. Therefore, the moment of persistence is not established by the very fact of its occurrence. Consequently, it should be understood that the moment of persistence does not exist. Thus, the statement "the moment of persistence exists" is merely a conventional expression. But the characteristic of persistence is not established by the very fact of its occurrence. Why? Because
Only this much was stated: "At the moment of dissolution it is not arising, yet it is not non-arisen"; it was not stated:

"at the moment of stability and at the moment of dissolution. Likewise, regarding the complete answers to these pairs—"not ceased, nor ceasing" and "not ceasing, nor ceased"—after stating "at the moment of arising it is future," the omission of the words "at the moment of stability" [is for the same reason].

Furthermore, in the section on "the time when it has passed beyond," after stating that "at the moment of dissolution, consciousness has transcended the moment of arising," the failure to mention "the moment of presence" indicates the absence of a moment of presence for consciousness.
For even in the Suttas, it is said: "The alteration of what is present is discerned.
Since no alteration is discerned in that single [moment] itself, [it follows that] "that in which alteration is discerned is the persistence of the continuity (santati)."
"It is not impossible to say [it exists]," meaning that what is present is said to be "standing" while possessing two moments.
Furthermore, as for the arising of matter at the moment of the cessation of consciousness mentioned here, that too must be examined:
"Is it the case that for whom the truth of origin ceases, for him the truth of suffering arises? It was stated, "No. And as for [the matter] at the moment of the arising of consciousness...
The cessation of matter has been stated, and that must be investigated: "When wholesome states arise for someone, do indeterminate states cease for them?

To which it was replied, "No," and so forth. Nor can it be said that the denial was made with reference to mind-originated matter alone, because there is no specific context concerning mind-originated matter, and because the term "indeterminate" applies to mind-originated matter as well as other types.

Because it does not occur [in that context]. If one were to argue that the reason for taking "unspecified" (*abyākata*) here as referring exclusively to mind-originated matter is because the *Saṅkhārayamaka* states that bodily formation arises and ceases simultaneously with mental formation, that too is no valid reason.
For by that statement, there is no denial of the simultaneous arising and simultaneous cessation of other types of matter with the mind, nor...
Neither is there an allowance for non-arising or non-ceasing, nor is there a prohibition against other indeterminate states (abyākata) that are not originated by consciousness;
therefore, since the state of being indeterminate has not been rejected, permitted, or prohibited for those [states] such as those born of karma (kammaja),

which arise and cease simultaneously with it, it is not possible [to claim] by this [argument] that the cessation of consciousness at the moment of its arising applies to those states born of karma and so forth.

It is impossible to speak of the cessation of consciousness at the very moment of its arising. Furthermore, when recollecting the *Yamakapāḷi*, it is evident that consciousness breaks up immediately after its arising;
therefore, at that moment, consciousness does not produce matter because it is in the process of perishing, nor does it act as an assistant to another factor that produces matter.
Thus, [the mind-door adverting consciousness] arises simultaneously with the rebirth-linking consciousness.
The season might produce matter at the moment of arising of the consciousness immediately following it.
This being the case, since matter and immateriality arise together at the very beginning, there would be no such thing as priority or posteriority;
moreover, consciousness revolves so rapidly that one could say that the matter which arises together with it is actually arising within that very same conscious moment. For this very reason:
From the moment of rebirth-linking onwards, it is not a condition by any means for those mind-non-originated [material phenomena] that arise together with itself;

and since that [matter] reaches its state of presence immediately after that [consciousness], the immediately preceding consciousness is a postnascent condition (*pacchājāta-paccaya*) for that matter, not a conascence condition (*sahajāta-paccaya*).
If this is so, then regarding the statement: "For whom bodily formation arises..."
If it is argued that one should say, "His verbal formation ceases," [the answer is] no;

because at the moment of the cessation of consciousness, there is no commencement of the arising of matter. For, in the direct sense (nippariyāya), matter is only arising at the very moment of the arising of consciousness;

however, once the moment of consciousness has passed, it does not perform its function as a pre-arising condition (purejāta-paccaya) for the production of its own matter, nor does the immaterial [consciousness] [perform its function] for that [matter].
The statement "it is not a postnascent condition" was said figuratively with reference to the failure to attain a specific state of stability and arising.
As for the phrase "But after that," this refers to the conclusion of the preceding discussion by the summary commentary beginning with "But here, as for that which...
and so forth; thus, by the statement "from then on, the succession of kamma-born materiality no longer proceeds."
"Simultaneous connection" means "after death.

However, as stated in the *Aṭṭhakathā* regarding "matter together with matter," etc., since there is no simultaneous arising or simultaneous cessation of material phenomena (*rūpa*) with immaterial phenomena (*arūpa*), nor of immaterial phenomena with material phenomena, [the connection] is established only between material phenomena and material phenomena, and between immaterial phenomena and immaterial phenomena.
The meaning is that the matter of the body is its constituent part; "massed-heap-nature" (*ghanapuñjabhāvo*) refers to the state of being a dense mass, not...
"Mass" (puñja) means a collection of things whose connections are loose, like a heap of sesame, mung beans, and so forth. "Simultaneous arising, etc. refers to the three modes already mentioned.

"Below" refers to the commentary on the *Rūpakaṇḍa*. It is stated that they "are indeed fully accomplished" (*parinipphannāva*) because it is taken as having been said in the commentary on the *Rūpakaṇḍa* that there is a way of speaking regarding the full accomplishment of derivative forms (*vikārarūpa*) and so on. What is the difference between "fully accomplished" (*parinipphanna*) and "accomplished" (*nipphanna*)?

A phenomenon that possesses intrinsic nature (*sabhāvadhamma*)—delimited by the past and the future, produced by conditions, and struck by the three characteristics—is "fully accomplished" (*parinipphanna*).

However, even a phenomenon lacking intrinsic nature (*asabhāvadhamma*) can be called "accomplished" (*nipphanna*) when it is being brought into being through such means as the attainment of name-grasping (*nāmaggahaṇa*) or meditative absorption (*samāpajjana*).
By the phrase "but the attainment of cessation," it should be understood that all designations based on clinging (*upādāpaññatti*) are indicated by way of a single part thereof.
The commentary on the miscellaneous discussion is finished.
Regarding the commentary on the discussion determining the sequence and so forth:
those [defilements] to be abandoned by seeing are stated first because they are to be abandoned first; those to be abandoned by the second [path] are stated second.

This is the sequence of abandoning (*pahānakkama*). Because the stages (*bhūmi*) that are progressively more refined are established in successive order, the sequence of the teaching is according to those [stages].

Expressions such as "the four foundations of mindfulness" (*cattāro satipaṭṭhānā*) constitute the sequence of the teaching itself, because the foundations of mindfulness and so forth can occur even within a single moment.

Discourses on giving (*dānakathā*) and the like are spoken in progressive order; however, this is not because there is an absence of establishing [their] arising and so forth, but rather because of giving and the rest.

Here, the term is "the sequence of the teaching" (*desanākkamavacana*). As for "sequence of the teaching," because there is no fixed determination (*vavatthāna*) as previously stated, and because it is impossible for numerous statements to occur simultaneously, it must be taught according to some prior or posterior order;

thus, by that very intention, it is called the "sequence" of the mere teaching itself. "Without distinction" (*abhedena*) means by way of grasping them as a whole, without making distinctions such as form (*rūpa*) and so forth.
This is the meaning. Since it is the object of the eye and so forth as well, it refers by way of a single part to the aggregate of form (*rūpakkhandha*) as a whole.

"In this way" means according to the method stated here; the intention is that consciousness (*viññāṇa*) is the sovereign, because of the statements: "The king is the lord of the six doors" and "States are preceded by the mind."

The statement regarding the aggregate of form (rūpakkhandha) that it is "with taints (sāsava) and subject to clinging (upādāniya)" is for the purpose of precluding the idea that the aggregate of form possesses that same nature as those phenomena that are without taints (anāsava), because such untainted phenomena do exist;

it is not for the purpose of precluding the existence of form that is itself without taints. In the phrase "only those without taints are mentioned among the aggregates," the word "only" (eva) should be understood as having the sense of exclusion (aṭṭhānappayutta); the meaning is: "only those without taints are mentioned among the aggregates."
The grouping together of all conditioned things by way of their commonality is the "grouping of all conditioned things under a single common category" (*sabbasaṅkhatasabhāgekasaṅgaha*).
For when all conditioned things, beginning with contact, are grouped together by way of their commonality, they constitute the five aggregates.

In this context, those belonging to the same class by virtue of the commonality of being subject to change (*ruppana*) and so forth should be understood as "common" (*sabhāga*). Among these, the function of conditioning the conditioned belongs to that which has the nature of exertion (*āyūhana-rasa*).
Volition (*cetanā*), being powerful, is called the "aggregate of formations" (*saṅkhārakkhandha*);

furthermore, other factors such as contact (*phassa*) and so forth—which lack specific characteristics such as being "malleable" (*ruppana*)—should be understood as such by virtue of their commonality in forming conditioned phenomena (*saṅkhata-abhisaṅkharaṇa*).

However, because the intrinsic natures (*sabhāva*) of touching and so forth cannot individually be designated by the term "aggregate," the Tathāgata, who is cognizant of the true nature of phenomena (*dhammasabhāva-viññū*), [established] the aggregates of contact and the rest.
It should be understood that [the view] has not been stated. Furthermore, by way of such suttas as:

"Bhikkhus, whatever recluses or brahmins are eternalists and proclaim the world and the self to be eternal, they all do so in dependence upon and based upon these very five aggregates of clinging, or one or another of them," it is shown that this is the ultimate limit of the objective basis for the grasping of a self and what belongs to a self.

They are to be seen; and by this [text] and by way of the sutta to be cited later, it is stated that view arises depending on the aggregates alone, and it cannot be said to depend on objects such as the limited (paritta), because there is no dhamma with intrinsic nature (sabhāva-dhamma) other than the aggregates and Nibbāna.
Furthermore, since there exist others denoted by the term "aggregate," such as the aggregate of virtue (sīla-kkhandha) and so forth, it is not the case that there are only five.
To refute this objection, he says: "And because it is included among others.

The afflictive nature of feeling should be understood by way of the suffering of suffering (*dukkhadukkhatā*), the suffering of change (*vipariṇāmadukkhatā*), and the suffering of formations (*saṅkhāradukkhatā*).

For one associated with lust and so forth, there is the suffering of change and so on; that which grasps the forms of woman, man, and so forth is rooted in the various corresponding intentions (*saṅkappa*).
Perception (*saññā*) is the origin (*samuṭṭhāna*). Just as bile and so forth are the proximate cause of a disease, the origin is the immediate cause;

whereas just as climate, food, and age are the primary causes, the source (*nidāna*) is the fundamental cause. In the phrase "mental factors are the attachments of the mind," the mind is described as being like a patient;
for perception (*saññā*) acts as the cause for the manifestation of feeling (*vedanā*)—such as pleasant perception—and because it provides the sustenance for the "food" that is feeling.

They are like enemies and like executioners; for in the *Āsivisa-sutta* it is said, "Bhikkhus, 'five executioners and adversaries' is a designation for these five aggregates of clinging," and in the *Bhāra-sutta* it is said, "Bhikkhus, 'the burden' is a designation for these five aggregates of clinging. Furthermore, regarding the past time...
“I was devoured by form, just as I am being devoured now by present form;
and if I were to delight in future form, I would be devoured by future form, just as I am being devoured now”—thus, by way of the discourse on being devoured, one is a devourer.
[He understands] that impermanent form is “impermanent form.”
"In the Yamaka Sutta, by such passages as 'he does not understand it as it really is,' the aggregates are shown to be impermanent and so forth.

Although the aggregates are stated without distinction in this Vibhaṅga, it should be understood that what is stated refers to the aggregates of clinging (*upādānakkhandhā*), since they are the most prevalent and are included within those [five aggregates].

"Taught by the Kinsman of the Sun": this means taught by the Kinsman of the Sun (*ādiccabandhu*), or they were taught [by him]. The elision of the nasal vowel (*anunāsika*) or the elision of the particle *nika* has been made for the sake of metrical ease (*gāthāsukhattha*).
"Unable to be grasped" means it is not appropriate to grasp it as being permanent (*nicca*) and so forth.
Although it appears in form and shape to be like a wooden board (*phalaka*), because it lacks the quality of hardness (*kharabhāva*), it does not perform the function of a board.
"It is not possible to take it and make it into a plank or a seat," he said. "It does not remain so" means that it is not permanent and so forth;

or rather, the meaning is that because it breaks up immediately after arising due to being grasped as permanent and so forth by craving and views, it does not remain having assumed those characteristics.
"The number of one hundred thousand koṭis": this is not intended to show a limit of calculation.
This, however, should be understood merely as a demonstration of many states. "Water-slime" (*udakajallaka*) means water-scum.

Just as a wind produced by the falling of drops on the surface of water gathers the water-slime together, forms it into a mass, and creates what is called a bubble, so too does contact—produced by an object entering the range of the sense-fields—gather the unbroken slime of the defilements (*kilesajalla*) through its status as a concurrent condition.

Having gathered [them] together, it is called "feeling" (*vedanā*). It should be understood that this is stated with reference to the feeling pertaining to the round of existence (*vaṭṭagata-vedanā*), which is produced by defilements (*kilesa*) acting as its primary cause and by [objects] acting as the gratification of the objective field.
Alternatively, four conditions have been stated as the maximum limit; however, [feeling] certainly arises even with fewer than these.
“Of various characteristics” means having diverse natures by way of color, fragrance, taste, touch, and so forth. He says that the form displayed by illusion is “illusion.

Since even the five aggregates of clinging have the very nature of being foul and so on, due to their state of being the locus for the impurities of the defilements, they must indeed be regarded as foul and so forth.
Nevertheless, because in some cases a certain distinction is easy to grasp, he says: “And especially,” and so forth.

In this context, because the four foundations of mindfulness bring about the abandoning of the four perversions, it is stated that they are to be viewed as impure and so forth with respect to the aggregate of form and the others, by virtue of being their objective domain.

One is not oppressed by the aggregates because their intrinsic nature has been thoroughly understood. For even a practitioner of insight does not fall into suffering when those aggregates undergo decay.
But regarding those whose taints are exhausted, there is simply nothing to be said; for they are not afflicted by the aggregates even in the future.

"He fully understands physical nutriment" means that because it has been stated, "With the arising of nutriment comes the arising of form," one who abandons desire and lust for internal form also abandons desire and lust for physical nutriment, which is its source of origin; this is the full understanding through abandoning (*pahāna-pariññā*).
Furthermore, when one comprehends internal material form, one also comprehends the physical nutriment that serves as its condition;

this is the full understanding through knowledge (*ñātapariññā*). And when it is said, "one contemplates its arising and passing away," this should be connected with the full understanding by scrutinization (*tīraṇapariññā*).

With reference to covetousness in the form of sensual lust, he says "the bodily tie of covetousness. For the abandoning of sensual lust occurs through the contemplation of the foul (*asubhānupassanā*).

"It happens": either by way of sensual lust, he speaks of the abandoning of all greed. Because it was stated that "feeling has contact as its condition," the full understanding of contact should also be applied here according to the method already explained for the full understanding of nutriment.
Since the aspiration for existence exists solely for the sake of pleasure, one who abandons craving for feeling crosses over the flood of existence (*bhava-ogha*).
Seeing all feeling as suffering, one does not perceive any previously unarisen suffering produced by oneself or another, nor any happiness destroyed;
thus, by abandoning the bases for resentment such as "He has done me harm," one breaks the bodily tie of ill will (*byāpādakāyagantha*).

Furthermore, grasping at the idea that "purity lies in a state of existence abundant in happiness in a happy destination," one misapprehends purity through practices such as the cow-vow (*gosīla*) and the cow-life (*govata*).
One clings only by way of aspiring for pleasure; thus, while abandoning craving for feeling, one does not take up the clinging to rules and observances (*sīlabbatupādāna*).
Mental volition (*manosañcetanā*) is indeed the aggregate of formations (*saṅkhārakkhandha*), whereas perception (*saññā*) is associated with it;
therefore, seeing perceptions and formations as non-self, one abandons desire and lust for mental volition, and one thoroughly examines and brings that [volition] to completion.
And thus it is said: “He fully understands perception, volitional formations...
