[and so on]. Because there is a grasping at a solid mass in consciousness due to ignorance, one who discerns that solid mass and views it as impermanent crosses over the flood of ignorance.
Since adherence to rules and observances occurs through the power of delusion alone, by abandoning that, one breaks the bodily tie of adherence to rules and observances.
“Monks, as for this which is called ‘mind,’ or ‘intellect,’ or ‘consciousness’:
therein the uninstructed worldling is not capable of becoming disenchanted, not capable of becoming dispassionate, not capable of being liberated.
Why is that? Because, monks, for a long time this has been clung to, craved, and adhered to by the uninstructed worldling.”

“‘This is mine, this I am, this is my self’—from such a statement, one who perceives consciousness as permanent clings to it through the clinging to views; therefore, perceiving it as impermanent, one does not cling to it.
The commentary on the discussion of the determination of the sense-bases and so forth is concluded.
The commentary on the Suttanta-bhājaniya is finished.
2. Commentary on the Abhidhamma-bhājaniya. 34.

Having thus explained how the aforementioned feelings are to be understood by way of their planes through the singlefold and other classifications, [the text] further [explains them] by way of association.
He said "Moreover" (*apica*) and so forth in order to state the various aspects of what is to be known, such as the manner in which it has been demonstrated.

Regarding the phrase "eightfold therein" (*aṭṭhavidhena tattha*), the word *tattha* (therein) is to be construed with the sevenfold division alone; for if it were construed with the sixfold division, the state of being eightfold would not exist.

It was stated solely for the purpose of completing [the number ten]; that is, it was stated only to complete the state of being tenfold, and not for the purpose of providing a method (*naya*) as in the ninefold division.
Why? Because the method (*naya*) has been applied there. For the application of the method consists in the analysis of that which is to be analyzed, and that [analysis] has been performed there.

And just as with the triad of the wholesome (*kusalattika*), so too this statement—"bodily contact-born feeling is pleasant, there is painful"—is explained as being for the sake of completion alone, because the method of the eightfold division has been applied there.

"Extension of grasping" (*gahaṇavaddhana*) means the grasping of something other than what was previously grasped; it is by way of the extension of grasping, not by way of the accumulation of something else while that which was previously grasped remains.

Alternatively, the word "extension" (*vaddhana*) has the sense of cutting off, as in "the growth of hair" (*kesavaddhana*); thus, the non-grasping of what was previously grasped is the cutting off, which is "extension.
"Extension of both" (*ubhayavaddhana*) refers to the extension of both types of persons—the ones who are "twice-fettered" (*dukatika*)—from both sides.
Or, "increase" (*vaḍḍhana*) refers to the occurrence [of both]; it is an increase of both, and that itself is the "increase-both" (*ubhatovaḍḍhanaka*).

The removal by means of that is the "removal of the increase-both" (*ubhatovaḍḍhanakanīhāra*). Alternatively, the method of increase is the "increase-removal" (*vaḍḍhanakanīhāra*); the increase-removal occurring from both sides is the "increase-both-removal" (*ubhatovaḍḍhanakanīhāra*).
In this context, regarding the "increase-both" [methods] based on pairs and based on triads, there are only the two-fold and three-fold divisions.
This is indeed the distinction. Other divisions are undifferentiated;

nevertheless, for the purpose of generating a variety of wisdom, for the purpose of warding off useless thoughts such as thoughts of relatives through the practice of reflection on the Dhamma, for the purpose of generating joy associated with the Dhamma in one who reflects upon this textual passage, and because each section taken up serves as an entrance to liberation, [the exposition is presented] by way of a twofold, threefold, and manifold division.

It should be understood that other classifications have also been stated; for when things are mutually dependent, one becomes distinguished by way of its specific difference, and thereby the others also become distinguished.
It is not only of one kind, but also of two kinds; nor is it only of one or two kinds, but also of three kinds;
nor even only of one... up to nine kinds, but also of ten kinds. For in this way those classifications are mutually dependent.
Therefore, it should be understood that one particular division, when being related to itself and when relating itself to other divisions, qualifies them;
thus, by virtue of that [particular division], they too are said to be worthy of being so designated.
As for the phrases "in seven ways" and so forth, they are stated solely to show the manifold nature [of the divisions], without regard for other specific subdivisions.
"In all those ways, he has shown the aggregate of feeling in its many aspects"—thus it is said.

Just as a king with a vast domain is unimpeded within his own territory, so too the Blessed One, by virtue of his possession of the unobstructed knowledge of omniscience, is capable of teaching in whatever manner he desires, owing to his own great range of scope;
this is the meaning. Having stated the dyads (duka), the triads (tika) have been explained.
It is appropriate that the triads (tikas) are included within the dyads (dukas); but how are the dyads included within the triads?
Even though they are stated later on, it is because the dyads have been joined to each respective triad by way of the relationship between the expectant and the expected.
It was stated that the functional mind-element (kiriya-manodhātu) is obtained through the mode of adverting (āvajjana), yet adverting itself is conditioned by eye-contact (cakkhu-samphassa).
It does not exist. For no subsequent state within the same cognitive series (*vīthi*) serves as a condition for a preceding one.
And as for those who say, "The advertence and feeling are so called because they arise from the impact with the eye," that too is not tenable.
For nowhere—in any Sutta or Commentary—is it stated that "the impact of the eye and visible form is eye-contact."
Or it has been said: if that [feeling] were also contact by way of the eye, then feeling co-nascent with eye-consciousness would also have contact by way of the eye as its condition;

thus, it should not have been excluded here in the commentary. Furthermore, since it is already included in the Canon in the passage, "There is feeling conditioned by contact by way of the eye which is indeterminate," one should not again say, "feeling born of contact by way of the eye."

"Could it be. This, however, is the intended meaning here: since there is no arising of eye-contact without the feeling of adverting, that [adverting] which produces it is fit to be called, by way of a secondary sense (*pariyāyena*), a condition for eye-contact because it serves that purpose;
but in the primary sense (*nippariyāyena*), feelings are obtained only subsequent to eye-contact.

Regarding the phrase "by way of thirty-four types of consciousness-arising": here, the fine-material and immaterial-sphere consciousnesses are not included because they themselves constitute the mind-door (*manodvāra*).
For the mind-door is the life-continuum (*bhavaṅga*) mind of all [realms], and death and rebirth-linking are not other than that.

However, within this twenty-fourfold classification, there is the occurrence of wholesome and other states—such as those conditioned by eye-contact—within a single uniform cognitive process (*samānavīthi*).

Although these are stated in the *Aṭṭhakathā*, in the *Pāḷi* itself they are presented by condensing the nineteen and twenty-four [categories]; thus, because it is stated that they are found within various sequences (vīthi) such as,
"There is a feeling-aggregate conditioned by eye-contact which is neither-clung-to-nor-liable-to-clinging, neither-defiled-nor-defiling,
without initial application and without sustained application," the fact that they are found within various sequences applies to the wholesome triad (*kusalattika*) as well.

They should be applied. In the Commentary (*Aṭṭhakathā*), however, because the conditionality beginning with eye-contact within a single cognitive series (*samānavīthi*) is absolute, its occurrence therein is shown;
it does not, however, exclude its occurrence in a non-identical series (*asamānavīthi*).
For that very reason, he said: "Those [conditions] may be stated by taking any one among the sevenfold and so forth. Indeed, not...
They are obtainable only within the same cognitive series (*samānavīthi*) through development that transcends the limits of decisive support (*upanissaya*).
With reference to their being obtainable in these three ways, it is said: "It is permissible to speak of them as being wherever they may stand.

By "these," he refers to the wholesome and other types of consciousness as they have been shown; and in this section on the description of feeling (*vedanā*), [he also refers to] that which precedes it.

Because it is easy to explain by way of consciousness, the connection with consciousness has been made. For that very reason, consciousnesses have been elucidated according to the sevenfold division by way of the triads of planes;
according to the twenty-fourfold division by way of the triads of doors; according to the thirtyfold division by way of the doors and planes;
and according to the manifold division by way of the triads of doors and planes. Therefore, "having established oneself in any one of these... [is said].
It is said: “They are applicable. The exposition of the wholesome and so forth should be made by way of the planes such as the sense-sphere (kāmāvacara) and others;
and those planes are included within the thirtyfold classification itself, not like the sevenfold classification where the door is not specifically mentioned.

Furthermore, because they are very clear in being obtainable here in both similar and dissimilar cognitive processes (vīthi), [the text says]: “…in the thirtyfold… they serve as indicators of pleasure.”
It has been stated. But why did they explain [the matter] by remaining within the thirtyfold classification alone?
Is it not the case that, since the doors, the triad, and the planes have already been touched upon, one should have explained them by remaining within the manifold classifications?

No; because that would exceed the scope of what is to be explained. For the sevenfold classification, since the doors have not been touched upon, is an inappropriate basis for explanation; whereas in the twenty-fourfold classification, the doors and the triad have already been touched upon.
The stages (*bhūmi*) were not established by taking the [nine] stages into account; rather, the "stages of the door" (*dvārabhūmi*) within the thirtyfold classification have been stated.
And those that were established here should be illustrated solely along with the stages, excluding the consideration of the triads (*tika*).
Therefore, this is the place for such illustration; however, if one goes beyond that, there is a transgression of the proper place.

Regarding the phrase "by way of the extreme limit of decisive support" (*upanissaya-koṭi*): here, in various contexts such as "relying on faith, one gives a gift," the natural decisive support (*pakatūpanissaya*) has been explained.

It would be logical to say that within a single context, visual contact and the rest are conditions for wholesome states and so forth by way of a mere trace of decisive support—just as birth is for aging-and-death—because they do not exist in their absence; however, here [it refers to] that which arises because of seeing the form of the *kasiṇa*.

Since it will be stated that "the feelings of the preliminary stage (*parikamma*) and so forth have eye-contact as their condition," these consciousnesses occurring in various cognitive series (*vīthi*) are obtained by way of the condition of eye-contact; thus, they do not constitute even a trace of a decisive support (*upanissaya*), let alone the pinnacle of such support.

Rather, the "pinnacle of decisive support" refers to the primary decisive support among all the strong and weak decisive supports, such as the preliminary stages and so forth. [As for] "the tip of a hair (*vālakoṭi*")...
In expressions such as "it is not discerned," the word *ādi* (beginning) means either a part or a limit (*koṭi*).

Furthermore, since the decisive support (*upanissaya*) for the feelings associated with sense-sphere wholesome states and so forth proceeds from the moment of seeing the *kasiṇa*-form onwards, that seeing is the "limit of the decisive support.

Alternatively, seeing is not a powerful decisive support in the same way that the preliminary stages (*parikamma*) and so forth are; rather, it is designated as the "limit of the decisive support" by virtue of its status as a subordinate decisive support.

It has been stated. By stating that there is an absence of [the state of] being obtainable as a decisive support (upanissaya) in the three doors beginning with the nose, he indicates that a "common cognitive sequence" (samānavīthi) is not included here.
For, just like seeing and hearing, smelling and so forth do not serve as decisive supports for the preliminary work of the kasiṇas;
thus, their non-inclusion is indicated. Or rather, although the air-kasiṇa should also be grasped by touching it, [this is] according to the former [method].
However, since that touching [of the goal] generally does not occur by itself without hearing [the teaching], its status as a decisive support (upanissaya) has not been stated.

One who has attained excellence through aspiration is "one perfected in aspiration" (ajjhāsayasampanna); it is said, "one whose aspiration is perfected. Regarding "proper conduct and secondary duties" (vatta-paṭivatta):
There is both minor and major duty (*vatta*), as well as the duty performed previously and the counter-duty (*paṭivatta*) performed afterwards.

Thus, he speaks of the eye-consciousness that has arisen at the beginning; however, those [consciousnesses] that arise thereafter—such as seeing the kasiṇa-form, seeing a spiritual friend, or seeing objects that inspire a sense of urgency (*saṃvega*)—are indeed supporting conditions (*upanissaya-paccaya*).
Therefore, it should be understood that he is showing the eye-consciousness together with its supporting conditions.

It is the non-seeing and non-regard for things as they truly are in their own-being. It refers to that which is bound to form and so forth by the thought "I am," and which is misapprehended by way of conceiving it to have another intrinsic nature;

the meaning is "of that which is misapprehended. It is of the defilement that has become firmly rooted through its state of arising again and again by way of grasping at an object, or of one in whom sensual lust and so forth have not been abandoned. It is "established in grasping" by means of investigation.

It is established. And here, by the phrase "through non-regard," etc., the investigation should be understood as occurring through the arising of delusion and the other [defilements], which are made manifest by their respective functions.
Because it occurs by way of overcoming the defilements arisen through the seeing of forms, it is said to be "rooted in the seeing of forms";
thus he says, "born with eye-contact as its condition. And here, regarding the eye-contact and the feeling belonging to the four planes...
The state of being a decisive support (*upanissaya-bhāva*) has been explained by way of another method, as it is here in the phrase "by way of development" (*bhāvanā-vasena*).

By means of the sequence of insight practice beginning with the contemplation of rise and fall— having applied the three characteristics through the comprehension of groups (*kalāpa-sammasana*) and having first comprehended the material object by discerning the material object at the outset— one performs the entire comprehension rooted therein.
Having said that it "occurs with respect to the primary object of form," he states, "having comprehended the object of form.
Here, it should be understood that "comprehension" (sammasana) refers to the entire process beginning with the discernment of name-and-form (nāmarūpa), which constitutes meditation (bhāvanā).

Furthermore, by the phrase "having comprehended the object of form," the specific object of form that serves as the objective support for the aforementioned eye-consciousness is meant, not just any object whatsoever. By means of the object...
For it shows visual contact. In this way, it should also be understood in the case of the phrase "defilement arisen with respect to a visible-form object.

As for the question, "Upon what is this tangible object supported?", the dependence upon the great primary elements (mahābhūta) should be applied according to possibility—just as in the case of the eye-door—by way of the water element and by way of mutual dependence.
[The passage] "Birth... is a powerful condition" refers to birth and the other factors mentioned above being seen as fearsome, by virtue of their state of being powerful conditions.

By seeing those [objects] as fearful, he demonstrates the state of being a powerful condition for either the mental contact (manosamphassa) that arises simultaneously with that [fear], or for the life-continuum mental contact (bhavaṅga-manosamphassa) which serves as its door.

Regarding the phrase "with mental objects" (dhammārammaṇe), it does not refer only to objects such as birth and so forth mentioned previously; rather, it refers to all things that serve as the basis for lust and other defilements.

Regarding the object of mental phenomena (*dhammārammaṇa*): by the phrase "supported by the physical basis" (*vatthunissita*), he shows the discernment of the object of mental phenomena through the method of discerning a portion of that same object consisting of mental phenomena, namely feeling and so forth.
"Mind-contact" (*manosamphassa*) is taken as consciousness because it serves as the cause of contact; that very [consciousness] is [the cause] of its own result.
It is not appropriate to speak of [consciousness] as being in the state of a result, because that would lead to a confusion between cause and result, thereby producing delusion in the listeners;
thus it was said: "For it is not possible to designate consciousness as 'born of mind-contact,'" and this is not because consciousness lacks the state of being co-nascent with mind-contact.
Or rather, it is because, according to the statement "the meeting of the three is contact," the faculty and the object [are required].
Consciousness, like the sense-faculties, is a specific condition for contact, but contact is not so for consciousness; therefore,

just as with the sense-faculties and their objects, consciousness also does not deserve to be designated by terms such as "born of eye-contact," and thus it should be understood that the status of being "born of eye-contact" and so forth was not applied to it.
The commentary on the *Abhidhammabhājanīya* is finished.
3. Commentary on the *Pañhapucchaka*. 150.
Having treated each respective aggregate as a single phenomenon by way of the arising of consciousness and material form, [it says]: "fifty-five phenomena of the sense sphere."

He said: In the passages beginning with "of one who is lustful," lust and the other [defilements] should be applied to the six doors, while virtue and the five other restraints (*saṃvara*) should be applied as appropriate;
however, comprehension (*sammasana*) occurs only in the mind-door (*manodvāra*).

Since there is the arising of covetousness, dejection, and so forth regarding phenomena of the fine-material and immaterial spheres, the restraint of mindfulness and the restraints of knowledge and energy should be applied from that point as well, according to the circumstances. By the word "encompassing" (*pariggaha*),...
It includes both contemplation by way of comprehension and reflection. "Those very same" refers to the four aggregates mentioned.

A "turning" (*parivaṭṭa*) is the revolving of the mere teaching when what is to be taught remains the same. Having considered that there is nothing lacking or superfluous in any of the three turnings, he said: "There is only one section.
The commentary on the Question-and-Answer Section is concluded.
The commentary on the Analysis of the Aggregates (Khandhavibhaṅga) is finished.
2. Analysis of the Bases (Āyatanavibhaṅga).
1. Commentary on the Suttanta Exposition (Suttantabhājanīya).
152. "By way of distinction" means that, like the word *āyatana*, it refers to the specific meaning of the words *cakkhu* (eye) and so forth, rather than their common meaning.

He explains the meaning by way of the word *cakkhati*, which has the sense of tasting—as in "he tastes honey, he tastes the sauce"—and thus states its meaning accordingly. "The eye, Māgaṇḍiya, delights in forms, rejoices in forms, and exults in forms."

According to the verbal root, the eye relishes visible form (*rūpa*). Although the ear and other [senses] possess a state of delighting in their respective objects such as sound, it should be understood that the word "eye" (*cakkhu*) is applied specifically to the eye because of its conventional usage, just as the words "mud-born" (*paṅkaja*) and so forth are used for lotuses and the like.

By the term *cakkhati*, which is established by the characteristics of grammar, he states the meaning. "It sees" (*cakkhati*)— *Note: The provided text fragment ends abruptly; the full passage would typically continue with a definition of the verb.*

"Explains" (*ācikkhati*) means he speaks clearly; the sense is that he makes it manifest. Since explaining consists precisely in distinguishing between the even and the uneven—just as one does when leading someone—he said, "and the meaning is 'he makes manifest'.
Alternatively, because verbal roots have multiple meanings, the word *cakkhu* (eye) should be understood here as having the sense of "making manifest.
[It is like] the form of a lizard or the form of a crab at times when it is affected by passion or corruption.
Furthermore, matter (*rūpa*) that undergoes a change of appearance (*vaṇṇavikāra*) "makes manifest" (*rūpayati*) the state of being present in the heart;

it makes it clear as if it were matter itself, meaning it displays it as if it possessed a physical form. Alternatively, the meaning of the word *rūpa* is "extension" (*vitthāraṇa*), and since extension is indeed making manifest, he says "it makes manifest.
Or, because verbal roots have multiple meanings, the word *rūpa* has the sense of "making manifest" alone.

It is to be seen. Regarding the word *rūpa* which denotes "color," its etymological derivation is *rūpayati* ("it manifests"); regarding the word *rūpa* which denotes "form" (matter), it is *ruppati* ("it is affected")—this is the distinction.
In the sense of "that which is illustrated is called [an example]," only the word (*vacana*) itself would be taken;
yet here, the word "word" (*sadda*) is not merely the verbal expression, but rather everything that is audible, for it is "heard" (*sappati*) by its own conditions and is made audible (*sappīyati*).
The meaning is "it goes. "It indicates" means that by way of its odor, it makes manifest its own substrate—which was previously unmanifest—saying, "This is fragrant," or "This is foul-smelling";

or else, it is as if it were slandering a concealed object such as a flower or fruit, saying, "There is a flower here, a *campaka* or the like," or "There is a fruit here, a mango or the like. This is because the digestion of food is rooted in the apprehension of taste.
Because it inclines toward the taste of food for the sake of life, it is called "tongue" (*jivhā*) according to its etymological characteristic, as it "invokes" (*avhāyati*) life.
Because it is the "coming" (*āya*) of base, tainted phenomena (*sāsava-dhamma*), it is specifically called "body" (*kāya*);

among the nose, tongue, and body—which do not lead to the cause of the unsurpassed [Nibbāna] and which are produced by karma rooted in sensual desire (*kāmarāga*)—the body is distinguished as the specific condition for that sensual desire.
Because they are specifically conditions for the outflow (āsava). For it is by means of that [tangible object] that beings, relishing the tangible, engage even in sexual intercourse.

"Place of arising" means the cause of arising. Alternatively, the four aggregates based on the body-faculty are specifically called "with outflows" because they serve as the primary causes for the outflow of sensual desire and so forth;
thus, the meaning is "the place where those arise. They bear their own characteristic (lakkhaṇa).
Those which ought to be designated by the term "base" (*āyatana*) according to their specific characteristics (*visesalakkhaṇa*)—namely, the eye and so forth—are spoken of in that way.

However, other phenomena (*dhammā*) that constitute the domain of the mind are spoken of by being brought into the state of a single base (*ekāyatanatta*) solely by virtue of their general characteristic (*sāmaññalakkhaṇa*).

Because the former [bases] are manifest through the subject-object relationship (*visayavisayibhāva*) consisting of coarse physical bases, objects, and mental apprehension, the others—the domains of the mind—which are not manifest in that way, do not [function as such] of their own accord.
The word *dhamma* is used here to illuminate the meaning "not bearing their own intrinsic nature" (*sabhāvaṃ na dhārenti*).

"Exerting themselves" (*vāyamanti*) means simply "performing their own function. Regarding this meaning, the word *āyatana* signifies a locus (*adhikaraṇa*), as in "that wherein they extend" (*āyatanti ettha*);
however, in the second and third [grammatical] cases, it signifies the agent (*kattū*). "And those" refers to the states of consciousness and mental factors (*cittacetasikadhammā*).
They are called *āyatanas* because they come (*āyanti*), arrive, and proceed toward their respective doors and objects.
"They extend" means that, because they were previously unarisen, latent, and obscure, they stretch them out from the past, making them manifest and producing them; this is the meaning.

The passage beginning with "Moreover" (*apicā*) is commenced in order to state the meaning of the word *āyatana* by way of conventional usage (*ruḷhī*). "Because of being dependent upon that" (*taṃ-nissitattā*)...

In this context, since the mind is not the support-condition (*nissaya-paccaya*) for the mind-consciousness and other mental states and mental factors, its status as their "door" (*dvāra*) and its status as their "support" (*nissaya*) should be understood [in this specific sense].
This is according to the meaning of the term (*atthato*), not according to the literal etymological meaning (*vacanatthato*).

For here, the literal meaning has been stated by such expressions as "it sees" (*cakkhati*), whereas the referential meaning (*vacanīyattho*)—namely, that the eye is [composed of] the four great elements—is not what is intended here.
It is as in the passage beginning with “confidence based on [the Buddha],” and so forth.

By the phrase “just that many,” he shows the state of being neither deficient nor excessive. In this regard, since there is no phenomenon whatsoever apart from the twelve bases (āyatana), there is no objection regarding excess;
however, the maintenance of their own specific characteristics (salakkhaṇa) is the universal characteristic (sāmaññalakkhaṇa) common to all.
Showing that a deficient enumeration would result, he says: “For the eye and so forth, too,” and so on. “Unshared” means unshared by visual consciousness and the rest.
Even though the eye and so forth have unshared objects, their non-inclusion in the base of mental phenomena (dhammāyatana) should be understood because they are taken [here] as doors.
Alternatively, it is called “unshared” with reference to their being unshared in terms of their status as doors and objects.
The inconsistency regarding the order of arising and so forth should be applied by means of the predominance of their appearance and other such factors.

By the phrase "among the internal ones" (*ajjhattikesu hi*), he shows that the internal bases are to be taught first because of their internal nature and because they are the objects [of consciousness].

For among those that ought to be taught first, the eye-base (*cakkhāyatana*) was taught earliest because it is the most manifest. Then follow the nose-base and the others; here, this is due to the absence of being of great service [to the mind].

The intention is that because they cannot be taught simultaneously due to their inability to be spoken of together, they must be taught in a single sequence; thus, they are taught according to the order beginning with the nose.
For even if they were taught otherwise, one could not object to it, nor can it be said that what ought to be cleared up was not taught.
"Gocaravisaya" means that which has a range or sphere of activity; [this refers to] the mind (*mano*). Of what?
But is this its range (gocara) or its object (visaya)? It is the range of all five, beginning with the eye.

By the phrase "from the determination of the causes for the arising of consciousness," he states the reason for mentioning visible forms and so forth immediately after the eye and the other [faculties].

"Difference in conditions" refers to the difference in kamma and so forth. "Difference in destinies" refers to the distinctions between the various realms of existence, such as hell and so forth, as well as the different modes of birth, such as being footless and so forth. "Difference in animals" refers to elephants, horses, and so forth.
There is the division of classes such as the Khattiyas and so forth; there is the division of persons according to the various distinctions in the mental continuums of individual beings.
Furthermore, the infinite variety of bases (vatthu) such as the eye and so on that has been described is itself the variety of the heart-base (hadayavatthu).

From that, the infinite variety of the mind-base (manāyatana) should be understood through its divisions such as the painful way of practice (dukkhāpaṭipadā) and so forth, as well as through the divisions of objective dominance (ārammaṇādhipati) and so on. In this [context]...

In the *Suttantabhājanīya*, insight (*vipassanā*) was mentioned; thus, by taking consciousness as that which approaches insight, the eighty-onefold division of the mind-base (*manāyatana*) was stated according to the *Niddesa*.
Blue is "homogeneous" (*sabhāga*) only to blue, while other colors are "heterogeneous" (*visabhāga*);

in this way, it should be applied to the various divisions such as those originating from wholesome states (*kusalasamuṭṭhāna*). "By way of objects consisting of phenomena belonging to the three planes" was stated previously.
This was said with reference to mental objects (dhammārammaṇa) excluding the eye and so forth.
*Īhanā* is the striving by way of active effort (*saparipphanda-kiriyā*). *Byāpāra* is the performing of an operation by way of thinking (*cintana*). Demonstrating the operation therein, he said:
"For it does not occur thus to the eye regarding visible forms and so forth. Demonstrating the striving, he said: "Not..."
And so forth: “...and those. However, both [of these] are respectively expressed as *īhā* (endeavor) and *byāpāra* (activity).
*Dhammatā* means either the very nature (*sabhāva*) or the capacity for causality. The status of being a sense-door and so forth for those things devoid of endeavor and activity is *dhammatā*.
And in this sense, the word *yaṃ* (which) has the meaning of *yasmā* (because). In the former case, the word *yaṃ* is a qualification of the arising. “Empty...”
Because of the statement, "Monks, 'village' is a designation for these six internal sense bases," they should be regarded as being like an empty village.

Just as when an empty village has been entered, whatever vessel one touches there is found to be empty, so too, when things grasped as permanent and so forth are investigated, [they are found to be empty].

"These are seen as truly empty. It is said that visible forms and so forth are "striking" (abhighātaka) to the eye and other faculties by way of giving rise to covetousness and dejection within the doors of the eye and so forth. There are six types of creatures: snakes, pythons, birds, dogs, leopards, and monkeys.

Their haunts are uneven terrain, caves, open spaces, villages, charnel grounds, and forests. Among these, by means of the eye and other faculties whose inclinations are toward such uneven terrain and the like...

Because one delights in the forest-like state of apprehended phenomena—which are similar to uneven ground, pits, caves, villages, and charnel grounds—the similarity of form and the other aggregates to "the uneven" and so forth should be applied accordingly.
The phrase "in the sense of having existed and then not existing" is stated separately because it encompasses the other four modes. Having existed...
For the very aspect of non-existence (*abhāvākāra*) consists of the aspects of arising, passing away, and so forth.
In this context, by the word "having been" (*hutvā*), he shows that existence in the middle is preceded by being devoid of a prior limit;

having stated that, he shows with the term "non-existence" that non-existence in the future limit is preceded by existence in the middle. By both together, he shows that impermanence has the characteristic of constant non-existence. This is the relinquishing of intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*).
“Change” (vipariṇāma) means either transformation through aging and dissolution, or the occurrence of a modification in the continuity [of the stream].

To preclude the notion that something might endure for a long time even though it is always absent, he said “temporary” (tāvakālika). That which is devoid of arising, passing away, and alteration is permanent;
it is not otherwise. Thus, “impermanent” (anicca) is used in the sense of the negation of permanence, with the intended meaning being its opposite of permanence.
“Oppression” (paṭipīḷana) refers to the state of being undesirable due to such factors as the nature of birth. Regarding the phrase “in the sense of oppression”:
the meaning is that it is so called because it oppresses the person in whom it occurs, or because it is itself oppressed by aging and the other [characteristics].

It is also called “because of constant oppression” because even for that which has a limited duration, it is constantly oppressed by arising and the other [characteristics] during its own moment of existence.
Having distinguished it from the previous general characteristic, he says: it is "painful" (dukkha) because it oppresses the person.
Because it is the opposite of pleasure, "pain" rejects and precludes pleasure; or rather, the word "pain" rejects pleasure by its very meaning—thus he said, "by way of rejecting pleasure."
There is no one who exercises mastery over it, nor is there mastery exercised over this; thus it is "not subject to mastery" (*avasavattanaka*).

Alternatively, "subject to mastery" (*vasavattanaka*) refers to the state of exercising mastery by oneself over another, or by another over oneself; since that does not exist for it, it is "not subject to mastery.
The meaning or intrinsic nature of being not subject to mastery is the "meaning of not being subject to mastery" (*avasavattanakaṭṭha*); and this is its general characteristic (*sāmaññalakkhaṇa*).

"By ten" means it is empty in the sense that another has no mastery over it within itself. And in this context, "ownerless" (*assāmikato*) is a qualification of the term "emptiness" (*suññatā*) itself.
Alternatively, because there is no state of mastery over these three bases for anyone who thinks, "Since this...
may it not come to pass," it is empty by way of that very absence of mastery over itself.
The meaning is as follows: This is not subject to anyone’s will, nor does it have any power to act according to its own will; thus, it is "not acting according to its will" (*akāmakāriya*).
By this, he shows it specifically in the sense of being devoid of mastery.

"Going to non-existence" (*vibhavagati*) means going to destruction. "Going to the transition of existence" (*bhavasaṅkantigamana*) means precisely the arising of another existence within the continuum.

The abandonment of the mode of occurrence as it has been proceeding within the continuity is the abandonment of its natural state. When it is said, "The eye is impermanent," since the words "eye" and "impermanent" have the same referent, the objection arises that other impermanent phenomena would also incur the status of being the "eye.
To prevent this objection, there is a distinction between words expressing specific and general characteristics, which consists in their denoting either a single part or the whole collection.
He said "Furthermore" (*apica*) and so forth in order to illuminate this.
What is being shown? The intention is: by one who speaks of the practice of insight (*vipassanā-cāra*), what characteristic is being shown?
"And what, Ānanda, is the perception of non-self? Here, Ānanda, a bhikkhu, having gone to the forest, or to the foot of a tree, or to an empty hut..."

Or he reflects thus: “The eye is non-self,” and so on... “Mental objects are non-self. Thus, it is said that one dwells contemplating non-self in these six internal and external bases without distinction;

this is stated for the purpose of clarifying the characteristic of non-self through the non-selfhood of both the causes—the eye and so forth—and the effects—the eye-consciousness and so forth—which are merely cause and effect.
"The teaching on the bases" refers to the statement: "Of the twelve... [up to] the characteristic of non-self.
Although the characteristics of impermanence and suffering are also shown here, the intention is that the characteristic of non-self alone is specifically demonstrated by them.
In the phrase *veti ca*, the word *iti* has the sense of completion (*samāpanattha*). In the phrase *iccassa*, the word *iti* refers to the fault that is to be attributed to what has been completed.
It has the sense of illustration. “In this way” means: when there is such a doctrine as “the eye is the self.

Or, in the phrase “of him thus,” the word *iti* has the sense of illustrating the manner of the fault in the opponent’s doctrine, as in “of one who speaks thus. “In this way” has the sense of illustrating the mode in which the fault occurs.

If it is argued that, regarding form as the self, there would be the application of a designation of ownership toward what belongs to the self—as in “let my form be thus”—[we reply]: No; [it is not so] because of [the statement] “my...”
Because it is grasped as "self. For material form (rūpa) grasped as "my self" would indeed exist exactly as desired when one wishes, "Let it be thus," due to its being subject to one's mastery;
yet even for one who desires it, that self consisting of material form is not subject to one's mastery.
"For affliction" means: thus, by way of suffering. "Making known" means: making known to others. Regarding the making known of the characteristic of non-self...
Because they are not the domain of others, it is shown that the proclamation of the characteristics of impermanence and suffering—which illustrate the characteristic of non-self—is not their domain.
Furthermore, this difficulty of proclaiming them arises from their being difficult to establish; thus, this is the reason why they do not become manifest.
The questioner says, “But these,” and so forth. Regarding the constant oppression mentioned below that occurs uninterruptedly in the bases (*ṭhāna*) and so on:
the analysis of the various elements (*nānādhātuvinibbhoga*) is the discernment of the eye and the other faculties from their collection as mere elements (*dhātumattatā*).
By the word “solidity” (*ghana*), he speaks by bringing all four solids into a state of unity through their solid nature. Wisdom itself is the disturbance of the continuity (*santativikopana*).
It should be seen. "According to its actual nature" means according to its non-erroneous intrinsic character (*sabhāva*).
For an intrinsic character, when it is being tasted—that is, when it is being relished through uncontradicted penetration—is called "flavor" (*rasa*).

The mention of the characteristic of impermanence and so forth elsewhere by way of "impermanence," etc., is because there exists a distinct apprehension of impermanence and so forth, which differs from the apprehension of form and so forth that occurs by way of "being afflicted" (*ruppana*) and the like. Indeed, it is not [grasped] merely by the delimitation of name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*).
The task is accomplished; furthermore, the aspects (ākāra) of impermanence and so forth should be seen as belonging to form and the other aggregates.

However, since those aspects do not exist in an ultimate sense (paramattha) but are merely the aspects of form and so forth, it is appropriate to remain within the mere intended meaning—that in the *Aṭṭhasālinī*, the status of the aggregates as the object of insight (vipassanā) having the characteristics (lakkhaṇa) as its object was stated—and not to overstep that. "Impermanent" (anicca).
And when one grasps [the mark] as "suffering" or "non-self," one does not grasp it as [the other marks]; likewise, when suffering and the rest are grasped, the others are not grasped.

Furthermore, the graspings of impermanence and so forth serve to turn back the perception of permanence and the like; they are dominated by the faculties of faith, concentration, and wisdom, and they constitute the three doors to liberation.
Therefore, since there is a mutual distinction among these modes being comprehended, the three characteristics have been taught.
The commentary on the Suttanta-bhājaniya is finished.
2. Commentary on the Abhidhamma-bhājaniya: 167.
The discourse on the delimitation of name-and-form is called "Abhidhamma discourse" because, unlike in the Suttanta, it proceeds by way of pairs of conditions.

Without explaining them according to the internal and external [classification], the sense bases to be directly known (*abhiññeyya*) have been taught in the *Abhidhammabhājanīya* by way of their non-separation. "Having approached" means:

for one who is disenchanted with all conditioned phenomena (*saṅkhāra*), who is inclined toward the unconditioned (*visaṅkhāra*), and whose mind has turned away [from the round of existence] through the lineage-knowledge (*gotrabhū*), there is the realization by means of the Path;
that is the meaning. For when that [Nibbāna] is being realized, having been attained, it becomes both the object-condition (*ārammaṇa-paccaya*) and...

Because the path, which is characterized by destruction, depends upon that [Nibbāna]—which serves as the dominant condition (*adhipati-paccaya*) and as the foundation for the formations (*saṅkhāra*) that are free from the nature of supreme relief—and because it exhausts lust and the other defilements, it is said: "By coming to that, lust and the others are exhausted.
For in the absence of the realization of that [Nibbāna], there would be no arrival at the non-arising and cessation of lust and the others. Thus it is stated according to the Sutta.
"Having released" means having released the words of the Sutta. Another meaning of the Sutta must be brought forth, as in the case of "having killed mother and father," and so on;
the meaning is not one that is led [to] by the words of the Sutta alone—this is the sense.
"One, different" refers to making something powdered or minute; he speaks of "making into powder" without great respect. Not...
“You know only one name”—the meaning is: “Do you not know even this much?
By saying “Surely it is known,” he restrains the opponent who, concealing his own knowledge, creates confusion by thinking, “Even if it was not known before, surely it is good that it is known now.
“Having analyzed” means: not remaining at the mere literal meaning, but having analyzed the hidden (līna) meaning.
The meaning is: having extracted and brought out, it is "spoken.

One asks—"What is called the destruction of lust (*rāga*) is the destruction of lust itself," and so forth—in order to cut through the statement of one who claims that the destruction of lust and the other defilements is merely non-existence, and that there can be no plurality in non-existence because of its very nature as non-existence.
For if the destruction of lust were not the destruction of hatred (*dosa*) and the rest, then [the destruction of] hatred and the others...
Furthermore, because greed and the other [defilements] have been destroyed, they become mutually distinct, differentiated, and separate;

thus, it follows that there would be a plurality of *nibbānas*. Moreover, since there can be no mutual distinction for that which lacks intrinsic nature (*nissabhāva*), it follows that *nibbāna* must possess intrinsic nature (*sasabhāvatā*).

There are nine things rooted in craving, beginning with "in dependence on craving, there is seeking" (*taṇhaṃ paṭicca pariyesanā*); among these, seeking and the others are the defilements that perform the acts of seeking and so forth.
It should be seen. One thousand five hundred defilements are mentioned in the *Nidānakathā*.

"He should be made to undergo [the penalty] because of coarseness" means he should be enlightened regarding, or restrained from, the fault of attributing coarseness to Nibbāna, which is extremely subtle.
"The object" refers to the tactile sensation of a clung-to (upādinnaka) body in sexual intercourse. Even for those such as cats and the like, there is the attainment of Nibbāna.

Why was it so stated? Is it not the case that for one who maintains that "Nirvana is the absolute non-arising and cessation of the defilements," the destruction of the defilements—their non-occurrence for some period—would not constitute Nirvana? No; because they share the commonality of being non-existence (*abhāva*).

For both absolute non-occurrence and non-occurrence for some time are simply non-existence; thus, there is no distinction. Or rather, for one who speaks with distinction, [the former] is non-existence.
"Attains": because it can be reached even by animals, it is coarse and gross, like an ornament clearly visible to them as well.
However, he rebukes him as if mocking him, saying that it cannot merely be worn on the ear, or that it cannot be worn because it is too large even for an ornament.

Thinking that the attainment of the destruction of defilements has occurred for him at the moment of the change-of-lineage (gotrabhū) by means of making Nibbāna the object, he said, "But you [say this] while the defilements are still unabandoned," and so forth.
Is it not impossible to say that the destruction of defilements is not attained merely by making something an object?
For the mind takes as its object everything—past, future, and so on—and not only that which is actually produced; thus, even the change-of-lineage [takes Nibbāna as its object].
Does it arise by taking as its object that state of non-arising of defilements which is to be brought about by the Path? No;

because for one who has not yet attained Nibbāna, there is no knowledge that takes Nibbāna as its object. For Nibbāna is not like other phenomena; rather, because of its extreme profundity, it cannot be grasped as an object by one who has not attained it.
Therefore, by that change-of-lineage consciousness, which is to be attained through a profound nature that transcends the characteristics of the three periods of time—

It must be so; for one who desires the mere destruction of the defilements, there would have to be a destruction of defilements already accomplished prior to the change-of-lineage (gotrabhu) consciousness.
Therefore he said: "You designate the destruction of defilements, Nibbāna, while the defilements are still unabandoned.
For if that which has not yet reached the destruction of defilements were made the object, then even the consciousnesses preceding the change-of-lineage would take it as their object.

"The destruction of defilements through the path is Nibbāna": the meaning is, "What is this Nibbāna that serves as the object of the path? By the words beginning with "the path," he explains the first two questions.
"And it is not anything whatsoever": they say that among form and so forth, Nibbāna is not any thing at all;
nor does it exist at any time; nor can it be described by way of pastness and so on. Relying upon that [Nibbāna], there is not even a slight portion (*ekadesamatta*) of ignorance or craving.
The meaning "that very thing, having come to that [state], never again comes to be" is appropriate.
The commentary on the *Abhidhammabhājanīya* is finished.
3. Commentary on the *Pañhapucchaka*.

168. “... pe ... not to be classified as having an object” means that just as those [states] with an object take some object that cannot be classified by way of being limited (*paritta*) and so forth, so too this [state] does not belong to any category that cannot be classified by way of its objective support (*ālambana*).
The commentary on the interrogation section is finished.
The commentary on the Analysis of the Bases (*Āyatanavibhaṅga*) is finished.
3. Analysis of the Elements (Dhātuvibhaṅga) 1.
Explanation of the Exposition According to the Discourses (Suttantabhājanīya-vaṇṇanā) 172.
Although it has been stated in the *Dhātusaṃyutta* and other texts: "Bhikkhus, I will teach you the diversity of elements; and what is that?"...
"Monks, what is the diversity of elements? The eye element... [and so on] ...the mind-consciousness element. Thus, the eighteen elements have been mentioned;
however, since they are also found in the Abhidhamma, they are not included here because they are common to both.

Instead, having taken the three sets of six elements as they appear specifically in the Suttas, it should be understood that the *Suttantabhājanīya* has been analyzed. "All elements" refers to all eighteen.

The word *dhātu* should be understood as established in the sense of a mere intrinsic nature (*sabhāvamatta*) within emptiness (*suñña*). "Unaffected element" (*asamphuṭṭhadhātu*) means a state not pervaded by the four great elements (*mahābhūta*). 173.
Regarding the "two earth-elements," this is a citation from the commentary; however, in the canonical text (*pāḷi*), it says simply "two."
It occurs [in the text], but the meaning is exactly as stated before. However, when the reading is *dvayaṃ*, this meaning is also possible:
that which has two parts (*avayava*) is a "pair" (*dvaya*); a pair of earth elements is "earth-element-pair" (*pathavīdhātudvaya*), meaning a collection of two earth elements.
Or, the two parts themselves combined are a "pair," namely, the pair of earth elements. "Therein... [the text continues].
"What is the earth element? The two-fold earth element; this is the earth element"—thus he answers in brief.

Regarding the statement "there is the internal, there is the external," here the terms *ajjhattika* (internal) and *bāhira* (external) do not denote the internal and external bases (*āyatana*) as they do in the "Internal-External Duka" (*Ajjhattika-bāhira-duka*), nor do they correspond to the terms *ajjhatta* (internal) and *bahiddhā* (external) mentioned in the "Internal-External Tika" (*Ajjhatta-bahiddhā-ttika*).

They have the same meaning; however, these terms denote both that which is bound by the faculties and that which is not bound by the faculties. Therefore, it was said: "Included within the continuum of sentient beings," and so forth.

Furthermore, the term *niyakajjhattā* (inherently internal) is not stated with reference to being born within one's own individual self (*paccattaṃ attani*), but rather it should be understood as being born within the continua of all sentient beings.
For by the expression "internal" (*ajjhattaṃ*) and "individual" (*paccattaṃ*), there is the inclusion within the continuum of sentient beings.

This shows its internal nature, not its individuality as a person. "By way of its own-nature and mode" means by way of the mode of being grasped through its own specific nature, distinguished from water and so forth.
"Head-hairs have the characteristic of hardness" is said because they possess an excess of hardness. "A separate portion" means merely a portion of earth.
“Empty” is the meaning. It should be understood that the brain is not mentioned separately here because it is already included by the mention of the bone-marrow.
“By this” refers to the passage beginning with “That is to say, head-hairs,” and so forth. “Having performed the work” means having performed the application, the effort, or the exertion;
for just as one desiring wealth performs work in ploughing and so on, so too one desiring Arahantship must perform the work in this act of attention (*manasikāra*).

The "prior impediments" (*pubba-palibodha*), such as one's dwelling and so forth, are mentioned in contrast to the "subsequent impediments" (*apara-palibodha*), which include minor impediments like long hair and the like.

Since attention (*manasikāra*) by way of the five factors— color and so forth— is common to both the attention to the repulsiveness of the elements (*dhātu-paṭikūla-manasikāra*) and the attention to the elements themselves,
the statement "at the end, attention should be practiced in this way" is said in order to show the attention to the elements already produced.

He said: By saying "devoid of mutual application (ābhoga) and reflection (paccavekkhaṇa)," he shows that because both cause and fruit are devoid of functional activity (abyāpāratā), they are merely elements (dhātumattata).
In this very same way, the lack of functional activity should also be understood for application, reflection, and so forth.
For these do not arise or perform their functions by first applying themselves to or reflecting upon their respective causes. "By way of characteristic" (lakkhaṇavasena):
This was said with reference to such statements as "hard" and "rough.
*Vekantaka* is a single type of iron. *Nāganāsika-iron* is a distinct variety of iron similar to iron, like the distinct variety known as *haliddi*.

*Kittima-iron* (artificial iron) is produced by mixing [iron] with *tipu*, *tamba*, and so forth, because it is brought into being through a process of manufacture. *Morakkha* and the others are indeed of those very names.
"Seas' pearls" is merely an illustration; for all pearls, indeed, are pearls. 174. *Appeti* means water (*āpo*);
it reaches the other three elements by way of cohesion, which is the meaning of "it flows" (*silesati*). *Yūsabhūto* means having become juice (fluid).
Regarding the phrase "moistening the kidneys, heart, liver, and lungs": here, the liver [is moistened] by filling its lower portion.
The others moisten them by trickling down little by little upon them.

The comparison of the clods of earth below should be understood as being intended solely to demonstrate the commonality of non-intervention (*abyāpāra*) between those who moisten and those who are to be moistened, not to demonstrate a commonality of position.
For in the *Satipaṭṭhānavibhaṅga*, it is stated that some of those to be moistened by the accumulated blood are situated below, while others are situated above.
Regarding the phrase "it will say": the lower part of the liver does not know, "Blood is staying in me," nor do the kidneys and so forth know, "The blood that is moistening us is staying [here].

This is how the construction should be understood. However, unlike the medicinal rule (*bhesajja-sikkhāpada*), where there is a restriction stating, "the milk belongs to those whose meat is allowable," no such restriction exists here.
175. "By way of sharpness" means by way of being whetted, by way of being keen. "Heat" (*santāpa*) is the state of being hot that exceeds the natural temperature of the body;
"fever" (*paridāha*) is a great burning that proceeds by way of consuming the body. This is the distinction between them.

"By which one decays" also makes sense as meaning that one decays through diseases of decay such as those occurring every day (*ekāhika*). Having heated it a hundred times and then cast it into water...
They say it is "boiled ghee" and "ghee washed a hundred times. The "flavors" (rasa) and so forth refer to chyle, blood, fat, flesh, sinews, bones, and bone-marrow.
Some, omitting the sinew, have stated that semen is the seventh constituent (dhātu). "Natural" means not subject to agitation, but always present.
Here, the "fire of the hungry ghosts" (petaggi) is understood as that which has actually emerged from their mouths.
176. "By way of movement" means by way of proceeding with urgency, or by way of vibration.

177. By this [statement], "In whatever space... [etc.]... that has been described," it is said in order to show that the space revealed by the kasiṇa has not been described here, whereas the space free from impurities (ajaṭākāsa) has been described.
179. The state of pervading pleasure and pain belongs to the body-dwelling wind because it serves as the condition for the arising of the tactile objects of pleasure and pain.

It is called "according to its strength" because of its capacity to pervade either a single part of the body or the entire body; likewise, it is so called because of its capacity to pervade in that same way by giving rise to mental states born of desire—either desirable or undesirable—for joy and grief.
Thus, by virtue of their pervading the body, it shows how one occupies the place of another and strikes down the other, demonstrating their mutual opposition.
Or rather, their "pervasion" (pharaṇa) is simply the coarse manifestation of mutual opposition.

The bases and objects, which serve as the causes for continuous occurrence, should be regarded as the locus of pervasion; and this state of having an opposite is shown by way of the person possessing both, because it is easy to perceive.
181. "With reference to defilement-desire (*kilesakāma*)" means that the intention is: with reference to the "intention" (*saṅkappa*) mentioned in the passage, "Intention is desire; lust is desire.
For that too is analyzed as "defilement-desire" because it afflicts and torments, arising from association with defilements, or because it arises from the basis of defilements.
"Connected with desire" means associated with desire, which is defined as sensual lust (*kāmarāga*).

Or [it means] "bound up with sensual desire. Even though other phenomena associated with sensual desire exist, it should be understood that the word *dhātu* (element) is conventionally established as being prefixed with "sensual desire" (*kāma*) specifically for *vitakka* (applied thought), because applied thought functions with a particular intensity of attachment to sensual desire. This same method applies to the "element of ill will" (*byāpādadhātu*) and the others.
"Harming" (*vihiṃsā*) is the causing of suffering to oneself and others. They "harm" (*vihiṃsanti*) means they wish to kill.

182. Although it arises in both [realms], sensual thought (kāmavitakka) is called a "breaker of the path" because, through its association with covetousness, it generates a course of action and breaks the course of non-covetousness.
As for "ill will," however, the term "ill will" indicates ill-will-thought; for that is the element of ill will.
Likewise, in the case of cruelty and the element of cruelty, they are treated according to their occurrence by way of ill will.
And the classification of the courses of kamma (kammappatha) should be applied by way of killing living beings and so forth. "In this" refers to the two triads.

"The discourse encompassing all" (sabbasaṅgāhikakathā) is the explanation given after grouping the other two pairs together with those that include all sense-sphere (kāmāvacara) and all wholesome (kusala) states.

Furthermore, when "in this" is said to refer to "this hexad," there arises the implication that by the term "sense-sphere element" (kāmadhātu), both the sense-sphere states and the renunciation-element (nekkhammadhātu) and so forth would be included.
"Should be made to obtain": the phenomena that are obtaining the state of the eye-element and so forth should be brought out and made to obtain [their respective objects] by means of seeing.

"Course" (*cāra*) means that which courses therein; what is it that courses? It is comprehension (*sammasana*). The course of comprehension is the "course of comprehension" (*sammasanacāra*), which is a designation for the phenomena belonging to the three planes.
The commentary on the Suttanta-bhājaniya is finished.
2. Commentary on the Exposition of the Abhidhamma (Abhidhammabhājanīya) 183.

"Of the eye" (*cakkhussa*) is stated by way of its specific cause through the relationship of an uncommon owner. For that [eye] is not shared with other persons, yet it is shared with respect to all visible forms such as blue and so forth.
"It discriminates" (*vidahati*) means being directed [by the mind] thus: "In this and that manner, you must proceed."
The meaning is "it produces as it were. Furthermore, the specific sense of the verbal root (*dhātu*) itself is illuminated by the prefix;

thus, even without the prefix, this word *dhātu* should be understood as expressing that same meaning. Since the establishment of the verbal root-word occurs in relation to the agent, object, state, instrument, and locus, these five meanings have been stated.
The "minerals" (*dhātu*) such as gold and silver refer to rocks and the like which serve as the seeds for gold and so forth.

Regarding the phrase "they bear their own intrinsic nature (sabhāva), thus they are elements (dhātuyo)," here too the grammatical derivation of the word *dhātu* should be understood as "that which bears (*dhātī*) [its nature], thus it is an element (*dhātu*).

For the word *dhātu* itself also possesses the sense of "bearing. Furthermore, since this sense of the agent is distinct from the previous one, the primary meaning of the word *dhātu*—the bearing of a mere intrinsic nature devoid of a sentient being—is stated separately.
In the expression "elements like elements" (*dhātuyo viya dhātuyo*), the word *sīha*...

Just as the word "lion" is established [as a designation] for men, so too the term *dhātu* (element), though established for the components of a rock, should be understood as being used metaphorically for the eye and the other faculties.

Knowledge (*ñāṇa*) and the object of knowledge (*ñeyya*) constitute "knowledge and the object of knowledge"; their components, which consist of their respective divisions, are the "components of knowledge and the object of knowledge" (*ñāṇañeyyāvayava*).

Among these, the divisions of knowledge are a portion of the element of phenomena (*dhammadhātu*), while the divisions of the objects of knowledge are all eighteen; thus, they are merely the components of knowledge and the object of knowledge.
There are elements (*dhātuyo*). Alternatively, the meaning is as follows: the intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*) that is to be known by knowledge is what is expressed by the word "element" (*dhātu*);

it is to be known by non-erroneous knowledge, not to be known by those who grasp erroneously through views and so forth. The parts (*avayava*) of that which is to be known by knowledge are the eye and the other [faculties].
The word "element" (*dhātu*), which is conventionally established for the parts that have dissimilar characteristics such as taste (*rasa*) and so forth, [is also applied] to such other parts.

It should be understood as being used metaphorically in relation to the eye and so forth, or else it is established (nirūḷha) in its primary sense for the eye and so forth, just as it is for taste and so forth.

By the phrase "this is a designation for that which is merely devoid of a soul" (*nijjīvamattassa*), he shows that the word *dhātu* is established in the sense of an object that is merely devoid of a soul.
"That which has six elements" is *cha-dhātuko*; that collection of phenomena which is called "a person" (*puriso*) in the world is composed of six elements, because of the six...
The meaning is that there is merely a collection of earth and so forth, which have the nature of being devoid of life; herein there is no living soul (jīva) or person (purisa).
Since the sequence of the eye and so forth was stated previously, here, while showing the sequence of the three elements within each triad, he says:
"by way of the successive determination of cause and fruit. The successive determination of causes and fruits is simply their state as cause and fruit.
In this context, "cause" (hetu) is intended to mean "condition" (paccaya). "Fruit" (phala) refers to that which has arisen from conditions; thus he says "the eye-element," and so forth.

The status of the mind-element (manodhātu) and the mental-object-element (dhammadhātu) as causes of mind-consciousness (manoviññāṇa) should be applied according to their respective possibilities, or rather, by way of the mind that serves as the door for that mind-element.
"By way of all" means by way of the thirty-five elements previously mentioned, beginning with the light element (*ābhā-dhātu*).
Since that which lacks an ultimate intrinsic nature can never be included within things that possess an ultimate intrinsic nature, he says: "existing by way of their own intrinsic nature.

Because the various appearances of color, such as the radiance of the moon and the sun, are indeed the light element, he says: "the light element is simply the visible-form element (*rūpa-dhātu*). [They are] bound up with form and so forth.

The phrase "or forms and so forth" was spoken as a connected statement with the intention that the "sign of the beautiful" (subhanimitta) refers to the aspect to be grasped by way of being an object of lust;

thus, he did not simply say "forms and so forth. Even though it lacks the status of being an object of lust, the second alternative was stated: "the beautiful element has wholesome resultant as its object.
The element of cruelty (vihiṃsādhātu) is volition, or the desire to harm others. Non-cruelty is compassion (karuṇā).
"Both" refers to the dhamma-element and the mind-consciousness-element. Regarding the inferior and so forth:

according to the previous method, the eye and other faculties that are despised are "inferior," those that are esteemed are "excellent," and those that are neither too despised nor too esteemed are "middling.

It should be understood that the middling element is stated here by extracting it from the "pair of the inferior" as it appears in the *Khandhavibhaṅga*. As for the consciousness-element, although it exists by way of the sixfold consciousness-element...

Although they are thus analyzed, it is said that "by the inclusion of the consciousness element (viññāṇadhātu), the mind element (manodhātu) is already included because it precedes and follows it"; therefore, he says: "The consciousness element... [is] merely the sevenfold summary of consciousness.

Because of the manifold nature of the many eye-elements and so forth, and because each of these has various modes, there is the world of many elements and diverse elements by way of those various elements.
It was said [by the commentator] that it is "merely the classification of the eighteen elements," stating:
"By way of the division into the eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, mind, and mind-consciousness elements. This is what is written in the Aṭṭhakathā.

In this context, the intended meaning is not a connection of the eye and so forth with the word *dhātu* alone, because it is a statement regarding the classification of that which has the intrinsic nature of cognizing.
When a connection is made with the term *viññāṇadhātu*, two mentions of "mind" (*mano*) need not be made, for there are not two mind-consciousness elements (*manoviññāṇadhātu*).

Alternatively, one could say: "eye... pe... body, mind-consciousness, and mind-element," since a copulative compound (*dvanda*) cannot occur when the members of the conjunction are not of equal status.
However, the reading here might be: "by way of the distinction between eye... pe... body-consciousness, mind, and mind-consciousness element."
The teaching on the aggregates (*khandha*) and bases (*āyatana*) is a concise teaching, while the teaching on the faculties (*indriya*) is an extensive teaching;

with reference to both of these, the teaching on the elements (*dhātu*) is neither too concise nor too extensive. Alternatively, the teaching on the elements as set forth in the *Suttantabhājanīya* is an overly concise teaching, whereas the teaching that should be given by way of the "light element" (*ābhā-dhātu*) and so forth, up to the "many elements" and "diverse elements," is an overly extensive teaching; [the present teaching] avoids both of these.
Having taken this into account, [the author] says: "Neither too brief nor too detailed.
This is because the eye-element is the basis for consciousness, just as the surface of a drum is for sound.

And by these similes, it is shown that just as when lifeless things such as the drum-surface and the stick come together, there arises sound and so forth which are themselves lifeless, so too when lifeless things such as the eye and visible form come together—

The occurrence of eye-consciousness and the rest in the conjunction of lifeless [factors] demonstrates the absence of an agent or an experiencer, because causes and effects are merely elements (*dhātu*).
"Like preceding and following" means that for some lifeless thing, there are certain lifeless things acting as its precedents and sequents.
Or rather, the mind-element itself, not overstepping its own moment, [is the cause] of the eye-consciousness and the rest, which likewise do not overstep their own moments.

The meaning is that although there is no actual state of being a "preceding" or "following" factor, they should be regarded as if they were preceding and following factors by virtue of their temporal sequence—earlier and later time.

It should be regarded as a dart and as a stake because of its association with the three kinds of suffering. "Hope-suffering" (*āsā-dukkha*) means suffering that is itself hope, or rather, suffering consisting in the frustration of hope.
For perception (*saññā*), even though it is unreal, perceives even the suffering of suffering as beautiful and so forth. That...
"And it produces frustration for her through the non-attainment of the desired beauty and so forth.
He said, "Volitional formations have karma as their predominance, because they are cast into rebirth-linking," and so on.

"Because of being followed by the suffering of birth" means because of being pursued by the suffering of birth that is produced by oneself; for birth has existence as its condition, and that birth is itself suffering. Like a lotus, it appears...
Just like a wheel of firebrands, material form (rūpa), when appearing in the guise of a woman or other such objects, gives rise to manifold calamities.

All harmful things—namely, passion and the like, as well as birth and the like—are hostile, non-existent, and terrifying; therefore, because they are the opposites of those [beneficial qualities], they should be viewed as the "deathless" (amata) and so forth.

"Even having let go of one [branch] and taking hold of another": by this, he shows the monkey's similarity [to the mind], for just as the monkey is unable to remain in the air even after letting go of the branch it has grasped, so too [the mind] is unable to proceed even after letting go of the object it has grasped without taking hold of another.
A "wicked horse" is a wild colt that, even when pierced by eight arrows, does not submit to training.
A dancer who has gone onto the stage is a "stage-dancer.

(184) By such statements as "dependent on the eye and forms," the use of both the singular and plural numbers regarding the doors and objects is due to their being conditions for consciousness occurring in either a single or multiple continua, and because they are of a single or diverse nature respectively.

Regarding the phrase "in all phenomena" (*sabbadhammesu*), here the word "all" (*sabba*) refers, by virtue of the context, to what has been previously mentioned: [phenomena] consisting of consciousness and those consisting of objects.
Or it should be understood as "it stands in every part. In the description of the mind-consciousness element (*manoviññāṇadhātu*), it says:
"Immediately after eye-consciousness element has arisen and ceased, the mind element (*manodhātu*) arises; immediately after the mind element has arisen and ceased, consciousness (*citta*) arises.
Just as the mind element arises immediately after the eye-consciousness element, so too [consciousness arises] immediately after the mind element.
The meaning can also be understood thus: "consciousness arises" refers to all consciousness that has occurred until another mind-element (manodhātu) is about to arise, taking it as a single unity.

For if this were the case, there would be no possibility of the mind-element that arises immediately after the mind-consciousness-element (manoviññāṇadhātu) being considered a mind-consciousness-element itself. This is because [the text] demonstrates the transition from the five sense-consciousness-elements to the mind-element.

This is for the purpose of showing that the mind, which is delimited by its own dissimilar intrinsic nature and its place of arising, possesses the state of the mind-consciousness element (*manoviññāṇadhātu*), and not merely because of its immediate succession.
Thus, it is appropriate to show this by attributing unity to that which has a dissimilar intrinsic nature.
Even if unity is not explicitly attributed, when one instance of a dissimilar intrinsic nature is shown, everything else of that same nature is understood by way of its commonality (*sāmañña*).

It should be understood that [the meaning] has been shown. If it is argued that, since the word "also" (pi) includes the mind-consciousness element (manoviññāṇadhātu), the mention of the mind-consciousness element in the passage, “Immediately after the mind-consciousness element, a consciousness arises...

such a mind-consciousness element arises,” excludes the mind-element consciousness (manodhātucitta) that arises immediately after the life-continuum (bhavaṅga), [we reply: No, because its status as a mind-consciousness element is not established.
For that which is raised as an objection cannot itself serve as its own resolution.
By the mention of the two types of mind—the mind-element (*manodhātu*) and the mind-consciousness-element (*manoviññāṇadhātu*)—it is shown that these two possess mutually exclusive natures;
thus, it should be understood that by this very statement, the possibility of the mind-element being the same as the mind-consciousness-element is precluded.

For its nature as the mind-element (manodhātu), which is distinct from the mind-consciousness-element (manoviññāṇadhātu), has been stated by such passages as: "Or rather, the first act of attention toward all phenomena arises," and so forth.
The phrase "all that" is merely an indication of the beginning;

for the mind-consciousness-element does not end with the impulsion (javana) stage, as there are also subsequent moments such as the registration (tadārammaṇa) and others. Thus, [it is explained] by way of the specific natures of the five sense-consciousness-elements and the mind-element.

Having shown all the mind-consciousness elements (*manoviññāṇadhātu*), he then spoke the passage beginning with "dependent on the mind" (*manaṃ ca paṭicca*) in order to show specifically the impulsive mind-consciousness element (*javanamanoviññāṇadhātu*) by way of the mind-door (*manodvāra*).
However, if it were understood here that only those consciousnesses ending with the impulsion (*javana*)— by way of the six doors—
are shown as the "mind-consciousness element," then [there would be an omission] regarding the death-moment, rebirth-linking, and the life-continuum (*bhavaṅga*).
Because they are not included [in the sixfold classification], the teaching would result in being incomplete; therefore, the meaning should be understood according to the method already stated.
Alternatively, it should be understood that other states with characteristics identical to those of the six-door consciousnesses are also indicated by the term "mind-consciousness element.
Regarding the word "dependent" (*paṭicca*) where it occurs, in such passages as "and the mind experiences their range and domain," it is mentioned separately.

What is appropriate [to do] here, however, is as follows: just as in passages such as "dependent on the eye" (*cakkhuñca paṭicca*), the word *ca* (and) groups [the mind] together so that advertence (*āvajjanā*) is made dependent on the eye and so forth,

so too in the passage where it says "dependent on the mind" (*manañca paṭicca*), the intention is that advertence must be understood as being dependent specifically on the life-continuum (*bhavaṅga*) reckoned as the mind-door (*manodvāra*).
The commentary on the Exposition of the Abhidhamma is finished.
3. Commentary on the Section of Questions:
Since the Section of Questions follows the method already stated above, it is self-evident.
The commentary on the Section of Questions is finished.
The commentary on the Analysis of Elements is finished. 4.
Analysis of the Truths (Saccavibhaṅga).
1. Suttantabhājanīya: Explanation of the Summary. 189.
"The sequence of the Dispensation" refers to the Noble Truths or the teaching on the Noble Truths. For the entire Dispensation of the Blessed One...
Since there is no word that is devoid of truth, it proceeds among the truths; or rather, the teaching—consisting of virtue, concentration, and wisdom—proceeds within them.

Therefore, because it proceeds therein, it is called *kama*. What proceeds? The teaching. The "procedure of the teaching" (*sāsanakkama*) refers to the truths as the bases for the operation of the teaching;
and by the designation of the whole, its parts are also so called.

"Thus" (*tathā*) means having that very nature. "Not otherwise" (*avitathā*) means not having a different nature from that. "Not in another way" (*anaññathā*) means devoid of any other mode. The distinction between these [terms] is as follows:

"unwantedness" through the states of suffering-as-suffering and the cause of suffering is the sense of oppression (*pīḷanaṭṭha*); burning in both ways, or association with the burning of the defilements, is the sense of torment (*santāpaṭṭha*).
Alternatively, oppression is the harming of the person; torment is the state of being sharp within oneself, which is the sense of torment.
And herein, the meaning of "oppression" (*pīḷana*) is the mode of manifestation of suffering by its own essential nature;
the others are, respectively, the modes of manifestation through the seeing of the origin, the path, and cessation—this is the distinction between all four.
