Regarding the term “striking the path” (*padaghāta*): here, the path already traversed is called the “path. And that means or cause by which a thought of sensual desire arises is the path traversed by it;
the striking of that [path] is “striking the path. “Having made them strive” (*ussukkāpetvā*) means having urged them upward, further and further.
"Having made it endowed with a distinction of peace" means having increased it.

Regarding the phrase "in the Vibhaṅgas" in the Pāḷi: in which Pāḷi? First, in the *Dhammasaṅgaṇī*, eight kasinas, ten foulness subjects, four divine abidings (*brahmavihāra*), and four formless attainments (*āruppa*) are analyzed. In the *Āgamas*, the ten recollections (*anussati*), the perception of repulsiveness in food, and so forth [are analyzed].

"The analysis of the four elements" (*catudhātuvavatthāna*) is explained here and there as "these [elements] and so forth. "In these three" refers to the three bases beginning with sensuality (*kāma*).
By the phrase "reckoned as wrong speech," he shows that they are to be abandoned by a single volition (*cetanā*).

Here, the noble disciple (*ariyasāvaka*) is either a wholesome worldling (*sakalyāṇaputhujjana*) or one in training (*sekkha*). "Transgressions of the door of body" refers to killing living beings and so forth, distinct from those caused by livelihood (*ājīva*).
The abstention [from each factor] should be applied separately.

However, "this" refers to the fact that, having taken all four types [of path factors] as one through their nature as the Path, this distinction of the Path—consisting in its being entirely similar, entirely dissimilar, or partially similar [to the fruit] by way of jhāna—occurs according to the rule of the foundational jhāna (*pādakajjhāna*). Here, it is by the rule of the foundational jhāna...
Making this the primary focus, he said: "In the *Aṭṭhasālinī*, however, the fixed order of insight (*vipassanā-niyāma*) is presented because it is not in conflict with any other doctrines;

here, however, the fixed order of the foundational jhāna (*pādaka-jjhāna-niyāma*) is presented because it excludes the doctrines concerning the person who has attained comprehension and the inclination toward jhāna.
It should be understood that the fixed order of insight is not rejected here either, as it is common to both systems. Furthermore, the views of other teachers will be explained later."

"Should be analyzed": explaining first the very same aforementioned fixed sequence of the foundational jhānas (*pādakajjhāna-niyāma*), he said, "First, by the fixed sequence of the foundational jhānas.
The intention is that this is stated in the *Aṭṭhasālinī* regarding the formless attainments (*ārūpa*) as "the fourfold and fivefold [jhānas]...
One might object: "Is it not stated there that 'in the formless realm, the threefold and fourfold jhāna arises,' and not 'the fourfold and fivefold jhāna'? True; however, in those [cases]...
However, since there is doubt regarding this, it should be understood that he spoke thus so as to show their arising;
by that, it is effectively stated that the fourfold and fivefold jhānas arise in meaning. And with reference to the aggregate [of factors], he said, "And that is supramundane, not mundane.
For it is only the fourth jhāna that arises there as mundane, not the fourfold or fivefold sets.
"Here, how? means: since there is no foundational jhāna (pādakajjhāna), how is it to be understood?

The intention is that the three higher paths arise for him right there in that same jhāna, having made that same jhāna the foundation for the cultivation of the subsequent paths, such as the first fruit and so on; however, after cultivating a path consisting of three or four jhānas, the immaterial jhāna arises for one who has attained it therein.
Since the development of the higher paths— whether based on a jhāna that is itself a fruit or on another jhāna— can arise by taking that jhānic fruit as its basis,

it should be understood that the attainment of prior volitional formations (*pubbābhisaṅkhāra-samāpatti*), which determines the jhāna factors and so forth, serves as the basis for the fruit as well, and is not something to be comprehended (*sammasitabba*).

This is because the knowledge of suffering and the rest have the six objects such as visible forms as their domain, whereas the intention of renunciation and the rest have as their objects various wholesome states such as the kasiṇas.
He says "accordingly" because the factors such as right speech have as their respective objects those things from which one must abstain.

"In accordance with that" means that virtue which produces non-remorse is a specific condition for effort; thus, the conformity of effort to virtue is stated, and this applies even to the associated [mental states].
Furthermore, since the text speaks specifically of the associated [states], it does not say "of one established on the plane of virtue," but rather "of one who is being established."
It has been said. "Non-confusion of the mind" refers to the state of the mind being guarded by the protection of mindfulness, which was mentioned in the phrase "having a single guard.
Therefore he said: "Thus... [omitted] ...for one who has well-established protection of the mind.

The state of being true knowledge (*vijjā*) regarding the knowledge of the destruction of the taints (*āsava-kkhaya-ñāṇa*) has been stated; thus, in the path known as the destruction of the taints, which is comprised of the three aggregates.

The aggregate of wisdom (*paññākkhandha*) is true knowledge (*vijjā*); since the state of being the "footing" (*caraṇabhāva*) has been stated for virtue (*sīla*) and the four meditative absorptions (*jhāna*), the other two aggregates are the footing.
That by which one goes to *nibbāna* is a vehicle (*yāna*); thus, insight itself is the vehicle, hence "the vehicle of insight" (*vipassanāyāna*).
Because virtue is a specific condition for concentration, and concentration is [a condition] for insight, the aggregate of virtue is [included] due to its assistance to serenity (*samatha*).

And it is included by the vehicle of serenity (*samatha*). One who discerns the danger in sense-desires by means of the vehicle of insight (*vipassanā*), while not abandoning the unworldly bliss of meditative absorption (*jhāna*) through the vehicle of serenity, avoids the wrong path of the two extremes.

Just as wisdom is the direct opposite of delusion, so too are virtue and concentration the direct opposites of hatred and greed, because they are to be accomplished by non-hatred and non-greed. This is due to the application of virtue, concentration, and wisdom.
It is beautiful in the beginning, middle, and end. For virtue and the other [factors] constitute the beginning, middle, and end of the Dispensation.

That which, when established upon it, makes one noble—whether at the stage of the path or the stage of the fruit—is the Noble Plane, consisting of the Dispensation comprised of the three aggregates known as the path and its fruit.
The commentary on the exposition of the Truth of the Path is finished.
The commentary on the Suttantabhājanīya is finished.
2. Commentary on the Abhidhammabhājanīya (206–214).
When the term "noble truth" is applied to the origin [of suffering], it refers to that which is entirely to be abandoned and is devoid of the state of being something to be fully understood.

It occurs with respect to the origin consisting of craving, but not with respect to the remaining defilements, remaining unwholesome states, and the remaining wholesome states with taints that are not to be abandoned or fully understood; thus, in that context, the origin is partial.
However, regarding the word "truth" (*sacca*), it is complete. Therefore, he said, "in order to show the origin completely. [The cessation of suffering...]
However, in this teaching on the Noble Truths, they are indeed exhaustive in terms of the Dhamma;

for there is no other phenomenon besides those that could be called "suffering" or "cessation" within the teaching on the truths. Nor is there any new path not already included in the sections on the eightfold and fivefold paths.
Therefore, he says [the Buddha] spoke of the origin alone "exhaustively" (nippadesato) in all instances.
Because something not previously stated was shown on all three occasions.

For even in the teaching of the Truths for the purpose of showing the arising of what was not previously known, the statement, "In this context, what is the origin of suffering? Craving," is intended to show that the word "Truth" (sacca) applies to craving alone.
However, by way of the teaching, having set aside each respective origin, suffering is [defined], and its cessation is defined by way of the abandoning of each respective [origin].

It is appropriate to say that the teaching on the Truths was given in order to show those [truths] without limitation, for in the teaching on the Noble Truths, the Path— whether by way of the eightfold,
the fivefold, or all supramundane wholesome states— is not mentioned, and thus suffering and the other truths are shown there only with their specific applications (sappadesa).
"Designated as a condition" means that it is the root of the suffering of birth and so forth, by way of karma and defilements.
The truth of cessation... [etc. ...is demonstrated in five ways; this shows the distinction between the teaching on the truths in general and the teaching on the noble truths specifically.

In that context, the phrase "the abandoning of the three roots of the wholesome and the remaining wholesome states associated with the taints" refers to the abandoning of their conditions—namely ignorance, craving, and clinging—or else it refers to the case when ignorance and the other factors have been abandoned.
It should be understood that this is stated by way of their non-arising; for wholesome states are not to be abandoned.

Furthermore, "abandoning" (pahāna) indicates the cessation (nirodha) to be attained through the function of the Path; or rather, it should be seen that "abandoning" refers to the state of the non-arising of craving and the other [defilements] within that very cessation.

Even though this was said for the purpose of showing the decisive support (*upanissaya*) for the fulfillment of the eightfold path at the moment of the supramundane path— thinking, “But if his bodily action, verbal action, and livelihood have already been completely purified, then this noble eightfold path of his reaches fulfillment through development”—
nevertheless, the phrase “but if... already” [indicates] that the purity of bodily action and so forth [is required].

Regarding the state of being a remote decisive support: for one who dwells without lust, without attachment, and without delusion toward the eye and so forth, contemplating danger, by means of that very insight leading to emergence, there comes about in the future the diminution of the five aggregates of clinging;
through the turning away from all formations, and through the distancing of the defilements as the craving for renewed existence is abandoned.
When the bodily and mental distress, burning, and fever have been abandoned, and bodily and mental happiness are being experienced by way of tranquility of body and mind,

there occurs— at the moment of insight leading to emergence— the state of being an immediate decisive support for the five factors beginning with right view, which are said to occur at that stage in such passages as: "The view of one who has become thus is his right view."

"He shows" means he indicates that the teaching of the five-factored path occurs by way of the inclination of those persons who easily awaken to the five-factored path through the influence of a more proximate decisive support (*upanissaya*).
Therefore, he says: "Because of the statement, 'Previously indeed...
[it] becomes perfectly purified,' etc. Thus, the word "from this statement" is an ablative expression denoting the means of teaching.

This is an indicative illustration; or, by the word "from his own speech," the meaning is that even the five-factored path was taught by the Blessed One as being "the way" (paṭipadā) in accordance with his own words.
Where? In the City of the Gods (Devapura). Therefore, in order to show that method of teaching, the section on the five factors has also been set forth by the compilers of the Dhamma.
Alternatively, it is by the very words, "But previously indeed for him... [that this is established].

By way of indicating the cause for the distinction in underlying intention (*ajjhāsaya*), it is taught that even the five-factored path (*pañcaṅgika-magga*) is indeed the way of practice (*paṭipadā*) according to the individual's inclination;
thus he said: "But previously... [etc. ...from the statement... [etc. ...it is taught.
Therefore, the meaning is that the Blessed One also set forth the group of five factors in order to demonstrate the method taught in the Sutta in the City of the Devas (*devapura*).
The entry into the teaching or the entry into development occurs through the jhānas; this is the application of the jhānas.
It should be understood that the presentation of four thousand methods for each section is for the sake of ease in counting.
However, according to how the text is established, one should follow the sequence of the text by joining five sections to each mode of practice and to emptiness and the other [two doors].

"Katam" (which) is understood [to mean "what"]. Therein, in the section on the eight factors, the construction should be made thus: "At that time, in the second jhāna and so forth, there is a seven-factored path.
And in the section providing a comprehensive summary, it is according to the factors actually present.
The commentary on the *Abhidhammabhājanīya* is finished.
3. Commentary on the Section of Questions (Pañhapucchakavaṇṇanā) 215.

Why is it said, "Thus also in the two preceding [sections]"? Is it not the case that in the Suttantabhājanīya, in the exposition of the practice leading to the cessation of suffering, the path was described as a mixture of mundane and supramundane?
For in its commentary, it is stated: "By way of learning and so forth regarding the four truths..."
This statement beginning with "knowledge regarding suffering" was spoken with reference to the arising of preliminary knowledge;

however, at the moment of penetration (paṭivedha), there is only a single knowledge. Thus, the mixed nature of right view—and likewise of right intention and the other factors—both mundane and supramundane, is shown:
"Furthermore, this so-called right view, in its preliminary stage, has various moments and various objects, but at the moment of the Path..."

And [it is said] in such passages as, "They are of one moment, of one object," and so forth? This is true; however, by way of the method of approach, even there the Noble Eightfold Path is shown through the gateway of the demonstration of the four foundations of mindfulness (the four truths).

And having done so, it is stated that "at the moment of penetration, however, there is only a single knowledge," whereby the single knowledge of the path possesses the nature of the knowledge of suffering and so on, and "at the moment of the path... there is only a single wholesome intention."

By such statements as, “When [right view] arises, this is called right intention,” the status of right intention and the other factors as being right intention and so forth within the path is determined.
Furthermore, after enumerating the eightfold path in the Pāḷi, in order to explain that very same path, it is said, “Knowledge regarding suffering,” and so on.
By this, even in the Suttantabhājanīya, the mundane nature of two factors and the supramundane nature of the other two is stated: “Thus...”
"Also in the first two" means "by this.
The commentary on the Section of Questions is finished.
The commentary on the Analysis of Truths is finished.
5. Analysis of the Faculties (Indriya-vibhaṅga) 1.
Commentary on the Exposition According to the Abhidhamma (Abhidhamma-bhājanīya-vaṇṇanā) 219.
It exercises lordship over the eye-door; thus, in its capacity as the eye-door, it exercises its own lordship over those [mental states] associated with that door.
The meaning is that it causes the state of supreme sovereignty. For in the apprehension of those forms, it (the consciousness) conforms itself to them, and they conform to it.

This same method applies to the others as well. That by which the person possessing it, or the phenomena associated with it, become "knowers" (aññātāvino)—that state of being a knower is the knowledge of having completed what was to be done.
In some instances, there are two, as in: “Bhikkhus, it is through the development and cultivation of two faculties that a bhikkhu whose taints are destroyed declares final knowledge...

[as] noble wisdom and noble liberation. For whatever is his noble wisdom, bhikkhus, that is his faculty of wisdom; for whatever is his noble liberation, that is his faculty of concentration,” and so forth.
Two: “Bhikkhus, it is through the development and cultivation of three faculties that the bhikkhu Piṇḍola Bhāradvāja has declared final knowledge...
[as follows]: the faculty of mindfulness, the faculty of concentration, and the faculty of wisdom. And: “Bhikkhus, there are these three faculties. Which three?
The faculty ‘I shall come to know the unknown,’ the faculty of final knowledge, and the faculty of one who has known.”
In such passages as, “These three... namely, the female faculty, the male faculty, and the life faculty,” there are three;
and in such passages as, “Brahmin, these five faculties have different domains... namely, the eye faculty... up to the body faculty”; “Five...
namely, the pleasure faculty... up to the equanimity faculty”; and “Five... namely, the faith faculty... up to the wisdom faculty.”

And there are five [categories] in such passages as these. Therein, in the Suttanta, the mention of "pairs" and so forth is because pairs and so on constitute the means of escape and other such factors.

However, all the faculties (*indriya*) are to be directly known (*abhiññeyya*), and since the teaching of the dhammas that are to be directly known is the Abhidhamma, they are all stated together here.

Because it arises having become an actual state for one whose taints are destroyed (khīṇāsava), it is said: "because it arises only for one whose taints are destroyed. It is called a *liṅga* because it leads to or makes known;
or else, it is a *liṅga* because by means of it something is marked (*liṅgīyati*).

What does it lead to, or what is marked by it? It is the power (*inda*) or the powerful one (*indo*); the mark of the powerful one is the "mark of Indra" (*indaliṅga*). The meaning of the mark of Indra is its essential nature (*taṃsabhāva*).
The meaning of "indaliṅga" is either the mark of Indra (*indaliṅga*) or the meaning of the word *indriya* as the mark of Indra; thus it is "the meaning of the mark of Indra.
"Produced" (*sajjita*) means brought forth (*uppādita*), and what is produced by Indra is "Indra-produced" (*indasiṭṭha*). "Juṭṭha" means practiced or cultivated.

Since these are the marks of Indra in the sense of karma, and are produced by him, they should be applied only to those [faculties] born of karma, and not to others. And those two meanings apply only to karma.

They are to be applied, and the others [the faculties] likewise to the Blessed One; thus he said, "according to what is appropriate. "By that" means by virtue of the Blessed One’s mastery over action.

"In this" means among these faculties. They "indicate" or manifest [the state of the person] through the success or failure of the fruit, because of the comprehension of the success or failure of the cause.
In such passages as "He cultivates that sign," even the making of the object is included.
Since it was stated [in the text] that they are "cultivated" (*āsevanā*), he said: “Some by way of cultivation of the objective field.

Although all [dhammas] are to be made into an objective field, the expression “some” is used because those not to be seen through insight are not to be cultivated due to the lack of frequent attention (*bahulī-manasikaraṇa*). For in their case, there is merely reflective observation (*paccavekkhaṇā*).
In such passages as “For him who cultivates that path,” etc., “cultivation” (*bhāvanā*) is what is meant by “cultivation” (*āsevanā*); thus, those [dhammas] which are to be developed are [meant].
Referring to faith and the other [faculties], he says: “some are for the sake of cultivation and frequenting. Sovereignty (*ādhipacca*) is the state of being a faculty-condition (*indriya-paccaya*).

And in the absence of the state of being a faculty-condition, there is the state of being followed by the gender-mark (*liṅga*) and so forth—which, while occurring in their own capacity as conditions within the continuum associated with them, do not arise in any other form. In this sense:

They are called *indriyas* because they exercise supreme sovereignty (*indati paramissariyaṃ karonti*). Following the method demonstrated regarding the eye and the other [faculties], the predominance (*ādhipacca*) of others over their respective concomitants should be applied as appropriate. "Below" refers to the *Aṭṭhasālinī*.
It is non-delusion itself, not four separate factors; therefore, in the phrase for the faculty of wisdom (*paññindriya*), it is non-delusion.

The intention is that their characteristics (*lakkhaṇa*) and so forth are to be understood as having been analyzed. The remaining [factors] are presented in their own form along with their characteristics and so on in the *Aṭṭhasālinī*.
Now, one might ask: "Are not the characteristics and so forth of the faculty of pleasure (*sukhindriya*) and the faculty of pain (*dukkhindriya*) stated there?

Although they are not explicitly stated, they are to be understood by way of the characteristics and so forth that have been stated for the faculties of mental joy (*somanassindriya*) and mental grief (*domanassindriya*).
These too have already been explained. How so? The faculty of pleasure has the characteristic of experiencing a desirable tangible object;

its function is the enjoyment of the desirable aspect; it is manifested as bodily gratification; and its proximate cause is the body-faculty. The faculty of pain has the characteristic of experiencing an undesirable tangible object;
its function is the enjoyment of the undesirable aspect; it is manifested as bodily affliction; and its proximate cause is the body-faculty.
And here, it should be understood that the "taste of enjoyment" belongs only to objects appearing as desirable or undesirable, and not to their opposites— that is,
to objects appearing in an undesirable manner or a non-desirable manner. Furthermore,
the attainment of the plane of the Noble Ones by sentient beings is both the common and the primary purpose of the Blessed One’s teaching.

He said: "Having fully understood internal phenomena," and so forth. In the *Aṭṭhakathā*, the sequence for teaching the life-faculty (*jīvitindriya*) is stated immediately after the female and male faculties;
that sequence accords with the teaching on the *Indriyayamaka*. However, here in the *Indriyavibhaṅga*, the life-faculty is mentioned immediately after the mind-faculty (*manindriya*).
This is because it protects both those preceding and following [faculties], namely the internal and external ones.

It should be understood that this is stated in the middle [of the text]. "Whatever is felt, all that is suffering" is said for the purpose of making known that as long as the life-faculty (jīvitindriya) continues to sustain the two-fold state of existence, there is no cessation of these feelings which are of the nature of suffering.

And by this, he makes known that the eye and so forth are to be fully understood (pariññeyya) because they are followed by suffering. Immediately after that, [the statement] is for the purpose of showing that they are to be developed (bhāvetabba).
This was said with reference to the faculty of final knowledge (aññindriya) associated with the path of cultivation (bhāvanāmaggasampayutta).

For cultivation follows immediately after seeing (dassana). Although it possesses the status of being a condition such as pre-arising (purejāta), he says "function" (kicca) specifically because it is a function that must be accomplished by way of the faculty-condition (indriyapaccaya), since it is not shared by others and because the discussion concerns the faculties (indriya).
[This refers] to the mental faculty (manindriya) by virtue of its being the forerunner.

It exercises mastery; it does not do so for others. For even the faculties associated with it perform their respective faculty-functions only as things to be accomplished, because they are mental factors (*cetasika*).

It should be understood that the governing topic—"to be accomplished by way of being a faculty-condition in all cases"—continues to apply here. [This applies] in the non-arising and the non-supporting.

“Conformity” (anuvidhāna) is the state of being a cause for the occurrence of those conditions. When pleasure and pain sensations arise by covering and pervading [the body], they become manifest in themselves by overcoming their co-nascent factors;
and the co-nascent factors, by virtue of that [sensation], appear as if they have attained the state of pleasure or pain.
Thus it is said: “attaining their respective coarse modes. Of that which does not exist...
One should apply the application of the mode of neutrality even to that which is unremoved, being associated with the unwholesome and its resultants;
or alternatively, the application of the modes of tranquility and refinement to pleasure and pain within their own respective classes.

The application of the modes of clarity, exertion, establishment, and concentration belongs respectively to faith and the other [faculties]. By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), the higher fetters (*uddhabbhāgiya-saṃyojana*) are included, as they are associated only with the Path.

And thus the function of the faculty has been shown; by that very fact, it is shown that for the [faculty] associated with the fruit, its function consists precisely in the subsiding and abandoning of the respective fetters.
Since all its functions have been performed, the *aññātāvindriya* (the faculty of one who has already known) lacks anything further to be done;

therefore, it is directed toward the Deathless (*amata*) and is a condition for being such, unlike the others which are occupied with other functions. Hence he said: "and the state of being a condition for being directed toward the Deathless."
220. "Even though this is so" means that although [these categories] encompass everything, they are called "all-encompassing" precisely because they include:
(1) wholesome and unwholesome energy and so forth, which are to be included under the category of the faculty of energy;

and (2) the eye and so forth, which are divided according to time, person, conditions, and so on, and are to be included under the category of the eye-faculty and so forth. They do not, however, include those things that do not exist on a particular plane.
The meaning is "their being inclusive. And by that, since there is no qualification [of the factors], there would be the undesirable consequence of taking all [factors] as belonging to all planes;
thus he shows that by excluding that [consequence], the statement regarding the inclusion of all [factors] does not indicate the inclusiveness of something non-existent.
The commentary on the *Abhidhammabhājanīya* is finished.
2. Commentary on the Section of Questions (Pañhapucchakavaṇṇanā) 223.

"Herein, it is not included" means it is stated because it has no object whatsoever. Why is it said, "Because it is mixed with matter, it is included among the material phenomena that are without objects"?
Is it not the case that, precisely because it is mixed, the life-faculty (*jīvitindriya*) [should be] among those without objects?
[It is] not included [in the category]. Is it not stated that the eight faculties are without an object? True, this is so;
however, this was stated with reference to the fact that a portion of the life-faculty is included among the material phenomena (rūpadhamma) which are without an object.

The intention is that, by way of the immaterial portion (arūpakoṭṭhāsa), it is included in the "perhaps" position because it possesses limited objects and so forth. But as for the possession of limited objects and so forth by way of the immaterial portion:

It should be understood that because there is an "indefinability" (navattabbatā) with respect to the category of form (*rūpa*), this is included in the "perhaps" position (*siyāpakkha*) by way of the mixed aggregate as a whole, and not by way of a single part.
For it is not the case that what is without an object (*anārammaṇa*) cannot be defined as having a limited object (*parittārammaṇa*) and so forth.
This is also evident from such statements as: "Form and Nibbāna are without objects; the seven faculties are without objects."

Among those things that cannot be defined as either having an object or being without an object, he shows their indefinability because they lack an object, not because that which has an object is itself indefinable, nor because that which is indefinable possesses an object.

For the term "indefinable" (navattabba) is not conventionally established in the sense of "having an object. Even if it were so, [it would contradict the statement]: "The three feelings, form, and Nibbāna—these phenomena are indefinable."

If it were not stated [in the suttas] that "it is associated with pleasant feeling," and so forth, then even though the term "indeterminate" (*navattabba*) refers only to those states that possess an object (*sārammaṇa*) because of its connection with limited objects and so on, one would have to say, instead of "two bases may have limited objects," etc., "the mind base may have a limited object... [and so on]...
an immeasurable object," and likewise, "the mental-object base may have a limited object... [and so on]..."
It may be said that it has an immeasurable object, and it may also be said that it is without an object;

for in the section on questions, there is no teaching that leaves anything remaining. Furthermore, regarding the statement "eight faculties may have an internal object," it should be understood that in the case of the life-faculty during the sphere of nothingness, because both the immaterial and the material are without an object, it is not to be defined [in those terms].
The commentary on the "Examination by Way of Questions" is finished.
The commentary on the "Analysis of the Faculties" is finished.
6. Analysis of Dependent Origination (Paṭiccasamuppādavibhaṅga).
1. Suttantabhājanīya: Explanation of the Section on Enumeration (Uddesavāra-vaṇṇanā) 225.
“‘What, venerable sir, is the doctrine of the Fully Enlightened One? ‘He is a proponent of analysis, Great King,’ [said] the Elder Moggaliputtatissa.”
Because it has been so stated, the disciples of the Perfectly Enlightened One are proponents of analysis (*vibhajjavādino*).

For they speak by analyzing the nature of those who follow the path of annihilationism (*venayika*) and so forth; or they speak by analyzing whether robes and other requisites are to be used or not used;

or they speak by analyzing the doctrines of eternalism and annihilationism, such as "the self and the world are eternal," because they set aside those questions that are to be set aside (*ṭhapanīya*), [thereby avoiding] the eternalism of the destruction of lust and so forth, and the annihilationism of bodily misconduct and so forth.
And because of their statement, they do not exclude the three questions—such as those to be answered categorically—and speak only of that which is to be answered analytically.
The "circle of the Vibhajjavādins" (*vibhajjavādimaṇḍala*) refers to the assembly or group of the Vibhajjavādins;
alternatively, it is also said to be the retinue of the Blessed One, the Vibhajjavādin. [This is] by way of illustrating the unerring meaning as stated by the teachers.

By one who does not misrepresent [the teaching]. By speaking such things as, "Ignorance is the cause and condition for meritorious and imperturbable volitional formations," and by speaking against the bases of debate such as the doctrine of a person (puggalavāda) when they have been rejected, one is said to deviate from one's own system;
thus, by one who does not so deviate. By one who does not exert effort through the activity of attributing faults to other systems. "This too..."
Some say that one should accept what is appropriate without conflating the doctrines of other schools.

One who speaks such things as, "As I understand the Dhamma taught by the Blessed One, it is this very same consciousness that wanders and transmigrates, and not another," is said to reject the Sutta; thus, one should not reject it. "As I..."

One who says, "I understand the Dhamma taught by the Blessed One such that these things called 'obstructive states' by the Blessed One are not sufficient to obstruct one who indulges in them," and "a transgression committed even in a dream constitutes an offense," and so forth, is said to be contradicting the Vinaya;
conversely, one who acts in accordance with it is following the Vinaya. Thus he contradicts it.
For one who breaks the continuity of the action contradicts the nature of things (*dhammatā*). When the *Suttanta* has been stated, one should look to the four great authorities (*mahāpadesa*);

and when the *Aṭṭhakathā* has been stated, one should look to the four great authorities: the *Sutta*, that which is in conformity with the *Sutta*, the tradition of the teachers (*ācariyavāda*), and what is personally approved by oneself (*attanomati*).
For by looking to these, one stands firm in the *Sutta* and the *Vinaya* and does not overstep them. "Dhamma" refers here to the text on dependent origination (*paṭiccasamuppāda*).

“Atthā” means for that purpose. Here, causes and their fruits are not intended. Having restated the meaning already stated—that “ignorance regarding suffering and so forth is ignorance”—the text further demonstrates it through other synonyms such as “ignorance regarding the past,” and so on. [It is shown] by such statements as:
“By this synonym, volitional formations are called ‘existence’; by this synonym, craving is called ‘clinging,’” and so forth.
"They explain" means they describe.

"A being" (satta) refers to the emptiness of a being (sattasuññatā), or rather, it is the conventional designation "being" applied to formations that are empty of a being. "And the very mode of conditionality" (paccayākārameva ca): the *ma*-kāra is used here merely for the euphonic junction of words (*padasaṃdhikara*).
"Therefore" (tasmā) is because the commentary on the meaning must be composed according to the method already stated, and because it is difficult to do so.
“I do not find a foothold”: the meaning is that by the power of his own knowledge, he does not find that method wherein, once established, it would be easy to provide a description.

However, pointing out the support, he said, “But this teaching,” and so forth. Here, “teaching” (*sāsana*) refers to the Dhamma of the Canon, or specifically to dependent origination (*paṭiccasamuppāda*).
For that [dependent origination] is adorned with various methods of instruction, such as the forward and reverse orders.
Because it has not been interrupted and continues even today, it serves as a support; and because it is the path of the ancient teachers, it is known as the *Aṭṭhakathā*.
To show the purpose for generating reverence with the words, “Listen to that, being composed,” he said, “For it has been said,” and so forth.
“Having made it a bone” means having made it one’s concern; or, making it as if it were fixed upon a bone so that it does not perish, he says “having made it a bone.”

"Having made [it so]. "Successive" (*pubbāpariya*) means existence from an earlier time to a later time. The meaning is that, starting from the very first undertaking, one attains a distinction in knowledge and a distinction in the destruction of the defilements at every moment.

Because it is the root cause of the rounds of karma, its result, and the defilements, and because it was mentioned first, ignorance (*avijjā*) is [the beginning] of dependent origination (*paṭiccasamuppāda*).

The Root. In this context, one should not apply the analogy that just as when the root of a creeper is seen, the removal of the creeper begins from that point, so too when the root of dependent origination (paṭiccasamuppāda) is seen, the teaching of dependent origination begins from that point.
For there is nothing for the Blessed One to distinguish as "only this has been seen" and "the other has not been seen," because everything has been seen by him.
Furthermore, from the very beginning, the teaching of dependent origination (*paṭiccasamuppāda*) has been presented starting from the root, just as one might take up a creeper from its root;

this is the intended commonality here. Alternatively, one should also apply the commonality of showing the root and so forth by way of the disposition of those to be enlightened and the nature of what is to be made known. Of that—
“Monks, as that youth grew up and his faculties matured, he was provided with the five cords of sensual pleasure...
which are alluring. Having seen a form with the eye, he became infatuated with forms that were pleasing and felt aversion toward forms that were unpleasing;
he dwelt without established mindfulness of the body, with a limited mind. He [failed to attain] that liberation of mind...”
“He does not understand liberation by wisdom as it really is. Wherever those arisen evil unwholesome states cease without remainder,
he— having thus fallen into attachment and aversion— whatever feeling he feels, whether pleasant, painful,
or neither-painful-nor-pleasant, he delights in that feeling, welcomes it, and remains clinging to it.”

When it has been said thus: "In this way, so too with the door of the ear and the others. "Abhivadato" means: one who speaks out through a powerful craving that has reached the state of vocal expression, saying "Aho, what happiness! Aho, what happiness!"—speaking thus with the notions of "I" and "mine.
Then, because it is impossible to release oneself from that powerful [craving], one remains clinging through attachment (*ajjhosāya*).
Even more powerful than that is the craving which constitutes *upādāna*; it is delight (*nandī*). And here, by means of such delight and so forth...

Craving has been mentioned; by the word "delight" (nandī), it should be understood that clinging—which has craving as its condition—is fourfold, both by way of being inseparable from delight and by way of the states of delighting in craving and views.
Furthermore, the passage beginning with "With birth as condition, aging-and-death" is stated in that very same Mahātaṇhāsaṅkhayavimutti Sutta.
With reference to rebirth-linking, the contact of the process, and so forth, which constitute the round of kamma-result, as well as the nutritive essence produced by kamma, it was said:
"The four nutriments have craving as their source," and so on. Furthermore, even the other nutriments that support the round do not exist when that [craving]—which is the origin of craving—is absent;
therefore, it is appropriate to say that they too "have craving as their source."
“From this or that” refers to the fourfold methods of teaching; it means from each respective teaching. It “leads to the penetration of the method” (*ñāyappaṭivedha*);
thus, “method” (*ñāya*) is the Path, or else it is Dependent Origination itself, according to the statement: “And his noble method has been well seen through wisdom.
Indeed, because it is all-beneficent and must be penetrated in various ways, by each respective...

"It conduces to his own teaching and to his own realization. Since the state of being "Samantabhadraka" (the All-Auspicious One) and the attainment of excellence in teaching are common causes for all four types of teaching, he said "specifically" (*visesato*) with the intention of stating the specific cause.
It should be construed as either "the teaching of this Blessed One" or "the teaching of this dependent origination. This is the analysis of the cause of its occurrence.
Ignorance and so forth are the cause; alternatively, it is the non-causality of primordial matter (*prakṛti*) and so forth—which are grasped as causes—and the causality of ignorance and so forth.
In this regard, some who are deluded grasp what is not a cause as "the cause," while others do not perceive anything as a cause at all.

Therefore, the teaching in direct order (*anuloma*) is given for the purpose of demonstrating the occurrence of volitional formations (*saṅkhāra*) and so forth through their respective appropriate causes.
Although the other [factors] may also exist for that purpose, their occurrence is not *solely* for that purpose because other purposes are present;

however, since this [ignorance] exists solely for that purpose, its being "for that purpose" is stated. Furthermore, it is stated for the sake of demonstrating the sequence of arising in the process of occurrence:
ignorance is the beginning which conceals the danger of occurrence, from which volitional formations arise, and from those, consciousness arises.
For one who is reviewing, there occurred prior to full enlightenment the penetration of various respective fruits;

in order to demonstrate that which was thus attained—the cause of aging and death and so forth, such as birth and so forth—according to and following that [penetration], the teaching in reverse order (paṭiloma) proceeded.
Alternatively, the connection is: "the teaching in reverse order proceeded for one who is reviewing."
For even though the Blessed One has descended [from the realm of the Buddhas], he surveys the world fallen into distress and teaches for the purpose of showing...

[as before] ...the preliminary stage. With the intention that "nutriments, craving, and so forth belong to the present time, while formations and ignorance belong to the past time," he said, "having brought back as far as the past time";
or else, the nutriments are to be produced by craving and thus belong to the future time.

Craving and so forth belong to the present; volitional formations and ignorance belong to the past. However, having shown the fruit directly, it is appropriate to show the succession of causes for that fruit by way of demonstrating its source;

thus, the nutriments produced by prior craving constitute the present period, craving and so forth are the past, and volitional formations and ignorance are even further in the past, for the purpose of showing that saṃsāra is beginningless.
The meaning "spoken" (*vutta*) as "as far as the past period" (*atītaṃ addhānaṃ*) or "as far as the more distant past period" (*atītataraṃ addhānaṃ*) is appropriate.

Or, the four nutriments (*āhāra*) that bring about the production of renewed existence in the future—[regarding them], I do not say "he nutries," nor would I say "he nutries"; in that regard, the proper question is: "Who indeed..."
“Venerable sir, he consumes it. Yet I do not speak in that way.
But if someone were to ask me, “For what purpose, venerable sir, is consciousness a nutriment?”—that is a fitting question, and this is the fitting answer:
“Consciousness as nutriment is for the production of renewed existence in the future.””
This is because of the statement [in the Sutta], because contact and volition are associated with it, and because edible food is the cause for its occurrence.
For by means of that [food], there is the accumulation of kamma-consciousness in one whose material body has been supported and who desires it.
Indeed, it is said that food is the decisive support (*upanissaya*) for faith and so forth, as well as for lust and so forth. Therefore, "those foods comprised within the cycle of kamma..."
In this method, "the present time" is consistent with the very same meaning as before.

From the passage beginning, "Thus, monks, with ignorance as condition there are volitional formations," [the Buddha] has ascended by way of demonstrating the source of the foods and the direct realization of the sequence of cause and fruit in the past and beyond that;
for those who do not understand without such a turning back [from the future], [he has taught it].
The meaning is that this teaching was set forth for the purpose of demonstrating that. "For the purpose of demonstrating the future time" means:

having shown the present cause—which is directly perceptible—to those who find it difficult to penetrate and do not see [the future], it is for the purpose of demonstrating that [future] by way of the succession of cause and fruit.
In view of the word "root cause" (*mūlakāraṇa*), the neuter designation "not without a cause" (*na akāraṇaṃ*) was employed.

He cites the sutta, demonstrating that if it were without a cause, the sutta would be contradicted. The status of being the head of the discourse on the round of existence (*vaṭṭakathā*) implies that the karma which is the cause of the round is also a cause [of suffering].
In that context, ignorance (*avijjā*) is also a cause of the craving for existence (*bhavataṇhā*); by that [ignorance], the danger [of suffering] is concealed.
Because craving arises within existence, ignorance is specifically the head [of the causal process] and is thus called the "root cause.
[The Buddha] said, "And so it is said, monks," and so forth, because if its prior limit were not known, one might grasp at permanence due to the absence of an arising [from that point].
By this, since there has been no prior arising before this, the non-knowing of a prior limit is due to its being unknown.
The word "said" (vuttaṃ) indicates this meaning.

When it comes to stating the results in the sequence of ignorance and craving as causes, the expression "those going to happy and miserable destinies" is used to avoid contradicting the rules of grammar (*saddalakkhaṇa*).
For in a *dvanda* compound, that which is more honored is placed first. It is said that the Savaras repeatedly [rub] the bone against the meat so that it does not stick.
Having heated it, having pounded it, and having made him drink hot water, they kill the cow by cutting out the entrails and the flesh from the anus.

Therefore he said, "Scorched by fire," and so forth. In this context, just as the cow to be slaughtered, being overwhelmed by ignorance, undertakes the drinking of hot water as described, so too does the worldling undertake the aforementioned karma leading to an unhappy destination. But just as...
Seeing the danger in drinking hot water, one undertakes the drinking of cold water under the influence of craving;

likewise, due to the dullness of ignorance (*avijjā*), one sees the danger in kamma leading to an unhappy destination and undertakes kamma leading to a happy destination under the influence of craving.
For in regard to suffering, craving follows ignorance, and in regard to pleasure, ignorance follows craving.

Thus, because it is shrouded by ignorance and bound by craving, this "body" refers either to the conscious body—the pentad of aggregates—or to the sixfold sense base, since it is said that "contact has the six sense bases as its condition," and it is called the cause of contact.
"Arisen" means produced. And "externally, name-and-form" refers externally to the conscious body—the pentad of aggregates.

Or the six sense bases (*saḷāyatana*). "Ittha etan" means "this is thus. The meaning is that for oneself and for others, the five aggregates and the twelve bases are established as having the nature of doors and objects, and are thus called by the name "dyad" (*dvaya*).

Elsewhere, it is said that "contact arises dependent on a dyad," referring to visual contact and so forth arising dependent on the dyads of eye and visible form; however, here [the dyad] refers to the internal and external [bases].
"The sense bases (āyatana). This is indeed what is called the 'Great Pair' (mahādvaya)," so it is said. This is the intended meaning here:

elsewhere, in such passages as "Dependent upon the eye and forms, eye-consciousness arises; the meeting of the three is contact," and so forth, it is stated that eye-contact and the rest arise dependent upon pairs consisting of "the eye and forms... [and so on] ...the mind and mental objects."
Furthermore, here [in the phrase] "this very body," the remaining phenomena that depend upon the eye and so forth are treated as being dependent upon the eye and so forth themselves;
thus, having taken the body of the eye and so forth as a unity under the designation "internal base" (*ajjhattikāyatana*), it is called "external name-and-form" (*bahiddhā nāmarūpa*).
And the objects such as visible form, likewise taken as a unity, are the "external bases. These are the internal and external bases.
“Dependent on [the six bases], contact is spoken of; therefore, this is called the ‘Great Duality. Having established it thus, it is said:
“And this meaning should be illustrated by means of one’s own five aggregates and six bases, as well as those of another.
For the eye and so forth, together with their supports, which are spoken of as “this body,” are one’s own five aggregates; while those spoken of as “external name-and-form” are...
Form and so forth belong to others. Likewise, this body consists of one's own internal bases (*āyatana*), while name-and-form external to oneself belongs to others as external bases.
Otherwise, if "this body" were spoken of merely in terms of the internal bases, it would not follow that one's own five aggregates (*pañcakkhandha*) are exclusively internal bases;
thus, the demonstration of both one's own and others' five aggregates would not be possible.
"The six bases" means the six causes of contact; by means of these bases acting as causes, the fool—being touched by the contact arisen therefrom—experiences pleasure and pain.
By the word "etcetera," [it is meant: "Or, monks, by one or another of these, for the wise man who has ignorance as an obstruction, craving..."

The passage beginning with "of one who is bound" (*saṃyuttassa*) and so forth should be applied here. For in that sutta, having established that volitional formations (*saṅkhāra*) are dependent upon ignorance (*avijjā*) and craving (*taṇhā*),
and having included consciousness (*viññāṇa*), name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), and the six sense bases (*saḷāyatana*) by means of the mention of the body (*kāya*), the Blessed One—

by showing the specific conditionality of feeling (*vedanā*) through contact (*phassa*) within this very body which is likewise dependent upon those [formations]— distinguished between the foolish and the wise.
The dependent origination (paṭiccasamuppāda) ending with feeling, rooted in ignorance and craving, has been shown regarding the past.
Furthermore, by demonstrating the distinction between the fool and the wise, it was said: "Bhikkhus, for the fool who is shrouded by that ignorance and bound by that craving..."
“The body has come into being; yet that ignorance of the fool remains unabandoned, and that craving remains unexhausted. For what reason?
Because, monks, the fool did not lead the holy life for the complete destruction of suffering. Therefore, monks, with the breakup of the body, the fool goes to a state of bodily existence;
having gone to a state of bodily existence, he is not liberated from birth... [and so on] ...from suffering, I say.”
Having shown craving— which arises from feeling and is accompanied by ignorance— and having established clinging and existence as dependent upon that [craving],

the Buddha taught dependent origination as rooted in both [ignorance and craving] starting from its emergence from present causes, by way of the passage beginning with "he enters upon a body" and so forth,
which demonstrates birth and the rest; and conversely, for the wise person, it is through the exhaustion of present causes.
From this point on, there is the reverse order of dependent origination (paṭiloma-paṭiccasamuppāda) based on both roots.
Because ignorance is a specific condition for karma leading to an unhappy destination, it is said that "one finds what is not to be found" (*avindiyaṃ vindati*);

likewise, because it is not a specific condition for what is to be found, it is said that "one does not find what is to be found" (*vindiyaṃ na vindati*). [This refers to] the eye-consciousness and so forth that depend upon the self.
The *āyatana* (source) is the occurrence and the production. Because it has not reached clear comprehension precisely due to its state of delusion, it makes [the object] unknown and unrecognized.

And regarding the phrase "it causes it to move within the limitless," by means of the fivefold characteristics of etymology (*niruttilakkhaṇa*)—namely, the addition of a vowel (*vaṇṇāgama*), the transposition (*vipariyāya*), modification (*vikāra*), destruction (*vināsa*), and the specific sense of the root (*dhātu-atthavisesa*)—one should understand that the letters *a*, *vi*, and *ja* are taken from the three locations [of the word].
By eliding the vowels of the other syllables and adding a second *ja*-sound to the [consonant], it is called "avijjā.
Having shown the meaning of the phonetic form (*byañjanattha*), he says "Furthermore" (*apicā*) and so forth in order to show the meaning of its intrinsic nature (*sabhāvattha*).
Because ignorance is unable to know the bases and objects of eye-consciousness and the rest—such that one could discern "this is the base" and "this is the object"—ignorance is their concealer.

It has been stated. Because it conceals the intrinsic nature of the bases and their objects, and because it conceals the state of dependent origination of ignorance and the rest, as well as the state of being dependently originated of aging, death, and the rest, it should be understood as the "concealing of dependent origination and dependently originated phenomena.
The formations (saṅkhāra) that have come under the term *saṅkhāra* are "formations conveyed by the word *saṅkhāra*. Even though [it is said] "with ignorance as condition"...
Volitional formations (*saṅkhārā*) are also included by the term "volitional formation" (*saṅkhāra*), yet they are mentioned separately because they are the primary focus of this teaching.

Therefore, in the phrase "of two kinds," one should connect the volitional formations included by the term "volitional formation" with the formations mentioned there [in the *Dhammasaṅgaṇī*], even excluding what was stated therein regarding the volitional formation that performs the act of forming (*abhisaṅkharaṇaka-saṅkhāra*). Thus: "the volitional formations included by the term 'volitional formation'."
Either the whole [collection] is mentioned, or a part of it is described here by way of being that which is to be explained in the formula "with ignorance as condition, volitional formations arise.
Therefore, it should be understood that the twofold nature is stated by way of including everything that is to be explained.

By the passage beginning "First, verbal formation ceases," etc., applied thought (vitakka), sustained thought (vicāra), in-breath and out-breath (assāsa-passāsa), perception, feeling, verbal formations, and so forth, are mentioned.
The bodily volition and so forth mentioned here are not those included within ignorance and formations (*avijjā-saṅkhāra*).
"Is agitated" means he thirsts. "Becomes" is said with reference to rebirth-existence (*upapatti-bhava*); "brings about" refers to kamma-existence (*kamma-bhava*).
"Death" is the passing away of the aggregates; it is called "death" because "by means of this they die. "Painful feeling is painful in its arising and painful in its persistence."
It undermines [the world] in two ways by way of its verbal expression. *Āyāsa* means exhaustion and despondency.

The word *kevala* expresses the sense of being unmixed, as in "the *sālaya* plants are *kevala*," and it expresses the sense of being without remainder, as in "*kevalā aṅgamagadhā*" (all of Aṅga and Magadha); therefore, it conveys the meaning in both ways.
In this context, "of that which is unmixed" means of that which is devoid of happiness, for there is nothing here whatsoever that is free from arising and passing away.
It has the function of deluding because it deludes either the person associated with it or the individual.

It has the manifestation of concealing because it is apprehended as a covering over the true nature of the object. It has the proximate cause of the taints (*āsava*) because of the statement: "With the arising of the taints, there is the arising of ignorance.

It has the function of accumulating because it exerts effort—that is, performs an activity—for the sake of producing rebirth-linking; or alternatively, "accumulating" (*āyūhana*) means the act of piling up.
It functions as the precursor to name-and-form; thus, it has the function of being a forerunner (*pubbaṅgamarasa*).

It is grasped by way of connecting with the previous existence; thus, it has rebirth-linking as its manifestation (*paṭisandhipaccupaṭṭhāna*). It is associated together with consciousness; thus, it has association as its function (*sampayogarasa*).
Because there is no mutual association [between itself and] matter, it disperses matter; thus, it has dispersion as its function (*vikiraṇarasa*). And so it is.

When rice and other grains are ground, they scatter and become powder; thus, since name (nāma) sometimes possesses the state of being wholesome and so forth, the term "having the manifestation of the indeterminate" (*abyākatapaccupaṭṭhāna*) was stated for the purpose of distinguishing it from those.

Alternatively, its indeterminacy should be understood as the absence of an object (*anārammaṇatā*), just as in the expression "insentient and indeterminate. The characteristic of the sense base (*āyatanalakkhaṇa*) is the characteristic of cohesion (*ghaṭanalakkhaṇa*).
Its characteristic is either coming or stretching. Its function is to serve as the cause for seeing and so forth; thus, it has the function of seeing and so on.

It is said to have "the manifestation of pleasure and pain" because unwholesome-resultant equanimity is comprised under pain due to its undesirable nature, while the other [resultant types] are comprised under pleasure due to their desirable nature.
Craving has the characteristic of being a cause because it is the origin of suffering; it has the function of delighting, according to the statement, "It delights here and there."
Because it is apprehended as the state of dissatisfaction of the mind or the person with respect to forms and so forth, it has the manifestation of dissatisfaction (*atittabhāva-paccupaṭṭhāna*).

Because craving-intensity manifests as sensual clinging (*kāmupādāna*), and the remaining [clingings] manifest as views (*diṭṭhi*), they have the manifestation of craving-intensity and views (*taṇhādaḷhatta-diṭṭhi-paccupaṭṭhāna*).
The characteristics and other [aspects] of existence (*bhava*) should be applied by way of kamma-existence (*kamma-bhava*) and rebirth-existence (*upapatti-bhava*).
By the word "etc. (ādi), there is the inclusion of such states as subsequent awakening (anubodha) and so forth. Ignorance regarding suffering and the other truths is non-practice (appaṭipatti);

the perversions of perceiving the beautiful and so forth in what is actually foul and so forth is wrong practice (micchāpaṭipatti). Alternatively, non-practice is that which is dissociated from views, while wrong practice is that which is associated with views.
It is not only ignorance that possesses the six doors and has the six objects as its domain; rather, this is also the case for other factors of dependent origination (paṭiccasamuppāda).
Regarding "immaterial phenomena," he said "in all [of them]. He said "neither within the range of both" referring to the mind-base (*manāyatana*).

For immaterial phenomena, because they lack shape, there is no nearness or farness by way of location; therefore, the range of the mind-base is not said to be either "reached" or "unreached" by the mind-base.

Since grief and the rest would exist, there would follow the undesirable consequence of having too many factors; therefore, the determination of the factors should be understood as being "only twelve.
For grief and the rest are not stated as being factors in their own right; rather, they are mentioned to show ignorance—the cause—as the root factor by way of its fruit.
Indeed, those [states] arise in the fool who is struck down by aging and death; thus, grief and the rest have aging and death as their cause.
It has been stated: “Touched by bodily painful feeling. And in the Sutta, suffering is included as the cause of aging and death;

thus it is stated by way of establishing those respective causes. Since, however, sorrow and the rest are subsumed under aging and death alone, it is therefore logical that they have birth as their condition. For if ignorance were the condition for aging and death...
A single summary may be made: "With birth as condition, aging-and-death, sorrow, and so forth, arise.
In this context, aging-and-death is included as a factor with absolute certainty; however, sorrow and the others are not certain, as they are absent in the form realm (*rūpabhava*) and elsewhere.
They are included merely by way of their manifest fruit in order to demonstrate ignorance. By means of that [summary], regarding future birth...

Since ignorance, acting as the cause for the subsequent rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*), has been shown, the uninterrupted continuity of the wheel of existence (*bhavacakkassa*) is thereby demonstrated.

Furthermore, the Sutta should be understood as proving precisely this point—that ignorance is the cause of sorrow and the rest—not merely that sorrow and the rest are the signs of old age and death for the fool.
For by the expression, "The uninstructed worldling... [the text establishes the causal role of ignorance].
Ignorance is shown to be the cause of sorrow and the rest; yet suffering is not suffering merely because it is the sign of aging and death.
The commentary on the section of the summary is finished.
Commentary on the Exposition of the Section on Ignorance.

226. For it has been said: “With ignorance as condition, there are volitional formations. By this, because ignorance is stated as the qualifying attribute and the volitional formations as the primary subject, he shows the reason for the volitional formations being that which is to be demonstrated. A father is described thus:
“Dīgha is dark-complexioned, Mitta is short, and Datta is fair-skinned.”
“Rasa” (taste) is the essential nature that is to be tasted and penetrated; “sarasa” (its own taste) is its own taste; “yāthāvasarasa” (the taste according to reality) is the taste as it truly is;
and because that very thing is to be characterized, it is the “lakkhaṇa” (characteristic). Thus, it is the “characteristic according to the taste of reality” (*yāthāvasarasalakkhaṇa*).

By the phrase “according to the method of the Suttas,” it is meant that only four [truths] are stated in such suttas as: “And what, monks, is ignorance? It is non-knowledge regarding suffering,” and so forth.

He says: "But by the passage beginning 'In the Nikkhepakaṇḍa... and so forth, he provides an exposition by way of commenting on the meaning of that very ignorance which was spoken of here in four places;
for it was spoken of in the Nikkhepakaṇḍa in eight places by twenty-five terms according to its functions and by way of its characteristics.
Indeed, the method of the Abhidhamma consists in analyzing that which is to be analyzed without omission.
"Jāti" (birth) means that which is born here; it is the place of arising.

Although ignorance does not take cessation and the path as its object, because it arises there—concealing them from one who wishes to know them, and by way of causing the apprehension of cessation and the path where they do not exist—it is said to arise therein; thus, those two also constitute a place of arising for ignorance.
And as the objective condition for others. Just as a sanghāṭi robe is for the monks' strength and a plow for oxen,

the characteristic (lakkhaṇa) should be understood as having the nature of ignorance (aññāṇa), etc., which turns back greed and other defilements that cause blindness toward objects such as suffering, and which acts as the objective condition for other [defilements] such as hatred.
"Atthattha" means "fruit of fruit. This is a reduplicative expression used for the purpose of making each and every meaning clearly manifest individually.
Alternatively, "attha" itself is "atthattha"; this is used to demonstrate the non-erroneous nature of the meaning, thereby distinguishing the meaning by means of the meaning itself.
For knowledge does not apprehend what is not a meaning as being a meaning. This should be understood in the same way for the expression "cause of causes" as well.

"Taking that aspect" means taking the aspect of the meaning, the object, and so forth. "Having grasped" means having introduced it into the mind, or having made it an object of the mind or of a person.
"Reviewing" (paccavekkhaṇā) is the re-examination of what has already been penetrated.

"Foolishness" (bālya) is the state of a fool characterized by ill-considered thinking and the like. "He understands" (pajānāti) means he knows by way of various modes (pakārehi). "Delusion" (pamoha) is powerful delusion. "Complete delusion" (sammoha) is delusion on all sides.

"Having suffering as its object" (*dukkhārammaṇatā*): by way of having suffering as its object; or, that ignorance which conceals has suffering as its object, and those phenomena associated with it have that [ignorance] as their state—that is "having suffering as its object.
Alternatively, "object-ness" (*ārammaṇatā*) is simply the object itself; since suffering is the object of this [ignorance], it is "having suffering as its object."
The intention is this: because they are difficult to see, [the truths] are deep not by their intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*); therefore, ignorance arises with them as its object.

However, because the others [the remaining truths] are deep by their very intrinsic nature, ignorance does not arise with them as its object. Furthermore, the phrase "but moreover" shows that cessation is even more profound than the Path, because the Path possesses a conditioned intrinsic nature (*saṅkhata-sabhāva*).
The commentary on the exposition of the section on ignorance is finished.
The commentary on the exposition of the section on volitional formations (*saṅkhāra*):
It "purifies" means it cleanses one from the fruit of demerit and from the defilement of suffering; it performs merit with an inclination toward welfare and happiness.

It is called "meritorious" (*puñña*) because by its accomplishment it fulfills the intention of the agent; according to the characteristic of etymology (*niruttilakkhaṇa*), it should be understood as "meritorious" because it fills (*pūraka*) and produces what is worthy (*pujja*).
The meaning is that it does not waver or move due to being extremely remote from the opposites of concentration (*samādhi*).
The term "of the body" (*kāyassa*) is used as a designation for the door in the sense of its master.
"Leading to merit" means leading to the attainment of existence. "Therein" refers to the Vibhaṅga Sutta, for that [merit] is taken there as the primary factor.
However, in the Sammādiṭṭhi Sutta, it is stated: "Friends, there are these three formations.
But this [teaching] was spoken by the Omniscient Victor, not by a Pacceka-jina (Solitary Victor); it is by way of these suttas that he [the Buddha] elucidated this meaning.
[The text] has been grasped. But how is this meaning illuminated by this grasping? To show that, he said:
"For in both the Abhidhamma and the Sutta, the same *tanti* (tradition/scripture) is set forth.
It is meant that because it is similar to the well-known Suttanta spoken by the Omniscient One, this too is known to be spoken by the Omniscient One.

It is said, “even those consisting of thirteen [factors]”; therein, since it is not evident that those dissociated from knowledge possess the quality of being "consisting of development" (*bhāvanāmaya*), he says, “For just as...,” and so forth.
Furthermore, the meditation on “earth, earth,” etc., as well as the preparation of the *kasiṇa* and the making of the disk, cause one to partake in development.
The states of consciousness and mental factors that occur in the mode of giving are “giving” (*dāna*). Among these, the volition of exertion (*āyūhana-cetanā*) constitutes the actual activity.
It is said that [the result] arises "with reference to giving" (dānam ārabbha) and "having made giving the basis" (dānam adhikicca); the same applies to the other cases.

The phrase "with a mind accompanied by joy" (somanassacittena) should be understood merely as an illustration of the occurrence of rejoicing (anumodanā); for one also recollects [the deed] with a mind accompanied by equanimity (upekkhā).
Even though it is dissimilar, it is similar to the fourth jhāna fruition (vipāka) in the Vehapphala realm and so forth, even among those without perception (asañña).

It is "form produced by past action" (*kaṭattārūpa*). Form itself is called "unshakable" (*aniñjana*) because it possesses the quality of being unshakable, due to its lack of suppression of the hindrances and other such disturbances, or because it is the cause of the "shaking" known as craving for form.
For this very reason, every fourth jhāna that has form as its object or a sign as its object is not, in the ultimate sense, called "unshakable."

When one holds a great balance (*mahātulā*) and measures with a small measure (*nāḷī*), one holds and measures the aggregate as a whole, not each individual *guñjā* seed or each individual grain of rice.

In the same way, the Blessed One also, having taken the immeasurable first wholesome volitions (*paṭhamakusalacetanā*) by way of their aggregate alone, shows them as being "one" because they belong to a single class. The same applies to the second [wholesome volitions] and so forth.
By not saying "occurring at the body-door" and instead saying "arising as it causes taking up, grasping, and moving," he merely shows a difference in phrasing.
For the occurrence at the body-door itself is what constitutes the causing of taking up and so forth.
Alternatively, by the former [expression], the door's character as a defining mark is stated; by the latter, the volition's production of informative matter is shown.
In this context, *ādāna* (taking up) is grasping by drawing [the object] toward oneself; *gahaṇa* (grasping) is the grasping of that which is associated [with consciousness];

*phandana* (trembling) is the stirring [of the body]. "Therein" (*ettha*) refers to the inclusion of bodily and verbal formations (*kāyavacī-saṅkhāra*), or the inclusion of bodily and verbal volition (*kāyavacī-sañcetanā*). In the Commentary (*Aṭṭhakathā*), supernormal volition (*abhiññā-cetanā*) is not included because it is not a condition for consciousness.
But why is it not a condition? Is it not also wholesome and subject to fruition (*vipākadhamma*)?

Is this so? It is true; however, when craving and ignorance are not yet severed within the continuum, its skillfulness (*kusala*) and its nature as a result (*vipākadhammatā*) are stated in terms of its active functioning, not because it actually produces a result.

Moreover, if it were to produce a result, it would produce one only of the fine-material sphere (*rūpāvacara*). For a kamma belonging to one plane does not produce a result belonging to another plane. And [it possesses] an object similar to itself.

That [state] would be subject to persistence (*tiṭṭhānika*), because in the *Cittuppādakaṇḍa* it is stated that for the fine-material-sphere resultant (*rūpāvacara-vipāka*), there is only an object similar to the kamma;

and furthermore, a fine-material-sphere resultant does not have a limited (*paritta*) or other such objects as its objective support, whereas the volition of direct knowledge (*abhiññā-cetanā*) has only limited and other such objects.
Therefore, it is understood that it does not produce a resultant. And regarding the fourth jhāna concentration produced within the kasiṇas...

The higher knowledges (*abhiññā*) are the benefits (*ānisaṃsa*). As it is said: "When his mind is thus concentrated," and so forth. Therefore, that [volition] is similar to the fruit of concentration;

yet, because it does not itself bestow a fruit, it is like the acquisition of conditions within that very existence—the benefit of generosity and virtue—since it too does not produce a karmic result (*vipāka*).

And just as volition associated with the higher knowledges is not so, likewise volition associated with restlessness (*uddhacca*) is also not so; this refers to that which is accompanied by restlessness.
Having extracted the Dhamma separately, it should be investigated because it is stated: "Knowledge regarding their result is the analytical knowledge of meaning (*atthapaṭisambhidā*).

Herein, this is the exposition following the path to the Deathless: even in the absence of seeing and development, those ordinary persons (*puthujjana*) and trainees (*sekkha*) for whom seeing and development ought to occur, are able to abandon [defilements] by means of those [faculties] at the time of their arising.

Unwholesome states are described as "to be abandoned by vision" and "to be abandoned by cultivation. However, because ordinary worldlings (*puthujjana*) lack the practice of cultivation, there is no consideration of what is to be abandoned by cultivation for them. Therefore, even though these [unwholesome states] arise in them, they cannot be abandoned by vision;
thus, they are not said to be "to be abandoned by cultivation. If they were so described, then by vision—
Certain [factors] to be abandoned by cultivation might at times serve as conditions—by way of object, object-predominance, or decisive support—for others to be abandoned by cultivation;

however, in the *Paṭṭhāna*, it is not stated that "those to be abandoned by vision are a condition for some of those to be abandoned by cultivation by any kind of condition. But for those in training (*sekkhā*), there exist [defilements] that can be abandoned by cultivation.

They are to be abandoned by cultivation. For that very reason, because they have been seen, abandoned, vomited out, released, relinquished, discarded, and utterly cast away by those in training (sekkha), they are not to be relished or rejoiced in;
and precisely because they are abandoned, they do not become causes for mental joy or non-distraction, nor do they produce mental grief.

And because they give rise to restlessness, those [objects] do not become for them objects of focus (*ārammaṇa*), objects of focus as a dominant condition (*ārammaṇādhipati*), or natural decisive support conditions (*pakatūpanissaya*).
For a noble one does not, by relying on what has been abandoned, give rise to defilements such as lust.
And it is said: "Those defilements that have been abandoned by the path of stream-entry—those defilements he does not repeat, he does not return to, he does not go back to... and so forth.

“...by means of the path of arahantship... one does not return [to them]. Furthermore, it cannot be said that these [defilements] can be abandoned merely by seeing ordinary worldlings (*puthujjana*), nor that they serve as conditions for others through any other cause. Thus: “One relishes and delights in wrong view;
with that as an object, lust arises, and wrong view, doubt, and restlessness arise. With doubt as an object...”

Because it is stated that "doubt and views give rise to restlessness," this expresses the state of views and doubt as being object-conditions for restlessness. Here, "restlessness" is said with reference to a mental arising accompanied by restlessness.
And having done so, in the exposition of the predominance condition (*adhipatipaccaya*), it says: "Holding a view dear, one relishes and delights in it; holding that [view] dear..."
It is stated only thus: "Having performed [the act], lust arises, wrong view arises"; it is not stated that "restlessness arises.

Therefore, although those things to be abandoned by seeing and cultivation cannot be defined as past and so forth, regarding those ordinary persons (puthujjana) in whom such a state of being subject to non-arising has been induced for those [defilements] abandonable by those two, the seeing [of the truths] occurring in them—
Those that can be abandoned by seeing, having depended on that [seeing], are "to be abandoned by seeing.
Those existing among those in training (sekkha) that can be abandoned by cultivation, having depended on that [cultivation], are "to be abandoned by cultivation.

Among these, those to be abandoned by cultivation do not produce a result when deprived of their companions; thus, volition to be abandoned by cultivation functions as a kamma-condition at a different time.

It was not stated [that these states produce results] because it is impossible to deny that for ordinary worldlings (*puthujjana*) who lack the vision and cultivation required to regard [objects with detachment], the production of results by the mental states associated with restlessness (*uddhacca*)—which arise toward their own possessions through desire and lust (*chanda-rāga*), etc.—cannot be prevented;

this is due to the fact that the three fetters (*saṃyojana*) and the defilements associated with them remain unsevered, leaving their companions undestroyed. Thus, regarding the phenomena associated with restlessness...
"It is stated in the *Vibhaṅga* that [this] is the result (*vipāka*).

If that is so, does it not follow that unwholesome states (*akusala*), which lack the quality of being seen or cultivated, would fall under the category of 'to be abandoned neither by seeing nor by cultivation' (*neva-dassanena-na-bhāvanāya-pahātabba*)?
It does not so follow, because those states that are not to be abandoned are explicitly stated to be 'neither to be abandoned by seeing nor by cultivation.'"
And because unwholesome states possess a nature that is opposed to what is not to be abandoned, does it follow that they cannot be included in this triad?
It does not follow; for the twelve unwholesome consciousness-arising types shown in the *Cittuppādakaṇḍa* are subsumed under two of the terms.
For just as, in the *Uppannattika*, all conditioned phenomena are subsumed by way of their intrinsic nature (*dhamma*), so too here...

Although those [states] not included by way of time are past and thus "not-to-be-stated" (*navattabba*), they were not mentioned because there is no "not-to-be-stated" among those things already grasped as being states of consciousness or material form;

likewise here too, it should be understood that "not-to-be-stated-ness" was not mentioned because there is no "not-to-be-stated" among those things grasped as being states of consciousness. For where a state of consciousness is necessarily "not-to-be-stated," [it would have been mentioned].
