In those cases where there is a fourth category, as in the aforementioned passages,

even here one must divide and distribute the arising of consciousness that is to be divided and distributed, by means of such statements as "it may be not-so-classifiable and have a limited object. Because that [fourth category] is absent,
it was not stated in that manner in the "arisen triad" (uppannatika) nor here.

Alternatively, just as in the form element (rūpadhātu) three great elements are called "with resistance" (sappaṭigha) because they share the same nature as that which possesses resistance, as it is said:
"For non-percipient beings, depending on one invisible and resistant great element, two great elements [arise];
depending on two great elements, one great element [arises]"; so too, for worldlings, those [states] occurring...

Since those things that possess the same nature as what is to be abandoned by cultivation (bhāvanāya pahātabba) may be called "to be abandoned by cultivation," there is no possibility of an objectionable consequence.

And this being so, even though they are occurring in worldlings (puthujjana), the desire and lust for one's own belongings—which are to be abandoned by cultivation—serve as a decisive support condition (upanissaya-paccaya) for desire and lust for the belongings of others; and lust serves as a predominance condition (adhipati-paccaya) for lust and views.

This meaning is established. However, just as three of the great elements (mahābhūta) in the visible-form element (rūpadhātu) are not ultimately resistant because they are not tangible, so too, the desire and lust (chandarāga) regarding one's own belongings that arise in worldlings—being devoid of the state of being an object for contemplation—are not ultimately abandonable by meditation;
thus, there is no relationship of asynchronous kamma-conditionality (nānākkhaṇika-kammapaccayatā) for those things abandonable by meditation.

It is not stated [that they are abandoned by seeing], nor is it stated that "those things to be abandoned by cultivation are a condition, by any kind of condition, for those to be abandoned by seeing.
For those defilements which are conditions to be abandoned by seeing do not continue to occur after seeing has taken place;
however, even for the restlessness-accompanied [defilement] which is a condition to be abandoned by seeing, there is merely a deficiency of its companion [the delusion] due to seeing.
It has been stated that no state of his has been brought to a condition of non-arising through seeing;

therefore, it is said that he must abandon it through exclusive cultivation. Consequently, for such a person, the statement regarding the production of a result when [the cause] exists as an associate, and the statement regarding the non-production of a result when it does not exist, are not contradictory.
If that [volition] is also to be excluded from being a condition for consciousness, why was it stated as "twenty volitions"?
To show the reason for this, he said: "But all these [twenty] occur with ignorance as their condition.

If that is so, should it not be stated as "twenty-one" including the volition of direct knowledge (*abhiññā-cetanā*)? No; because the reason for its non-mention has already been stated, and that same reason applies to the non-mention of the others as well.
"Reason" (kāraṇa) refers to the reason by which one [type of formation] is mentioned as being "one," based on the statement regarding the commonality of volition and verbal expression;

it shows that for that same reason, the other [type] should also be mentioned. And it shows that for the reason by which the other was not mentioned, even the one that was mentioned should not be mentioned.
Because there is no distinction [between them], the immovable formation (*āneñjābhisaṅkhāra*) is simply the mental formation (*cittasaṅkhāra*).
"Manifest" means that its connection [to suffering] has not been shown.
"Having grasped it with the perception of pleasure" indicates the activity of craving (*taṇhā*). "The equipment of craving" means the retinue of craving;
or, the meaning is that which is fashioned or adorned by craving through such notions as "pleasure" and "beauty. For craving is the origin of suffering.
Not knowing [the truth], one cultivates volitional formations with the thought: "Oh, that after the breakup of the body, following death, I might arise in the company of wealthy kṣatriyas!
"Amaratapa" (the austerity of immortality) refers to the practice of difficult deeds undertaken for the sake of not dying; or it is austerity for the sake of becoming a deity;

or, because it is painful, "māra" means that which kills, and thus "amaratapa" is austerity that [paradoxically] leads to death. The word "adiṭṭha" (unseen) is used in the sense of the seen (*diṭṭha*).
The term "immortal" (amara) should be understood as being applied to those who have died, just like [the term] "immortal" is used for gods.
The formation of merit is said to be similar to a fall from the realm of the gods because it generates the suffering of falling into birth and so forth.
And the fruit of merit, when grasped through its delightful nature and its quality of gratification, is like the crest of a lamp-flame or the edge of a sword smeared with honey.
And that purposeful volitional formation of merit is like licking the place where one has spat.
Like a fool who, through the perception of pleasure, thinks, "Pleasant is the touch of this young woman’s soft,
hairy arm," the person— overcome by defilements, overwhelmed by anger and lust, and lacking self-control— is like one wishing to die.
At the moments of performing, fruition, and presence, one undertakes a non-meritorious formation that is loathsome and painful, like eating poison.
This should be compared to playing with excrement for that which is accompanied by greed, and to eating poison for that which is accompanied by hatred.

Just as even a city of ogres, though full of danger, becomes a cause for the perversion of perceiving it as happiness due to the abundance of sensual pleasures, so too it is with the immaterial karmic results.
Because their arising and passing away are not perceived due to their continuity, and because their transformation is not grasped due to the long duration of their continuum,
they serve as causes for the perversions such as the notion of permanence— even though they consist in the suffering of the transformation of formations;
thus, their resemblance to a city of goblins and the resemblance to walking toward it should be applied to the formative activity of the imperturbable (*āneñjābhisaṅkhāra*).
*Tāva* is a particle that requires a subsequent correlative; therefore, the meaning is: "First, it is established that ignorance is a condition for volitional formations (*saṅkhāra*);

however, this other point must also be stated. By saying "all these [volitions] arise with ignorance as their condition," he demonstrates that they serve as conditions for the volitions associated with direct knowledge (*abhiññā*).
Through the knowledges of others' minds, past lives, and the future, [one knows] the [volitions] of others...
And it should be connected with the time of knowing one’s own deluded mind.
"Due to being bewildered by ignorance" means due to being bewildered by ignorance which conceals the danger of existence and so forth.

Regarding "of lust and so forth," the arising [of these states] should be understood as occurring with reference to ignorance at the times of relishing lust, views, doubt, restlessness, and dejection, which are associated with ignorance. Having made [ignorance] heavy...
Relishing (*assādana*) should be associated only with ignorance (*avijjā*) that is conjoined with lust (*rāga*) and views (*diṭṭhi*).

Since relishing consists of lust and the views that are not dissociated from it, it should be understood that by the very mention of "relishing," both the aforementioned ignorance and the views—which honor [that ignorance]—are stated.
Furthermore, because lust and the other [defilements] are mentioned explicitly in the text, the formations (*saṅkhāra*) conjoined with them have ignorance as their object (*ārammaṇa*), and so forth.

[The text] shows this. He says "whatever" (*yaṃ kiñci*) in order to include everything—both that which was not mentioned and that which was mentioned—in the statements regarding the object-predominance, proximity, and other conditions for the first impulsion, whose object is ignorance. "By the method stated" means by the method stated in terms of transcendence and the aspiration for existence.
"A doctrine of a single cause is reached" expresses the consequence of a fault; for a doctrine of a single cause is undesirable [because it implies that] everything [arises] at all times.
[It is] because of the attainment of occurrence and the attainment of a single similar nature.

Since [the cause] does not exist in three ways, but exists only in the fourth way by process of elimination, there is a purpose in illustrating a single cause and fruit; therefore, it is not untenable.
Regarding the determination of feeling according to contact: "Monks, dependent on a contact to be felt as pleasant, a pleasant feeling arises... [and so forth].
Because of the definition of pleasant feeling and so forth through such passages as "pleasant feeling," etc., and "dependent on the eye... the meeting of the three is contact;
conditioned by contact is feeling," etc., according to the correspondence between pleasant-feeling-producing [objects] and so forth with visual-contact and so forth;
and because, even when the eye, visible forms, and so forth are common [to all], there is no reversal of pleasant feeling and so forth by way of contact; and because, when [the factors] are common—

And the meaning is: because there is no confusion among the eye-contact-born [feelings] and so forth due to the specific impact of the eye and other faculties upon mental attention toward visible forms and so on;

and because, even when other conditions are common, there is no confusion regarding the coarse or subtle nature of the pleasant and other feelings born from eye-contact and so forth, by virtue of their being contact;
thus, the non-perverted causal status of the aforementioned contact for the pleasant and other feelings is precisely "according to the feeling" (*yathāvedanaṃ*).

The determination of contact, or the ascertainment of the distinction between cause and fruit through the distinction between fruit and cause—thus, in both cases, "ascertainment" (*nicchaya*) is called "determination" (*vavatthāna*).

"Kamma and so forth" refers to kamma, nutriment, temperature, and so on, which are not manifest [as such], because the subsiding of disease occurs through the counteracting of phlegm. This is because of the statement:
"In one who contemplates gratification, craving increases. Therefore: "O monks, regarding things that are conducive to fettering..."
The meaning is that by this sutta—“For one who dwells contemplating gratification, craving increases; with craving as condition, clinging arises;
with clinging as condition, existence arises”—it is stated that craving is the cause of volitional formations (*saṅkhāra*).

Furthermore, in order to show that ignorance (*avijjā*) is the cause of that [craving] as well, he said: “Because of the statement, ‘With the arising of ignorance, there is the arising of the taints (*āsava*). Craving...

Furthermore, since the four types of clinging—namely, the taints of sensual desire, existence, and views—are evident as causes for volitional formations (*saṅkhāra*), these two suttas likewise demonstrate that ignorance alone is the cause of volitional formations.
For by the expression "one who perceives gratification," it is shown that ignorance, whose function is to conceal danger, is the cause of craving (*taṇhā*).
Because one is ignorant, one therefore engages in meritorious volitional formations and so forth.
"He conditions" (*abhisaṅkharoti*): because the state of ignorance (*avidvasubhāva*) is evident as the cause for the formations (*saṅkhāra*), it is described by way of being the cause of formations;
this is because the formations are absent in one whose taints are destroyed (*khīṇāsava*), and because [ignorance] is not common [to all].

Since the bases, objects, and so forth are common to the meritorious formations (*puññābhisaṅkhāra*) and the rest, ignorance—which conceals the danger of meritorious existence and the like—is [the cause] of the meritorious formations and so forth.
Alternatively, the meaning should be understood as "the uncommon cause. "Contrary to its station" (*ṭhānaviruddha*) means contrary to its existence (*atthitā*).
However, some say that "stations" (*ṭhāna*) refers to rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*) and so forth;

if this were the case, then the preceding consciousness would not invariably be a condition contrary to the station of the succeeding consciousness, for even the life-continuum (*bhavaṅga*) is a proximity-condition (*anantarapaccaya*) for the life-continuum, and the impulsive moment (*javana*) [is likewise].
"Swift-going" (*javanassa*) refers to consciousness; since crafts and the like do not possess a place for rebirth-linking and so forth, they are not intended here.

Action (*kamma*) is a condition that is contrary to matter by virtue of its nature as bending and being subject to transformation, and by virtue of the opposition between having an object and lacking an object;
milk and the like are [contrary] to curds and the like by virtue of the opposition between their natures, such as sweet and sour tastes. Light has the function of non-cognizing.
Just as molasses and the like, which lack the function of intoxication, are conditions for the function of intoxication of liquor;

and as the hair of cows and sheep are conditions for *dabbā* grass; and as curds and the like are conditions for *bhūtiṇaka* grass—here, "rattā" refers to rams—and yet these [conditions] are not themselves results of kamma:
so too, although ignorance has suffering as its result, the volitional formations of merit and the imperturbable, which do not have that same result, [arise from it].

The meaning is that its status as a condition is not untenable. Even though it is non-resultant (*avipāka*), because it is unwholesome (*sāvajja*), it is a condition only for unwholesome volitional formations (*apuññābhisaṅkhāra*) that are non-opposed and similar to it, and not for others.
To prevent this objection, it was said: "Conditions for phenomena are established as opposed and non-opposed, and likewise similar and dissimilar. Therefore, regarding that point:
Making it clear, he said: "Thus this is ignorance," and so forth.

*Niyati-saṅgati* means the fixed order (*niyati*)—like the sequence of pearls strung on a thread or the arrangement of indestructible gems—and the meeting or conjunction (*saṅgati*) that arises through that fixed order;
by means of that, beings undergo transformation into states such as human, deva, or bird.

"Attained to transformation through destiny, association, and state" (*niyatisaṅgatibhāvapariṇatā*): they explain the meaning as "having attained various modes, transformed by destiny, association, and state.

And by means of these conceptualizations, ignorance makes the mind unwholesome and causes it to proceed toward any one among the [three courses of action], such as merit and so forth; showing this meaning, he said:
“Thus, due to ignorance,” and so forth.
“A fool who lacks a guide” means one who is devoid of a virtuous friend (kalyāṇamitta) who leads one to the path of arahantship.
Alternatively, it is called a “guide” because the knowledge culminating in the path of arahantship leads to Nibbāna by showing what is even and what is uneven; he is devoid of that.
"Without a guide. "Having known the Dhamma" means: having known the Dhamma consisting of the discourses and so forth that illuminate the Four Noble Truths by relying upon true persons (*sappurisa*);
or else, having known Nibbāna—the most excellent of all phenomena—by means of path-knowledge (*magga-ñāṇa*) itself.
However, because the realization of the remaining truths depends upon that [knowledge of Nibbāna], it is stated as if it occurred at a prior time, even though it actually occurs simultaneously.
The commentary on the exposition of the section on formations is finished.
Commentary on the exposition of the section on consciousness: 227.
That consciousness which arises with the aforementioned formations as its condition must be produced by that very same kamma.

Regarding the phrase "it is worthy," he said: "The thirty-two types of mundane resultant consciousness are included. However, in the *Dhātukathā*, in the exposition of the terms "included" and "not included" with respect to the dissociated [factors], it says: "Those phenomena which...
by way of volitional formations as a condition for consciousness... [and so on] ...by way of the six sense bases as a condition for contact, and by way of contact as a condition..."
“Those phenomena that are dissociated from feeling—by how many aggregates, etc., are those phenomena comprised?
Excluding the unconditioned as an aggregate, those phenomena are comprised by one aggregate, eleven bases, and eleven elements.
By how many are they not comprised? They are not comprised by four aggregates, one base, and seven elements.”
By way of this statement, the inclusion of all consciousness, contact, and feeling has been established.
For if consciousness, contact, and feeling were here only partial, there would have been an answer similar to that for "resultant states" (*vipākā dhammā*).

Therefore, it should be understood that in that context, consciousness and the rest are taken by way of the *Abhidhamma-bhājaniya* as having formations as their condition. And the formations conditioned by ignorance [are treated] in the *Abhidhamma-bhājaniya*.
It should be understood that since both wholesome formations of the four planes and unwholesome formations have been mentioned, it is precisely these that are included in the *Dhātukathā*.

However, in the *Dhātukathā*, "existence" (*bhava*) is not included according to the method of the *Abhidhamma-bhājaniya* for the purpose of demonstrating the distinction between kamma-existence and rebirth-existence.
This being the case, instead of citing [the formula] "with clinging as condition, existence," it is stated there specifically as "kamma-existence," and so forth.

Existence (*bhava*) has been extracted by way of this method. The phrase "the result is the cause" establishes that consciousness possesses the condition of volitional formations (*saṅkhāra-paccaya*) because it is a result;
and in order to establish that, it was stated: "because in the absence of accumulated karma there is an absence of result. Explaining that, he says:
"And the result," and so forth.

"Generally at the conclusion of a javana associated with greed": since it is stated that immediately after a javana accompanied by joy there occurs a registration (tadārammaṇa) accompanied by joy—due to this rule regarding registration—it should be understood that this is said with reference specifically to those [javana moments] accompanied by joy.
However, because at the conclusion of a javana associated with all three roots (tihetuka), a registration moment sometimes occurs that is rootless (ahetuka), [the word "generally" is used].
Therefore, he said, “for the most part. Or “once” is to be understood as in the case of “two or three nights,” etc.

However, they say that [the thoughts] arise only twice. In the expression “two or three nights,” since the word *vā* (or) is absent, it is appropriate to understand that the mention of “two nights” is made merely for the sake of euphony;
or alternatively, it is for the purpose of showing a continuous succession of three nights. But here, the word *vā*...
It should be understood that the meaning of "alternation" (*vikappana*) was stated with reference to an occasional occurrence at a single time; thus it is said, "or at once" (*sakiṃ vā*).

For it is precisely for this reason that, in order to show that [the mind] must be investigated in terms of the occurrence of the registration-mind (*tadārammaṇa*) at that single moment, he says, "But in the reckoning of the occurrence of consciousness," and so forth.
Therein, "in the reckoning of the occurrence of consciousness" refers to the discussion on resultant [consciousness] regarding a powerful object such as a visible form.
This was said with reference to the reckoning of the occurrence of consciousness. For in that context, only two instances of the arising of registration (*tadārammaṇa*) are mentioned.

The intention is that registration, which experiences the object of the impulsion (*javana*), would not arise if that object were to perish after only one moment of consciousness remaining within its proximity.
"A corresponding rebirth-linking" refers to the rebirth-linking of the miserable states for unwholesome-resultant [consciousness].
The rebirth-linkings (*paṭisandhi*) of the wholesome resultant states of the sense-sphere and so forth are appropriate to their respective destinies in the realms of desire, form, and the formless.
Considering that the discussion on rebirth-linking has a vast scope, [the author] first demonstrates the course of existence (*pavatti*) by saying, "But in the course of existence...

and so forth. The reason for not mentioning the restriction or non-restriction of doors for the two rootless [resultants] and others is that those which constitute the life-continuum (*bhavaṅga*) are themselves the doors, as are those which constitute death and rebirth-linking.
Because they do not arise through the life-continuum (bhavaṅga) or through any other door, it is impossible to say that these [consciousnesses] have either a fixed or an unfixed door;

thus, the fine-material-sphere (rūpāvacara) consciousnesses have a fixed object. This is because when the active fine-material-sphere resultant of a single being arises with respect to a particular object such as the earth-kasiṇa, it does not arise with respect to any object other than that. Therefore, the fine-material-sphere consciousnesses possess a fixed object.
Thus it was said. Therein, "of that" refers to the thirty-two-fold occurrence [of consciousness].

Because of the influence of the occurrence of the faculties, there must be a distinction of doors—namely, the eye-door and the ear-door—and because that [occurrence] is dependent on the distinction of the cognitive process (*vīthi*), there must also be a distinction of processes.
And when that exists, there is seeing or hearing immediately after the adverting [consciousness].

Immediately following that, there must be a determination of consciousness according to the sequence beginning with "receiving" (*sampaṭicchana*) and so forth. This being the case, the existence of both receiving and investigating (*santīraṇa*) is established;
it is not merely seeing and hearing by the power of the sensory faculties' activity, nor is it the case that the sensory faculties themselves perform the functions of seeing and hearing.
Demonstrating this point, he said: "Due to the determination of consciousness according to the distinction between the doors and the cognitive process... (*dvāravīthibhede cittaniyamato*).

And thus: if there is the arising of a registration consciousness (tadārammaṇa) following a first wholesome state, that [registration] which arises immediately after the first wholesome state is called "following" (*anubandhati*) the productive [kamma];
that which arises immediately after a second wholesome state or others is called "following" what is similar to the productive;
and that which arises immediately after an unwholesome state is similar to the productive because it belongs to the sense-sphere (*kāmāvacara*).
The eleven consciousnesses that take that as their object (*tadārammaṇa-citta*)... [etc. ...do not take that as their object;

thus, because they do not possess the state of taking that as an object, they have received the name "taking that as an object" (*tadārammaṇa*). The meaning is that they do not assume the state of taking that as an object, nor do they proceed by way of taking that as an object.
Alternatively, when the impulsion (*javana*) has impelled with respect to a name or a clan, the "taking that as an object" does not [arise] as the object of that impulsion.
They seize [them], meaning they do not take them as objects. "Material and immaterial phenomena" refers to phenomena belonging to the fine-material and immaterial spheres.

Having said this, the qualification "having the knowledge of direct higher power (abhiññāñāṇa) as its object" is for the purpose of showing that, because it has limited (paritta) and other such objects, it is similar to sense-sphere (kāmāvacara) states and does not give rise to a subsequent result-object (tadārammaṇa).
Phenomena fixed in falsehood (micchattaniyata-dhammā) are established through cultivation just like the Path.

Furthermore, because it is of great strength and proceeds with momentum and continuity, it cannot be accompanied by a subsequent registration (tadārammaṇa); thus, registration is excluded in those cases.

Although the phrase "with reference to supramundane states" alone would suffice, the separate mention of "states fixed in the rightness [of liberation]" is made because states fixed in the rightness and states fixed in the wrongness are mutually opposed, thereby emphasizing their relative strength.
This is for the purpose of showing that [the rebirth-linking consciousness] does not serve as the objective support (ārammaṇa) for itself.

Having thus shown the occurrence of consciousness during the course of existence (pavatti), he said, "But as for what was stated," etc., in order to show it regarding rebirth-linking (paṭisandhi). "By what, where?
means by which consciousness and in which existence (bhava). There are nineteen types of rebirth-linking by means of those respective consciousnesses.

"Arising material and immaterial phenomena at the moment of rebirth-linking"—this means that by means of this or that consciousness, this or that rebirth-linking occurs in this or that place; thus it is said. "Of that" refers to the consciousness.
"Having come" means as if having arrived. "Gopakasīvali" refers to one named Sīvali, born into the Gopaka clan, who was a protector for the welfare of the king.
Because it is devoid of the activity of recollecting [past] karma and so forth, it is called "death in confusion.

For in that state, the appearance of karma and the rest occurs precisely through non-activity. Regarding this, some state the reason: "When a fly is being crushed, the first sense-door adverting consciousness does not disturb the life-continuum because of the existence of something being thought of by itself. This, however, is...

It is without cause because there is no other object to be thought of apart from the object of the life-continuum (bhavaṅga), and because at the time of the arising of another consciousness, the mere subsisting of the life-continuum is impossible. However, the reason for this here may be:

because of the statement, "At that time, these [thoughts] hang upon him, hang down toward him, and hang all around him," [it follows that they occur] only when three impulsion-moments (javana) have not yet arisen.

It must arise with the presentation of the object as kamma and so forth; for through the occurrence of many sequences of javanas, there is a downward suspension (*ajjholambana*) and a complete suspension (*abhippalambana*).

Therefore, without turning back the mind-door adverting consciousness (*manodvārāvajjana*), that very mind-door adverting consciousness first turns back the life-continuum (*bhavaṅga*) toward the object such as kamma;
then, because of the strength of the tangible object (*phoṭṭhabba*), in the second sequence, the cognitive process of body-consciousness (*kāyaviññāṇa-vīthi*) occurs.
When [the process] proceeds toward a present tangible object, then, after the mind-door impulsion has impelled in sequence upon the kamma and so forth grasped by the preceding series of impulsions,

it either enters the life-continuum— known as either the root-life-continuum or the adventitious life-continuum— with that same object (tadārammaṇa), or, in the absence of such an object, it simply remains in the life-continuum. At this point, one dies.

The meaning is that one passes away by means of a death-consciousness (cuticitta) that has that same object as its immediate predecessor, or—in the absence of such an object—by means of a death-consciousness designated as the life-continuum (bhavaṅga).
For it is the life-continuum itself that proceeds having become the death-consciousness; thus, here the death-consciousness is called the "life-continuum.
It was said, "The sphere of the mind-door is light," with reference to its light manifestation among immaterial phenomena (*arūpadhammā*).
"Light" means that the object of the mind-door, which is an immaterial phenomenon (arūpadhamma), presents itself as a light appearance.

Furthermore, because consciousness does not first arise toward the strong object of the body-door, which is a material phenomenon (rūpadhamma), but rather first arises toward the objects of the mind-door such as kamma and so forth, this demonstrates the lightness of the objects of immaterial phenomena. Even in the absence of material objects, [the mind-door functions].
Or rather, the expression "immaterial phenomena" (arūpadhammā) should be understood as being intended solely to show those things for which it is the object.
Therefore, because the mind proceeds toward them with ease in the case of light karma and so forth, the lightness of the object consists in its being easily grasped by the mind.
Since the classification of karma and the rest is infinite in detail—by way of planes, types of consciousness, and so on—he said "in brief."

Since karma and the rest manifest only while the defilements such as ignorance and craving remain uninterrupted, and because the mental continuum (cittasantāna) thereby becomes inclined, bent, and directed toward another existence, it is said: "swayed by the power of unabated defilements.

For when the continuum is swayed, the rebirth-linking consciousness (paṭisandhicitta), which is a single part of that continuum, is likewise swayed; and by virtue of being swayed in one part, [the whole is affected].

“Without the bending of the continuum, there is no existence. However, in all cases they determine that “for a death bent toward rebirth in an unhappy destination, the preceding javanas are unwholesome; for the other [type of death], they are wholesome.

“Bhikkhus, consciousness, while persisting, persists either clinging to the gratification in signs or clinging to the gratification in secondary characteristics. And if at that time one should die...”
"It is possible that he will be reborn in one of two destinations:

either in hell or in the animal realm"—so it is said. Therefore, proximate unwholesome action is a decisive support (*upanissaya*) for rebirth-linking in an unhappy destination, and wholesome action is a decisive support for rebirth-linking in a happy destination.
An "inferior object" is one that serves as the cause for lust and so forth; thus, he speaks of an "unpleasant object" as being suitable to be the object of unwholesome-resultant consciousness.
For even that [pleasant object] becomes a cause for lust by way of intention (*saṅkappa*).

Alternatively, the state of being inferior consists precisely in its being the cause for lust and so forth that are co-nascent with the kamma producing unwholesome-resultant consciousness, or with the proximate death-moment javanas that are similar to it. For that...
An object that produces remorse later might, by way of its kamma-nature, become an undesirable object for unwholesome kamma-result;
otherwise, the result of unwholesome kamma occurring with a desirable object would not have the sign of the kamma as its object.
For it is not possible for an unwholesome result to have a desirable object. And in the case of the five sense-doors, when [an object] comes into range...
The present kamma-sign should be understood as that which has arisen in the continuity of the object of a deed recently performed, and as something resembling it;
otherwise, that very same sign would both establish the object for rebirth-linking and produce the rebirth-linking itself.

Furthermore, unlike those things that serve as the proximate conditions for rebirth-linking, [the kamma-sign does not appear with the thought], "In this, you must proceed," to the rebirth-linking consciousness.
Furthermore, the impulsion-moments occurring near the moment of death would have to produce rebirth-linking as if they were proceeding without grasping at an object.

For it is said: "Because of what has been done and accumulated. At that time, however, how could those [impulsions] be considered "done" or "accumulated" when they are proceeding in the same cognitive process (vīthi) as the [death-moment], yet are not experienced with relish, and are neither mundane nor supramundane?
They have fruits that belong to the same category.
Either he has previously committed that evil deed which results in painful experience,
or he has subsequently committed that evil deed which results in painful experience, or at the time of death he possesses and has adopted wrong view.
"Because of that, with the breakup of the body, after death, he reappears in a state of deprivation, a bad destination,
a lower world, even in hell"— by such a sutta, it is stated that at the time of death, right view or wrong view, when fully perfected and undertaken,
gives rise to rebirth through its concomitant volition; and it is not by means of weak five-door javanas that wrong view or right view [functions].
Or it is fully undertaken and observed. And he will say:

"For all this activity, beginning with the discernment of wholesome and unwholesome states and ending with the process of death, occurs solely through consciousness belonging to the mind-door, not through that of the five doors;
therefore, in the performance of all such activity, the process-thoughts accompanied by impulsions (sahajavana) are excluded."

For it is said there: "He does not discern any phenomenon whatsoever," and thus it is stated, "Mind precedes all phenomena," meaning that he does not discern even a single wholesome or unwholesome state.

Furthermore, the occurrence of those [mental factors] through whose manifestation pleasure or pain follows is excluded in the case of the five sense-doors, as is the undertaking of wholesome or unwholesome kamma.

"Of that same kind" means: rebirth (cuti) occurs immediately after the registration consciousness (*tadārammaṇa*), and the subsequent rebirth-linking (*upapatti*) occurs only through the mind-door (*manodvāra*), not being included within the cognitive series of the life-continuum (*sahajavanaka-vīthicitta*).

With this intention, it should be understood that here, death is stated to occur immediately after a five-door registration consciousness, and rebirth-linking immediately thereafter. In that context, [the lifespan] consists of the remaining five thought-moments (*pañca-cittakkhaṇa*).
Referring specifically to the rebirth-linking consciousness that has arisen with respect to a present object such as visible form, it is said:

"The rebirth-linking consciousness having a present object is a condition for the life-continuum having a present object by way of the proximity condition. Furthermore, referring to that which has arisen during the remaining single moment of the life-span, it is said:
"The rebirth-linking consciousness having a present object is a condition for the life-continuum having a past object by way of the proximity condition."
It should be understood that this is what is meant by the phrase “a condition.
“Or for a pure [consciousness]” means for a cognitive series (javanavīthi) that has a sublime kamma-sign as its object and is devoid of registration (tadārammaṇa).
That cognitive series, moreover, should be regarded as the proximate cause (upacāra) for a sublime resultant consciousness. However, some [teachers] say that...
They say that the cognitive process (vīthi) ends with the sublime (mahaggata). Eleven types have past objects; seven types have indeterminate objects.
Why is it said, "By this same method, the rebirth-linking (paṭisandhi) immediately following an immaterial-sphere death (āruppacuti) should also be understood"?
Is it not [already stated] in such passages as, "For one established in a happy destination (sugati) attained by means of the earth-kasiṇa jhāna and so forth"?
Is this rebirth-linking also excluded by that rule? No; for in that context, it is stated that the rebirth-linking occurs only immediately after death in the fine-material sphere (*rūpāvacara*).

For there, by such passages as "either a sign such as the earth-kasiṇa or a sublime consciousness (*mahaggata-citta*) enters the range of the mind-door, or [the objects] of the eye and ear," it is shown that the rebirth-linking follows immediately after death specifically in the fine-material sphere.
It is understood that this has been stated. Furthermore, by way of application according to what is possible, this rebirth-linking (paṭisandhi) is also restricted to that very [realm].
However, there is no rebirth-linking in the fine-material sphere (rūpāvacara) immediately after death in the immaterial sphere (arūpāvacara).

And in the immaterial sphere, with each successive death, there is a rebirth-linking into the lower levels; thus, there is no rebirth-linking with an indeterminable object (navattabbārammaṇa) following death in the fourth immaterial realm.
Therefore, for the purpose of showing this distinction— that right there, rebirth-linking with a past object belongs to the sense sphere (*kāmāvacara*),
while other rebirth-linkings may have past or present objects as appropriate, and furthermore, formless-sphere rebirth-linking has either a past or an inexpressible object,
whereas sense-sphere rebirth-linking has a past or present object— a separate extraction has been made.
Thus, by way of object, from a single type of death in a happy destination of the sense-sphere (kāmāvacara), there are two types of rebirth-linking (paṭisandhi) in miserable destinations;
from death in a miserable destination, there are two types of rebirth-linking in happy destinations;

from death in a happy destination of the sense-sphere, there are five types of rebirth-linking in happy destinations according to the two, one, and two modes of the sense-sphere, fine-material sphere (rūpāvacara), and immaterial sphere (arūpāvacara); and likewise from death in the fine-material sphere.
Fivefold rebirth-linking has been shown by way of two kinds of immaterial death, each corresponding to two types of sense-sphere and immaterial realms, thus making eight kinds in total.
However, because death in the miserable destinies is of only one kind, the two-fold rebirth-linking in the miserable destinies was not shown;
in order to show that, he said, "But for one situated in a miserable destiny... and so forth. As for those previously mentioned—
“Of two, two, and five kinds, and also of five, eight, and two kinds—altogether twenty-four are these rebirth-linkings.

By the passage beginning with “Because of having performed wholesome kamma of the sense-sphere,” the various modes of the asynchronous kamma-condition have been shown; therefore, in order to show specifically the mode of the decisive-support condition, he says: “For it has been said,” and so forth.
"Along with the first," etc., means along with the mixed consciousness.
"Two or three decads arise abridged" is stated with reference to those born from a womb; for elsewhere, many groups (kalāpas) arise together.
Indeed, even in the state of a Brahmā, because many fathoms in height are occupied, many groups arise simultaneously, such that the material phenomena (rūpa) exceed thirty.

Because odors and tastes have been excluded, even though the eye, ear, heart-base, the set of seven [mental aggregates], and the life-faculty exist there, they are not mentioned because of their multiplicity.
However, in the Commentary (Aṭṭhakathā), it is stated that even there the decads of the eye, ear, and heart-base, as well as the nonad of the life-faculty, arise;
whereas in the Canon (Pāḷi), it says: "At the moment of rebirth in the fine-material realm, excluding the gods who are non-percipient beings..."

It is said, "five bases appear, five elements appear"; likewise, it is stated—"in the form element there are six bases and nine elements"—to show the bases and elements existing therein according to the inclusion of all categories.
And in the *Kathāvatthu*, the existence of the odor base and so forth, as well as the nose base and so forth, is [acknowledged] therein.
This was rejected by such statements as: "Is there a nose-base there? Yes. Is there a smell-base there?

One should not say so," and so forth; for it is impossible to assert the existence of smells and tastes there—just as one can assert the existence of the earth element and so on among the non-tangible bases—without the earth and other elements possessing their own intrinsic nature, which is distinct from the impossibility of being touched.
This is because there is no such thing as an intrinsic nature of smell or taste that is devoid of the state of being smell or taste.

Furthermore, if they were called "bases" (*āyatana*) on the grounds that they lack the causal status of olfactory contact and so forth, there would be no reason not to call them "smell-element" (*gandhadhātu*) and "taste-element" (*rasadhātu*), since the term *dhātu* denotes that which is insentient and devoid of a living soul; thus, their status as phenomena (*dhamma*) remains.

Furthermore, their status as bases (āyatana) must be accepted unconditionally, because there is nothing else characterized by the definition of "maintaining its own nature" (sabhāvadhāraṇa) and so forth;

and the fact that phenomena are bases is stated categorically in the *Yamaka*: "Is a phenomenon a base? Yes. Therefore, even if they lack the status of being the bases of smell and taste, some essential nature of being a base must be predicated of them.
And if the nature of the earth element and so forth were something other than the nature of the tangible (phoṭṭhabba),...
If there were some other intrinsic nature of theirs apart from their being odors and tastes, they would be included in the dhammāyatana.

However, since they possess the nature of odor and taste as well as the status of being bases (āyatana), it follows that "odor is both itself and a base, thus it is the odor-base (gandhāyatana)," and "taste is both itself and a base, thus it is the taste-base (rasāyatana). Therefore, their status as the odor-base and taste-base is indeed established.
It can be prevented; and because of the statement, "there are three nutriments," the absence of physical nutriment (*kabaḷīkārāhāra*) therein is understood.
Therefore, the enumeration of material form (*rūpa*) should be made in such a way that it does not contradict the Canon. For in this way, the nature of things (*dhammatā*) is not subverted.

Regarding "from the wool of birth" (*jātiuṇṇāya*), they also say it means "wool taken after splitting open the womb. "Difference in origin" (*sambhavabheda*) means difference in existence. It is said that *nijjhāmataṇhikās* do not conceive a fetus even after indulging in sensual pleasure, due to their constant affliction by suffering.
Regarding the phrase "among the *rūpī* Brahmas who are of apparitional birth" (*opapātika-yoni*), [the author] distinguishes the *rūpī* Brahmas from those of apparitional birth.

In explaining the statement, "at the minimum, thirty among those born of moisture and by apparition," he says, "but at the minimum," and so forth; however, this does not accord with the canonical text (*pāḷi*).
For in the canon, there is no mention of the birth of moisture-born beings belonging to the sense-sphere (*kāmāvacara*) who are without noses.
It has been stated. For in the *Dhammahadayavibhaṅga*, it is said:

"At the moment of rebirth in the sense-sphere realm (*kāmadhātu*), for some eleven bases (*āyatana*) appear; for some ten bases; for others another ten bases; for some nine bases; and for some seven bases appear.
It is not said that "eight bases appear. Likewise, it is said that "ten bases appear."
It should have been stated three times; for while a birth without a nose exists, it should have been stated three times that "nine bases manifest," yet that was not said.
Thus, in the questions concerning the manifestation of elements and so forth, even in the *Yamaka*, the co-occurrence of the nose, tongue, and body is mentioned.

The identity of the aggregates and so forth between death and rebirth-linking constitutes non-difference (*abheda*); their lack of identity constitutes difference (*bheda*). This is merely an introduction to the method (*nayamukha*).
Having shown what was stated and having included everything that was not explicitly stated, he said: "This, first of all, is the method regarding the formless planes (arūpabhūmi) alone.

Because the access concentration (upacāra) of those belonging to the fine-material and immaterial realms is powerful, there is no rebirth in a miserable destination after falling away from them; thus he said, "from death in certain happy destinations.

Regarding the phrase "rebirth-linking in certain miserable destinations," the purpose of the inclusion of the word "certain" (ekacca) is as follows: [The text continues:]... [the purpose of the inclusion of the word "certain"]... [the purpose of the inclusion of the word "certain"].
This must be investigated. However, the intended meaning here may be as follows:

among those described as "possessing diverse bodies and diverse perceptions," there are certain beings in the states of deprivation (*vinipātika*) who possess rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*) with three roots and so forth.

Taking their rebirth-linking to be a "rebirth-linking in an unhappy destination" (*duggati-paṭisandhi*) by virtue of its being a state of deprivation, [the text] intends to exclude the notion that this rebirth-linking occurs only through death from *all* happy destinations, rather than through death from *certain* happy destinations. Therefore, it is for the purpose of precluding that [misconception].
The phrase "rebirth in some miserable state" (ekaccaduggati) is employed. For rebirth in a state of misery occurs only after death from *some* happy state, not after death from every happy state.
Alternatively, rebirth in a miserable state is twofold: that which follows immediately after death from *some* happy state, and that which follows after death from a miserable state.
Here, excluding the latter, he says "rebirth in some miserable state" in order to include only the former. [This refers to] death without root-cause (ahetuka-cuti).

“Rebirth with a cause” (sahetuka-paṭisandhi) should be applied as twofold or threefold. For, as in the case of the frog-devaputta and others, there can even be a rebirth with three roots (tihetuka) following a death without roots (ahetuka-cuti).

And in the cases such as “rebirth in a certain miserable destination following death in a certain happy destination,” it should be applied accordingly according to the opposite of each respective instance.

Regarding the specific distinctions: the meaning is that whatever is applicable—such as "the passing away of some from an unhappy destination" and "the rebirth-linking of some in a happy destination"—that should be applied accordingly.
The neuter designation is used by way of referring to the mere state of being applicable; alternatively, it should be understood as having the sense of the gerundive (*yojetabba*).
This applies in cases such as "having an object that is not sublime and external" and "having an object that is sublime and internal."

However, a contrary application must not be made. For there is no rebirth-linking in the formless planes with a non-magnanimous external object following a death-consciousness that has a magnanimous internal object.
The reversal of the statement "from a four-aggregate formless death-consciousness, there is a five-aggregate sense-sphere rebirth-linking" has already been applied by oneself.
[Likewise,] from a death-consciousness with a past object, [there is rebirth-linking] with a present object...
And there is no reversal of this term "rebirth-linking" (paṭisandhi). Thus, only the distinction regarding the difference [of rebirth] has been shown in detail;
however, the distinction regarding the absence of difference should be applied in each respective case by way of connecting death and rebirth-linking within those very instances, such as:
"from the five aggregates of the sense-sphere, the five aggregates of the sense-sphere... [and so on] ...from the state without applied thought and sustained thought..."
Regarding the phrase “without applied thought and without sustained thought,” for the four aggregates, however, the four aggregates are already included by themselves.

It is possible to understand it through this very method; therefore, no distinction between the undifferentiated [categories] was shown among the five aggregates and so forth. “Therein, without a cause” means without a cause in that context.
“The bondages of the joints of the limbs and members” refers to the bondages of the joints of the limbs and members; [the term refers to] those who cut them.
It should be understood that the phrase "when the eye and so forth have ceased" is stated with reference to their reaching a state of extreme weakness.
For even immediately after the five-door consciousnesses, death has been shown previously. And in the *Yamaka*:
"Does the mind-base cease for one in whom the eye-base ceases? Yes. Or for one..."
But when the mind-base ceases, does the eye-base cease for that person? For those who are passing away with a mind but without eyes, the mind-base ceases, but the eye-base does not cease for them.
For those who are passing away with eyes, both the mind-base and the eye-base cease.”
By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), the cessation of the eye-base (*cakkhāyatana*) and so forth together with the death-consciousness (*cuticitta*) is stated.

That which has obtained the remaining conditions for consciousness—namely, ignorance (*avijjā*) and the rest—is the "condition consisting of what remains" (*laddhāvasesapaccaya*), which is volitional formation (*saṅkhāra*).

When its danger is concealed by ignorance, [volitional formation] becomes the basis for the arising of craving (*taṇhā*) toward that object of action (*kamma*) and so forth, which serves as the objective field (*ārammaṇa*) and the locus of rebirth for the rebirth-linking consciousness (*paṭisandhiviññāṇa*).

Because it has not been abandoned and because the preceding continuity has undergone transformation, consciousness proceeds leaning, inclining, and tending toward the place of rebirth-linking; thus it is said, "craving leads.

"Concomitant formations" refers to the volition co-nascent with the impulsion-consciousness proximate to death, or alternatively, all factors such as contact and so forth. At that point of rebirth-linking—

They "cast" consciousness toward objects such as kamma; the meaning is that, as if casting it, they function as the cause for the establishment of consciousness by way of rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*) upon that object.

"That" refers to that consciousness, which is treated as a unity by way of the continuity of consciousness consisting of the death-consciousness, the rebirth-linking consciousness, and the consciousness immediately preceding them.

"Being bent by craving... [and so on]... "it proceeds. By this, he shows that—through the continuity of the stream (*santati*)—the acts of bending, throwing, abandoning the former support, seeking another support, and proceeding without a support belong to that very same single consciousness, and not to another.
Furthermore, by saying "through the continuity of the stream," he refutes the false grasping that "this very same consciousness runs on and transmigrates, and it is not another."
He rejects it. For when there is the principle of diversity (*nānattanaya*), there is the principle of unity (*ekattanaya*) by way of the continuity of the stream.
The object of action and so forth, which binds one to the personal existence of a previous birth, should be seen as like a rope tied to a tree on the near shore;
consciousness is like the man; craving is like his desire to cross over the boundary; and the volitional formations of throwing are like the effort of crossing. Just as...
And just as that man, while establishing himself on the further shore, whether finding support from something tied to a tree on the further shore or not finding such support,
establishes himself upon the earth solely by means of his own strength and effort; even so, this [consciousness],

whether finding support in the five-aggregate existence (*pañcavokāra-bhava*) or not finding support in the four-aggregate existence (*catuvokāra-bhava*), is bound to a heart-base (*hadayavatthu*) that is itself bound to the personal continuity of another becoming.
Or it proceeds solely through kamma associated with the object. Therein, "relishing" means reaching or obtaining;
the meaning is that it attains [the object].

"From the linking of another existence, etc. means from the connection to the beginning of another existence, or alternatively, from the intervals between other existences, birth-sources, destinies, stations of consciousness, and abodes of beings.

The meaning is "due to their re-linking. "Kamma" refers to the kamma that produces rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*). "Formations" (*saṅkhārā*) refers to the projecting formations (*khipanaka-saṅkhārā*) associated with the impulsion consciousness (*javana-viññāṇa*) proximate to death.
Regarding the phrase "caused by sound, etc.": here, an echo is caused by sound; a lamp is caused by another lamp and so forth; a seal impression is caused by stamping;
a shadow is caused by a face reflected in a mirror and so forth. "They exist without going elsewhere" means they exist without having gone to the location of the conditions such as sound.

Just as [sounds and so forth] have their causes because they did not exist prior to them, so too this rebirth-linking consciousness does not go to the location of its cause and become caused by it because it did not exist prior to that; therefore,

this [consciousness] has not come from the previous existence to the location of its cause like echoes and the like from sounds and so forth, nor has it arisen there without a cause, like sounds and the like.

The meaning is: "without [the original sound], like echoes and so forth. Alternatively, the phrase "they exist without going elsewhere" means that having been present previously in the location of the condition, they do not exist as its effects by going elsewhere from there, because they were non-existent prior to their arising;

nor is it the case that they do not have sound and so forth as their conditions. This should be applied according to the method already stated: "This is the same principle" as in the case of seeds, sprouts, and so forth.
This shows that a correlation should be made, as far as possible, among all things arisen from causes and conditions.

For here too, if there were absolute identity between the consciousness that is the cause and the consciousness that has arisen from that cause, one who belongs to the human destiny would not become one belonging to the divine destiny; if there were absolute difference, there would be no fruit for one who possesses the karma.
Therefore, just as in the case of [the expressions] "a seed is red" and "its fruit is red," [one says] "I was formerly... [and so on].
Otherwise, there would be the loss of conventional designations such as, "Venerable sir, there was a seer named Rohitassa.
Therefore, when there is a continuity of the stream within causes and their effects, one should not absolutely maintain either identity or difference.
And here, by the negation of absolute identity, he precludes the view that "pleasure and pain are self-made," and by the negation of absolute difference...

“Happiness and suffering are produced by another” refers to the state of being arisen from causes and conditions; “fortuitously arisen” refers to the same. “In this case” means within a single continuum (*ekasantāne*).
The cultivation of the four sweets, lac-dye, and so forth, is the volitional formation (*abhisaṅkhāra*) of mango, citron, and other seeds.
Here, the sentient being is like the seed, karma is like the volitional formation, and the continuity of sprouts and so forth from the seed is like [the continuity] of the sentient being.
The continuity of rebirth-linking consciousness and so forth should be understood as being like the existence of a sweet fruit with red filaments produced from its very seed,
and likewise, the existence of the fruit from that very formative action (abhisaṅkhāra) is due to the being who performed the karma alone;
and the acquisition of knowledge and the training in crafts performed in the body of a child [are likewise to be understood].

Furthermore, medicinal applications do not enter an aged body; nevertheless, proficiency in knowledge, mastery of crafts, and freedom from disease exist in the aged body on account of those [applications].

And this does not belong to anyone else, because it arises only in that aged body included within its own continuum (*saṃtati*), and not from anything else apart from the study of knowledge and so forth as they were applied.

Because it does not exist in the absence of that [cause]. Likewise here too, in the context of the continuum, one should connect the passage thus: "Whatever fruit there is, this belongs to nothing else, nor is it from anything else.
By the phrase "nor from anything else," he shows only the absence of the fruit when the formations (saṅkhāra) are absent; he does not intend to exclude other conditions.

As for what was said, the words "to that we reply" (*tattha vadāma*) are to be supplied as the remainder of the sentence. Or, the connection is: "In the absence of the enjoyer, the conventional designation (*sammuti*) of 'enjoyer' is established. "It bears fruit" (*phalati*) is the conventional designation of bearing fruit (*phalati-sammuti*).
"Even though this is so" means that even when there is no transmigration and [the doctrine] is established by avoiding the aforementioned faults.
"Prior to its occurrence" means prior to the moment of the accumulation of karma. "And after" means after the occurrence of the ripening [of that karma].
If [karma] is a condition because it has been performed despite its result not yet having ripened, then the state of having been performed is the same for those whose results have already ripened.
He said, "Nor does it constantly bring about a fruit," in order to dispel the apprehension that even for those [actions] there might be the production of a fruit.
By the phrase "neither because of its existence nor because of its non-existence," he avoids the faults already mentioned regarding reliance on existence and non-existence.
It is merely the performance of that act of standing as a guarantor, the act of purchasing goods, or the act of contracting a debt and so forth.

That is merely the performance of the action itself. That very [action] serves as the condition for the handing over of that object, whether it be the giving of a counter-commodity or the repayment of a debt;
the meaning is that its fruit is the handing over of what was not previously fruitful, and so forth.
"Without distinction" means generally, without making such divisions as "a three-rooted [kamma] for a three-rooted [result]," and so on; that is, by way of a collective whole.

The meaning. In all instances, the decisive support condition (*upanissaya-paccaya*) should be applied by way of powerful karma. For it will be stated later in the *Paṭṭhāna-vaṇṇanā* that "weak [karma] does not constitute a decisive support condition.
By the phrase "without distinction," all meritorious volitional formations (*puññābhisaṅkhāra*) are included together.
Regarding the phrase "the twelvefold division of unwholesome volition (*akusalacetanā*)," why is that which is accompanied by restlessness (*uddhacca-sahagata*) included here?

This must be investigated. In the case of rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*), there is a restriction that a single consciousness has such-and-such a condition, but not so during the course of existence (*pavatta*). For during the course of existence, the intention is that it is a condition for all seven [types of consciousness].

It was stated that "even in the world of the sense-sphere deities (*kāmāvacara-deva*), undesirable forms and so forth do not exist"; however, this refers to the time when the portents of death (*pubbanimitta*) appear to the deities.
How could there not be the undesirability of the *milāta-mālā* and so forth?

Regarding the phrase "that very same [volition] in both existences," here the mental formation (*cittasaṅkhāra*), which consists of twenty-nine types of volition (*cetanā*), is treated as a single unity by way of its nature as a mental formation;
thus it is said, "that very same. However, that specific portion which is the sense-sphere mental formation (*kāmāvacara-cittasaṅkhāra*) pertains to the thirteen [types of consciousness].
And the condition for the nine [realms] should be understood. For it is by way of being a partial condition that the whole has been stated.

And where a detailed exposition has already been made, wishing to provide a mere summary from that point onward, he says, "starting from the beginning. By this, the passage beginning with "in two realms" is stated. "By way of the plane of the third jhāna..."

By this, it should be understood that the plane of the fourth jhāna—excluding the base of non-perception (asañña) and the formless bases (ārūppa)—is included by virtue of the commonality of having a single body and a single perception. "According to possibility" means:

among the twenty-one wholesome and resultant states of the sense-sphere and fine-material sphere, [the jhāna factors] occur in the rebirth-linking and the course of existence for fourteen; they occur only in the course of existence for seven. This is "according to possibility."
"Of the four consciousnesses" is stated with reference to [the four] existences (bhava) and so forth;

however, the conditionality of the three consciousnesses included within those four for the three stations of consciousness (viññāṇaṭṭhiti) should be applied accordingly. In the non-conscious abode of beings, although consciousness is absent due to the condition of formations (saṅkhāra), the phrase beginning with "Moreover" (apicā) was said to show that even there, consciousness has formations as its cause. And in this...

It should be understood that the fact that volitional formations of merit and so forth serve as conditions for consciousness—such as wholesome resultant consciousness—in its occurrence within the miserable destinies and so on, is already implied by the method explained regarding the various states of existence (*bhava*); therefore, it was not stated explicitly here.
The commentary on the exposition of the term "consciousness" is concluded.
Commentary on the Exposition of Terms for Name-and-Form (Nāmarūpapadaniddesa) 228.

The distinction in the teaching of name-and-form in the Suttantas and the Abhidhamma constitutes a difference in method of presentation. Although the phrase "three aggregates" does not appear in the actual text (pāḷi), it should be understood as having been stated here because it is indeed expressed by implication through its meaning.
The term "of egg-born and those who do not become" should be construed together. "The beginnings of the continuity" means the roots of the continuity of the [mental] groups (kalāpa). Even though...

At the moment of rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*), the material phenomena that are modifications (*vikāra-rūpa*) do not exist; however, the material phenomena that are characteristics (*lakkhaṇa*) and delimitations (*pariccheda*) do exist.
Therefore, avoiding those [modifications] which are not fully established in the ultimate sense (*paramattha*), he says "from the material phenomena" (*rūpa-rūpato*).

As for the phrase "but in the sensual existence (*kāmabhava*) for the rest of the spontaneously born (*opapātika*)," although they are indeed called "spontaneously born" in the sensual existence, [the distinction is made here].

Since there are none [of the other types of birth] by which the inclusion of the word "remainder" (sesa) would be purposeful, it should be understood that the inclusion of "remainder" was made because, among the egg-born and womb-born, the apparitional and moisture-born are what remain.

Alternatively, having stated the apparitional beings such as those of the Brahmakāyika realm, he said "the remaining apparitional beings" with reference to those others; and since they also exist as formless beings, he specified "in the sensual existence" (kāmabhava).

It should be understood that although it was not stated, the enumeration of phenomena regarding the name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) of those with incomplete sense bases can be understood from the method explained in the exposition of consciousness mixed with matter (*rūpamissakaviññāṇa*), according to how they occur; thus it was not explicitly mentioned.

At the minimum, there are exactly two groups of eight, consisting of those produced by temperature (*utu*) and mind (*citta*); therefore, referring to the time when sound is present, [it says] "at the maximum..."
"Of two novices," it is said. Regarding "previously," they say it refers to the *Khandhavibhaṅga* (Analysis of the Aggregates), for there it is stated:
"Arising three times in each single moment of consciousness. Or rather, it is stated right here with reference to the series beginning with the dyad and ending with the heptad;
thus he says: "The seventy kinds of kamma-originated [matter] were previously stated. And that, as it arises, in each single moment of consciousness...
It is said, "arising three times in each single moment of consciousness," with the intention that it arises three times.
"Determined in the four directions" means that their heads are joined together and they are determined in the four directions by way of their roots;
standing while embracing one another, they are like a split bamboo fence.

And regarding the phrase "in the five-aggregate existence during its occurrence," this is said with reference to matter produced by kamma that does not generate [subsequent] matter at the time of the occurrence of the fivefold sense-consciousness, and with reference to the condition of consciousness as a co-nascent factor.
For at that time, there is only name (nāma) arising from that;

however, it can be said that both [name and form] always exist due to the condition of kamma and consciousness, and matter is sustained by the condition of subsequently arisen consciousness. "Among the non-percipient beings," and so forth.

This was stated with reference to the condition of kamma-viññāṇa; and since it occurs in the five-aggregate existence (*pañcavokārabhava*) during its active process, it is logical that this was said with reference to times other than the moment of the arising of the life-continuum (*bhavaṅga*) and so forth—namely, the time of the arising of material form from a kamma other than the one producing the life-continuum, the time of the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*), and times other than those when the life-continuum and so forth arise.
For at the time of the arising of the life-continuum and so forth, [matter] arises solely through the very same kamma that produces it.
It can be said that form, being a result, has kamma-consciousness as its condition.
For even during the course of existence, while form and name proceed by means of kamma, they do not proceed independently of consciousness as their co-nascent condition.

"In all cases" refers to both at rebirth-linking and during the course of existence. [Therein] name-and-form has consciousness as its co-nascent condition, and [it] has kamma-consciousness as its condition.

And name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) should be joined according to their respective occurrence. In the expression "name-and-form" (*nāmañca rūpañca nāmarūpañca nāmarūpan*), the term *nāmarūpa* is identical in form to the word *nāma* through its own partial component, and to the word *rūpa* through its own partial component.
Therefore, according to the rule "the single remainder of those that are identical in form," the place of the term *nāmarūpa* stands for both [of the others].
The non-perception of the terms "name-and-form" (nāmarūpa) is to be understood.
That which is other than fruition (vipāka) is non-fruition (avipāka). Since it is considered twofold from that [perspective], it should be connected thus: "this is indeed appropriate.

In the phrase "at the moment of wholesome consciousness, etc.," by the word "etc.," just as in the moments of unwholesome and functional consciousness, so too in the moments of resultant consciousness, there is that which is originated by karma not producing a result.

It should be understood that [the condition] is included. However, at the moment of resultant consciousness (*vipākacitta*), both [the object and the condition] are found due to the condition of formative consciousness (*abhisaṅkhāraviññāṇa*) according to the method previously stated; thus, in order to exclude such moments of resultant consciousness, it is said: "at the moment of wholesome and other types of consciousness.

The phrase "according to the Suttanta method" is stated because the decisive support condition (*upanissayapaccaya*) for material phenomena is not mentioned in the *Paṭṭhāna*, whereas it is mentioned in the Suttas.

However, having established that "when this exists, that comes to be; when this does not exist, that does not come to be; this is its decisive support (upanissaya), its source, its cause, and its origin," it is stated that "name-and-form has consciousness as its decisive support" (viññāṇūpanisaṃ nāmarūpaṃ), thereby expressing the status of form as being decisively supported by consciousness.

And in the *Vanapattha-sutta*, the forest grove, village, town, city, district, and person are the decisive supports for the maintenance of the postures, and from those [supports], the robes and other requisites [arise].
The acquisition of the requisites for life is said to occur both with difficulty and without difficulty;

however, forest groves and the like do not partake in being the object-condition (*ārammaṇa-paccaya*) or the decisive support-condition (*upanissaya-paccaya*) for postures or the acquisition of robes and so forth.

Therefore, according to the method of the Suttas, the nature of a decisive support-condition should be understood as non-existence in the absence [of that factor]. For the mind, it is the formative consciousness (*abhisaṅkhāra-viññāṇa*).
At the time of rebirth-linking and so forth, where karma is the object, it cannot even be said that it is merely an object-condition;
thus, from the perspective of the Suttanta method, the status of matter as a condition is stated in only one way.
For when it is said that this condition exists for matter—which is itself subject to doubt—it cannot be said that it exists for mentality.
Because the process of existence (*pavatta*) is well-known, he takes up the obscure matter of rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*) and asks, "But how is this so? and so forth.
It should be understood that from the standpoint of the Sutta, the name [aggregate] arises with consciousness as its condition, while from the standpoint of reasoning, it is the material form.

Having established this through reasoning, he strengthens it by means of the Sutta, saying, "And even for that which is produced by kamma," and so forth. The phrase "only of that produced by mind" refers to that which is produced by mind (*cittasamuṭṭhāna*).
Because only name-and-form (nāmarūpa) is seen as it occurs, therefore, by speaking of that alone, the unsurpassed Wheel of Dhamma has been set in motion.
For the intended meaning is that the setting in motion of the Wheel of Dhamma is the illumination of emptiness (suññatā).

Alternatively, by the very statement of the mere nature of name-and-form, the mere nature of the truth of suffering (dukkhasacca) in its occurrence is expressed; and by the illumination of the truth of suffering, its origin (samudaya) [is likewise shown].
Its cessation and the path leading to its cessation have indeed been revealed. Since suffering cannot arise without a cause,
since that which does not cease would not exist [as a phenomenon], and since cessation cannot be attained without a means,
the proclamation of the Four Noble Truths should be connected with the setting in motion of the Wheel of Dhamma.
The commentary on the exposition of the terms for name-and-form is finished.
Commentary on the Exposition of the Terms for the Six Bases (Saḷāyatana): 229.
And the phrase "by way of determination" refers to the four primary elements, the six bases, and life, as they occur respectively.
This was stated with reference to the state of being a condition for the six sense bases (*saḷāyatana*) as they arise, by way of such factors as co-nascence, support, prenascence, and faculty;
however, it should be understood that the sense bases such as visible form (*rūpāyatana*) are not included because they lack the nature of being co-nascent, supportive, or protective.

Furthermore, their status as object-conditions (*ārammaṇa-paccaya*), object-prenascence (*ārammaṇa-purejāta*), and so forth, applies only to those [bases] that are included within a continuity (*santati*).

And it is not the case that their status as conditions is indefinite, like that of the eye and so forth, which function in only one way. [The text continues: "In a definite manner... up to the life-faculty.
Here, by the word *evaṃ* (thus), the inclusion of the visible-object base (*rūpāyatana*) and the others should also be understood.
Regarding the term *saḷāyatana*, although the words *chaṭṭhāyatana* (the sixth base) and *saḷāyatana* (the six bases) differ phonetically...

There is no identity of form (*sarūpatā*); however, since the sixth base (*chaṭṭhāyatana*) is in fact just one part of the six bases (*saḷāyatana*), there is identity of form in respect to a single part.
Thus, it should be understood that a "single-remainder compound" (*ekasesa*) based on partial identity of form has been employed.

For they accept a single-remainder compound based on partial identity of form even for things that are identical in meaning, as in: "crooked and curved are 'curved'. Therefore, a single-remainder compound must indeed be formed for those things that are identical in meaning in respect to a single part.
Alternatively, by applying the grammatical rule of "single remainder" (*ekasesa*)—either as "the sixth base and the mind-base are the sixth base," or "are the mind-base";

or "the sixth base and the sixth base are the sixth base," or "the mind-base and the mind-base are the mind-base"—it is called "the six bases" (*saḷāyatana*) together with the eye and the other [senses].
This very [term] is the name based on the condition of single remainder.
Showing the meaning by way of the mind-base (*manāyatana*), which has name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) as its condition, he said:
"The sixth base and the six bases [together] are called 'the six bases' (*saḷāyatana*); thus it is formed by the elision of one member.
For even the aforementioned elision of one member is, in terms of meaning, indeed formed as "the sixth base and the six bases. And in all cases, when the elision of one member is made...

It should be understood that the singular designation is made by way of the commonality of being expressible by terms such as "the sixfold base" (*saḷāyatana*) for those [bases] formed by the *ekasesa* (single-remainder) compound.

Regarding the statement "it will be explained in the section on the indeterminate" (*abyākatavāra*): although it is stated in both the unwholesome (*akusala*) and wholesome (*kusala*) sections that "the sixth base has name as its condition," the intention is that only the resultant sixth base is taken in the Suttanta-bhājaniya; therefore, it is specifically the indeterminate section that is intended.

It should be understood that they are mentioned by way of their capacity as producers [of results]. However, in the method of relations (*paccayanaya*), even that which is non-resultant is mentioned as a condition in such passages as, "At least it becomes the sixth," and so forth;
this should be understood as having been mentioned because of the desire to state [the conditions] without omission.

"Included here" means included here by the method of single-remainder (*ekasesanaya*). In that regard, in the section on the indeterminate (*abyākata*) within the distribution of worldly resultants (*lokika-vipāka-bhājaniya*):
The intended meaning is that it should be understood as "analyzed.

"Neyya" means "to be known. Regarding "the heightening and lowering": here, the heightening (*ukkaṃsa*) consists in the state of being a condition in seven ways, whereas the state of being a condition in eight ways, or again in nine ways, or even ten ways, constitutes the heightening;
the lowering (*avakaṃsa*), however, consists in [the state of being a condition] in ten ways.
The state of being a condition should be understood as ninefold, then eightfold, and then sevenfold;
however, the two extremes—the maximum and the minimum—should not be combined based solely on the sevenfold state of being a condition, because there is no minimum beyond that.
By the phrase "acting as an associate to the heart-basis," it is shown that, unlike in the formless realm, name does not exist without an associate, namely the heart-basis.
This merely shows that name is a condition for the sixth base;
it does not intend to convey the meaning that name is a condition in the same way that the heart-base is. For the base is a dissociation condition (*vippayutta-paccaya*), whereas name is not;
and name is a condition such as the cause of kamma-result (*vipāka-hetu*), whereas the base is not. During the course of existence (*pavatta*), these are immaterial phenomena (*arūpa-dhammā*).
Conditions are for kamma-born materiality only when it has reached the stage of subsistence (ṭhiti), not while it is arising;
thus, the dissociated-presence-non-disappearance conditions, as well as the postnascent-dissociated conditions and so forth, should be applied only to the eye-base and the others.

Regarding the phrase "for the remaining mind-base," because the phrase "but in the existence consisting of the five aggregates" follows here, this refers to the five-aggregate existence (pañcavokāra-bhava).
It should be understood that while it is thus occurring, the remaining sense-base (manāyatana) is described by means of the five types of consciousness.
