The state of being a common condition for name-and-form through such factors as co-nascence, and the state of being an uncommon condition through such factors as association, should be applied according to what is possible.
The commentary on the exposition of the section on the six sense-bases is finished.
Commentary on the Exposition of Contact (Phassapadaniddesavaṇṇanā): 230.
Regarding the statement, “Contact has the sixth base as its condition,” this passage from the Abhidhamma-bhājanīya is spoken with reference to the formless realm (āruppa).

Therefore, he says, “‘Contact has the sixth base as its condition’ is according to the canonical text. The term “internal” (ajjhatta) refers exclusively to that which is included within one’s own continuity (sasantati).
It grasps it. For that [object], being produced by karma included within one's own continuity (*sasantatipariyāpanna*), serves as a condition for such contact;
however, external and unappropriated forms and so forth serve as the objective field (*ārammaṇa*) of contact.

They do not, like the eye and other faculties, serve as a condition for contact by way of being the manifestation of the signs of defilements and karma included within one's own continuity—this is the first teacher’s position.

They were not included [in the first teacher’s doctrine]. However, in the second teacher’s doctrine, they were included because it was impossible to exclude them when the state of being a condition exists in whatever way it may be.
If a single contact were to arise from all the sense-bases (*āyatana*), then the singular expression “contact conditioned by the six sense-bases” would be appropriate.
Alternatively, even if all contacts were to arise from a single sense-base, likewise from all sense-bases...
One might argue that because all contact arises [from the sense bases], there is no differentiation of contact according to the differentiation of the sense bases;

thus, a statement regarding it as being "one" would be appropriate on account of that non-differentiation. However, since such a thing is impossible, he objects with the words, "Not from all sense bases," and so forth.
Or rather, it is precisely for the purpose of making known another rule that is impossible that he says, "Nor from a single sense base do all..."

It is said, "contact," yet it should be understood that this very statement—that "a single contact does not arise from all sense bases"—is the reason demonstrating the inconsistency of speaking of a "single contact. Alternatively, this was stated by way of illustration:
just as not all contacts arise from a single sense base, so too a single contact does not arise from all sense bases; therefore, the expression "a single [contact]" is used.
"It is not logical. However, showing that a single contact can arise from multiple bases, he said, "In this regard, the answer is as follows," and so on.

[He explains: "A single [contact] may originate from multiple bases; a single [contact] may originate from multiple bases. One should discern these five ways in the case of the sixfold conditionality;
the same application applies to the remaining cases as well. And likewise: "Present forms and so forth, and the present [consciousness]."
This was said with reference to "form-form" (rūparūpa) included within the base of mental phenomena (dhammāyatana).
The phrase "merely by way of being an object-condition" (ārammaṇapaccayamattena) was said with reference to all that is not present, as well as other bases of mental phenomena.
The commentary on the exposition of the factors of contact is finished.
Commentary on the Exposition of the Section on Feeling (Vedanāpada-niddesa-vaṇṇanā) 231.

Regarding the phrase "of the rest": although the five [types of contact], such as eye-contact and so forth, which constitute the adverting [consciousness], are indeed conditions for the receiving [consciousness] by way of proximity and other modes, nevertheless, because proximity and the others are included within the decisive support (upanissaya), they are not mentioned separately for the investigating and the registration [consciousnesses].
It is stated as "in one way" (*ekadhā*) by way of that [contact] which is common to all.
It should be applied thus: for the resultant feelings of the three planes as well, that contact—consisting of the conascent mind-contact—is a condition in eight ways.
Since some maintain that even a condition may be non-clung-to (*anupādinnaka*), the phrase beginning with "but that which... refers to the mind-door adverting contact.
The state of being a condition has been stated; and that should be understood as being for the purpose of showing merely the heading.

By this method, the fact that every contact—whether immediately preceding or not immediately preceding—is a decisive support (*upanissaya*) for its respective resultant feeling should be applied accordingly.
The commentary on the exposition of the section on feeling is finished.
Commentary on the Exposition of the Footings of Craving (Taṇhāpadaniddesa-vaṇṇanā) 232.
“By way of ‘mine-making’” means by way of endearing; that is to say, by way of craving for gratification.

In this context, feeling should be regarded as like a son, while the forms and other objects that serve as conditions for feeling are like milk and so forth, and the nurse who provides the milk and such is like [the source of] the feeling.
There are six [types of persons] who provide the six objects, such as visible forms, like painters and so forth.

In this context, the physician should be understood as a provider of the mental object (*dhammārammaṇa*) by means of elixirs (*rasāyana*), medicinal herbs, and the life-force sustained thereby. The object-condition (*ārammaṇapaccaya*) is merely the object for that which is arising;

it is not a producer in the same way that the decisive support-condition (*upanissaya*) is. Therefore, it is said "in one way" (*ekadhā*) with reference specifically to the decisive support that acts as a producer.
It has been stated. Alternatively, by means of the decisive support (upanissaya), the object-decisive-support (ārammaṇūpanissaya) is included;

and by that, through its nature as an object, other modes of being objects of the same nature are also illustrated. Thus, it should be understood that the state of being a condition is stated specifically by way of the decisive support.
By the words "because" (yasmā) and so forth, it is shown that not only is there resultant pleasant feeling alone, but all three kinds of feeling are resultants, with a specific distinction.

This shows that craving is a decisive support condition (*upanissaya-paccaya*), and that the others are so as well without distinction. However, because equanimity is peaceful, it is spoken of as "pleasure" (*sukha*);
therefore, the intention is that it too is a decisive support for craving by way of being craved even more intensely.

Furthermore, equanimity that is the result of unwholesome kamma (*akusala-vipāka*) should be classified under suffering (*dukkha*) because it is undesirable; the other [equanimity] is classified under pleasure because it is desirable.

It can be said that both suffering and pleasure serve as decisive supports (upanissaya). Regarding the statement "with feeling as condition, craving arises," since this would imply that craving must arise for every instance of feeling because such a condition exists,
the text says "and with feeling as condition" and so forth, in order to preclude that [unrestricted] consequence.
Is it not the case that, since there is no statement saying "feeling accompanied by underlying tendencies is a condition for craving," it is impossible to prevent this over-extension?
No; because this is occurring within the context of a discourse on the round of existence (*vaṭṭa*).

For since the round of existence cannot exist in the absence of underlying tendencies, it is stated by implication that [feeling] is a condition only when accompanied by underlying tendencies. Alternatively, [the phrase] "with ignorance as condition" (*avijjāpaccayā*)...

Because it occurs in succession, it is understood that the condition is indeed accompanied by underlying tendencies (*anusaya*). Furthermore, regarding the statement "with feeling as condition, craving arises" (*vedanāpaccayā taṇhā*), this restriction is understood:
craving arises *only* with feeling as its condition, and not without feeling; it does not mean that craving must necessarily arise whenever there is feeling as a condition.
Therefore, there is no over-extension (*atippasaṅga*) of the principle.

“Vusīmato” means of one who has lived [the holy life]; the meaning is: of one who has completed the residence of the holy life (*brahmacariya*). Alternatively, “vusi” refers to the Path (*magga*) because it is “lived” (*vussati*);
he is “one possessed of vusi” (*vusīmā*) because that Path has been traversed by him. Or else, the supreme fruit (*aggaphala*) is called “vusi” because its residence is fully accomplished;
he is “one possessed of vusi” because he possesses that fruit.
The commentary on the exposition of the term *taṇhā* (craving) is finished.
233. Commentary on the exposition of the term *upādāna* (clinging):
The statement "the self is eternal" is said in order to demonstrate a subsequent view while clinging to a preceding view.
For just as this view clings to what precedes it by way of strengthening it, so too do views such as "there is no gift" and so forth.
However, the inclusion of the term "self" refers to the clinging to a self-theory (*attavādupādāna*); thus, this should not be regarded as a demonstration of the clinging to views (*diṭṭhupādāna*).

Alternatively, the phrase "and the world" refers to a grasping distinct from the grasping of a self, which constitutes the clinging to views, as indicated here by the mention of the preceding and subsequent views.

It should be understood that it is "said. Regarding the phrase "in the brief and detailed exposition of the Dhamma," he thus determines the brief and the detailed according to the brief and detailed exposition of the Dhamma: "In brief, it is the intensity of craving; in brief, it is merely view; but in detail...
Here, in the compound *dhammasaṅkhepavitthāre*, the locative case should be seen as having a sense of selection (*niddhāraṇe*).

The clinging to a self (attaggāha)—the thought that there exists some permanent or perishable self that is the master of those [elements] such as the primary elements (pakati-aṇu-ādi), which is preceded by the grasping for their eternity or the grasping for the annihilation of the body—occurs only occasionally;

therefore, it is said "for the most part" (yebhuyyena). Alternatively, it is connected with the statement: "For the most part, first comes the clinging to the doctrine of self (attavādupādāna)," and so forth.
Even though the javana-process of craving for existence occurs first for one who has taken rebirth-linking— since it must proceed due to the inclination toward existence—
he did not state the initial arising of sense-desire clinging (*kāmupādāna*), thinking that such craving for existence is not an intensity of craving (*taṇhā*).
However, if no distinction were made between craving and sense-desire clinging, then all craving would [erroneously] be considered sense-desire clinging.

In the case of the *karaṇa* (instrument), other types of craving besides sensual lust that have reached a state of firmness are called "clinging to sense-pleasures" (*kāmupādāna*); thus, its inclusion as something to be abandoned by the path of Arahantship has been stated.
The mental states (*cittuppāda*) that serve as the basis for arising are the "object" (*visaya*). The five aggregates of clinging (*pañcupādānakkhandhā*) are the "attachment" (*ālaya*);

because one delights therein, beings are "delighting in attachment" (*ālayarāmā*). For this very reason, that delighting in attachment is manifest both in one's own continuum and in the continua of others.

By the term "decisive support" (*upanissaya*), the object-decisive support (*ārammaṇa-upanissaya*), the proximity-decisive support (*anantara-upanissaya*), and the natural-decisive support (*pakatūpanissaya*) are stated; thus, the inclusion of the proximity-condition (*anantara-paccaya*) and others is also effected.
The commentary on the description of the term "clinging" (*upādāna*) is finished.
The commentary on the description of the term "existence" (*bhava*).

234. Since *kamma-bhava* is called "existence" (*bhava*) by way of conventional designation for its fruit, he says, "It is existence because it comes to be," speaking thus while making the definition of *upapatti-bhava* (existence as rebirth) common to both.

"It goes to existence" means that, by virtue of producing its fruit, it proceeds during its own occurrence facing toward existence; or rather, here "going" is intended to mean simply being brought into being.
Regarding the phrase *saññāvataṃ bhavo saññābhavo*, one should understand that there is an elision (*lopa*) of the suffix *-vant-*;

alternatively, by substituting the letter *a* for its meaning, the reading *saññābhavo* is also valid. That which is scattered, spread out, or expanded is called a *vokāra*; or else, scattering itself is *vokāra*.
Because it occurs in a single location, it is called "a single *vokāra*" (*eko vokāro*), meaning the arising of a spreading in a particular place.

"Associated with volition... [etc. ...is included"—having thus shown that it is designated as "kamma" by way of its leading to accumulation, he speaks of its being included within the existence of kamma (*kammabhava*) in a figurative sense.
However, in the primary sense, volition alone is the existence of kamma. For it is said:
"The existence of kamma is associated with three aggregates, one base, and one element; it is dissociated from one aggregate..."
“With one base and with one element, it is associated with some [factors]. Rebirth-existence (*upapattibhava*) consists precisely of the aggregates of rebirth mentioned in all three triplets.

As it is said: “Rebirth-existence, sense-desire existence (*kāmabhava*), perception existence (*saññābhava*), five-aggregate existence (*pañcavokārabhava*), is comprised of five aggregates, eleven bases, and seventeen elements,” and so forth. For if...
There might be the inclusion of even those things not grasped (*anupādinnaka*), and it would have to be stated as "by means of the twelve bases (*āyatana*) and the eighteen elements (*dhātu*).

If it is argued that this repetition is not logical—on the grounds that since *saṅkhāra* and *bhava* are distinct categories of phenomena (*dhamma-bheda*), *saṅkhāra* itself was not stated again—it is not so;
for *saṅkhāra* was stated again as "existence" (*bhava*) because it constitutes a portion of existence. By the other...
Or, disregarding the distinction between the phenomena (dhamma), it was stated that "this repetition is purposeful" according to the intention of the accuser.

In the Commentary, the nature of karma— which produces the sensual existence (kāmabhava) and so forth— as being "the sensual existence" and so on, is expressed by way of the terminology of the fruit (phalavohāra).

It was said thus: not counting those included within as separate, but treating them as merely internal, and doubling the sense-sphere existence (*kāmabhava*) and so forth by way of kamma-existence (*kammabhava*) and rebirth-existence (*upapattibhava*), he said, "six existences.

"Without distinction" means without making a division according to the types of clinging (*upādāna*). And because they are comprised by way of including the twelvefold classification through that very non-division of clinging, it is stated as "six existences."

Some say that because it is stated that companionship with cattle and dogs results from the complete undertaking and adoption of the cow-vow and the dog-vow, the cultivation of jhāna does not succeed for one who clings to rules and observances;
thus, they claim that such clinging does not lead to rebirth in the fine-material or immaterial realms.
However, [the author] says, "That should not be accepted," because, in the manner that will be explained, such clinging functions as a condition [for continued existence].
And the misapprehension of a path to purity where there is no pure path is the clinging to rules and observances (*sīlabbatupādāna*).

Thus, it is not tenable that the production of fine-material and immaterial-sphere jhānas occurs through such a misapprehension of a path to purity. Hearing the *Purāṇa*, the *Mahābhārata*, the abduction of Sītā, the ritual for animal sacrifice, and so forth, is "hearing what is not the true Dhamma" (*asaddhammasavana*).
By the word "and so forth," one includes reliance upon unworthy persons, the failure to perform merit in the past, and one's own wrong aspirations.
It includes. "Included within that" means that they are indeed included within that sensual existence (*kāmabhava*) produced by misconduct and produced by good conduct.
And it is said that they are "included" because they are partially included within the existence of perception (*saññābhava*) and the five-aggregate existence (*pañcavokārabhava*). For it is not...

These [three] are entirely included within the existence of sense-desire (*kāmabhava*). "Possessing distinctions" means possessing the distinctions of happy destinies, miserable destinies, humans, and so forth.

And the statement that the clinging to rules and observances (*sīlabbatupādāna*) is a condition for existence (*bhava-paccaya*) at the end, rather than being mentioned sequentially like the clinging to a self-theory (*attavādupādāna*), is because it does not manifest frequently and because it serves as the cause for the clinging to a self-theory.

Regarding the phrase "by the classifications of the root-condition" (*hetupaccaya*), the path-condition (*maggapaccaya*) should also be mentioned here; for view-clinging (*diṭṭhupādāna*) and the others are indeed path-conditions.
The commentary on the exposition of the terms for existence (*bhava*) is finished.
Now begins the commentary on the exposition of the terms for birth, aging-and-death, and so forth.
235. It is said that "birth" (*jāti*) is simply the arising of the state of rebirth (*upapattibhava*);

therefore, it is stated: "not the state of rebirth. However, since birth is the birth of one who is being born, it can be asserted that even the state of rebirth is a condition for birth, because it does not exist in the absence of birth.

For the state of rebirth is also described as the proximate cause (*padatthāna*) for the birth of material form (*rūpa*), just as it is said: "Accumulation (*upacaya*) has accumulated material form as its proximate cause; continuity (*santati*) has uninterruptedly following material form as its proximate cause."
The disparagement and non-disparagement of arisen aggregates, as well as their inferiority and superiority; by the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), it includes distinctions such as beauty and ugliness.
He says "in the internal continuum" because there is no other cause that produces a distinction apart from what occurs within the internal continuum itself.
"By this or that" refers to various phenomena of suffering other than aging and death, such as the loss of kinsmen and so forth. "By way of the limit of decisive support" (*upanissaya-koṭiyā*)...

The meaning is: by way of decisive support (*upanissaya*), by the characteristic of decisive support. For that which is not included in the *Paṭṭhāna*—namely, the presence [of a state] when [another] exists and its absence when it does not exist—is called "the limit of decisive support" (*upanissayakoṭi*) according to the method of the Suttantas.
The commentary on the exposition of the terms birth, aging, death, and so forth, is finished.
Commentary on the Discourse on the Wheel of Existence (Bhavacakka-kathāvaṇṇanā) 242.

*Samitaṃ* means joined together; the sense is "uninterrupted. *Kāmayānassa* means "of one who desires," or alternatively, *kāmayāno* is one for whom desire (*kāma*) is the vehicle (*yāna*); [the text refers to] that desirous one. *Ruppati* means he is afflicted by sorrow.
*Pariyuṭṭhānaṭṭhāyī* means one whose habit is to persist in obsession (*pariyuṭṭhāna*). Alternatively, the reading is *pariyuṭṭhaṭṭhāyino*.

In this context, "it obsesses" (*pariyuṭṭhāti*) means an obsession (*pariyuṭṭha*), namely the obsession of views (*diṭṭhipariyuṭṭha*). One who stands by that is called "one who stands by the obsession" (*pariyuṭṭhaṭṭhāyī*);

such is the meaning to be understood. "The five portents" refers to those five stated as: "the garlands wither, the clothes become soiled, sweat breaks out from the armpits, a change of color comes over the body, and the deva no longer delights in his celestial throne."

The meaning is "the signs preceding death. For upon seeing them, through the power of desire for existence (*bhavachanda*), intense sorrow arises in the devas regarding the state of rebirth (*upapattibhava*), which consists of the aggregates produced by kamma. "A fool" means one who is ignorant;
by this, he shows ignorance to be the cause. "Threefold" refers to its causes: hearing talk of the formless realm (*arūpa*), performing deeds, seeing [omens], and the approach of the time of death.
The suffering of sorrow and so forth. "They accomplish the outflows" means they cause the outflows to cease or bring them to an end;

this is the meaning. "This being so" means: given that there is no beginning due to the state of being unknown and so forth. "The statement of having a beginning," etc.: that which has this [beginning] is "having-a-beginning" (*ādima*), namely the wheel of existence (*bhavacakra*).

The state of that is "the state of having a beginning" (*ādimatta*); the speaking of that is "the statement of having a beginning" (*ādimattakathana*). It serves the purpose of excluding specific [other] qualities.
Or, if the word "beginning" (ādi) were taken in its primary sense, it would follow that ignorance exists everywhere—at the beginning, in the middle, and at the end;
thus, the statement that ignorance is [only] at the beginning would be contradicted. "By the mention of ignorance" means by the production or the description of ignorance, or by its non-abandonment;
the meaning is: by causing it to be present within one's own continuum. "Kamma and so forth" refers to...
The rounds of kamma and its result. Ignorance (avijjā) is called "the primary factor" because it is predominant as the cause of the round [of existence].
It "speaks," thus it is a "speaker" (vada). Or, it is "to be felt" (vedeyya), meaning it experiences pleasure and so forth, or it knows all objects;
the meaning is that it knows and is known by itself and by others through such terms as "happy" and so on. Or, by means of Brahmā and so forth...
*Attanā vā*: the word *vā* has the sense of the word *ca*. Therefore he said, “devoid of an agent and an experiencer,” using a compound in the sense of *ca*.
“Empty of the twelvefold emptiness”: it is empty by way of the twelvefold emptiness of ignorance and the other [factors].
Alternatively, having taken the fourfold emptiness as one, it is “twelvefold” because of its twelve constituent parts; thus the meaning is that it is empty of that twelvefold emptiness.

"By way of bringing forward from the past" means that this wheel of existence (bhavacakkam) has its conclusion in delimited feeling, because it brings about present-resultant [kamma] from the past; for even a single portion of the wheel of existence is called "the wheel of existence.

Alternatively, because feeling is a condition for ignorance accompanied by craving, and from that [feeling] come volitional formations (saṅkhārā), it is so called by way of such sequential connection.
It is logical that the wheel of existence (bhavacakra) ends with feeling; thus it should be applied as having craving as its root.

For both [craving and ignorance] mutually enter into one another. Indeed, ignorance, by concealing the true nature of phenomena (dhammasabhāva) and producing a distorted adherence, leads those of a speculative temperament through the cycle of existence (saṃsāra), or else it leads them through the cycle of existence, which is the process of the formations (saṅkhāra) and so forth.
Because it causes [the cycle] to proceed, it is called the "leader of saṃsāra. The term "arising of the fruit" (*phaluppatti*) is a designation for the agent.

For here, the arising of present fruits such as consciousness is seen; moreover, it demonstrates that even those [fruits] not yet seen do not cease without having produced their own fruits—namely, ignorance and volitional formations—which belong to the previous existence.
Alternatively, the wheel of the previous existence is connected with the second [wheel].
"Is stated" means it reveals the non-interruption of craving and the other causes for the arising of the fruit known as feeling;
therefore, the meaning is that it reveals the non-interruption of the causes of the first wheel of existence (*bhavacakkā*), which serve as the reasons for the arising of the fruit.

Or alternatively, [it means] the non-interruption of ignorance and the other causes for the arising of the fruits such as volitional formations (*saṅkhāra*), without those causes producing their own fruit.

The first wheel of existence (bhavacakra) demonstrates only non-interruption—that is, the continuous succession of the causes of consciousness and so forth, such as volitional formations—and does not, like the second wheel, show the conclusion; thus it is said: "because it demonstrates the non-interruption of the causes for the arising of the fruit.
In the phrase "with consciousness as condition, name-and-form," having spoken of the kalala-body whose sense-bases are incomplete, from that...
Since the occurrence of the six sense bases (*saḷāyatana*) was stated above as “with name-and-form as condition, the six sense bases,” he said, “because it illustrates successive occurrence.
Since the arising of the sense bases in their sequential order was not stated here in the phrase “with existence as condition, birth,” he said, “because it illustrates simultaneous arising.
That which has three joints preceded by cause and so forth is the wheel of existence (*bhavacakra*), having the sequence of cause-result-cause-result. By way of cause-result and cause-result:
That which has a fourfold classification of its constituent factors (*aṅga*) is called "the fourfold compendium" (*catubhedasaṅgaha*).

"Modes" (*ākāra*) are so called because, although not explicitly stated in their specific form, they are scattered throughout those various compendia and are made manifest by the inclusion of items such as ignorance (*avijjā*) and volitional formations (*saṅkhāra*);

or alternatively, "modes" are the ways in which past causes and so forth appear. Having become connected through defilements, karma, and results, and through results, defilements, and karma, [they arise] again and again.
“They revolve” means that the name “wheel” (vaṭṭa) is applied to them, thus they are called “three wheels”; or, because they are parts of a wheel, they are called “wheels.
“Determined by the beginning and end of the joints” means determined by the prior and posterior [limits] of the joints.

“Whatever volition there is, that is becoming; the formations associated with volition are the exertion”—this is from this Exposition of the Knowledge of the Stability of Phenomena (dhammaṭṭhitiñāṇabhājanīya).
This was stated according to the *Paṭisambhidāmagga-pāḷi*, for therein it is said: "Volition is existence" (*cetanā bhavo*).

However, in the exposition of existence (*bhavaniddesa*), under the phrase "by way of meaning" (*sātthato*), it is shown according to the *Vibhaṅga-pāḷi*: "Volition alone is formations; but existence includes those associated with volition as well.
And: "In that context, what is the meritorious formation? It is wholesome volition pertaining to the sense sphere," and so forth.
For it is stated in the *Vibhaṅga-pāḷi* that volition (*cetanā*) is the nature of formations (*saṅkhārā*). In that context, the *Paṭisambhidā-pāḷi* states:

"They are formations because they are associated with volition and, being subject to result (*vipākadhamma*), they are conditioned by the function of forming (*abhisaṅkharaṇakicca*) which is called 'exertion' (*āyūhana*) and possesses result.

In the *Vibhaṅga-pāḷi*, however, it is said: "All karma leading to existence (*bhavagāmikamma*) is 'existence as karma' (*kammabhava*)," thus [defining them] by way of their being a condition for existence.
They are called "existence" (*bhava*) because they bring about rebirth-existence (*upapattibhava*) by way of leading toward existence, by being associated with and assisting karma,

and by having the nature of karma; furthermore, in the *Paṭisambhidāmagga*, volition (*cetanā*) is called "existence" because the function of producing rebirth-existence belongs preeminently to volition,
while in the *Vibhaṅga*, volition is [called] such because the function of constructing existence (*bhavābhisaṅkharaṇa*) belongs preeminently to volition.

By the passage beginning with “wholesome volition,” volition is stated to be “formations” (*saṅkhāra*); therefore, since both [terms] can appropriately be used for both meanings according to their respective methods, there is no contradiction here.
“Grasping” refers to sensual clinging (*kāmupādāna*) by way of its function; “clinging” refers to the other types.
“At the end of the accumulation” means at the conclusion of the accumulation mentioned in all three alternative interpretations of the meaning.

When the two alternative interpretations were stated regarding the formations of accumulation (*āyūhana-saṅkhāra*), he said "prior to that" (*tassa pubbabhāga*); when the third was stated, he said "associated with that" (*taṃsampayuttā*).

Because the mental activity of a young child is predominantly composed of the life-continuum (*bhavaṅga*) and is generally incapable of accumulating karma that produces another existence, it is said here:
"because of the ripening of the sense bases" (*paripakkattā āyatanānam*). By this, [it is shown that] there is delusion at the time of performing the deed.
This shows delusion as a condition for karma, not merely that which is associated with karma.
"Accumulations of karma" (kamma-sambhārā) refers to those things that accumulate and increase karma;

or, karma itself is the formative existence (saṅkhāra-bhava), while ignorance, craving, and clinging—which assist it—are the accumulations of karma; or else, karma is the existence that bestows rebirth-linking (paṭisandhi).
The volitional formations of accumulation (*āyūhana-saṅkhārā*) as previously described, as well as ignorance (*avijjā*) and so forth, are the "accumulations of kamma.
By applying the grammatical rule of "single remainder" (*ekasesa*)—that is, taking both "kamma" and "accumulations of kamma" as simply "accumulations of kamma"—he says "accumulations of kamma.
The ten factors are called "kamma" because, through their status as companions to kamma, they resemble kamma and assist it; thus they are designated as "kamma."
It is called "concise" (*saṅkhepa*) because ignorance and the rest, as well as consciousness and the rest, are condensed therein; that is, karma and its result.
Alternatively, it is called "concise" because karma and its result are thus condensed; that is, ignorance and the rest, and consciousness and the rest.

It should be understood that the singular number is used by virtue of the commonality of the state of being concise. Or, since the word "concise" is a designation for a part, "karma-concise" means the karmic portion.

"Thus arisen" means arising from karma; therein too, it is "thus arisen" in the sense that volitional formations arise from ignorance, or it is "thus arisen" by way of the three links and so forth—this is the meaning of the wheel of existence (*bhavacakra*).
"Ephemeral" (*ittara*) means subject to passing away; the meaning is that it is subject to destruction.
By this word "impermanent" (*anicca*), which indicates the possession of arising and passing away, and which indicates the attainment of change...
And by the word "moving" (*cala*), it indicates the negation of persisting for a period of time; by "unstable" (*adhuvam*), it indicates the negation of firmness and insubstantiality.
"Causes themselves are the requisites" means *hetusambhārā*. In the phrase "by way of occasion and by way of cause," what is stated here is the "occasion" (*ṭhāna*);
furthermore, the common cause for each respective thing is the "requisite" (*sambhāra*), while the uncommon cause is the "cause" (*hetu*). Thus.

The meaning is: when, in this way, it is taught that phenomena arise solely from causes, that by the cessation of causes the round of existence (*vaṭṭa*) is cut off, and that phenomena are taught for the sake of their cessation—then "the holy life" (*brahmacariya*) exists here; "and beings" (*satte ca*):
here the word *ca* has a conjunctive sense, meaning "thus the holy life exists, and eternalism and annihilationism do not occur. For in this way, [beings] are dependent upon causes.
When there is the mere arising of phenomena (dhamma), no sentient being (satta) is apprehended; and if such a being were apprehended, there would be either eternalism or annihilationism.
When that being is not apprehended, it is said that there is neither annihilation nor eternalism.
"From the source of truth" means from truth itself, or from the source of truths. "Wholesome and unwholesome kamma" refers to the discourse on the cycle of existence (vaṭṭa).

Because it is currently occurring, it is understood as being "with taints" (*sāsava*). "Without distinction" means that, without making a distinction between volition and those factors associated with volition, all that wholesome and unwholesome karma is called the "truth of origin" (*samudayasacca*); for [in the Sutta] it is said: "Craving...
and the remaining wholesome states that are with taints," thus without making a distinction between volition and what is associated with volition.
"Is stated" means that it is stated as the "truth of the origin" (*samudayasacca*) without making a distinction among the noble truths.

"In the bases" (*vatthūsu*) means in the objects (*ārammaṇesu*), or in the bases such as the eye and so forth which are to be concealed. "Because they are the foundation for sorrow and so forth" means because they are the causes thereof;
and together with the volitional formations (*saṅkhāra*) accompanied by ignorance established by them, they also serve as the condition for the manifestation of another existence.
This is the intended meaning. Since the death-consciousness (cuticitta) serves as the proximity-condition (anantarapaccaya) for rebirth-linking consciousness (paṭisandhiviññāṇa), it is said:

"And it is a condition for the manifestation of another existence. However, that death-consciousness, if devoid of ignorance (avijjā) and volitional formations (saṅkhāra), does not serve as a condition for another existence;
therefore, in order to show its companions, it is said: "Because it is the basis for sorrow and so forth. "In two ways" means:
It is twofold: by means of its own inherent nature (*sarasena*) and by way of being a condition for other phenomena (*dhammantarapaccayabhāvena*).

By the statement "with ignorance as condition, volitional formations arise" (*avijjāpaccayā saṅkhārā*), he demonstrates that volitional formations are dependently arisen; thereby he shows: "The question 'Who, indeed, performs the volitional formation?
is not a valid one. Thus, this is the prevention of the view of an agent (*kāraka*). It is the prevention of such views as these.
By this, he states the refutation of the view that [the self] "sobs, laments, and is afflicted. For grief and the rest are dependent on conditions and lack autonomy;
thus it is said: "With birth as condition, aging-and-death, grief... [and so forth] come to be. "Like a carbuncle and a boil" means:

like the small boils that arise upon a carbuncle while it is being cooked for the purpose of bursting the carbuncle; or like the boils that appear when a carbuncle breaks open in many ways. The transformations of the carbuncle include its swelling, discharging pus, and oozing, and so forth.
One whose eye is overcome by a cataract does not see forms; and even when seeing something, he sees it erroneously.
In the same way, one overcome by ignorance does not engage with or see suffering and the other truths, or engages with them wrongly.
Thus, ignorance is like the cataract, and because it is produced by oneself and is the cause of one’s own wandering in saṃsāra, it is like the worm.

Furthermore, formations are like the interior of a treasury; consciousness, which finds no footing without the appropriation of formations, is like a prince who finds no footing without the appropriation of a commander-in-chief.
Thus, the commonality here is the failure to find a footing without appropriation. By "the sign of rebirth," he refers to the object such as karma. By "conceiving":
It is so called because it makes [the object] its objective support, or because it cogitates by means of the associated initial application (*vitakka*).

Name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) is like an illusion (*māyā*) due to its manifold variety, such as gods, humans, beasts, birds, and so forth. The six sense bases (*saḷāyatana*) are like a thicket of trees, because they attain specific growth through specific bases.
It is so called because of the clashing of the sense bases—which consist of the subjects and their objects—due to their mutual orientation toward one another. Herein...

It should be understood that two similes each have been stated because the formations and the other [aggregates] share a resemblance in pairs with a treasure chest, a location, a navigator, and so forth.
"Deeply radiant" (*gambhīrāvabhāsa*) means that being deep itself, it shines, is manifest, and is seen.

"The state of having arisen and come about through the condition of birth" (*jātipaccayasambhūtasamudāgataṭṭha*) means the state of having arisen from the condition of birth and, being thus produced, having successively arrived higher and higher in accordance with its own conditions.
The meaning is "non-continuity. Alternatively, the meaning of "arisen" (*sambhūta*) and the meaning of "come-to-be" (*samudāgata*) together constitute the meaning of "arisen-and-come-to-be.
For it has been said: "Old age and death do not exist without birth as their cause, nor do they arise from anything other than birth.

Thus, the meaning of "arisen through the condition of birth" is stated. And in this way, the meaning of "come-to-be through conditions" is that whatever birth there is, in whatever manner it occurs...

The meaning is that there is a condition, which is the manifestation corresponding to that [condition]. Here, however, by "in forward and reverse order," he means that from the arising of the condition comes what is termed the "forward" (anuloma) arising of the conditioned, and from the cessation [of the condition] comes what is termed the "reverse" (paṭiloma) cessation.
Furthermore, proceeding from the beginning to the end is the forward order, and from the end [backwards]—
The "initial departure" refers to the reverse-order teaching beginning with, “What is the source of these four nutriments? and so forth;

and it refers to the summary of the two connections through both the reverse-order teaching starting from the middle and the forward-order teaching beginning with, “Dependent on the eye and forms, eye-consciousness arises;
the meeting of the three is contact; conditioned by contact is feeling,” and so forth, as well as [the section on] “things that fetter.”

In such passages as, "Bhikkhus, for one who dwells contemplating gratification in phenomena, craving increases; with craving as condition, clinging arises," there is a single connection and a twofold summary.

It is called "penetration" (*paṭivedha*) because the intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*) of ignorance and the other factors is penetrated. For it is said: "Of those various [factors], in those respective places..."
“Penetration (*paṭivedha*) is the non-perverted intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*), characterized by its own specific mark (*salakkhaṇa*), which is to be realized regarding the teachings already stated.
A portion of the unwholesome formations (*apuññābhisaṅkhāra*) is accompanied by lust (*sarāga*); the other is free from lust (*virāga*).
Alternatively, because it is not an antidote to lust, every unwholesome formation that increases lust is *sarāga*, while the other, being an antidote, is *virāga*. “For a long time, indeed, this—”

Monks, for the uninstructed worldling, consciousness—which is clung to, cherished, and grasped as "this is mine, this am I, this is my self"—is said to be the distinguished basis for the misapprehension of a self; thus, the meaning of emptiness regarding consciousness is profound.
This is because of the powerful adherence to the notions of agency, transmigration, and selfhood, such that [the worldling] insists: "The self cognizes; the self transmigrates."
The profundity consists in the non-exertion, the non-transference, and the manifestation of rebirth-linking;

and the dissociation [of name from form] arises because of the non-association of name with form and form with name, while the non-dissociation of name with name is to be understood through their co-arising and co-ceasing.

Furthermore, when non-dissociation is intended, it applies to form with form as well in the cases of the single and fourfold sense-sphere existences (ekacatuvokārabhava). Alternatively, [this refers to] name-and-form in those same single and fourfold sense-sphere existences.

The distinction between them should be understood as their mutual separation due to not functioning together, and their non-separation due to functioning together within the fivefold existence (*pañcavokārabhava*).

The sense of "predominance" (*adhipati*) refers to the state of being a faculty-condition (*indriya-paccaya*). The meanings of "world" (*loka*) and so forth, which were stated in the passage, "This is a world; these are doors;

this is a field," should be applied to the five [faculties] beginning with the eye. Because the mind-base (*manāyatana*) also disintegrates, [it is called a world] in relation to mental contact (*manosamphassa*) and the rest.

And these meanings arise precisely because they function as doors and fields. Illumination—characterized by the suitability for manifesting forms and so forth that have come into the range [of the senses]—is the objective state (*visayibhāva*) of the eye and the other [senses], while for the mind-base (*manāyatana*), it is the act of cognizing.

The sense of "striking together" (*saṅghaṭṭana*) applies specifically to the five [types of contact], such as eye-contact, though it should also be applied to the other six. Furthermore, touching (*phusana*) is the intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*) of contact (*phassa*).

Contact is its function; the others are its modes of manifestation. It is described by way of its function as "the experiencing of the flavor of the object," and by way of its characteristic as "that which is felt.
Because of the strong tendency toward the misconception that "a self feels," the meaning of "lifeless" (nijjīva) regarding feeling is profound.
The being-felt of a lifeless feeling is "lifeless-feeling"; it is precisely this lifeless-feeling.

The meaning is the state of being felt by that which is devoid of a living soul (*nijjīva*). The meaning of grasping (*ādāna*) is common to all four types of clinging (*upādāna*); the meaning of seizing (*gahaṇa*) applies to sensual clinging (*kāmupādāna*), while for the other three, it has the sense of dogmatic adherence and so forth.
Furthermore, because of the expression "the wilderness of views," it also has the sense of the difficulty of transcending views.
Alternatively, because they are firmly grasped, the sense of being "difficult to transcend" should be applied to all four [nutriments].

Regarding the compound "throwing into the womb, destinies, stations, and abodes," one should understand that there is no elision of the locative case-ending; therefore, it forms a compound with the words *āyūhana* (accumulation) and *abhisaṅkharaṇa* (volitional formation).
In the phrase "the aging-and-death factor has death as its preponderance," the profound aspects such as destruction (*khaya*) and so forth are shown precisely in the context of death.
For aging (*jarā*) is the occurrence of the state of being broken and so forth through the complete exhaustion of ever-new [states];

or rather, it should be understood that the meaning of "exhaustion" (*khaya*) is stated for aging. For it is appropriate to say that "exhaustion" is the departure from the state of being new. The meaning of "transformation" (*vipariṇāma*) applies to both.

Alternatively, the state of exhaustion and passing away (*khayavaya*) should be applied to aging by way of the continuity of the stream, while the state of dissolution and transformation (*bhedavipariṇāmatā*) should be applied to death by way of conventional and momentary [analysis].

*Atthanayā* means the methods (*nayā*) for meanings (*atthā*). Because unity and so forth are led (*nīyanti*) or conveyed (*gammenti*) by way of such states as ignorance and other meanings, unity and the rest are called their "methods.

For they are called "methods" (*nayā*) because they lead (*nīyanti*). Alternatively, the meanings themselves, when being led—that is, when being known—by way of unity and so forth, are called "meaning-methods" (*atthanayā*).
Or, they are called "methods" (*nayā*) because meanings are led by means of them; thus, meanings are led by unity and the rest.
They are led by the words beginning with "one" (*eka*), therefore the meanings such as unity and so forth are called "modes of meaning" (*atthanaya*).
By way of the non-interruption of the continuum, the seed reaches the state of a tree and proceeds as a tree; thus it is spoken of as "unity.
In this way, here too, it shows that the non-interruption of the continuum of ignorance and the other factors constitutes "unity."

"Of one whose continuum is indeed broken" means that by grasping at diversity devoid of continuity, one who perceives "one being has perished" and "another being has arisen" adopts the view of annihilationism (*ucchedadṛṣṭi*).
"From whatever [source]" means: if the arising of one thing could occur from another, why would oil not arise from sand or milk from sugarcane?
Therefore, there is no cause for anything whatsoever; thus one adopts the view of causelessness (*ahetukadṛṣṭi*), even though [a cause] does not exist.

It should be understood that, according to the circumstances, one adopts the doctrine of determinism (niyativāda) because oil, milk, bodies, and so forth arise from sesame seeds, cows, semen, blood, and so on, due to their fixed causality. Why?
Because no one, having shattered this wheel of existence (bhavacakra), has transcended the fear of saṃsāra even in a dream.
The connection is with the word "exists" (*atthi*). "Difficult to overcome" (*durabhiyāna*) means difficult to transcend.
"Like the wheel of a thunderbolt" (*asanivicakkaṃ ivā*) means like the circle of a thunderbolt; for that indeed exists only as a crushing, never existing without crushing.
In the same way, the wheel of existence (*bhavacakkam*) is called "constant crushing" because it invariably produces suffering.

Having split [the world] with the sword of knowledge, he has transcended the fear of *saṃsāra*; demonstrating that there is no one else who has done so, he said, "And this too has been said," and so forth.

"Tantākulaka" means a tangled mass of threads; those born like a tangled mass of threads are "tantākulakajāta," meaning they are excessively entangled by defilements (*kilesa*), karma, and its results (*vipāka*). A nest for the bird *guṇā* is a "guṇāguṇḍika. Due to the absence of growth...
One does not transcend the fourfold *apāya*— namely, the state of misery because it is a destination of suffering, an evil rebirth because it is a miserable heap,
and a downfall because it is a precipice— nor does one transcend *saṃsāra*, as described in the passage beginning with "the succession of aggregates. Alternatively,
the entire *saṃsāra* itself is designated here by the names *apāya* and so forth according to its meanings such as increase and decrease, solely because it is a mass of suffering.
The commentary on the Discourse on the Wheel of Existence is finished.
The commentary on the Suttanta-bhājaniya is finished.
2. The commentary on the Abhidhamma-bhājaniya.
243. Dependent origination (paṭiccasamuppāda) is explained by way of a conceptualization of meanings that are vast and extensive, like the earth and space.

For it is as if it were spreading out and expanding the earth and space—which are themselves unspread and unextended—by being spread out and expanded in common to all beings and all minds, rather than being confined to each individual mind.

The Blessed One demonstrates this by means of the *Suttantabhājanīya*. In that context, the phrase "by way of various states of consciousness" (*nānācittavasena*) is said with reference to the fact that the conditions and conditionally arisen phenomena—both those not co-nascent and those co-nascent—that reside within various states of consciousness have been shown.
These methods (*nayā*) possess nine root-terms, thus they are "nine-rooted methods. By each individual method, there are four sets of four sections.
It is said, "because they are included," but here it should be stated, "by each respective tetrad.
For the sections on the tetrads of method (*naya*) are established here because the tetrads shown possess the nature of methods.
1. Commentary on the Tetrad of Conditions (*paccaya*).

Without taking ignorance as a constituent factor, he says, "No, because it is not a constituent factor," referring to those factors such as "with ignorance as condition, volitional formations" and so forth, which are stated as conditions and conditionally arisen phenomena following that [ignorance].

And having done so, in the *Niddesa* he treats ignorance separately by asking, "In this context, what is ignorance? and then asks, "In this context, what is the volitional formation conditioned by ignorance? and so forth.
The formations and so forth, which possess their respective conditions, have been excluded. Among the three modes, the first section enters into the second section and so on;
because it is common to all the various distinctions such as specific conditions, it includes those particular sections and is therefore called "comprehensive" (*sabbasaṅgāhaka*).
For the first section alone does not refer merely to the sixth sense-base (*chaṭṭhāyatana*), but rather to both name (*nāma*) and contact (*phassa*).
The name [of the condition] is mentioned not only for the sake of the sixth base (*chaṭṭhāyatana*), but also for the sake of the contact (*phassa*);

it is stated as having omitted the factor of the sixth base in order to show that specific distinction in meaning by which the teaching of the *Mahānidāna Sutta* proceeds, and not because of a complete suppression of all factors.
Thus, its inclusion is stated in the second section.
"In each of the four sections" means in each individual section. "Otherwise" means that it is stated as "volitional formation" (*saṅkhāra*) in a manner different from the *Suttantabhājanīya*.
"Not stated" refers to the fact that in those four sections—such as "form" and "the six sense bases"—sorrow and the rest are not mentioned, whereas they are mentioned in the *Suttantabhājanīya*.
It should be understood that what was stated there is stated here "otherwise," namely as the "sixth sense base."

"By way of being common to all instances" means, according to the method already stated, by way of being common to all occasions, or by way of being common to all states of existence (bhava) which are the bases for the occurrence of consciousness.

Since even the triad of aggregates [feeling, perception, and formations] is equally both the fruit and the condition for consciousness in the absence [of the fourth aggregate, matter], he says "without distinction.
However, because of the statement, "The meeting of the three is contact," consciousness is a specific condition for contact; therefore...

Contact is the distinguished fruit; and although the other factors associated with the condition possess the status of being nutriment-conditions (*āhāra-paccaya*), the mental volition (*manosañcetanā*) has the distinguished function of providing the nutriment of consciousness (*viññāṇāhāra*).
Thus, volitional formations (*saṅkhāra*) are its distinguished condition. "Merely non-mind-moments" means devoid of the measure of a mind-moment.
"Its meaning" refers to the meaning of that which was stated beginning with ignorance (*avijjā*), as explained in the commentary on the *Suttantabhājanīya*.
It should be understood in the same manner as previously stated.

Regarding the phrase "the root-factors, etc.": here, that tetrad in which the word *hetuka* (root-factor) is mentioned should be understood as being called "root-factor" because it is associated with the term *hetuka*.
The word *hetu* (root-cause) indicates the destination (*gati*) by way of precluding the state of being dissociated while not yet having become dissociated.
It is stated that the "tetrad of causes" (*hetukacatukka*) is explained by way of the condition of non-disappearance (*avigatapaccaya*), meaning that [the cause] is indeed a destiny (*gati*).
Regarding the phrase "in three ways, four ways, or five ways," the word "or" (*vā*) should be understood as also providing the alternative "or in six ways.

For concentration (*samādhi*) is a condition by way of the three common conditions: the jhāna, the faculty, and the path. Clinging (*upādāna*) [is a condition] for existence (*bhava*) by way of the path-condition (*maggapaccaya*).

"Seven" refers to [the factors] excluding sensual clinging (*kāmupādāna*). However, the manner in which sensual clinging serves as a condition for existence (*bhava*) has already been explained under craving (*taṇhā*), and thus it is not mentioned here.

The intention [of the text] is that, according to the statement "they act as conditions by way of the co-nascence condition (*sahajātapaccaya*)" in this tetrad, they are conditions. This is the meaning.
For indeed, there is nowhere a condition that does not exist for its own dependently arisen [phenomenon] according to its respective conditions;

however, because this tetrad is stated specifically by way of the co-nascent condition (*sahajāta-paccaya*), they say that only this [condition] applies here. "The first section" should be stated as "the first tetrad.
Regarding the absence of such [conditions] for existence (*bhava*) and so forth: if the first tetrad were [to apply] solely by way of the co-nascent condition...
Existence (bhava) has been stated [as a condition] for birth (jāti), yet birth is not a co-nascent condition (sahajāta-paccaya) for death.

Just as in the case of the "non-disappearance tetrad" (avigata-catukka) and others, it is not stated that "birth is conditioned by existence, having existence as its cause," and so forth—because existence and the other factors lack the status of a non-disappearance condition and so on—likewise here too, it would not be proper to say "birth is conditioned by existence," and so forth. For the very mention of a "condition" (paccaya) for them...

Because there is no other statement here indicating a specific condition—as there is, for example, in the case of the "arisen-together" (sahajāta), "indicative," "included," and "not-disappeared" tetrads—this tetrad was not stated by way of the arisen-together condition alone;
nor is it the case that it was not stated, nor do existence and the others constitute arisen-together conditions. Therefore, this tetrad was not stated solely by way of the arisen-together condition.
Furthermore, since the remaining conditions are possible, this [tetrad] should not be combined with the phrase "of existence and so forth."

This was stated with reference to the general possibility of ignorance and the other factors existing together through co-nascence (*sahajāta*), as well as their existence through the remaining modes of conditionality.

This is the meaning here: since there is no other statement indicating a specific distinction among the conditions, it might be said that no conditions for ignorance and the others exist apart from co-nascence; thus, this tetrad would be undertaken solely on the basis of the condition of co-nascence.
And it is not that these do not occur; therefore, this [formula] has not been undertaken in that way.
It is stated, "In the Mahānidāna Sutta, dependent origination is taught with eleven factors," and therein, in the passage beginning, "With name-and-form as condition, consciousness;
with consciousness as condition, name-and-form; with name as condition, contact," it occurs twice.
When name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) is taken as a single unit, it is called the ninefold [dependent origination]; when taken as two units, it is called the tenfold.

However, it should be understood that it is stated thus because, when ignorance (*avijjā*) and volitional formations (*saṅkhāra*)—which are mentioned elsewhere—are joined for the purpose of showing the three time-periods (*addhattaya*), it becomes elevenfold.
Regarding the phrase "for the purpose of encompassing the teaching of the Mahānidāna Sutta," for in that [sutta], the eye-base (*cakkhāyatana*) and so forth [are included].

Just as, having included the sixth base within both form and name, the phrase "contact has a condition consisting of name-and-form" was stated to show the complete condition for contact in terms of form as well as the complete condition in terms of name, so too here,
by showing the specific distinction demonstrated therein, this is for the purpose of encompassing that teaching regarding dependent origination occurring within a single moment of consciousness.
The meaning is that by including the sixth base (chaṭṭhāyatana) within "name" (nāma), it is stated: "With name as condition, contact.

Because this was taught with reference to the location where matter arises, the words "of this" (*imassa*) are understood as an ellipsis, and not [as referring] to the previous [bases]; for this very reason he said, "For this...
and so forth. And here, by way of the mode of birth (*yoni*), even those born from moisture (*saṃsedaja*) are included among the "spontaneously born" (*opapātika*) by virtue of having complete bases.

It should be understood that [the term] is stated having been made [complete]. Or rather, in order to show the womb of all-perfected sense bases (*āyatana*) through the womb of striving (*padhāna*), it is said, "of those born spontaneously" (*opapātikānam*).
For it is precisely by way of this demonstration of inclusion that even in the *Dhammahadayavibhaṅga*, the mention of "those born spontaneously" and "ghosts" (*petā*) and so forth was made;
the mention of "moisture-born" (*saṃsedaja*) was not. Within a single moment of consciousness, by means of the six sense bases...
There is no occurrence of contact, nor is there, for a single unwholesome contact, any sense-base—excluding the sixth sense-base—that occurs simultaneously and serves as its condition;
furthermore, since the object-condition (*ārammaṇa-paccaya*) is not a productive factor here, it is not included.
Therefore, this is stated for the purpose of showing that one cannot say, "contact [arises] with the six sense-bases as condition."
He said, “But because of this...,” and so forth.
Although the six sense bases (saḷāyatana) may arise for some even during the first two stages of the womb, they do not arise during the stage of the embryo (kalala) and so on;
therefore, he said, “because of their constant non-arising. However, in the latter two stages of the womb, for those in whom they do arise, they arise constantly.
"Thus" (iti) means: whatever distinction there is from this tetrad or from the method (naya).
The commentary on the Tetrad of Conditions (paccayacatukka) is finished.
2. Commentary on the Tetrad of Causes (hetucatukka).
244. "At the very moment of birth" means that it exists beyond that point; this is the sense.

Because there is no fixed rule for the non-disappearance condition (*avigata-paccaya*), the inclusion of "existence" (*bhava*) as the cause for "clinging" (*upādāna*) was not made. One should connect this by understanding that because the non-disappearance condition does not exist, the inclusion of "existence" as the cause for "birth" (*jāti*) and so forth was not made.
However, just as in the case of consciousness which is not perceived as long as its basis (*vatthu*) exists...
The physical basis (vatthu) remains a non-disappearance condition even for consciousness that arises subsequent to it;
likewise, clinging is a non-disappearance condition for birth and so forth as they are comprised within existence, and existence may be a non-disappearance condition for birth.

If this were not the case, then because birth and so forth are included within the aggregate of formations (saṅkhārakkhandha), consciousness would be a non-disappearance condition for mentality (nāma), and mentality, due to its occurrence at a different moment, would be a non-disappearance condition for the sixth sense base (chaṭṭhāyatana).
"Na siyā" (it would not be) means that, just as here, there too the mention of a cause should not be made;

therefore, it cannot be established that the non-apprehension of birth and so forth exists only until grasping (*upādāna*), nor can it be maintained that the absence of becoming (*bhava*) at the very moment of birth is the cause.

This is because the conditioned characteristics (*saṅkhatalakkhaṇa*), such as birth and the rest—which are phenomena lacking intrinsic nature (*asabhāvadhamma*)—are themselves included within "becoming."

Furthermore, because a dharma that lacks intrinsic nature (*asabhāva*) does not exist as a distinct state of being in the ultimate sense (*paramattha*), conditions such as cause and so forth do not exist;

thus, clinging (*upādāna*) is not invariably a non-disappearance condition (*avigatapaccaya*) for becoming (*bhava*). However, becoming is not a non-disappearance condition for birth (*jāti*), nor is birth a non-disappearance condition for aging-and-death (*jarāmaraṇa*).
Therefore, due to the absence of a fixed rule regarding non-disappearance conditions and the non-existence of such a condition among becoming and the others—[the following applies].
It is logical that the inclusion of "cause" was not made [in the definition of nutriment].
But would it not then follow that the statement, "Name has consciousness as its cause; the sixth base has name as its cause," could not be said?
For there is no non-disappearance condition for birth and so forth—which are included within name—for anything else, nor is there the state of being a non-disappearance condition for anything else.
Is it because they are non-substantial phenomena (*asabhāvadhamma*)? No, because they are not included under the term "name" (*nāma*).

For "name" is defined by the function of bending (*namana*); and since that function belongs only to substantial phenomena (*sabhāvadhamma*), the three aggregates that constitute substantial phenomena are alone called "name.
Therefore, the inclusion of "root" (*hetuka*) there is appropriate; however, here, "existence" (*bhava*) is that which comes to be (*bhavati*), and birth and the other [factors] do not.
They do not occur through the application [of the formula] "with existence as condition, birth comes to be; with birth as condition, aging-and-death comes to be.

Therefore, because there is no fixed rule that birth and the rest are included under "existence" simply by virtue of existing—as *saṅkhārā* are included under "formations" (*saṅkharaṇa*)—the term "cause" was not employed in the manner previously stated, on account of the absence of such a restriction.
With the words "But some," etc., he states the opinion of the Elder Revata. For here, the immaterial aggregates are included under "existence" (bhava).
Indeed, it is said: "In this context, what is existence conditioned by clinging? Excluding clinging itself, it is the aggregate of feeling... [and so on] ...the aggregate of consciousness.
It was stated, "Because there is no passage stating [them]," yet even though such a passage exists, birth and the other factors possess their own intrinsic natures just like clinging.
It is logical that no separate category [of existence] should be established simply because there is no such distinct entity to be established as "not being.

However, it has been stated: "Birth is for those who are being born, and aging-and-death is for those who have been born; thus, 'with existence as condition, birth arises; with birth as condition, aging-and-death arises.

Just as in the case of the statement, "With name as condition, contact arises," where it is asked: "In this context, what is name? With the exception of contact, the aggregate of feeling... [and so forth]."
The aggregate of consciousness. This is called "name. [In the formula] "With name-and-form as condition, the six sense bases," there is name and there is form.
Therein, what is name? The aggregate of feeling, the aggregate of perception, and the aggregate of mental formations.
This is called "name. Therein, what is form? The four great elements and that form dependent upon which the mind-element [arises].

And when it is said, "The mind-consciousness element occurs; this is called form," the locus for what ought to be stated regarding that name-and-form which is the condition for contact and the six sense bases has been indicated.

Likewise, even though there are distinctions between what is to be excluded and what is to be included, it cannot be said that there is no locus for what ought to be stated concerning that existence which is the condition for birth.
The commentary on the Tetrad of Causes is finished.
4. Commentary on the Tetrad of Mutuality. 246.
Because it is stated without limitation, clinging (*upādāna*) is included within becoming (*bhava*); therefore, there is no separate [category] for clinging that has arisen as a condition.
To show that because of the absence of a persisting entity, it cannot be said that "clinging has existence as its condition," he says, "But since existence is without limitation," and so forth.
If this were the case, it would follow that one could not say "consciousness has mentality as its condition";
however, the intention is that "mentality" is taken here only as something limited, being both that which has arisen from conditions and that which serves as a condition.

Just as in such passages as "with name as condition, the sixth base; with name as condition, contact," where name is taken while excluding that which has arisen by way of condition, so too here it is not impossible to take existence while excluding that which has arisen by way of condition in the phrase "with existence as condition, clinging.
Therefore, just as there is no fixed rule regarding the non-disappearance of the condition for clinging...

It should be understood that because the necessity of mutual conditionality does not exist in the case of *bhava* (existence) according to the method previously stated, it was not said: "With *bhava* as condition, there is also *upādāna* (clinging).
And here, by "mutual condition," the associated, dissociated, and presence conditions (*sampayutta-vippayutta-atthipaccaya*) may be intended. "With *nāmarūpa* (name-and-form) as condition..."
For it is said, "consciousness," yet the physical basis (vatthu) is not a mutuality condition for unwholesome consciousness; rather, it is a pre-arisen dissociation condition.

Likewise, it is said, "name-and-form also has the sixth base as its condition," yet the sixth base is not a mutuality condition for the eye-base, the [other] sense-base supports, or mind-originated matter; rather, it is a post-arisen dissociation condition.
The commentary on the Mutual Tetrad is finished.
247. Commentary on the Matrix of Methods Rooted in Formations, etc.:
"Because there is no other previously unstated condition for existence (*bhava*) to be mentioned, the method rooted in existence [is not treated here]."

It has been said [that ignorance is conditioned by name]. If that were so, then statements such as "ignorance is conditioned by the sixth sense-base" and others rooted in the sixth sense-base and so forth would not be tenable.
For in the statement "ignorance is conditioned by name," it is said that all four aggregates are "name" when they are conditioned by ignorance.
In this regard, the intended meaning might be as follows: [it refers to] specific types of name, such as the sixth sense-base and so forth.

It should be stated that ignorance (*avijjā*) functions as a condition; therefore, [the conditions] rooted in the six sense bases (*chaṭṭhāyatana*) and so forth have been mentioned. However, whatever name serves as a condition for ignorance could likewise be stated here in the phrase "ignorance conditioned by existence" (*bhava-paccayā avijjā*), as there would be no difference in what is being asserted. Consequently, it was not mentioned because it is not something new.
Furthermore, by the inclusion of the term "existence" (*bhava*) here, all phenomena (*dhammas*) possessing intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*) that serve as conditions for ignorance are intended.
It should be understood that [ignorance] was not mentioned because it would lack novelty; one would not say "one should grasp birth and so forth" [if they were already included].

It was asked, "Could it also have been stated that 'with ignorance as condition, ignorance [arises]'? However, just as when it is said "with name as condition, contact," it is not stated "with contact as condition, contact," because the condition is grasped by excluding what has arisen from that condition, so too here it would not be stated; therefore—

Since the word "existence" (*bhava*) functions as a general term for both phenomena that possess intrinsic nature and phenomena that lack intrinsic nature by way of their state of being, it cannot be said that this [word] is not a condition for ignorance.
Therefore, it should be understood that the method based on existence (*bhavamūlakanaya*) was not stated here.
Just as in the case of "with clinging as condition, existence," the word "existence" refers to a specific portion of existence when it has not been separately grasped previously.
When stated from the beginning for the purpose of clarifying the conditions, it indicates them without remainder; this is not the case with the word *nāma*.

For these linguistic expressions (*nirutti*) possess such a nature. It should be understood that it was said, "It might also have been stated as 'with ignorance as condition, [there is] ignorance,'" according to this very intention.
And by this same intention, it was said, "Because existence (*bhava*) is without exception, clinging (*upādāna*) is also [conditioned] by existence."
"It was not stated"—this meaning should be understood as having been stated in the section on the mutuality condition (*aññamañña-paccaya*).

In that context, by the phrase "because they have been cut off," it is as if the status of birth, aging, and death as conditions for ignorance is affirmed. However, for those things currently being born, there is birth;

it is not that birth is [the condition] for those currently being born. And for that which is currently aging and passing away, there is aging and death; it is not that aging and death are [the condition] for that which is currently aging and passing away.

Birth and the other [links] do not serve as conditions for ignorance within a single moment of consciousness; therefore, because they are impossible [in that context], methods rooted in them were not included.
However, since there is indeed a sequential order [of arising], it should be understood that the phrase "because it has been cut off therein" was stated.
For this very reason, he said "Moreover... and so forth.
The commentary on the *mātikā* is finished.
Commentary on the Exposition of the Unwholesome (248–249).
[Objection: "Would it not follow that clinging (*upādāna*) becomes a condition for clinging? For is this not a fault? Indeed, sensual clinging (*kāmupādāna*)..."
Is it not true that view-fuel (*diṭṭhupādāna*) is a condition for the other [fuel]? True;

however, because sense-desire fuel (*kāmupādāna*) is already included by the mention of craving (*taṇhā*), and because—unlike the case of name-and-form—it lacks a specific conditional relationship, it is only view that is taken as "fuel" here, being the condition for existence (*bhava*) which itself has craving as its condition.
Thus, this fault has been stated. And because, in the place of "fuel"...

The conditionally arisen and the condition are one and the same; therefore, as in the explanations of "contact has name as its condition" and "the six sense bases have name-and-form as their condition," the condition is not analyzed separately in the explanation of "existence has clinging as its condition.
Or, even though sensual clinging is included by virtue of being a condition for existence, if it were not stated [specifically] as "excluding clinging,"...

He shows that the phrase "excluding clinging" (*ṭhapetvā upādānaṃ*) was stated in order to preclude the possibility that sense-desire clinging (*kāmupādāna*) could be a condition for sense-desire clinging, or that view (*diṭṭhi*) could be a condition for view—thereby avoiding the fallacy of a condition being the very same as its own effect. 252.

Consciousness is the producer of mind-originated matter (*cittasamuṭṭhānarūpa*) which supports the eye-base (*cakkhāyatana*) and so forth; [it is] the nutriment-condition (*āhārapaccaya*) for the accumulation (*upacaya*) of the eye-base and the rest.
Regarding the statement "condition," with the intention that even that which does not produce it [is a condition], he said, "of whichever mind-originated materiality," and so forth.

The phrase "for even those" means that for the temperature, nutriment, and continuity [materialities] as well, consciousness is indeed a condition by way of the supporting, originating, and postnascent conditions.

254. *Yathānurūpaṃ* (accordingly): the great elements (*mahābhūta*) are the co-nascent and other conditions for the five [mental aggregates]; the physical basis (*vatthu*) is the pre-nascent and other conditions for the sixth;
mentality (*nāma*) is the post-nascent and other conditions for the five; and [mentality] is the co-nascent and other conditions for the sixth. This is "accordingly. 264. *Yassa* (of which):
this should be construed as "of whichever arisen mentality or consciousness there exists the state of being a concomitant condition (*sampayutta-paccaya*)."
272. By stating, “even with contact as condition,” the occurrence of the very name that ought to be described by way of having contact as its condition is shown through its own arisen condition;
thus, [the author] says “tathāpi” (even so) and so forth, demonstrating that there is no purpose in stating again “excluding contact.”
280. Since there is no resolve (*adhimokkha*) either, the connection is that the basis for clinging (*upādāna*) is indeed abandoned.

However, the reason why the word [“resolve”] is included for the sake of completing the meter is stated to be the absence of craving (*taṇhā*) in those [states] accompanied by mental grief (*domanassasahagata*);

thus, its connection with that [absence of craving] should be applied. “In all cases” refers to the third consciousness and so forth, in such passages as “with craving as condition, there is resolve.”
The text has been abbreviated by showing only the distinction in the answers. "Below" refers to the sections on the arising of consciousness and so forth.
The commentary on the Exposition of the Unwholesome is finished.
[Now begins] the commentary on the Exposition of the Wholesome and the Indeterminate.
292. *Pasāda* means faith (*saddhā*).

306. From such statements as, “Non-greed (*alobha*) is the source for the arising of kamma,” it follows that the wholesome roots (*kusalamūla*), being active, are the sources of volitional formations (*saṅkhāra*);
they are not [the sources] in the case of results (*vipāka*) cast forth by the momentum of kamma, which are mere reflections of the kamma accompanied by non-greed and so forth.

Non-greed and the other [wholesome roots] occurring [in this way] should be understood as being "fallen into the stream" (sotapatita) because they lack a causal basis, just as in the case of the fivefold sensory consciousnesses (*pañcaviññāṇa*).
Functional states (*kiriyadhamma*) should be known as having abandoned the ground of ignorance (*parihīnāvijjāṭṭhāna*), precisely because they are mere functionings and thus lack a karmic cause.
Why was it stated that the third and fourth sections are impossible? Is it because visual consciousness and the others [do not arise] from the accumulation of the eye-base and so forth?

Are they not postnascent conditions? They are; however, it should be understood that the statement "because of impossibility" was made with reference to the non-arising of the mind-originated [matter] that supports that [consciousness].

But by way of co-nascent and postnascent consciousness, even then there is mentality-materiality conditioned by consciousness; and by way of the co-nascent and prenascent material eye, etc., which are co-nascent and prenascent with the postnascent mentality, [there is also materiality conditioned by consciousness].
And because the six sense bases are obtained through the condition of name-and-form (*nāmarūpa-paccaya*), the third and fourth sections are not impossible.
The commentary on the exposition of the wholesome and the indeterminate is finished.
[Now begins] the commentary on the exposition of the wholesome rooted in ignorance (*avijjāmūlaka-kusala*).

334. "By way of delusion" means: with respect to the wholesome fruit, because it possesses danger due to its impermanence and other characteristics—being like the seed of a poison-tree that has a sweet taste—and with respect to the wholesome state that produces it, because one does not see its disadvantage. Development for the purpose of transcending is "development as transcending";
or, development that consists in transcending by means of substitution of opposites (*tadaṅga*) and suppression (*vikkhambhana*) is "development as transcending."

Likewise, the statement "they are not found here" is said with reference specifically to the absence of ignorance as a condition for volitional formations (saṅkhāra) in its aspects such as non-disappearance;

however, since volitional formations and so forth do serve as non-disappearance conditions for consciousness and so forth, one cannot say that it is impossible to apply the formulation: "volitional formation conditioned by ignorance," "consciousness conditioned by volitional formation," "having volitional formation as its cause," and so on.
