Thus, the tetrad of non-disappearance and the others are also applicable.

These [terms] are not found here. For the method has been shown by way of application according to what is available, starting with: "With consciousness as condition, name-and-form; 'name' is that which is associated with consciousness," and so forth.
The commentary on the description of wholesome states rooted in ignorance is finished.
Now begins the commentary on the description of resultant states rooted in the wholesome.
343. It was said: "But there is nothing at all that needs to be said regarding asynchronous (nānākkhaṇika) kamma as a condition.

Does this mean that both wholesome roots and unwholesome roots are conditions by way of kamma-condition? They are not. However, they act as a condition just like kamma itself when it is conjoined with volition (cetanā) which has become a kamma-condition.
Therefore, it should be understood that this was stated because they have, as it were, attained a state of unity [with that volition]. Just as...

Since karma does not produce a result (vipāka) without the roots of the wholesome and unwholesome, these are called "decisive support" (upanissaya) for the result by way of a figurative sense (pariyāya).

Likewise, because they become unified and conjoined with karma, they serve as conditions for those things born of karma; thus, their status as a "kamma-condition" (kammapaccaya) is stated by way of a figurative sense.
"This" should be construed as "this root-of-the-wholesome condition and this root-of-the-unwholesome condition."

Since the roots of ignorance—both wholesome and unwholesome—are not the producers of functional (kiriyā) states, just as they are the producers of wholesome and unwholesome resultant states, it is said that "they do not obtain the status of decisive support (upanissaya).

Attention (manasikāra) also does not act as a decisive support for ignorance, in the same way that wholesome and unwholesome states do, because it merely serves to introduce the impulsion process (javanavīthi);
rather, it is merely the revolving of the life-continuum (bhavaṅga) for the purpose of the occurrence of those things that have ignorance as their decisive support.

For those actions in which ignorance has been abandoned, ignorance is neither their producer nor their cause; it is merely their object (*ārammaṇa*). And having established this, [the following statements are justified]:

"A wholesome state is a condition for an indeterminate state by way of the decisive support condition (*upanissaya-paccaya*)," and "A state subject to ripening is a condition for a state that is neither subject to ripening nor subject to non-ripening by way of the decisive support condition."
And thus, in such cases as these, the functional states (*kiriyā*) are not mentioned by way of being a decisive support condition (*upanissaya-paccaya*).

Furthermore, by way of the formula "with ignorance as condition, volitional formations arise" (*avijjāpaccayā saṅkhārā*), the wholesome method rooted in ignorance is stated; by way of the formula "with volitional formations as condition, consciousness arises" (*saṅkhārapaccayā viññāṇaṃ*), the resultant method rooted in both the wholesome and the unwholesome is stated. However, the functional states are not included by the mention of "volitional formations," nor...

And it should be understood that because consciousness does not undergo grasping through the act of grasping, the method of action (kriyā-naya) rooted in that [grasping] is not applicable, and thus it was not mentioned.

"Due to its manifold divisions" means that in the first method, the root terms such as ignorance (*avijjā*) and so forth—which exist for a single moment of consciousness—are apprehended by way of being various conditions, such as co-nascent conditions (*sahajāta-paccaya*), at the end of the action; therefore, by way of those conditions, the root terms beginning with the ninefold [set] are [included].
The intention is that [the classification] is by way of the methods (*naya*), or else by way of the four tetrads in their many varieties.
Regarding the phrase "and in the resultants of the wholesome and unwholesome," it should rather be stated as "in the wholesome and unwholesome, and in the results of the wholesome and unwholesome.
For in the first and last methods, the mode of conditionality (*paccayākāra*) has been explained; it is said "as manifoldly or as a unity" for the purpose of demonstrating that.
Furthermore, in the later method (*pacchimanaya*), the mode of conditionality (*paccayākāra*) is not explained through its many divisions; rather, it is stated as "in one way" (*ekadhāva*).
"In one way" means by way of the single conditionality of the root-terms (*mūlapada*), or by way of a single method (*naya*), meaning in a single manner;
or the intention is that it is according to the first tetrad alone. Regarding the "division of dhamma-conditions," this refers to ignorance (*avijjā*) and so forth.
In the diversity of the conditional relations of phenomena (*dhamma*): in the diversity of the conditions for phenomena such as aging and death (*jarāmaraṇa*) by way of birth (*jāti*) and so forth;

or in the diversity of the momentary conditions such as ignorance (*avijjā*) for phenomena such as contact (*phassa*) delimited by the time of the arising of this or that state of consciousness. Regarding the sequence of the scriptures and so forth: the sequence of the scriptures... [etc. ...the sequence of practice (*paṭipattikkama*).
For in the mode of conditions (*paccayākāra*), the mastery of the texts, the hearing of their meaning, and the reflection on the meaning of the texts [are taught] as "aging and death..."
He employs the term "successive order" because the practice of meditation must be carried out in sequence, beginning with [the contemplation]: "It is impermanent, conditioned... [and so on]...

subject to cessation," and so forth. "From that" means from that which generates the various distinctions of knowledge; there is no other further duty. For the making of an end to suffering is dependent upon that.

355. "Three foundations of mindfulness" (tayo satipaṭṭhānā): this provides an extraction of the meaning of the term *satipaṭṭhāna*, rather than a demonstration of the meaning of the term *satipaṭṭhāna* as it is used here in the text.

They conduct themselves accordingly. Some disciples listen attentively... [and so on] ...and they do not act contrary to the Teacher’s instruction.
In this regard, monks, the Tathāgata is neither pleased nor does he experience pleasure;
he is neither displeased nor does he experience displeasure. He experiences neither pleasure nor displeasure.

"Furthermore... 'to happiness. His disciples listen attentively... [as before] ... they conduct themselves accordingly.

“Mindful and clearly comprehending. This, monks, is the third.

Thus, being undrenched by aversion and attachment, the constant presence of mindfulness, and the transcendence of both—these are called the foundations of mindfulness (*satipaṭṭhāna*). It is said that only Buddhas possess the constant presence of mindfulness, and not Paccekabuddhas and others.
The prefix *pa-* signifies “commencement” (*ārambha*), and since commencement implies “proceeding” (*pavatti*), he says: “the meaning is ‘that which should be set in motion.’”
*Satipaṭṭhāna* is that which is established by means of mindfulness (*sati*) acting as the instrument; thus it is *satipaṭṭhāna*.
Grammarians maintain that the word *ana-* is frequently used to express the sense of the object (*kamma*), and likewise they maintain it expresses the sense of the agent (*kattā*).

Therefore, in the third method, it is stated: "It establishes itself (*patiṭṭhāti*), thus it is *paṭṭhāna*. In this context, the prefix *pa-* illuminates the sense of intensity and plunging (*pakkhandana*); thus, having plunged in...

“Having leapt forward, it proceeds”—this is the meaning,” he said. Again, when the word *sati* (mindfulness) and the word *paṭṭhāna* (foundation) are used in the sense of the abstract state (*bhāvattha*), he says “Alternatively,” and so forth.
By this, it is understood that in the former sense, both the word *sati* and the word *paṭṭhāna* have the sense of the agent (*kattuattha*).
Specifically, because the body and feeling are the causes of gratification, for the sake of abandoning them, [one contemplates] those bases of craving.
The contemplations on the foulness and suffering of things gross and subtle are easy for those of dull and sharp wisdom who are temperamentally dominated by craving;

thus they are called the "path of purification" for them. Likewise, the contemplations on impermanence and non-self regarding mental phenomena—which are the specific causes for abandoning views—are easy for those of dull and sharp wisdom who are temperamentally dominated by views, since these phenomena have reached a state of great differentiation even though the differentiations themselves are not overly numerous.
For the purpose of abandoning those [views], these are easy to practice for those of dull and sharp faculties.
"These [factors] are the path of purification for them. One who is keen and a follower of serenity (samatha-yānika), while grasping a gross object, does not remain fixed upon it;
rather, having entered into jhāna and emerged from it, he grasps the feeling. Thus it is said: "Because of not being stuck on the gross object.

The fact that those contemplations are the path to its purification has been stated.
Regarding the phrase "of them therein," here the word *tattha* (therein) is to be construed with the word *pahānatthaṃ* (for the purpose of abandoning).

Since the five strands of sensual pleasure are found especially in the body, the body is specifically the basis for the flood of sensuality; and through the grasping at happiness within existence, there is delight in existence (*bhavassāda*).

The underlying tendency to aversion underlies feeling;
thus, feeling—which consists of the suffering of suffering, the suffering of change, and the suffering of formations—is specifically the basis for the bodily tie of ill will.

Because there is a misapprehension of a self as eternal through the grasping at permanence in the mind, such as "purity comes through virtue" and so forth, the mind is the basis for the clinging to rules and observances. [This occurs] through the delimitation of name-and-form.

For one who does not see what has come to be as it truly is, there arises the dogmatic adherence to the views of "existence" and "non-existence" (bhava-vibhava-diṭṭhi), namely the insistence that "this alone is the truth.

Consequently, through his [attachment to] phenomena... [and so on] ...by way of relishing pleasant feeling, he becomes indifferent to the next world and gives rise to the misconception that "there is no giving," and so forth;

“Fear arises” means that through the failure to understand the true nature of phenomena (*dhammasabhāva*), fear arises; thus, phenomena [are to be understood] through the approach of fear... [and so on].
The status of the basis for those not explicitly mentioned should be applied according to the method already stated.
“With the arising of nutriment, there is the arising of the body; with the arising of contact, there is the arising of feeling; with volitional formations as condition, there is consciousness.”

Because of the statement, "With consciousness as condition, name-and-form [arises]," the nutriments—edible food, contact, mental volition, and consciousness—which constitute the origin of the body and so forth, become fully understood through the thorough knowledge of the body and so on;
thus he says, "for the sake of the full understanding of the fourfold nutriment. "The method of the treatise" (*pakaraṇanaya*) refers to the method of commentary in the Sinhalese language.
Some also say it is the method of application for preachers of the Dhamma in the *Nettippakaraṇa* and *Peṭakopadesa*.
"By way of refuge" means by way of supporting the body and so forth, as well as wholesome states and so forth. In the sense that "they remember and go by means of this," it is *sati* (mindfulness).
In this context, the convergence upon the single [state of] Nibbāna is "convergence in unity. Indeed, it is to demonstrate this very point that he said, "Just as...
and so forth. Or else, because it is the cause for entering the single Nibbāna, the nature of the foundations of mindfulness is one due to its sameness.
Oneness (*ekatta*), convergence therein (*tatra samosaraṇaṃ*), and sharing that same nature (*taṃsabhāgatā*) constitute "convergence in oneness" (*ekattasamosaraṇaṃ*).

However, in order to show that they serve as the cause for entering into a single *nibbāna*, he said, "For just as... and so forth. In this sense, refuge, oneness, and convergence should be understood as being stated together because they act as the causes for the single state of the foundations of mindfulness (*satipaṭṭhāna*);
in the previous [explanation], they were treated separately. Alternatively, [the terms] may be understood by way of "refuge" (*saraṇa*) or by way of "going" (*gamana*).

When there is a meaning [of convergence], that very act of going is "convergence" (*samosaraṇa*). Alternatively, when "convergence" is not expressed by way of the meaning of the word *sati*, it is simply "retention" (*dhāraṇatā*) that is called *sati*.

Since there is no other meaning for the word *sati* besides these two, the former is the cause for the existence of mindfulness (*satibhāva*), while the latter is the cause for its single nature (*ekabhāva*).
Thus, even in the case of Nibbāna as the point of convergence, those foundations of mindfulness (*satipaṭṭhāna*) together are the causes for the single nature of mindfulness.
"By way of fourteenfold" refers to the sections on mindfulness of breathing (*ānāpānapabba*) and so forth as taught in the *Mahāsatipaṭṭhāna Sutta*.
Likewise, it should be understood that "contemplation of phenomena (*dhammānupassanā*) by way of fivefold" applies here as well.

And in this context, the similarity to merchandise ready for sale should be seen as the power of the respective development of the foundations of mindfulness (*satipaṭṭhāna*). For these are the "pastures" of the bhikkhu. Indeed, it is said: "In his pasture..."
“...bhikkhus, practice in your own ancestral domain,” and so forth.

A bhikkhu is one who exists through the practice of body-contemplation (*kāyānupassanā*) and the rest; thus, by saying “he dwells contemplating the body,” etc., it shows that this [practice] is restricted to the bhikkhu. He is a *santa* (peaceful one) because he is tamed by the restraint of the sense faculties; he is "one who has entered the fixed course" (*niyata*) by means of the four paths; he is a "brahmacārī" (one living the holy life) due to his supreme conduct.

Having laid aside the rod through the non-infliction of physical punishment and the like, such a person should be understood by the designations of "brāhmaṇa" and so forth, owing to his having banished evil, stilled evil, and shattered the defilements.

Commentary on the Summary of the Contemplation of the Body (*Kāyānupassanā-uddesa-vannanā*). "Unmixed" (*asammissato*): although feelings and the other [aggregates] are also dependent upon this and bound to this, the meaning is that even when the contemplation of feelings and so forth is included here under the heading of "the body," it is unmixed with them.

This is for the purpose of preventing the adherence to the notions of a whole (*avayavin*), the pursuit of conventional designations (*samaññā*), the running after [concepts], and the grasping of a core (*sārādāna*).

By analyzing the body into its major and minor limbs, those [limbs] into hair and so forth, and hair and so forth into the primary elements and derived matter, he said, "Thus, there is no [self] in the body," and so on.
Even for those who maintain the existence of a whole (*avayavin*), they do not grasp at a whole in the case of a collection of parts such as the components of a palace or a city.
However, some might still run after conventional designations (*samaññā*), thinking that there is some entity called a "city" that exists.
The example of the city is given regarding the running after designations such as "woman" or "man.
As for the statement, "whatever woman or man one sees," is it not the case that there is no seeing of women or men by means of the eye? It is true that there is not;
however, by way of the perception (*saññā*) that occurs in the form "I see a woman" or "I see a man," it is said, "whatever one sees."

It has been stated. Or, regarding wrong seeing (*micchādassana*), that which one sees through a [wrong] view is not truly seen; it is not the visible base (*rūpāyatana*), or rather, that [visible base] is not it—this is the meaning.

Alternatively, that which is called the collection of the primary and secondary elements consisting of hair and so forth is not what is seen, or rather, what is seen is not as previously described—this is the meaning. "That which is seen, he does not see."

The meaning is that he does not see with the eye of wisdom (paññācakkhu) that visible form-base (rūpāyatana)—consisting of the collection of primary elements and derived matter such as hair and so forth—as it truly is.
"Not contemplating other phenomena" means not contemplating other intrinsic natures; it is said that he does not contemplate it under any aspect other than its impurity and so forth.

He calls the "earth-body" (pathavīkāya) the earth consisting of hair and so forth "body" (kāya) because it is a collection of phenomena (dhamma), [and] [he refers to] the earth characterized by its specific mark (lakkhaṇapathavī) alone.
Or, taking as a collective the various divisions of the entire body as they occur in a temporal sequence of before and after, one speaks of it as "the body"; so too in other cases.
"Internal and external" refers to the state of being a single combined object for internal and external phenomena.
The meaning is "it does not exist"; or rather, the meaning is that this [state] does not exist as a combined object of internal and external phenomena.
"Of the defilements in the three realms of existence" means of the defilements whose domain is the three realms of existence (*bhavattaya*).
"Universal" (*sabbatthika*) means existing everywhere; because it is desirable in every mind—whether sluggish or aroused—it is universal. All...

Alternatively, they are "universal" (*sabbatthika*) because the factors of enlightenment (*bojjhaṅga*) are to be cultivated when [the mind] is either sluggish or excited; that is, they are needed for all occasions.
"Internal contraction" means internal shrinking, which is to say, laziness (*kosajja*).

Having established that the abandoning of the two hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*) has been stated without distinction by both [the first two foundations of mindfulness], he now states the specific distinction of what is abandoned by each one.

He said "by way of distinction" (*visesena*) in order to show this; or, showing the purpose of the removal of covetousness and dejection, he said "by way of distinction," etc., rather than saying "having removed the hindrances.

For the purpose of this [passage] is to show the abandoning of favoring and opposing, and so forth, which are the direct opposites of the development of the contemplation of the body (*kāyānupassanābhāvanā*).
"Development of the body" (*kāyabhāvanā*) refers to the development of the contemplation of the body.
This is what is intended. "By that" refers to the statement regarding the abandonment of attachment and so forth.

The meditation subjects that are beneficial in all circumstances (*sabbatthika-kammaṭṭhāna*) are: recollection of the Buddha (*buddhānussati*), loving-kindness (*mettā*), mindfulness of death (*maraṇassati*), and the development of the foul (*asubha-bhāvanā*).

It is said that when these meditation subjects beneficial in all circumstances are maintained by the practitioner through mindfulness and clear comprehension (*satisampajañña*), they are sustained by the power of mindfulness and clear comprehension.
Because that [mindfulness] must be maintained without interruption, or because serenity is mentioned [in this context] due to its inclusion within the aggregate of concentration (samādhikkhandha).
The commentary on the summary of the contemplation of the body is finished.
Now begins the commentary on the summaries of the contemplation of feelings and so forth.

By the words "only" (*kevalaṃ*) and so forth, [the author] shows the limit of what is to be understood here; that is, he demonstrates the boundary of what should be known. *Addasa* and *adakkhi* are two words with the same meaning.

*Sammaddaso* means one who sees correctly. Regarding the phrase "also from pleasure and pain": because it has been stated that there is pleasure in the knowledge of the stability and change of pleasure and the other [feelings], and pain in the ignorance of their change and stability, the meaning is that all three should be contemplated as pleasure, and all three should also be contemplated as pain.

It should be construed as being "by way of" the various distinctions of the sense-sphere (kāmāvacara) and other planes—such as those based on objects like visible forms, mental factors like desire, predominants like wisdom, and concomitants like knowledge—as well as the various distinctions of wholesome, unwholesome, their results, and functional states, and further by way of the various distinctions such as prompted (sasaṅkhārika), unprompted (asaṅkhārika), with a basis (savatthuka), and without a basis (avatthuka), etc., indicated by the word "etc. (ādi).

"Of the nature of emptiness" (suññatādhammassa) means of that which has the essential nature of emptiness as it appears in the "Emptiness Chapter" (Suññatāvāra) in the passage beginning, "They are dhammas; they are aggregates," and so forth.

By way of this [phrase]. With the words "Granted that here... and so forth, he shows the objection that since [the defilements] have already been abandoned previously, their abandonment again should not be mentioned;

For in mundane development (*lokiyabhāvanā*), what is abandoned in the body has not been suppressed in regard to feeling and the other aggregates.

Even if it were not to arise [again], one must still speak of its further abandonment because that non-arising of covetousness and dejection (*abhijjhā-domanassa*) occurs there through the cultivation of the specific antidote.
Alternatively, both [aspects] should be applied to both cases, since both are possible: what is abandoned in one instance is likewise [to be understood as] abandoned in the others.

for it has been said in all four [foundations] that "the five aggregates are the world.
The commentary on the summary of the contemplation of feelings and so forth is concluded.

A row of fingers. "Of the penetration of characteristics" means of the penetration of the characteristic of foulness (*asubha-lakkhaṇa*) or the penetration of the characteristic of the elements (*dhātu-lakkhaṇa*).

“Horizontally delimited by one another”: how so? Because two hairs do not exist together as one. “Abode” (āsaya) means support (nissaya); the meaning is “condition” (paccaya).

“The nails are horizontally delimited by one another” is said with reference to their being established separately. Indeed, to demonstrate that very point, he says: “Two nails do not exist together as one.
“Even the subtle” refers to the subtle inner skin of the mouth and so forth, which is subtler than the aforementioned gross skin; or [it refers to] the skin among the bodily parts.
Because it is difficult to discern due to its being so subtle, it is called "subtle" (*sukhuma*).
For that [subtlety] becomes manifest to one who sees by peeling back the skin in the manner described.
As for the "layer of palm-sugar," this refers to the sap of ripe palm fruit which is smeared onto a palm-leaf strip, dried, and then scraped off as a layer.

"Thus, three [each]"—by these words "thus" and "mere," it should be understood that even those not explicitly mentioned, such as the ankle bones and so forth, are indicated. "Playing marbles" refers to marbles used for play by tying them with a string and striking them against one another.
In that context, "the place where the shin bone is established" means the place where it stands after having entered into the knee bone;
this is the intended meaning. The place where that bone is established upon the hip bone is like a large *puṇṇāga* fruit with its tip cut off.
A "lead-head" is a cloth strip placed upon the head after it has been wrapped with a lead band. "Round balls" refers to pellets pierced by a spindle for spinning thread;
a row of such round balls is called a "row of round balls. An "avalekhana-satthaka" is a scraping instrument used for scraping sugarcane.
"Delineated by the portion of the kidney" means demarcated by the boundary of the kidney-shaped section.
“Sakkharasudhāvaṇṇaṃ” means plaster-colored by the Marumpas. They also read the variant “setasakkharasudhāvaṇṇaṃ,” which means having the color of white sugar and the color of plaster.
The connection is: “wherein food and drink, having fallen, remain.

The inclusion of the term “visamacchinna” (unevenly cut) is used to show that just as water flows unevenly from a bundle that has been cut unevenly, so too does the body flow out unevenly—above, below, and across—from the openings of the hair-pores and other apertures.
Extremely pungent, excessively hot food, and so forth, are "dissimilar nutriment" because they are dissimilar to the elements functioning at the time of heat.

"By the power of the single-ness object alone" means by way of an object that has a single nature, which—due to the absence of the agitation of various objects—is established by a well-concentrated mind whose hindrances have been suppressed. For that is the single-ness object.
While being established [in this way], it generates delight in oneself, an especially pervasive joy, and the mental happiness (*somanassa*) that experiences desirable aspects.
For there can be no establishment of unity for one who has not transcended joy and bliss without delight and mental happiness.

"But in a general sense, by way of commonality" means without making distinctions regarding the specific colors of the repulsive elements, but rather by way of the commonality of both serenity (*samatha*) and insight (*vipassanā*).
The meaning is as follows. "In three ways" refers to the methods such as *anuloma* (direct order) and so forth, which will be explained later.

Regarding the phrase "for six months," it should be understood that this is said because even when the recitation is delimited by a period slightly less than half a month, the six months still constitute the delimiting period.

Indeed, the mention of "six months" is intended to prevent the lapse into another month while the [period] is being delimited; it is not for the purpose of showing the completion of the entire six-month duration.
"Teachers" (ācariyā) refers to the teachers of the commentaries (aṭṭhakathācariyā).

"Characteristic" (lakkhaṇaṃ) means the characteristic of the elements as being repulsive. "Not fit for people" (ajaññā) means they are unfit to be introduced to the public; it is said that they are loathsome.
"Bones in succession" (paṭipāṭiyā aṭṭhīni) means bones standing in a row, positioned edge-to-edge. There is no so-called "self" (attā) here whatsoever.
He shows that this "conglomeration" (saṅghāṭo) is merely a heap of bones, nothing more than bones themselves.
"Bound by many joints" means that this heap of bones is bound and connected by numerous joints. "By no one" negates the existence of a self that binds it.
"Urged on by old age" means urged on by the approach toward death through the process of aging.

The primary element (mahābhūta) is delimited by derived form (upādārūpa) through such designations as "blue," "yellow," "fragrant," or "foul-smelling. Derived form is delimited by the primary element because that which depends upon it does not exist apart from it.
The mutual delimitation of shadow and light consists in their relationship as the condition for the arising of shadow and the producer of light, respectively.
Because the aggregate of form (rūpakkhandha) has been thus encompassed, the bases (āyatana) and doors (dvāra) of the eye and so forth, which are included within it, are likewise delimited.
By way of this [condition], the formless aggregates (*arūpino khandhā*) become manifest through their respective doors; and "bases and doors" (*āyatanadvārāni*) means either the bases and the doors.
Thus, it is said "by way of the base of visible forms (*rūpāyatana*) and so forth.

"With conditions" (*sappaccayā*) means by virtue of having conditions; it is said that they arise being dependent upon conditions. Alternatively, a condition that is common, similar, or appropriate is a "condition" (*paccaya*); therefore, they are "with conditions" (*sappaccayā*).

"To such an extent" means a section that has become proficient in the manner already described. "The learning itself is the connection to the learning" (*uggahova uggahasandhi*). It is called a "connection" (*sandhi*) because the manifestation [of the object] is connected—that is, joined—here by way of the syllables and so forth.

"It manifests" means it manifests by way of the syllables and so forth; this is the meaning. "In possession of five factors": (1) being endowed with coming and going that is neither too far nor too near is one factor;
(2) being free from constant noise by day and having little sound or clamor by night is another; (3) being free from contact with gadflies, mosquitoes, wind, heat, and creeping creatures...
One [reason]: while dwelling in that lodging, robes... and requisites arise without difficulty;
this is one. Another: elder bhikkhus who are learned dwell in that lodging; this is one.
"Endowed with five factors" means endowed with the factors of exertion—namely, being free from illness, modesty, faith, wisdom, and energy.
“Uṭṭhānakadāyanti” means that which is to be given as grain from those fields by way of a harvest; this is the meaning.

Herein, the field yielding eight jars should be regarded as the duty of washing the face, and the one yielding sixteen jars as the duty of eating and consuming, because of their relative lightness and heaviness.
Furthermore, whatever suffering arises from that, and other [states], are [to be understood] through the attention to the thirty-two aspects (dvattiṃsākāra-manasikāra).
And because it does not turn back, he said, "The work must be done right here. "To this extent" means by fixing the attention thirty times in a single day.
"Having accomplished a thousandfold increase" means having applied a debt increased a thousandfold. "It is to be drawn out" means it is an extraction (*uddhāra*).
"Indeed, growth is so called. "With a pure mind" means with a mind free from defilements such as distraction.

Regarding the hair and so forth, those who are attached to the skin take the term "skin" (*taca*) to mean the beautiful complexion and the hide, and thus they become attached [to the body], thinking, "My skin is the color of gold," and so on.

Among them, it is said that two do not travel by the same path; the meaning is that they flee in whatever manner [necessary]. In this context, the thirty-two parts of the body should be understood as being like thieves because they bring about harm by serving as the basis for lust and other defilements.
Since action alone is the basis for the attainment of distinction, the development of the meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna) is called "cultivation" (bhāvanā). Therefore it was said:

"For one who attends to it, absorption (appanā) is reached. Alternatively, it is stated that the basis or object of the cultivation of action reaches absorption by entering into the state of being the object of absorption.

By the phrase "of a proud nature," he shows that it is devoid of tranquility due to its association with the capacity for arrogance. For it should be understood that the mind, when expanded toward various objects in such a manner, is likewise devoid of tranquility.
He says this with reference to what is stated in the *Visuddhimagga* regarding the case of the question asked while holding [the Elder’s] hand:
"In that context, it is said—'The Elder Mālaka, it seems, took the Elder Abhaya, the Dīgha-bhāṇaka, by the hand and said: "Friend Abhaya, first... [and so on].
Having said, "Learn this question," he spoke thus: "The Elder Mālaka was an attainer of the thirty-two first jhānas among the thirty-two divisions;
if he entered one by night and one by day, he would attain them again after more than half a month.
But if he entered only one per day, he would attain them again after more than a month."

However, it should be understood that this [passage] has been brought forward by way of illustration to establish the point that for one who attends to each [part] individually, there are thirty-two [parts]. By the phrase "situated on the side of what is not clung-to" (*anupādinnaka-pakkhe*),

it is shown that for one capable of grasping them by placing them on the side of what is not clung-to— just as the Elder Mahātissa who dwelt at Cetiyapabbata did, or like the novice attendant of the Elder Saṅgharakkhita—
one can [perceive them] even in a living body by way of the ten kinds of beauty (*dasavidha-asubha*).
It should be understood that when [the parts] are present, the attainment of access concentration is shown. However,
when the head-hairs and so forth are grasped by way of the "being" (satta) as being "in his body," the manifestation does not occur there in the same way as it does when one's own body—
free from the grasping of a "being" as in the phrase "in this body"— is manifest and ever-present with the basis of the "I-conceit" shattered.
With the intention that, until absorption is reached, there is only the contemplation of danger (*ādīnavānupassanā*) in that context, he said:
"But it should be understood as the development of insight (*vipassanābhāvanā*) consisting in the contemplation of the foul (*asubhānupassanā*).
(357) Cultivation (*sevanā*) at the beginning is *āsevanā*; intensification is *bhāvanā*; and doing it repeatedly is *bahulīkamma*. This is the distinction between them.
“By full understanding of the basis” means by the thorough knowledge of the body, which is the basis for covetousness and dejection.

“Appitā” means brought to an end; and since that [ending] is the state of being destroyed, he said “destroyed. It should be understood that the meaning “established in non-occurrence” is also expressed by the term “appitā” through the derivation of the word.
“Made with its limit removed” means the limit that is to be made now.
"Vigatanta" means "those for whom these [defilements] do not exist"; the sense is that they have become such.
"Kammaṭṭhāna" (meditation subject) is the basis for the attainment of distinction, which is action itself; or, it is the starting point for the undertaking of development within action.
And since that is contemplation, he says "the meditation subject of contemplation," the intention being that it is described as contemplation.
The commentary on the exposition of the contemplation of the body is finished.
Commentary on the Exposition of the Contemplation of Feelings (Vedanānupassanāniddesa): 363.
"Experiencing with full awareness" (*sampajānavediyana*) means experiencing while being fully aware. "Object" (*vatthu*) refers to the objective basis for pleasure and so forth.
The compound *vatthuārammaṇā* should be understood as meaning "that which has the physical basis (*vatthu*) as its object (*ārammaṇa*).
By the phrase "it is a mere conventional expression" (*vohāramattaṃ*), he shows that the statement "I feel a pleasant feeling" is spoken merely by way of conventional usage.
"Having joined energy and concentration" means that through the predominance of the energy of endurance (*adhivāsanavīriya*) and through the balance (*samatā*) of that [concentration], both—
"Having joined together. "Together with the analytical knowledges (paṭisambhidā)" means together with the supramundane analytical knowledges.

Alternatively, even regarding the mundane ones, it should be understood that the phrase "together with the analytical knowledges" is said with reference to their capacity to arise therein at the time of their occurrence.

"One who reaches the goal simultaneously" (samasīsī) means that having become one whose head is simultaneous [with the Buddhas], he attains final nibbāna in the stage immediately following the stage of reviewing (paccavekkhaṇa).
By way of brief attention, [this is taught] in the Mahāsatipaṭṭhāna Sutta; by way of detailed attention, in the Rāhulovāda, the Dhātuvibhaṅga, and so forth.
With the word "only" (*eva*) in the phrase "only in the pentad of contact," he shows the equality of the comprehension across all three doors.
Since the determination of name-and-form (*nāmarūpa-vavatthāna*) is intended, the following is for the purpose of showing the complete comprehension of form: "the physical basis..."
He said, "It is called the body born of kamma," meaning not the six bases such as the eye and so forth.
However, in order to establish that the body born of kamma is the physical basis (vatthu), the Sutta passage, "And this consciousness of mine is supported here, bound up here," has been cited.
Since for some people the contact and consciousness are not evident, he spoke with reference to those [for whom they are not] by way of contact: "By way of contact..."
“...or indeed... [as before] ...it does not become manifest. However, because feeling is manifest to them and to all other beings who are to be trained, he said:

“But it becomes manifest by way of feeling. What is called *satadhota-sappi* (hundred-times-purified ghee) is ghee that has been repeatedly melted and poured into water a hundred times, and then taken out.
"Having set aside" means having extracted it separately from the collection of the four aggregates. In certain discourses such as the Mahāsatipaṭṭhāna Sutta,
after first explaining the material meditation subject (rūpa-kammaṭṭhāna), the immaterial meditation subject (arūpa-kammaṭṭhāna) is subsequently shown by way of feeling,
having been set aside from the immaterial heap through the full understanding of the known (ñāta-pariññā).
It is shown having been excluded from either the category of the fully understood (*pariññāta*) or from the categories of the formed (*rūpa*) and the formless (*arūpa*).

Furthermore, it should be understood that among those [meditation subjects] where full understanding through knowledge (*ñātapariññā*) was first mentioned, this is included therein; whereas among those where it was not mentioned, the statement that "the meditation subject on the formed was first explained" refers to the meditation subject on the formed as a mere object of feeling (*vedanā*), which is abbreviated and not recorded in the canonical text (*pāḷi*).

“Mental phenomena that are desirable and pleasing,” and so forth—in this manner it is stated that the six types of worldly joy (*gehasita-somanassa*) belong only to one who contemplates gratification in the five strands of sensual pleasure.
Therefore, he says: “The six feelings of worldly joy are dependent on the bait of the five strands of sensual pleasure.
The commentary on the description of the contemplation of feelings (*vedanānupassanā-niddesa-vaṇṇanā*) is finished.

Commentary on the Description of the Contemplation of Mind (Cittānupassanāniddesa): 365. Even when there is dissociation from some defilements among those states associated with defilements, because they are defiled by those [defilements] with which they are associated—and which are similar to them in their state of being defiled—there is no purification even by means of the others; thus he said.
“They do not resort to the final stage. The word “twofold” is a separate statement for the purpose of distinguishing [them] from those possessed of lust and those possessed of hatred.
Because they do not approach insight, it is said: “There is no room here at all.
The commentary on the description of the contemplation of mind is finished.
In the Exposition of the Contemplation of Mental Objects (Dhammānupassanāniddesa), in the commentary on the Chapter on the Hindrances (Nīvaraṇapabba): 367.
He says "by way of frequent occurrence" because [the hindrances] are absent at the time of understanding that there is no coupling of the dark and the bright.
"Beautiful" refers to sensual desire as well. For that [object] is called "beautiful" by way of its mode of being grasped;
and because it serves as the sign for another sensual desire occurring in that mode, it is also called a "sign.
"Inappropriate attention" is attention that is not a means for the welfare and happiness one desires. "Therein" refers to the object that is to be accomplished.
And [it applies] to both kinds of beautiful object.
"The foul" means the jhāna of the foul; that, moreover, should be understood as occurring in relation to the ten kinds of foulness and to [the parts of the body] beginning with head-hair.
For it is stated in the *Girimānanda Sutta* that "perception regarding head-hair and so forth is the perception of the foul. Herein, regarding the fourfold improper attention:
It should be understood that the mention of "proper attention" (*yonisomanasikāra*) is made for the purpose of showing [the path] in its entirety.
Among those, however, what is intended here is the attention directed toward the foul as "foul," or else the others as well, because they are conducive to that.
For one who knows the proper measure in food, sensual lust—finding no opportunity due to the absence of being overcome by sloth and torpor—is abandoned.

They say this. However, by developing the perception of repulsiveness in nutriment (*āhāre paṭikūlasaññā*), the vision of the foulness and so forth of its transformation, its support, and its primary condition, as well as the vision of the body’s dependence on nutriment for its maintenance, his sensual desire (*kāmacchanda*) is indeed abandoned;
for according to the Abhidhamma method, all greed (*lobha*) is the hindrance of sensual desire.
He said: "By means of the path of arahantship.
Regarding "the directed, the undirected, and the pervasion of the quarters": the state of being directed (*odissakatā*) occurs by way of oneself, one's dearest friend, and neutral persons;

the state of being undirected (*anodissakatā*) occurs when a boundary has been established; and the pervasion of the quarters (*disāpharaṇatā*) occurs by way of pervading a single direction during the grasping of loving-kindness (*mettā*).
It should be understood. Alternatively, the directional radiation may be specified, such as by way of a monastery, a road, or a village;

or it may be unspecified, being directed toward the eastern and other quarters without reference to a monastery or similar location. It is with reference to these two kinds of acquisition (*uggaha*) that it is said: "of the specified and unspecified directional radiations.
Furthermore, acquisition should be seen as extending up to the threshold (*upacāra*); once acquired, its repeated practice is development (*bhāvanā*). In this regard: "All..."
Or, it is fivefold by way of these categories: "beings," "living creatures," "creatures," "persons," and "those comprised within individuality.

Alternatively, it is twentyfold when non-specific pervasion (anodhisopharaṇā) is practiced fourfold toward each of these: "May they be free from enmity, free from affliction, free from distress, and may they maintain themselves in happiness.
Or, [it is twentyfold] by way of: "all women, men, noble ones, ignoble ones, deities, humans, and those in the states of deprivation."
There is sevenfold or twenty-eightfold limited and all-encompassing loving-kindness (mettā) that proceeds by way of taking beings as its object;
and there is tenfold directional loving-kindness that proceeds by way of taking directions as its object.

Alternatively, within each direction, according to the application of beings and so forth, women and so forth, and enemies and so forth, there are four hundred and eighty varieties of both non-limited and limited all-encompassing loving-kindness to be understood.
"Bending the body" means bending the body in various ways.
"Grasping the sign in overeating" means grasping the sign of sloth and torpor in overeating;
it is the grasping of the cause and non-cause of sloth and torpor, thinking, "When this much has been eaten, there is a cause for sloth and torpor; when that much has been eaten, there is not."
This is the meaning. Because the ascetic practices (*dhutaṅga*) depend upon energy, he says: "also by talk that is suitable and dependent on the ascetic practices.

Since remorse (*kukkucca*), which occurs through the grieving over what has been done and left undone, shares the same characteristic as restlessness (*uddhacca*) and is of the very nature of non-tranquility, the lack of tranquility of the mind is stated as "restlessness-and-remorse" (*uddhaccakukkucca*).
For one who is well-versed (*bahussuta*) and investigates the meaning and so forth according to the text and its meaning, there is no distraction of the mind.

It is said that "restlessness and remorse are abandoned even by great learning" because of practice according to the rules and the undertaking of appropriate counter-measures, as well as the regretting of what has been done and left undone. Furthermore, associating with the elders brings about the virtue of the elders;
thus, because it leads to the tranquility of the mind, its function of abandoning restlessness and remorse is stated. However, those who uphold the Vinaya dispel remorse regardless of seniority.

It should be understood that "virtuous friends" has been mentioned. It is called *ṭhānīyā* because one stands (*tiṭṭhati*) upon it; thus, those which are the standing-points for doubt are "doubt-standpoints" (*vicikicchā-ṭhānīyā*). Alternatively, they are called *ṭhānīyā* because one should stand (*ṭhātabba*) upon them; thus, those in which doubt stands are "doubt-standpoints.
Granted, even doubt consisting of eight factors is abandoned through great learning and thorough inquiry; nevertheless, [this particular doubt] is rooted in doubt regarding the Three Jewels.

Having identified [the term] as "doubt regarding knowledge" (*ñāṇa-vicikicchā*), he said, "with reference to the Three Jewels. Regarding the phrase "one who has mastered the Vinaya," he said, "even for one who has attained mastery in the Vinaya," because such a person effects the abandonment of that doubt which was described as "hesitating regarding the training" (*sikkhāya kaṅkhati*).
The expression "one who abounds in resolve known as faith capable of conviction" refers to the resolve characterized by the faith of penetration (*anupavisana-saddhā*).

For one who is habitually intent upon resolution (*adhimuccana*). It should be understood that resolution is simply the act of producing resolve (*adhimokkha*). Alternatively, resolution is the state of being inclined toward faith (*saddhā*).
The commentary on the section on the hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*) is finished.
Kha. Explanation of the Chapter on the Factors of Enlightenment (Bojjhaṅgapabba).

Taking the meaning of the aggregates and so forth from the textual tradition (pāḷi) to be the "meaning of the aggregates and so forth," he says: "The abundance of inquiry based on the meaning of the aggregates... pe ...and of the insights.
By this, he shows that inquiries apart from the textual tradition do not lead to wisdom as effectively as inquiries based on the meaning.

By the word "mandattā" (due to dullness), the inability of energy and the other [faculties] to perform their own functions is stated, just as the water element and so forth are unable to do so amidst a mass of fire.
Regarding the phrase "as he was taking out his bowl, having heard it," they say that because he possessed the five supernormal powers, he heard it with the divine ear (*dibbasota*).

"Due to the absence of affection characterized by clarity" means due to the absence of affection known as *pasāda*. "The coarse dust on the back of a donkey appears even coarser" means that because of its extreme coarseness, it is similar to that [dust].
“Stirring, clarification, sharpening, satisfying, and encouragement” [is said].
The commentary on the Chapter on the Factors of Enlightenment is finished.
The meaning is that the first [factor] and the others are explained by way of serenity (samatha), insight (vipassanā), and pure insight (suddhavipassanā). [They are] associated with the Path (magga).

"Mindfulness is called 'contemplation of the body'"—this was stated by way of its derivation. Thus, first of all, "the teaching on the foundations of mindfulness rests upon the person" means that the teaching on the foundations of mindfulness is stated having been distinguished by way of the derivation of terms such as "one who contemplates the body.

For it is not possible to assert that a single person possesses multiple [foundations] simultaneously, because that would entail the undesirable consequence of the simultaneous occurrence of multiple instances of mindfulness and clear comprehension.
However, when speaking of phenomena (dhammas) that are distinct from their respective functions after having touched upon the person (puggala), [the author] says "But regarding the body...
and so forth, showing that even for a single mindfulness, there is a multiplicity of names due to the difference in function.

For just as the person who contemplates the body and so forth differs according to the distinction of phenomena—since phenomena themselves constitute the functions of the person—it is not the case that one phenomenon is the function of another phenomenon.

There is no division of that [mindfulness] by way of a division in its nature; therefore, mindfulness is indeed one, but when perfected on the path as the abandoning of the four perversions, it receives four names according to the different functions of that abandoning, though there is no difference in the entity itself. This is the intended meaning here.
The commentary on the Suttantabhājanīya is finished.
2. Commentary on the Exposition by Way of Abhidhamma (Abhidhammabhājanīya) 374.
In the Exposition by Way of Abhidhamma, it is stated according to its textual source: “And how, bhikkhus, does a bhikkhu dwell contemplating the body as a body?
Here, bhikkhus, at whatever time... [omitted] ...he dwells with sluggish direct knowledge contemplating the body as a body; whatever mindfulness there is at that time... and so forth.

Having taught the specific applications of mindfulness (satipaṭṭhāna) by way of persons, [the Buddha] again taught the method of the pure application of mindfulness (suddhika-satipaṭṭhāna-naya) by way of each individual factor that accomplishes the four functions, without referring to a person and without making distinctions based on the scriptures, as follows: "In this regard, what is the application of mindfulness? Here, at whatever time a bhikkhu...
[with slow direct knowledge]... at that time, whatever mindfulness there is," and so forth.
"Is stated"—this is the distinction here between these two methods.
The commentary on the *Abhidhammabhājanīya* is finished.
The commentary on the *Satipaṭṭhānavibhaṅga* is finished.
8. Analysis of the Right Strivings (Sammappadhāna-vibhaṅga) 1. Commentary on the Suttanta Exposition (Suttantabhājanīya-vaṇṇanā) 390. Regarding "strivings for a purpose":
they are understood as being for the sake of the non-arising of unarisen evil states and so forth; thus, they remain exactly as they have been grasped.

The word *sammā* (rightly) is an illuminator of this meaning: "it indeed accomplishes that goal. Its meaning is that it is the cause for the non-arising of unarisen evil and so forth regarding the intended goal;

that is to say, it is the primary cause. With reference to the fact that the word *sammā* illuminates the sense of "means" (*upāya*) and "methodicalness" (*yoniso*), it is said: "having the means as their exertion, having methodicalness as their exertion. One who has entered upon the practice (*paṭipannaka*).

"Devoted to development. "Intense application and practice" (*payoga-parakkama*): it is application itself that is effort; thus it is "application-effort. These terms—beginning with "exerts himself"—should be construed with the phrases beginning with "practicing, he exerts himself.
"Unarisen" refers to those that have reached a state where they cannot yet be called [existent], namely:
those not yet attained to the plane, those whose objects have not been grasped, those not suppressed, and those not eradicated.
391. Regarding "desire for the Dhamma" (*dhammacchanda*): it is not a separate phenomenon distinct from craving, views, or the desire for effort;

rather, it is the very nature of what is desirable. Showing this, he says, "desire as its own-nature" (*sabhāvacchando*). In that context, it should be understood that in such passages as "whatever desire for sensual pleasures," craving is called "desire.
Furthermore, [it is said]: "Are all recluses and brahmins, dear sir, proponents of an absolute [view], possessors of absolute virtue..."
