Regarding the statement, "If phenomena were not to arise, they would lead to harm," it is said in the Commentary that "only serenity and insight (samatha-vipassanā) should be understood here.
However, he rejects this, arguing that it is not tenable because, while those two exist as non-arisen states prior to the path, the path itself— when not yet arisen—
does lead to the harm of the round of existence (vaṭṭa).
There was great reverence; therefore, thinking, "It is not possible to obtain [the requisites] according to one's desire out of reverence for the Saṅgha," he did not go forth with the Saṅgha.
"Are they not too weak? means "Are they not indeed too weak? Since there is no other powerful cause for steadying oneself than the attainment of peace, [it is said]:
"Having fallen away from that, they were unable to steady themselves."
He said: "Indeed, when the great rope is cut, the strands of thread cannot support [the load].

Having shown the basis for serenity (samatha), he spoke thus—"In this way, serenity and insight, having arisen... lead [to the goal]"—with the intention that insight (vipassanā) shares the same destiny as that [serenity].

In that context, regarding the phrase "of those not yet arisen," the intention is that this is the determination (*vinicchaya*) of the term "not yet arisen" found either in the two-fold discourse on the right exertions (*sammappadhāna*) or in the canonical text (*pāḷi*). "These very ones" means those that have already arisen within the beginningless cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*).
The fourteen major duties (*mahāvatta*) are stated in the *Khandhaka*:

the duties toward guests, residents, those departing, the expression of appreciation (*anumodana*), the meal hall, alms-rounders, forest-dwellers, dwellings, the bathhouse, the restroom, teachers (*ācariya*), preceptors (*upajjhāya*), co-residents (*saddhivihārika*), and pupils (*antevāsika*).
Beyond these, there are others that must be performed occasionally at times such as when one has been subjected to a censure-act (*tajjanīyakamma*) or during the period of probation (*pārivāsika*).
The eighty-two minor duties (*khuddakavatta*) should be understood as having been thus described. For they are not to be practiced in all circumstances;

therefore, they are not included among the major duties (*mahāvatta*). In that regard, beginning with the words, "I shall prescribe the duty for monks who are on probation (*pārivāsika*)," it continues:
"One should not confer full ordination... [and so forth] ...one should not walk up and down on a walking-path while those walking on the path are on the ground."
Sixty-six rules have been stated, ending with those concerning the duties to be observed in one’s natural state; following that, there are others such as:

"Monks, a monk who is on probation (pārivāsika) must not live in a common residence under one roof with a monk who is senior to him in the probationary period, nor with a monk subject to being sent back to the beginning (mūlāyapaṭikassanāraha), nor with a monk subject to the trial period (mānattāraha), nor with a monk undergoing the trial period (mānattacārika), nor with a monk subject to rehabilitation (abbhānāraha). And so forth.
Because they are not different from those duties to be performed by a regular monk (*pakatatta*), they are not counted separately;

rather, because they must be performed toward other individuals such as those on probation (*pārivāsika*) or those senior in standing, they are combined according to those cases and counted as five each, making seventy-one rules of conduct (*vatta*).

Regarding the rules for one against whom a formal act of suspension (*ukkhepanīya-kamma*) has been carried out, it is stated under the heading of the establishment of the rules: "Not [behaving] toward a regular monk..."
The acceptance of salutation, rising from one’s seat for a bhikkhu... pe ...and back-massage during bathing—this constitutes one [offense] regarding the acceptance of such things as salutation;
and there are ten others, beginning with "A bhikkhu of normal status (pakatatta) must not be accused of failure in virtue" (sīlavipatti).
Thus, there are eighty-two [rules]. Among these very rules, some are the duties (vatta) for those who have undergone a censure-act (tajjanīya-kamma), and some...
By the inclusion of what was not previously mentioned, it should be understood that there are eighty-two rules, including those such as the *pārivāsika* (rules for one undergoing probation).
Here, the "object" (*tadārammaṇa*) is so called by way of experiencing its fruition;

and the "kamma" is said to be "arisen after having been experienced and passed away" (*bhutvā vigatuppanna*) by way of its mere having existed and passed away—since its unripened fruition has not entirely ceased—rather than in the manner described in the *Aṭṭhasālinī*.

The impulsion (javana) that has passed away after being experienced by way of lust and so forth, as well as the remaining conditioned states reckoned as "past" because they have arisen and ceased, is called "arisen past.
Therefore, here it refers only to resultant [consciousness] as "arisen by way of providing space," and not to kamma as well, as was the case there.
By "latent defilements" (anusayita-kilesa), those not yet abandoned and to be abandoned by the Path are intended.

Therefore he said: “The past... [etc. ...should not be so described. For, according to the simile of the mango tree, it cannot be said that those [past states] possess the status of being present or arisen.
The object attained by means of grasping the sign (nimitta) should be regarded as like a milk-exuding tree that has been struck;

the object in which defilements are included because they have not been suppressed should be regarded as like a milk-exuding tree that has not been struck. Grasping the sign and the unsuppressed defilements—these are the two factors.
Or, individuals are like milk-trees that have been cut or not yet cut. "In the same manner as before" should be elaborated by connecting it thus:
"Just as in the case of [defilements] that have arisen but are not suppressed, one cannot say 'they will not arise in this particular place' because they have not been eradicated.
"In the Pāḷi" refers to the Paṭisambhidāmagga Pāḷi. The fact that those defilements abandoned by the Path alone cannot be described in three ways is not evident.
An unfruitful tree was brought as an illustration to make this clear;
and for the purpose of showing that the past and so forth have not been abandoned, he said, "It should be illustrated by means of a fruitful tree.

In that regard, just as fruits capable of arising on a tree that has been cut down do not arise once it is cut, and thus they have never been, are not, and will never be possessed of their own intrinsic nature, they cannot be described in terms of the past and so forth.

In this way, the defilements abandoned by the path are to be understood. And just as the usefulness of cutting [the tree] is seen in that fruits will arise when there is no cutting, and will not arise when there is cutting, so too should the usefulness of the cultivation of the path be applied.
The commentary on the Suttantabhājanīya is finished.
3. Commentary on the Section of Questions (Pañhapucchakavaṇṇanā) 427.

Regarding what was stated in the Section of Questions: "Because there is no other energy besides that which has energy as its chief, it should not be said whether they have the Path as their dominant factor or do not have the Path as their dominant factor," herein [the phrase] "they have the Path as their dominant factor" means:
It should not be understood that the very fact of their being inexpressible [as path] is the reason for the absence of any other energy (vīriya).

Rather, it is stated that because there is then no dominant influence (adhipati) consisting of desire (chanda) or consciousness (citta) that has not yet become the Path, they cannot be called "dominated by the Path.
Alternatively, the intended meaning is that, just as with desire and consciousness, there is an absence of any other dominant influence such as energy that has not yet become the Path.

It should be understood that at that time, because the right efforts possess the status of being predominant (adhipati) in the sense of being the Path, it was stated that they "should not be said to have the Path as their predominance.
The commentary on the interrogation section is finished.
The commentary on the Analysis of the Right Efforts is finished.
9. Analysis of the Bases of Psychic Power (Iddhipādavibhaṅga) 1.
Explanation of the Exposition according to the Discourses (Suttantabhājanīyavaṇṇanā) 431.
Of the word *iddhi*, the first [meaning] is the sense of the agent (*kattū*), and the second is stated as the sense of the instrument (*karaṇa*); of the word *pāda*, there is one...
The meaning is stated as the instrument (*karaṇa*). Success (*iddhi*) is stated as that which is to be accomplished;

however, success—which is both being accomplished and what is to be attained—is not in grammatical apposition with the "foot" (*pāda*), which is the instrument for attaining it. Therefore, one cannot say, "by the first meaning, success itself is the foot, thus 'success-foot' (*iddhipāda*).
Likewise, success—consisting of growth—that is to be achieved by the instrument of the act of succeeding, [is not in apposition] with the instrument of the act of attaining.

Regarding the word *pajjitabbā* (“to be understood”): since it is impossible for two grammatical instruments (*karaṇa*) not to share a common substratum (*asamānādhikaraṇatā*), one cannot say, "the basis of success (*iddhipāda*) is the foot of success (*iddhiyā pādo*) in the sense of the second [definition].

Therefore, the construction is appropriate as follows: in the first sense, the basis of success is the foot of success (*iddhipādo*); in the second sense, success itself is the foot, thus the basis of success (*iddhipādo*).

From the scriptural passage, “If one develops concentration through desire… this is called concentration through desire,” it is understood that the compound is stated by eliding the word *adhipati* (predominance), such that “concentration with desire as its predominance” is termed “concentration through desire.

However, according to the commentary (*aṭṭhakathā*), it is stated by way of showing the meaning of the word *adhipati*: “Concentration caused by desire or abounding in desire is ‘concentration through desire.’”
It should be understood. Some say that "consisting of exertion" (*padhānabhūtā*) means "consisting of energy" (*vīriyabhūtā*).

For the term "exertion" (*padhāna*) is used for the purpose of excluding conditioned formations (*saṅkhata-saṅkhāra*) and the like. Alternatively, it is called a "formation" (*saṅkhāra*) because it forms various specific qualities; thus, it refers to all energy.

In this context, the term "exertion" is used to exclude anything other than that which accomplishes the four functions; therefore, "consisting of exertion" means "consisting of the best" (*seṭṭhabhūtā*).
This is the meaning. However, because fourfold energy (*vīriya*) is intended here, the plural form is employed.
"In the sense of a foundation" (*adhiṭṭhānaṭṭhena*) means in the sense of being the foundation for both types of supernormal power (*iddhi*).

By the phrase "serving as a foot," it refers back to the previously stated meaning of "basis of power" (*iddhipāda*), where the word *pāda* was taken in the sense of a "means" (*upāya*) and applied accordingly through a separate method of compound construction.

This should be understood as having been stated with reference to the state of being the agent and the instrument of the supernormal powers (*iddhi*) that will be described as preceding their acquisition;

or, alternatively, it refers to the state of being the agent-supernormal power (*kattiddhibhāva*) of the supernormal power to be accomplished by means of the bases of power (*iddhipāda*)— such as desire (*chanda*) and the rest— as explained in the *Uttaracūḷabhājanīya*, and to the state of being the instrument-supernormal power (*karaṇiddhibhāva*) of those very factors, desire and the rest.
In the exposition of the basis of psychic power consisting in energy (*vīriyiddhipāda*), energy (*vīriya*) appears twice:

in the phrase “endowed with the volitional formation of striving and concentration through energy” (*vīriyasamādhipadhānasaṅkhārasamannāgata*). Therein, the first instance is a qualification of concentration, meaning “concentration dominated by energy” (*vīriyādhipati samādhi*);
the second shows the factor of being endowed [with it]. For in all cases, there are only two factors of being endowed: concentration and the volitional formation of striving.

Furthermore, while zeal and the other factors are qualifiers of concentration, the "volitional formation of striving" (padhāna-saṅkhāra) is qualified by the word "striving" itself and not by zeal and the others;
thus, the predominance of energy (vīriyādhipati-tā) is not stated here as belonging to the volitional formation of striving.
Rather, it is energy itself—standing as a qualifier of concentration—that is expressed by the term "volitional formation of striving" by way of being a factor of possession (samannāgama-aṅga).

Nor is it said that there is an endowment with two kinds of energy. However, because concentration is distinguished by zeal (*chanda*) and the other factors, and because the volitional formations of striving (*padhānasaṅkhāra*) and the remaining phenomena are associated with that very same [concentration] as thus distinguished, the four bases of psychic power (*iddhipāda*) are taught by way of these distinctions of concentration.
And the state of being a distinguishing factor belongs to zeal and the others by virtue of their respective roles as supports.

In the passage, “It becomes ‘the basis of psychic power consisting in concentration due to desire’... [etc]... the basis of psychic power,’” the word *pāda* (foot/basis) is used in the sense of a support;

thus, by way of the sense of a means (*upāya*), the status of being a basis of psychic power is attributed to desire and the others. For this very reason, in the *Uttaracūḷabhājanīya*, the status of being a basis of psychic power is stated for desire and the others alone, beginning with: “The four bases of psychic power: the basis of psychic power consisting in desire,” and so forth. And in the *Pañhapucchaka*: “The four...”

Although the summary is given here by way of the words, “In this case, a bhikkhu [possesses] concentration of desire,” and so forth, the state of being wholesome and so on is explained again specifically for desire and the others.
For it is precisely for the purpose of showing the basis-factors of success (nissaya-iddhipāda) that the means-factors of success (upāya-iddhipāda) are shown;
otherwise, there would not be a fourfold division. This is how the determination of the meaning should be understood according to the text.
433. *Rathadhure* means in front of the chariot. Even one of low birth, such as a Caṇḍāla, does not obtain positions such as commander-in-chief despite possessing qualities like service;
thus it is said: "Having purified his birth... [he] relies upon his birth. *Amantanīyo* means unworthy of consultation regarding what is beneficial or harmful.
When there was a desire [to see him], how could they not grant permission? Thus, the Elder Raṭṭhapāla did not eat even seven meals.
Having obtained the permission of his parents and gone forth, he realized the supramundane Dhamma by relying solely on *chanda* (zeal);
thus it is said, "like the Elder Raṭṭhapāla.
The Elder Mogharāja relied upon *vīmaṃsā* (investigation); therefore, the Blessed One gave him the discourse on emptiness, beginning with: "Behold the world as empty."

He spoke; and because he did not answer the question when asked twice for the purpose of suppressing pride dependent on wisdom, it is said that the repeated arousal of desire is like its "presence" (upaṭṭhāna), while energy is like its "heroism" (sūratta) due to its state of strength.
It is also [like a king] because of its leadership, according to the statement: "The king is the lord of the six doors."
It is the state of the mind being similar to a distinguished genus.

"By way of non-differentiation" means: what is the meaning of speaking by combining the three factors each—such as desire (*chanda*) and so forth—and by mixing the bases of success (*iddhipāda*) with success itself (*iddhi*)?
In that context, they are called "success" (*iddhi*) because desire, energy, and so forth are successfully accomplished (*ijjhanti*) by means of it; it is "successful" (*ijjhati*) [itself].
"Supernormal power" (*iddhi*) refers, without distinction, to the formations consisting of concentration (*samādhi-padhāna-saṅkhāra*).

The bases of supernormal power such as the basis of desire (*chanda-iddhipāda*) and the basis of concentration (*samādhi-iddhipāda*) are specific; however, the "basis" (*pāda*) itself is non-specific because it is common to all supernormal powers.
Therefore, in order to show that it is appropriate to include it not only among the specific ones but also among the non-specific, [the author] says:

In all instances, he says that it is even appropriate to say, "it stands upon its feet. "Right there" means in the bases of psychic power consisting of desire-concentration, effort-formation, and volition;

the meaning is: in those very four beginning with desire. "For one who possesses desire, what concentration would not succeed?"—thus, that which is developed by way of the cultivation of concentration is "concentration-developed."
"Here, however" means that there is nothing new in this discourse on analysis (*bhedakathā*) because it is not a discourse on non-analysis (*abhedakathā*).

For those three factors which, in the discourse on non-analysis, were stated simply as "success" (*iddhi*) and "bases of success" (*iddhipāda*), are in this discourse on analysis both "successes" and "bases of success," while the remaining ones are only "bases of success.
Thus, showing the absence of anything new, he said: "Zeal, concentration," and so forth. These...

Indeed, these three... [as before] ...are not without [the others]; therefore, the remaining four associated aggregates (sampayutta-khandhā) would be called "success" (iddhi) by virtue of the accomplishment of those three, but not by their own intrinsic nature (sabhāva).
Thus, they are the bases of success (iddhipāda) themselves, but not the success itself.

It should be understood that this was stated in this way because of their status as the cause for the former. Alternatively, there is the state of being success and the state of being the basis of success for the three.
The remaining factors are also the bases of success (iddhipāda); in order to establish all of this, he said: "For these three... [as it is said] ...not without [them].
Therefore, because they succeed (ijjhanti), they are success (iddhi).

And because they succeed only together with their associated states and not without them, the associated states are the bases of success; furthermore, because those three factors are included therein, they too are bases of success.

This shows that they exist. Furthermore, to show that there is also a figurative application of the term "supernormal power" (*iddhi*) to the associated aggregates (*khandhas*), he says, "But as for the associated [aggregates]," and so forth.
Among the four aggregates, one part possesses the nature of supernormal power;
all four possess the state of being a "basis of supernormal power" (*iddhipāda*) in the sense of being "a foot of supernormal power. Moreover, the four aggregates are also "supernormal power itself."
By the phrase "the foot is the basis of success" (iddhipāda), the state of being a basis of success is shown, and not that of anything else;
thus he says, "it is not a designation for anything else. By this, he refutes the claim that "success (iddhi) is unproduced.
He does so considering that the description of the attainment of success and its preliminary stages as "success" and "basis of success" is unprecedented [if taken in that sense].
He asks: “In what sense is it *iddhi*, and in what sense is it a *pāda*? The implied remainder of the answer is: “It is acquisition (*paṭilābha*) and the preliminary stage (*pubbabhāga*).

Furthermore, because the means (*upāya*) itself becomes established for its own fruit by virtue of being a means, he says: “In the sense of being a foundation (*patiṭṭhāna*), it is a *pāda*. It is stated that desire alone...
[and so on] ...investigation alone is the “foot of success through investigation” (*vīmaṃsiddhipāda*); therefore, the four aggregates are not themselves the success (*iddhi*).

Whether the bases for psychic power (iddhipāda) are simultaneous or belong to different moments, it is precisely these factors—desire and so forth—which, acting as the predominant elements, are the bases for psychic power in all instances;
this is the intended meaning of those masters of the commentaries.

For, in order to make clear the bases for psychic power that serve as the means and are presented by way of qualifying concentration in both the Suttanta-bhājaniya and the Abhidhamma-bhājaniya, [the following is stated].
"The section on the *Uttaracūḷa* has been explained. "Some" refers, it is said, to the elders residing at the Uttaravihāra monastery.
The commentary on the *Suttantabhājanīya* is finished.
2. Commentary on the *Abhidhammabhājanīya*.
444. In the *Abhidhammabhājanīya*, for the purpose of showing the meaning of "basis of psychic power" (*iddhipāda*) as "contact...
[etc. ...exertion and non-distraction" in one who has become thus, exertion and non-distraction are mentioned, while consciousness and wisdom are condensed.

As for the statement "four thousand methods are analyzed," this must be investigated because there is no complete set of sections including those with and without the supernormal powers (*sādhipati*).
For there are no "dominants" (adhipati) that exist as dominants over other dominants; rather, in each presentation of the bases of psychic power (iddhipāda), one section on the dominant is obtained.
Thus, sixteen hundred methods are obtained for each.
The commentary on the *Abhidhammabhājanīya* is concluded.
3. Commentary on the Section of Questions (Pañhapucchakavaṇṇanā):
But surely all four predominants can be obtained in a single moment?

However, they do not act as predominants for one another, because it has been stated that "the four bases of psychic power (iddhipāda) do not have the Path as their predominant. For this very point is illustrated by the simile of the princes.

Does it illuminate [this]? No; because there is simply no second dominant factor (adhipati) at a single moment, and because it is stated that "they are not dominated by the Path," the simile of the prince illustrates precisely this point—that they do not act as dominants—rather than the coexistence of dominants.
How is this to be known? Because it has been rejected. For in the commentary on the Exposition of the Dominant Condition (adhipatipaccaya-niddesa), it is said:

It is asked: "But why is the teaching here given in the manner of 'the desire-dominant [faculty] for those associated with desire' and so forth, instead of saying as in the exposition of the root-cause condition (hetupaccaya), 'roots for those associated with roots'? [The answer is:
"Because they do not exist simultaneously in a single moment. And even when the four dominant factors (adhipati) coexist—
The qualification “of one who is developing the path dominated by investigation (vīmaṃsādhipateyya) while possessing the noble path” need not be made,
because there is no path that does not have investigation as its dominant factor. Furthermore, regarding the state of desire and the other factors acting as mutual dominants,

the statement that desire and the rest have investigation as their dominant factor— expressed in such passages as “setting aside investigation, [the path] associated with it”— [is intended to show their specific predominance].

It should not be said [that they are co-existent]. Likewise, by such statements as “the four noble paths may have the path as their dominant factor, or may not be said to have the path as their dominant factor,” the co-existence of the dominant factors has likewise been rejected.
The commentary on the section of questions is finished.
The commentary on the Analysis of the Bases of Psychic Power is finished.
10. The Analysis of the Factors of Enlightenment. 1. The Suttanta Exposition.
Commentary on the First Method 466.
Regarding the commentary on the *Oghataraṇa-sutta*:
"Establishment is by way of the defilements; accumulation is by way of volitional formations. Likewise, establishment is by way of craving and views..."
Accumulation by means of the remaining defilements and volitional formations. Establishment by way of craving; accumulation by way of views.
Establishment by way of the eternalist view; accumulation by way of the annihilationist view. Establishment by way of dullness; accumulation by way of restlessness.
Establishment by way of devotion to sensual pleasure; accumulation by way of devotion to self-mortification. By way of all unwholesome volitional formations...
It is a foundation; it is the exertion by way of all mundane wholesome volitional formations.
These should be understood according to the modes mentioned there but not stated here [in this context]:
"He reflects upon the Dhamma that has been rightly practiced; he views it from the perspective of its arising; he proceeds having assumed its aspect."

The enlightenment factor of equanimity has the characteristic of reflexion (*paṭisaṅkhāna*). And having established it thus, the equanimity regarding formations (*saṅkhārupekkhā*) is mentioned because of the predominance of the function of equanimity, according to the statement: "Reflexion, steadiness, and neutrality in grasping.
As for the purpose of the sequential arrangement, it is that each preceding factor serves as the cause for each subsequent one.
467. Since it is only when mindfulness is strong that it is called the "mindfulness-enlightenment factor," wisdom (*paññā*) is included here for the purpose of illustrating its state of strength;

it is not any kind of mere retentive memory. Rather, showing that mindfulness is the "recollection" (*saraṇa*) which is the cause for the arising of the wholesome, he says, "or the duty," and so forth.
"Standing at the head of one's duties" means: "Oh, may they indeed hear my Dhamma, and having heard it..."
Without thinking, "May they have confidence in the Dhamma, and having gained confidence, may they manifest that confidence toward me," one should instead think:
"The Dhamma has been well-expounded by the Blessed One... [as above] ...by the wise; oh, that they might hear the Dhamma from me! Having heard it, may they understand the Dhamma;
and having understood it, may they practice for the sake of its realization! It is based on the excellence of the Dhamma that such compassion arises.
The meaning is that it was spoken by the Elder Mahākassapa out of compassion and sympathy, as if standing in the preeminent position of the cause of liberation, thinking:
"Not only the Teacher, but I too shall teach the Dhamma in detail to others exactly as I have heard it and mastered it.
It was prompted by him through such factors as his long-standing observance of the proper conduct (*vatta*).

The immaterial factor has been mentioned; or rather, because it possesses the nature of a real entity, the words "made" (*kata*) and "spoken" (*bhāsita*) are considered to denote the immaterial factor that has become an action.
Thus he said: "body-intimation... [etc. ...the factor.
Regarding the state of being the originator of the factors of enlightenment (*bojjhaṅga*), it applies to the six preceding ones each in relation to their own immediate successor, and to all others.
Or they should be connected according to their respective turn by way of their origination. Regarding "the bait of the round of existence in the sense-sphere world" (*kāmaloka-vaṭṭāmisa*):

some say it is craving together with the aggregates that have it as their object; others say the lust for the five strands of sensual pleasure and the objects thereof are the "sensual bait" (*kāmāmisa*), while the lust accompanied by eternalism and annihilationism—which proceeds by way of grasping at a world through such views as "the self and the world are eternal"—and its objects [are the "bait of the round"].

The "worldly bait" (*lokāmisa*) refers to worldly conditions (*lokadhammā*), while the "round's bait" (*vaṭṭāmisa*) is the lust that generates saṃsāra, arising through a delight in the round, as well as its object.
They are called "preliminary" (*pubbabhāga*) because they precede the Path.
The commentary on the first method is finished.
Commentary on the Second Method (Dutiyanayavaṇṇanā) 468–469.
The phenomena to be directly known (*abhiññeyyā dhammā*) are: "All beings subsist by nutriment; the two elements; the three elements;
the four noble truths; the five bases of liberation; the six unsurpassed things; the seven grounds for praise."

The phenomena classified as such include the eight bases of mastery (*aṭṭhābhibhāyatana*), the nine successive dwellings (*navānupubbavihāra*), and the ten grounds for the wearing away [of defilements] (*dasa nijjaravatthu*);

as well as the aggregates (*khandha*) and so forth, shown by the statement: "All, O monks, is to be directly known" (*sabbaṃ, bhikkhave, abhiññeyyaṃ*). "Speech" (*vāna*) means the binding together of existence (*bhava*) and so forth, or the proceeding toward objects that are pleasant and agreeable.
The energy that arises in one who resolves upon the walking meditation (caṅkama) should be understood as being accompanied by insight (vipassanā).

"By this much" means: "by this much, those [states] mixed with both the mundane and the supramundane have been explained. "He does not grow weary when speaking of the mundane" means that because it originates from bodily intimation (kāyaviññatti), which is mundane, he is beyond reproach.
"Not obtained... rejected" refers to that which is not obtainable in the fine-material sphere (rūpāvacara).

The meaning is that even though joy (pīti) without applied thought and sustained thought (avitakkavicāra) is obtainable when based on the joy factor of enlightenment (pītisambojjhaṅga), it is excluded; thus, it is not called "the joy factor of enlightenment.

Alternatively, the meaning is that while joy factors that constitute the joy factor of enlightenment are indeed obtainable, those without applied thought and sustained thought which are not obtainable in the sense-sphere realm (kāmāvacara) are excluded;
therefore, a joy factor of enlightenment without applied thought and sustained thought is not mentioned.
“Internal liberation” (*ajjhattavimokkha*) means that the path which has emerged from being intent upon internal phenomena is here called “internal liberation”;

this is the intended meaning. “It should not be excluded” means that it should not be rejected, because mindfulness and the other factors in jhānas such as the kasiṇas—which are based on insight (*vipassanā*)—partake of penetration (*nibbedhabhāgiya*). However, those who do not extract [these factors] are like those who lack insight regarding enlightenment (*bodhi*).

Meditative absorption (*jhāna*) is not the proximate cause of the Path, nor is it an absolute cause; furthermore, they do not omit it by considering that the Path is the culmination of the function of absorption in the same way that it is the culmination of the function of insight (*vipassanā*).
In this context, by the mention of "kasiṇa-absorption," the formless attainments (*āruppa*) dependent upon them should also be understood as included.

The reason the meditative absorptions based on the foul (*asubha*) are not mentioned is because only that which is without initial application and sustained application (*avitakkavicāra*) is intended here.
The commentary on the second method is finished.
Commentary on the third method (470–471):
Having spoken of the state of being based on partial cessation, complete cutting off, and escape-seclusion, [he speaks] of the state of being based on tranquillity-seclusion.
It is called "speechless" because the enlightenment factors to be developed here have been stated in such passages as, "he develops the mindfulness enlightenment factor," and so forth.
For it is in the *Abhidhamma-bhājanīya* that the fruit-enlightenment factors, which are to be realized by one who has developed the [causal] enlightenment factors, are explained.

It is said that the term *vossagga* has two meanings—the sense of relinquishment and the sense of leaping forward—thus indicating the twofold nature of relinquishment. "In the manner already stated" refers to...

By way of the complete eradication of its factors and by way of making that state the object of inclination; it is "turning over" at the moment of insight (*vipassanā*) and "turned over" at the moment of the path (*magga*).
The commentary on the third method is finished.
The commentary on the Suttantabhājanīya is finished.
2. Commentary on the Abhidhammabhājanīya 472.
“By way of equanimity” indicates that it is a description of its intrinsic nature; it shows that [equanimity] does not exercise any activity regarding decrease or increase.

The meaning is "by way of looking on from the perspective of rebirth. Since "looking on with equanimity" (*ajjhupekkhanā*) refers to an equanimity superior to mundane equanimity, it is appropriate here that only the supramundane is intended.
The commentary on the *Abhidhammabhājanīya* is finished.
The commentary on the Analysis of the Factors of Enlightenment is finished. 11.
Analysis of the Factors of the Path.
2. Commentary on the Abhidhamma Exposition.
490. Furthermore, because it is stated in the *Abhidhamma* section on the analysis of supramundane consciousness (*lokuttara-citta-bhājanīya*) that "at that time there are four aggregates...

[and so on] ...there is the Eightfold Path," here too, in the *Abhidhamma* analysis, while giving a teaching in accordance with the *Abhidhamma*, he does not apply the prefix "noble" (*ariya*) to the term "Eightfold Path."
493. "At that time" refers to worldly time; it shows that these [factors] have a function in addition [to their own].
Because they cause a person to abandon wrong speech and so forth by producing abstinence (*virati*), the five beginning with right view are called the "factors that cause [the others] to act.
For abstinence is the activity consisting of right speech and so forth, and these factors cause that [abstinence] to be performed. "By way of abstinence" means by way of the activity of refraining.
The meaning is: "not by way of being a prompter nor by way of being an agent. To show this... [etc. ...the sense is:

even in the supramundane moment, these five [factors] are the prompters for the triad of right speech and so forth within a single moment, thereby demonstrating their superiority in function (*kiccātirekatā*).

There are twenty factors belonging to the unwholesome side: ten beginning with wrong view (*micchādiṭṭhi*) and ten unwholesome states conditioned by them; and ten beginning with right view (*sammādiṭṭhi*).
Because ten wholesome states arise with that as their condition, there are twenty wholesome factors; this is the name given to them in the Mahācattārīsakasutta.

"Conducive to merit" (*puññabhāgiyā*) means existing within the portion of merit; the meaning is that they constitute a part of the volitional formations of merit (*puññābhisaṅkhāra*). They are "ripening in the acquisitions" (*upadhivepakkā*) because they ripen into the aggregates as acquisitions, or because they ripen therein.
Having pointed out the five-factored path, each individual factor is questioned therein, and for each one, there is a determination of its specific occasion.
Having provided the answer [to each individually], it is said that this is "asking separately and answering separately. However,

when one asks all five together and provides the answer by defining the occasion for all five at once— as in the counter-explanation beginning with "In this context, what is the wisdom of right view?"—
this is not "asking and answering separately," because it is a counter-explanation given as a single, collective response.

Regarding the phrase "there is a name": it should be understood that in the section on the five factors (*pañcaṅgika*), the separate questions and answers concerning right view and the other factors—which are the performing factors (*kāraka-aṅga*)—are made with reference to the arising of the Path through the cultivation of each one individually.
For speech and the other factors are accomplished through prior purification, not by means of the access concentration (*upacāra*) of the Path.
The commentary on the *Abhidhammabhājanīya* is finished.
The commentary on the *Maggaṅgavibhaṅga* is finished.

1. Suttantabhājanīya: Commentary on the Matrix (Mātikā) 508.
The perfection of preliminary duties for jhāna consists of the restraint of the Pātimokkha and so forth; the recollections on the foul (asubhānussatiyo), and the supramundane jhānas.
And by saying "there is nothing outside of this," he includes every possible mode [of asceticism].

By the statement "the doctrines of others are empty of recluses," he shows the absence even of those who are perfected in the preliminary duties that constitute the state of a recluse. Regarding the training rules (*sikkhāpada*), which are to be trained in by not transgressing the words as they are expressed in terms of the mental body (*nāmakāya*) and so forth, there is the volition of abstention (*virati-cetanā*) characterized by non-transgression.

Or, regarding the portions of training that are to be mastered through fulfillment, he says, "In the training precepts," which means that each specific training—such as the training of a bhikkhu—which constitutes a portion of the training precepts, is to be practiced; thus, this is an exposition of the phenomena (dhamma) to be trained in.
[He also mentions] contentment with whatever one has obtained and so forth, praise for such mutual contentment, and the absence of anxiety when nothing is obtained.
"Having obtained it, one uses it without attachment" shows these qualities. "One who practices the development of jhāna" is an exposition that clarifies the state of being a practitioner.
By means of the passage beginning with "in the forest," etc., he explains the classification of the lodging; by means of "little noise," etc., he explains its freedom from defects;
and by "suitable for seclusion," he explains its benefits. Thus he said: "An exposition of the classification of the lodging... [and so on]... and its clarification."
The commentary on the *mātikā* is finished.
Commentary on the Exposition (Niddesa): 509.
Since the teaching is expressed by means of words such as *diṭṭhi* used in the sense of the action (*kammattha*), it is said: "Because it is seen, it is a view (*diṭṭhi*)," and so forth.
"In the sense of its own-nature" means in the sense of being non-perverted. Since one who is training disciplines the body and so forth, and not otherwise, he says:
"In the sense of what is to be trained, it is the Vinaya. Alternatively, the Vinaya refers to the training rules (sikkhāpada) which are to be trained in;

or, the three aggregates (khandha) are to be trained in, and thus it is called Vinaya because it is like a discipline (vinaya). He says "by way of giving instruction" because the three trainings constitute the Teacher’s act of giving instruction.
"By way of right view as a condition" means by way of right view being the condition. For one training in the three trainings, right view becomes fulfilled. This is because of the statement:
"Therefore, bhikkhu, you should first purify the very beginning among wholesome states;
and what is the beginning of wholesome states? It is virtue that is well-purified and view that is straight. Thus, it is preceded by right view.
The three trainings (*sikkhattaya*). And regarding these two meanings, the three trainings are called "view" (*diṭṭhi*) by way of metaphorical designation for both the fruit and the cause;
or rather, the intention is that they are so called because they are a part of oneself through wholesome states (*kusaladhamma*).

Because it is the Blessed One’s act of training, the discipline (*vinaya*) consists of the three trainings; moreover, that training is by means of the Dhamma alone, through its non-unequal nature, that is, by means of the Dhamma of the teaching.
Or, because it proceeds by way of the Dhamma and does not proceed by way of punishment and the like, it is called "Dhamma-Vinaya.
"For the sake of the state of faultless Dhamma" means for the sake of the supreme, faultless Nibbāna, or for the sake of unshakable liberation of mind.
Because the three trainings are the cause for the higher knowledge and so forth regarding the things to be known through higher knowledge and the rest, they are called "Dhamma-Vinaya. "Of this..."

The phrase "in this" (*imasmin*), being repeated, serves as a restriction; or rather, it is said with the intention that the word *eva* has been elided, thus [the author] says, "a restriction has been made.
(510) Regarding *bhikkhu*: by adding the letter *ka* in the sense of "none other," the word is extended to express the meaning "by way of the nature of begging" (*bhikkhanadhammatāya*).
However, in the reading *bhikkhaka*, the meaning is "one who begs" (*bhikkhati ti bhikkhako*). *Jallikaṃ* means mixed with dust.

"Stained" means unmixed with what is not stain; it is simply stain itself. The explanation "one who wears tattered robes" is stated because the word *bhikkhu* is conventionally established (*nirūḷha*) for one who wears tattered robes.

One for whom there remains a limit (*odhi*)—that which is to be developed or abandoned—is "limited" (*odhisī*); but since an Arahant lacks that, he is "without limit" (*anodhisī*), and thus it is said:

"Bhikkhus are so called because of their abandonment of defilements without limit. Alternatively, the word *odhi* is conventionally established in the sense of a specific portion [of the defilements].
All paths and all defilements have been developed and abandoned by the Arahant, yet they are not called "the flood" (oghā).
It should be understood that this etymology (*pahāna*) is stated by way of the method of breaking apart (*bhedana*).

By the words "one in training" (*sekha*) and so forth, the meaning expressed by the term *bhikkhu* is shown according to its qualities; whereas previously, it was shown by way of its manifestation as "by name and by designation," and by way of its etymology as "he begs" (*bhikkhati*) and so forth.

Regarding the statement, "A bhikkhu who is in training (*sekha*)," seven types of trainees are mentioned; and regarding "one who has broken [the bonds] of evil... [and so on]... a bhikkhu," only one whose taints are destroyed (*khīṇāsava*) is mentioned.

This pair does not accord with the following two points: "The term 'trainee' refers to the seven noble ones together with the worldling of good character, whereas by the term 'one who has broken,' the four who stand at the fruit-attainments are meant. This [former presentation] is a non-figurative (literal) exposition.
It should be understood that it has been stated: "In the remaining places, the 'virtuous worldlings' (puthujjanakalyāṇaka) and others are mentioned. One might ask:

"Is it not true that the one who possesses the virtue of a monk (bhikkhusīla) is also mentioned by way of formal admission? He is indeed mentioned, but he is not intended here, because what is intended here is one who produces all types of jhāna.

The word of the Blessed One is the "ground" (ṭhāna) because it is the cause for performing the act of full ordination; "fit for the ground" (ṭhānāraha) means suitable for that. The meaning is that the proclamation of the motion and the threefold announcement is complete and has not been stated out of order.
511. In the non-figurative sense, the intention is that virtue (*sīla*) consists in undertaking, abstention, and the state of non-transgression.
With reference to non-covetousness and so forth, the figurative nature of mental virtue has been stated. They say that the city architect is a teacher of the science of sites (*vatthuvijjā*).
The fourfold nutriment consists of eating and so forth; or rather, it consists of what is to be chewed, what is to be swallowed, what is to be tasted, and what is to be consumed.
One who is endowed with restraint according to the Pātimokkha has his sense faculties covered, because the three types of good conduct have restraint of the sense faculties as their sustenance;

or else, restraint according to the Pātimokkha serves as the decisive support for restraint of the sense faculties. Thus, one whose sense faculties are covered by restraint according to the Pātimokkha is called "restrained by restraint according to the Pātimokkha.
With this intention, the term "restrained" (saṃvuta) means "one whose sense faculties are covered."

He stated the meaning. Regarding the phrase "by the Pātimokkha and by restraint," it should be understood that this was said with the intention that, apart from the Pātimokkha itself, other forms of virtue—namely, physical non-transgression and so forth—are included by the mention of [the term "restraint"].
However, the second meaning was stated with reference to the identity of purpose between both.
513. Regarding the statement "all immorality," he said, "one practices even with the mind," intending to include covetousness and the rest.
"Thus, therefore, in order to show that," [it was said]. "Therein" refers to the improper conducts described by way of bodily transgression and so forth.
"He incurs the forfeiture of an article of value" means he incurs a *thullaccaya* (grave offense).

"Grown upon" (*aropimo*) means produced on land belonging to the Saṅgha. "Counter-action" (*phātikamma*) refers to an action consisting of an article of value. "Punishment" (*daṇḍakamma*) refers to the manual labor (*hatthakamma*) as previously mentioned. "Bathing" (*sināna*)—that by which one bathes—is things such as bath-powder and the like.
One who speaks agreeably even with falsehood is called a "flatterer" (*cāṭu*). One who desires flattery for oneself is a "flatterer" (*cāṭukāma*);
the state of being such is "flattery" (*cāṭukamyatā*). The intention is that there is no place where mung-bean soup does not enter, because it is not incompatible with any kind of food.
One who "waits upon," supports, or nourishes is a "servant" (*paribhaṭa*); or alternatively, a servant who is part of one's retinue is a "personal attendant" (*paribhaṭa*).
The work of a storekeeper is said to be performed for laypeople.
"Exchange of alms" (*piṇḍapaṭipiṇḍa*) means giving alms for the sake of receiving alms, or taking back alms after having given alms.

Some say that "improper management of the property of the Saṅgha and the property of a shrine" refers to the misappropriation of what belongs to the Saṅgha or a shrine, treating it as if it were one's own private possession.
514. "Gocara" means a place where cows graze; it is like a grazing ground, a place to be frequented constantly.
Alternatively, the "cows" are the sense faculties such as the eye; the place to be frequented by them is the "gocara.
An improper grazing ground is an "agocara," while any other suitable one is called a "gocara."
Taking the word *vā* to also have the sense of "shaking off," he said: "or having shaken off their stains.
(515) Those for which the measure (*mattā*) is inferior or subsequent are "trifling" (*oramattakāni*).

"To be performed by restraint" means they are counter-measures to be accomplished merely by the restraint of body and speech, or they are to be dispelled by the mere restraint of the mind, thinking: "I shall not do so again."

Or rather, the duties to be performed for restraint are to be carried out by means of the restraint of the sense faculties (*indriya-saṃvara*) alone. One who dwells in a forest hermitage or lives in the countryside is a "forest-dweller" (*āraññaka*).

The very determination of the mind is the "manifestation of determination" (*adhiṭṭhāna-avikamma*). Here, "instruction" (*desanā*) is intended by the term "manifestation of emergence" (*vuṭṭhāna-avikamma*).

In that regard, because of the statement, "The duties to be performed through the arising of thought are dependent upon attention (*manasikāra*)," [one acts] for the sake of the purification of the Pātimokkha restraint.
The Teacher’s intention is that the faults (vajja) have been described as those which must not be transgressed and which lead to non-offenses.
"Of the fourfold" refers to the fear of self-reproach, reproach by others, punishment, and an unhappy rebirth. 516.
Regarding the phrase "here, monks," it is with reference to the fact that only a monk is intended that he says: "But the remaining training rules are [treated] by way of a summary of their meaning."
"It was said thus for the purpose of showing the meaning of the word *sikkhā*.
However, the mention of "bhikkhus" is made by way of the foremost assembly to indicate all four assemblies who produce all the meditative attainments (*jhāna*).

Alternatively, since the "bhikkhu" is intended here in terms of his qualities, it should be understood that "all training" (*sikkhā*) is intended here. Regarding the phrase "by undertaking the entire training": [the commentary continues].
That undertaking by which all the trainings are undertaken is called a "total undertaking" because it performs the function of all undertakings even though it is only one;
indeed, there is no need to speak further regarding the many [other types].

"In every way of training" means by way of the modes such as non-transgression, instruction, rising from [seclusion], observance of duties, and so forth. By means of transgression, the making of the remainder [of the training] complete is also effected.
Having in mind [this], he said, "Even for one who has broken [the precepts]," and so forth.
Since the cultivation of purifying the mind from things that obstruct it is called "devotion to wakefulness," he said, "cultivation.
Regarding "well-grasped": this is called "well-grasped" because there is nothing before or after it; this is its—
"Condition," etc., refers to the encompassing [factor].

520–521. "Engaged" means undertaking [the practice]. The connection is shown as follows: "By exercising both constant mindfulness and discernment, one becomes devoted to the practice of wakefulness. 522. Regarding the statement, "Even for the mundane... he says":
this indicates that through the cultivation of insight (vipassanā), the foundations of mindfulness (satipaṭṭhāna) and so forth [converge] upon a single object.
They do not arise together; even when they do arise, the faculties and powers are included within the factors of enlightenment (bojjhaṅga) themselves.
For by the inclusion of the joy factor of enlightenment (pītisambojjhaṅga), the faith faculty and the faith power, which are its necessary conditions, are already included, because it is said:
"Gladness has faith as its proximate cause. Only five of the path factors (maggaṅga) arise at the moment of insight (vipassanā).
It should be understood that this was said with reference to this meaning. 523.

*Sampajañña* (clear comprehension) is the thorough, correct, or even-minded understanding of what is purposeful and so forth; that itself is clear comprehension. By the word "by that" (*tena*), the intention is that although mindfulness (*sati*) is not mentioned in the brief enumeration (*uddesa*), it is nevertheless stated in the detailed exposition (*niddesa*) by the term "mindful" (*sato*), precisely because it is associated with mindfulness.

Clear comprehension of the purposefulness of going forward and so forth is "clear comprehension of the purposeful" (*sātthaka-sampajañña*). Likewise for "clear comprehension of the suitable" (*sappāya-sampajañña*).

Furthermore, regarding "clear comprehension of the resort" (*gocara-sampajañña*): when one does not abandon the resort consisting of the meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*), whether engaged in the sphere of the alms-round such as walking forward and so forth, or in other activities, this is clear comprehension of the resort. Regarding "clear comprehension of non-delusion" (*asammoha-sampajañña*): it is simply the absence of confusion regarding walking forward and so forth;

thus, it is clear comprehension through non-delusion. Regarding the phrase "two kinds of talk": this refers to talk concerning what has been said and what has not been said, or talk concerning what is done and what is not done. The meaning is: "I shall indeed carry out what is said"; therefore, because of being easy to speak with, one gives a reply.

"By means of the meditation subject as the very spearhead" (kammaṭṭhānasīseneva) means by means of the meditation subject as the foremost; the sense is "having made the meditation subject the primary focus.

By this, he shows that one does not abandon the meditation subject—either that which is about to be explained starting with "Even a bowl is insentient," etc., or that which is being practiced according to one's disposition.
Regarding the word "therefore" (tasmā), it is connected with the phrase "they say that a Dhamma talk must indeed be delivered."
Regarding the connection: "in fear" means in fear of foreign armies and the like;

"in the remaining places" means in places other than where rice gruel is taken. The phrase "only standing or walking" is stated with reference to the postures that must be formally resolved upon (*adhiṭṭhātabba-iriyāpatha*); it is not by way of prohibiting sitting, which must necessarily be done at times such as eating.
This refers to the Elder Dārucīriya.
“Therefore, Bāhiya, you should train yourself thus: ‘In the seen there shall be just the seen; in the heard, the sensed, and the cognized, there shall be just the cognized.

When, Bāhiya, for you there shall be just the seen in the seen, just the heard in the heard, just the sensed in the sensed, and just the cognized in the cognized, then, Bāhiya, you will not [be] by that;
when, Bāhiya, you are not [bound] by that, then, Bāhiya, you will not [be].”
“Where you are not, Bāhiya, there you are not. Since you are neither here, nor elsewhere, nor in between the two, this is the end of suffering.
With these words, he realized arhatship.
They say that "carrying across" (*vītiharaṇa*) means carrying on one's side for the purpose of avoiding stumps and the like, or for the purpose of avoiding the foot already placed down.

Alternatively, the distinction between these terms is as follows: "bringing forward" (*āharaṇa*) lasts until the foot is placed down, while "carrying across" (*vītiharaṇa*) refers to the movement beyond that point.
"Without interval" (*avīci*) means continuously.

The statement "even in the first impulsion... there is none" is said with reference to the absence of lust and so forth regarding "woman" or "man" within the cognitive series of the fivefold sense-consciousnesses.

For therein, through improper adverting and apprehending, greed arises toward a desirable object such as a woman's form, and aversion arises toward an undesirable one. However, in the mind-door, [the perception] of "woman" or "man"...
There is lust and so forth; the root of that is the five-door javana, or else, as previously stated, the entire process beginning with the life-continuum (bhavaṅga).

Thus, "full understanding of the root" is explained by way of the root of the mind-door javana. However, its "guest-like and temporary nature" refers specifically to the five-door javana, by way of its being something new and more recent.
They say that the *maṇisappa* is a species of snake found in the island of Sri Lanka. "Moving" means shaking.
*Atiharati* means he brings [the food] as far as the mouth. *Vītiharati* means he carries it from there as far as the stomach, or he carries away what has entered the stomach while observing it.
*Allattañca anupāleti* means he protects it so that it does not become excessively decomposed by the winds and other internal elements.
*Ābhujati* means he attends to the search for food, its swallowing, its state of being digested or undigested, and so forth; the meaning is that he discerns these things.
Indeed, it is precisely the application that effects the discernment of each respective object which is called "right application" (*sammāpayoga*).

Alternatively, "discernment" (*vijānana*) is the mental engagement (*ābhujana*) consisting of such thoughts as, "By resorting to right practice, there is no so-called 'self' within that experiences [anything].

"In an improper place" (*aṭṭhāne*) means in an unsuitable location occupied by humans or non-humans, such as a field or a sacred grove (*devāyatana*). "From the vessel" (*tumbato*) means from a water-container such as a bamboo tube or the like. "That" (*taṃ*) refers to the discarded water.

In the passage beginning with "going" (*gata*) and "going" (*gamana*), since the shifting of the body forward and backward was already mentioned by the inclusion of "advancing and retreating," it should be understood that here only the act of "going" itself is intended; or else, the distinction between these will be stated later.

By the phrase "by so much," the meaning is that *sampajañña* regarding the range of movement does not become manifest merely by the statement of the occurrence of the four postures without relinquishing the meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*). Thus, in the Sutta, the meditation subject remains unmanifested.
The phrase "it occurs" means that while one is attending to [the meditation object] during walking, standing, or sitting, those [mental states] occurring during sleep remain unmanifest.

Because it consists of bodily and other types of activity, and because it arises from the functional process of adverting (āvajjana), it is called "impulsion" (javana). Alternatively, all activity proceeding through the six sense doors is termed "activity-based occurrence. The second jhāna is called "silence" because it is devoid of verbal formations (vacī-saṅkhāra).
526. "A place for practice" (upāsanaṭṭhāna) refers to the practice of attending to the meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna-upāsana), which is like the training and application of archers in their craft.

The meaning is "a basis" (*ṭhāna*). Indeed, to demonstrate that very same meaning, he says "the path of yoga" (*yogapatha*). "He washes his head" means he makes known his freedom from slavery through the slavery of desire;
or else, he washes away the iron dust thrown [on him] by those who have entered upon wrong practice.
529. This is found in the *Adinnādāna-pārājika* according to the method of the Vinaya; according to the method of the Suttanta, it is in the *Āraññaka-sikkhāpada*.
The phrase “five hundred bow-lengths behind” refers to a forest-dwelling (*āraññika*) bhikkhu.
For he is called “a forest-dweller who lives in a remote lodging” in the Sutta because he dwells in a wilderness according to the method of the Vinaya.

530. That which they call a “slope” (*nitumba*) or a “river-grove” (*nadīkuñja*), that is a “cleft” (*kandara*); this shows that even in a place not on a mountain, a location where a river turns in a difficult passage is a cleft.
531. By the phrase "shown after dividing," he indicates the reason for placing the exposition at the end:

namely, that it is to be divided. 533. Secret action is *rahassa*; that which is fit for it, or suitable for it, is *rāhasseyyaka*. For secondary derivatives (*taddhita*) are indeed diverse. Alternatively, *rahassa* means that which is good in secret;
that which is fit for it is *rāhasseyyaka*. 536. *Paṇihita* means well-placed.
537. *Pariggahitaniyyānaṃ* means having the nature of an outlet that has been grasped;

the meaning is that it is endowed with the nature of an outlet through its thorough application to the body and so forth. Alternatively, "grasping" (*pariggaha*) refers to the knowledge that grasps the body and so on;
the meaning is that one has established the foundation of mindfulness (*upaṭṭhāna*) as an outlet by means of its association with that [knowledge].
542–543. “By way of undergoing transformation” means by way of the mind’s state of undergoing transformation.

“By way of including everything” means by way of including all anger contained within the seven formations. And it should be understood that this inclusion of everything is made because the abandonment through complete eradication (*samucchedappahāna*) is also intended.

546. “With reference to this,” it means with reference to the statement “two states. Although “torpor and drowsiness” was indicated in the singular, the change in grammatical number to the plural—“are present”—is made in the detailed exposition (niddesa).

The phrase “by way of the continuity of cessation” refers to the continuity of the factors (aṅga) or the continuity of their intrinsic nature (sabhāva), for the purpose of precluding the absence of continuity.

550. The perception of light (*ālokasaññā*) is so called because it is free from the distortion of sloth and torpor (*thinamiddha-vikāra*), being the perception that is their opposite. For this very reason it is said: "This perception becomes light. 553.

The phrases beginning with "Because of having vomited it up" and "Because of having released it," as well as those beginning with "It becomes light," have been stated [in the commentary] as "Because of having abandoned it," etc.
Alternatively, by means of the word "etc.," both sets of explanatory terms are included; therein, whatever synonyms there are for these [terms], they are precisely those.
It should be understood that this was stated with the intention that these are "mutually synonymous terms. By the word *paṭimuñcati* ("he fastens"), he demonstrates exertion and overcoming.

Because it is free from obstruction (*nirāvaraṇā*) and is directed toward (*ābhujati*) while being clearly comprehending (*sampajāna*), it is "unobstructed application" (*nirāvaraṇābhoga*); it is "open" (*vivaṭā*) because its nature is such. 556.

It should be understood that "transgression of the object" (*vatthujjhācāra*) is spoken of by way of a figurative expression for its cause—the remorse (*vippaṭisāra*) rooted in the transgression of an object due to indecision, such as thinking, "Was it the wrong time? Or was it not?"* *Note: The original text contains a reference to a specific commentary number (556) and a portion of the Pali text regarding the definition of *vatthujjhācāra*. The translation reflects the technical exegetical style.*

562. "They defile" (*kilissantī*) means they cause defilement; or, by virtue of their inherent nature of being accompanied by passion, they themselves become defiled. For when they arise, they do not arise free from defilements. 564.
And in this very *Vibhaṅga*, the passage beginning with "he is endowed" has already been stated in various places. 588.
"By way of exposition" (*niddesavasena*) means by way of the exposition beginning with "In this context, what is equanimity? That which is equanimity," and so forth. "By this..."
They say that this is by way of a secondary explanation (paṭiniddesa), beginning with the words, "He is endowed with equanimity. By the passage, "In this context, what is... [etc.
...by means of this equanimity he is endowed," the person is indicated; he is then explained further by the words "fully endowed" and so forth.
Alternatively, he is indicated up until the word "possessed of," and is then explained further by the phrase, "Therefore he is called 'equanimous'."

By means of these [terms], the exposition and the sub-exposition are to be joined. By way of "modes" (*pakārena*), they establish and set forth the meaning of the word *upekkhaka* through the modes of phenomena such as "looking on with equanimity" (*upekkhanā*) and so forth, and through the modes of persons such as "endowed with equanimity" (*upeto*) and "fully endowed with equanimity" (*samupeto*).
For "looking on with equanimity" (*upekkhanā*) is the cause for the meaning of this term "equanimity" (*upekkhā*); indeed, it is by way of looking on with equanimity that there is equanimity.

Likewise, regarding the terms "endowed" (*upeta*) and "fully endowed" (*samupeta*), they explain them by showing the reason as "having approached" (*upāgata*) and "having fully approached" (*samupāgata*);
thus they reveal the reason for each respective meaning both in terms of the Dhamma and the person.

Or else, they show the reason for the very meaning of "equanimous" (*upekkhaka*) by saying, "he is endowed with this equanimity," and so forth, [and] by [explaining] "equanimity, thorough equanimity, fully endowed," and so on.

They analyze by showing the distinction between the words (*byañjana*). Alternatively, the distinction of the phrasing (*byañjanavibhāga*) consists in providing a separate explanation of the meaning for the word "equanimous" (*upekkhaka*)—which is subsumed under the term "equanimity" (*upekkhā*)—through such passages as "that which is equanimity, the act of equanimizing," and "one is endowed with this equanimity.
In every respect, it is the state of being unknown, the state of being concealed.
The profundity [of the base] consists in the absence of any exhaustive delimitation, even when it has been cognized in some way.

(602) Regarding the phrase "for the attainment of the higher plane," this should be connected specifically with the passage "by surmounting perceptions of form. Alternatively, since the base of infinite consciousness and so forth are also the higher planes for the base of infinite space and so forth, this is not inconsistent in any context.
(610) In the description of the base of infinite consciousness, [it says]: "Infinite consciousness"—that very same space is pervaded by consciousness.
"He attends to it as infinite and pervades it; therefore it is called 'infinite consciousness'"—here, "by consciousness" (*viññāṇena*) is an instrumental case used in the sense of the accusative.
It is said in the *Aṭṭhakathā* (Commentary) that he attends to that very same space-pervading consciousness as "consciousness.
Or rather, this is its meaning: [he attends] to that very same space-pervading consciousness by means of the consciousness of the base of infinite consciousness (*viññāṇañcāyatana-viññāṇena*).
"He attends to it" means this: he attends to that very space pervaded by consciousness, in the mode apprehended by it;

thus that consciousness pervades the infinite. For the second immaterial-sphere practitioner, while attending to that very consciousness together with the mode of pervasion which the first immaterial-sphere practitioner pervades as infinite space, [attends to it].
"It is said that it pervades the infinite.

(615) "One causes that very consciousness to cease" means: that which was previously attended to as "infinite consciousness"—that very [consciousness] is the meaning. For one causes that very thing, which has become the object, to cease by means of the third formless attainment, just as the sign of form was [caused to cease] by the first.
The commentary on the Exposition is finished.
The commentary on the Suttanta-bhājaniya is finished.
2. Commentary on the Abhidhamma-bhājaniya 623.
In the presentation of the fivefold method within the Abhidhamma-bhājaniya, regarding the phrase "five jhānas" and "therein, what is... [the following is said]:

It is introduced by the words, "the first jhāna," and so forth. This is because only the four jhānas—the first, third, fourth, and fifth—are presented, and because it is specifically the second jhāna whose distinction is being shown.
The commentary on the *Abhidhamma-bhājaniya* is finished.
3. Commentary on the Section of Questions (Pañhapucchakavaṇṇanā) 640.
Regarding the phrase "In these three jhānas, they may be supramundane and have an immeasurable object":

the intention is that when categorized in this way, during the time of the path or the time of the fruit, they are indeed supramundane. [These are] the space-kasiṇa of limited extent, the light-kasiṇa, the breath-meditation, and the fourth divine abiding.
They should be understood as being included in the fourth [category], the "basis-in-all-places.

It should be known that the statements, "Buddhas, Paccekabuddhas, and those whose taints are destroyed have cultivated the path and realized the fruit," and "they will cultivate it and realize it," are spoken with reference to the lower paths and fruits. From the perspective of the wholesome...
For this discussion was set forth regarding thirteen fourth [jhanas], yet one cannot see the paths and fruits of Arahantship by means of a wholesome fourth jhana.
Regarding the phrase "from the functional, thirteen," since there is no supramundane functional fourth jhana, it should have been said "twelve";
or alternatively, including the fourth jhana of the trainee's fruit within the thirteen wholesome ones, it is said "from the functional, thirteen."

It should be understood that one speaks together with the Asekha as the fourth. Herein, it should be seen as "having everything as its basis" (*sabbatthapādaka*) because the superknowledges (*abhiññā*) and other qualities possessed by those whose taints are destroyed (*khīṇāsava*) serve as the basis for all [meditative attainments].

For there is no cycle of existence (*vaṭṭa*) remaining for them. Alternatively, it is so called because, like the fourth jhāna based on the limited space-kasiṇa (*paricchinnākāsakasiṇa*), it is equal to the "all-basis" type in its indeterminability (*navattabbatā*).
The state of being "based everywhere" (sabbatthapādakatā) is to be understood [here].

Mental formations (manosaṅkhārā) refer to perception and feeling, or else to all four aggregates. Regarding the phrase "taking a sign as object" (nimittam ārabbha), it should be stated here that "the sign is Nibbāna.

In the passage, "An internal state is a condition for an internal state by way of the object-condition" (ajjhatto dhammo ajjhattassa dhammassa ārammaṇapaccayena paccayo), [the word] "internal" (ajjhattā)...

Because it is stated that "the aggregates are a condition for the knowledge of the modes of supernormal power, the knowledge of recollecting past lives, the knowledge of the destination according to karma,

the knowledge of the future, and for advertence, by way of the object-condition," the knowledge of the destination according to karma does not know only what has occurred in another's continuum— unlike the knowledge of others' minds—
but also knows unmanifest matter within one's own continuum, just as the divine eye does.
It makes manifest karma that was previously hidden. Therefore he said, "at the time of knowing one's own karma.
The commentary on the interrogation of questions is finished.
The commentary on the Analysis of Jhāna is finished.
13. Analysis of the Illimitables (Appamaññāvibhaṅga) 1.
Explanation of the Exposition According to the Discourses (Suttantabhājanīyavaṇṇanā) 642.
"Everywhere" (sabbadhi) is said with reference to an unrestricted pervasion by way of direction and location; "all-encompassing" (sabbattatāya sabbāvantaṃ) refers to its pervading all that exists.
It is because of the word *satta* (being). Therefore he said: "for the purpose of seeing without limitation. The word *tathā* or the word *iti* was not stated;

the meaning is that those two [words] which follow upon the phrase "with a mind accompanied by loving-kindness" were not stated because they would find no place as locations for its pervading and so forth, and thus it is stated again: "with a mind accompanied by loving-kindness."

643. Loving-kindness (*mettā*) guarded by moral shame (*hiri*) and moral dread (*ottappa*) does not decline; the intention is that there is no occurrence of failure in the face of passion (*rāga*) and affection (*sineha*), which are like immediate enemies.

645. "Having resolved" (*adhimuñcitvā*) means having fully extended [the mind]. Showing this, he said, "by way of excellence" (*adhikabhāvena*), or else, having resolved with a powerful act of conviction (*adhimokkha*). 648.
"As already stated above" refers to the phrase "in every way, entirely, in all respects, everything," specifically regarding the undertaking of the training (*sikkhāsamādāna*) in its entirety.
In the *Jhānavibhaṅga*, the meaning is stated as: "the entire training" and "training in every way that ought to be trained.

Here, however, the meaning is appropriate as "the entire world" by means of every limit—through self-equality and through being joined with all beings—and "the entire world" by means of the modes of pervading every direction and limit.

650. "By way of the destruction of adversaries" means by way of the destruction of the immediate and remote adversaries—namely, lust, ill-will, and so forth—of loving-kindness and the other [immeasurables]. "That which is immeasurable is 'harmless'" (avero); "the state of being harmless" (averabhāvo) is its meaning, or this is its significance.

653. "Destiny" refers to states such as hell; "clan" refers to outcaste families and the like; "possessions" refers to the lack of gain for food and so forth. By the word "and so forth" (ādi), disfigurement and other such conditions are included. The commentary on the *Suttantabhājanīya* is finished.
3. Commentary on the Section of Questions (Pañhapucchakavaṇṇanā) 699.
However, by the phrase "but in this... it is said," [the author] indicates that those [immeasurables] mentioned in this Vibhaṅga are purely mundane;
thus, he distinguishes them from the Khandhavibhaṅga and others. Consequently, it is not admitted elsewhere that supramundane (lokuttara) immeasurables are taught.
The commentary on the Section of Questions is finished.
The commentary on the Analysis of the Illimitables is finished. 14.
The Analysis of the Training Precepts (Sikkhāpada-vibhaṅga).
1. Commentary on the *Abhidhammabhājanīya* 703.
"In the sense of being a foundation" means by way of association (*sampayoga*), by way of decisive support (*upanissaya*), and by way of providing space.

That which is called "liquor" (*surā*) is made by mixing and kneading various ingredients such as flour-cakes, rice, and parched grain. [Likewise, there are liquors made from] various ingredients such as the flowers of the *madhuka* tree, the fruit of the jackfruit tree, sugarcane, and *muddika* grapes.
*Rasa* refers to fermented liquor that has been aged for a long time; the meaning is *āsava*.
"Because they are associated with that" means because they are associated with abstinence (*virati*), or because they are associated with volition of abstinence.
"Only courses of kamma" means that among the various categories such as the jhānas—which are not common to all—these belong exclusively to the category of courses of kamma.
They say that even the drinking of intoxicants is mentioned as a distinct course of kamma in the passage: "Bhikkhus, the drinking of intoxicants, when indulged in...

leads to hell. If this were so, there would be eleven courses of kamma; therefore, its inclusion should be understood as being subsumed under the aforementioned courses of kamma by virtue of its being an auxiliary and its sharing the same nature.

The fact that these have beings—whether female or male—as their object should be understood as being due to their having as objects the formations (saṅkhāra) grasped by those [beings]. For it is said: "The five training precepts have limited objects," and it will further be stated:
"For all of these, having made the things to be transgressed their object, they desist precisely through volitions of enmity."
Gorūpasīlaka was naturally virtuous. The phrase "for the sake of even a single kākaṇika coin," and so forth, is stated with reference to speaking falsehood out of greed (*lobha*).
Furthermore, when speaking falsehood out of hatred (*dosa*), it is the schism of the Saṅgha (*saṅghabheda*) that has reached its ultimate limit [in gravity].

However, when speaking falsehood out of hatred for the purpose of bringing about another's ruin, one should apply the degrees of slight or great offense (*appasāvaja-mahāsāvajja*) according to the specific qualities of the person involved.

And according to the desire for the undertaking of weak or superior [levels of] commitment, only two are included, because those consisting of relinquishment, the minor [offenses], those based on knowledge, and those based on supernormal power enter precisely into the categories of "by one's own hand" and "by command.

It was stated with reference to the conventional morality (pariyāyasīla) characterized by volition that all five courses of action are indeed [included]; however, the morality of abstinence (viratisīla) belongs to the category of the Path. "Of these," refers to the remaining types of morality.
712. It was stated [above] as "by way of being a constituent part," but it should rather be said as "by way of being a foundation.

In this context, however, regarding the section on the training rules (*sikkhāpada*), abstentions from actions are not mentioned because for an Arahant—who has abandoned the five things that render one incapable and has entirely ceased from the enmities to be avoided—such abstentions do not exist;
whereas for those in training (*sekkhā*), even though they have abandoned the five enmities, [the abstentions are mentioned] due to their similarity to that state.

Since there exists the presence of unwholesome states that are themselves enmity, as well as greed and other factors that are the causes of enmity, the arising of the abstentions (*virati*) will certainly not fail to occur.
Furthermore, bodily actions and so forth originating from the unwholesome are indeed enmities—namely, bodily misconduct and the rest—and from these, the abstentions do indeed arise;
for this reason, even the three higher paths, though they are not themselves the fruit [of the lower paths], possess the nature of the Eightfold Path.
Furthermore, in the section on training (*sikkhāvāra*), those phenomena that are results (*phaladhamma*) are not to be trained in because they are not to be cultivated;
nor are those active phenomena (*kiriyadhamma*) that arise for one who has already completed the training. Therefore, no indeterminate (*abyākata*) states were included among the trainings.
The commentary on the *Abhidhammabhājanīya* is concluded.
2. Commentary on the Section of Questions (Pañhapucchakavaṇṇanā) 714.
“By way of abstention from what is encountered” means: by way of abstaining from that which ought to be abstained from with respect to an object encountered—that is, present.
The commentary on the Section of Questions is finished.
The commentary on the analysis of the training rules (*sikkhāpadavibhaṅgavaṇṇanā*) is finished.
15. Analysis of the Discriminations (*paṭisambhidāvibhaṅga*).
1. The Suttanta Exposition (*suttantabhājanīya*).
1. Explanation of the Section on Compendium (Saṅgahavāravaṇṇanā) 718.
Having shown "this is the same method" in brief, he said "of the classification of phenomena," etc., in order to show that very method in detail.
