*Nijigīsana* is the desire to deceive and take for oneself a great deal by means of a small gain; its state is *nijigīsanatā*. It is either the mode of occurrence of that very desire or the act of searching concomitant with it.
866. Regarding "vaṇṇasampannaṃ pokkharaṃ vaṇṇapokkharaṃ," it should be understood that there is an elision of the first member of the compound (pubbapadalopa).
Alternatively, "vaṇṇapokkharatā" means the fullness of color. He says "it causes to proceed" because, as in the phrase "atthajāpikā," the word *japa* here signifies arising.
867. Because it proceeds by way of elevation, similar to pride (*seyya*), it is stated in both cases that "it causes conceit (*māna*) to arise."

868. However, since *hīnamāna* (inferiority-conceit) occurs by way of being subservient (*onati*), it does not deserve to be defined by the word *māna* alone; therefore, in its definition, it is stated as "one who fancies oneself inferior" (*omānaṃ jappeti*).
872. One who enjoys the kingdom through the king’s wealth is a *raṭṭhiya*, one who depends on the king. 879.
"Without referring to a person" means that, just as in the definitions of the conceits of superiority (*seyyamāna*) and so forth, [one does not say] "oneself superior to others," etc.

"He burns" refers to a person who is superior and who gives rise to conceit; thus, even when this person is in a state of "conceit regarding superiority," the meaning is that it is stated simply as "he despises others" without specifying the particular individual who causes the conceit to arise.

For "excessive conceit" (*atimāna*) is the conceit that arises by surpassing others, regardless of who those others may be. 880. *Mānātimāna* is a conceit higher than the preceding conceit; it should be understood that the prefix *ati-* expresses the sense of the word *upari* (above). Alternatively, *mānātimāna* is a conceit that has transcended the preceding conceit.
881. Among the species of birds, the crow is considered inferior; therefore, it is said, "like the species of crow. 882.

It is said that the Elder was of a hateful temperament (dosa-carita). For this reason, they say that from the very beginning he spoke by means of a skillful method rather than saying, "You have not yet exhausted the taints (āsava). Alternatively, the intention is that because of his hateful temperament, he quickly produced dispassion (virāga) at the third stage of the verse.
883. "Desire accompanied by conceit" (māna-anugata-chanda) refers to desire associated with conceit, or conceit-desire that has followed the nature of conceit.

884. "Vilambana" (dallying) should be understood as that which is connected with the act of dallying, such as the honoring of women and men and so forth. In this context, *vilambana-paṭibhāna* is a ready wit that is appropriate, apt, and polished.
887. *Amaravitakka* (thought of immortality) is a thought associated with talk of not dying; it is a thought for the sake of one's own non-death or for the sake of becoming a deity.
888. *Parānuddaya* is the state of one who has compassion for others (*parānuddaya*); it is the making of compassion toward others by way of passion (*rāga*). Its nature is that very quality.
*Parānuddayatā*: the state of having compassion for others, or the state of one who rejoices in others' success and so forth—this is *parānuddayatā*.

Such is the nature of lust (*rāga*). Regarding the phrase "therein" (*tattha*), the meaning is appropriate as referring to dwelling in association with that which is characterized by compassion for others.

890. One who aspires to not being despised aspires to the very object of not being despised, namely the strands of sensual pleasure (*kāmaguṇa*). Thus he says: "Having become dependent on the five [strands of] sensual pleasure... and so forth.
The commentary on the Singlefold Exposition is finished.
(2. Commentary on the Twofold Exposition: 891.
*Upanayhati* means "binds. The vowel *a* expresses the sense of immediate succession (*anantara*), or it is a substitute for the vowel *ā* which expresses a limit (*maryādā*).
Having made it concise, it is said that "establishment" (*aṭṭhapanā*) refers to what was stated as "immediate establishment" (*anantaraṭṭhapanā*), and so forth.

In this context, the mode of occurrence of that which has first arisen is the boundary (*mariyādā*); establishing by way of strengthening that very [mode] without transcending it is "boundary-establishment.
The meaning is that it is merely the establishment of the natural state, devoid of any further qualification.
892. *Niṭṭhuriyaṃ* means spitting; it is called *niṭṭhuriyaṃ* because it is like spitting. "Having shown" means having bitten with the teeth.
By that, he shows that the showing [of the teeth] is *paḷāsa*. The occurrence of seizing with the yoke is the "coming forth" (*āyana*) of *paḷāsa*.
Victory is the burning away of evenness; it is called *āhāra* because it brings that [victory] forth. "He does not give the *dhura*" means he does not grant leadership.

894. One performs duties such as sweeping the courtyard of the cetiya with the body in order to inform others: "How could one who is thus endowed with proper conduct and possessed of faith commit bodily misconduct and the like?
*Aticca* means having committed a transgression (*accaya*). *Āsaranti* means they come;
the meaning is that they proceed toward concealing [the fault] once again. *Konāmevaṃ karoti* refers to either cutting off or covering up, or it is a term for concealing.
"Not speaking rightly" shows that one who does not speak rightly is a deceiver. "Neither the belly nor the back can be known" means that because he lacks actions corresponding to his mind,
it is impossible to know him as being "of such a mind and of such conduct," since his true qualities cannot be discerned through mere outward appearance.

The goat itself is the "goat-eater" (ajāmiga). Nelakoṭi is a young calf. Just as that yakkha, having displayed a corresponding form, devours those who come and go under the perception that they are "goats," so too does this [deceit] deceive various people by means of the estimation of qualities similar to their own.
Therefore, this deceit should be understood as a deception more powerful than illusion (māyā). For this very reason, it is called "craftiness" (parikkhattatā).

908. Even in the absence of personality-view (*sakkāyadiṭṭhi*) and the rest, that fetter which exists is called "external fetter" (*bahiddhā-saṃyojana*) because it is a fetter directed toward the external; it serves as a distinguishing characteristic for the person who possesses that external fetter.
The commentary on the Exposition of Pairs (*Dukaniddesa-vaṇṇanā*) is finished.
(3. Commentary on the Exposition of Threes (*Tikaniddesa-vaṇṇanā*).

909. Since they stated that "the unwholesome roots themselves are the roots of the round," it follows that by those [statements] the active manifestation of the roots of the round was explained; thus he said, "By the three... explained. 919.

The view that "the world is eternal" and so forth is considered by those who hold to speculative views (*diṭṭhigatika*) to be the holy life (*brahmacariya*), the supreme conduct that leads to liberation;
thus he said, "of what is agreed upon by those who hold to speculative views. Regarding the results (*vipāka*) of the fine-material and immaterial realms:
It is said, “the Great Brahmā,” with the intention that his lust for existence (*bhavarāga*) is predominant.

(920) Regarding the question “of what kind?”—taking it to mean “in what manner established”—he says, “the shape of its form. “Establishment by conceit” means establishment by means of conceit (*māna*) through such modes as superiority, or establishment consisting of conceit itself.
(921) “Terror of the mind” is dejection (*domanassa*), or hatred (*dosa*), or the volition and other factors associated with them.

922. "By way of the ease of teaching" means that, with respect to the three periods of time, the teaching is easy for one who is characterized by doubt—thinking "he hesitates, he doubts"—but it is not so for one characterized by delusion;
this is the intended meaning. Regarding the phrase "having heard the distinction of complexion and so forth," some say:
"The kṣatriya-being is of a pale complexion. Why? Because he delights in the forenoon, and in the forenoon the shadow..."

Having heard their distinction of color—namely, that the Brahmins, Vessas, Suddas, and Jīvas are of white, yellow, black, and dark colors respectively—and having heard their distinction of shape as described by those saying, "It is pervasive," "it is circular," and so forth, [he thought]:
"For they indeed possess white, yellow, black, and very dark shadows at midday, evening, night, and at times of extreme darkness.
Thus he understood their differences in color and their differences in shape.
923. By treating the two words *purisa-puggalo* as a single compound, this conventional discourse (*sammuti-kathā*) proceeds from the perspective of those who understand [the term] thus;
or, showing that this is indeed another word denoting a person (*puggala*), he says "But this... and so forth.

Alternatively, it is said "man" (*purisa*) precisely because it is a person (*puggala*), and not merely one endowed with the male faculty (*purisindriya*); for the sake of demonstrating this as well, he says "man-person" (*purisa-puggala*).

It should be understood that this is what was stated. Regarding "in the eight types of afflictions": these are those arising from bile, phlegm, and wind; those born of seasonal changes; those caused by external factors; those resulting from an imbalance of the humors (*sannipāta*);

and those produced by karma. "Previously performed" refers to more ancient karma; they maintain that it includes [karma] to be experienced upon rebirth (*upapajjavedanīya*), and they indeed reject [karma] to be experienced in subsequent lives.
"By way of being rooted in an order" means that even one who, having given an order, causes suffering such as execution or imprisonment, that [suffering] is also rooted in that [order].
The intention is that it does not exist;
rather, it is rooted solely in the creation by a Supreme Lord (*issaranimmāna*). 924. The "burning" (*anudahana*) of delusion is stated because of its nature as a cause of burning;

however, non-penetration (*asampaṭivedha*) should also be understood as "burning" in the sense that, by its very nature, it is opposed to the bliss of penetration and is thus suffering. And having established this, [it is said]: "Equanimity-feeling is the bliss of knowledge..."
"...suffering due to ignorance," it is said.
Regarding "in objects with various signs" (*puthunimittārammaṇesu*): this refers to objects that possess the nature of various signs by way of the sign of the beautiful (*subhanimitta*) and so forth;

or alternatively, it refers to objects such as the sign of the beautiful that exist in various natures. Although there is a similarity between the descriptions of laziness (*kosajja*) and negligence (*pamāda*), [the latter] is characterized by a lack of expansion (*avipphārikatā*).
"Laxity of conduct" is indolence; "negligence," which is defined as the lapse of mindfulness, is heedlessness—this is the distinction.
(931) "Living with respect" refers to living with a sense of shame (*ottappa*); "living with deference" refers to living with reverence toward elders.
"Not taking up" means not receiving instruction; the meaning is a lack of regard. Like the dryness of a piece of wood, or its lack of moisture, it is a lack of pliancy (*amudutā*).
“Lack of virtue” (*asīlya*) means a lack of virtuous conduct and a lack of mental pliancy.
934. “Censure” (*upārambho*) may be the arising of a state of consciousness associated with hatred.
936. Since the word “does” (*karoti*) is also appropriate in the sense of placing, as in the phrase “he places a stone here,” he says: “‘Does’ (*karoti*)...”

"...it sets aside. Here, it should be understood that this adverting consciousness is mentioned among the "minor bases" (khuddakavatthu) because it is an immediate cause for unwholesome states, or because its function is conducive to them.
The commentary on the Exposition of the Triads is finished.
(4. Commentary on the Exposition of the Tetrads, §939.
The word *iti* is a particle used for indication; this shows that it has the same meaning as the word *evaṃ*. Regarding the phrase "the causes of various states of existence" (*bhavābhavahetu*):

here, "state of existence" (*bhava*) means that by which things come into being or are born, namely, medicinal substances such as ghee and the like. When that very state of existence becomes more excellent and fully developed—

Non-existence (*abhava*). Or, because they are to be abandoned through the noble lineages (*ariyavaṃsa*) that delight in meditation, all cravings—excluding the previous three types of craving—should be understood as having been stated thus:

"They arise with existence and non-existence as their cause. "By this" means by the wrong course of desire and so forth. "Do not go" means they do not proceed; the meaning is that they do not perform various actions. "By this" means by such a wrong course of desire and so forth. "Going according to one's inclination" means going in whichever direction among desire and the rest one is inclined.
“Fear of waves,” etc.: just as there is fear caused by signs such as kings, so too there is a trembling of the mind caused by signs such as waves; this is called “fear of waves.
According to such statements as, “Monks, ‘fear of waves’ is a designation for anger and distress,” it refers to anger, distress, gluttony, the five cords of sensual pleasure, or women.
In that context, by the mention of the five cords of sensual pleasure and women, one should understand that desire and lust based upon them are also included.
Greed is indeed gluttony. The disciplinary measures of the Vinaya include such acts as the formal act of suspension (ukkhepanīyakamma).
In the Nidāna-vagga, it is said: “Then the wanderer Timbaruka went to the Blessed One...
and said this: ‘Master Gotama, is pleasure and pain self-made? ‘Do not say so, Timbaruka,’ the Blessed One replied,” and so forth.
Because it has come [from that source], it is called the "Timbaruka view.
The commentary on the exposition of the tetrads is finished.
(5. Commentary on the Exposition of the Pentads.
940. "But not allowing [the mind] to come" means it should be understood as not being a condition for its arrival.
941. "From anointing" means from the cause of increasing flesh through filling [the body], and from accumulation.

"There is comfort for one who lies down after eating during the summer season"—this seasonal comfort is called "the pleasure of lying down" (*seyyasukha*); it is the pleasure of the posture of reclining.
The meaning is as follows: *vata* refers to the ascetic practices (*dhutaṅga*). *Tapa* refers to the duties prescribed in the Khandhakas, or else it means energy (*vīriya*).

If it is argued that the mention of "austerity" (*tapa*) and "holy life" (*brahmacariya*) need not be made because the duties of the Khandhakas and the abstention from sexual intercourse are already included by the mention of "virtue" (*sīla*), we say no.

This is because [the author] intended to show that austerity and the holy life are grasped for the purpose of making them distinct from other forms of virtue and for showing their role in causing one to become a deity; furthermore, it is to show the occurrence of external fetters.
Or rather: for them, non-violence, the cow-vow (*govatā*), the performance of difficult austerities, and abstinence from sexual intercourse are, respectively, virtue (*sīla*) and the other [factors].
And they practice these while making a resolution (*paṇidhāya*) for that divine realm. Otherwise, through faith, inclination, and so forth, they conceptualize [the self] in such ways as:
"O sir, when this self—which possesses form, consists of the four great elements, and is born of mother and father—is destroyed at the breaking up of the body, it perishes," and so on.

942. In the section on misfortunes (*vyasana*), it should be understood that by the mention of the misfortunes of relatives, wealth, and illness, the sorrow and other states caused by them are included. Regarding "repulsiveness in seeing and hearing" (*dassana-savana-paṭikūlatā*):

here, it should be understood that among the five disadvantages (*ādīnava*), impatience (*akkhanti*) itself—which is the cause of those [disadvantages]—is stated by breaking it down [into its components]; or rather, it refers to those causes such as unpleasantness (*appiyatā*) which are rooted in impatience.
These include faults such as wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) and frivolous speech (dubbhāsita).
The fear that arises at the time of death on account of wrong livelihood is called "the fear of livelihood" (ājīvakabhaya).

However, in the reading "the fear of a livelihood-claimer" (ājīvikābhaya), the meaning should be understood as the mental terror arising from the sign of a false ascetic, which occurs when one perceives the non-attainment of the necessary requisites.
"Fame" (*kittisadda*) means renown; its opposite is ill-repute (*asiloka*) or infamy (*akitti*). Therefore, he said "fear of censure.
943. "Exultation" (*uppilāvana*) refers to a state of lack of tranquility characterized by elation, or the mode of joy that serves as the cause for such lack of tranquility.
The commentary on the exposition of the pentads is concluded.
(6. Commentary on the Exposition of the Sixfold Set 944.

By the passage beginning, “He is prone to anger and bears ill will,” etc., it is stated in the Sutta that resentment and the rest—having anger and so forth as their cause—are the auxiliary causes for anger and the rest;
therefore, anger and the rest alone are the roots of dispute, and thus they alone are mentioned here. [Likewise] is the adherence to one's own views (*sanditthiparāmāsa*).
[It is] due to being dogmatically attached to one’s own view.

945. "Without support" means being devoid of venerable persons who serve as a support. "The characteristic of heedfulness" is the non-abandonment of mindfulness, or the persistence in the application of what is wholesome.
"Being properly engaged" means being thoroughly intent through the influence of leaning toward that [wholesome state]. "Socializing with the crowd" occurs by way of the defilements.
Socializing (*saṅgaṇikā*). The gratification in hearing talk connected with women and in hearing the sound of women is the "contact of hearing.
The gratification in giving to or receiving from a woman is the "contact of enjoyment. 946.
They proceed together with joy; thus they are called "joyful mental explorations" (*somanassupavicārā*), which are associated with unwholesome joy.
It should be understood that here the "investigations of form" (*rūpavicāra*) and so forth are intended, as are the "investigations of equanimity" (*upekkhupavicāra*).

By the phrase "associated with that," it is shown that by the inclusion of "investigation" (*vicāra*), "initial application" (*vitakka*) is also included; thus, through the occurrence of initial application, the expression "he applies himself to initial application" (*upavitakketi*) is also implied.

947. Regarding "associated with ignorance" (*aññāṇasampayutta*): they say that in states of consciousness accompanied by doubt (*vicikicchā*) or restlessness (*uddhacca*), equanimity (*upekkhā*) is delusion (*moha*). Furthermore, even equanimity associated with greed (*lobha*) is not non-worldly (*gehasita*). 948.
The "fortuitous originationist" (*adhiccasamuppannika*), grasping at the thought, "The self has arisen fortuitously;

it will continue to arise," is one who holds an eternalist view (*sassatadiṭṭhi*). Showing that [the latter's] view is similar to such a one, [the text says]: "Of the fortuitous originationist alone."
He said: Regarding the phrase "he is not born" (*na so jāto*), here the particle *jātu* is stated as "born" (*jāto*) by changing the vowel *u* to *o*;

or rather, this should be seen as another particle having the same meaning as that. "The view regarding all taints" (*sabbāsavadiṭṭhi*) means the view that has come down in the discourse on all taints (*sabbāsava*).
The commentary on the exposition of the sixfold set is finished.
(7. Commentary on the Exposition of the Septet. 951.
Since there is no other septet among the sixty-two views, the seven annihilationist doctrines (*ucchedavāda*) themselves are not stated here as such, but are called "seven views.
The commentary on the exposition of the septet is finished.
(8. Commentary on the Exposition of the Eight: 952.
Mental states that arise in the manner of sinking down, such as "I must perform some work," are the causes of indolence;
or rather, they should be understood as causes of indolence because they serve as the proximate causes for further indolence.
Regarding the phrase *māsācitaṃ maññe*: here, the word *ācita* expresses the meaning of the word *tinta* (soaked), and the word *maññe* expresses the meaning of the word *viya* (like).
With this intention, the meaning “like a soaked bean (*tintamāso viyā*)” is clarified; or alternatively, the meaning is “like a heap of beans (*māsacayo viyā*)”.
957. *Pharati* means “it touches”; the meaning is “it strikes. “By another cause” refers to: “Today you ate at an improper time.”
When told, "Therefore you have committed an offense," he conceals the relevant reason with another, irrelevant reason, such as saying, "I ate at the proper time yesterday, therefore I am not guilty.
This means that he diverts the discussion by using an unrelated cause to hide the pertinent one.

"Diversion" (*vikkhipana*) refers to the removal of the discourse from its subject matter so that it does not adhere to it, leading it away externally; this is "leading away externally" (*bahiddhā apanāmanā*).

958. “Those who maintain the doctrine of non-perception” (*asaññīvādā*) refers to persons who demonstrate their views; or, those dogmatic attachments (*abhinivesa*) by which they declare the self to be non-percipient are the “doctrines of non-perception. “The sign of the formless attainments” (*arūpasamāpattinimitta*) refers to space and so forth.
The commentary on the Exposition of the Octad (9) is finished.
(9. Commentary on the Exposition of the Nonad (Navakaniddesa).
960. Because the tenth [type of pleasure] was not mentioned, it is said: "They are explained solely by way of their arising among beings. 963.

*Sukhavinicchayaṃ* means the determination of pleasure regarding what is to be cultivated and what is not to be cultivated. *Ajjhattaṃ sukhaṃ* refers to the pleasure of renunciation (*nekkhammasukha*) which is to be cultivated. Regarding the phrase "two determinations" (*vinicchayā*), this refers to what is called in the world "the pleasant" and "the unpleasant":
"Sātaṃ asātanti yamāhu loke... (That which is called 'pleasant' and 'unpleasant' in the world...)
“Depending upon that, desire arises;
having seen both dissolution and origination among forms,
a person makes a judgment in the world.”
This was stated in its exposition (niddesa).

Regarding the phrase "here it is called 'determination' (vinicchaya)': that which is expressed by the word 'determination' in this Vibhaṅga text by way of being the condition for desire-and-lust (chanda-rāga), is [also] expressed by the word 'thought' (vitakka) in the Sakkapañha Sutta by way of being the source of desire."
"Thus it has come"—this shows the state of the thought's determination (*vinicchaya*) and its inclusion here.
"Strong conviction" (*balavasanniṭṭhāna*) means grasping an object after having determined it through powerful craving (*taṇhā*).

Although other [mental factors] also possess the quality of being conditioned (*saṅkhata*), the conditionality of the conceit "I am" (*asmīti*) and "I am this" (*aham asmi*) is particularly prominent.
Having [conditioned] it, pride is called "the conditioned" (*saṅkhata*). Alternatively, the conditioning of oneself as "I am" by way of superiority and so forth is the conditioned.

Herein, because the occurrence [of the mind] such as "they will be" and so forth is characterized by craving and views, the state of being subject to fluctuation (*iñjita*) and so on is also predicated of those.
The commentary on the Exposition of Nines is finished.
(10. Commentary on the Exposition of Tens: 970.
Skillful planning, such as the arrangement of casting a net, is "contrivance" (*upāya-cintā*); it is so called because it conceals the state of its being wrong.
It should be understood that the delusion (moha) occurring in that mode arises by way of reflecting on a means [to conceal it].
Furthermore, the perception or intention that occurs when viewing the absence of danger in the evil deed already committed is "reviewing" (paccavekkhaṇā);

the delusion arising in that mode—which either conceals its false nature or views the absence of danger in the manner of reviewing—is likewise to be understood. "Perceiving as liberated" (vimuttasaññitā) is associated with overestimation (adhimāna).

Some say that "wrong liberation" (micchā-vimutti) is an unwholesome state of consciousness occurring in the form of the thought, "I am liberated," which arises from the perception of being liberated through one's own view,
as held by the followers of other sects (titthiyā). However, when liberation is grasped as being like the fruit [of the path],
it would be more appropriate to say that in a consciousness associated with wrong view, the view itself is wrong knowledge (micchā-ñāṇa), while the concentration (samādhi) is wrong liberation.
The commentary on the *Dasakaniddesa* is finished.
Commentary on the *Taṇhāvicaritaniddesa*: 973.
Regarding the phrase "by way of grasping as a collective," they say it means by way of grasping craving (*taṇhā*), conceit (*māna*), and views (*diṭṭhi*) in common. "In this way, thus..."
However, grasping without making a distinction [between the two] as "otherwise" should be understood as grasping at a collection (*samūhagāha*).
"Another aspect" means an aspect belonging to another's mental continuum. "Exists" means it is always present; this is the meaning. "Sinks" means it perishes.
"By way of doubt and discursive thought" means by way of such discursive thought as: "Could I be, or could I not be? "By way of aspiration and imagining" means...
“May I indeed be successful!”—it is by way of such an aspiration and its conceptualization [that this is said].
“With pure heads” (*suddhasīsā*): they are called “with pure heads” because craving, conceit, and views share a common head, as they do not depend on any distinction.
In that context, by means of the “heads of views,” craving is shown through view; and by means of conceit and views, which have their root in the “head of the head,” [conceit is shown].
He said himself: "In this way, these... pe ... should be understood as phenomena that are wanderings of craving.

Regarding the view and conceit [factors] as well, the expression "wanderings of craving" should be understood as being applied because, although view and conceit are mutually dissociated, they are not dissociated from craving;
rather, they are so designated because they are rooted in craving and have craving as their primary factor.
974. *Avakkarī* is a particle meaning "in various ways" (*nānābhāve*); thus, that which is not made in various ways is *anavakkari*.
Having done that—or, alternatively, having not done what is to be separated—he says, "having made [them] undivided" (*avinibbhogaṃ katvā*), showing it in this way.
Or there is the reading *anavakāriṃ karitvā*; therein, *avakiraṇaṃ* means scattering, the separation of parts from a whole.

"Avakāri" means that without making a distinction from that which is "avakāri," one takes even the five aggregates as a single whole and, failing to separate them from a self, acquires the desire, conceit, and views of "I am. Regarding "asitabyābhaṅgitāya":
by means of this equipment, namely the sickle and the carrying-pole, the acts of reaping and threshing are called "asitabyābhaṅgī."
976. “Having made a distinction” means having analytically separated form and the other aggregates from the self. “By means of this form...

by means of this consciousness, one acquires the desire ‘I am’”—in all such instances, the meaning of the word “by means of this” should be understood as “by means of form and so forth that are not analytically separated from the self. For those things which are not analytically separated from the self, which are not external to it, and which are grasped as simply “I,” [are what is meant].
Craving that arises by approaching and taking up form and so forth is said to be "dependent on the internal";
craving that arises by approaching and taking up those things which are distinct from the self and considered external is said to be "dependent on the external.
One thinks, "I am eternal," or "There is no destruction for me through a sword or an umbrella," thus imagining that there is no ruin for oneself through such auspicious objects as a sword.

The meaning is as follows. The phrase "for each one" is stated for the purpose of showing that even all thirty-six [types of craving] can occur for each individual throughout the beginningless and endless cycle of saṃsāra, both in the past and the future;
or alternatively, it is stated with reference to the attainment of each individual person according to their respective circumstances.

This too is said by way of considering craving, conceit, and views as independent, for the purpose of showing that for an ordinary person (puthujjana), some of these may occur in the long-term present.
The commentary on the exposition of the investigation of craving is finished.
The commentary on the analysis of the minor bases is finished. 18.
The Analysis of the Heart of the Teaching (Dhammahadayavibhaṅga).
1. Explanation of the Section on the Compendium of All (Sabbasaṅgāhikavāravaṇṇanā) 978.

By the passage beginning with “The five aggregates,” [the text] refers to the aggregates and so forth, which are distinguished by various classifications such as: those included within the occurrence of the elements; those pertaining to the planes of existence; those pertaining to the internal bases;

those produced by wholesome kamma such as giving; their respective results (vipāka); those objects to be known through direct knowledge (abhiññeyya); the two dyads of objects; the triads beginning with the seen; the pentads beginning with the wholesome; and the two dyads of the mundane (lokiya). These are further divided according to the categories of form, etc.

Because it includes [the factors] without remainder and because the second section and those following are incorporated herein, the first is called the "all-inclusive section" (sabbasaṅgāhika-vāra) as it is stated in its entirety; the second is called the "section showing arising and non-arising.

In that context, however, their mere existence is stated by means of such questions as, "In the sense-sphere realm (kāmadhātu), how many aggregates (khandha) are there? How many bases (āyatana) are there? and so forth.
The non-application of specific actions— such as "exists," "becomes," or "is found"— is because they are understood through the general action of being manifest;

therefore, it is appropriate to call this "the section showing possibility and impossibility," while the fourth is "the section showing arising and non-arising at the moment of rebirth," since it speaks of manifestation and non-manifestation therein.

979. Just as they ask, there is an unerring explanation corresponding to the question; because it is understood that even an answer given by others is the word of the Omniscient One (sabbaññu) since it was produced [in accordance with his teaching], it is indeed called an "Omniscient One’s explanation. What need is there to mention one given by the Omniscient One himself?
This is the intended meaning. 2. Commentary on the Section on Arising and Non-arising: 991.
“And of those born in the sense-sphere” (kāmadhātu-sambhūtānaṃ): the meaning is, of sense-sphere beings who have gone to the fine-material sphere (rūpadhātu) by means of supernormal power (iddhi).
Regarding the phrase "due to the absence of the sense-base of smell and so forth":

if, because of that absence, the sense-bases of odor and so forth do not perform the functions of being a sense-base and so on, then in the case of non-percipient beings (*asaññasatta*), the sense-base of form (*rūpāyatana*) would likewise not perform the function of being a sense-base due to the absence of the sense-base of the eye.
Consequently, the statement, "At the moment of rebirth for the gods who are non-percipient beings, two sense-bases become manifest," and so forth, [would be contradicted].

It should not be said [that they are not elements]. The spheres such as the sense-sphere (kāmāvacara) and so forth are called "elements" (dhātu) because they serve as the basis for sentient beings arising therein, or for the phenomena included therein.

Likewise, those groups of beings (sattanikāya) within which sense-sphere beings and others arise—being called "origins of beings" (sattuppatti) because the arising of those beings occurs therein—are also [elements].
Furthermore, there is no such thing here as a non-included location (*apariyāpanna-okāsa*) or a non-included realm of beings (*apariyāpanna-sattanikāya*) that could be called a "plane" (*dhātu*).
Demonstrating this point, he said: "Whether by way of location or by way of the arising of beings, there is no such thing as a 'non-included plane' (*apariyāpanna-dhātu*).
By the phrase "by way of the arising of beings," he includes both the world of space and the world of beings together, [showing] that such a non-included plane does not exist.
It shows non-existence. Or, "arising of beings" (sattuppatti) means arising by way of the state of a being;
the aggregates of clinging that arise by way of various existences as dwellings for beings are called "elements" (dhātu) because they serve as similar bases for those things included therein.
Thus, the meaning is that there is no such thing as an "unincluded element" (apariyāpannadhātu).
3. Commentary on the Section on the Included and the Unincluded (Pariyāpannāpariyāpannavāra-vaṇṇanā) 999.
"Delimited by way of existence and by way of plane": herein, all appropriated aggregates arising elsewhere [in other planes] should be understood as being included in their respective [planes].
6. The Section on Productive Karma and the Measure of Life Span (Uppādakakamma-āyuppamāṇavāra)
(1. Commentary on Productive Karma 1021.

Having explained the classification of the aggregates and so forth by way of their arising from the elements and so on, in order to show the classification by way of those beings who possess the diversity of elements, the karma that produces them, and the result of that karma, [the text says] "three..."

The sixth section, beginning with "the gods," has commenced. For it is the aggregates (khandha) and so forth themselves that are divided according to the gods who have become the three elements, according to the kamma such as giving, and according to the acquired aggregates delimited by their respective lifespans. Some say [the lifespan] is four *doṇas* of mangoes, while others say six *doṇas*.
The commentary on the productive kamma is finished.
(2. Explanation of the Lifespan Measure: 1024.
"The three people" means three groups of people; this is the intended meaning. 1025.
"Radiance" (*ābhā*) refers to beautiful light.
1026. Like a mass of gold, it is "radiant as a mass of gold" (*kañcanapiṇḍasassirikā*).
In that context, although one should say *subhākiṇṇā*—meaning "strewn with beautiful radiance"—the vowel *ā* is shortened and the final letter *ṇa* is changed to *ha*, thus it is called *subhakiṇhā*.
Alternatively, it is *subhakiṇṇā*, meaning "strewn with beauty. In the preceding terms as well, [the word] *parittaṃ*...

The compound should be construed with the word *subha* as follows: "Those for whom beauty (*subha*) is limited are the Parittasubhas; those for whom beauty is immeasurable (*appamāṇa*) are the Appamāṇasubhas.

[Verse 1027] Since these were explained in relation to the preliminary stage (*pubbabhāga*) of the attention to the object, they refer to the cultivation of the limited and other kasiṇa objects either at the moment of absorption (*jhāna-kkhaṇa*) or subsequently.
The meaning is this: through the act of adverting (*āvajjana*), there is no diversity in the object or the attention of the jhāna;

however, through preliminary development (*pubbabhāga-bhāvanā*) and the preliminary adverting, such diversity does exist. For by means of preliminary development, the jhāna takes as its respective object limited earth-kasiṇas and so forth;
and by means of the preliminary stage, through the adverting to each respective kasiṇa, there occurs the respective attention (*manasikāra*). [As for] desire and the rest...

However, they are also present at the moment of absorption (*appanā*). In this context, "aspiration" (*paṇidhi*) should not be understood as the longing of craving (*taṇhā*), but rather as the longing of desire (*chanda*).
"Resolution" (*adhimokkha*) is certainty. "Directing" (*abhinīhāra*) is simply the engagement of the mind.

But if what is intended by "longing for existence" (*bhava-chanda*) and "aspiration for existence" (*bhava-patthānā*) are those factors that determine specific types of existence, then they are applicable even during absorption; for when absorption has arisen...
Therefore, it should be understood that even subsequently they are still operative.

However, when the object is qualified by the fading away of perception (*saññāvirāga*) and so forth, the attention (*manasikāra*) proceeding toward it in such a manner determines the specific state of existence (*bhava-visesa-niyāmaka*);
since this occurs only in the preliminary stage (*pubbabhāga*), it is said: "The object and attention are described as belonging to the preliminary stage."

"Vast fruits" means vast fruits such as peace, happiness, long life, beauty, and so forth. "They see well" means they see with the eye of wisdom (*paññā-cakkhu*) as well as with the physical eye and the divine eye (*dibba-cakkhu*).

Regarding the statement, "As long as that evil karma has not been exhausted," he says, "Karma alone is the measure. The intention is that the determination of the lifespan limit for the *abbuda* hell and the others is made solely by way of karma.
"The absence of a place to hide" means there is no place free from those sensual pleasures, being constantly surrounded by a host of celestial nymphs of the same kind; this is the meaning.
"What determines? means: what does jhāna determine regarding rebirth? "The nine Brahmā-worlds" refers to all nine, beginning with the Brahma-pārisajja, having been purified.
"At the summit" means: in the Vehapphala [heaven]. "The best existences" means: they are the highest existences because there is no going beyond them;
for that very reason, they are designated as the "heads of existence. "In these three places" refers to the locations beginning with the Vehapphala.

It was said with this very intention. However, regarding those non-returners (*anāgāmī*) who have been reborn in the nine lower planes prior to the *Vehapphala* realm, because they are reborn in the formless realm (*arūpadhātu*), it was stated:

"For one who has passed away from the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) and is being reborn in the formless realm, seven underlying tendencies (*anusaya*) underlie for some, five for some, and three for some. This was not said with reference to those reborn in the *Vehapphala* realm and so forth.
The intended meaning here may be that this was said with reference to those who have been reborn [in the higher realms].

As for what was stated—that "for noble disciples reborn in the nine Brahma-worlds, there is only rebirth there, and not rebirth in the lower planes"—by this, only rebirth in the lower planes is precluded, not rebirth in progressively higher levels within those very worlds, nor rebirth in the Vehapphala realm, nor rebirth in the formless realm (*arūpadhātu*). [Regarding] "in the plane of the first jhāna..."
"Having been reborn as a non-returner, he purifies the nine Brahma-worlds and, stationed at their summit, attains final Nibbāna"— this too was said with reference to one who ascends step by step;
therefore, it should be understood that this does not preclude the rebirth of one who has not reached the summit into the formless realm (arūpadhātu).

This commentary was spoken with reference to a noble disciple who, having developed the path either elsewhere or there itself, passed away and was reborn there with the lust for the form realm not yet suppressed. For this very reason, it says:
"of noble disciples reborn in the nine Brahma-worlds," "a non-returner reborn in the plane of the first jhāna," and "non-returners reborn in these three places."

And in all cases, the term "arisen" (nibbatta) has been employed. Furthermore, for one who has been reborn there, once the lust for the fine-material realm (*rūparāga*) has been suppressed, there will be no further longing for existence;
thus, the cutting off of lust for the immaterial realm (*arūparāgupaccheda*) will certainly occur as well.
As for an ordinary person (*puthujjana*) who has been reborn there and, having developed the Noble Path, has suppressed the lust for the fine-material realm by means of the immaterial states—

Alternatively, this meaning may be intended: when the Path has arisen, there is no longing for existence because one sees the danger in the state of existence that has been produced; it is by virtue of this that the Yamaka-pāḷi proceeds.
The commentary on the measure of the lifespan is finished.
7. Explanation of the Section on What is to be Directly Known, Etc. 1030.

The purification by overcoming doubt (*diṭṭhikaṅkhāvitaraṇavisuddhi*) that apprehends specific characteristics through the apprehension of general and specific characteristics—such as “matter has the characteristic of being molested (*ruppana*);
contact has the characteristic of touching”—is full understanding through knowledge (*ñātapariññā*). Beyond that, up until...
The full understanding by scrutinization is the "conformable" [full understanding]; it extends from the contemplation of rise and fall up to the path, which is the full understanding by abandoning.

Regarding the phrase "in each respective case": first, that which is to be said concerning the aggregates and so forth has already been stated in the sections on the interrogation of questions in the *Khandhavibhaṅga* and other such texts;

furthermore, since causes and so forth are included within the aggregates and so forth, that which is to be said concerning them in their respective sections on the interrogation of questions is likewise stated.
It should be understood as "already stated.
The commentary on the section beginning with "to be directly known" is finished.
The commentary on the *Dhammahadayavibhaṅga* is finished.
Thus ends the sub-commentary on the word-by-word explanation of the *Sammohavinodanī*,
the root commentary on the *Vibhaṅga*.
Homage to that Blessed One, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Self-Awakened One.
Abhidhamma Piṭaka: Vibhaṅga-aṇuṭīkā 1.
Khandhavibhaṅga (The Sub-commentary on the Analysis of the Aggregates)
1. Commentary on the Suttantabhājanīya:
Since the four noble truths are included within the Four Truths, the truths are taken in their entirety by the phrase "one who sees the four truths" in the verse.
Therefore, explaining that meaning in its full extent, he says: "The four truths," and so forth.
In this context, "collected" (*samāhaṭāni*) means brought together; the intended sense is that they have been grasped as one by the mind.

Furthermore, by the term "collected," he shows that this is a compound formed by way of a collective aggregate (*samāhāra*). For that very reason, even though its agent has been expressed, the neuter designation "the Four Truths" (*catusaccaṃ*) is used, just as in the case of "three turnings" (*tivaṭṭaṃ*) and so forth.
Indeed, its feminine gender is not established by the inclusion of words such as "bowl" (*patta*), just as in the expression "five bowls" (*pañcapattaṃ*).
He saw—that is, he perceived—the fourfold yoke and the three worlds, which are the Four Noble Truths;
the meaning is that he penetrated them by way of the clear realizations (*abhisamaya*) of full understanding, abandoning, realization, and cultivation.

But why, when the infinite and immeasurable qualities of a Buddha—such as Great Compassion and Omniscience, which are not shared with others—are present here, is there mention instead of the vision of the Four Noble Truths, which is shared with disciples and Paccekabuddhas?
Reflecting on the objection that [the Buddha] praises the Blessed One [when he himself has already attained his goal], he says, "Even though there are disciples," and so forth.

Therein, by the phrase "because it was not previously done by another," he shows the Blessed One’s non-commonality and unsurpassed nature regarding the vision of the Four Noble Truths, both in relation to the disciples and—by the words "and therein"—in relation to the Paccekabuddhas.
It is because [this vision] is perfectly manifest through its extension into the mental continuums of others.

Because of the power of his teaching, and because the vision of the Four Noble Truths has been expanded within the mental continuums of those to be trained, it has been well-proclaimed among gods and humans.
To show that the word *nātha* is used in the world in the senses of "one who entreats," "one who torments," "lord," and "head," it is said:
"He protects (*nāthati*), therefore he is a protector (*nātha*)," and so forth. In this context, since the Blessed One, by virtue of his very vision of the Four Noble Truths, [is the one who...]

Having reached the pinnacle of both seeking the welfare and happiness [of others] while burning away the calamities of the defilements, and of requesting [others] to practice for their welfare, he has revealed himself by means of that very [title].

Therefore, without touching upon the extraction of the meaning (*atthuddhāra*), he spoke the passage beginning with “he seeks the welfare and happiness of those to be trained,” showing the meaning of the word *nātha* by way of the extraction of the words (*paduddhāra*). Or else, by this phrase “the seer of the Four Truths,”...
The power of the Blessed One’s knowledge has been revealed as not shared by others;

therefore, in order to manifest his power of compassion—which likewise is not shared by others—through the word "Nātha" (Protector), the phrase "of those to be trained" (*veneyyānaṃ*) and so forth was stated.

The construction is: the Blessed One, endowed with supreme sovereignty of mind, is called "Nātha. Likewise, [he is so called] because he is endowed with supreme sovereignty of mind toward all beings...
It should be construed as "he rules by means of his qualities. By "sovereignty over the mind" is meant mastery over the mind through noble psychic powers (*ariyiddhi*) and so forth.

"He rules by means of his qualities" means that he exercises sovereignty through the Dhamma by means of his own qualities such as virtue (*sīla*), which have reached the highest excellence; this is the meaning.
Because one who has become thus is called "the Conqueror of All," it is said: "he conquers. And so it was said: "In the world with its devas..."
“Monks, in the world... [as before] ...he is the conqueror, unconquered; therefore he is called the ‘Tathāgata.
Thus he shows the word *nātha* (protector) in the sense of sovereignty in two ways.
The construction is: “the praise of the teaching through its eighteenfold division. By means of qualities that are of equal number (*samānagaṇanaguṇehi*) means by those whose enumeration is equal.
By means of the qualities acting as instruments— that is, by means of the unsurpassed vision of the Four Noble Truths as previously described,

which serves as the proximate cause (*padaṭṭhāna*) for omniscient knowledge (*sabbaññutaññāṇa*) and mastery over the ten powers (*dasabala*). For, through the perfect awakening to the Truths, in accordance with his original aspiration,

[the Buddha] attained a preeminent state regarding material and immaterial phenomena by way of three hundred and sixty million approaches, distinguished by the dense variety of functions, aggregates, activities, and objects within the mental continuum.

By means of the unique quality of a Buddha known as the "Great Vajira-knowledge" (mahāvajirañāṇa)—which arises through the process of contemplation—the Blessed One was firmly established in Perfect Self-Enlightenment (sammāsambodhi).

Thus, while analyzing phenomena according to their divisions into wholesome and so forth, and according to their divisions into contact and so forth, he became capable of teaching the compendium of Dhamma (dhammasaṅgaṇī) in four ways by means of the "Chapter on the Arising of Consciousness" (cittuppādakaṇḍa) and the rest. Likewise, he was endowed with the qualities of a Buddha, such as unimpeded knowledge regarding the past (atītaṃsa).
The Blessed One was capable of teaching the aggregates and so forth by analyzing them according to their divisions, such as the past and so on. Therefore it is said:
“...the Vibhaṅga as previously described... Having stated “because it was spoken by the Omniscient One,” he further says “showing that it could not have been taught by one who is not omniscient”;
by this, [he demonstrates] the positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya* and *vyatireka*) between the *Dhammasaṅgaṇī* and the *Vibhaṅga*.
It clarifies precisely that which has been proclaimed by the Perfectly Enlightened One. Regarding the "qualities such as perfect enlightenment":

it reveals qualities such as the Perfect Enlightenment (*sammāsambuddhatā*) of the Buddha Jewel, and the well-expounded nature (*svākkhātatā*) and the well-practiced nature (*suppaṭipannatā*) of the Dhamma and Saṅgha Jewels.

But is it not the case that the qualities of the Blessed One alone are clarified by the passage beginning with “the seer of the Four Truths”? True; however, by that very same [passage], the qualities of the Dhamma and the Saṅgha are also [clarified].
The qualities are "discerned" because there is no other way for them to arise from that source;
or, by means of those [qualities], the Dhamma and its support, the Saṅgha, are likewise said to be described. Thus it is said: “He discerns the Buddha and so forth...
In the phrase *atītaṃse*, it means in the past section; that is, in the prior limit (*pubbante*). “Unobstructed” (*appaṭihataṃ*) means not obstructed; it refers to the obstruction of knowledge.

It is ignorance, or else the entire mass of defilements. Since that has been abandoned by the Blessed One together with its underlying tendencies (*vāsanā*), his knowledge regarding the past is said to be entirely unimpeded due to the abandonment of the veil of the knowable (*ñeyyāvaraṇa*).
This same method applies to the others as well. But are these separate, individual types of knowledge, or are they simply the knowledges that function with respect to the past and so forth?
Is it so? They say that the "unimpeded knowledges regarding the three times" are indeed three distinct knowledges belonging to the Blessed One.
However, being one and the same, the "unimpeded knowledge regarding the three times" is simply the knowledge of omniscience (*sabbaññutaññāṇa*).
"Every bodily action" refers to whatever bodily action was to be performed by the Blessed One. "Preceded by knowledge" means having knowledge as its precursor. "Following after knowledge" means...
The meaning is that as the Blessed One performs every bodily exertion, he does so having delimited it with knowledge, such that it proceeds only accompanied by knowledge.
The same method applies to the other two phrases as well. "Of desire" means of the desire for agency;

the meaning is the desire to perform beneficial action through the longing for the absolute welfare of beings due to the conjunction with great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*). "Of the teaching of the Dhamma" means...

Regarding the discourse on the Dhamma: because of the Blessed One’s inexhaustible and immeasurable eloquence and his perfection of skillful means, the teaching of the Dhamma never comes to an end even when it is being expounded continuously;
rather, it only increases further and further. "Of energy" refers to the enthusiasm for practicing for the welfare of others. "Of liberation" refers to liberation as the fruit.

And herein, the non-decline of concentration and the other factors should be understood as being unique to these [Buddhas] because their respective opposites have been abandoned along with their latent tendencies (*savāsanā*);
however, for zeal (*chanda*) and the rest, it is also due to their conjunction with Great Compassion (*mahākaruṇā*). The remainder is easy to understand. 1.

"Those very same phenomena" refers to those very phenomena comprised within the triplets and dyads, such as the wholesome and so forth; in the *Suttanta*, they are categorized by way of the aggregates (*khandha*) and so on.
The construction is: "when [the aggregates] have been spoken of, they are analyzed by way of the aggregates and so forth. One might ask:

"Are they not, however, spoken of in the Suttanta by way of the analytical knowledges (paṭisambhidā)? Even if they are not spoken of in their specific form, they are indeed spoken of in terms of meaning, because the analysis of knowledge regarding cause and effect and so forth has been stated in such passages as, "knowledge of aging-and-death, knowledge of the origin of aging-and-death," and so on, in the *Paṭisambhidāmagga*.
Or, because they are included within the *paṭisambhidā* (analytical knowledges), those states are indeed spoken of in the Suttanta by way of the *paṭisambhidā*.

"Therein" means in that Suttanta. "In brief" means by way of summary. For in the Suttanta, the aggregates and so forth are taught merely by way of enumeration and exposition (*uddesaniddesa*), and not by way of further detailed explanation (*paṭiniddesa*) and so on;
thus it is said that they are spoken of there "in brief. Alternatively, "therein" refers to the *Dhammasaṅgaṇī*.
For even there, the aggregates and so forth are stated in brief by such passages as, "At that time, however, there are four aggregates.
It is called *vibhaṅga* because the aggregates and so forth are analyzed (*vibhajīyanti*) therein, or by means of it.

It is called *pakaraṇa* because those very same [aggregates] are scattered forth (*pakirīyanti*) or established (*paṭṭhapīyanti*) therein, or by means of it. Thus, it is the *Vibhaṅga-pakaraṇa*, being both a *vibhaṅga* and a *pakaraṇa*.

“By that which indicates the meaning of the word *ādi*”: as in [passages] such as “Thus, or in such a manner, he abstains from dancing, singing, instrumental music, and the viewing of spectacles,” it is by that which illuminates the meaning of the word *ādi*. “By that which indicates the sense of modality (*pakāra*)”:
as in [passages] such as “Thus indeed, monks, the fool is full of fear, while the wise man is free from fear,” it is by that which clarifies the sense of modality. “The whole by means of a part...”
By the phrase "it shows," he demonstrates that in the passage "the aggregate of form... up to ... the aggregate of consciousness," the word *iti* has the sense of illustration (*nidassana*).
For the word *iti* is indeed seen to have the sense of illustration in such instances as: "‘It exists,’ Kaccāna, this is one extreme," and so forth.
Alternatively, it has the sense of completion (*parisamāpana*), as in: "Therefore, monks, become my heirs to the Dhamma."
[They] are not heirs to material things. [I have compassion for you, thinking:
‘How may my disciples be heirs to the Dhamma, not heirs to material things?’—as in such passages as these. For this concludes the Suttanta-bhājaniya by way of showing a portion of it, namely:
“The five aggregates: the aggregate of form... [and so on] ...the aggregate of consciousness,” since its meaning has been thus summarized.
“In that regard” means in the Vibhaṅga treatise. Regarding the phrase “of those excluding Nibbāna”:
if the Khandhavibhaṅga is stated at the beginning because it has fewer terms than [the other categories] excluding Nibbāna...

[is it not the case that] the Saccavibhaṅga [should have been first], since it encompasses all phenomena together with Nibbāna, and because the Truths (sacca) have fewer terms than the aggregates (khandha), which themselves encompass all phenomena along with the sense bases (āyatana) and so forth?
Should it be stated at the beginning? No; because even there, in the *Dukkhasaccavibhaṅga*, the aggregates alone are analyzed in part.
As it is said: "In that regard, what is the Noble Truth of Suffering? Birth is suffering... [and so on] ...in brief, the five aggregates of clinging are suffering.
However, here the aggregates are analyzed without exception; thus, for those things excluding Nibbāna... [and so on] ...because they consist of fewer terms.
The analysis of the aggregates (*khandhavibhaṅga*) has been stated at the beginning.
Furthermore, there are three kinds of persons to be enlightened: those confused about form, those confused about the formless, and those confused about both;
likewise, those who prefer brevity, those who prefer detail, and those who prefer neither too much brevity nor too much detail; and those with sharp faculties and those with dull faculties.
And [the classification] as "those of medium faculties. Among these, the teaching on the aggregates (khandha) is for the benefit of those confused about the formless;

the teaching on the bases (āyatana) is for those confused about form; and the teaching on the elements (dhātu) is for those confused about both. Likewise, the teaching on the aggregates is for those who prefer brevity;
the teaching on the bases is for those who prefer neither too much brevity nor too much detail; and the teaching on the elements is for those who prefer detail. For those of sharp faculties...
The sequence of the teaching on the aggregates, bases, and elements should be understood according to this purpose and this order:
the teaching on the aggregates is for those of medium faculties, the teaching on the bases for those of medium faculties, and the teaching on the elements for those of dull faculties.
Furthermore, these three—the aggregates and so forth—when understood by way of occurrence, cessation, and the causes of both, lead to the realization of things as they truly are.
The *Saccavibhaṅga* (Analysis of the Truths) was taught for the purpose of showing that "it is so, and not otherwise.

Furthermore, since that realization of things as they truly are depends specifically upon the faculties (*indriya*), the *Indriyavibhaṅga* (Analysis of the Faculties) was taught. And since the "lordship" (*indaṭṭha*) of the faculties consists precisely in their specific causal status toward their respective conditionally arisen effects—among those phenomena that serve as conditions—the [next section] demonstrates the distinction between conditions and the conditionally arisen.
The teaching on the analysis of the modes of conditionality (*paccayākāra-vibhaṅga-desanā*).

The teaching on the analysis of the foundations of mindfulness, the right efforts, the bases of psychic power, the factors of enlightenment, and the factors of the path—through which there arises an unerring understanding of the nature of the modes of conditionality and of the aggregates and so forth, by means of right attention (*sammā-manasikāra*) toward the foundations of mindfulness and the rest.

And this right attention toward the foundations of mindfulness and the rest occurs through this practice; thus, there is the teaching on the analysis of the meditative absorptions (*jhāna*) and the immeasurables (*appamaññā*).
The teaching on the analysis of the training rules (*sikkhāpada-vibhaṅga*) is given because right practice (*sammāpaṭipatti*) arises for one established in this much virtue;
the teaching on the analysis of the knowledge of discrimination (*paṭisambhidāñāṇa-vibhaṅga*) is given because these are the benefits of the aforementioned right practice;
and the teaching on the analysis of the defilements (*kilesa-vibhaṅga*) is given because these specific types of knowledge arise only when these defilements are abandoned, and not otherwise.

Thus, when the aggregates and so forth have been taught in detail, the teaching on the *Dhammahadaya-vibhaṅga* occurs at the conclusion in order to show that for one who understands them even in brief, the goal is accomplished. In this way,
the reason for the sequence of the teaching of these eighteen great *vibhaṅgas* should be understood.

"Of form and so forth" means of form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness. "Because of the absence of the nature of being felt and so on" means, respectively, because of the absence of the nature of experiencing, cognizing, and volitional formation.

For form does not have the nature of being felt and so forth, nor do feeling and the rest have the nature of being affected (ruppana) and so forth; therefore, by including form and the others within feeling, [the text speaks of] "the four aggregates," and so on.
The aggregates (khandhas) should be taught by way of summary. Because there is no other [nature] apart from being subject to change and so forth:

since there is no summarized nature to be expressed as a "heap" by taking up past [aggregates] and so forth as something other than the intrinsic natures of being subject to change, experiencing, and so on;
for the state of being mental factors and so forth is not the intrinsic nature of feeling and the rest. "In the lower enumerations" means in the enumerations below five.

“Inexhaustible” means without end. For if one were to speak of form and so forth without including even a few, or not including even one, a teaching given by way of the aggregates would not be possible as a comprehensive inclusion of all conditioned phenomena. “Of an aggregate” means of an aggregate in the sense of a heap.
Therefore he said, “For it is not,” and so forth. “By phenomena that have divisions” means by phenomena that possess distinctions.

By the phrase, “It shows the range of the word *khandha* together with its literal meaning,” he demonstrates that the word *khandha* functions as a designator for the sense of a ‘heap,’ just like the word ‘heap’ (*rāsi*), because it exists as a synonym.
However, in the case of qualities (*guṇa*) and so forth, its function is merely as an application to that object, not as a designator;
thus he says, “In the quality... [etc. ...not the literal meaning of the word.”
The term *khandha* is the word *khandha* applied to the words *sīla* (virtue) and so forth. For this very reason, it is said:

"It illuminates the sense of a 'heap' as distinguished by qualities such as virtue. The phrase "some" refers to the Elder Dhammasiri. "In this context" means in the passage: "the aggregate of virtue, the aggregate of concentration," and so on.
And not only he [the Elder], but also the teachers of the commentaries maintain that it has the sense of a quality (*guṇattha*) in this instance.

They are indeed intended [in this sense]. For it is stated in the *Aṭṭhasālinī*: “In such passages as ‘the aggregate of virtue’ and ‘the aggregate of concentration,’ [the word *khandha* is used] in the sense of a quality (*guṇa*). But is it not the case that the word *khandha* by itself is also used in such instances as:
“O student, he is a speaker in praise of three aggregates,” and “Friend Visākha, the Noble Eightfold Path is not comprised within the three aggregates”?
Is it seen as denoting virtue and so forth? No; because even there, its application to virtue and so forth is shown only by way of delimiting the specific context or subject matter.
The meaning is that the word *khandha* does not function in the sense of the word *paññatti* (concept/designation); thus, like words such as *nirutti* or *vohāra*, it is not a synonym for *paññatti*.
When one says "a log of wood" (*dārukkhandho*), this indicates that the word *khandha* functions specifically as a designation (*paññatti*).

[The text] shows this. Regarding the term "aggregate" (*khandha*) in "the aggregate of consciousness": the word *khandha* used here in the phrase "consciousness is the aggregate of consciousness" is established in the sense of a collection (*samudāya*).

It is established in that way because it refers to a mass of consciousness gathered together by the synthesis (*abhisaṃyūhana*) of wisdom, which distinguishes between its divisions such as the past and so forth.
By virtue of that very conventional usage (*ruḷhi*), it applies [metaphorically] to its individual parts (*tadavayava*) through that establishment in the sense of a collection.

"It occurs even in a single consciousness. Herein, it should be understood that just as the state of being "wholesome" (*kusala*), which is established in a collection of consciousness associated with knowledge (*ñāṇasampayutta*) in the sense of being produced by skill (*kosallasambhūta*), is applied by convention to even a single part of that collection when it is dissociated from knowledge (*ñāṇavippayutta*);

or alternatively, having grasped some characteristic (*nimitta*), even though there is something else associated with that characteristic, [the term] applies to one specific thing alone by way of conventional usage.
Even in the absence of a formal cause (*nimitta*), the continued usage of a term regarding an object by virtue of long-standing convention is called "conventional usage" (*ruḷhi*).

For example, one who lies on the earth is a "buffalo" (*mahiṃsa*), and those that go are "cows" (*gāva*); in this same way, the conventional nature of the word "aggregate" (*khandha*) should be understood.

In the phrases "from a heap" (*rāsito*) and "from a quality" (*guṇato*), the ablative case should be seen everywhere as having the sense of the locative or as an expression of separation (*nissakkavacana*). "Having determined" (*niyametvā*) means having defined or established.

“Piṇḍa” means a collection. Therefore, since only five aggregates (khandhas) have been mentioned, and since there ought to be a sixth aggregate by way of Nibbāna—given that the meaning of “aggregate” is both “a portion” and “a heap”—it is logical that the meaning of “aggregate” is indeed “a heap.

[This applies] to those phenomena whose intrinsic nature consists of being subject to change (ruppana) and so forth, which are divided into categories such as the past and so on, as expressed in the passage beginning: “Or for those things which have a distinction by way of the past, etc.”
This shows that when things are apprehended as distinct individual components, it is impossible for a single Nibbāna— which is devoid of such divisions—

to possess the sense of being a "heap" (koṭṭhāsa), just as it cannot possess the sense of being a "mass" (rāsa). By this, it should be understood that the reason why even a designation (paññatti) is not included among the aggregates has been stated.
But why, in this context, are feeling and perception included as separate aggregates, while the aggregate of formations (*saṅkhārakkhandha*) is not included as it is with contact and the others?
It is for the purpose of showing their specific distinction as the roots of dispute and so forth. For householders, the cause of dispute is attachment to sensual pleasures.

And this has been said: "Furthermore, monks, it is because of sensual pleasures, originating from sensual pleasures, having sensual pleasures as the basis, that [disputes arise] regarding sensual pleasures themselves..."
“The mother disputes with her son, and the son also disputes with his mother,” and so forth. This refers to the adherence to views among those who have gone forth.
And it has been said: “Those who, grasping at views, engage in disputes, saying, ‘This alone is the truth,’ and so forth.
Among these, attachment to sensual pleasures arises through the relishing of feeling, while adherence to views arises through the perversion of perception. Through the perversion of perception...
For there is a perversion of the mind; through the perversion of the mind, there is the perversion of views, conceit, and craving.
Thus, one who is greedy for feeling and whose perception is perverted wanders in saṃsāra. For in one who is greedy for feeling, craving is established with feeling as its condition;
and from that, with craving as its condition, grasping arises—thus the wheel of existence turns. In one whose perception is perverted...

And because of the statement, "For conceptual proliferation (papañca-saṅkhā) has perception as its source," there is no cessation of the cycle of existence (saṃsāra) due to the non-cessation of the proliferations of views,
conceit, and craving. Thus, the fact that the causes of attachment to sensual pleasures and adherence to views— which are the grounds for dispute— are themselves the cause of the cycle of existence,
is stated without including them within the aggregate of formations (saṅkhārakkhandha), in order to show this specific distinction of being the root of dispute and so forth.
It should be understood that feeling (vedanā) and perception (saññā) are included as separate aggregates.
Regarding the term "locations" (okāsesu): because they serve as the bases for the activity of differentiation, the past and so forth are called "locations. By the word "iti":
by the word "iti" as it is stated in the Commentary (*Aṭṭhakathā*) in the phrase "derived matter" (*upādāyarūpa*). By the sense of "illustration" (nidassana): by way of providing an example.
"Entirely" (sabba) means the method of classification divided into eleven bases. And this "classification" refers both to what has been classified as "the four great elements...
[and] derived matter," and to this present classification. "In the coarse, etc.
means among the coarse, subtle, inferior, superior, distant, and proximate. And the classification beginning with "the eye-base" refers to: "The eye-base... [and so on]."

The analysis that occurs as follows—"the sense base of the tangible, the female faculty... [and so on] ...edible food, visible forms, sounds, odors, tastes, and tangibles"—is to be applied according to what is possible (*yathāsambhava*), that is, as appropriate.
Whatever analysis is suitable for each of the eleven locations should be applied there.
This applies likewise to the aggregate of feeling and the others, just as it does to the aggregate of form.
It was stated that the classification should be applied to the eleven sections as far as possible;
likewise, the meaning is that the classification should be applied to the aggregate of feeling (vedanākkhandha) and the others as far as possible to those eleven sections.
Therein, first, the aggregate of feeling is classified under the first five sections by way of the triad of feelings, beginning with pleasure.

In the other [set], it is analyzed by way of the wholesome triad, the feeling triad, the meditative attainment dyad, and the with-taints dyad. As for the aggregate of perception (*saññā-khandha*), however, in the first five sections it is analyzed by way of the six doors of contact;

in the other, the dyad of the gross, it is analyzed both by way of the dyad of impingement-contact and by way of the aforementioned wholesome triad and so forth. In the remaining [sections], it is analyzed solely by way of the wholesome triad and so forth. Likewise...
The aggregate of volitional formations (*saṅkhārakkhandha*). However, the dyad of contact involving aversion (*paṭighasamphassaduka*) is not found here at all.
And herein, the exposition is given specifically by way of volition (*cetanā*) for the purpose of showing that among the phenomena of the aggregate of volitional formations, volition is predominant;
for it is as such that it is called "the aggregate of volitional formations. "Therein" means in that detailed explanation and restatement of the aggregate of consciousness. "But that dyad," however—

The pair consisting of the mind-element (manodhātu) and the mind-consciousness-element (manoviññāṇadhātu). For that pair which was taught as "mind-element" and "mind-consciousness-element" in the teaching on the seven consciousness-elements is referred to simply as "mind-consciousness" (manoviññāṇa) in the teaching on the six groups of consciousness.

"By way of the canonical method" means by way of the method found in the *Khandhavibhaṅga* (Analysis of the Aggregates) of the Pāḷi. "In another manner" refers to the different manner found in the *Dhammasaṅgaṇī* and its commentary (*Aṭṭhakathā*).
1. Explanation of the Description of the Aggregate of Form (Rūpakkhandhaniddesavaṇṇanā) 2.
Regarding the word "kiñci" (whatever), it has the same meaning as "ekaccaṃ" (some); thus he says:

"'Kiñci' is an indication of non-restriction by touching upon a particular variety. By both [terms], it is shown that there is no restriction, whether by not touching upon a variety of modes or by touching upon them.
By the two words "whatever" (*yaṃ kiñci*) occurring [in the text]. "The intended meaning" refers to form (*rūpa*). "Exceeding" (*aticca*) means having transcended.
"Because it occurs" (*pavattito*) means because of its occurrence. "For the purpose of restriction" (*niyamanatthaṃ*) means for the purpose of exclusion.
Here, in the word "kiñca," the term *kiṃ* expresses a question and indicates a causal sense; furthermore, this is the nominative case used in the sense of the instrumental.
The word *ca* is a rhetorical ornament; thus he says, "For what reason do you say [this]?

However, in the second interpretation, having transformed the interrogative pronoun *kiṃ*—which functions in the sense of a reason according to the method already stated—into the accusative case by connecting it with the verb "do you say," he says: "Do you state that reason."
"The breaking up of the prior continuum" means the destruction of the prior continuum;

and here, by way of mentioning its destruction, he shows precisely the arising of something dissimilar within that continuum. For this very reason, he says: "Because it demonstrates the arising of a dissimilar continuum.
But is there not also a dissimilar arising among immaterial phenomena when opposing conditions coincide? True, there is; however, that is not more manifest.

And it is this [meaning] that is intended here as the more evident one. For this very reason, he said: "In the encounter with cold and so forth. Likewise, the Blessed One said: "It is affected by cold, and it is affected by heat," and so on.
Now, showing that the word *bheda* (change) directly denotes the occurrence of a transformation (*vikārāpatti*), he said:
"And change... It is simply the arising of a dissimilar form, not the alteration of what has already arisen.
This is the intended meaning (*adhippāya*). By this, he rejects the Kāpiliyan theory of transformation (*pariṇāmavāda*).

Having in mind the objection that "if change consists in a difference from the preceding continuum or an arising of something dissimilar—that is, being subject to alteration (*ruppana*)—then such being the case, there would be an over-extension (*atippasaṅga*) of the definition," he says, "of the immaterial aggregates," and so forth.
Here, by the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) in the phrase "by cold and so forth," [he includes] heat, hunger, thirst, and the like.
They are conjoined; in this way, the conjunction of nutriment and so forth should also be understood. "By which" means by which encounter with cold and so on.
"Therein" refers to among those material phenomena (*rūpadhamma*). Or, the connection is: "of nutriment and so forth that has reached the moment of stability.

Just as there is an encounter with cold and so forth for material phenomena at the moment of their stability, in the same way, there is no encounter with anything else for the immaterial aggregates (*arūpakkhandha*).
Because they change very rapidly, non-material phenomena (arūpadhammā) do not possess a manifest transformation like that of material phenomena (rūpadhammā);
therefore, the connection is that they are not said to "be affected" (*ruppanti*) nor to "have the characteristic of being affected" (*ruppanalakkhaṇā*).

To show the meaning of the term "is affected" (*ruppati*) by way of its analysis as an agent-noun (*kattusādhana*) and an object-noun (*kammasādhana*), the Commentary states: "It is disturbed, struck, and oppressed."
Explaining the meaning of what was stated as "it breaks," he said, "By this it is agitated," and so forth. "Acts of anger and so on" refers to the acts of provoking, clashing, and oppressing.
Here, the word *kopa* (anger) should be understood as a synonym for agitation (*khobha*).
When the meaning is expressed by way of the agent and the object—being both the agent and the object—it is designated as the primary elements (*bhūta*) and derived matter (*upādāya-rūpa*).

The meaning: "It is divided by the word *ruppati* in the sense of the object-agent" means that when the word *ruppati* has the sense of the object-agent (*kammakattuttha*), then the word *bhijjati* should also be understood as having that same meaning.

In this context, when the word "is afflicted" (*ruppati*) has the sense of the object, then in phrases such as "by cold," etc., the instrumental case has the sense of the agent (*kattuattha*). But when the word "is afflicted" (*ruppati*)...

Whether it refers to the agent (*kattū-attha*) or the object of the agent (*kammakattū-attha*), in that case, the word for the instrument (*karaṇa-vacana*) should be understood as being used in the sense of the cause (*hetu*).

By the passage beginning with “That which is afflicted” (*yaṃ pana ruppati*), he shows the reason for using the term even when the words refer to the meanings of the agent or the object, such as in “it is disturbed” (*kuppati*).

Although the word *attha* can also be a synonym for intrinsic nature (*sabhāva-paryāya*), as in “the meaning of oppression” (*pīḷanaṭṭha*) and so forth, here—in the phrase “in what sense” (*kenaṭṭhena*)—it is a synonym for the denotable object (*abhidheyya-paryāya*).

“Intended” means he said, “In what sense? In the sense of being affected (ruppana), according to the nature of the question,” the meaning being that it is by way of being denotable by the word *ruppana*.
For this very reason he said, “Being affected is not merely the literal meaning of the word.

“Of that phenomenon” means of that dhamma characterized by its own intrinsic nature, which is divided into the primary elements (*bhūta*) and the derived matter (*upādāya*). And this characteristic of being affected is distinct from hardness and so forth, just as impermanence and so forth are distinct [from them].

It should not be grasped. For the *tanti* (the textual tradition) is a specific formulation; however, it should be understood as a specific intrinsic nature (*sabhāvavisesa*) of hardness and so forth, devoid of immaterial phenomena (*arūpadhamma*).
