"By falling into a swoon" means by the occurrence of a swoon, which is delusion (*moha*). "Water that sustains the eon" refers to the water rained down by the great clouds that sustain the eon.
Water. "In that way" means that because of its salty nature, if there were saltiness, the earth would dissolve by the water, as happens at the time of the world's dissolution (*kappa-vaṭṭhāna*).
However, it should be understood that for beings in the *Lokantarika* hells, their bodies dissolve even though there is no salt, due to the power of their evil karma, as if there were salt.
"For that very reason" means precisely because the hell with a rich substrate has been described; for [such a thing] does not exist in Avīci.
They inflict the fivefold torture and other forms of punishment. 3.
Having included matter that has reached the stage of being an artifact (*pakaraṇappatta-rūpa*), the heading (*mātikā*) is established; this is the connection to be supplied.

The intention [of the author] is stated thus: because it is said that [matter] "has entered into the reckoning among past things by way of its own specific mode" (*tappakārabhāvena*). By the words "Indeed not," etc.,...

This shows that there is no purpose in mentioning the primary elements (*bhūta*) and the derived matter (*upādāya*) for the sake of excluding other phenomena (*dhamma*) or for the sake of excluding other modes of expression.
"In that demonstration" means in the demonstration of the subsequent enumeration. "Because of having that nature" means because of having the nature of the primary elements and the derived matter.

By the words "And not," etc., it is shown that the nature of the primary elements and the derived matter is not [the same] because, due to being included in the past category, even that which has that nature is enumerated otherwise.
And because it has been calculated in that way as being of a non-existent nature, he shows that it is not a valid reason. By the statement, “Internally...
is found,” he shows that according to the second method, there is not only the aforementioned fault, but also the fault of non-pervasiveness.

However, this is not a valid reason, because the state of being a cause was not intended here; for the state of being derived matter (upādāyarūpa) from primary matter (bhūtarūpa) does not exist in the past.
The "reason for counting" is what is intended here, because from it the aforementioned faults might arise.
Regarding the word *kinti*: here, *kiṃ* is a specific inquiry into the nature of that which was previously grasped generally as "form" (*rūpa*).
The term *iti* has the sense of illustration, not the sense of a reason. Therefore, of that form which is past and ceased... [and so on] ...by way of the past.

It is included and has entered into the enumeration in the previous section. Why is that? By means of showing the distinction through the analysis of the primary elements (*bhūta*) and the derived matter (*upādāya*), he specifically demonstrates: "The four... [and] matter.
For this is an illustration of all those specific instances pointed out here, such as the eye-base (*cakkhāyatana*) and so forth. And there is no lack of distinction from the previous method;
for in that [previous] case, there was merely the demonstration of the intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*) of matter as consisting of the primary elements and the derived.
Thus it was said. Therefore, the *Aṭṭhakathā* says: “Past matter, too, consists of the primary elements (*bhūta*) and so forth.
Here, however, by means of the primary elements and derived matter (*upādāyarūpa*) serving as an illustration, the manifestation of all the specific classifications of matter is shown.

And by doing it thus, there is no room here for the fault of non-pervasiveness (*abyāpitadosa*), since [the text asks]: “What matter is internal... [and] clung-to (*upādinna*)? It is the four [primary elements]... and matter.”
Because it is intended to show another specific distinction. And thus he said: "In this way, the meaning is to be understood in all cases.
Regarding "by way of figurative teaching" (*pariyāyadesanā*): *pariyāya* is a figurative approach, a turning around, or a deviation from the essential nature;

the meaning is that there is no direct application. A discourse (*suttanta*) is called a "figurative teaching" because it consists of, or is characterized by, such a figurative teaching. For a discourse...

The teaching of the Dhamma that ought to be taught according to the inclinations of those to be trained—stating its existence by way of a figurative indication rather than stating it through a direct and exhaustive definition—is called "figurative teaching" (pariyāyadesanā).
For that very reason, it is called the "teaching in accordance with what is suitable" (yathānulomasāsana).

In contrast, the Abhidhamma is the teaching of the Dhamma that ought to be taught through a direct and exhaustive definition; thus, it is called "non-figurative teaching" (nippariyāyadesanā), which is why it is termed the "teaching in accordance with the Dhamma" (yathādhammasāsana).
It is said: "To speak by way of determination" means to state [the meaning] with certainty as a location. Likewise, the connection is as follows:

just as in the *Bhaddekaratta-sutta* and other discourses, the state of being past and so forth—the state of being past, future, and present—should also be demonstrated here in the *Khandhavibhaṅga* according to the divisions of time (*addhā*), because it belongs to the Suttanta-bhājaniya section.

“Sannipatitaṃ” means come together. “By way of continuity” means by way of preceding and succeeding [moments]. Because the subsequent is equal in measure to the preceding, it is neither deficient nor excessive;
for that very reason, it is of a single mode. Alternatively, it is neither deficient nor excessive by way of the time of its occurrence, and it is of a single mode due to its identical nature.
By this, he shows that it is not interrupted by a dissimilar utu (seasonal change). “The same applies to nutriment” refers here to nutriment that is dissimilar.

“Sabhāgekāhāra” (a similar kind of nutriment) refers to that which has been consumed many times and even over many days without interruption. For it is said: “Prior to that, there is the past arising from dissimilar temperature and nutriment;

subsequent to that, there is the future. However, others maintain that since it is stated as “arising from a single nutriment,” the application [of the term] is appropriate only to a single instance of nutriment.
Regarding the phrase “by way of the five doors”: here, starting from the five-door adverting consciousness...
The continuum of consciousness that proceeds from the moment of the object until the impulsion, or until the registration, constitutes a single cognitive series (*ekavīthi*).

"Arising from a single impulsion" means arising from a single impulsion-moment. Furthermore, here the distinction between the past and so forth should be understood by way of the continuum without reference to time, and by way of time without reference to the continuum.

"Of these" refers to the root-conditions (*hetu-paccaya*). "Of the aggregate" refers to the material aggregate (*rūpa-kalāpa*). Regarding "kamma, proximity, and so forth": the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) should be applied separately to both "kamma" and "proximity.
Therein, by the first "and so forth," the inclusion of the decisive-support condition (*upanissaya-paccaya*), nutriment (*āhāra*), and others is to be understood;
by the second, the inclusion of the immediate (*samanantara*), proximate (*anantara*), decisive-support, and others is to be understood. And herein, of the arising of consciousness—
The application regarding the state of being a producer should be understood as follows: for the former [the mind], by way of conditions such as the immediate antecedent (kamma-anantara), etc.;

for the latter [the materiality], solely by way of kamma and so forth. Likewise, support should be understood for the arising of consciousness by way of the pre-arisen (purejāta), for the other by way of the post-arisen (pacchājāta), and for both by way of the co-arisen (sahajāta).
For this very reason, he said: "It should be applied according to what is possible. Regarding the moment of arising (uppādakkhaṇe):
"At the moment of the function of the cause": the "function of the cause" (hetukicca) means the causing of the arising of whatever is to be produced;
and that [function] should be understood as completed at that moment because the fruit has arisen and because there is nothing further to be done thereafter.
As for the other [condition], the construction is that its "function of being a condition" (paccayakicca) is to be seen in all three moments.

6. "Of the turning away from the undesired name" means that by showing that [the undesired name] is not the cause for the turning away, he shows that it is not the cause for obtaining the desired name.
"In the state of existence as a fortunate deva or human" means in the state of existence as a deva or human endowed with excellence, one who possesses such excellence.

"The state of perfected beauty" means the state of increased beauty. "Precisely because of that" means precisely because of the lack of excellence; the sense is: precisely because of being unaccomplished. Of those very...
Elephants and the like do not become causes of pleasure because, through being recollected and so forth, they are conditions for suffering.
"Of these" refers to the forms of elephants and so on. With the words "of this or that," etc., he explains the meaning as previously stated.
The construction is: "That which is produced by unwholesome action performed by oneself becomes a condition for suffering. "Therefore" means because karma [functions] within whichever continuum...
Once arisen, it becomes a condition for pleasure and pain right there and not elsewhere; therefore [it is said].

The phrase "but in the Commentary" indicates a particular opinion. Therein, regarding the statement "there is nothing called undesirable," since the status of being desirable for that which is born of wholesome karma is certain by means of the double negation, he does not restrict it by saying, "only that born of wholesome karma is desirable."
Showing that the restriction should be understood here as “only what is born of wholesome kamma is desirable,” he says, “even that which is born of unwholesome kamma,” and so forth.
How can that which is born of unwholesome kamma be beautiful, such that it might be called “desirable” for others?

If [it is argued] that for certain animals in the miserable states (duggati) there is excellence of form and so on, while for beings in the happy states (sugati) there is deformity due to the outflow of unwholesome kamma—
Since it appears as if through a wholesome outflow (*kusala-nissanda*), how can it be born of unwholesome kamma?
Alternatively, this was said with reference to those forms which, though unpleasant to some, appear as pleasant;
even so, just as the human form—which is born of wholesome kamma—appears unpleasant to certain animals and the like, yet remains the very result of wholesome kamma.
In terms of its function as an object, that which is desirable is indeed called "agreeable" (iṭṭha) in its actual nature;

likewise, even though something born of unwholesome kamma may appear agreeable to some, it is in fact called "disagreeable" (aniṭṭha) in its actual nature because it serves as the object for an unwholesome result.
This must be accepted in this way. Otherwise, [the Buddha would not have said]: "It is impossible, it is out of the question, that one who has committed a bodily misconduct..."
Otherwise, there would be a contradiction with the scriptural passage beginning, “Could a desirable, lovely, and pleasing result arise?
For this very reason, he says, “But for one born of wholesome karma,” and so forth. “Of all” means of both oneself and others. It must be stated that there is an absence of the desirable;

just as it was said, “There is no such thing as an undesirable result born of wholesome karma,” so too, although it is true that “there is no such thing as a desirable result born of unwholesome karma.”
It is not stated in the *Aṭṭhakathā*, but by that demonstration of the method (*naya*), the absence of what is born of unwholesome karma is indeed already expressed;
thus, the intention is that this should be determined and stated by way of commentary.
By this, he shows that the restriction of the preceding term must be understood as "only that which is born of wholesome karma is desirable."
Now, with the words “of elephants and so forth as well,” he explains that same point. Regarding the phrase “of wholesome resultant [consciousness]”:
here too, the meaning is that it is the object specifically of wholesome resultant consciousness. Furthermore, “of humans” should be regarded as a mere illustration;

for this method has been shown to apply such that the object produced by unwholesome karma is the object of unwholesome resultant consciousness alone, and the object produced by wholesome karma is the object of wholesome resultant consciousness alone.
But why does it settle as agreeable alone toward an object that is mixed with both the agreeable and the disagreeable? To this he says:
"By means of a desirable object... it is possible to say [so]. It is well said;

for those who maintain that "the agreeable and the disagreeable are definitively distinguished by result (vipāka) alone" have correctly defined the distinction between desirable and undesirable objects. "Following that" means according to the mode of result.
Having followed the determination of desirable and undesirable objects. "In all places" means in both happy and miserable destinies, or among all objects.
By the very word "undesirable," their desirability is excluded; thus he says, "and similarity is simply the state of being form and so forth.

Since it is stated in the Sutta that only desirable forms and so forth are the strands of sensual pleasure (*kāmaguṇa*), [the undesirable] is the opposite of the desirable, just as an enemy is the opposite of a friend.
It is said that "unpleasant" is intended [by the term *aniṭṭha*], as stated: "Unpleasant... [etc.]... like a conventional designation. If it is asked:

"Since all [objects] are described here as 'forms that are dear and agreeable' (*piyarūpaṃ sātarūpaṃ*), how can forms and so forth that are unpleasant attain the status of objects of sensual pleasure (*kāmaguṇa*)?
It is because even those [unpleasant things], by way of perversion (*vipallāsa*), serve as the basis for craving; thus, their state of being "dear" is what is intended. If this is so, then how...
He said, “excessively,” etc., because the sutta passage beginning with “forms cognizable by the eye that are desirable” and so forth is being interpreted.

He stated, “in both the passages concerning the inferior and the sublime,” etc., in order to show that the exposition in the Pāḷi proceeds by way of forms bound to the sense faculties (indriyabaddharūpa).

The genitive case is used in the sense of a partitive relation (avayavayoga), not in the sense of an agent; this is the intended meaning. [The phrase] “of those various beings” refers to forms bound to the sense faculties.

Regarding the question of why, in the exposition, the meaning is stated by way of the force of karma (*kamma-javasena*) and not by way of the four continua (*catusantati*), he says: “In the *Sattasantāna*... [it is] so stated.

For, having stated the meaning by way of the force of karma because it is the primary factor, the commentary (*aṭṭhakathā*) applies the principle of extension (*atidesa*) to the remaining factors with the words:

“Thus also in the case of those arisen from temperature (*utu-samutthāna*), etc. By the phrase “by this or that” (*tehi tehi*), in this sense, the word “of them” (*tesaṃ tesaṃ*) refers to the agent (*kattari*).

It is suspected that this is a genitive expression (*sāmivacana*). If that were so, it would indicate that the quality [of being supreme] is obtained either in the sense-object (*visaya*) or in the genitive case, as shown by the passage beginning with “not solely by way of kamma.
Furthermore, the mention of “kamma” here should be understood as an illustration (*upalakkhaṇa*).

“Become the ultimate limit” means having become the highest limit. For this very reason, he said: “For whomever they are pleasing, for him alone they are supreme. “Of these” refers to the strands of sensual pleasure (*kāmaguṇa*). “By way of their intrinsic nature” means by way of their characteristic (*lakkhaṇa*).

By the passage beginning, “Because of relishing and revulsion toward one and the same [object],” he shows that the commentary on the Sutta—beginning with “since those very same forms, etc., one person relishes”—is stated as the reason for the state of being desirable or undesirable.

The mention of “desirable and undesirable” means that, just as with Nibbāna, there occurs an adherence to the desirable and undesirable among other objects due to a perversion of perception (*saññā-vipallāsa*); this is the intended meaning.
"Vibhāga" means non-confusion and detail; thus, for the word "vibhatta," the meanings "determined" and "manifested" are stated.

"Of others" refers to those who are exceedingly wealthy or exceedingly poor. Regarding the phrase "this becomes both desired and undesired," it should be understood that by the word "and" (ca), the meaning "it also becomes undesired and desired" is expressed. [The text continues: "The undesired as desired..."
The application of the terms is respectively: taking what is desirable as "undesirable," and taking what is undesirable as "desirable.
Regarding the phrase "due to the occurrence of a transformation of the faculties, etc.," the word "etc. includes previous karmic formations (*pubbābhisaṅkhāra*) and so forth.

For, even without a perversion of perception (*saññāvipallāsa*), one takes the desirable as "undesirable" and the undesirable as "desirable" by virtue of volitional formations (*abhisaṅkhāra*) that occurred in a prior moment of consciousness.
"By that result" means by that result of wholesome and unwholesome [kamma].

"The desirability and undesirability of the object" indicates, respectively, the desirability of the Buddha’s form and so forth, and the undesirability of excrement and so forth, of the object where that [result] arises.
Even though a perversion of perception exists, this demonstrates the determination of the result by way of the object.
"Only a wholesome resultant arises with a desirable object, and an unwholesome resultant arises with an undesirable object"—
this is the demonstration of the determination of the resultant by way of the object.

"For the purpose of demonstrating the determination of the object" means for the purpose of showing that whatever is the object of a wholesome resultant is called "desirable," and whatever is the object of an unwholesome resultant is called "undesirable."
For a result is determined by its object; thus, it becomes the determiner of its own supportive object.

This is because an object that serves as a condition for suffering in one sense-door can produce a pleasant result in another sense-door, and an object that serves as a condition for pleasure in one sense-door can produce a painful result in another sense-door.
The construction is as follows: by showing the determination of the object through its result—that is, by way of its maturation (vipāka)—the state of being desirable or undesirable is demonstrated.

7. By means of the reason consisting in the sense of being difficult to grasp, the difficulty of penetrating the characteristic (lakkhaṇa), which is the intrinsic nature (sabhāva) of the faculties and so forth, [is shown];

thus, by means of the sense of being easy to grasp, the ease of penetrating the characteristic is to be understood. Regarding the phrase "not stated as 'distant'": it is because of the characteristic.

“‘Distant’ refers to that which has not been mentioned. Regarding the phrase “even though it has been stated,” this means that even though the subtle form has been described by way of its characteristic as being “distant.
Regarding the word “splitting,” since it is said to mean “mixing together,” he says, “making a mixture.
However, because splitting also involves making a division, therefore in the second alternative, for the word “splitting,” [he explains it as] “separately.”
He stated the meaning as "making. In the third alternative, however, "breaking" means "destroying. Therefore he said:

"Making nearness into distance, and making distance into nearness. For it is not possible to make something distant without destroying its state of nearness, nor likewise for the other. By means of making nearness...

It does not break nor destroy; nor does it break by making a distinction through separation—either by distance of location or by difference of characteristic—and it does not break by mixing through proximity of location or similarity of characteristic.

This is the construction of the sentence. The phrase "the meaning should be seen in three ways" briefly stated the matter, which he then explains in detail with the words beginning "for it does not," and so forth.
The connection is made by bringing in the word *karoti* (makes), as in "he makes separate" (*visuṃ karoti*) or "he makes mixed" (*vomissakaṃ karoti*).

By the phrase beginning with "even here," just as in the expression "it breaks [the object] far away from its location" (*okāsato dūram eva bhindati*), what is intended is the making of that which is distant from its location into something proximate to its location—

that is, destruction is "breaking"— so too, in the expression "it does not break [the object] far away from its characteristic" (*na lakkhaṇato dūram bhindati*), it is likewise [from its characteristic].
This shows the meaning of non-breaking and non-destruction as the non-making of nearness through the characteristic of distance.
With reference to the sense of making a mixture and making a division, he said: "And here, in the phrase 'breaking,' breaking is stated otherwise.
In the latter method, with reference specifically to the sense of destruction, he said: "And here, in this context, breaking is stated otherwise."
The commentary on the description of the aggregate of form is finished.
2. Commentary on the description of the aggregate of feeling. 8.

"The sensitivities of the eye and so forth" refers to the sensitivities of the eye, ear, nose, and tongue included within a coarse physical existence, as well as those included within a mind-made existence.
And the sensitivities of the eye and ear. They "deserve the designation 'body'" because, being included within the body and being parts of the body, they deserve to be called "the body.
For the term "body" (kāya) refers to the personal organism (attabhāva), as in "personality-belief" (sakkāyadiṭṭhi) and so forth;
it also refers to the physical body made of kamma (karajakāya), as in "he creates another body from this body" and so forth. "Based upon that" means based upon the eye and the other [sensitivities].
"Physical" is said figuratively; in the absolute sense, however, they are purely mental. As it is said:

"At that time, there is a mental feeling born of contact with the corresponding eye-consciousness element, which is neither pleasant nor unpleasant, a feeling born of mental contact that is neither-painful-nor-pleasant," and so forth.
By the statement, "For the eye and so forth are not the physical sensitivity of the body," [it is shown that] it is dependent upon the physical sensitivity of the body.

This shows that feeling (*vedanā*) is, in the primary sense (*nippariyāya*), bodily. By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) in the phrase "in the state of being bodily, mental, and so forth," states such as wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate are included.
"By that" refers to the absence of the state of past and so on by way of time-period (*addhā*) for a portion of pleasant feeling and the rest.

However, some here [hold] that because it was shown in the manner previously demonstrated, it is by way of time-period (*addhā*) due to its obviousness, [as in] one moment (*ekamuhutta*) and so on, or morning (*pubbaṇha*) and so on.

They say: "Just as with matter (rūpa) due to temperature and so forth, no distinction of feeling (vedanā) is perceived; and thus, its classification into past and so on has not been shown by way of time.
With reference to the fact that even feelings occurring as a continuum must be grasped as a collection by means of consciousness, he says: "a collection of feelings" (vedanāsamudāyo).
"By those" means by way of their state as past and so on, according to duration and time. "In this" refers to this [context].
In the *Vibhaṅga*, "parts of feeling" refers to the specific types of pleasant and other feelings that are distinguished by their nature as bodily, mental, and so forth.
If parts of feeling are taken here, they must be understood as delimited by moments (*khaṇa*), not delimited by a continuity (*santati*);

thus he says, "But in a single continuity," and so on. "Among them" means among the divisions such as pleasure and the rest. "Division" means distinction. "Of that" refers to the distinction of pleasure and the rest.
And just as it is here, so too in the phrase "those associated with it and productive of it," it should be understood that a specific [feeling] such as pleasure is referred to by the word "it" (taṃ).

The connection is: "it is worthy of being a delimitation of the continuity. The intention is that the delimitation is stated solely by way of the moment of the continuity (santati-khaṇa), and not by way of the duration or time-period (addhā-samaya).
“‘Those who have reached the past, future, and middle’ means those for whom the function of the cause has been completed but the function of the condition has not yet been completed;
however, that [phrase] is an illustration of the method stated as ‘having transcended the functions of cause and condition. Thus he said:

‘By the phrase “those who have reached the past, future, and middle,” he shows the method stated by way of the functions of cause and condition. Herein, regarding wholesome, unwholesome, and functional feelings...”
Just as in the case of material form (*rūpa*) and as in the case of resultant states (*vipāka*), it cannot be said in an absolute sense that this is a "productive cause" (*janakahetu*);
however, in a figurative sense, it may be called a cause because it serves as an immediate condition (*anantarapaccaya*).

11. The function of heating (*santāpanakicca*) means the function of burning. "Confusion regarding birth and so forth" refers to [confusion] concerning birth, intrinsic nature, persons, the mundane, and the supramundane.

"Without causing confusion or intermixture. "Of a similar kind" means of one and the same genus (*ekajātiya*). The connection is to be understood as follows: those of that same genus which are pleasant and those which are neither-painful-nor-pleasant are "excellent" (*paṇīta*).
"In a similar division" refers to a common classification such as the different planes of existence (*bhūmantara*) and so forth.

"Of the elements that have been built up" refers to excellent material phenomena (*rūpadhamma*) produced by the emergence of a sublime form. "Of those that are oppressed" means of those that are squeezed or pressured.
"Of those that have been mixed. "Both" refers to the pair beginning with pleasure. And here, agitation and turbulence should be understood by way of bodily pleasure;
soaking by way of jhāna-pleasure; intoxication by way of sensual pleasure; likewise, covering. Pouring should be understood by way of all [three];
alternatively, covering or pouring should be understood by way of all.
"And by way of the distinction between intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*) and so forth" means by way of the distinctions such as intrinsic nature, person (*puggala*), mundane (*lokiya*), and so on.
In the exclusively sublime supramundane (*lokuttara*), there is inferiority and sublimity by way of the inferior and sublime paths (*paṭipadā*).

In the exclusively inferior unwholesome, there is inferiority and sublimity by way of zeal (*chanda*) and so forth, as well as grossness and subtlety (*oḷārika-sukhumatā*). For it is said in the Commentary: "That which is gross is inferior; that which is subtle..."

"It is refined. Regarding the unwholesome states and so forth, grossness and subtlety are described progressively on the basis of each category according to internal subdivisions such as those accompanied by hatred, and according to their respective groupings;
they are not so described by way of the wholesome, unwholesome, and so forth. Thus he says: "Even when explaining according to their respective groupings, there is no reversal [of the order].
"Due to the prevalence of hatred" means due to the predominance of defilements. "In that way" means due to the prevalence of hatred.
But how is there an abundance of defilement among wholesome states? By way of decisive support (*upanissaya*):

wholesome phenomena occurring in a continuum where defilements predominate do not yield abundant or extensive fruits, because they have been crowded out by the defilements—just as crops crowded out by weeds and the like do not yield abundant or extensive fruits.
"In that way" means due to the dullness of the defilements. The dullness of the defilements regarding wholesome states should also be understood according to the method already explained.
Regarding the phrase "craving for the gross and the subtle": here, the commonality of the grossness and subtlety of craving is stated by way of its internal distinctions.

For just as, through the commonality of grossness, the various grades of craving—gross, more gross, and most gross—are included, so too, through the commonality of subtlety, the various grades—subtle, more subtle, and most subtle—are included. This refers to the basis for craving that is most subtle.
And here, insight-knowledge should be understood as extending up to the peak of existence (*bhavagga*). 13.
"If there were": if there were non-association, that is, if it were unconnected.
"From the proximity of the unwholesome" means from the proximity of the state of being unwholesome, that is, from unwholesome feeling associated with greed and so forth.
“Unwholesome” refers to unwholesome feelings accompanied by hatred and so forth, which are far away in the sense that they are to be removed.
“Wholesome, being far from that” means wholesome feeling—such as the wholesome feeling of the sense-sphere and so forth—which is far from that unwholesomeness.
The statement “it is not possible” expresses the impossibility of removal; this is explained by the passage beginning with “for if it were so,” and so on. Therefore...
Since extracting from the near by means of the distance follows the same method as extracting from the near itself, there would be no distinction in meaning;
rather, it is the relative distance and proximity based on successive reference points that is intended here.
Therefore, the intention is that it is impossible to perform an extraction from the near into the near, because there is no distinction in meaning and because such a thing is not intended.
Having considered the objection that there is indeed a distinction in meaning based on the desire for a more emphatic expression, he says:

"Because nearness and nearer-ness, as well as remoteness and remoter-ness, are not intended here. "Yā" refers to unwholesome feeling (*akusalavedanā*). "Tato" means from wholesome feeling (*kusalavedayita*).
Regarding the phrase "of the remote mentioned here," it refers to the unwholesome feeling within this *Vedanākkhandhavibhaṅga* [in relation] to wholesome and indeterminate [feelings].
Regarding "the distance" spoken of in the passage beginning with "far from feelings," etc.:
because it is absolutely dissimilar to that which is called "far," there is no proximity in relation to it; thus, one cannot extract proximity from distance.
This is the intended meaning here: as for those feelings mentioned below, by whichever feeling they are far...
It has been stated that that very [feeling] is not to be extracted from its vicinity (*santika*) by any means whatsoever.
By "vicinity," he refers specifically to the feeling already mentioned. By "divided," it is meant divided according to the categories such as those accompanied by greed (*lobha*).
"In that very place" means precisely in the sense expressed by the word "vicinity. This is what is meant: "Unwholesome feeling is in the vicinity of unwholesome feeling."

Thus, even "remoteness" (dūrabhāva) is obtained with respect to unwholesome feeling itself when it is analyzed by way of being accompanied by greed and so forth. The same applies to the remaining [feelings]. Having considered the objection:
"If remoteness is obtained from proximity, then by the very same principle by which remoteness is obtained, one could also extract proximity from that which is remote," he said:
"It is not possible to derive proximity from the remote by taking each [instance] in turn."

"Uddharitun" (to extract), etc. Its meaning is as follows: although that which is obtained from what is distant may be obtained in the sense of being dissimilar (*visabhāga*), nevertheless, that which is obtained there from what is proximate (*santika*) is obtained only in the sense of being similar (*sabhāga*). Thus, it may be said that "from the proximate, the proximate has been extracted.
Therefore, because distance exists in the sense of being dissimilar, and [proximity] in the sense of being similar...
Proximity is desired; therefore, the intention [of the question] is: since those associated with greed and those associated with hatred are dissimilar and thus far apart, how could they be near?
One might object: "Is it not the case that a similarity in their unwholesome nature (akusala-sabhāgatā) is indeed found? To this, he gives the reply: "Because they are dissimilar," and so forth.
In that context, [the term] does not function without grasping at a distinction; thus, it refers to a distinction or difference.
Dissimilarity proceeds precisely by grasping what is non-existent. Regarding "distance":

because that which is intended here as distance does not pervade the similar, it is impossible to extract the near from the distant. For if there were pervasion of the similar, there would be proximity;
thus, the intention is that it would then be possible to extract the near from the distant. This is shown by the words beginning with "No, indeed."
He makes this very point clear: "Sabhāgatā" means commonality; "bheda" means distinction. "Having included within" means having pervaded.

Because it pervades what is dissimilar (*visabhāga*), and because of its proximity (*santikatā*), it is possible to extract "the distant" from the "proximity" mentioned below, since it functions by pervading the specific dissimilarities intended here. This is that same point.
He makes it clear with the words beginning, “unwholesomeness” (*akusalatā*).
The commentary on the description of the aggregate of feeling (*vedanākkhandha*) is finished.
3. Commentary on the Description of the Aggregate of Perception (*saññākkhandha*).
17. *Tassāpi*: of that [perception] as well. *Tabbatthukatā*: because it has the eye as its basis (*cakkhu-vatthuka*). *Paṭigha-viññeyyo*:

to be cognized through resistance (*paṭigha*), meaning it is to be understood by way of resistance as previously described. *Uttarapadalopaṃ katvā*: having elided the latter member of the compound in the first word.
The intention is that this refers to the state of being cognizable, not to the act of arising. *Vacanaṃ*: sound; the meaning is "name" (*nāma*). *Vacanādhīnā*: dependent upon speech.
"Dependent on sound for its apprehension" means that its grasping is subject to the name (*nāma*). Whatever needs to be said regarding this has already been stated in the *Nāmarūpa-duka*.
"Designation" (*adhivacana*) refers to those things which possess a designator, a declarer, or an indicator; thus they are called "designations," just as one says "the noble son.
"Born from that" means born from the immaterial aggregates (*arūpakkhandha*), which are termed "designation. This is because they are included within the immaterial aggregates.
In order to show that the meaning already stated is also possible in the case of "contact" (*phassa*), he says, "Or, it is simply contact itself," and so forth.

Not only in the case of contact pertaining to the mind-door, but also in the case of contact pertaining to the five doors, the aforementioned sense—namely, that "designation-terms" (*adhivacana*) are those which function with reference to the state of being cognizable—is possible. "Thus" (*iti*) means for that reason. "By that method" (*tena pariyāyena*).
By way of the mental-contact-born method. "Born from that" means born even from contact at the five doors.

"Because no other kind is possible" means because the method of contact-born-through-aversion is impossible [in this context]. Being born from contact through aversion is its exclusive characteristic;
being born from contact through designation is another mode.

"If this is so": if the perceptions arising through the five-door contacts are called "born of designation-contact" both figuratively and literally, then it would be appropriate to say the same of the other four immaterial aggregates as well.

This being the case, why is it that perception alone is called "born of designation-contact"? To answer this, he says: "Of the three aggregates," and so forth. Therein, "of the three aggregates" refers to...

Of the aggregates of feeling, mental formations, and consciousness. "In terms of meaning" means in terms of the meaning stated as: "They are 'designation-contact' because they proceed by depending upon designation," and so forth;
that is, in terms of their etymological derivation (*anvatthatā*). "Even its own [non-occurrent] name" refers to the name "born of designation-contact," which is indeed not occurring in itself.
"Expression of phenomena" (*dhammābhilāpa*) means natural linguistic expression. Previously, regarding the four formless aggregates...

Having stated that even though conventional usage arising from contact with designations is common [to all], it occurs specifically through perception by way of conventional metaphor (*ruḷhi*), he now says "Or else" (*atha vā*) and so forth,
in order to show that this [usage] is established in perception as being common to the other aggregates of form. Regarding the phrase "after becoming impassioned,
in looking and so forth," the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) includes such things as listening after becoming impassioned, just as looking after becoming angry is included.
It should be understood that this is so because, through such acts as listening attentively, it is possible for redness and other qualities to be known;

however, in order to demonstrate by way of illustration how perception born of eye-contact becomes manifest, he said: "Looking occurs when there is a meeting of the object with eye-consciousness," and so forth.

He further stated: "From the sense-base of the sensitive organ (*pasādavatthuka*)," because when looking is not manifest, the knowledge of redness and so on does not occur, whereas when it is manifest, it does occur.
“Thus. “Thinking of something else”: thinking of some other matter than that which was previously spoken by him or manifested by him through the body.
For this very reason, he said, “known.
The commentary on the description of the aggregate of perception is finished.
4. Commentary on the Exposition of the Aggregate of Volitional Formations (Saṅkhārakkhandhaniddesa). 20.
Regarding the phrase, “‘At its lower limit’ refers to this [first instance],” this was stated with reference to the first occurrence of the expression “at its lower limit.
For its meaning should be understood in the locative sense. Therefore he said: “For therein the primary [factor] is shown.”
Taking this meaning—that striving is shown at its very lowest limit—he raises an objection with the words, “If it were so,” and so forth.

The other [respondent], showing that the restriction here must be understood as “striving is shown only at the lowest limit,” resolves that objection with the words, “By way of having reached the upper limit,” and so forth. It is the showing of striving itself; for in striving...
"Even though it is not explicitly shown, it is effectively shown by implication. Therefore, it was said in the *Aṭṭhakathā*:

"But the formations associated with that [consciousness] are already included when that [consciousness] is grasped. Since whatever is found at the lower limit is also found at the upper limit, he said:
"For the lower limit encompasses everything. To show that the second [section] is a description in the instrumental case:
He said, “The connection is ‘having come. For the action of coming is stated there as an instrument (*karaṇa*) in its lowest limit (*heṭṭhimakoṭiyā*).
And just as with the action of coming, so too the state of being an instrument in its lowest limit is possible for the action of speaking; thus he said, ‘Or even in the former,’ and so forth.
‘In the forty-ninefold variety’—this refers to those [mental states] that have come down in the Pāḷi among the mundane (*lokiya*) arisings of consciousness.”
This was stated with reference to the upper limit of the phenomena belonging to the aggregate of mental formations (saṅkhārakkhandha).

If the upper limit were taken together with the miscellaneous phenomena (yevāpanaka-dhamma), it would have to be called "fifty-three"; however, by way of supramundane (lokuttara) consciousness-arising, it is "fifty-seven."
The commentary on the exposition of the aggregate of mental formations (*saṅkhārakkhandha*) is finished.
In the commentary on the miscellaneous discussion,
the meaning of the term *samuggama* is shown both in its actual sense and by way of synonyms as "in birth, in initial arising."

As for the classification, it is called "arising" (uggamana) in conjunction with [conditions]. Regarding the investigation of *with what* it is in conjunction, *from where*, and *how* it arises, he says:
“In conjunction with this or that condition,” and so forth. “Right there” means precisely in the five-aggregate existence (pañcavokārabhava), for it is there that the five aggregates arise complete.
“Of those already attained” means of those attained in their various modes; “of those pertaining to rebirth-linking” (paṭisandhikānaṃ).

The meaning is as follows. Here, it should be understood that by the mention of "spontaneously born" (*opapātika*), the "moisture-born" (*saṃsedaja*) are also included, because they are capable of arising at that time, being comprised within the five aggregates. In this regard, the moisture-born increase after having arisen, whereas the others do not;
this is the distinction between them. It is said that some ewes in the Himālayas have very fine-fibered wool.
They do exist; it is with reference to their wool that it is said, "the wool of a born sheep," because those hairs are exceedingly fine.

However, some say: "The wool produced from a specific type of sheep that is not mixed with common goats or other such animals is 'birth-wool' (jātiuṇṇa), and that too is [the wool] produced at that very moment. "Of one taken after splitting open the womb" means:
Others [say]: "Of such a shape" means having the shape of a drop of oil that remains at the tip after a thread of wool has been dripped.
"Resemblance of color" means that which is concealed by visible form and concealed by shape.

"Roots of continuity" means those that serve as the roots for the continuity of matter (*rūpa-santati*) in that existence. "By way of being a collection of various faculties" means by way of being a composite of various faculties, such as the eye and so forth, as appropriate. "Principal limb" means the head, the supreme limb.
The intention is that this does not refer to the completeness of each respective aggregate (*khandha*), because it is stated only with respect to a single part of each aggregate.

"Of those belonging to the sense-sphere" (*kāmāvacarānaṃ*) means of sentient beings belonging to the sense-sphere. "Of one whose sense-base has been lost" (*parihīnāyatanassa*) refers to the case of one who has lost a sense-base such as the eye.
In that regard, for one born in an unhappy destiny (*duggati*), it is by way of the tenfold set consisting of the eye for the blind, and the tenfold set consisting of the ear for the deaf.
For one who is both blind and deaf, the cessation of the continuity of the faculties should be understood by way of both [the eye and the ear].

For a eunuch, however, the loss of the faculty of sex has already been stated. Likewise, for one who is blind, deaf, and noseless, [there is cessation] by way of the eye, ear, and nose faculties respectively.

But that contradicts the text of the *Dhammahadayavibhaṅga*; this will be made clear later. For those belonging to the fine-material sphere (*rūpāvacara*), however, [cessation occurs] by way of the eye, ear, base, and life-faculty.
Regarding "the four heads of the continuity": the loss of the heads of continuity should be understood by way of the others.
"Of these" refers to the five aggregates (*pañca-khandhā*). "By way of being the basis" means by way of being the foundation for investigation.

"The five aggregates arisen at rebirth and during the course of existence" indicates the five aggregates both at the moment of rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*) and at the moment of the ongoing process (*pavatti*).

“Specification in the locative case” means that “in the five aggregates” is a specification in the locative case (*bhumm-niddesa*). “In another way” means when the sense of selection (*niddhāraṇa*) is not intended.

“When there is the sense of characterizing a state by means of another state” is stated because the meanings of object (*visaya*) and so forth are impossible here. “Both” refers to the material and the immaterial.
“The continuity of the material and immaterial” refers to the continuity of matter that originates matter and the continuity of the immaterial. “Basis” (*vatthu*)...

In order to show that the statement, "it is weak at the moment of arising," refers neither exclusively to the moment of rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*) nor exclusively to the physical basis (*vatthurūpa*), he said: "It was stated with reference to the weakness of all material phenomena at the moment of their arising.

The phrase "For at that time," etc., is a statement of the reason for what has been said. In this context, "that" (*taṃ*) refers to material form. "Because it is projected by kamma" (*kammakkhittattā*).
This was not stated with reference merely to the state of being born of kamma; rather, it was said with reference to the lack of stability at the very first arising of what is born of kamma.
Demonstrating this, he said, "Even though there is mindfulness," and so forth. "After that" means after that rebirth-linking.
He said, "in a similar continuity," because it is established in a way that is not the same in a dissimilar continuity as it is in a similar one.
"Aṅgabhāva" means the state of being a cause. For this very reason, it is said to be "the state of being an associate.

"Of those phenomena" refers to the mental and mental-adjunct phenomena that arise together with [the rebirth-linking consciousness] at the moment of rebirth-linking (paṭisandhi). "Then" means that at the moments of stability (ṭhiti) and dissolution (bhaṅga), there is no arising of material form (rūpa) at all.
It is only at the moment of arising (uppāda), through the acquisition of conditions such as the immediately preceding condition (anantara-paccaya), that the mind possesses its state of strength.
Not otherwise. Therefore he said: "And when there is the arising of form, at that moment of arising.

"In whatever modes" means by way of the modes of nutriment, faculty, condition, and so forth. "Conditions exist according to possibility" means that contact and the rest function as conditions by way of nutriment and so on, as appropriate.
For this has been stated in the *Paṭṭhāna*: "At the moment of rebirth-linking, the resultant indeterminate..."
"Nutriments are a condition by way of nutriment-condition for the associated aggregates and for the matter produced by kamma (kaṭattā-rūpa)," and so forth.
"Arising together with the death-consciousness," or "arising with the death-consciousness as its cause.
"As if arising from those preceding it" means, for example, as if arising from those immediately preceding it that are close to the death-consciousness.

Form does not arise in another existence; thus, it shows that even though [form] arises by means of the death-consciousness (*cuticitta*), the non-interruption of the root of the round (*vaṭṭamūla*) is not the cause for the production of form by the death-consciousness, because the subsiding of the root of the round has occurred.
"Of the formless" (*arūpassa*) means of the formless realm (*ārūppa*).
"By temperature" means by the temperature that has arisen at the moment of the subsistence of the rebirth-linking consciousness (*paṭisandhicitta*).

"When matter has originated" means when matter has originated at the moment of the dissolution of the rebirth-linking consciousness; immediately after the rebirth-linking [consciousness], the first bhavaṅga-consciousness originates matter.

"The moments of arising and cessation" refers to the moment of arising of the first consciousness among the sixteen consciousnesses mentioned above, and [the moment of cessation] of the sixteenth consciousness.
Some say this refers to the moment of cessation; however, it should be understood as referring specifically to the moments of arising and cessation of material form (*rūpa*).

"Only at the moment of its existence" means that if it is grasped precisely during the moment when that temperature-element (*utu*) is present, it is said to have "a lifespan of sixteen mind-moments," because its duration is delimited by exactly sixteen consciousnesses (*citta*). [This applies to] the moment of arising.
"Without taking [the moment of arising]" means that, at the time when the temperature is present, the moment of arising is not taken; rather, the moment of cessation is taken.
Thus it is said, "matter has a lifespan of seventeen mind-moments," because one mind-moment is taken together with the moment of arising.
It is also said, "having a lifespan of more than sixteen mind-moments," because the moment of cessation is excluded.

Having thus shown that whether the moments of arising and cessation are grasped or not grasped, there may be a lifespan of sixteen or seventeen mind-moments, or even a lifespan of more than that, he now says "But because...
and so forth, demonstrating the position regarding those [moments] remaining therein.
In that context, "when they have arisen during the moment of its duration" means during the moment of the duration of that temperature (*utu*).

Since rebirth-linking (paṭisandhi) is included among the sixteen types of consciousness that have arisen, the moment of arising of the temperature-element is taken as occurring within the moment of its own existence;

thus, because the moment of cessation is not taken [at that time], it will be stated in the Aṭṭhakathā: "While the material form is still persisting, the sixteen types of consciousness arise and cease, and that [material form] ceases together with the seventeenth consciousness."
A lifespan of more than sixteen mind-moments is intended. Or, when the moment of cessation (nirodhakkhaṇa) has been grasped, a lifespan of sixteen mind-moments is intended;

such is the connection. And here, the phrase "a lifespan of more than sixteen mind-moments" is stated on the assumption that the arising-moment (uppādakkhaṇa) of the rebirth-linking consciousness (paṭisandhicitta) is included. For, in the *Paṭiccasamuppādavibhaṅgavaṇṇanā*, it is said:

“Two life-continuum moments, adverting, seeing, receiving, investigating, determining, five impulsion moments, two registration moments, and one death-consciousness—thus fifteen mind-moments have passed; then, [the object remains] for the duration of one remaining mind-moment.
Likewise, ending with the registration moments, there is one death-consciousness.
And he will say: "At the conclusion of that [process], rebirth-linking consciousness arises upon that very same object which lasts for only a single moment of consciousness.
Therefore, the fact that matter has a lifespan of sixteen moments of consciousness is indeed established as meaningful. Thus he said:
"A lifespan of sixteen moments of consciousness is intended. Nevertheless, having arisen, it serves as a condition for the vibration of the life-continuum (bhavaṅga).
It exists [already], not merely as it is arising; thus, its duration of seventeen mind-moments (*cittakkhaṇa*) should be understood.
The subtlety of the essential nature of nutritive essence (*ojā*) is due to its being a derived form (*upādārūpa*).

And herein, the nutritive essence ingested by the mother acts as a condition for the arising of the eightfold materiality consisting of nutritive essence within that continuum, like an external ointment for an embryo. This is through the continuity of materiality produced by nutriment (*āhārasamuṭṭhāna-rūpa*).

Just as nutritive essence (*ojā*) produces the remaining types of serenity-nutriment (*santati-ojā*), so too the nutritive essence in the stomach does not produce material form because it is temperature-originated (*utusamutthāna*); rather, it produces [material form] only in the location of what is clung-to (*upādinnaka*).
It should be understood that [this nutriment] travels via the nutrient-ducts (*rasaharaṇī*) and pervades the body.
In the phrase "and consciousness itself" (*cittañceva*), the word "and" (*ca*) conjoins only its counterpart—kamma—and not the mental states associated with consciousness.

Having said this, he stated: "Because it is the precursor of the mind. When it was asked: "Does it grasp the arising of consciousness—as in such passages as 'consciousness has arisen'—or does it grasp a single dhamma like the volition of karma? [the reply was:

"Just as for matter originated by consciousness, the mental factors associated with consciousness are the originators, so too for matter originated by karma, those associated with karma are the originators."
Having raised this objection, he said, "And [it is] kamma-originated," etc., in order to state the resolution to it.

"Of matter" means either of the moment of matter or of the duration of matter. This should be regarded as a mere demonstration of the method, because the point that material and immaterial phenomena manifest simultaneously at the very moment of rebirth-linking is not intended here. For this very reason, he said:
“Furthermore, because of the simultaneous arising of both the material and the immaterial,” he says.

Just as the restriction “only at the moment of rebirth-linking” should not be accepted, so too the restriction “manifestation occurs only at one and the same moment” should not be accepted; showing this, he says “But this is not...
and so forth. “For the purpose of illustrating that very thing” means for the purpose of illustrating the lack of simultaneity, not for the purpose of illustrating simultaneous arising.
For this refers to the discourse on the delimitation of the course [of existence].
"If it were so" means: just as the fruits [falling from a tree], if material and immaterial phenomena were to revolve with such slowness or rapidity;

"because they do not belong to the same duration" means because they do not belong to the same time; "without gaps" means without intervals. By this, he clarifies that their occurrence is indeed continuous.

This concludes the discussion on the delimitation of the path. Mental-born material phenomena (*cittaja-rūpa*) and so forth do not proceed in such uninterrupted succession as do kamma-born material phenomena (*kammaja-rūpa*);

therefore, he says, "with reference to the proceeding of kamma-born material phenomena. Alternatively, because kamma-born material phenomena are the primary basis for the others, they are predominant;
thus it is said, "with reference to the proceeding of kamma-born material phenomena. This is because they are not produced by a mental state (*acittuppādaka*).
The cessation-attainment (nirodhasamāpatti) should be understood as resembling Nibbāna because it is free from affliction (*abyābajjhatā*).
"Stepping foot upon foot" means placing one's foot near the foot already stepped upon due to having short legs (*lakuṇḍakapādatā*).
For it is one who has short legs and a quick pace who is intended here; thus he says, "the meaning is 'stepping very quickly. "They cease together" means...

This was stated on the understanding that, in this context, "matter" (rūpa) refers specifically to that produced by kamma (kammaja). However, matter born of temperature (utuja) certainly continues to function even after death.
"As previously stated" refers to the classification of duration (addhāna) mentioned as: "Seventeen thought-moments for matter; for the immaterial, one part of that."

"Arising together" means arising simultaneously; for this word *eka* has the sense of "simultaneous. "One mode of appearance" means one mode of appearance that is to be seen by means of full understanding through knowledge (*ñāta-pariññā*).
For in this way there would be sixteen modes; otherwise, there would be twenty, or even more than these modes.
"Of that" refers to the final kamma-born [matter]. "In the sixteenfold [set]" refers to the final sixteenfold set.
In the sixteenth consciousness that has just passed. "Of the last" means: of the final consciousness therein.
Not accepting the reason for the exclusion of the final kamma-born [consciousness]—just as there is no state of simultaneous cessation—[the author] speaks with apprehension, saying, "But if...
By the words "all too," etc., he demonstrates the over-extension (atippasaṅga) in that case. That which must be excluded is non-simultaneous arising and simultaneous cessation.

It should be understood as having a single arising and a distinct cessation. At that time, neither of these two exists because they have not yet arisen. For this very reason, it is said: "Because of the non-arising of kamma-born matter.
"Prior to that" means before the arising of the subsequent kamma-born matter.

"Of another" refers to a consciousness other than the one that arose at the moment of its own arising. Regarding that which arises at the moment of its duration (*ṭhitikkhaṇa*), there is a state of single arising.
Because there is no state of various cessations for that which has arisen at the moment of dissolution, he said: "excluding the material phenomena arisen at the moments of stability and dissolution.

By the word "tena" (by that), [he means] by that material phenomenon. By the phrase "a connection like that of a chain," he shows that here the term "paveṇī" (succession) is intended to mean an uninterrupted connection.
"Aññathā" (otherwise) means taking even that which is interrupted and calling it "paveṇī."

When it is being stated: since material phenomena (rūpadhamma) do not possess the status of an immediate condition (anantarapaccaya) as non-material phenomena (arūpadhamma) do, the number "forty-eight" was stated without including the material phenomena that arise at the moment of the dissolution (bhaṅgakkhaṇa) of material phenomena. However, if those were included, there would be forty-nine;
therefore he said, "The statement regarding the forty-nine types of kamma-born [matter] ought to have been made."

“Because it is well-illuminated” means because it is clearly illuminated by way of happiness, or because it is thoroughly illuminated by way of showing the method (*naya*). For this very reason he said, “By this method,” and so forth.
In that context, *taṃ* refers to matter (*rūpa*). “By that” means by matter. “In both cases” means during the occurrence of subsequent kamma-born matter, and prior to that.
“Of another” means of a consciousness other than that which arose at the moment of the duration (*ṭhiti*) of a single consciousness.
“Of that” means of matter (*rūpa*). And here, by the phrase “ceasing at the occurrence of the final matter born of kamma,” one should understand the matter that has occurred prior to that.
“By the matter that constitutes the four continuities,” and so forth, is a demonstration of the inclusion and application as previously stated.
“In this” refers to this illumination of non-simultaneous arising and simultaneous cessation. “At the moment of presence” refers to the moment of presence of both the immaterial and the material.
Because both arisen material and immaterial [phenomena] have been shown. Regarding "of that which has not been shown":

just as it is here, so too there, it refers to that which has not been analyzed and shown. But why, in this illustration by means of the last [category], is the inclusion of thirty-two types of kamma-born matter made?
He says: "Thirty-two... ...is joined. From that kamma they are born; thus, they are "born of that kamma" (*taṃkammajā*). Among those, "he constructs" (*saṅkharoti*).
It is both a formation (*saṅkhāra*) and life (*jīvita*); thus, "life-formation" (*jīvitasaṅkhāra*) refers to vitality (*āyu*). They are called "life-formations" because they are formed by life;
these refer to heat and so forth.

"At the moment of arising of another" means that the material form which has arisen at the moment of arising of a particular consciousness belongs to another [consciousness], namely, the seventeenth [moment] after it.
"At the moment of arising" and "at the moment of presence" are connected with "arisen at the moment of presence of another.

Regarding the phrase "it is said [that this is] the intended meaning," although this contradicts the canonical text (*pāḷi*), it is stated for the purpose of showing that it has been handed down in the commentary (*aṭṭhakathā*);
such is the intended meaning here. Why? Because the canonical text proceeds with reference to mind-originated matter (*cittasamuṭṭhānarūpa*), whereas in the commentary...

But as for the statement that it is "kamma-born matter," by what reason does that contradict [the previous point]? To this he says: "Because... must exist," the intention being that it has already been produced.
Therefore, it is said in the Commentary: "And this same rule regarding the moment applies both to that which is originated by mind and to that which is originated by kamma and so forth.
"By these" refers to the Twin Suttas as they have been cited, beginning with: "The bodily formation is originated by mind," and so on.
"By these commentarial passages (*aṭṭhakathāpadeso*)"—the intention is that there is indeed no [passage] demonstrating simultaneous arising (*ekuppāda*) and simultaneous cessation (*ekanirodha*).
For it is said: "From the moment it arises together with that consciousness, until the seventeenth [moment], it ceases together with it," and so forth.

Furthermore, by the phrase "by these," [it refers to] the commentarial passages occurring by way of demonstrating simultaneous arising, non-simultaneous cessation, non-simultaneous arising, and simultaneous cessation.
It should be understood that they have been "taken" (gahita); or rather, the meaning is "by both of these teachers. Regarding the phrase "the third part":
the connection is that by means of that [third part], the duration of sixteen mind-moments (*cittakkhaṇa*)—the third... [etc. ...is stated as the duration.

And by "the third part," the moment of dissolution (*bhaṅgakkhaṇa*) is intended, starting from the moments of arising (*uppāda*) and presence (*ṭhiti*). In which [dissolution] there are eleven mind-moments...

It should be applied thus: when fifteen mind-moments have passed, it has a remaining life-span of five mind-moments; and when [fifteen] have passed, it has a remaining life-span of one mind-moment—both of these being within that very same object.
Furthermore, both of these should be understood as having entered the range of the mind-door and the five doors respectively.
However, it is not possible to cognize an object that has already passed by even a single mind-moment.
Having in mind what was stated thus in the *Paṭiccasamuppādavibhaṅga-aṭṭhakathā*, he says “for it is not possible,” etc., showing that [the statement] was made in that way.
“Fifteen” means that more than fifteen mind-moments have passed; this is the connection.

By the words “therefore,” etc., he demonstrates precisely that which cannot be said, namely, that not even a portion of a moment has been grasped. Thus, first of all, matter does not have a lifespan of seventeen mind-moments.
Nor does it have a lifespan of sixteen mind-moments plus a third; rather, it is shown to have a lifespan of exactly sixteen mind-moments.
But why is it that, although material form shares the same state of being impermanent and conditioned, it is born with such a long lifespan? Because of its slow rate of transformation.
For immaterial phenomena possess an object, are preceded by consciousness, and—according to their respective power—function by way of manifesting their own objects.
They "occur" because they cease immediately after the accomplishment of their respective functions; thus, they are of rapid revolution.
Therefore the Blessed One said: "Bhikkhus, I do not see even a single other dhamma so rapidly revolving as this, namely, the mind (citta).
However, material phenomena (rūpadhammā) are without an object (anārammaṇā); they [are distinguished] from immaterial phenomena (arūpadhammā) by way of having an object.

They must be analyzed. And this analyzability of theirs, which conforms to conventional usage, results from their own slow revolution and the rapid revolution of those [mental states], being accomplished in sixteen or seventeen mind-moments;
thus, in this case, it is matter alone that has become long-lived. Furthermore, because the three aggregates exist in dependence upon a mere continuum of objects for swift consciousness.

Because consciousness consists merely in the apprehension of an object, it undergoes rapid transformation; whereas material form, due to its dependence on the great primary elements which arise slowly, undergoes slow transformation.
Among the various elements, only the Tathāgata possesses knowledge of them as they truly are;

and by him, it was stated that material form alone is a pre-nascence condition and also a post-nascence condition for that same [consciousness]. Therefore, one should not [conclude] here based on the commonality of their being impermanent and conditioned.
One should consider whether matter and non-matter have an equal lifespan. Following the method already stated, one must reach the conclusion here that matter alone has a long lifespan.

Furthermore, having demonstrated how it is that matter does not have a lifespan of seventeen mind-moments, nor a lifespan of sixteen mind-moments plus a third part, [we shall now address] that which is stated in the Commentary regarding the arising of matter at the moment of the mind’s duration (*ṭhitikkhaṇa*).
In that context, not yet granting the mind its status at the very moment of its stationing, he says, "That which here...
must be investigated," and then, citing the textual passage from the *Yamaka* beginning with the sections on "arisen" and "arising," he says, "In the *Cittayamaka*," and so forth.
Therein, "a complete answer" refers to an answer given without omitting either of the two *yamaka* terms. "And the future at the moment of arising" means at the moment of arising...
And the mind that has not yet arisen is not ceased; the meaning is "that which is currently ceasing.

This demonstrates the absence of a moment of duration (*ṭhitikkhaṇa*) for the mind. Thus, the fact that the term "at the moment of duration" is not mentioned in the sections on "the arisen and the arising," etc., demonstrates and makes known this point: that there is no such thing as a moment of duration for the mind.
For [this is] not [the case] in the Abhidhamma, the teaching of the nature of phenomena (*yathādhammasāsana*), where [such a moment] is found.

The intention is that a reason for not mentioning [the moment of duration] is seen. He says, "In the Suttas as well," and so forth, showing that it is not only in the Abhidhamma that the non-mention [of duration] indicates the absence of a moment of duration for consciousness, but rather that this is also the case in the Sutta-piṭaka.
In that context, "change" (aññathatta) means a difference between what precedes and what follows.
By saying "enduring as possessing two moments," he expresses the state of endurance belonging to the present. Change...
However, it should be understood as referring precisely to the continuity [of the stream].
And here, some raise this question: "In whatever manner a phenomenon arises, does it disintegrate in that very same manner, or in a different manner?
If it disintegrates in that very same manner, there can be no occurrence of aging. If, on the other hand, it disintegrates in a different manner, then it is simply something else."
"In every respect, there is simply an absence of a moment of duration," they say.

In that regard, even though arising and cessation have a single dharma as their substratum, the moment of arising is one thing and the moment of cessation is another. For the "moment of arising" is designated in dependence upon the state of arising, while the "moment of cessation" is designated in dependence upon the state of cessation.
And since the state of cessation is distinct from the state of arising, [these moments are distinct] even within a single dharma possessing intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*).
If it were otherwise, one would fall into the position that one phenomenon arises and another phenomenon ceases;
thus, as there must be a state facing cessation just as there is a state of cessation, this must be accepted as being both stability and decay.
If this is so, why is the moment of stability not mentioned in the Canon? It is because of conformity with the inclinations of those to be trained.
It should be understood that the text proceeds by way of guidance and vision. For even the teaching of the Abhidhamma sometimes occurs in accordance with the inclinations of those to be trained.

Thus, for example, the arising of form is taught by dividing it into "accumulation" and "continuity. Furthermore, the teaching on the dyads such as "associated with a cause" should be cited here as an illustration.
“Or for whom? and so forth is the question; “No” is the answer. “The truth of origination ceases” refers to the moment of cessation of the arising of consciousness. This is the intended meaning here:
if matter were to arise at the moment of the destruction of consciousness, then—taking that as the truth of suffering—it would not be possible to say “No,” and yet this has been stated. Therefore...
It is understood that "at the moment of the cessation of consciousness, there is no arising of matter. But this is not a valid reason.
For it may be said that "no" refers either to the immaterial world (*arūpaloka*) or to matter originated by consciousness (*cittasamuṭṭhānarūpa*).

This is indeed the nature of the Yamaka teaching, namely, its application according to what is possible. By this, the statement beginning with "nor is it only matter originated by consciousness" and so forth is refuted.

It should be understood thus. Alternatively, according to the principle of proximity (*paccāsatti*), that truth of suffering (*dukkhasacca*) which is to be produced by the truth of origination (*samudayasacca*)—namely, that which consists of mind, mental factors, and matter dependent upon them—does not arise at that time;
therefore, the answer is "no," but this does not apply to everything.
"Because of the statement regarding simultaneous arising and simultaneous cessation" means: "Is it the case that for whom bodily formation ceases, for him mental formation ceases?
Yes," thus because of the statement regarding simultaneous arising and simultaneous cessation. "By that statement" means by the statement beginning with "for whom bodily formation.
"Of other material phenomena" refers to material phenomena born of kamma, temperature, and nutriment. "Simultaneous arising, simultaneous cessation, and so forth" [refers to these].

Here is the application of this: [it refers] to those things such as kamma-born matter, whose state of being indeterminate is not prohibited by simultaneous arising, nor permitted by simultaneous cessation, nor prevented by non-arising, nor denied by non-cessation. "By this" means by the textual passage beginning with "In whom wholesome states arise," and by the statement of reasoning that "it is not only mind-originated matter.
"Recollection of the Yamaka-pāḷi" means according to the literal sense of the Yamaka-pāḷi on consciousness as it has been shown.
While recollection is present. "The state of breaking up" means the breaking up of consciousness, which is its cessation due to the absence of stability.
It does not even attain the status of an associate, because it lacks the nature of a condition through such factors as being a support or a basis.

For it is only at the moment of arising that consciousness is powerful by obtaining conditions such as the immediate (anantara) condition. And this being so—meaning, and thus, by temperature (utu) as well, of the *bhavaṅga* consciousness...

"When there is the production of material form precisely at the moment of its arising. "In that moment of consciousness" means in the moment of that consciousness; the sense is "even during two moments.

"Precisely by that" means precisely by way of its extremely rapid revolution. Alternatively, "precisely by that" means precisely by way of the state of arising throughout the entire single moment of consciousness due to the slowness of the revolution of material form.
"That" refers to the consciousness. [It refers to] the rebirth-linking consciousness (*paṭisandhicitta*).

Since material phenomena that arise together [with consciousness] also act as conditions for one another through such relations as co-nascence (*sahajāta-paccaya*), just like the associated mental states (*sampayutta-dhamma*), it is said:

"after rebirth-linking" (*paṭisandhito uddhaṃ*). Since consciousness is indeed a condition—by way of co-nascence and so forth—for those things originated by consciousness (*cittasamuṭṭhāna*), it is stated:

"of those not originated by consciousness" (*acittasamuṭṭhānānaṃ*). "Immediately after that" (*tadanantaraṃ*) refers to the consciousness with which [the matter] arose simultaneously; [it refers to] that consciousness...
"Immediately after": "that" refers to material form (*rūpa*). "Immediately after that mind" means the mind that arises immediately after the co-arisen mind.

If it were so—that is, if the entire moment of consciousness (*cittakkhaṇa*) consisted of matter in the very process of arising, such that the commencement of the arising of matter occurs at the very moment of the mind's arising—then [the author] says: "No, because there is no commencement of the arising of matter at the moment of the cessation of the mind."
"At the moment of consciousness" (*cittakkhaṇe*) means at the moment of the consciousness that arises together with itself. "That" (*taṃ*) refers to material form (*rūpa*).

"The function of being a condition for the origination of material form and the function of being a pre-arising condition" (*rūpasamuṭṭhāpanapurejātapaccayakiccaṃ*) means both the function of originating material form and the function of being a pre-arising condition.

"The non-attainment of the distinction in the acquisition of stability" (*ṭhitippattivisesālābhaṃ*) means the non-attainment of that distinction which is obtainable through the acquisition of stability. This is what was said: "That with which it arises, at that very moment of consciousness..."
The statement, "Form arises itself," is spoken by way of a figurative expression (*pariyāya*).
Whatever is stated in relation to something else as its correlate (*sambandhibhāva*) should be connected with that [correlate] even if it stands at a distance; thus he said, "After that... [etc.
...the connection is with this. Therefore, in the word "from that" (*tato*), the pronoun *taṃ* refers back to "death" (*cuti*).
It is said: “The meaning is ‘after passing away’.

Regarding the phrase “there is none”: although it is stated in the *Aṭṭhakathā* that there is no simultaneous arising or simultaneous cessation of material phenomena with immaterial ones, nor of immaterial phenomena with material ones, the intention is that such [simultaneity] does indeed exist in the manner we have described.
Because a fourth mode is being mentioned, it is said: “He spoke three modes.”
By stating, “It is the bodily transformation of those very forms,” and so forth, he demonstrates the state of being a transformation and so on for things that are fully accomplished (*pariniṣpanna*).
By saying, “Everything that is fully accomplished is indeed conditioned (*saṅkhata*),” the method of exposition regarding full accomplishment is shown.

“Delimited by the prior and subsequent limits” means delimited by the states of manifestation and destruction, or delimited by arising and passing away. [This is illustrated] by such expressions as, “Let this one be named Datta,” and so forth.

"Naming" (nāmakaraṇa) means the taking of a name. "Attainment" (samāpajjana) refers specifically to the cessation of the mental body (nāmakāya) through the sequence of serenity (samatha) and insight (vipassanā) in the attainment of cessation (nirodhasamāpatti).
By the word "etc. (ādi), the establishment of the designations for the seven kasinas and so forth is included.
"Being produced" (nipphādiyamāna) means being accomplished (sādhiyamāna).
The commentary on the miscellaneous discussion is finished.
Regarding the commentary on the discussion determining the order of sequence, etc.:
since the order of teaching is indeed found among the order of arising and so forth, it is said, "the order of teaching beginning with 'the four foundations of mindfulness'."

It has been stated. Regarding "by way of successive exaltation" (*anupubbukkaṃsato*): the successive exaltation of the discourses is stated because of their progressive elevation through the sequential presentation of the discourses on giving, virtue, the danger of sensual desires, and so forth, culminating in the discourse on renunciation. By this, he shows that this "order of exaltation" is indeed a distinct order.
Nevertheless, he states the reason for its inclusion within the sequence of the teaching on giving and the rest: "because there is no fixed determination regarding its origin and so forth."
In this context, the word "beginning" (ādi) includes the sequence of stages for the practice of abandonment.
By the phrase "the object-domain of the eye and so forth," it is intended that [feeling] is the range of the five material faculties; thus he says, "partially," and so on.
