"Partially" means by way of the external gross sense-bases. "Therein" refers to the manner stated in the passage: "Whatever one feels, that one perceives."
"For the purpose of excluding that which has that nature" means for the purpose of excluding the nature of phenomena free from taints (*anāsava*).
The meaning is that those free from taints are mentioned only among the aggregates (*khandha*), because [the term] is also mentioned among the aggregates even for those with taints (*sāsava*).

[Objection: But is it not the case that there exists a phenomenon free from taints which is not included among the aggregates? [Reply: True, it exists. However, within the context of the aggregates, only those free from taints that are comprised within the aggregates are taken; thus, this is not a fault.

Just as contact and the others are included within the aggregate of volitional formations (*saṅkhārakkhandha*) because they are specifically of the nature of forming the conditioned through their functioning in accordance with that [volition], feeling, perception, and consciousness are not so;
therefore, like material phenomena, they are stated separately as distinct aggregates.
By this, it should be understood that the absence of a separate designation by the term "aggregate" for contact and the others has been stated. By that—
It is said: “But touching and so forth,” and so on. Regarding the phrase “and such suttas as these,” the word “etc. (*ādi*) includes:
“Bhikkhus, when there is form, by clinging to form, by adhering to form, fetters, attachments, and bondages arise.
When there is feeling... perception... volitional formations... consciousness, by clinging to consciousness, by adhering to consciousness...”

“fetters, adherences, and bondages arise,” as well as such scriptural passages as, “one dwells obsessed with the thought, ‘I am form,’ ‘form is mine’”—this is how the inclusion [of these texts] should be understood. “By this” means by the sutta shown by himself.
And “by way of the sutta to be spoken” refers to the passage beginning with, “Bhikkhus, when there is form,” which will be cited in the commentary.

“By way of the Sutta. By the phrase “it cannot be said [to have] limited objects, etc.,” he shows that even a view with an indeterminate object arises depending on the aggregates themselves, let alone one whose object is the aggregates. “For the sake of feeling” means for the source of feeling.

“Because of concealing” means because of making it appear attractive. “By way of abundance” means by way of preponderance; for the aggregates of clinging (upādānakkhandhas) are characterized by abundant occurrence, whereas the others are not.
"Having made a fold" means having bound a fold resembling a parasol. "In the basis" (vatthumhi) refers to the bases such as the eye and so forth;

this is said with reference to the feeling pertaining to the round of existence (vaṭṭagata-vedanā), for that is what stands here in the state of being visible. "By the deficient" means by the bases and by the defilements being deficient.
Regarding "by illusion" (māyāya): since the employment of illusions such as Indra’s net is "illusion," he says, "the form shown by illusion is 'illusion.'"

"‘Yes’ [is the answer]. By the phrase “from its being the basis, etc.,” the word “etc. includes the object, the associated factors, and so forth. “In some cases” refers to the aggregate of form and others.
“Some specific [meditation subject]” refers specifically to the foul (asubha) and so on.
“Of that” refers to internal form. For one in whom the abandoning of all lusts is possible by way of the abandoning of sensual lust.
Referring to this, it says: "He speaks of the abandoning of all greed by way of sensual lust.
"Should be applied" means that one who abandons desire-and-lust for feeling also abandons desire-and-lust for the contact that is its origin; thus it should be applied.
The application of the three kinds of full understanding is indeed evident.

"Than that" means because one does not see the production of suffering and the destruction of happiness [resulting from it]. "It breaks" means it destroys. "That" refers to the nutriment of mental volition (*manosañcetanāhāra*);

one grasps it and examines it through the full understandings of knowing and scrutinizing. "Abandoning that" means abandoning ignorance (*avijjā*). "Misapprehended" means grasped by way of permanence and so forth through views reckoned as misapprehensions (*parāmāsa*).
"One who sees consciousness as permanent takes up the clinging to views"—this is the meaning of the passage beginning with "tadevidaṃ... [and so on].
It should be illustrated by such sūtra passages as: "Consciousness runs on and wanders about, and not another.
The commentary on the discussion determining the order and so forth is finished.
The commentary on the Suttantabhājanīya is finished.
2. Commentary on the Abhidhamma-Bhājaniya 34.
"Having stated that" means having stated that which is to be known by way of plane, beginning with "all feeling belonging to the four planes," and so forth.
Regarding the phrase "shown by way of association, etc.," the word "etc. here includes the distinctions of root, genus, plane, faculty, physical basis, and contact-born.
It encompasses the state of being fully demonstrated without remainder.

Although the word *taṃ* (that) is a reference back to what was previously stated in its general sense, nevertheless, because it is appropriate to refer to what has immediately preceded—since it is impossible in any other context—it says:
“The application [is] ‘eightfold... and “Because of the absence of an eightfold nature.”
By this, he shows that it is impossible.
It is stated merely for the sake of completion (*pūraṇattha*), meaning because there is nothing previously unestablished (*apubbatābhāvato*).
"By way of the increase of grasping" means by way of the augmentation of grasping. And here, "grasping" (*gahaṇa*) should be understood as speaking (*kathana*).

Its "augmentation" (vaḍḍhana) is the mention of what has not been stated in each respective place. Therefore he said: "Augmentation is the grasping of something other than what was previously grasped," and for that very reason it was said: "by way of the accumulation of something else upon what was previously grasped.

As for the statement, "The word 'augmentation' has the sense of cutting off," this should be understood in the same way that a non-cleaver is called a "cleaver" (sivā), or that what is seen is called "unseen" (adiṭṭha).
“Leading out the method” (*nayanīharaṇa*): “Method” (*naya*) is that which leads; it is the teaching. Its “leading out” is its setting forth.

“The method of expansion” (*vaḍḍhanakanaya*) is the method of teaching that proceeds by way of the aforementioned expansions. “Other divisions” refers to the divisions such as the singlefold, fourfold, and so on.
To the question, “If they are not distinct, why were they mentioned? he says, “Nevertheless,” and so forth. Therein, “for the purpose of generating the various distinctions of wisdom” means:

The meaning is: for the purpose of producing the analytical knowledge of phenomena (*dhamma-paṭisambhidā*) in those to be trained, by means of wisdom that has reached differentiation regarding the domain of phenomena;
and for the purpose of generating the analytical knowledge of phenomena in those to be trained through the bases of knowledge (*vijjā-ṭhāna*) and so forth.

It is stated, "because each section taken up serves as a gateway to deliverance," because the section on comprehension (*sammasana-vāra*) constitutes the objective domain for the classification of phenomena to be directly known (*abhiññeyya-dhamma*).

The other classifications have also been stated; thus, by way of the diversity found within the two-fold and three-fold classifications, those other classifications—though not themselves diverse—are stated according to the reasons already mentioned.
Having shown the mutual dependence of the classifications with the words beginning “Not only...,” he shows their distinctness with the words beginning “Therefore...”.

He shows by the phrase "independent of other classifications," etc., that these sevenfold and other classifications do not proceed according to numerical sequence while depending on further subdivisions, as is the case with the *duka*-rooted [matrices] and so forth;
rather, these are stated solely by way of their commonality of manifoldness, independent of other classifications.
This is because the referents of the *duka*, *tika*, and *catukka* [matrices] must be understood in relation to one another as appropriate.

Because they are stated by way of the relationship between the subject and the object of dependence—just as the triads (tikas) stated after setting aside the dyads (dukas) are said to be "inserted" therein—so too, even though the triads are stated after the dyads have been spoken, they are considered "inserted" because they are stated in relation to the meanings of the dyads and triads.
Thus he says: "Because they are joined further on... and so forth.
"In the same row" means in one and the same row. "By the impact of the eye" means by the striking against the visible object.
"That" refers to the impact of the eye and the visible object. "Producing that" means producing that visual contact. "That" refers to the feeling of adverting.

But is it not stated that contact is the condition for feeling, and not that feeling is the condition for contact? No; because the arising of consciousness is being referred to under the heading of "feeling."
"By way of being the purpose of that" means by way of being the purpose of eye-contact. "Purpose" (*payojana*) means that which causes one to act; it is the fruit.
The intention is [to refer to] the resultant states of the fine-material and immaterial spheres; for those are not included here. For this very reason he said:
"Because they themselves have become the mind-door," and so forth. "From that" means from the life-continuum (*bhavaṅga*). "Of the wholesome and so forth conditioned by eye-contact, etc."...
Here, by the first word "ādi" (etcetera), such terms as "conditioned by ear-contact" and so forth are included; by the second, unwholesome states and so on.

Because wholesome and indeterminate states of the sense-sphere alone have been applied in the passage beginning with "by way of the eight wholesome consciousnesses of the sense-sphere," it is stated in the Commentary that "being found within the same cognitive process (*vīthi*) is what was intended.
[This applies] to those excluding the triads of feeling, the "also" (*pi*), and the "with-visible-object" (*sanidassana*).
By way of nineteen triads, there are nineteen twenty-fourfold groups.

If it were to be applied that wholesome states and so forth are obtainable even in a dissimilar cognitive series (*vīthi*), then why was it applied only to the similar series? To this he says: “But in the Commentary...,” and so forth.
“For that very reason” means precisely because they are not excluded from the dissimilar series.
"Connection with consciousness" (*cittasambandha*) means a connection with consciousness; having established this connection, it is a designation for feeling by way of the heading "consciousness.

"By way of the triads and planes" means by way of the triads such as the wholesome triad, and by way of the planes such as the sense-sphere plane. "By way of the doors and triads" means by way of the doors of arising such as the eye, and by way of the triads such as the wholesome triad. "In whatever place" refers to that which is to be illustrated.

"Because there is no distinction in the meaning, [the term applies] to any one among the sevenfold classification and so forth"—this is the construction. "And the door is not left unmentioned" is the connection.
By this, he shows the distinction between the sevenfold classification and the thirtyfold classification.

Although the planes (bhūmi) are mentioned in both cases, by specifically naming the planes such as the fine-material sphere (rūpāvacara), it is shown that they are obtainable within a different cognitive process (vīthi).
He said: "And here, the state of being obtainable in both similar and dissimilar cognitive processes (*vīthi*) is very clear.
They are "illuminators of happiness" because the aggregate of feeling (*vedanā-khandha*) is analyzed by way of the doors, the bases, and the objects.

"Not established with reference to the planes" means they are not established by way of having reference to the planes as something to be explained; the meaning is that they are not taught through a classification of planes.
"Free from what is to be expected" means being devoid of specific doors and so forth that one might desire, because the door-planes have not been included here.
Regarding the phrase "by way of the ultimate limit of decisive support" (*upanissaya-koṭiyā*), both the literal and figurative senses of the "ultimate limit of decisive support" are shown;
in order to demonstrate the specific "ultimate limit of decisive support" intended here, it is said: "relying on faith," and so forth. In that context, regarding "of the decisive supports":
[This refers to] those things that serve as the decisive support (*upanissaya*) for feeling. "Seeing" means eye-consciousness, or the grasping [of an object] after having seen.

"By way of being a low-grade decisive support" means by way of being a base or inferior decisive support. If smelling and so forth were to be decisive supports, they would necessarily be natural decisive supports (*pakatūpanissaya*).

And since a natural decisive support occurs only within the same cognitive sequence (*ekavīthi*), the statement here regarding its non-attainment indicates that it does not occur within a different cognitive sequence (*nānāvīthi*).

He shows this with the words, “In the doors of the nose, etc. The phrase “of the preliminary work for the kasiṇas, etc. refers to the preliminary work for the kasiṇas, the attainment of jhāna, the production of insight, its development, and so forth.
“Non-attainment of that” means the non-attainment of the decisive support (upanissaya), and that is because it is impossible to know the practice of others through smelling and so on.

Since Bodhisattvas in their final existence and others may attain that [support] even without hearing [the teaching], it is said “for the most part” (yebhuyyena) to indicate that this refers to the root decisive support (mūla-upanissaya).

"Of perfected aspiration" means one whose aspiration is perfected through the attainment of the necessary conditions for turning away from existence (*vivaṭṭūpanissaya*). "By that" refers to the statement, "Thus visual consciousness. "Its supporting condition" means that which serves as the supporting condition for the subsequent seeing of kasiṇa-forms and so forth.

Regarding the phrase "the reaching of firmness," he says, "or of one who has not abandoned sensual lust and so forth," because this is the unique characteristic of sensual lust and the other defilements.
The discussion concerning the arising of lust and aversion toward desirable and undesirable objects begins with the words, "Lust has arisen," and so on.
Since these have been mentioned [previously] and not as a specific function, he says "by way of non-regard," etc., to show them as stated according to their specific functions.
The meaning is "arisen feelings. "By another mode" means by another mode consisting in the transcendence of the defilements that have arisen conditioned by eye-contact.
Regarding the phrase "likewise by way of development," here the word "likewise" refers to the four-plane feeling of eye-contact.

This draws out the very same meaning as that stated by way of another mode: that the state of being a decisive support (*upanissaya*) is itself expressed through a different formulation. Here, "development" (*bhāvanā*) is the alternative mode;
all comprehension (*sammasana*) should be understood as development, not merely the full understanding (*pariññā*) consisting in the abandoning of the hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*).
And "of each other" refers to the mutual relationship among the great elements within the tangible object, and by way of the water element as well.

"Of these" (*tesaṃ*) refers to birth and the other [links of dependent origination]; here, this genitive case is used in the sense of the object. The connection is that it shows the state of being a powerful condition for the conascent mental contact.
Or, "of that seeing" (*tassa vā dassanassa*) means of that knowledge belonging to the sense-sphere which proceeds by way of seeing birth and the others as fearful.
That very same consciousness, which was described as having the status of a cause for contact in the phrase "mental contact" (*manosamphassa*) by way of being the fruit of its own fruit,

is not fit to be described as having the status of a fruit for that contact— expressed as "born of eye-contact" (*cakkhusamphassaja*) and so forth— by way of being the fruit of its own fruit. Furthermore,
although it is obtained [as contact] through the phrases "mental contact" and so on, it [arises] dependent upon consciousness.
Having stated that the fact of contact being a condition was not mentioned for the sake of avoiding a confusion between cause and fruit, [the author] says "or because" and so forth,
in order to show that although contact is indeed a condition for consciousness, consciousness is not its specific condition in the same way that contact is; thus,
the fact that consciousness is born from eye-contact and so forth was not mentioned.
The commentary on the *Abhidhammabhājanīya* is finished.
3. Commentary on the *Pañhapucchaka*. 150.
"That respective collection" refers to that respective collection of phenomena consisting of states of consciousness, as well as the collection of all material phenomena without exception.

"And as they occur" means that restraint (*saṃvara*) occurs at the sixth door [the mind] through the mental application (*upavicāra*), while the other [restraint] occurs through the six sense bases (*chaḷāyatana*);
thus, "as they occur. "From that" means from covetousness, dejection, and so forth. "As appropriate" means according to what ought to be restrained.

"In some cases" he speaks generally regarding those very same cycles (*parivaṭṭa*). Or, "in some cases" means in some particular place within those cycles. "Even a little" means even a small amount. The intention is that there is only one delimitation, and not a variety as found in the *Āyatanavibhaṅga* and other such texts.
The commentary on the Section of Questions is finished.
The commentary on the Analysis of the Aggregates is finished. 2.
The Analysis of the Bases (Āyatanavibhaṅga).
1. Commentary on the Exposition of the Suttanta (Suttantabhājanīya) 154.
"By way of being uncommon" means by way of being unique (*āveṇika*). To establish their state of being uncommon by way of their opposites, he shows a common example [for comparison], saying:
"Just like the meaning of the word 'sense base' (*āyatana*). Alternatively, it refers to the meaning of the eye and so forth.
Thus, the meaning of "base" (*āyatana*) is distinguished by terms such as "eye" and so forth; with reference to that specific meaning of base, he says:
"Because it is unique, like the meaning of the word 'base'.
If the word "eye" had the meaning of "savoring objects," then this designation would also apply to the ear and the other [senses], which would result in the fallacy of over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).

Avoiding [other interpretations], he said, "It is mindfulness" (*sati*), and so forth. In the second interpretation of the meaning: "it sees" (*cakkhati*) means that it announces what is even or uneven as established by consciousness;
the sense is that it is as if announcing, or as if making it manifest.

Since the word *rūpa* is intended here as a term for color—like a visible form (*rūpa*) cognizable by the eye, as if possessing a grasp, as if possessing a physical image—he said, "the detailed explanation."
"Or the meaning of the word *rūpa*.

"Speech alone" means sound accompanied by intimation (*saviññattika-sadda*). "Is conveyed" means it is led toward [the object]. By stating that the apprehension of flavor (*rasaggahaṇa*) is the root of swallowing, he shows that flavor is an indirect cause of life.
For the apprehension of flavor has flavor as its cause, and the apprehension of flavor has [the swallowing] as its cause.
Swallowing, and life for the sake of that [swallowing]. Furthermore, swallowing should be understood as being rooted primarily in the apprehension of taste.
A "location" (*desa*) is so called because fruit is seen or indicated by it; thus he says, "the location of arising means the cause of arising.
"In that manner" means in the form of the eye-base and so forth. "Become the range of the mind" means having become the range of the mind alone. "By the common characteristic alone" means...
Without grasping specific characteristics such as experiencing and so forth, [the sūtra] speaks by means of the common characteristic known as the state of being a phenomenon (*dhamma*).

Having brought them into the unity of a single base (*ekāyatana*), these twelve are spoken of as having a single intrinsic nature (*ekasabhāva*); for there would be no purpose in speaking of them as distinct.

Indeed, the teaching on the bases (*āyatana*) is for the purpose of showing the distinction between the doors and the objects. "From the prior end" (*pubbantato*) means from the preceding portion, that is, from the state of being cooked (*pākabhāva*). For the state of being cooked is the prior end of phenomena possessing intrinsic nature (*sabhāvadhamma*), while the state of disintegration is the subsequent end.

In such contexts as "place of residence," the word *āyatana* does not function by way of explaining the meaning of the term as it does in the case of the [twelve] sense bases (*āyatana*) and so forth;

rather, it is used because the word is conventionally established (*nirūḷha*) in reference to specific things like temples and the like. Thus he says: "to state the meaning of the word *āyatana* by way of conventional usage (*ruḷhi-vasena*).
"Mind" (*mano*) refers to the mind that serves as a door. Regarding "the state of being a support" (*nissaya-bhāvo*), here the support is similar to a support; this is the similarity.
And they are to be understood as such because their existence is dependent upon that fruit. The meaning of "to be spoken of" (*vacanīyattha*) is the meaning of "existence" (*bhāvattha*).
"To that extent" (*tāvatvato*) means "from that much. "The objection regarding deficiency" (*ūnacodanā*) refers to the objection: "Why were fewer than twelve not mentioned?
If the class of phenomena (*dhammajāta*) that is unique to eye-consciousness and so forth is the *dhammāyatana*, then, this being the case, [the same would apply] to the eye and the other [senses].

Anticipating the objection that "it might be the nature of the sphere of mental objects (dhammāyatana)," he says, "Even though," and so forth. Regarding the phrase "by way of being both door and object":
it is not uncommon [to the mind] merely by way of being an object; rather, the elliptical addition is that it is possible for it to be uncommon by way of being both door and object.
Regarding "by way of their mostly simultaneous arising, etc.": generally speaking, the eye-sphere and the others arise together for someone at some time.
For it is said: “At the moment of rebirth in the sense-sphere realm (kāmadhātu), eleven bases (āyatana) arise for some.
Therefore, first of all, the order of arising of the bases is not tenable. Nor is the order of abandoning tenable, because wholesome and indeterminate states are not to be abandoned.
Nor is the order of practice tenable, because unwholesome states and certain indeterminate states are not to be practiced. Nor is the order of planes (bhūmi) tenable...
This is because eight of the eleven bases belong exclusively to the sense-sphere (*kāmāvacara*), the others are included within the four planes of existence, and some are supramundane (*lokuttara*).
Thus, the application of logical consistency regarding the order of arising and so forth should be understood.

Those things in whose presence the personal identity (*attabhāva*) is manifested—namely, the eye and the other [senses]—are the objects of excessive affection, such that one thinks, "This is my eye," and so forth.
Just as they are internal, so too their status as faculties that perform functions such as seeing is primary; thus it is said: "by way of being internal and by way of being possessors of objects.
"In the order of the nose and so forth" means in this sequence: nose, tongue, and body.
Alternatively, the eye and the others are mentioned first because they have present objects, whereas the mind has some present objects and [some past or future].

The statement "some have an object that need not be specified" was spoken later. Even among those with present objects, the four types having derived matter (*upādārūpa*) as their object were mentioned first, followed by those having primary matter (*bhūtarūpa*) as their object.

Furthermore, even among those with derived matter as their object, the sequence of teaching for the eye and so forth is intended to illustrate that they apprehend objects more remotely and more distantly, and more rapidly and swiftly. For the pair of the eye and ear—
"Having a distant range" was stated first. Even among those, the eye was stated first because its range is even more distant;
for even while seeing a river current from afar, one does not hear its sound. Between the nose and the tongue, the nose was stated first because its activity is swifter;
for the odor of food is perceived as soon as it is placed before one. According to their respective locations...
Or rather, this is the order of their teaching. For in this body, the foundation for the eye is at the very top;
below that is the ear; below that, the nose; below that, the tongue; and likewise, the body is generally situated below those.

The mind, however, is mentioned last because it is formless (*arūpī*). Following each of these [internal bases], the external bases are mentioned because they are the respective objects of experience for each.
"Stated" means "this very meaning has been stated"; in this way, too, the sequence of these [terms] is to be understood.

"From that" means from the differentiation of the heart-basis (*hadayavatthu*). For while one mental consciousness (*manoviññāṇa*) proceeds depending upon a certain heart-basis, another does not proceed depending upon that very same one.
"By way of exposition" means by way of exposition in brief and in detail.
It should be applied in such ways as: “That which originates from the wholesome is a counterpart of that which originates from the wholesome,” and so forth.

“Similarity” (sabhāva) means the relationship between the subject and the object, as well as the fitness for the production thereof. “Causal efficacy” (kāraṇasamatthatā) means the capacity existing as a cause, that is, the state of being a condition.
“The state of being a door, etc. means the state of functioning as a door with respect to the doors and objects. In this sense:
Regarding the meaning stated immediately before: "Yasmā" means by which natural law (*dhammatā*) or by which state of being a door and so forth acting as a cause.

"Sambhavanavisesanaṃ" expresses a reference to the action; the sense is: "that arising, [which occurs] through the power of the natural law. "Rittakāneva" means precisely those that are devoid of permanence and other such qualities.
"Visamādiajjhāsayāni" refers to those whose underlying intention (*ajjhāsaya*) is directed toward unevenness and the like.
They are called "having uneven dispositions, etc. (*visamādiajjhāsayāni*) because they possess uneven dispositions, etc., namely the eye and so forth.
Because of delighting in the eye and so forth—which are like snakes and other creatures dependent on an uneven state, etc.—and in the mind which is like a monkey dependent on a forest;
for "forest-state" (*vanabhāvo*) means "forest-disposition" (*vanajjhāsayo*).
“Secluded from the prior limit” means being devoid of the preceding stage. For here, the “prior limit” (*purimanta*) refers to the initial portion prior to arising.

“The subsequent limit” (*aparanta*) means in the later stage; the meaning is “after dissolution. Indeed, a phenomenon possessing intrinsic nature (*sabhāvadhamma*) is delimited by arising and passing away.
It is with reference to this that it was said: “They have gone to non-deposition, they are broken; there is no heap remaining in the future. Thus, it is always non-existent.

It is not the establishment of non-existence at all times—that is, saying it does not exist at any time—but rather, because it is delimited by arising and passing away, there is a negation of its constant existence;
thus he says, "the characteristic of impermanence. "The relinquishing of its own nature" refers to reaching the state of dissolution.
"Transformation" means that without a continuity through the stages of arising and aging, there is no undergoing of change; thus he says, "or the undergoing of transformation within the continuity."
“By way of being subject to birth and so forth” means by way of having the nature of birth, aging, sickness, death, and so on. “Unpleasantness” (*aniṭṭhatā*) means not being desirable;
the meaning is suffering (*dukkhatā*). The “previous general characteristic” refers to the characteristic of suffering previously stated in its general sense as “in the sense of oppression.
For individual phenomena that proceed in the mode of suffering by way of conditions, the act of suffering belongs to the person alone.
Because it is painful by way of its nature, he said: "It is suffering because it oppresses the person. "The word 'suffering'" refers to the Teacher’s statement, "it is suffering.
By the phrase "there is no controller over this," he demonstrates the meaning of "non-self" (*anattā*) as "there is no self (*atta*) over this";
however, by the phrase "nor is this a controller," he shows it as "non-self" in the sense that "this is not a self. "Self" (*attan*) refers to one's own internal essence.
He speaks with intentional meaning (*sandhāya*). "In another" means in something other than that. The same principle applies here to the phrase "in another and in oneself.
"That does not belong to this" means that the aforementioned imagined power-wielding quality (*vasavattaka*) does not belong to this eye and so forth;
by this, the inclusion within the fourfold emptiness (*catukoṭika-suññatā*) should be understood. "It is empty of that mode of power-wielding."
Since the meaning of "lack of mastery" (avasavattana) must be shown in both ways, he first states "of another," etc., to show one of them, and then shows the other with "or else," etc.

If the meaning were taken as "one who is a master is a *sāmika*, not a non-master is an *assāmika*," there would be no purpose for the qualification of "emptiness" (*suñña*) in the term "from the state of being without a master" (*assāmikato*). [The phrase] "acting according to one's will" (*kāmakāriyaṃ*)...

It is "to be made according to one's wish" (*yathākāmakaraṇīya*). He shows this by distinguishing it for the purpose of demonstrating non-subordination (*avasavattanattha*), because it comprises the meaning of two compounds.
He says, "In the continuity, the arising of dissimilar states is here called the transition of state (*bhāvasaṅkantigamana*)," meaning precisely the arising of another state within the continuity.
Likewise, in that dissimilar arising, there is the disappearance of the prior form and the relinquishing of the original state (*pakatibhāva*).
He said: "The relinquishing of the mode of occurrence as it proceeds within the continuity. Or, *bhāva* means "becoming," which is a specific state;
the transition of that is *bhāvasaṅkanti*. For a phenomenon possessing its own intrinsic nature (*sabhāvadhamma*), having reached the moment of arising and the moment of stability, breaks up;
thus it is said that it transitions from the state of arising to the state of aging, and from there to the state of dissolution. As it thus transitions—

And this should be applied according to the moment (*khaṇa*): from the moment of its own acquisition onwards, there is the relinquishing of its own nature by means of aging and death, which is the abandoning of its original state.
Furthermore, the phrase "by way of priority and posteriority" can also mean "by way of the priority and posteriority of moments.
The term "on account of being one in meaning" (*ekatthatta*) refers to having a common substratum (*samānādhikaraṇa*), and not to the relationship between a qualifier and a qualificand.
Because of identity. When it is said, "The eye is impermanent," it is already said that "the impermanent is the eye";

thus, it follows that "whatever is the eye, that is impermanent; whatever is impermanent, that is the eye. Therefore, he says: "It would follow that other impermanent phenomena also possess the nature of being the eye."
And by those characteristics of impermanence and suffering, the characteristic of non-self (anattalakkhaṇa) alone is specifically demonstrated, as in such passages as:

"What is impermanent, that is suffering; what is suffering, that is non-self," and so forth. "For the purpose of demonstrating the mode of the characteristic of fault" means for the purpose of demonstrating the mode by which the fault is to be characterized. "Thus by suffering" means thus by various kinds of suffering, such as eye-disease and the like.
Regarding "for the sake of affliction": "of those that illuminate the characteristic of non-self" means they are the means for making known the state of non-self.

For the impermanence and suffering found through such things as the breaking of a jar or being pierced by a thorn do not, by themselves, serve as absolute causes for the realization of the non-selfhood of sentient beings.
However, that which is found through dependence on conditions, constant oppression, and so forth— [...is the cause for the realization of non-self.]
For indeed, the eye and the other [faculties] function in dependence upon conditions such as karma and the great primary elements;
therefore, they arise having not existed before and perish having existed, and thus they are impermanent. Because they are constantly oppressed, they are suffering.
And being such, because they do not admit of mastery, they are non-self. This can be seen by those established in comprehension who have accumulated the equipment of knowledge.
But how is their "having been followed by non-existence" to be known? From seeing their alteration at every moment.
How is that known? Through reasoning (*yutti*). What is the reasoning here? It is the apprehension of a difference.
For if there were no alteration of the eye and so forth at every moment, then this subsequent apprehension of a difference, which occurs when external conditions have varied, would not take place.

For if there were no such moment-to-moment alteration (aññathatta) in that [object], how could there be a perception of difference later on, in the absence of any external specific condition? Yet, such a perception of difference does occur.
Therefore, there is indeed a moment-to-moment alteration in them, which, by increasing gradually, becomes more manifest later on. Likewise...
Indeed, the discernment of the distinction [between the two] is due to the instability and the fatigue of the body's inhalations and exhalations.
For the inhalations and exhalations are unstable because the winds proceed in alternating succession.
If there were no subsequent difference in the body whether during inhalation or exhalation, there would be no distinction between them; yet such a distinction is observed. Therefore...
The inhaled breath, becoming otherwise in due course, reaches such a state.

Since that which is the condition for the out-breath, and conversely, that which is the condition for the in-breath when there is an out-breath, remains the same, the establishment of the body’s alteration is proven by the instability of the in-and-out breaths.
Likewise, even fatigue, in the absence of any other distinction, occurs later...
There would be no [sustenance] for the body by which it dispels fatigue through the practice of various postures and so forth.

Alternatively, there is the apprehension of distinction even by way of the classification into form and so on; for that specific quality which is subsequently apprehended in the body and in things not bound to sense-faculties—such as milk, water, cloth, flowers, fruits, medicinal herbs, grains, and the like—with respect to their forms, odors, tastes, touches, and so forth.

Thus, in the absence of any external condition for change, how could the differentiation of color, strength, and so forth, as well as the differentiation of taste, potency, post-digestive effect, and specific action, be perceived in these things during their stages of aging and so on, if there were not a moment-to-moment alteration? But as for that "natural" matter such as stone and the like—how is it there?
Even in that case, there is indeed the perception of differentiation due to the distinction between the contacts of cold and heat. [This occurs] moment by moment.

"Without change at every moment, it is not tenable. And since there is a distinction among material form and the other aggregates, the distinction among the primary elements (mahābhūta) that serve as their support is also established.
For a distinction among supported things cannot exist without a distinction among their supporting primary elements.

Thus, first of all, through the perception of specific differences among material phenomena, change at every moment is established; and from that, the non-existence [of permanence] after having been is proven.
However, the distinction among immaterial phenomena (arūpadhammā) is grasped by way of their objects (ārammaṇa) and so forth.
For wherever immaterial phenomena arise with respect to an object, they cease right there; they do not migrate elsewhere.
And the objective phenomena themselves do not persist beyond their own respective moments. This point should be understood through such examples as a lamp and the like.
For indeed, at every moment, visible forms and so forth are different, as they are in a lamp’s flame; likewise when streams of milk fall, or when the wind blows, the impacts are different.
Just as there is this difference in these things from moment to moment, how much more so for consciousness and mental factors!

Furthermore, due to the diversity of sounds and even the distinctions among sounds, there is a difference from moment to moment in the consciousness and mental factors that have those sounds as their object.
From that, there is the apprehension of distinction. For when one rapidly turns over a text that is well-mastered, a difference among the sounds produced by the mind is observed;
indeed, there can be no difference in the effect without a difference in the cause, just as in the case of musical sounds.

In the same way, there is an apprehension of distinction among immaterial phenomena due to a difference in their objects. By this very fact, their state of alteration from moment to moment is established.
This is to be understood. This same method applies even when distinguishing by way of the different types of phenomena associated with the planes of birth.

Thus, through the apprehension of the distinctions between material and immaterial phenomena, the state of changeability at every moment is established. Since they exist having previously been non-existent, the eye and so forth are established as impermanent;
because they are impermanent and thus constantly oppressed, they are suffering; and because one lacks mastery over them, they are non-self.
Therefore the Blessed One said: “What is impermanent, that is suffering; what is suffering, that is non-self.
He speaks thus, specifying the meaning of the word *abhiṇha* (frequently) as “occurring without interval. “By way of mere elements” means by way of the state of being mere elements.
“From the aggregate” means from the mass [of the eye] together with its constituent parts, such as the physical eye. This term “of the eye, etc. refers to the phrase “from the aggregate.”

With reference to the word *pada*, the genitive case is used for the sake of connection; with reference to the word "separating" (*vinibbhujana*), it should be understood as having the sense of the object (*kamma*).

"The four masses" (*ghanāni*) refers to the masses of continuity (*santati*), collection (*samūha*), function (*kicca*), and object (*ārammaṇa*). Regarding the phrase "from the grasping of occurring form and so forth":

that which occurs by way of being affected (*ruppana*) and so on is "occurring," and that which is the grasping of form and so forth is "grasping of form and so forth"; thus, the compound is "occurring-grasping-of-form-and-so-fort," from which [the genitive] should be construed.
"Because the apprehension of impermanence and so forth exists" means that because there is found a knowledge of impermanence and so forth distinct from the knowledge of form, feeling, and the rest.

By this, he states the distinction between the state of impermanence and so forth [of the object] and the state of being subject to change (ruppana) and so forth, even though the objects such as form possess the nature of impermanence and so forth.

Now, in order to make that very distinction clear by way of its being the objective domain of the full understanding consisting in knowing and scrutinizing, he says "For it is not... and so forth. "Not to overstep" means...

Here, the characteristics (*lakkhaṇa*) and the possessor of characteristics (*lakkhaṇavanta*) are stated to be distinct. In that context, it is not appropriate to overstate the case by asserting a mutual contradiction—namely, that they are non-distinct—on the grounds that the aggregates (*khandha*) are said to be the object of insight (*vipassanā*) which has the characteristics as its object. Why? Because it was stated:

"But those modes," and so forth. Furthermore, the underlying intention here should be understood as the clarification that the characteristics are merely the modes (*ākāra*) of form and the other aggregates.

For it is precisely by observing formations as they are in their intrinsic nature— thinking, “It is impermanent, suffering, and non-self”— that one observes the characteristics [of impermanence, etc.].

Just as there is a distinction between impermanence and the other characteristics according to the method already stated, so too, although impermanence and the others share the commonality of being characteristics,

they are distinguished by their being the respective objects of different types of knowledge, by their having different opposites, and by their association with different faculties, as they constitute the three doors to liberation.
Showing that there is mutual differentiation, he said, “And grasping it as ‘impermanent,’” and so forth. This is indeed easy to understand.
The commentary on the Suttanta-bhājaniya is finished.
2. Commentary on the Abhidhamma-bhājaniya.

155. "By way of pairs of conditions" means by way of the two conditions: internal and external. "Not disconnectedly by way of internal and external" means without confusion, both by way of the internal and by way of the external.

167. "Inclined toward the unconditioned" (visaṅkhāraninna) means leaning toward Nibbāna. "Completely liberated from formations" (vinimuttasaṅkhāra) means being thoroughly liberated from formations through the liberations of complete cutting off and subsiding, and by the abandoning of the desire and lust bound up with them; it is so called because of its state as the supreme consolation.
And [it is] by way of being a destination (*gati*) and a foundation (*patiṭṭhāna*); for it is said, "Nirvana is the destination of the Arahant. There is also the reading *ṭhitibhāvena*.
"In the absence of its realization" means in the absence of the realization of that Nirvana. "Led" means brought forth; the meaning is "manifested.
"Crushed" means split apart. "Do you not know yourself? means "Do you not indeed know? "What... [the rest follows].
"You know one thing, but do you not know this [other]?"—to the opponent who thus creates a diversion, the proponent binds him with the words "Is it not known?
and so forth. "Having analyzed" means having analyzed the meaning of the statement: "Because they arise at the end of the destruction of lust and the other defilements.
The construction is: "They do not exist due to the destruction (khaya) of lust and the rest. And as for the intrinsic nature (sasabhāvatā) of Nibbāna...
The connection is with the word "has fallen into" (*āpannā hoti*).

By means of making Nibbāna the object—which serves as the cause; for this instrumental case (*karaṇavacana*) has the sense of a reason (*hetu*). Or, for one who desires the mere destruction of defilements (*kilesakkhayamattataṃ*) as Nibbāna, the construction is:

"there must be the destruction of defilements. Thus, in Nibbāna, which is the mere destruction of defilements, the various defilements to be destroyed are of many kinds and diverse types, as is the Path.

It exhausts the defilements by way of specific categories. This refers to the same two preceding questions: "Having made what kind of exhaustion of defilements, namely Nibbāna, its object, does it exhaust which defilements?
"That very same" means exactly that which was stated as "not even a mere portion of ignorance and craving."

And here, regarding this objection that nibbāna is non-existent because it is said that "nibbāna is simply the destruction of the defilements," there follows this demonstration of its existence and non-existence according to scripture and reasoning. For the Blessed One said:
"There is, bhikkhus, that which is unborn, unbecome, unmade, and unconditioned.
And: "There is, bhikkhus, that sphere wherein there is neither earth, nor water, nor fire, nor air..."
And so on; likewise:
“Profound, hard to see, hard to understand, peaceful, sublime, beyond the sphere of logic, subtle, to be experienced by the wise”;
and: “Bhikkhus, I will teach you the unconditioned and the path leading to the unconditioned—the undecaying, the taintless.”
Truth, the further shore, the subtle, very difficult to see, undecaying, stable, visible, non-manifest, free from proliferation,
peaceful, deathless, sublime, auspicious, secure, the destruction of craving, wonderful, marvelous, free from calamity, possessing a nature free from calamity,
Nibbāna, unafflicted, dispassion, purity, liberation, non-attachment, the island.
"Monks, I shall teach you a shelter, a protection, a refuge, and a final resort, as well as the practice leading to that final resort"— through such Sutta passages as these,

and through portions of the Abhidhamma such as "the unconditioned phenomena (appaccaya-dhammā), the unformed phenomena (asaṅkhata-dhammā), and all form and the unformed element (asaṅkhata-dhātu)" and so forth,
it is taught precisely as ultimate reality (paramattha-bhāva). For [that which is] devoid of intrinsic nature (sabhāva) [cannot be so taught].

It is logical that mere non-existence should possess such qualities as profundity, unconditionedness, and so forth, as well as the status of being an indeterminate phenomenon (*avyākata-dharma*) and the like; and this has indeed been stated.
Therefore, Nibbāna is not mere non-existence.
Furthermore, this proponent of non-existence should be asked: "If the non-existence of defilements is Nibbāna, then is this non-existence a single [entity]?"
Or could it be manifold? If it were one, then since it would be both produced and realized by a single path alone, it would follow that the higher paths are purposeless;
for it is never seen that a single thing can be accomplished by multiple sequences of action.
Now, if it should be argued that while this absence of defilement is indeed one, it is not to be produced by the paths, but rather to be realized—then [the objection remains].
This being so, it follows even more clearly that the Path is useless because the defilements have not been abandoned.

And if the Path does nothing, what purpose would it accomplish toward the realization of the absence of defilements? Furthermore, since the function of the various Paths is specifically determined by the abandonment of the three fetters and so forth, there must be a distinction in the absence of defilements according to the distinction between the abandoners.
This being so, multiplicity cannot exist without a distinction in intrinsic nature (*sabhāvabheda*).

By way of the designation "plurality," its "having an intrinsic nature" (sasabhāvatā) is implied. Furthermore, if it were argued that "there is a metaphorical application of plurality to those things which are non-existent because of their plurality," then, in that case, there would also have to be a metaphorical application of "having an intrinsic nature" to those things which are non-existent because of their having an intrinsic nature.

Likewise, they would also possess the state of being defilements, conditioned phenomena, and so forth, because of their being defilements, conditioned phenomena, and so forth; yet this is not tenable.
The metaphorical designation of them as "many" is not tenable. If it is argued that even their status as "one" cannot be asserted because they lack intrinsic nature (*asabhāvatā*), we say no;
for, by virtue of the commonality of non-existence (*abhāva-sāmānyataḥ*), there is a designation of unity through the conventional term of non-difference based on that commonality of non-existence.
And if unity exists, one does not escape the faults previously stated.
And if there were multiplicity, then the possession of intrinsic nature (*sasabhāvatā*) would be established.

Even if it were the case that just as multiplicity implies the possession of intrinsic nature, so too the possession of intrinsic nature in general would not deviate from multiplicity—such that multiplicity would follow for Nibbāna even on the side of its possessing intrinsic nature—is that not so?
Why? Because of the non-differentiation of that generality. For it is not possible to say that just as the state of being hard...
Just as existence does not deviate from its own nature, so too, its own nature should not deviate from the state of being hard.
For if that were the case, it would follow that all other phenomena are non-existent; therefore, multiplicity depends upon its own nature, but its own nature does not depend upon multiplicity.
Thus, there is no occurrence of multiplicity for Nibbāna, which possesses its own nature. For "one... [is said].
This is because of such statements as: "Truth has no companion; there is one goal, not many goals.
Furthermore, here the "absence of defilements" refers to the total eradication, absolute abandonment, and non-arising cessation of lust and the other defilements.

Since that [cessation] is a single unity, it must be accomplished by a single path alone due to the absence of any distinction in its function; thus, the classification of the paths according to seeing and so forth is established.
It could not be so. For that [cessation] is intended as the very abandonment of the defilements.

And this distinction of the path occurs—due to the states of being slightly sharp, sharp, sharper, and most sharp among the faculties such as faith—even when there is a single capacity for the abandonment through eradication, by way of a specific realization;
thus, it is appropriate only for Nibbāna to possess its own intrinsic nature (sasabhāvatā). As for the non-existence of the defilements...
It might be thought that [nibbāna] should be accomplished by the path—lest the path be rendered useless—but it is not something to be realized.
For what intrinsic nature (sabhāva) could there be in it that might be realized by means of that [path]?

Furthermore, that absence of defilements (kilesābhāva) ought to be established by a single path alone, rather than by four, lest there be a division of nibbāna into four parts or a distinction among different types of nibbāna. Therefore...
The entire argument turns back [against you]:

the distinction between the paths beginning with the path of seeing would not exist. Furthermore, if non-existence were to become existence, and its status as a functional phenomenon (*bhāvadhammatā*) were thus admitted, then—just as that conditioned phenomenon would incur the status of being a conditioned phenomenon through aging, death, and so forth—it would likewise incur the status of being a phenomenon for many defilements.

Since the undesirable consequence of its being manifold and so forth would also be difficult to avoid, one should understand that Nibbāna is a single, conditioned state possessing its own intrinsic nature (sasabhāva), as opposed to anything else which lacks such a nature.
If this is so, why is it said to be "the destruction of lust, the destruction of hatred, and the destruction of delusion"? It is because it is to be attained by means of destruction.

Cessation (*khaya*) is indeed the noble path. As it is said: "Knowledge of cessation, knowledge of non-arising. Because it is to be attained by means of that noble path—which is a synonym for the destruction of lust and the other defilements—it is stated:
"Nibbāna, which is the destruction of lust and so forth, is the ultimate goal, profound, subtle, hard to see, and difficult to realize.
Or rather, it is because it is to be reached by way of the abandoning of lust and the rest, as follows:
It is also stated elsewhere: "The crusher of intoxication, the remover of thirst," and so forth.

Furthermore, just as the escape (nissaraṇa)—which is the opposite of, and possesses a nature contrary to, those sensual pleasures and material forms that are subject to full understanding—is discerned, so too [is it discerned] by means of that which is the opposite of all conditioned phenomena, together with their intrinsic natures.
There must be an escape by way of a state that is diametrically opposed [to suffering]. And that which is this escape is the unconditioned element (asaṅkhata-dhātu).

Furthermore—insight-knowledge having conditioned phenomena as its object, even the knowledge of conformity (anuloma-ñāṇa), abandons defilements by way of their partial overcoming (tadaṅga-vasena), but it is not able to abandon them by way of total eradication (samuccheda-vasena). Likewise, [knowledge] having conventional truth (sammuti-sacca) as its object in the first jhāna and so forth...
Knowledge abandons defilements only by way of suppression, not by way of eradication. Thus,
because knowledge that has conditioned phenomena as its object and conventional truth as its object is incapable of eradicating defilements through their total destruction,
it possesses an object whose intrinsic nature is the opposite of that noble path-knowledge which effects such eradication.

It must exist; it is the unconditioned element (*asaṅkhata-dhātu*). Likewise, the statement, “Bhikkhus, there is that which is unborn, unbecome, unmade, and unconditioned,” is a word indicating the ultimate existence of Nibbāna, because it was spoken by the Blessed One with an unerring meaning.

For whatever has been spoken by the Blessed One possesses an unerring meaning, just as in the case of: “All conditioned phenomena are impermanent, all... [phenomena are suffering, all phenomena are non-self].”

“Formations are suffering; all phenomena are non-self. Likewise, the word *nibbāna* refers in some instances to the ultimate reality as it truly is, because of the presence of figurative usage (*upacāra-vutti*), just like the word *sīha* (lion).

Alternatively, there certainly exists an unconditioned element (*asaṅkhata-dhātu*) in the ultimate sense, because its intrinsic nature is liberation from the aforementioned opposites, just as in such expressions as “the earth-element” or “feeling,” and so forth.

The existence of the unconditioned element (asaṅkhata-dhātu) in the ultimate sense (paramattha) should also be understood through both the methods [of the Abhidhamma] and through logical reasoning (yutti).
The commentary on the *Abhidhammabhājanīya* is finished.
3. Commentary on the *Pañhapucchaka*.
168. “Kiñci” means some object. “Ālambanatō” means by way of making it an object.
The commentary on the section of questions is finished.
The commentary on the Analysis of the Bases (Āyatanavibhaṅga) is finished.
3. Analysis of the Elements (Dhātuvibhaṅga) 1.
Explanation of the Exposition According to the Discourses (Suttantabhājanīyavaṇṇanā) 172.
"And as it has come down in the Abhidhamma" refers to the questions and inquiries in the Abhidhamma-exposition (Abhidhammabhājanīya) within this Analysis of the Elements.
And they appear in the *Nikkhepakaṇḍa*, the *Dhammahadayavibhaṅga*, and so forth, as they have been set forth in the teaching.

Just as the aggregates and other categories that have come down in the Suttanta and the Abhidhamma are analyzed in the *Khandhavibhaṅga* and other sections according to the method of exposition used in the Suttantas—
namely, by way of the Suttanta-Bhājaniya— so too here the eye-element and the others ought to be analyzed by way of the Suttanta-Bhājaniya.

In that regard, since there is no other mode of teaching for the aggregates and so forth— distinct from the Abhidhamma teaching— that has been brought down in the Suttantas as a comprehensive summary,
they were taught in the *Suttanta-bhājaniya* by way of the aggregate of form (*rūpakkhandha*) and the rest. However, since such a [comprehensive] mode exists for the elements (*dhātu*), he said,
"It is analyzed in the Suttantas themselves...," showing that they are taught here by way of the three sets of six elements.
"It should be understood. Therefore, it is said in the Commentary: "All elements, having been condensed by way of six groups of six elements.

But how is there an inclusion of the eighteen elements within each of these six groups of six? It is by way of their commonality of intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*), support (*nissaya*), door (*dvāra*), object (*ārammaṇa*), and association (*sampayoga*).

In that regard, first, in the initial group of six, the earth, fire, and air elements are, by way of their intrinsic nature, the tangible element (*phoṭṭhabbadhātu*). The water element and the space element...

A portion of the dhamma-element consists of the seven consciousness-elements. By the inclusion of the four elements here, the remaining material elements are subsumed under the designation of their supports—since they exist in dependence on those [four]—or by way of being the doors and objects for the consciousness-element;
and by the inclusion of the consciousness-element, a portion of the dhamma-element is included through its association with that [consciousness]. Thus, there is a complete inclusion of all elements.
It should be understood as follows. In the second group, the six elements are included by way of their intrinsic nature; they constitute a portion of the base of mental phenomena (*dhammāyatana*).
The seven consciousness-elements are included through association with them, and the remaining elements are included because they serve as their respective supports, doors, and objects.
The same method applies to the third group of six as well. Thus, herein, the inclusion of the eighteen elements within the six groups of six elements should be understood.
Therefore it was said: "All elements, having been condensed by means of six [elements] each.

It is "empty" (suñña) in the sense of being empty of a self; thus, because they possess their own intrinsic nature (sasabhāvatā), the term "element" (dhātu) is used here. Hence he said: "The word 'element' is conventionally established in reference to mere intrinsic nature within what is empty.
Space is the very limit of form, characterized by the state of being devoid of this or that [form]. That from which it is devoid—
Since there can be no non-contact with those things that have limits if they are all-pervading, he says:
"the state of not being pervaded by the four great elements. For the elements function within limits.

(173) Not accepting the previous point—that there is no such thing as a composite whole separate from its parts—he states the second meaning without the composite whole, beginning with "or two," and so forth. "Produced individually in oneself" (*paccattaṃ attani jātattā*) means individuality (*pāṭipuggalikataṃ*).
"A separate component" means a single earth-component that is distinct and unmixed with other components such as hair and so forth.
"Application" refers to the application of meditation. "Energy" refers to the exertion that brings about the development of meditation. "Exertion" refers to the corresponding volition.
"Of the attention to elements, repulsiveness, and beauty" means of the attention to elements, the attention to repulsiveness, and the attention to beauty.
“By way of non-malice” means by way of being devoid of the volition [thinking], “I am producing this; this production is mine.
“Performing” means they give rise to mental application (*ābhoga*) and reflection (*paccavekkhaṇā*).

“By way of characteristic” means by way of intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*). Since that [characteristic] is the hardness and rigidity of the earth element, he said: “It is stated with reference to the expression ‘hardness, rigidity,’ and so forth.”
Vekantaka is a type of iron capable of cutting through all other metals. For it "cuts" (vikantati) or slices, thus it is called *vikanta*;
being a *vikanta*, it is termed *vekantaka*. It is "like iron" (*lohassadisa*) in that it remains dense and solid like the dross of iron.
However, when heated and beaten, it disperses as it is cut away piece by piece.
If it is not soft, smooth, or workable, it is therefore called "base metal" (*lohavijaṭī*). Regarding "with tin, etc.":
brass (*kaṃsaloha*) is made by mixing tin; bell-metal (*vaṭṭaloha*) is made by mixing lead and tin;
and *ārakūṭa* is made by mixing lead and copper. Furthermore, that which comes from the pure lead element is also called "bronze" (*pittala*).
What they say is not intended here; rather, taking only that which is mixed as previously described, it is called "artificial.
The phrase "by way of illustration" is stated because pearls have many varieties according to their source.
For there are eight sources of pearls: the elephant's frontal globe, the boar's tusk, the serpent's head, the cloud-peak, the bamboo joint, the fish's head, the conch, and the oyster shell.
Among these, those born from the frontal globes of elephants are yellow in color and devoid of radiance. Those born from the tusks of boars are the very color of a boar’s tusk.
Those born from the heads of serpents are of colors such as blue and are extremely pure and rounded. Those born from clouds are brilliant and their forms are difficult to distinguish;
they remain dispelling the darkness during the night and serve exclusively for the enjoyment of the gods. Those born from bamboo joints are the same color as the *kāra* fruit.
They are not radiant; moreover, those *veḷuva* [pearls] grow only in places that are the domain of non-human beings (*amanussa*).
Those born from fish have a color similar to the back of a *pāṭhīna* fish; they are round and light, yet devoid of luster. Those born from conchs have the color of a conch shell’s skin;
though they may be the size of a *kola* fruit, they too are indeed devoid of luster. However, those born from oysters are endowed with a particular excellence of luster.
They exist in various shapes. Thus, among the eight kinds of pearls according to their species, those produced from fish, conchs, and oysters are oceanic;
some say that certain ones produced from snakes are also oceanic, while the others are non-oceanic. Therefore it was said: "Oceanic pearls" is merely an illustration;
for all pearls, indeed, are simply pearls. Or, this [distinction] is mentioned in the Commentary because of their abundance.
It is said: "Pearls means ocean pearls. For in the world, ocean pearls are generally what are seen.
Even among those, only those produced by oysters [are true pearls]; others are sometimes glass.
Here, however, there is no such restriction, because only the state of being liquid is intended.
175. “By way of being sharpened” means by way of a sharp state produced through such processes as heating. For here, “sharpening” refers to the manifestation of heat.
“Ordinary” is intended to mean the natural bodily heat. “Always” means at all times, as long as the life-faculty continues to function.
“Peta-fire” refers to the fire of hungry ghosts (nijjhāmataṇhika-peta). “Here” refers to this discourse on the external fire element.

176. *Vāyanaṃ* (blowing) means seed-sowing; however, because that proceeds with force, it is said: "by way of proceeding with urgency. *Samudīraṇaṃ* (agitation) means the drying of what is moist, or the state of being the cause for the arising [of matter] in another location within the aggregate of primary elements (*bhūtasaṅghāta*).

177. It is said: "because of the mention of unobstructed space (*ajaṭākāsa*)," meaning that the preparation of the delimiting space (*paricchedākāsa*) is performed by depending precisely upon the unobstructed space found in such things as wall-cavities.
179. "By way of being the condition for the production of the tangible objects of pleasure and pain" means by way of being the producer of desirable and undesirable tangible objects.
By way of being a condition (*paccayabhāvena*). To the question, "Of what, then, is it the state of being a condition? he says: "of the body, the parts of the body, and the limbs.

And the term "by way of being a condition" is used in the instrumental case to express the cause (*hetumhi karaṇavacanaṃ*). For by that which has become the cause, there arises the aforementioned capacity for the contacts of pleasure and pain.
By the phrase "just so," he recalls the statement: "according to its strength, [whether] a single part of the body or the entire body."
Thus, by means of this mode of pervading established through a metaphorical application (*phalūpacāra*) to oneself. "Of these" refers to pleasure and so forth.
By the phrase "pervading is simply their coarse manifestation," he shows the meaning of pervading for these [feelings] in its primary, non-metaphorical sense.
"Possessing both" means possessing pleasure and pain, or joy and grief; or else, possessing the locations where there is pervading and non-pervading.
181. Here, "intention" (saṅkappa) refers to that which is stated in the explanatory passages such as "intention is desire" (saṅkappo kāmo).
For in those instances, it is precisely defilement-desire (kilesakāma) that is meant, as in the passage: "A man's desire is the passion of intention" (saṅkapparāgo purisassa kāmo), and so forth.
As for object-desire (vatthukāma), it is called "intention" because it is intended and conceived in various ways; it is not, however, applied thought (vitakka). This is the point here.
The meaning has already been stated. However, in order to show the meaning by way of applied thought (*vitakka*), the passage beginning with “That too indeed” is stated in the *Ṭīkā*.

If it is argued that even there the same meaning as before is intended, then the particle *pi* (too/also) would be redundant in its sense of "conjoining," and the phrase “because of the arising from intimacy with the defilements” could not be said;
furthermore, later on he will say, “By the mention of ill-will (*byāpāda*), he shows the applied thought of ill-will.”

The intention is that "defiled desire" (kilesakāma) is distinguished because it is associated with defilements (kilesasampayutta). Regarding the phrase "bound to sense-desires" (kāmapaṭibaddhā), it should be understood that here the term "desire" (kāma) includes both objective sense-objects (vatthukāma) and sensual passion. 182.
"Arising in both places" means arising in both [categories]: among sentient beings and among formations (saṅkhāra); thus, there is the mode of a sentient being and the mode of a formation.

Or it arises by way of grasping both aspects of the object. In order to show that the distinction of the courses of action (*kamma-patha*) and the destruction of the courses of action constitute the "breaking of the courses of action," the phrase beginning with “by association with covetousness” (*abhijjhā-saṃyogena*) was stated.
Similarly, the construction is that it shows the thought of cruelty (*vihiṃsā-vitakka*) by means of cruelty.
And the meaning of “by cruelty” (*vihiṃsāya*) is “by the term ‘cruelty’. [This occurs] according to possibility, by way of killing living beings (*pāṇātipāta*) and so forth.
By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), taking what is not given, false speech, slander, harsh speech, and idle chatter are included. By the "all...

[passage], it refers to the desire-element and the renunciation-element as they are grasped by their respective factors. "Two by two" refers to the elements of ill-will and cruelty, and the elements of non-ill-will and non-cruelty.
With the words "But 'here'... and so forth, [the author] shows that there is no confusion between defilement and purification, nor is there any undesirable consequence.
Through the method of contrast (*byatirekamukhena*), he establishes the very same meaning as previously stated by means of vision (*dassanena*).
The commentary on the Suttanta-bhājaniya is finished.
2. Commentary on the Abhidhamma-bhājaniya.
183. Since the word *visesa* (distinction) carries both the sense of being "exclusive" (*āveṇika*) and the sense of "excellence" (*atisaya*), both of these are shown by the statement:
“It is not shared with other persons, yet it is shared with all visible forms such as blue and so forth.

For a designation can be made on the basis of an exclusive cause, as in “the sound of a drum” or “a sprout of barley”; and it can also be made on the basis of an excellent cause, as in [the description of the knowledge that] “of past, future, and present undertakings of kamma...”
“He understands result as it really is according to its basis and its cause. Thus, the meaning is precisely that of the word *dhātu*.
For the meaning expressed by the term *dhātu* is illuminated by the prefix (*upa-sagga*).

The distinction between the meanings of "differentiation" (*vidhāna*) and "sustaining" (*dhāraṇa*), which is not evident in the former [definition], is made clear here. Parts (*bhāgā*) are components (*avayavā*) characterized by dissimilarity and possessing distinct natures; [the term refers] to those.

As for their occurrence: the functional mind-element (*kiriya-manodhātu*) is related to the resultant mind-element (*vipāka-manodhātu*) by way of decisive support (*upanissaya*); the resultant mind-element is related to the resultant mind-consciousness-element (*vipāka-manoviññāṇa-dhātu*) by way of contiguity (*anantara*) and so forth;

and all others are related to the latter solely by way of decisive support. Furthermore, the mental-object element (*dhammadhātu*), whether consisting of feeling and so on, is related to mind-consciousness by way of co-nascence (*sahajāta*) and so forth when it is co-nascent, and by way of contiguity and so forth when it is not co-nascent; it is also related by way of decisive support, object (*ārammaṇa*), and so forth.

“Condition”: in this way, the causal relationship of the mind-element (manodhātu) and the mental-object-element (dhammadhātu) toward mind-consciousness (manoviññāṇa) should be applied according to their respective possibilities.
Since the mind that has become a door is also called “mind-element” in the Sutta, he says, “or by way of the mind that has become a door.
The connection is that the causal relationship of that mind-element toward mind-consciousness should be applied according to its respective possibility.

"By the previous method" is a qualification because the second method has already been analyzed by way of the inferior triad (*hīnattika*). "And of the various elements, such as the eye-element (*cakkhudhātu*)," is the connection [of the phrase].
For there are not two mind-consciousness-elements (*manoviññāṇadhātu*) in the demonstration of the division of the eighteen elements; this is the intended meaning.

The demonstration of the analysis of the aggregates (*khandha*), bases (*āyatana*), elements (*dhātu*), and faculties (*indriya*) by way of summary (*saṅkhepa*) and so forth is because these [categories] comprise the majority of the phenomena to be fully understood (*pariññeyya-dhamma*). This concludes the teaching on the truths (*sacca-desanā*).
However, because it was already extremely concise, [the details] were omitted here.

The passage beginning with "of that which is devoid of a living being" (nijjīvassa) and so forth is stated because the teaching on the elements (dhātu-desanā) is intended specifically to illustrate the emptiness of sentient beings (sattasuññatā).
It is said by way of the intention that the former method may also apply to other elements that occur in sequence; thus, [it says] "or the mind-element alone," and so forth.

The second method has been stated. In that context, although there is no state of being a precursor or a follower, even in the absence of any intentionality regarding precursors and followers, the mind-element (*manodhātu*) is described as being like a precursor and a follower solely by virtue of its immediate antecedent time and its immediate subsequent time.
By the phrase “because it is incapable of occurring without grasping another [object],” this demonstrates the absolute dependence of consciousness upon an object (*sārammaṇatā*).
This refutes the doctrine of consciousness (*viññāṇavāda*) as it has been propounded thus: "Consciousness arises by itself, manifesting as blue and so forth, even without an object.

184. The construction is as follows: "Of those belonging to one and various continua" means of the doors belonging to one continuum—that is, belonging to an undivided continuum—and of the objects belonging to various continua—that is, belonging to divided continua.
"Being of one and various kinds" means because the eye and so forth are each of a single kind.
Because the objects are of many kinds, such as blue and so forth, there is a distinction in the terminology used for the eye, visible forms, and so on;

this is done to show the specific point that even a single factor, such as the eye, serves as a condition for consciousness, whereas visible forms and the rest must be combined in their multiplicity. But what is the reason [for this]?
Is it that even a single factor such as the eye is a condition for consciousness, whereas factors such as visible forms are always multiple?

It is because of the distinction in their mode of being conditions. For the eye is a condition for eye-consciousness by way of the conditions of support (*nissaya*), pre-existence (*purejāta*), faculty (*indriya*), and dissociation (*vippayutta*);

yet it acts as a condition only through its actual presence, since consciousness exists when the eye exists and does not exist when it is absent. Therefore, the eye is its condition by way of presence (*atthi*) and non-disappearance (*avigata*).
"It is said that it is a condition. Its state of being a support (nissayatā) should not be understood as clinging by way of a single part, because it is formless;
rather, it is by way of its existence being bound to that [support], like students, subjects, or men in relation to teachers, kings, or lords.
And the other conditions should be understood according to their respective specific characteristics. Furthermore, this state of being a condition does not exist in only one [of the factors].
In order to show that even a single eye serves as a condition for eye-consciousness, the singular expression "dependent on the eye" (*cakkhuñca paṭicca*) was employed in the Pāḷi.
As for visible form, although— like the eye— it acts as a condition by way of the conditions of pre-existence, presence, and non-disappearance, it does so prior [to the arising of consciousness].
Because it is helpful precisely at the moment it has arisen and exists; nevertheless, it becomes a condition only when multiple [factors] are combined, by way of being an object (*ārammaṇa*).

For that consciousness which occurs discerning a causal phenomenon—whether it be its intrinsic nature or a merely conceptualized mode—and while other things also possess the status of conditions, it [is distinguished] because of its own nature of having an object.
Because it is that which must be relied upon by whatever [consciousness] is incapable of occurring without support, due to being the cause for its occurrence by clinging to it,

it is called an "object" (*ārammaṇa*) since it is to be resorted to (*ālambanīya*). Since consciousness acquires the condition of an object in proportion to the apprehension of the object's intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*),
therefore, when eye-consciousness occurs having taken visible form as its object, it occurs only while making manifest that very intrinsic nature of the object.

And for him, whose functioning is dependent on the sense faculties, the perception of the objective field’s own nature does not occur merely by way of the color of one or two *kalāpas*, nor even by way of the color of a few *kalāpas*;
rather, it occurs by way of the color that has entered the range of the senses in accordance with mental application (*ābhoga*).
Thus, showing that many forms indeed serve as conditions for consciousness through their collective operation, the Blessed One said: "In regard to forms..."
He indicated this by using the plural form "and [the others].
But as for what was stated—"The visible-form base is a condition, by way of object-condition, for the eye-consciousness element and for the states associated with it"—how is that so?
That too refers to whatever kind of visible-form base serves as an object-condition for eye-consciousness.
It was said with reference to exactly that. But what kind [of object] is it? "Aggregated" (samudita) is the meaning clearly evident here.

And having established this, what some say—that "eye-consciousness and the rest have the act of perceiving as their object by way of perceiving the sense-base (āyatana), not by way of perceiving the substance (dravya)"—is indeed logical.
Nor should the status of having an aggregate as its object (samudāyārammaṇatā) be suspected in this case.
Because there is no enjoyment of the collection as a whole, the color-phenomena (vaṇṇadhammā) that have come together serve as the object-condition (ārammaṇapaccaya).
But how can those that are individually incapable become an object when combined? Is it not the case that the blind, who are unable to see individually, do not see when combined?
This is not an absolute rule, for those who are individually incapable [of carrying] are capable [of doing so] in tasks such as carrying a palanquin when combined.
