Because of this seeing: since it is impossible to grasp the individual color of the hair and so forth in the place where they reside, yet it is possible to grasp them when they are gathered together in that very same place, their collective functioning (*saṃhaccakāritā*) is even more clearly evident.
By this, objections such as whether the object of eye-consciousness is a single atom or a collection thereof are refuted.
It should be understood that this same method applies to the passages beginning with “dependent on the ear and sounds,” and so forth.

Thus, the meaning is obtained as follows: by the word “also” (*api*) in the phrase “by the mind-element also” (*manodhātuyāpi*), not only is the mind-consciousness-element (*manoviññāṇadhātu*)—which concludes with the impulsion (*javana*)—included, but rather the life-continuum (*bhavaṅga*) and the registration (*tadārammaṇa*) states are also included.
In this way, too, the meaning is obtained; that is, it is possible.

"When this is so" means when, through the occurrence of the mind-element (*manodhātu*), there is the demonstration of the nature of mind-consciousness-element (*manoviññāṇadhātu*) for those mental states occurring prior [to it].

Even though the mind has the state of having come into being, there is certainly no undesirable consequence (*pasaṅga*) of the mind-element becoming the mind-consciousness-element, because it is precisely by virtue of its own specific nature that it becomes the mind-consciousness-element.
Because it has already been demonstrated. Now, he makes that same meaning even more evident with the passage beginning, "The five consciousness-elements and the mind-element.
"By way of a dissimilar nature" means by way of a nature different from the five consciousness-elements.

"And by way of the place of arising" means by way of the specific places of arising delimited by the mind-element, the functional mind-consciousness-element, and so forth. Now, [he explains] the inclusion as a unity.

In order to show that the aforementioned meaning can occur even without [the specific conditions], it is said: “Even when not brought forward,” and so forth. Therein, “by way of generality” means by way of similarity.

“Of that” refers to the consciousness that has arisen immediately after the life-continuum (bhavaṅga). “Because the state of mind-consciousness-element is not established” means because the state of mind-element (manodhātu) is not established;
for it is not the case that [consciousness] arises as mind-consciousness-element, ceases, and then—immediately thereafter—[another arises].

The statement, “Cognition arises... [and so on]... the corresponding mind-consciousness element,” establishes that the consciousness arisen immediately after the life-continuum (bhavaṅga) possesses the nature of the mind-element (manodhātu).
For once the nature of the mind-element is established, it follows that this [subsequent consciousness] serves as its successor; such is the intended meaning.
As for the statement illustrating the nature of the mind-consciousness element regarding the consciousness that has arisen as the mind-consciousness element:
One might ask: "Since such a mind-element (manodhātu) would also be shown to be nothing other than the mind-consciousness-element (manoviññāṇadhātu), how could it be excluded [from that category]?
To this he says: "For that which is raised as an objection cannot itself be the solution.
Having thus kept in mind the objection that five-door adverting (pañcadvārāvajjana) would likewise incur the status of being the mind-consciousness-element, [he responds].

He said, “Of the mind-element as well,” and so forth. The specific nature (sabhāva) distinguished by the five consciousnesses and the mind-element is the specific nature of the five consciousnesses...

[etc. ...by way of that. Regarding “of the death-moment, rebirth-linking, and the life-continuum”: this includes the registration-moment (*tadārammaṇa*) within the category of the life-continuum when it is stated thus.
Alternatively, in the phrase “ending with the impulsion,” the registration-moment should also be understood as included because its object is the same as the object of the impulsion.
For this very reason, he said: “Or by means of the six-door consciousnesses,” and so forth.

It is appropriate to treat it separately; for although adverting (āvajjana) may have visible forms and other objects as its domain, it does not—unlike impulsion (javana)—experience the flavor of the object.

Therefore, in such a case, it must indeed be treated separately. As for the word “and” in “and the mind” (mano ca), it is used in the same way as in expressions such as “dependent on the mind” (manañca paṭicca).
It does not have the sense of "combining," but rather the sense of "distinction" (byatireka) should be understood.
The commentary on the *Abhidhammabhājanīya* is finished.
3. Commentary on the *Pañhapucchaka*.
"By the method stated below": because when the limited-object status and so forth of the dharma-element and the mind-consciousness-element are being demonstrated by the passage beginning,

"for one who is lustful toward the fifty-five sense-sphere phenomena," the meaning thereof has been explained in the *Khandhavibhaṅga-vaṇṇanā* and other works by the method beginning, "having made each respective aggregate a single phenomenon by way of the matter associated with the arising of consciousness."
The commentary on the Section of Questions is finished.
The commentary on the Analysis of the Elements is finished. 4.
Analysis of the Truths (Saccavibhaṅga).
1. Commentary on the Suttanta-bhājaniya: Explanation of the Summary (Uddesa) 189.
There is nothing apart from the Truths, because [the teaching] proceeds by way of demonstrating the cause for both occurrence and cessation, as well as for that which is neither.
"It moves among the truths" means it proceeds with the truths as its objective domain; for a teaching has as its domain the meaning that is to be taught.
"It moves among these" means it proceeds among these Noble Truths by way of accomplishing functions such as full understanding (*pariññā*).
To make it clearer, he shows that the essential nature of the meaning—described as "consisting of virtue, concentration, and wisdom"—is taken as the agent of the act of moving.

“Of what nature is it? he asks. “By way of that designation” means by way of its metaphorical application. By this, he shows that the Teaching (sāsana) is, in the primary sense, the very nature of the meaning (atthasabhāva), while in a figurative sense, it is the nature of the words (vacanasabhāva).

“Having that nature” means having the nature of suffering and so forth. “Not having the nature of something else” means having a real nature by way of being oppressive and so forth. “Devoid of other modes” means...
It is devoid of such aspects as non-affliction and so forth. "In two ways" means by way of the suffering of suffering (*dukkhadukkhatā*) and by way of being the cause thereof.
The fever of the defilements such as lust is the burning of the defilements. Causing the continuum not to expand is the harming of the person.

"Its own sharpness" refers to the quality of being painful and sharp by its very own intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*) as a conditioned phenomenon. "By its own essence alone" means by its very own intrinsic nature.

By the seeing of the origin as a massed-together state, of the path as being free from the torment of defilements, and of cessation as being subject to no change, the respective meanings of suffering—namely, being conditioned, tormented, and subject to change—are made manifest. Therefore it is said:
"The other [meanings] are modes of manifestation through the seeing of origin, path, and cessation, respectively. "Pervading" means throughout existence (*bhava*) and so forth.
And having spread out among various objects. Because roots have multiple meanings, after stating that "ūhana" means "piling up," he further clarifies that meaning as "the production of suffering.

For even in the single-aggregate existence (*ekavokāra-bhava*), suffering is produced as a heap because it is a collection of many phenomena, let alone in the four- or five-aggregate existences. And here, the sense of pervading—
The word *āyūhana* should be understood as having the sense of a synthesis, formed by adding the letter *y* to its root-form. Regarding the term *nidadāti*:
because it is the absolute cause of suffering, he says "this is that suffering" and so forth, showing that it produces [suffering] as if pointing it out.
Just as the source of a disease is revealed by the sight of the disease itself, so too... [the connection... is made manifest. ... *Saṃyoga*... etc.
"By seeing": the meaning is that the state of conjunction (*saṃyoga*) is revealed by the seeing of cessation (*nirodha*), which has the nature of disjunction (*visaṃyoga*);
and the state of impediment (*palibodha*) is revealed by the seeing of the path (*magga*), which has the nature of deliverance (*niyyāna*).

"Those": the states of conjunction and impediment. "In this": when this [object] exists as the objective support (*ārammaṇa*). "Seclusion from arising" (*samudaya-viveka*) is the sense of seclusion (*vivekaṭṭha*). And cessation is so called because it has the nature of the destruction of craving (*taṇhākkhaya*).
It is secluded from its origin; therefore, by seeing that the origin is not secluded, the meaning of seclusion of cessation is revealed.

Furthermore, by seeing that even the Path—which is the cause for the attainment of Nibbāna—is conditioned due to its having conditions, the unconditioned meaning of cessation, which is without conditions, is revealed. Likewise, [it is revealed] through the nature of being subject to death.

By the passage beginning with “seclusion” (*vivekā*), he demonstrates this meaning: that for one who sees suffering perishing, the sense of the deathless (*amataṭṭha*) becomes manifest in cessation, which is by nature not subject to death.

The others [the remaining three meanings] are [manifested] through the vision of the origin and the vision of suffering. Here, through the vision of the origin, the sense of cause (*hetuṭṭha*) becomes manifest:

“This is not the cause for the attainment of Nibbāna; rather, this is the cause. Likewise, [through the vision of suffering, the sense of peace becomes manifest] regarding that which is supremely profound...
The meaning of vision is manifested by the seeing of cessation— which is extremely subtle and difficult to perceive— just as the eye’s function is manifested by seeing subtle forms;

whereas the meaning of predominance of the path is manifested by the seeing of suffering, just as the majesty of a lord is manifested by seeing the multitude of people afflicted by various diseases and the poor.
In order to show these [factors], such as the cause-condition (*hetu-paccaya*) and so forth, by way of their essential nature, it is said: "Therein, by way of cutting off impediments," and so on.
Therein, "by way of cutting off impediments" means by way of abandoning the origin (*samudaya*). It is because of the statement, "states having the Path as their dominant" (*maggādhipatino dhammā*);
for although jhānas and so forth do possess the status of being objects of dominance (*ārammaṇādhipati*), they are not called "states having jhāna as their dominant" (*jhānādhipatino dhammā*).

Such things as these were not stated; rather, it was simply said, "states dominated by the Path. Therefore, the state of being an object-dominant (ārammaṇādhipati) for the factors of the Path is preeminent.
Hence he said: "Or, specifically, the factors of the Path become object-dominants.
That is their mode—namely, the mode of those states that proceed by way of reviewing the factors of the Path after having treated them with reverence.
The aspect (ākāra) known as the objective-predominance condition is the meaning of predominance for the Path. However, the former meaning of predominance was stated by way of co-nascent predominance.

The phrase "the meaning of what is to be fully understood" (abhisametabbaṭṭha) speaks of the state of having to penetrate precisely those meanings already mentioned, such as oppression and so forth, by bringing them together into one; by this, it shows that the word *abhisamaya* has the sense of an object (kamma).
"Abhisamaya" means knowledge (*ñāṇa*). "Mode of occurrence" (*pavatti-ākāra*) refers to the specific mode of thorough understanding (*parijānana*) and so forth.
For that [mode] is established through non-delusion at the moment of the Path (*magga*), and subsequently it becomes manifest through review (*paccavekkhaṇā*) and other such processes.

Furthermore, the third method is shown by treating the mode (*ākāra*) as an "object" (*attha*) because it is to be reached (*araṇīya*) by knowledge. It is also shown by way of the classification of objects through oppression (*pīḷana*) and so forth.
There is a division according to the object, such as "perception of form" (*rūpasaññā*) and "perception of sound" (*saddasaññā*).

[The prefix *saṃ-*] signifies that which is loathsome, censurable, and unsubstantial. By means of the phrases "coming together" (*samāgama*) and so forth, he explains the prefix *saṃ-*'s function of indicating the sense of conjunction through both positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya* and *vyatireka*).
In cases such as "arisen" (*uppanna*) and "manifested" (*udita*), it refers to the word *panna* alone.
Because the meaning of "arising" (uppatti-attha) is not found when the word *ita* is employed, whereas it is found when the word *u* is employed, [the commentator] says:
"In this case as well, 'thus arisen' (*evam uppannaṃ*) means 'arisen' (*uditaṃ*)," thereby indicating that [the prefix *ud-*] signifies the sense of arising.
"Used separately" means used without the words *āgata* and *ita*. "Possessing its root" (*sadhātukaṃ*) means possessing the root contained within itself. For that very reason...

These are called "prefixes. "The state of being secluded from suffering" means the condition of being free from suffering. "In the cessation" refers to Nibbāna. "Having set aside" means having set aside by way of qualifying it with the term "non-arising.
"The conditionality of cessation" means the state of being an object-condition for the Path that is cessation.
"By way of the person, the realization, and the state of the dhamma" means by way of the person, the dhamma, and the state of that which is to be realized.

"Fruits" refers to the noble fruit (*ariyaphala*). "Of that" should be understood as the state of being the practice for the attainment of the cessation of suffering—which constitutes the final goal—and for the attainment of the cessation of suffering which constitutes the clear realization (*abhisamaya*).

"At the time of penetration" refers to the conventional designations such as "Buddha" and so forth in their direct sense; thus he says, "occurring at the time of penetration. "Precisely for that reason" means precisely because it has been revealed by that [penetration].

"The state of being its cause" means that birth and so forth are causes of suffering by way of being its basis (*adhiṭṭhāna*), not by way of being its source (*pabhava*) as is the case with the Truth of Origination.
The state of being oppressed by arising and passing away is the suffering inherent in formations (*saṅkhāradukkhatā*). "Merely occurring" means *pavatti* (occurrence).

Thus. "Function is the essence" (*rasa*) shows that the meaning of essence is the state of being a function. "In regard to proceeding and ceasing" (*pavatti-nivattīsu*) is the locative case used for specification.
"Unchangeability" (*avikāratā*) is the absence of change, which is permanence.
"Of the mirage, illusion, and self" (*marīci-māyā-attānam*) refers to the knowledge of the noble ones (*ariyānaṃ ñāṇassa*), namely, the knowledge of the Noble Ones (*ariya-ñāṇassa*). By that...
The knowledge that proceeds in accordance with the knowledge of the Noble Ones' path is also included. Therefore he said, "of one who grasps it as it truly is," and so forth.

"Of these" refers to the two knowledges: penetration and reviewing. Therein, for the knowledge of penetration, the state of being penetrable constitutes its objective domain (gocara), while for the other [reviewing], it constitutes its object (ārammaṇa).
Whether it be the state of being penetrable or the state of being an object, it pertains to the knowledge of penetration.
The state of being a *gocara* (range) belongs to the former, while the state of being an *ārammaṇa* (object) belongs to the latter.

Because the state of being the producer of the affliction (*bādhaka*) has been separately grasped as the "state of being the origin of the affliction" (*bādhakappabhava*), craving (*taṇhā*) is not grasped here by way of its state of being the affliction itself;
this is because [the text] intends to clarify the causes of occurrence and non-occurrence without confusing them. And having done so, even in the *Abhidhammabhājanīya*:

This explanation of the meaning is indeed appropriate. Anticipating the objection that, even so, the restriction "suffering alone is the oppressor" would be untenable and would entail the consequence [of suffering] being the origin [of suffering], he says:

"Or like birth and the rest," and so forth. He says, "By the determination of the sense of 'oppressor' in both ways," because there is a restriction regarding both the state of being an oppressor and the act of oppressing. For just as... [the state of being an oppressor].
“Certainty regarding suffering” means that there is likewise certainty regarding the fact that suffering is oppressive.

Since the state of craving alone as the origin [of suffering] is shown in the *Suttantabhājanīya*, he says “not without craving,” and so forth, in order to demonstrate the restriction by way of craving.
This is the commentary on the *Suttantabhājanīya*. By the phrase “without wholesome states,” and so forth, he expresses the predominance of craving as the cause of suffering.
For in this way, by serving as the cause for the diversity of karma, it specifically becomes a cooperative condition (*sahakārikāraṇa*) for karma.
"In both ways by way of necessity" means that the Path alone is the outlet (*niyyāna*), and the outlet alone is the Path; thus, it is by way of these two kinds of necessity.
"Truth of speech" (*vacīsacca*) refers to truthful speech and the volition (*cetanā*) that originates it; therefore he says, "the truth of abstinence, namely, the abstinence from false speech."
Some, however, say that "the truth of abstinence is abstinence through undertaking. Even for them, the truth of abstinence is not merely the act of undertaking;
rather, it is non-deception regarding what has been undertaken. And since that is the truthfulness of one's promise, it is indeed the abstinence from false speech.

Therefore he said: "For the word 'truth' is not conventionally established in reference to other types of abstinence. Even when there is an understanding of suffering and its origin, only to the extent that...
The cultivation of wisdom for the purpose of realizing cessation and the path is preeminently concerned with the meaning of the latter two truths;
showing that this realization is the cause for the absence of dispute, as elucidated in the Sutta, he says, “But for him...,” and so forth.
“There is no possibility” means there is no ground for establishing one’s own doctrine. By the very acquisition of a new existence...
It is said, "attainment, presence, and being first," because the attainment and manifestation of birth and so forth for sentient beings occurs.
Alternatively, their status as "first" and so on should be understood according to the sequence of the Blessed One’s teaching itself. The phrase "by means of full understanding, etc.
refers to full knowledge (*pariññā*), abandoning (*pahāna*), realization (*sacchikiriyā*), and cultivation (*bhāvanā*); furthermore, this is an ablative construction used in relation to another word.

The function of knowledge of the Dhamma (*dhammañāṇakicca*) is the function of awakening to phenomena as they truly are (*sabhāvadhammāvabodhakicca*). By stating that "the things to be fully understood (*pariññeyya*) and so forth are limited to this much," he shows that there is nothing further to be known beyond this.
Hearing [the teaching] that is appropriate and fitting for the nature of the Noble Truths of suffering and so forth, or that has come down through the succession of teachers.
*Anussava* (tradition) is [knowledge] according to what has been heard.

*Ākāraparivitakka* (reflection on aspects) is the grasping of the common mode of being, such as hardness in the case of touch, or impermanence and so forth, in other ways than through hearing. *Diṭṭhinijjhānakkhanti* (acceptance of views after reflection) is the finding pleasure in, and the contemplation by means of, wisdom—which consists of seeing—of the aspect as it was reflected upon, that wisdom being termed "view.
Like the sun with its radiance, one touches and realizes cessation.
It destroys the darkness of the defilements. It is said, “O monks, he who sees suffering,” and so forth, that one sees all four truths.
“Seeing at different times” refers to a gradual realization (*nānābhisamaya*). “Seers of one” means those who see a single truth.

“It should not be construed” means that if it were construed [with the previous phrase], then since seeing all would be subsequent to the other forms of seeing, it would follow that there is no cessation of seeing.

Furthermore, regarding the distinct realization of the truths, one would fall into the error of abandoning only a portion of the three fetters and so forth—which are to be abandoned by the first path and the others—through the vision of suffering and the rest.

If that were the case, it would follow that there is a state of being on the path of stream-entry only partially, and immediately thereafter, a state of being a stream-enterer only partially with respect to the fruit that is to be attained; therefore, there is no distinct realization of the truths.
It is not tenable. Just as a multiple simultaneous realization (nānābhisamaya) is not tenable, so too is the realization of objects (ārammaṇābhisamaya).

For if the realization of the Four Truths were intended to occur by way of making [the truths] the object, then since the Path does not itself take itself as its own object, the realization of the Truths would be incomplete.
If it is argued that the Path is taken as an object by another Path, and thus it is complete—this being the case:
If one path were taken as the object by another path, and that [other] by yet another, there would be an infinite regress;

therefore, it is not logical that the realization of the Four Truths (*catusaccābhisamaya*) occurs through the penetration of an object. Rather, it is logical precisely according to the method already stated.

Furthermore, the knowledge of the path (*maggañāṇa*) consists in the cultivation of delimitation and eradication, having taken as its object that which is to be delimited and that which is to be eradicated.

It is not appropriate [to take anything else as an object] because it has not emerged from that; rather, only Nibbāna, which has emerged from all conditioned things (*saṅkhata*), is appropriate as an object.

The view of non-causality (*ahetukadiṭṭhi*) is included by the mention of the view of non-action (*akiriyadiṭṭhi*), considering that in the ultimate sense (*paramatthato*) activity is simply the operation of causes.

"Sets in motion" means it engages, or it is the cause for setting [the world] in motion. "Withdraws" means it retracts, causes it to go to destruction, or serves as the cause for liberation through such states as dissolution (*palokatā*). "From the primary" means from the natural state, which is also called "inefficacious" (*abyatta*).
“Time creates beings; Time destroys people; Time keeps watch while others sleep;
for Time is indeed difficult to overcome. Such is the doctrine of those who maintain the theory of time (*kālavādin*).
[They argue: “The sharpness of the thorn, the roundness of the wood-apple fruit and so forth, and the various forms of the bodies of animals, birds, reptiles, and so on...”
The proponents of intrinsic nature (sabhāvavādins) maintain: "By whom were such states as consciousness and so forth caused?

They are established by their very own nature; thus it is with everything, for herein no one has the power of free will. The proponents of necessity (niyativādins) maintain: "The world is fixed, like a cut thread or an unbreakable gem; herein there is no human effort whatsoever."
“Whatever proceeds by chance, whatever ceases by chance,
whatever pleasure and pain [arise] by chance— therefore, people desire whatever they wish. Thus, those who maintain such a doctrine,
known as the proponents of chance (yadicchāvādin), and the proponents of fortuitous origination (adhiccasamuppattivādin) are included here among the proponents of inherent nature (sabhāvavāda).
Thus they should be understood as being included [within the category of eternalism]. He says, "The world proceeds by means of atoms," with reference to the Ājīvaka doctrine;

for that is a grasping at what is not the cause. However, the Kaṇāda doctrine asserts the occurrence and cessation of the world through the conjunction and disjunction of atoms under the influence of the Lord's will.
"The non-occurrence of the primary [cause]" means its non-transformation into the state of the Great One (mahat) and so forth, its lack of manifestation.

Or: "I am one, nature is another"—when, through such knowledge of the distinction between the natural self (*pakati-purisa*) and others, the undifferentiated grasping of one's own pleasure, pain, and delusion has been ceased, it is said that the exertion (*padhāna*) does not proceed according to the aforementioned method; this is liberation (*vimokkha*), say the followers of Kapila (the Sāṃkhyas).
By the word "etc. (*ādi*), the inclusion of such [views] as proximity to Mahābrahmā and conjunction (*saṃyoga*) should be understood.

"Unity" (*ekatta*) means from the state of being one; thus, even though it is one, it is spoken of [as such]. "Three" refers to the distinction of their functions. "Those" refers to the virtues of right speech and so forth.

Since the manifestation of desire occurs by way of desire even while conforming to conviction, the basis of psychic power consisting of desire (*chandiddhipāda*) is mentioned together with the faculty of faith (*saddhindriya*) and the power of faith (*saddhābala*).
At such a time, it is helpful for concentration through the cultivation of the sign of equanimity (*upekkhānimitta*).
Equanimity should be understood as having such functions by way of its association [with other mental factors].
"The state of being a harasser" is due to its nature of striking down by way of withdrawing [the mind].
"The two noble truths" refers to the pair of the truths of origin and the path. "By that very [reason]" refers to the aforementioned words beginning with "suffering."
[This is] precisely because [the term] expresses "that which is to be fully understood" and so forth.

"Inclusion by the first term" refers to the inclusion within the first term of this tetrad by means of the phrase: "suffering, but not a noble truth. "Dependent upon that" refers to the word "suffering" as dependent upon the word "noble truth.

"Inclusion by the fourth term" refers to the inclusion by means of the phrase: "neither suffering nor a noble truth. "The remaining defilements and so forth" refers to the defilements with the exception of craving.

The remaining unwholesome states, the wholesome roots associated with the taints (*sāsava*), and wholesome phenomena associated with the taints—these are indeed described in the *Abhidhamma-bhājanīya* as being "origination" (*samudaya*) by way of their nature as arising, but not as being the Noble Truth of Origination. Therefore, it is said: "Origination, but not the Noble Truth.

As for "the other factors of the path," these refer to right view of the fruit (*phala-sammā-diṭṭhi*) and so forth. Regarding the phrase "by this method," the application here is as follows: there is origination...

There is that which is not a noble truth, there is that which is a noble truth; there is that which is not origination, there is that which is both origination and a noble truth, and there is that which is neither origination nor a noble truth.
Therein, the first term has its meaning already explained. Cessation is a noble truth but not origination;
craving is both origination and a noble truth; the states associated with the path are the fruits of recluseship.
And because that [craving] for the abandoning of which the holy life is lived under the Blessed One does not exist, it is neither origination nor a noble truth.

The other two truths are noble truths; in the sense of being the producer of this or that [suffering], they may be considered origination, but not in the sense of that for the abandoning of which the holy life is lived under the Blessed One. This also applies to the other two tetrads.

The first term has already been explained. Among the remaining ones: the noble truth of the origin (*samudaya-ariyasacca*) is not cessation; the unconditioned element (*asaṅkhata-dhātu*) is both cessation and a noble truth;

the states associated with the path and the fruits of recluseship (*sāmaññaphala*) are not, in the sense of being that for the realization of which the holy life is lived under the Blessed One, either cessation or a noble truth. As for the other two truths:

The noble truth [of cessation] might be subject to cessation by virtue of its nature to cease, but it is not that for the realization of which the holy life is lived under the Blessed One in the sense of suchness (*tathattha*). Likewise, the noble truth of cessation is not the path;

rather, the noble path is both the path and the noble truth. Furthermore, those phenomena associated with the path and the fruits of recluseship (*sāmaññaphala*) are for the sake of whose cultivation [the holy life is lived].
In the Blessed One, the holy life is lived in the sense of suchness; therefore, it is neither the path nor a noble truth.

The other two truths might be the path because they constitute the state of the path as it arises, but they are not that for the sake of which the holy life is lived in the Blessed One in the sense of suchness.
"Peaceful" means the same [as "calm"]. In the same way, for the others as well, the action should be understood as being devoid of an agent;

when that [action] occurs solely through its own conditions, it is merely a conventional expression to say that "the collection of conditions performs the action. This same method applies even to those things that lead to extinction (*nibbuti*).

"Possessing taints" (*sāsavatā*) refers to impurity because of the oozing of the filth of the defilements (*kilesa*). "Of suffering and so forth" refers to suffering, its origin, and the path. "The state of being the origin and so forth" [refers to these].

The connection is as follows: suffering has the nature of both origin and path; origin has the nature of both path and suffering; and the path has the nature of both suffering and origin—but cessation does not have the nature of suffering and so forth.
"Mutual possession" (*aññamaññasamaṅgitā*) refers to the conjunction of suffering and the other truths with one another's individual essences.
"Of craving" (*taṇhāya*) is the locative case used in the sense of a locus. "Of renewed existence" (*punabbhavassa*) refers to that which is designated as renewed existence.

"Of future suffering. "Of those who maintain the doctrine of primordial nature (prakṛti)" refers to the followers of Kapila. "Manifestations" (vikāra) refers to the distinct [evolutes] such as the Great One (mahat) and so forth.

"From manifestation" means from becoming evident, or alternatively, from prior transformation. "And having dissolved back" means that subsequently they have gone to dissolution into primordial nature;

having abandoned their diversity, they are held within in a state of equilibrium as the [unmanifested] factors such as the sattva and so forth. Therefore he said: "They remain in the very state of primordial nature."
“By way of their natural state” means by way of their state of inefficiency. “By way of origination” means by way of the state of being an origin, namely, craving.
Otherwise, ignorance and the other factors associated with it would also be found to have the status of origination.

“Because they are undifferentiated” means because they have reached their natural state through the absence of irregularity. When “mutations” are mentioned in a general sense, they are shown in their specific form by the words “great,” and so forth.
In this context, "Great" (*mahanta*) means one of great intelligence (*mahābuddhi*). For the followers of Kapila (*Kāpila*) designate that very thing as the "Great Resolve" (*mahāajjhāsaya*).
There are six non-specific principles (*aviśeṣa*): the five subtle elements (*tanmātra*), such as form and so forth, and ego-consciousness (*ahaṅkāra*).

There are eleven faculties (*indriya*): the eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, speech, hand, foot, anus, generative organ, and mind. There are five specific elements (*bhūtavisesa*): earth, water, fire, air, and space.
By the phrase “standing in their very natural state,” he explains the meaning of the term “unmanifested. “Sagabbhā” means possessing seeds, that is, not empty.
“In the threads” means in the yarns that serve as the inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*). The same applies to the potsherds. For they declare the cause to be threefold:
the material cause (*upādānakāraṇa*), the instrumental cause (*nimittakāraṇa*), and the inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*). Among these, the spinning wheel, the shuttle, the stick, and so forth—
The material cause (*upādānakāraṇa*) is [the threads]; the weaver is the efficient cause (*nimittakāraṇa*); and the threads are the inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*). Regarding "in two atoms":
this refers to two ultimate atoms (*paramāṇu*), whether they consist of the earth element or the elements of water, fire, and air.

"Producing the conventional expression of 'here'" means that by way of such expressions as "the cloth is here in these threads," "the jar is here in these potsherds," or "the mat is here in these *bīraṇa* grasses," it produces the cognition and linguistic usage of cause and effect.

Through that which constitutes the relationship, the cognitions and conventional expressions regarding existing things arise here. That [inherence] is a relation of inseparable co-existence (*samavāya*) between things established simultaneously, like a cow and its horns.
However, conjunction (*saṃyoga*) is a relation between things established separately, like a tree stump and an army.
The construction is as follows: the triad (*tiaṇuka*)—the fruit—is related to the three atoms by way of inherence, as if it were a single unified entity. Regarding the term "inhering" (*samaveta*):
“Connected as if it were a single unity”—this is the explanation of the meaning.
“Of great magnitude” means a single effect of large dimension, such as the great earth and so forth, which they call a "substantial effect" (*kāriya-dravya*).
Since they consider those very causes by which the substantial effect is initiated to be already included within that [effect], he said: “by those [causes] included within itself.”
"By means of causes. Since the effect is inherent in the cause when there is inherence (*samavāya*), the cause might be considered present in the effect;

however, showing that this is not the case, he says: "Because of the absence of inherence, the cause does not exist in the effect; thus, the effect is empty of causes. Regarding "the distinction of nutriment":

this refers to specific types of nutriment, such as edible food (*kabaḷīkāra-āhāra*) and so forth. Regarding "the distinction of phenomena conditioned by that": this refers to what are comprised of the six bases consisting of the objects of ingestion, ignorance (*avijjā*), and volitional formations (*saṅkhāra*).

The "distinctions of phenomena that serve as conditions" (*tappaccayadhammabhedā*) refers either to the specific phenomena acting as conditions—namely, the nutritive essence (*oja*), the eightfold materiality, feeling, rebirth-linking consciousness, and name-and-form—or to the specific phenomena produced by them. The construction is:
"or by way of objects such as visible forms. "By way of the two vehicles" means by way of the two vehicles of serenity (*samatha*) and insight (*vipassanā*).

Although serenity and insight are indeed conjoined at the moment of the path, just as the designations "emptiness" and so forth apply, so too might the designations "serenity" and "insight" apply to the path by way of its approach; thus he said, "it is stated by way of its approach.
Alternatively, for one whose faculty of wisdom is predominant, the path is insight, while for the other, it is serenity; this is how the meaning should be understood here.
The "arising of concentration" (samādhijāti) is simply the state of being concentrated (samādhāna). "Precisely because of that" means precisely because it is an activity conducive to concentration.
"Having taken up and weighed" means having grasped, as it were, and having deliberated and applied thought (vitakka). "Of the two" refers to right view and right intention.
This is a designation [using a singular] for the sake of brevity, just as in the expressions: "dependent on one aggregate, three aggregates [arise]," or "one great primary element..."
"...dependent on the three great elements.
"To fathom" means to penetrate with knowledge. Its "smoothness" is due to its being impossible to grasp. Its "subtlety" is due to its being graspable by subtle wisdom.
He said, "by the word 'iti' [it means] 'in this sequence,'" intending the sense that "iti" signifies this.
“He shows the sequence of understanding. Regarding the phrase “by such modes,” the meaning signified by the word *evaṃ* (thus) is what is expressed by the word *pakāra* (mode);
thus it is said: “by the word *evaṃ*, he shows the method that serves as the cause for understanding. Alternatively, *iti* has the sense of illustration;
by means of it, he illustrates, by way of referring back, to the various distinctions already mentioned. The word *evaṃ* has the sense of “this”; therefore, [the phrase] is “by such modes.”
"By such benefits," meaning "by such as these.
The commentary on the enumeration is finished.
1. Exposition of the Truth of Suffering (Dukkhasaccaniddesa).
Commentary on the Exposition of Birth (Jātiniddesavaṇṇanā) 190.
By the phrase “In the exposition of birth and so forth,” he explains the meaning of the word “therein.

“The matrix of suffering” refers to the enumeration of the specific types of suffering, such as the suffering of suffering and the others. “In the two phrases” refers to these two phrases: “suffering in a figurative sense” and “suffering in a non-figurative sense.”

"By way of suffering itself" refers to suffering in the primary sense (*nippariyāya-dukkhatā*). "It qualifies the name by its intrinsic nature" shows that it is a designation according to its actual meaning (*anvattha-saññā*). By means of the preceding word *dukkha*, which expresses the suffering of intrinsic nature;
for that [word] qualifies the latter meaning of the suffering of formations (*saṅkhāra-dukkha*) because it functions as a qualifier through the state of delimitation (*avacchedaka-bhāva*).
For that [latter term] must be delimited, since it is common to both what is to be excluded and what is to be grasped.
"Ten" refers to the specific modes such as transformation (*vipariṇāma*) and resolution (*adhiṭṭhāna*).
Here, "conciseness" (*saṅkhepa*) means the condensation of the meaning to be taught; and since this is common to their various divisions, he says:
"Conciseness is the universal" (*sāmañña*). "Having included within" means having made them part of the interior, or having subsumed them. "In both ways" means...
Both in brief and in detail. "Vibhāga" (analysis) is the classification of common portions; thus he says, "The detailed exposition, however, is the distinction.
"Excluding other distinctions" means including other types of analysis. 191.
"In another sense" is a locative expression used in the sense of a genitive, as in "a foundation in all cases"; thus he says, "even in the sense of a genitive."
For the word *aparattha* is thus established. Its establishment, however, is to be understood by the rule: "It is seen [to apply] even by other [suffixes].

And because the word occurs in this way, he said, "Or 'of those, of those,'" etc., demonstrating that what was stated in the Canon (*pāḷi*) according to the masculine gender is shown in the Commentary (*aṭṭhakathā*) according to the locative case.
*Aparassa* means "of another being. The distinction such as "human" and so forth...

Showing that rebirth-existence (*upapattibhava*) is the destination (*gati*), while the aggregates (*khandhā*) characterized by the commonality of being a kṣatriya and so forth—which constitute its specific distinction—are birth (*jāti*), he said, "by way of the five destinations," and so on.
"Grass-form" means a variety of grass;
the meaning is a specific kind of grass. "Thus" (*evaṃ*) is used as an illustration. By that, [he refers to] the aforementioned manner.
First, one refers to the manifestation of consciousness. "Taking that as a basis" means starting from that point.

"Because it makes for the state of a noble one" means because it is the cause of the state of a noble one; for that which performs an action is called a "cause" (*karaṇa*). Alternatively, it is "noble virtue" (*ariyasīla*) because it resembles a noble one;

for even the fourfold purification virtue of the virtuous worldlings (*puthujjanakalyāṇaka*) resembles the virtue of a noble one. "Modifications of mode" refers to the various modifications of modes such as arising and so forth.
"Arising together" (*sahuppādakā*) means the aggregates in the state of arising, accompanied by their origination. "By way of bases" (*āyatanavasena*) means by way of complete or incomplete bases.
"By way of birth-origins" (*yonivasena*) means by way of birth-origins such as egg-born and so forth.

"By each single term alone" means that, just as in the second method, all sentient beings are encompassed by two terms each—such as "birth" and so on—through the distinction of complete or incomplete bases and birth-origins.
Birth has been shown [in the previous context], but it is not so here. Here, however, by means of each single term, all sentient beings are encompassed without distinction.

In both cases—that is, in the former and latter methods—the exposition in terms of "being" (bhāva) alone is appropriate. Regarding the rule for case-endings (*vibhatti*) when [the sense] is not already expressed (*anabhihite*):
the phrase "not expressed" (*nābhihite*) means that production (*nibbatti*) is manifest (*pākaṭā*), that is, clearly evident (*abhivyattā*).
“Of two pairs” means: in the one-aggregate existence (*ekavokāra-bhava*), by way of the sense-base of visible form (*rūpāyatana*) and the sense-base of mental objects (*dhammāyatana*);

in the four-aggregate existence (*catuvokāra-bhava*), by way of the sense-base of mind (*manāyatana*) and the sense-base of mental objects. “The rest” refers to the five-aggregate existence (*pañcavokāra-bhava*). “Of five” means: by way of the sense-bases of eye, ear, mind, visible form, and mental objects.
For these indeed arise at the moment of rebirth in the five-aggregate [existence] within the fine-material realm (*rūpa-bhava*). In the sense-sphere realm (*kāmadhātu*),...
The construction is: "of those arising at the moment of rebirth-linking.

"Of those with deficient or non-deficient faculties" means of beings whose sense-bases (*āyatana*) are incomplete or complete. For the deficiency of the sense-bases must be understood precisely by way of the faculties.
In that regard, for one with deficient faculties, there are seven, nine, ten, or again ten; for the other, by way of eleven sense-bases.
The inclusion should be understood as follows: "Of seven" refers to the seven [bases] by way of the sense bases of body, mind, visible form, odor, flavor, tangible object, and mental phenomena;
for this is said with reference to those born from a womb. "Of nine" refers to the nine [bases] excluding the sense bases of eye, ear, and sound;
for this is said with reference to the blind and the deaf. "Of ten" refers to the ten [bases] excluding the sense bases of eye and sound. Again, "of ten" [refers to the same].

[This refers to] those [objects] excluding sound from the ear-sphere. These two [terms], "blind" and "deaf," are stated by way of the blind and the deaf respectively. "Of the eleven" means excluding sound. "The state of being suffering" (*taṃ-dukkha-bhāvo*) refers to the state of suffering in a figurative sense (*pariyāya-dukkha-bhāvo*).
Therein, "by way of preventing its arising" means by way of prohibiting its production in such things as blue and red lotuses, that is, by speaking of its non-existence.
"In the cause for the arising of suffering" means in the place where suffering arises, which serves as the cause for the arising of suffering.
Commentary on the Exposition of Death (193).
"Of the breaking up of the aggregates" means of the destruction of the aggregates. "It" refers to that breaking up of the aggregates.
"The cutting off of the continuity" means the absolute severance of the continuity. "By way of its state" means by way of the state of conventional death. "By way of being a part of it" means...

"Because it is a constituent part of that [life-faculty]" means it is stated as "the name of that very thing" for the sake of non-confusion, since there is a severance of the entire continuity of the life-faculty produced by a single kamma.

Indeed, conventional death is the death at the exhaustion of birth; furthermore, that death at the exhaustion of birth is twofold: death by external agency (*upakkama-maraṇa*) and natural death (*sarasamaraṇa*).
Therein, natural death is also twofold: death through the exhaustion of the lifespan (*āyukkhaya-maraṇa*) and death through the exhaustion of merit (*puññakkhaya-maraṇa*).
It is twofold. In this way, their status as being a part of that [same category] should be understood. Of these, death through external effort is untimely death;
death by its own nature is timely death. Because beings are separated from the aggregates of the state of attainment (sampattibhava) by means of death, it is said:
"He separates them from the aggregates of the state of attainment."

“Kāraṇattha” means the sense of root (mūla). For a root is called “the beginning” (ādi), as in such passages as: “And what is the beginning of wholesome states? Virtue that is well-purified and view that is straight. Therefore he said: “The meaning is ‘having the cutting of the joints and bonds as its root.

Because such causal activity contains within it the activity of the result, it is stated as “included. For the bringing about [of ruin] by those who bring it about is accomplished together with the offense to be brought about. Commentary on the Description of Sorrow (Soka-niddesa-vaṇṇanā)
194. That which leads to or brings about happiness is *hita*, meaning the cause of happiness.
"Misfortune regarding wealth" (*bhogabyasana*) refers to a specific meaning based on the words *bhoga* and *byasana*; likewise for "misfortune regarding virtue" (*sīlabyasana*).

"Specific compound" (*samāsavisesa*) refers to a specific type of compound formed through grammatical coreferentiality (*samānādhikaraṇa*), such as "misfortune that is indeed disease" (*rogoyeva byasanaṃ*) or "misfortune that is indeed wrong view" (*diṭṭhi eva byasanaṃ*). [Examples include] food, drink, clothing, vehicles, and so forth.

"Enjoyment" (*bhoga*) is intended here in the sense of that which is to be enjoyed, and it exists as a collection of phenomena (*dhammasamūha*). "Their destruction" refers to the calamities of relatives and wealth;

since these must be designated by way of their modified states, they are mere designations (*paññattimatta*). That which is called "fully accomplished" (*parinipphanna*) is the pentad of aggregates (*khandhapañcaka*).

Because it does not possess its own intrinsic nature (*asabhāva*), designation is "not fully accomplished" (*aparinipphanna*) and is also "unproduced" (*anipphanna*); thus it is said: "the state of being not fully accomplished."
“Having had this in mind, he said they are ‘unproduced’ (anipphanna). For a designation (paṇṇatti) is not produced by anyone.

Furthermore, in order to show that the conventional term ‘unproduced’ is also applied elsewhere to things that are not fully produced (aparinipphanna), he said: ‘Only because of their being unproduced,’ and so forth.
While it is true that here ‘unproduced’ is stated as ‘not fully produced,’ the term ‘produced’ (nipphanna) does not refer exclusively to what is fully produced, nor does it refer to everything.”
Showing that it is a dhamma possessing intrinsic nature (sabhāvadhamma), he said, “And in the Khandhavibhaṅga,” and so forth. The connection is that “its being produced” has been stated.
This is because, although it possesses intrinsic nature, its non-produced state is not produced by anything.
“Constricted thinking” refers to the occurrence of dissatisfaction toward the object, due to its being the opposite of joy and mental pleasure, and due to its association with hatred.
*Antonijjhāna* is "internal brooding," which is the act of brooding (*cintana*) by way of burning away one's own support.

*Kukkucca* is remorse (*vippaṭisāra*), which consists of mental distress regarding one's own deeds done or left undone—whether skillful or unskillful—even though it possesses the nature of subsequent grieving.
The distinction between these two should be understood as follows: *antonijjhāna* as described above is sorrow (*soka*).

“‘At the moment of the impulsion in the mind-door’ (manodvāra-javana-kkhaṇe) is said with reference to clear, sustained contemplation; however, the other [type] is indeed found even in the impulsions of the five doors.
Therefore he says ‘body-consciousness, etc. ‘Of grief’ (domanassassa) means of grief in the mode of sorrowing, or of that which has various pathways even in the mode of sorrowing.
For that too is simply suffering. ‘Otherwise’ (aññathā) means in the mind-door impulsion.”
...thus it is taken. "Therein" means among those [states] having the body as their basis and those belonging to the mind-door.
195. Commentary on the Description of Lamentation (*parideva*):
"Making a sound of wailing" means having wailed; the meaning is, having lamented. It is the state of agitation in a person.
For whichever being it arises, there is for that being a state of instability. Or, it presents a state of agitation (*sambhama*) that has entered within by making it manifest;
thus, it is "presented as agitation" (*sambhamapaccupaṭṭhāna*).
"Beating with fists and so forth" refers to *muṭṭhipothanā* and the like.
"By which grief": from the suffering previously mentioned, such as "beating one's own body with fists," and so forth. "With that as its cause" means having lamentation as its cause.
Commentary on the Exposition of Suffering and Grief (196–7):

For one overcome by bodily pain, the state of being a necessary condition for bodily pain should be understood at times such as when one employs a practice that brings about similar suffering out of a desire for a remedy. "By this suffering" refers to the suffering of the loss of hands and feet, lack of protection, and so forth.
Commentary on the Exposition of Despair (Upāyāsa-niddesa-vaṇṇanā) 198.
"Sitting in painful places" and so forth refers to painful places and the like. The connection is that these serve as the basis for mental grief (*domanassa*), which is despair (*upāyāsa*).
Commentary on the Exposition of Association with the Unpleasant.

199. By the phrase "a compound with another expectation is not capable," he shows that this is the case; [it means] that the negative particle *a-* is not a prohibitor of that [compound] by which the compound is formed.
"The latter two" refers to these two words: "conjunction" (*samodhāna*) and "mixture" (*missībhāva*).

"By way of their meaning" means that it is applicable to the formations (*saṅkhāra*) by way of the meaning of conjunction and the meaning of mixture. And by those formations being present, [the designation applies] to the person (*puggala*).
The construction is: "there is a conjunction.
"Mere grasping of that" means mere grasping of the object that has entered the range of the senses.
This concludes the commentary on the description of desire.

201. "At that time" (*taṃ kālaṃ*) means the period subsequent to the cessation of the death-consciousness (*cuticitta*). Regarding the word "even" (*yampi*), the pronoun *yaṃ* is used in the sense of an instrumental case;

thus, its meaning is stated as "even by which" (*yenapi*). Regarding the phrase "whatever he desires" (*yaṃ icchaṃ*), when the pronoun *yaṃ* refers to "time," then because the non-attainment is the primary factor in the expression "he does not obtain" (*na labhati*), the desire is qualified [by that non-attainment]; hence it is said: "qualified by non-attainment. (*alābhavisiṭṭhā*)
"Desire is what is expressed. When the word "which" (*yaṃ*), functioning as a reference to an action, refers to the phrase "does not obtain," then desire is subordinate and non-obtainment is primary;
thus he said, "In that case, non-obtainment qualified by desire is what is expressed."

“Those devoid of moral shame and dread of blame are called ‘the cut-off’ and ‘the profligate,’” thus he said: “By a group that is cut and broken means by a group of profligates who are shameless. “Ragsmen” (kappaṭika) are those who wear stitched rags.
“Desiring what is unobtainable” means having a desire for an object that is unobtainable.
*Commentary on the Description of the Aggregates of Clinging* (Upādānakkhandhaniddesavaṇṇanā)
202. "Because such a basis exists" is said with reference to a comprehensive grasp by way of generality.
The meaning is: "by suffering that is exceedingly manifest, as it were, too clearly.
The commentary on the description of the truth of suffering is finished.
2. Explanation of the Exposition of the Truth of Origin (Samudayasacca-niddesa-vaṇṇanā) 203.
"Like the word *mano*" means like the word *mano*. "By the suffix *ika*" means by the suffix *ika* in the phrase "leading to renewed existence" (*ponobhavikā*).

"Because its meaning has been made known" means because its meaning has been explained. For here, the sense of "habitual practice" (*sīla*) is the meaning of the suffix, and that is expressed by the suffix *ika*.
The non-employment (*appayoga*) of the word *karaṇa* (instrument) when it denotes an action is [the case here], for there is non-employment of words whose meaning has already been stated.
Since it has been said that [craving] "gives renewed existence when other conditions are assembled, but does not give it in their absence," he says:

"Even though it does not give, it indeed gives renewed existence," because it does not deviate from its own nature. For this very reason he says: "Because of having a common nature, because of being under its influence."
And so it is said. Therein, "nature" (sabhāva) is the act of craving. "Power" (ānubhāva) is the capacity to produce a fruit when conditions come together.

Regarding the phrase "in the others," this refers to the remaining defilements and so forth. Craving, which acts as an assistant to karma that yields results during the course of existence (pavatti), is intended by the term "ripening in the substrate" (upadhivepakkā);
thus he says, "according as it has arisen in the substrate," and so on. "According as it has arisen" means by way of its own conditions.
In the sense of having been produced. *Nandana* means delighting, exulting, or being elated. *Rañjana* is the transformation of the mind by means of a variety of colors, as with a cloth dyed by dye;

or it is the act of causing delight. "By connection with lust" (*rāgasambandhena*) means by connection with the word "lust" (*rāga*); it is expressed in the masculine gender as "of that which has arisen.
"Lust for existence in the fine-material and immaterial realms will be explained separately"—here, the verb is "will explain" (*vakkhati*).
It should be understood in the sense of an action-base (*kammattha*).
By the phrase "the eye with its physical basis," the entire decad of the eye is meant; by the second [phrase], the eye together with its constituent parts.
"Aperture" refers to the hollow portion of the ear. "Ear-attachment" refers to the earlobe. In terms of color and shape, it is like a patch of red woolen cloth.
In terms of its function, they consider it to have a soft, moist, and sweet taste. "Taken in their generality" means taken without being distinguished by way of their objects.

"Distinguished by their objects" means distinguished by the objects of the eye and so forth. Herein, "arises" refers to the fact that there is no linguistic usage of difference between the general and the particular—just as with the whole and its parts—as in the case of "a tree is a *siṃsapā*. For not every...

A *siṃsapā* is a tree. Therefore, because there is a distinction in the action (*kiriyā*), in expressions such as "the wealthy eat while lying down," the state of being "arising" (*uppajjamānā*) is stated here as the characteristic of the action, whereas in the other case, it is stated as that which is characterized.
Since it is not accepted that "one who is arising exists," he states the existence of the action of arising (*uppādakiriyā*) with some reservation. By that, regarding arising—
The meaning of this [term] *satī* is "this is its purpose. In the phrase "arising" (*uppajjamānā*), "arising" is stated as the cause, while the other [factor] is stated as its fruit;

thus he says, "For it is as if it were employed by that. Alternatively, "arising" refers to craving's habit of arising there, its nature of arising, or its capacity for arising. And in that very context, of that [craving]—
The quality of arising is due to the absence of occurrence in any object other than *sakkāya* (the existing body). Capability [to arise] exists through the concurrence of conditions;

otherwise there is incapability, which is why it does not arise at all times. Regarding the phrase "when settling, it settles," the meaning here should also be understood according to this same method.
The commentary on the exposition of the truth of the origin is finished.
3. Commentary on the Exposition of the Truth of Cessation: 204.
Because the fading away of craving is its disintegration, like the fading of turmeric dye, he says, "by way of reaching its destruction."
"Ceased as something cut off" means "by way of proceeding into non-occurrence. "Relinquishing" means "casting away" or "abandoning";
thus he said, "by way of relinquishing through lack of concern, and by way of abandoning.
"Like its non-occurrence" means like the non-occurrence of that bitter *alābu* creeper. Even though it is the cause for non-occurrence...
Nibbāna is understood as the non-occurrence of craving; thus he said, "as if its non-occurrence," just as in the case of "the destruction of lust" (*rāgakkhayo*).
"Becoming a state of non-occurrence" means attained through the non-occurrence of craving; the sense is that it is what is to be attained.
It is stated for the purpose of showing that even though craving has ceased by coming to Nibbāna, it can still be said to have ceased with respect to things that are dear and pleasant.

The Exposition. And here, because both the Path and Nibbāna are the means for the complete eradication of craving, two similes—beginning with "Or the former simile"—are applied respectively to both cases;
however, that which serves as the basis for both [similes] is indeed applicable to both instances.
The commentary on the exposition of the truth of cessation is finished.
4. Commentary on the Exposition of the Truth of the Path 205.

Regarding the path fabricated by the sectarians (*titthiya*), such as that consisting of the knowledge of the interval between ordinary men (*pakati-purisa-antara*) and so forth: "It causes one to attain the noble" means it causes one to attain the noble fruit of recluseship (*ariya-sāmaññaphala*).
“Having the nature of abstaining from its opposite” means having the nature of abstaining from wrong speech (*micchāvācā*), which is the opposite of that right speech (*sammāvācā*).
Divisive wrong speech is slanderous speech; or rather, all wrong speech is divisive by way of deceiving others and so forth.
Thus it is said: “by the abandoning of divisive wrong speech. For, by virtue of its function of deceiving and so forth, [wrong speech] is harsh and non-supportive.
Right speech, being the opposite of false speech and the like, has the nature of embracing through its quality of affectionateness;

it functions by embracing the people who receive well-spoken words based on those conditions, as well as the associated mental states. Thus, it is characterized by embracing (*pariggaha-lakkhaṇa*). Therefore, it is said:
"It possesses the function of embracing both people and the associated [states]. Such activity includes tasks such as making robes; that which is to be done includes dyeing robes and so forth.
"Niravajjasamuṭṭhāpanakiccavā" means having the function of originating that which is blameless, or having the function of originating in a blameless manner.

Regarding the phrase "and originating associated states," here "originating" (samuṭṭhāpana) refers simply to the occurrence of associated states by way of being conducive to its own function, which is the opposite of wrong action;
or it refers to their "lifting up" (ukkhipana) through bodily activity.
It is like the throwing away of a burden. Purification (*vodāpana*) is the cleansing of the associated states, or rather, the cleansing of one’s livelihood itself.
"Associated with views" (*diṭṭhekaṭṭhā*) means those things that are to be abandoned simultaneously with views; this should be understood by way of the right view of the first path alone.
There is also a reading: "ignorance and so forth associated with views. In this alternative, there is an inclusion of the right view of all four paths.
It has been done. However, regarding the right view of the higher paths, pride—which is to be abandoned by each respective path—should be understood as the "station of views.
For that [pride] is a station for views because it functions in the mode of "I am. "He makes manifest" means he penetrates through the penetration of function.
"By that very factor" means by that very path-factor known as right view; that is, by that which has thus proceeded and serves as the instrument.
"Or by that reason. For the word *aṅga* also has the sense of "reason. "Therein" means in the path, or in the arising of the path-consciousness.
"Of this very [path]" means of that which is included within the Noble Path (*ariyamagga*).

Although volition (*cetanā*) is indeed found in one who abstains from what ought to be abstained from, because abstinence (*virati*) alone is predominant at that time, he said: "or the abstinences at the time of abstaining."
“Subhāsitādi” means right speech (*sammā-vācā*) and so forth; by the word “and so forth” (*ādi*), right action (*sammā-kammanta*) and right livelihood (*sammā-ājīva*) are included.

“Bhāsanādi,” however, refers here to bodily good conduct (*kāya-sucarita*) and so forth. “Because it is not a factor of the Path” (*amaggaṅgattā*) means because its intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*) is not that of the Path.

To demonstrate that very fact—that volition (*cetanā*) is not of the nature of the Path—it is said: “Of a single knowledge,” and so forth. In that context, the triad of functions beginning with right speech refers to [the abandoning of] wrong speech and so forth.
The volition of the path does not possess the nature of severing the three evil qualities; therefore, its status as right speech and so forth is not established at the moment of the path.

"In the establishment of that" means in the establishment of the three functions. However, just as it possesses the character of well-spoken speech and so forth in the prior stage, so too might it possess that character at the moment of the path.
This being the case, just as there [in that prior stage]...

If a single right intention were to perform three functions, and each of the factors beginning with right view were to perform four functions, then a single volition of the path would have to accomplish the three functions of right speech and so forth;

and if that were the case, there would be no three factors of right speech and so on within the path, and the Noble Path would consequently consist of only six factors. It is for this reason that he said, "by a single volition," and so forth.
But since this [volition] does not exist [at that moment], and because of the statement regarding the path as a condition, volition does not constitute the path;
therefore, at the moment of the path, it is the abstinences themselves that are right speech and so forth.

Expansion is happiness (*sukha*). Tranquil happiness is equanimity (*upekkhā*), for it is said: "Equanimity, however, is described as 'happiness' because of its tranquility. Regarding "thought and so forth," these very factors—directing the mind and so on—are stated by way of their manifest terminology.
Vitakka (initial application) is an auxiliary to vocal expression because it constitutes the volitional formation of speech. By the phrase "blameworthy...
[etc.]... is an auxiliary," he shows that vitakka is a specific condition for abstention (*virati*) just as it is for the volitions that originate vocal expression.
Or, since speech determines vocal expression, he refers here to abstention from verbal misconduct; for that [abstention], being right speech, is the opposite of wrong speech.
Saṃyaminī. Therein, just as one who is unrestrained from wrong speech, such as deception and the like, will certainly not be restrained from wrong action either—as it is said:
“One thing... [is] not to be done”—so too, one established in right speech through non-deception and so forth, fulfills right action as well;
thus he said: “The differentiation of speech... [is] helpful. This is because there is no fixed end to the occurrence of phenomena.

Just as "going" (*gati*) is said to mean "arising" (*nibbatti*), so too do the characteristics of taste (*rasa-lakkhaṇa*) belong to the state of occurrence (*pavatti-bhāva*); thus he says, "or in their nature as functions, etc. "Delighting" (*abhinandana*) means delighting by way of craving and so forth.
"Memorizing" (*uggaha*) is the act of bringing [the words] to the tongue;

"inquiring" (*paripucchā*) is the inquiry into the meaning. Since both of these depend upon hearing, he says, "they come under the heading of the knowledge of hearing" (*savana-ñāṇa*). "Grasping" (*pariggaṇhana*) is the apprehension [of the object] after it has been delimited by knowledge.
"Of that" means of the application.

"That" refers to the improper attention (*ayoniso-manasikāra*) directed toward the sign of beauty, which is the cause for the arising of sensual thought. "Of that" refers to the sensual thought. "Gata" means going or occurrence; its "means" (*upāya*) is the path gone by.
"The unity of what is to be abandoned" refers to the commonality of the state of being abandonable.

The meaning is that, having grasped the fourfold path collectively as a unity by way of its nature as the "path"— namely, the fourfold path consisting of the stream-entry path and so forth— it is expressed with the singular term “assā” (of them).

The mutual similarity of the entire path, as well as its dissimilarity and partial similarity, consist in its being entirely similar, entirely dissimilar, or partially similar by way of the jhāna factors.
"Thus, it should be connected as 'this very distinction. The connection is: 'He spoke, having made the fixed course of insight (vipassanā-niyāma) his primary task.
"But here," however, means "in this *Sammohavinodanī*. Regarding the statement "he comprehended... up to...
turning away," this was said with the intention that he speaks while placing the opinion of the first Elder (Thera) foremost; otherwise, the other opinions would also have been shown here.
The construction is: “Having made the fixed course of the foundational jhāna (pādakajjhānaniyāma) the primary focus, he says [this].
Why was it said, “Insight... should be seen”? For there is no rejection of that [insight] here. Indeed, it has been stated:
“Some say that insight leading to emergence (vuṭṭhānagāminivipassanā) determines the fixed course. This is not so. “Even here” means even here in the fixed course of the foundational jhāna.
The meaning here is that the "certainty of insight" (vipassanā-niyāma) is not excluded. For this very reason, he says, "Because it is common.
By the phrase "But here," it should be understood that the first Elder’s position is also included. If this is so, why is the certainty of insight mentioned separately?

It is for the purpose of showing that [the position] is not inconsistent with the three doctrines. And the "other teachers' doctrines" refer to the doctrines concerning the jhāna of comprehension (sammasita-jjhāna) and the individual's disposition (puggala-ajjhāsaya).

“‘In the formless realm, there are the threefold and fourfold jhānas... [and so on] ... it is not mundane’—this was established by making it a canonical tradition (*tantra*) in the ancient commentary (*porāṇa-aṭṭhakathā*) that has come down in the Theravāda;
thus he says, ‘The intention is that it is stated in the *Aṭṭhasālinī*, having been included therein.
By the words ‘in which,’ he speaks with reference to those [realms] excluding the final jhāna. For therein, in the arising of the formless [attainments],”
There is doubt regarding this, but not regarding the other. When "the fourfold and fivefold jhāna" is stated, it is considered without distinction as both with and without taints (*sāsavānāsava*).

Showing that the phrase "and that is supramundane" was spoken for the purpose of excluding the tainted from among those common terms where both what is to be rejected and what is to be accepted apply, and that "not mundane" was spoken to demonstrate the nature of what has been excluded, he said: "The aggregate... [etc.]..."

"Yes, it is so. Otherwise, because there would be no deviation [from this rule], the qualification "supramundane" (*lokuttara*) would be redundant. "The three paths" refers to the second path and those following.
"Belonging to that jhāna" means belonging to the third or fourth jhāna, such as the fruit of stream-entry (*sotāpatti-phala*).

"Also belonging to other jhānas" means that paths also arise belonging to jhānas other than the third and fourth—that is, belonging to the fourth jhāna as well. By the word "also" (*pi*), [it is implied that they may belong to other levels].

The meaning is that those jhānas consist of either three or four jhāna-factors. If this is so, then even in the fourfold plane of existence (catuvokārabhava), just as in the fivefold plane of existence (pañcavokārabhava), since the Path possesses the state of being three- or four-jhānaka, by what means is there a fixed determination of its jhāna-factors and so forth? To this he says:

"The prior volitional formation and attainment which determine the jhāna-factors and so forth. And "prior volitional formation and attainment" refers to the foundational [concentration] by virtue of its state of being free from passion for the phenomena it has transcended.
The formless attainments or the attainment of fruition are those that perform the preliminary volitional formations for insight. Therefore, he said "the basis.

They are not to be comprehended because the attainment—which determines the factors of jhāna—is not to be comprehended, since the threefold and fourfold jhānas to be comprehended do not arise therein, and because there is no distinction in the other case. "Of fruition" means even of the fruition belonging to the fourth and fifth jhānas.
"Of the knowledges of suffering, etc. means of the knowledges of suffering and its origin (*dukkha-samudaya-ñāṇānaṃ*).

"Having as their object each respective wholesome object" means that among the sense-sphere realm (*kāmāvacara*) and so forth, whichever wholesome state arises together with the intention of renunciation (*nekkhamma-saṅkappa*) and so on—these [knowledges] have that respective wholesome state as their object;
thus they are "having each respective wholesome object as their object," by virtue of being such. "Having as their object each respective thing to be abstained from, etc. means...
Because it has as its object such things as the basis for deception and so forth. For it is called "abstinence" (*virati*) precisely because it is that which must be transgressed against.
The term "of the factors" (*aṅgānaṃ*) should also be connected here with "renunciation-intention and so forth," since a whole cannot exist without its parts.

It is a "specific condition" because right effort is impossible for one whose virtue is broken or whose virtue is impure, just as [physical] exertion is impossible for one who lacks concentration (*samādhāna*).

Virtue is a specific condition. Although this meaning is appropriate by way of virtue already established previously, he said "also of the associated [state]" to show that it is indeed obtainable by way of co-nascence as well.
And since only co-nascence is intended here, he said "and of the associated alone," and so forth.
Confusion is negligence; its opposite is non-confusion, which is diligence (*appamāda*). That...
"Guarding of the mind" is what is meant by "the state of the mind being guarded.
By the word "and" in the phrase "and the aggregate of virtue," the aggregate of concentration is also included. Because virtue has patience as its primary quality, it accomplishes non-hatred;
because it is the direct opposite of sensual desire, which is the foremost of the hindrances, concentration accomplishes non-greed.
It should be seen. "The Teaching" (sāsana) refers to the teaching of realization (*paṭivedha-sāsana*), and they also call it the "holy life of the Teaching" (*sāsanabrahmacariya*).
The commentary on the exposition of the Truth of the Path is finished.
The commentary on the Suttanta-bhājanīya is finished.
2. Commentary on the Exposition of the Abhidhamma (Abhidhammabhājanīyavaṇṇanā) 206–214.
Why was it said, “That which is devoid of the state of being fully understood and is exclusively to be abandoned”?

Is it not the case that craving (*taṇhā*) also possesses the state of being fully understood, since it is described as the objective basis for craving, just like the eye and so forth? As it has been said: “Craving for forms (*rūpataṇhā*) is a lovely thing in the world... [SN 35.84].
“Pleasant form—herein this craving arises when arising, and herein it settles when settling,” and so forth.
For the state of being fully understood (*pariññeyyatā*) consists in the necessity of transcending by means of abandoning the defilements bound up with that [craving].
And this absolute necessity for abandonment applies not only to craving, but also to all remaining defiled phenomena (*saṃkilesadhamma*). For thus, in their entirety...

Is it the case that vision and cultivation are absolutely abandoning? This is true; nevertheless, just as the state of being "to be fully understood" (*pariññeyya*) is conventionally established for the five aggregates of clinging—which are the objects to be abandoned by the abandonment of craving—when it is said, "The noble truth of suffering is to be fully understood," this is not so for craving itself.
For craving, however, its status as the "origin" (*samudaya*), as expressed in such passages as "this craving leads to renewed existence," is far more prominent.

In order to show that the state of being abandoned is well-established [as a specific category], it is said: "in those things which are exclusively to be abandoned and devoid of the state of being fully understood.
That which has a portion not included [within a category] is "with a portion" (sappadesa); the meaning is "one part. "Therein" refers to the term *ariyasacca* (noble truth).
"Origination" (*samudaya*) means the sense of origination. "In order to show origination without exception" indicates that here only origination is taken up.

The passage beginning with “But from the cessation of suffering” (*dukkhanirodhā panā*) was stated in order to show the reason. In that context, “cessation of suffering” (*dukkhanirodhā*) refers to both suffering and its cessation.
Regarding the phrase “in the teaching of the Noble Truths” (*ariyasaccadesanāyaṃ*): it means just as in the teaching of the truths (*saccadesanāyaṃ*), so too in the teaching of the Noble Truths.

“From the standpoint of the Dhamma” (*dhammato*) means they are indeed exhaustive in terms of the Dhamma to be taught. For in the passage beginning with “and the remaining defilements,” there is merely a difference in the manner of the teaching.
This is the distinction. Therefore he said, “For there is nothing other than that,” and so forth. “There is nothing new” means that, in terms of the Dhamma, there is nothing new.

“Of that” refers to the origin (samudaya). “In all three sections” refers to the major sections divided into the eightfold, the fivefold, and the inclusive [summaries], as well as the five sub-divisions contained within them.
“Of the new” refers to [the passage] beginning with “and the remaining defilements,” and so forth.
"Of craving, which has not been seen before. For here, the statement regarding the origination of the remaining defilements and so forth constitutes "seeing what was not seen before.

Although there is no distinction between the second and third sections, this is stated thus because, among the five categories, something not previously seen is shown at each successive stage. That [first section] shows a specific distinction of origination, while the other shows a specific distinction of the path.
And its non-existence prior [to that moment] has already been shown by way of the Dhamma.

If this is so, why is craving (taṇhā) included in the second and subsequent sections, or even in the first section? To this he says: "Also for the purpose of showing a previously unknown origin," and so forth.

"Kevalāya" means independent of other defilements and the like. "Not stated by way of the teaching" means not by way of the Dhamma; this is the intended meaning. Therefore, suffering and the rest are [included] there in the teaching of the Noble Truths.
It should be understood that these have been shown in a limited way by way of a particular method (*pariyāya*).

However, since the teaching of the Abhidhamma is a discourse that is free from such methods (*nippariyāya-kathā*), it is stated in the Commentary: "in order to show the origin without limitation (*nippadesato*).
