The term *paccayasaṅkhātaṃ* means that which is regarded as a condition, that which has become a condition, or a category of conditions.
"Of these" refers to wholesome states (*kusaladhamma*). "By way of the abandoning of conditions" shows the cessation of the fruit through the cessation of the cause;
or rather, the abandoning of the wholesome is stated by way of the abandoning of the defilements bound up with them, as in: "Monks, even states (*dhammā*) are to be abandoned by you.
Thus, the abandoning of the wholesome is stated figuratively (*pariyāyato*), not absolutely (*nippariyāyato*), because they do not exist [independently].
He said: "For wholesome states are not to be abandoned. And just as it is with wholesome states, the same principle applies to indeterminate states as well.

"Cessation" refers to the unconditioned element (asaṅkhata-dhātu). The meaning is that "abandonment" refers to that state of non-occurrence of craving and so forth which constitutes the nature of cessation, namely Nibbāna.
Thus it is called abandonment.

The connection is as follows: by the phrase "purification of bodily action, etc.," he shows that the noble path has a more remote dependence on the purification of preliminary bodily action, vocal action, and livelihood.
The intention is that this illustrates the fivefold nature [of the path] as it occurs, but not that the noble path itself possesses five factors.
"An indicative illustration" means a demonstration of its indicative character; by this, [the word] "from the statement" [is explained].
This shows that the word is used in the ablative case (*nissakkavacana*) in the sense of cause (*hetuattha*). Alternatively, "from the word" means because of the existence of such a statement.
The meaning is that even a single part of the path is itself the path. It was set forth by the compilers of the Dhamma through the process of recitation (*saṅgāyana*).

The entry into the teaching by way of the meditative absorptions (*jhāna*) refers to the teaching itself under the heading of jhāna, as in: "He develops supramundane jhāna. Likewise is the entry into the teaching by way of cultivation (*bhāvanā*).

"Recitation of the text" (pāḷigamana) means the occurrence of the text, the teaching of the reading. "According to the factors as they actually occur" means according to the factors such as initial application (vitakka) that are obtainable in that arising of consciousness.
The commentary on the *Abhidhammabhājanīya* is finished.
3. Commentary on the Section of Questions (Pañhapucchakavaṇṇanā) 215.
"Of that" means of the Suttanta-bhājaniya. "But in this way" refers to the manner beginning with: "Furthermore, this so-called right view, in its prior stage, has various moments and various objects.
And "having done thus" refers to the fact that only the supramundane path possesses the nature of the truth of the path.
Because it is intended [as such]. "By that" means by that reason; the meaning is: because it was pointed out and explained as referring specifically to the Noble Path.
The commentary on the section of questions and answers is finished.
The commentary on the Analysis of the Truths (Saccavibhaṅga) is finished.
5. Analysis of the Faculties (Indriyavibhaṅga) 1.
Commentary on the Exposition according to the Abhidhamma (Abhidhammabhājanīyavaṇṇanā) 219.
"By way of the eye-door" means by reason of the state of being the eye-door. "By those [consciousnesses] occurring through that door" means by those [consciousnesses] that proceed within that door.
[They are so called] because of the mind and mental factors. For these [factors] possess that door as their sphere of activity; thus they are "door-possessors" (*taddvārika*).
But do not those [mental factors] based on that [same physical basis] also exercise that lordship (*indaṭṭha*)? Therefore, it was said in the *Aṭṭhakathā*:

"Because of being sharp when [the faculty] is sharp, and because of being dull when [it is] dull. True, they do exercise it; however, even those based on that [physical basis] are here referred to specifically as "door-possessors."
Indeed, the eye itself is called the "basis" (*vatthu*) in the sense of being a support, precisely because its state as a door has not been relinquished.

Alternatively, since its lordship (*indaṭṭha*) is manifest among those associated with that door, it is said "by those associated with that door. Demonstrating that lordship means being followed by others and possessing supreme sovereignty, he says:
"For that... they follow it. In this context, "that" refers to the eye; "they" refers to those associated with that door. [The word] *kiriyā* expresses the locus of action.
The word *āvī* means "manifest," as in such terms as *vijitāvī* ("one who has conquered"); thus he says, "the knowledge of having completed one's task.
In some places, six faculties are mentioned in the Sutta, as follows: "Bhikkhus, there are these six faculties. Which six? The eye-faculty... [and so on] ...the mind-faculty.
Why, then, are the faculties not mentioned in the Sutta in the same way as the aggregates (*khandha*) and so forth?
He said, "In that regard, in the Suttanta," and so forth, because [these faculties] were not taught together [in the Suttanta] but were taught in the Abhidhamma.

Regarding the phrase "by way of being the means of escape (*nissaraṇa*), etc.": here, among the supramundane [faculties], those included within the Path (*magga*) are the escape; the others are the fruit of escape.

The faculty of faith (*saddhindriya*) and the rest produced by relying on turning away (*vivaṭṭa*) are the means of escape. Among the others, some consist of active occurrence (*pavatti*), while others...
The means for its occurrence should be understood.
Being an actual state for one whose taints are destroyed (*khīṇāsava*), it is a property belonging only to one whose taints are destroyed, like the sixfold equanimity (*chaḷaṅgupekkhā*).

"Two meanings" refers to the sense of being the mark of Indra (*indaliṅga*) and the sense of being established by Indra (*indasiṭṭha*). "By way of their own respective conditions" means by way of their individual conditions such as karma and so forth.
"In a continuity accompanied by that" means in a continuity accompanied by the female faculty (*itthindriya*) and in a continuity accompanied by the male faculty (*purisindriya*).
"In another mode" means in a mode other than that of a woman, etc. The construction is: the state of being followed [by the body] is the predominance (*ādhipacca*) of the female and male faculties.
"In this meaning" refers to the meaning of predominance.
"Of these" refers to the three beginning with the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown.

That which was described as the faculty of pleasure and pain having the function of experiencing desirable and undesirable aspects should be understood precisely by way of the intrinsic nature of the object (*ārammaṇasabhāva*), and not by way of conceptual construction (*parikappa*) as in the case of certain types of mental joy-faculties and so forth;
showing this, he says, "And here," etc.
Although the life-faculty (*jīvitindriya*) is taught immediately after the male-faculty (*purisindriya*) even in the *Rūpakanda*, that is the material life-faculty;
furthermore, in that context, the female and male faculties are not mentioned after having spoken of the mind-faculty (*manindriya*).

However, here [in the *Aṭṭhakathā*], showing that the sequence of the faculties as stated is in every respect consistent with the teaching on the *Yamaka*, he said: "That [sequence] of the teaching on the pairs of faculties..."

“...comes together. Regarding “of the preceding and succeeding internal and external [factors]”: the preceding ones are the internal [faculties] such as the eye, etc., and the succeeding ones are the external [phenomena] such as the femininity faculty, etc.
The intention is that what is stated between them is for the purpose of illustrating how both types are mutually supportive.
Therefore, even in accordance with this other method of teaching, it is appropriate to state the sequence of the life-faculty (jīvitindriya).

[The author] shows this. Although it is stated thus here, later, in the determination of functions (*kicca-vinicchaya*), he will show the determination of the functions of the life-faculty (*jīvitindriya*) immediately after the mind-faculty (*manindriya*), and of the female and male faculties immediately after that, according to the sequence as it appears in the canonical text (*pāḷi*).

All that suffering [is to be understood] by way of the nature of the suffering of formations (*saṅkhāra-dukkha*), or by way of the suffering of suffering (*dukkha-dukkha*) and so forth, as appropriate.
"Of one who maintains the two-fold personal existence" means of one who maintains the two-fold personal existence by way of the material and the immaterial.
For here, the life-faculty (*jīvitindriya*) is taken as being twofold, according to the material and the immaterial.

By the word "occurrence" (*pavatti*), he illustrates that the feelings must be made to occur by the life-faculty, which has the function of making co-nascent phenomena occur. "Associated with the path of development" (*bhāvanāmaggasampayutta*).
By this, he excludes the faculty of final knowledge (*aññindriya*), which is the fruit. Furthermore, the mention of "cultivation" (*bhāvanā*) here could have been omitted;

for since it is stated that [the path] "is to be cultivated," the state of being cultivation is already evident. The phrase "immediately after seeing" (*dassanānantara*) is said with reference to the lack of intervention by anything of the same class or level, and not in the sense of the condition of immediate succession (*anantarapaccaya*).
“Of that” means of the state of being a condition by way of faculty (*indriya-paccaya*). “Because it is not shared with others” means because it is not common to other things that are not faculties.
Having thus defined the specific function through its capacity, he shows it also from the perspective of the treatise:
“because it occurs within the discussion of faculties. “Of others” refers to other co-nascent states (*sahajātadhamma*) that possess the nature of faculties. By which [states] they...

They exercise lordship, yet they lack mastery over themselves; because they lack the nature of being a precursor to the mind-faculty (*manindriya*), they themselves, in every respect, remain under the sway of the mind-faculty alone.
Therefore he said: “And those associated with it as well,” and so forth. If this is so, how can they possess lordship? [The answer is:
“It is merely the causing of the associated states to conform to their own mode of being, characterized by pleasure and so on.”
This meaning has already been stated. By the phrase "because they are mental concomitants" (*cetasikattā*), he shows the predominance of consciousness over the associated states;
for it is because of this that they are called "mental concomitants" (*cetasika*).

"In all respects" refers to the description of their function, from the exercising of mastery and the protection of co-nascent states, up to being the condition for the state of being directed toward the Deathless for the associated states. "In non-arousing..."
The phrase “and when there is no support” (*anupatthambhe ca sati*) should be supplied and connected [to the preceding]. For the meaning of a word does not deviate from its actual existence;

thus, what is meant is: “even in the absence of people acting as a support. “Of those conditions” (*tappaccayānaṃ*) refers to the conditions such as karma, which serve as the basis for the signs of woman, man, and so forth.

“The state of being a cause for their occurrence” (*tappavattane nimittabhāvo*) means the causal status in the production of the material form that takes on the appearance of the sign of a woman and so on.
It should be understood that "itself" refers simply to the presence of the femininity faculty (*itthindriya*) and so forth therein.

For when something exists, another thing comes to be, and when it is absent, that other thing does not come to be; therefore, the former is the cause of the latter. By the phrase "the state of being a sign is conformity," he shows that the word *anuvidhāna* has the sense of an object (*kamma*).
"As if having attained the state of pleasure and pain" means having themselves attained the intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*) of pleasure and pain.

The meaning is: "as if it were pleasure" and "as if it were pain. The attainment of the neutral aspect (*majjhattākāra*) by one who is not [actually] present... should be understood by way of unknowing-equanimity (*aññāṇupekkhā*) and so forth.

Regarding "of a similar kind": unwholesome equanimity is [compared] to unwholesome pleasure and pain; indeterminate equanimity to indeterminate [pleasure and pain]; and wholesome equanimity to wholesome pleasure.
Within that too, this meaning should be applied by distinguishing it according to the division of planes (*bhūmi*).
All of that should be illustrated according to the classification of gross and subtle as stated in the *Khandhavibhaṅga*. By the word "etc."—that is, by the word "etc.

used in the phrase "sensual lust, ill will, etc."—the fact that the faculty of one who has already known (*aññātāvindriya*) is intent upon another function is stated with reference specifically to its being the decisive support for the severing of the fetters (*saṃyojana*). For even that [faculty] has the function of the subsiding and abandoning of the higher fetters.
It can indeed be so. Alternatively, because the faculty of one who has already known (aññātāvindriya) is non-proliferative, its function of subsiding and abandoning need not be mentioned;

for that reason, even the faculty of final knowledge (aññindriya) is not explicitly cited as having that function in the Commentary. For the fruit that follows immediately after the path proceeds by way of the subsiding of the defilements—according to such statements as "by that faith which was not yet subsided"—and not in the other way.
Otherwise, the Noble Ones would at all times have the fever of the defilements unabated.

However, for the other [the worldling], the state of having the function of being calmed should be understood by way of conventional usage (*ruḷhivasena*), just as there is the designation "being" (*satta*) applied to those who lack desire and lust.
Here it may be asked: Why are only this many faculties mentioned, and why are these very ones mentioned? Because the sense of predominance (*ādhipaccattha*) is possible in their case.

This is so. "Sovereignty" (*ādhipacca*) is what is meant by "lordship. This sovereignty is powerful with respect to its own function, yet it is indeed obtainable for other intrinsic phenomena (*sabhāvadhamma*) as well.

For those things produced by conditions (*paccayuppanna*) exist in dependence upon their conditions. Therefore, they follow after those [conditions], and those [conditions] are followed by them. True, this is so; nevertheless, there is a distinction between them.

This specific distinction has indeed been shown in the Aṭṭhakathā by such statements as: "For in the occurrence of eye-consciousness and so forth, the predominance of the eye and the other [faculties] is established.
Furthermore, among the five aggregates, the six internal bases are the basis for the designation of a "being" (satta-paññatti).
First, those [faculties] are stated from the beginning as "the eye-faculty … the mind-faculty" by way of their predominance (*ādhipacca*).
However, life (*jīvita*) is mentioned in order to show that the phenomenon by which they proceed is the cause of their persistence.
Furthermore, these phenomena dependent on the faculties are designated as "woman" or "man" by virtue of these [life-faculties].
The two factors [faith and wisdom] are for the purpose of vision. This mass of phenomena, designated as a "being," while proceeding by way of continuity, becomes defiled by these feelings;
thus, the pentad of feelings is for the purpose of showing this. Then, for those seeking purification, the pentad beginning with faith is for the purpose of showing the equipment for cleansing.
After that, it is shown that these [beings] are purified by means of these [factors] which constitute the equipment for cleansing.

The three faculties beginning with "the faculty of 'I shall come to know the unknown'" (anaññātaññassāmītindriya) are stated at the end for the purpose of showing that [the noble ones] have attained purity and have completed their task.
In all instances, the phrase "taking it in the sense of predominance" (ādhipaccatthaṃ upādāya) should be applied. Since the intended meaning is established by this much, others are not mentioned.

Alternatively, these alone are stated for the purpose of showing the support and so forth for both the process of existence (pavatti) and its cessation (nivatti). For, regarding the process of existence...
Specifically, these are the six internal sense bases (*āyatana*) which serve as the fundamental support. As it is said: "The world has arisen in the six," and so forth.

Its arising occurs through the female and male faculties (*indriya*), for the manifestation of the mass of beings generally occurs due to the signs of lust for the bodies of those of the opposite sex.
For this has been stated: "Great King, indeed, from the conjunction of three things, there is the descent into the womb."
[The conditions are: "There must be the union of the mother and father here, the mother must be in her fertile period, and a conception must be present.

It is a "station" because it is to be maintained by the life-faculty (*jīvitindriya*). Therefore he said: "Life, stability, sustenance, maintenance," and so forth. "Experience" is by means of the feelings (*vedanā*);
for it is through the influence of feeling that there is experience of all objects, whether desirable or otherwise. As it has been said:
—“It feels, it makes feel; therefore, monks, it is called ‘feeling’ (vedanā).

Thus, for the purpose of showing the support, the arising, the persistence, and the enjoyment of the process [of existence], fourteen faculties have been taught, beginning with the eye-faculty and ending with the equanimity-faculty.
And just as these [faculties] pertain to the process of existence, so do the others pertain to its cessation. For, by means of that which is based on turning away (*vivaṭṭa*),...
The five faculties beginning with faith (*saddhā*), once generated, are the support for cessation.

Their arising is by means of the faculty "I shall come to know the unknown" (*anaññātaññassāmītindriya*), because it arises first. Their persistence is by means of the faculty of final knowledge (*aññindriya*). Their enjoyment is by means of the faculty of one who has known (*aññātāvindriya*), due to the enjoyment of the supreme fruit.
Thus, these very same faculties have been taught. To this extent, there is no mention of others, because the intended purpose has been accomplished.
By this [method] as well, their sequence of teaching should be understood as having been explained.

Regarding the phrase "wholesome and unwholesome energy, etc.," here the word "etc. (ādi) should be seen as including wholesome concentration and so forth, as well as indeterminate energy and so forth.
Regarding the phrase "conditions, etc.," the word "etc. includes location, object, and so on, as well as the aforementioned energy and other factors.
And it includes the eye-faculty and so forth. Thus, these terms beginning with the faculty of energy (*vīriyindriya*) and those beginning with the eye-faculty (*cakkhundriya*) are all-inclusive.
"By that" refers to the explanation of the classification of the planes (bhūmi) beginning with "even though this is so.

"By the exclusion of that" means by the exclusion of [the notion] that all [faculties] belong to all planes. "The state of not including what is non-existent" refers to that which is not found in a particular plane.
The function of the faculty as a unifier.
The commentary on the *Abhidhamma-bhājaniya* is finished.
2. Commentary on the *Pañha-pucchaka*.
Here, when it is stated that "the seven faculties have no object" (*anārammaṇā*)—thus being spoken of as exclusively objectless—the life-faculty (*jīvitindriya*) is not included;
yet in the *Ṭīkā*, it is stated by forming the compound *anābhaṭṭhaṃ*. Among material phenomena (*rūpadhamma*), it is included as being reckoned as "matter" (*rūpa*).
By way of the immaterial category (*arūpakoṭṭhāsa*), that is, by way of its immaterial nature, it is included in the alternative of "might be" (*siyāpakkhe*).

Why? Because it possesses limited objects and so forth. However, since the inclusion within the "perhaps" category is appropriate only in the case of that which is a mixture of the material and immaterial, and not for a single part, he said, "the intention," being unwilling to accept that [status] for a single part.
Now, to clarify that meaning, he said, "But by way of the immaterial portion," and so on. "Indeterminable" means [indeterminable] by way of having limited objects and so forth.

Regarding "the state of being inexpressible": in response to the objection, "But how can that which lacks an object be inexpressible in terms of the category of form (*rūpa*)," he says, "For it is not without an object," and so forth.
By the phrase "among those whose objects do not exist or are non-existent," he shows that the compound "without an object" (*anārammaṇa*) is a *bahirattha-samāsa*.
"Among those inexpressible" means among those that cannot be defined by way of having an object. "The state of being without an object" means because of being devoid of an object.

In passages such as, "Nine faculties may have limited objects, may have exalted objects, may have immeasurable objects, or they may not be described as having 'limited objects,' nor as having 'exalted objects,' nor as having 'immeasurable objects,'" it does not show that only that which possesses an object is subject to being indescribable.
And just as there is this way of speaking regarding what is indescribable for that which possesses an object, [so too is it for that which does not].
Thus, even for that which is without an object (*anārammaṇa*), there is no restriction regarding that which possesses an object (*sārammaṇa*).

Showing that this too is not a fixed rule—that it cannot be said to possess an object exclusively—he said, "or the state of possessing an object for that which is not so defined. This is to be connected with the phrase "he does not show that.
He elucidates that very point with the words beginning "for it is not," and so forth.

In this context, having considered the objection that "form and Nibbāna cannot be described as being associated with pleasure and so forth, but not because they have limited objects and so on," he says, "But even so," and so forth. Therein, the connection is: "even so, it may be stated.

"It might also be stated that it is without an object" means that the base of mental phenomena (*dhammāyatana*), being without an object, should be stated thus by setting it apart from those things that possess an object.
It might be so. If the term "inexpressible" (navattabba) were to apply only to those [factors] that possess an object (sārammaṇa), it would not have been stated [in this way];
and since there is no other reason for its not being stated, he said: "For in the section on the posing of questions, there is no teaching that leaves anything remaining.
Therefore, the intention is that the term "inexpressible" applies even to those [factors] that lack an object (anārammaṇa). As for the statement: "The eight faculties might be..."
When it is said, “It has an internal object,” the state of not being definable by way of having an internal object and so forth is stated;
that is stated with reference to the life-faculty’s having as its object merely the absence of consciousness during the first immaterial attainment at the time of the base of nothingness.

It is not stated for the purpose of showing that what possesses an object is undefinable, nor for the purpose of showing the absence of being undefinable by way of having a limited object and so forth in the case of that which lacks an object.
In order to show this, he said: “And here [in the passage] beginning with ‘Eight faculties may have an internal object’.
In that context, the word *iti* in the phrase “may have an internal object” (*siyā ajjhattārammaṇā*) has the sense of “etcetera” (*ādi*).

By means of that, through the inclusion of the remainder of the canonical text, the meaning stated in this passage—namely, “they may be described as having an internal object, or as having an external object, or as having both an internal and external object”—is indicated.

In demonstrating the life-faculty (*jīvitindriya*), he said: "The indeterminacy (*navattabbatā*) of the life-faculty... [etc.]... should be understood," the meaning of which has already been explained.
The commentary on the interrogation of questions (*pañhapucchakavaṇṇanā*) is finished.
The commentary on the analysis of the faculties (*indriyavibhaṅgavaṇṇanā*) is finished.

225. Regarding the term “vuttattā” (because it was spoken): what is the characteristic of this ablative case? It has the characteristic of a cause (*hetu*).

If that is so, does it follow that the state of being a Vibhajjavādin is caused by that [speech]? For were the disciples of the Buddha Vibhajjavādins simply because they were spoken to by the Elder Moggaliputtatissa?
This is not so. For a cause is threefold: the indicator (*ñāpaka*), the producer (*kāraka*), and the accomplisher (*sampādaka*).

The claim by some that there is no sense of accumulation (*upacaya*) should not be accepted as authoritative.
"By way of its opposite" means by way of persisting contrary to the Vinaya.

By demonstrating that what is blameworthy is blameless and so forth, one who divides, destroys, or confuses another formal act (*kamma*) violates the nature of things (*dhammatā*), perceiving it erroneously.
*Mahāpadesa* means "great authorities"; it refers to the great grounds (or causes) spoken after citing the Buddha and others as great authorities.
Alternatively, *mahāpadesa* means "great occasions"; what is meant is that these are the great bases for the establishment of the Dhamma.
Herein, this is the word-analysis: it is called an *apadesa* because it is cited (*apadisīyati*); that which has the Buddha as its authority (*apadesa*) is "Buddha-authority" (*buddhāpadesa*).

This same method applies to the remaining [great authorities] as well. In terms of its meaning, this Great Authority (*mahāpadesa*) is the criterion for determining whether something brought forward by anyone—such as "I heard this directly from the Blessed One"—is "Dhamma" or "non-Dhamma. But what is that criterion?
It is precisely the testing of the sutta and so forth against that which was thus brought forward. If this is so, how can there be four? There are two [criteria] for the Dhamma...
The Blessed One and his disciples are the authorities (*sampadāya*). Among them, the disciples are threefold according to the Saṅgha, the group, and the individual.
Thus, there are four [authorities] based on the distinction of those from whom one may point out: "This Dhamma was received by me from such-and-such. Therefore he said:

"I have heard this directly from the Blessed One," and so forth. It is also stated in the *Nettippakaraṇa*: "The appeal to the Buddha, the appeal to the Saṅgha, the appeal to many elders, and the appeal to a single elder."

Regarding the phrase "Sutta, Suttānuloma, Ācariyavāda, and Attanomati as the four Great Authorities" (*mahāpadesa*): here, the three Piṭakas included in the three Councils (*saṅgīti*) are called *sutta* in the sense of indicating the meaning and so forth.

*Suttānuloma* refers to the four Great Authorities themselves, exactly as previously stated, because they are in conformity with the aforementioned *sutta*. This is because, by means of grasping the meaning of the Canon (*pāḷi*), they establish [the teaching] within the nature of reality (*dhammatā*).
The *aṭṭhakathā* (commentary) is the "Teacher’s Statement" (*ācariyavāda*). One’s own realization through the grasping of the method is "one’s own opinion" (*attanomati*).

Here, it should be understood that the status of a "Great Authority" (*mahāpadesa*) is stated for the Sutta, the Teacher’s Statement, and one’s own opinion because they possess the nature of being causes for determining whether something is Dhamma or non-Dhamma when brought forward by anyone. One should remain established, not obstructing and not contradicting [them].

And by way of the opposite of that, one "runs too far. Having stated the meaning of a single term in one manner, to state its meaning again in another manner or to describe it through other methods is called "redundancy" (*niddisati*).
For example, after stating, "Ignorance does not allow for the penetration of the true nature and characteristic of the truth of suffering," and so forth, [to say] again: "This..."
Although ignorance is stated to be "non-knowing regarding suffering and so forth," there is also the statement that "it is a portion of the truth of suffering," and so on.
Alternatively, it is the restatement of a meaning already expressed as a cause by expressing it again as its fruit;

this is the re-exposition of that same matter, just as after saying "with consciousness as condition, name-and-form [arises]," one then says "with name-and-form as condition, the six sense bases [arise]."

[This is] the statement. Alternatively, the meaning here should be understood as follows: it is a restatement and further demonstration of the very same point already stated in such passages as, "All this wheel of existence (bhavacakra) is both karma and its result; it is threefold by way of defilement, karma, and result," and so forth, showing its division into two types, three types, and so on.

“Designation by way of a being” (sattavohāro) means the conventional term “being. For when one takes as a basis those phenomena that have become an aggregate and are occurring by way of a continuity, the conceptualization of a “being” arises.

To then encompass and understand that [conceptualization] exactly as it is—without falling into the extremes of regarding it as something other than those phenomena, nor as something not other, nor as having absolute non-existence—is difficult for the unskilled and hard to accomplish within the nature of things (dhammatā).

The "mode of conditionality" (*paccayākāra*) is the state of being a condition—by way of conditions such as cause (*hetu*) and so forth—with respect to a conditioned phenomenon such as volitional formations (*saṅkhāra*), which arises from a conditioning phenomenon such as ignorance (*avijjā*).
This is the meaning of "dependent origination" (*paṭiccasamuppāda*).
"In the manner stated" refers to the manner stated in the passage beginning with, "Without misrepresenting the Teacher," and so forth. And here, although all [the modes]...

The commentary on the meaning should be composed according to this very method; however, showing that the commentary on dependent origination (*paṭiccasamuppāda*) is of greater importance, he speaks thus.
"The Dhamma of the Pāḷi" refers to the word of the Buddha contained in the Three Piṭakas. "Dependent origination" refers to the textual discourse on dependent origination.

"Having made it beneficial" means having made it for one's welfare; that is, having acted in such a way that it brings about benefit. Or, "having made it a bone" means having made oneself desirous of it. [This refers to] the specific types of knowledge consisting of what is heard, reflection, and so forth, as well as the specific destruction of defilements through the stages of partial abandonment, suppression, and so on.

Ignorance (*avijjā*) is the root cause of the cycle of existence (*vaṭṭa*), because it conceals the dangers inherent in the realms of existence and the like, because it serves as a powerful decisive support, and because it acts as a specific cause for kamma.
Furthermore, although the cycle of defilements (*kilesavaṭṭa*) is the cause of the cycle of kamma—which in turn is the sign for the cycle of resultant rebirth—it is [still considered a root].
Ignorance (*avijjā*) is mentioned first for the purpose of showing that [the cycle] is rooted in ignorance.

For craving (*taṇhā*) also arises only in relation to objects whose dangers have been concealed by ignorance, perceiving them as gratifying, and not otherwise. Furthermore, one should connect the similarity of showing the root and so forth;
that is, by showing the root, middle, and end of the creeper, one should apply the similarity of showing those same parts to dependent origination (*paṭiccasamuppāda*).

Although everything is seen by the universal eye (*samantacakkhu*), at the time of teaching, it is intended that only a partial view is presented by means of the eye of knowledge of the teaching (*desanāñāṇacakkhu*), according to what is to be awakened.
[This applies] to one who asserts "I" through craving accompanied by views or accompanied by conceit, or "mine" through the other [craving]. "From delighting" (*abhinandanato*)—
For by this [term], the occurrence of craving accompanied by rapture (*sappītika-taṇhā*) is shown.
By "rejoicing" (*abhivadato*), the occurrence of that which is even stronger than that—accompanied by views (*diṭṭhi*) or accompanied by conceit (*māna*)—is shown.

By "remaining attached" (*ajjhosāya tiṭṭhato*), however, the occurrence of that which is even stronger than that—accompanied by views or as mere craving alone—is shown. For it is after having swallowed and fully digested [the object] that one remains [attached].
“Clinging” (*ajjhosāna*). “Conditioned by that” means conditioned by craving (*taṇhā*). But how is it that all four kinds of clinging are expressed by the word “delight”?
To this he says: “By way of delight,” and so forth. Therein, “by way of delight and non-separation from that”:

through its nature as delight, there is the clinging of craving (*taṇhūpādāna*); through non-separation—that is, the inseparability—from that delight which is craving, there is the clinging of views (*diṭṭhūpādāna*).
It should be understood that it is "stated. By the phrase "by way of delighting in views," he expresses that view itself possesses the quality of delight (*nandi*).
"Rebirth-linking and process-contact, etc. refers to the contact, mental volition, and consciousness that have arisen during both rebirth-linking and the course of existence.

Furthermore, the term "consisting of the round of kamma-result" (*vipākavaṭṭabhūte*) should be regarded as a qualification of the "process" (*pavatta*). "Supports for the round" means they are the decisive supports for the three rounds of existence.

The others are not born of kamma. "In that" refers to the aforementioned fourfold nutriment. "They are fit to be called" means that because craving is their source and decisive support, it is appropriate to call them "having craving as their source.
Just as the Noble Path is called "the method" (ñāya) because it is the middle way that avoids the two extremes, so too is dependent origination.
He said: "The 'way' (ñāya) is the path, or it is dependent origination itself. It leads to one's own realization because it is to be penetrated by means of a realization free from delusion.
And the phrase "it leads" is stated by way of metaphorical treatment of the cause as the agent, just as [it is said] "the truths that produce the noble state are the Noble Truths.
[Terms such as] "nature" (pakati) and so forth were discussed below in the *Saccavibhaṅga* in the section on the perversion regarding causes.
[The examples] have already been shown. They take what is not a cause to be a "cause," as the followers of Kapila and others do;
they do not understand anything as a cause, as other foolish worldlings (bālaputhujjana) do. "Of the others" refers to the three—teaching and so forth—starting from the middle up to the end.
"Even though the state of having that purpose is possible" means even though the state of showing the occurrence [of things] by way of their respective causes is possible.
"Because there is another purpose" means because there is another motive. For it is said in the Commentary:
"In order to demonstrate the causes by which one has personally attained suffering, such as aging and death;

and in order to demonstrate the sequence of cause and fruit, having traced it back through the determination of nutriment and its source all the way to the past, and then starting again from the past."
The three purposes for the three [sections] respectively are: "for the purpose of demonstrating the future period, beginning from its origination by way of causes";
"the penetration of each respective fruit" means the comprehension of birth and so forth as having aging-and-death and so forth as their respective fruits;

"surveying" refers, in the first alternative, to surveying the sign of insight (*vipassanā-nimitta*), and in the second, to the sign of the teaching (*desanā-nimitta*); [and] "become the clinging to sensual pleasures."
Craving is the specific condition for existence—which is comprised of the nutriment of mental volition—as well as for the other nutriments associated with it and those caused by it;
thus it is said: "The craving for nutriment and so forth belong to the present time. By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), everything up to consciousness (*viññāṇa*) is to be included.
Regarding the phrase "the craving for nutriment and so forth," here "nutriment" refers to that which is included within the present cycle of kamma.
Having established the half-yojana [unit], and taking those things included within the cycle of future kamma-results (vipāka), it is said:
“Or, food is to be produced by craving; the future time-period. “To be produced” means to be brought into existence in the future.

“It is joined” means that after having directly shown the present food which has become the fruit, [the connection is made] by such statements as: “Craving is the cause for that; its cause is [craving],” and so forth.

The vision of the succession of effects and the succession of causes is included under "reasoning" (yutti) because it conforms to the inclinations of those persons who awaken to such truths, and because it does not contradict the intrinsic nature of phenomena (dhammasabhāva).

If craving and the rest belong to the past period, then since formations and ignorance are already included by the mention of craving, for what purpose are they mentioned again? To this he says: "Formations and ignorance are even further in the past than that."

"Certainly" (addhā) is said for the purpose of showing that saṃsāra has no beginning. Alternatively, by the commonality of being "past," even that which is more remote in the past should be understood as included.

"Bringing about the production of renewed existence" means they are conditions for rebirth in a new existence. "Because of this statement" means because of the existence of the words spoken in this manner.
First, the nutriment of consciousness (*viññāṇāhāra*) is the cause for the production of renewed existence; but how are the others so? To this he says: "Because they are associated with that...
[and] because of the nutriment of physical food. The connection is: "The four nutriments are the bringers about of the production of renewed existence in the future.

The state of being a decisive support (*upanissaya*) for faith and the other [faculties] occurs at the time of relinquishment and so forth; for lust and the other [defilements], it occurs at the time of one who is greedy eating food and so forth. By this—

The accumulation of wholesome and unwholesome kamma-consciousness has been shown in due order. "Therefore" means because the four nutriments, which bring about the production of renewed existence in the future, are being taken up;
therefore. "The former instance itself" refers to the meaning stated in the passage beginning with "craving for nutriment and so forth belong to the present time.
"In the past" means in the past period. "Beyond that" means beyond that past period, in the present.

And in the future period, [it is taught] by such statements as, "With volitional formations as condition, consciousness arises. "Directly perceived" means those things that have become directly perceived because they are included within present existence.
"The present cause" refers to craving and so forth currently occurring, which are the causes for nutriment and the rest.
He cites the sutta: "From the arising of the taints comes the arising of ignorance. "Of the cause of the round" means of the cause of the round of kamma-result.
Or, [it is] because of the cause of the entire cycle (*vaṭṭa*). For unwholesome karma is indeed a condition for both the cycle of karma and the cycle of defilements (*kilesavaṭṭa*).
By the phrase "also being the cause of craving for existence (*bhavataṇhā*)," he states that ignorance (*avijjā*) is also a condition for the cycle of defilements.

And by the passage beginning with "In this way, monks, it is said," etc., he demonstrates, under the pretext of showing that the heads of the cycles—namely ignorance and craving—are themselves conditioned.
This clarifies that for all conditioned phenomena (*saṅkhata-dhamma*), there is no discernible prior limit due to their functioning as a continuous succession of cause and effect.
"Ignorance (*avijjā*) follows craving (*taṇhā*)" expresses the superior power of ignorance over it, because craving proceeds by overcoming [the understanding of] suffering (*dukkha*).
For beings overcome by ignorance engage in the practice of self-mortification—a suffering characterized solely by harm—even while they are agitated by craving.
"Craving follows ignorance": this states that craving is more powerful than ignorance because it proceeds by overcoming ignorance with respect to pleasure.

Even though ignorance remains powerful in the experience of tainted pleasure by concealing its existing dangers, craving—being even more powerful than that—leads beings toward ignoble pleasures that consist of vast misfortune.
The following of ignorance [by craving] has been stated.
Alternatively, the connection is that the "group of six bases" (āyatanachakka) is the "body. Regarding "the remaining phenomena based on the eye and so forth":

this refers to those phenomena that constitute the bases of the eye and so forth, as well as those bound up with them, which are included within one's own continuum. By the very mention of the "eye and so forth," they are understood to be precisely those dependent upon the eye and so forth.

"Having grasped" means having taken hold. "The collection of eye, etc. refers to the aggregate of the five aggregates belonging to others, which is the collection of phenomena such as the eye and so forth.
"Touched by contact" means touched by a contact that has arisen—like one touching an object—as something to be experienced as pleasure or to be experienced as pain.
For when contact arises in such a manner, there is the conventional expression that the person possessing it is "touched."
Just as the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*) are a specific condition for contact (*sparśa*), so too are they for feeling (*vedanā*);
showing this, he said, "the state of the six sense bases being a specific condition for feeling. "Dependent upon that" means dependent upon the six sense bases.

"Rooted in ignorance and craving belonging to the past period" means rooted in the ignorance and craving that constitute the past period. In both instances, by the word "body" (*kāya*), [the physical body is meant].
The pentad of the aggregates subject to clinging (*upādinnakkhandha*) is taken [as the object]. "Approaching that" means rebirth, the grasping of rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*).

"The root of both" means the root of ignorance (*avijjā*) and craving (*taṇhā*). "Because it has become non-realization" means because it is the opposite of realization (*abhisamaya*). "Of ignorance" means when ignorance exists. "Grasping" means the state of being graspable.
"Therefore" means because, even though they possess the nature of formations (*saṅkhāra*) as conveyed by the word "formations," [they arise] with ignorance as their condition.

The formations (*saṅkhārā*) are mentioned separately by way of their predominance, according to the analogy of "the cow and the calf. Therefore, regarding the phrase "even though they are mentioned therein":

among the formations included under the term *saṅkhāra*, one should exclude and not include the formative formation (*abhisaṅkharaṇa-saṅkhāra*); rather, the other formations are to be applied [to the definition].
In this way, the dual nature of the meaning—as that which extracts and that which is extracted—is shown without confusion.

“By way of being that which is to be described here”—by this [phrase], although formations (*saṅkhāra*) exist as conditions for ignorance (*avijjā*), he indicates the very same status of predominance as previously stated, even though they have already been mentioned by the word "formations. The connection is: "‘Formations conditioned by ignorance’—a portion of that [whole] has been stated.
In this interpretation of the meaning, by means of the word "formations" (*saṅkhāra*), [the text functions] by way of inclusion.
Although ignorance conditioned by formations is included among the formations already mentioned, it is taken separately here because it is the primary factor to be explained;
thus, the distinction is that "in the former [case], those were excluded. Therefore he said:

"The twofold nature was stated by way of including everything that is to be explained. Even though it is included under the general category, it is taken separately for the purpose of indicating its preeminence.
As it is said: “The equipment of merit and knowledge.
That accumulation by which wholesome and unwholesome states are called “states subject to ripening”—what, then, is that?
It is the state of active engagement within a continuum where craving and ignorance remain unsevered. Therefore he said: “Rebirth-linking... has the function of accumulating.”
However, because volition is its primary factor, it is stated [as such] after performing the function of volition.
"The making of a heap" and "the accumulation" are stated because of the production of a fruit—consisting of both the material and immaterial—which has been formed into a heap.

Regarding the statement, "The state of being without an object is the state of being indeterminate," this is said by taking the state of being without an object as belonging to the indeterminate, since only that which is indeterminate is without an object.
"Base" (*āyatana*) and "conjunction" (*ghaṭana*) should be understood as the mere occurrence of phenomena through their respective doors.

"Non-comprehension" and so forth are included in the exposition of the term "ignorance" (*avijjā*). Because of its connection with the term "ignorance," the feminine gender designation is used for "disassociated from views. "Because of the absence of shape" means because of the absence of a physical structure.
"Because of the existence of sorrow and so forth": rather than stopping at "with birth as condition, aging-and-death," [the text] subsequently mentions sorrow and the rest as well.

Because those [factors] mentioned exist, there arises the contingency of having too many factors (*aṅga-bahutta*), that is, when the factors of dependent origination (*paṭiccasamuppāda-aṅga*) are found to be numerous.
Regarding the phrase "only twelve": how can they be only twelve? Is it not true that grief (*soka*) and the others are also distinct phenomena mentioned in the teaching on dependent origination?
True, they are mentioned, but not as separate factors; showing this, he says "for not," and so forth. In that regard:
"By the fruit" means by that which has become the fruit—namely, sorrow and so forth, which are comprised within the factors of aging and death (*jarāmaraṇa*).

"In order to show the root factor": these sorrows and so forth were mentioned for the purpose of demonstrating the uninterrupted continuity of the wheel of existence (*bhavacakra*), by way of explaining how one falls into delusion through such things as sorrowing, thereby showing the ignorance (*avijjā*) factor which serves as the root of this teaching on dependent origination (*paṭiccasamuppāda*). "Those for whom aging and death are the cause... [is the definition of "beings"].

Sorrow and the rest have aging and death as their cause; the state of having that [aging and death] as their cause is "having aging and death as the cause" (*jarāmaraṇakāraṇatā*). That which has aging and death as its sign is "having aging and death as the sign" (*jarāmaraṇanimitta*).
Regarding the phrase "for those having that as their sign," here *taṃ* refers to the sutta. "For those having that as their sign" means for sorrow and the rest, which have suffering as their sign.
"From that onwards" means from the future second existence onwards, for the rebirth-linking in the third existence and so forth.

“Causes that have become causes” means being the cause of a cause. For volitional formations (*saṅkhāra*) are the cause of rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*), and ignorance (*avijjā*) is the cause of those.
He says this with reference to the sutta beginning, “The uninstructed worldling.

Ignorance is shown to be the cause of sorrow and so forth because, by demonstrating how the uninstructed person is overwhelmed by ignorance, it is stated that [sorrow] arises from that. “Not for the fool are sorrow and so forth... [the rest of the verse follows].
In order to make clear the meaning already stated—that there is a sutta which establishes that aging and death are the cause [of suffering]—the passage beginning with "And not" was spoken.
By this, he shows that it is not only aging and death as a cause that constitute suffering; rather, ignorance as a cause should also be applied here according to the method already explained.
Thus, having made a single synthesis of sorrow and the rest with aging and death, [the text continues].
The twelve factors of dependent origination (paṭiccasamuppāda) are to be understood.
But why is the teaching here concluded with aging and death (jarāmaraṇa)? Is it because there is no further process beyond that?

It is not that there is none; for one whose defilements (kilesa) have not been abandoned, there is the manifestation of rebirth-linking (paṭisandhi) from karma, following the death (cuti) which culminates in consciousness (viññāṇa) and the other factors.
Old age and death, which consist in the occurrence and the cessation of that [process], are the cause for the production of renewed existence (*punabbhava*).
However, since they are already indicated by birth through the formula "with existence as condition, birth," they are not stated again;
nor is there anything further beyond them, because there is no further occurrence. And for the continuum produced by a single karma, old age and death constitute the conclusion.

When the cycle of defilements exists, there is the arising of renewed existence through karma; but when that is absent, the teaching is given as ending with aging and death, concluding with the words, "This, indeed, is the end of suffering.

Furthermore, since for all things subject to arising, there is no aging without death—just as a wall does not crumble without first being baked—and since there is no death without aging due to the absence of any breaking apart without prior baking, therefore these two together constitute a single factor.

It is stated [as such] neither because it arises simultaneously in both locations like name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), nor because of an equality of function in its status as a sense-base (*āyatana*) like the sixfold base (*saḷāyatana*).

Furthermore, since this manifestation of renewed existence (*punabbhavābhinibbatti*) which has reached its conclusion is illustrated, [the sequence] beginning with "with consciousness as condition, name-and-form" and so forth is established;

and because in the absence of defilements and karma that [renewed existence] would not occur, [the sequence] beginning with "with ignorance as condition, volitional formations" (*avijjāpaccayā saṅkhārā*) is established.
Alternatively, it is explained by way of its meaning that the wandering about due to the non-stability of the three rounds of existence (*vaṭṭattaya*) is demonstrated.

Or else, by the inclusion of "aging," there is the grasping of name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) and so forth as they proceed through the stages of being fully matured, more fully matured, and so on, as well as sorrow (*soka*) and the rest;
likewise, ignorance (*avijjā*) is included as that which exists during the time of such maturation. As it has been said:
“Monks, as that prince grew up and his faculties matured, he lived surrounded and provided with the five cords of sensual pleasure:
forms cognizable by the eye... [and so on] ...tangible objects cognizable by the body... which are alluring.
Having seen a form with the eye, he became infatuated with a pleasing form and felt aversion toward a displeasing form.”

"And he dwells with unestablished mindfulness of the body and with a limited mind; he does not understand as it really is that liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom wherein those evil, unwholesome states cease without remainder," and so forth.

For here, by the mention of "with lust" and so on at the six sense doors in one whose faculties are matured, there is the implication of liberation through its inseparable connection [with those states].

Furthermore, ignorance—which serves as the condition for sorrow and the rest—is revealed through the lack of clear comprehension. Moreover, from the statement, "Sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair arise from what is dear," [ignorance is shown] by way of the taints of sensual desire (*kāmāsava*) and the taints of existence (*bhavāsava*).
And from the statement, "When one dwells obsessed with the thought 'I am form,' 'form is mine'...
sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair arise due to the change and alteration of form."

Because of the statement beginning with “the uninstructed one,” which refers to the taint of views (*diṭṭhāsava*), and because of the taint of ignorance (*avijjāsava*), the arising of sorrow and so forth is illustrated;

thus, by the mention of that [ignorance], the taints are included by virtue of being its causes. Furthermore, since they themselves have the nature of aging, they are included by the mention of aging.
And because of the statement, “With the origin of the taints, there is the origin of ignorance,” and because ignorance has the taints as its cause, [the taints are included] by the mention of aging.
This is the grasping. And from that, the wheel of existence (bhavacakra) revolves with the formula: “With ignorance as condition, volitional formations arise.

Furthermore, by stating “With volitional formations as condition, consciousness arises” and then saying “With existence as condition, birth arises,” the revolving of the wheel of existence is shown because it does not remain stationary.
For here, through consciousness, renewed existence for one shrouded in ignorance is shown; and through birth, [renewed existence] for one associated with craving is shown.

Because both [ignorance and craving] follow along in both places, this meaning is illustrated: that the wheel of existence (bhavacakra), driven by the causes of ignorance and craving, revolves without stopping.
Thus, although the teaching ends with aging and death, it does not indicate the absence of further occurrence beyond that, as its purpose is not that;
nor can it be said that the repetition is solely for the purpose of showing another condition.
This is because both [types of action] are established by a single teaching together. Likewise, whatever action has ignorance as its cause should be understood to have craving as its cause as well;
and whatever has craving as its cause should be understood to have ignorance as its cause as well. Why? Because the two roots of existence are not mutually separable.
For just as, with craving as a condition, there arises the formative action of kamma-existence caused by sensual clinging (*kāmupādāna*), so too...
By saying this, he shows that ignorance is not a condition for volitional formations (*saṅkhāra*) without craving for existence (*bhavataṇhā*).

Likewise, while teaching that very same condition of ignorance, he shows that craving for existence is not a condition for the kamma-process of becoming (*kammabhava*) without ignorance. Furthermore, there are volitional formations and so forth which have as their conditions ignorance and the rest occurring previously;
and there are becoming and so forth which have as their conditions craving, clinging (*upādāna*), and the rest; likewise, [those] which have craving as their cause and clinging as their condition.

It should be understood that the sequential relationship of these factors has thus been shown: existence; conditioned by ignorance, volitional formations; conditioned by existence, birth; conditioned by volitional formations, consciousness; conditioned by birth, aging and death; and conditioned by consciousness and so forth, name-and-form and so forth.
The commentary on the section of the summary is finished.
Commentary on the Exposition of Ignorance (Avijjāpada-niddesa-vaṇṇanā) 226.

"He is spoken of as a father" means he is spoken of by way of being a father, such that one says, "So-and-so is the father of so-and-so. And when he is spoken of, it is said with the aim of removing doubt by distinguishing him from other friends and relatives; showing this, the author says, "Dīgha...
[etc. ... Datta. "As it really is" means non-perverted. "By way of function and kind" means by way of its function of concealing and by way of its place of arising.
"By way of being the cause for grasping" means by way of being the causal state for grasping. The connection is made by supplying the word "preventing others, such as equanimity (*aññāsetā*)," etc.
"Concealing" means occurring in the mode of concealing. Because they occur in that manner, the ignorance associated with them has suffering as its object.
Therefore, because they are not deep by nature, ignorance arises having that [suffering] as its object, which causes their difficult-to-see nature.

The others are cessation and the path. Although they are equal in being sublime, untainted, and so forth, the phrase beginning with “of the path” was stated in order to show the distinction between that which has conditions and that which is without conditions.
The commentary on the exposition of the term *avijjā* (ignorance) is finished.

In the commentary on the exposition of the bases of formations (*saṅkhārapadaniddesa*), by the phrase “it purifies from the fruit of demerit,” he states that merit is free from the suffering of its ripening (*vipākadukkha*);

by “from suffering,” he states it is free from mental suffering (*ceto-dukkha*); and by “from defilement,” he states it is free from the suffering of the defilements (*kilesa-dukkha*). “From the fruit of demerit” means—
By the phrase "by this," he shows that merit is beneficial for the future.

By the phrase "from the defilement of suffering," he shows its benefit and happiness during the course of existence (*pavatti*). "By its accomplishment" means by the production of benefit and happiness. "One who produces what is worthy of honor" means one who produces what is praiseworthy.
Regarding the statement, "In such ways as 'this merit increases,' even the fruit of merit is called 'merit,'" he says: "It approaches merit; it approaches a fortunate rebirth."
"Initial cultivation" (*ādibhāvanā*) refers to the cultivation that occurs regarding the kasiṇas by means of [the formula] "earth, earth," and so forth.
Here, in the phrase "earth, earth," the word *iti* has the sense of "beginning" (*ādi*) or the sense of "manner" (*pakāra*). By this, the inclusion of the other kasiṇas is intended.
"Initial cultivation" means cultivation that is initial; for that is called "preliminary work" (*parikamma*). "Making a disk" (*maṇḍalakaraṇa*) means making a kasiṇa-disk.

“By the relinquishing of the object to be given” means by way of the renunciation of the thing to be offered. “Generosity” (*dāna*) is so called because it is that by which mental states (*citta*) and mental factors (*cetasika*) are given.
“Therein” means among those mental states and mental factors. “With reference to generosity” means with regard to the renunciation being produced by them.
Or, having set aside [the result] just as it comes forth; “on account of” (*adhikicca*) is a synonym for that very same thing. Or, [it refers to how it arises] by way of the associated [factors].

The act of giving, while being produced, reaches its culmination by way of completion; having done so [it ceases]. For the accomplishment of kamma such as giving occurs solely through volition (*cetanā*).
"In the others" refers to passages such as "having undertaken virtue" and so forth.
"Even though dissimilar" connects with "kamma-produced matter (*kaṭattārūpa*) that is unlike itself. [This occurs] even without the fruition of the fourth jhāna.

“Of that which is reckoned as craving for form” means: he refers to the craving for form mentioned here in the phrase “craving for form. “Guñja” means a substance to be carried that is the size of a guñja fruit;
likewise with “rice grain.
By saying “merely a difference in wording,” he states the absence of a difference in meaning; thus, he speaks of the absence of a difference in meaning regarding the “body-door.”
"For it is precisely the occurrence [of the action] that constitutes the taking up and so forth of evil. By "the former" is meant the phrase "occurring at the door of the body";
for that is a characterization of the door by way of describing mere occurrence. By "the latter" is meant the expression "taking up" and so forth.
"In the mention of bodily and verbal formations" refers to the summary (uddesa); "in the mention of bodily and verbal volition" refers to the detailed exposition (niddesa).

“Of consciousness” means of rebirth-linking consciousness (*paṭisandhiviññāṇa*). However, it is indeed a condition for both that which is co-nascent (*sahajāta*) and that which is immediate (*anantara*).

The phrase “wholesome states and states subject to ripening” is stated with the intention that here the volition of direct knowledge (*abhiññā-cetanā*) occurring in the mental continuum of trainees (*sekkha*) and worldlings (*puthujjana*) is intended, and not the other kind.
Therefore, the aforementioned volition of direct knowledge is also a condition for rebirth-linking consciousness.
It might be argued that [this consciousness] is wholesome because it possesses a wholesome nature or because it is subject to fruition, like other wholesome or unwholesome volitions;
however, this is inconclusive with respect to supramundane wholesome states, for they are not a condition for rebirth-linking consciousness (*paṭisandhi-viññāṇa*).
Or, if it were said that it is so called because it "gives fruition," even then it is inconclusive with respect to "past" (*ahosi*) karma, for there is no production of fruition from that.
He said, "It is not by the production of a result that there is wholesomeness and the quality of being subject to result.

For it is simply because its occurrence in a continuum where defilements have not yet been abandoned takes on the same mode as the occurrence of other things subject to results—which is characterized by activity and exertion—that it is called "subject to result" (vipākadhammatā) and is also described as "wholesome" (kusala) in the sense of being blameless. Even so, if it were subject to result...

Regarding the question, "How is it that volition pertaining to direct knowledge (*abhiññā-cetanā*) is without fruition (*avipāka*)?"—it is said, beginning with "But that... in order to demonstrate its impossibility.
For if volition pertaining to direct knowledge were to produce a fruition, it would have to produce either a fruition belonging to its own plane or one belonging to another plane.
In this regard, first of all, the production of a fruition belonging to another plane is untenable due to the absence of the necessary conditions, and likewise because it is not observed to occur.
Therefore he says, “Not indeed,” and so forth. It would produce either a state belonging to its own plane with an indeterminate object, or one with a limited (paritta) object and so on;

however, because among those [objects] it possesses an object identical to its own karma—as demonstrated in the case of the fine-material-sphere (rūpāvacara) resultant—and because the volition of direct knowledge (abhiññā-cetanā) has limited objects and so on, it would not produce an indeterminate object. Likewise, because it has exclusively an indeterminate object.

It is impossible that the resultant consciousness of the fine-material sphere (*rūpāvacara-vipāka*) would not arise with a limited (*paritta*) or other such object; therefore, he said, “with an object similar to itself,” and so forth.
In this context, *tiṭṭhānika* means possessing the three states by way of rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*), the life-continuum (*bhavaṅga*), and death (*cuti*).

By means of the wholesome [consciousness], such as the earth-kasina (*pathavī-kasiṇa*) or the water-kasina (*āpo-kasiṇa*), the object of the resultant consciousness is shown to be made non-different [from it].
He said: “Because it was stated in the *Cittuppādakaṇḍa*... [etc.

... ‘The fine-material-sphere triplets and fourfold jhānas, both from the wholesome, the resultant, and the functional, as well as the resultant of the fourth jhāna, the base of infinite space, and the base of nothingness—these states are not to be described as having a limited object, nor as having a sublime object, nor as having an immeasurable object.’”

Since it is stated that the resultant consciousness of the fine-material sphere has exclusively an indeterminable object, he says: "And there is no resultant consciousness of the fine-material sphere that has a limited (paritta) or other such object.

This impossibility establishes the absence of a result for the volition of direct knowledge (abhiññā-cetanā) when it has a limited or other such object, but not for that which has an indeterminable object.
For since that [volition] with an indeterminable object does exist, the [absence of result] is not universal; thus, [the argument] does not apply to the non-arising of the result.
To show another reason for this, he said, "And in the kasiṇas," and so forth.
Since the higher knowledges (abhiññā) are the unfolding of concentration, they are merely a benefit of concentration; thus it is said, "similar to the fruit of concentration.

However, the volition of higher knowledge is merely the accomplishment of whatever desired function—such as resolution, transformation, or hearing divine sounds—and it does not bear fruit at a later time, but is to be experienced in the present life (diṭṭhadhammavedanīya).
They do not have results as kamma-result (vipāka), but rather they should be understood as having the aforementioned benefits as their fruit.

Some, however, maintain: "Meditative absorptions (jhāna) belonging to the same plane are powerful due to the acquisition of repeated practice; therefore, because they possess the nature of meditative attainment (samāpatti), they yield kamma-results.

But the direct knowledges (abhiññā), although they too possess the nature of jhāna, do not yield such results because that [nature of attainment] is absent in them, [occurring instead] upon various objects."

They say, "The adventitious [consciousness] is weak, therefore it does not give a result. That is not a valid reason, because mastery over even direct knowledge (abhiññā) exists through repeated preliminary work (parikamma).

As for what they say: "When the impulsions (javana), which have acquired proficiency through being of the same nature as the basic jhāna, have properly attained mastery and are endowed with the eight factors such as purity..."

"When the extraordinary [state] has arisen, the superknowledges (*abhiññā*) are produced; and since those [superknowledges] belong to the fourth jhāna, their fruition (*vipāka*) would have to be produced on the plane of the fourth jhāna.

However, because that [fruition] is accomplished by the very power of the foundational jhāna (*pādakajjhāna*)—as described above—with its superior qualities, it does not yield fruition due to a lack of opportunity (*anokāsatā*).
That too is not a valid reason, because [the superknowledges] are not themselves fruitions.

Of those [formations]. For if they possessed the quality of yielding fruition (*vipākadāyibhāva*), it would be logical to urge that there is no room for fruition; yet their state of being non-fruition (*avipākatā*) is precisely as stated by the aforementioned method.
"It does not exist" means it does not exist as a condition for consciousness.

Thinking that even the volition of restlessness (*uddhaccacetanā*) has been stated without distinction from the volition of direct knowledge (*abhiññācetanā*), [the author] considers that the word "in fruition" (*vipāke*) does not merely express the capacity for fruition, but rather expresses the actual presence of fruition.

He said: "It should be investigated. And so it has been stated: "For the word 'resultant' does not denote that which is fit for resultancy in the same way that the term 'dhamma subject to resultancy' does.
Regarding this, what is to be investigated has already been explained above. However, the definitive conclusion here is as follows:
because the volition of restlessness gives rise only to a process-resultant (*pavatti-vipāka*), and not to a rebirth-linking resultant (*paṭisandhi-vipāka*).
Therefore, in the *Vibhaṅga*, result is mentioned by way of that [kamma] which yields its result in the course of existence (*pavatti-vipāka*).

However, since it is volition that gives both types of results [in the present and in the future] that is called the asynchronous kamma-condition (*nānā-khaṇika-kamma-paccaya*), that [condition] is not stated for it in the *Paṭṭhāna* because of the absence of such [a dual-resulting function].
As for what is said in the Commentary, "it should be excluded from the status of being a condition for consciousness," that—

This was said with reference specifically to rebirth-linking consciousness (*paṭisandhiviññāṇa*). The statement, “In this way, even restlessness-intention (*uddhaccacetanā*) does not exist,” is also said by taking up merely the absence of a conditionality for consciousness.
Thus, one should see that there is no contradiction here between the Canon (*pāḷi*) and the Commentary (*aṭṭhakathā*) regarding the giving of a result by restlessness-intention.
“Herein” means: in the giving of a result by restlessness-intention. “In the *Amataggapatha*” means: in the treatise so named. “In the continuum of an ordinary person (*puthujjana*”).”

Because it has been stated that this meaning—namely, that unwholesome states are to be abandoned by vision (*dassana*) and are to be abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā*) within the continuum of those in training (*sekkha*)—is what is intended, the passage beginning with "But for ordinary persons (*puthujjana*)" was spoken.

By the phrase "are not so called," he shows the absence of any figurative application (*pariyāya*) of the term "to be abandoned by cultivation" to the external fetters (*bahiddhā-saṃyojana*) and so forth that operate in ordinary persons. With the words "If they were so called," etc., he demonstrates that very same point through logical reasoning.

And he clarifies this through scripture as well. In that context, "of some" refers to desire, lust, and so forth, regarding one's own belongings. "Some" refers to the view of a self-identity (*sakkāyadiṭṭhi*) and the like.

"At any time" means at any period, such as the past and so on. "From oneself," etc., is a figurative expression. "Depending upon" means taking it as a decisive support-condition (*upanissaya-paccaya*).
"Of the others" refers to those [defilements] not to be abandoned by insight. The connection is: "and they are not non-existent. And having done thus, as stated in the aforementioned scripture...
By the mention of "restlessness" (uddhacca), a state of consciousness accompanied by restlessness is intended, and not restlessness occurring anywhere whatsoever;
such being the meaning. "Tad" refers to the view (diṭṭhi). Why was it said, "because it cannot be described as past and so forth"?

Is it not the case that only those things yet to come (anāgata) are to be abandoned? No; for in the primary sense, only those states ready to arise are called "future," whereas those to be abandoned [are future only in a secondary sense].

However, the statement that they "are not capable of arising" refers to their being indescribable in terms of pastness and so forth. "In relation to vision" means with reference to the path of vision that has been cultivated.
"Due to the absence of an associate" is because of the lack of the cooperative cause consisting of those things to be abandoned by vision.
"They do not produce a result" means that even when some [defilements] are destroyed, as in the case of the destruction of all defilements, there is no result caused by them.

The intention is that such a particular karma does not ripen. "The ripening has been stated in the Vibhaṅga" refers to both types of ripening—the distinction between rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*) and the course of existence (*pavatti*).

"Of the unwholesome" means of those unwholesome states in the continuum of an ordinary person (*puthujjana*) as previously specified. "Not to be abandoned" means those whose intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*) is not to be abandoned.

Of the wholesome and so forth. "The state of being reprehensible" (*sāvajjatā*) is the nature of being opposed to that which is not to be abandoned. The phrase "In this way too," and so forth, shows the internal fault [in the opponent's position].
By this, he demonstrates that even if those unwholesome states were not included in the third category of this triad (*tika*), they would nonetheless result in being "indeterminable" (*navattabba*).
For anything not included in its entirety within the triads and dyads (*duka*) by way of its intrinsic nature (*dhamma*) results in the consequence of being indeterminable.

He says, "It does not incur [the offense]. Now, he elucidates that non-incurrence of the state of being "not to be spoken of" by way of reason and illustration, beginning with the words, "In the section on the arising of consciousness," and so forth.
"Wherein" means in which triad (*tīka*). "Niyogato" means by necessity, absolutely.
"Of those" refers to the phenomena comprised within the three terms. "As in the aforementioned passages" means as in the three [passages] previously mentioned, beginning with the first.

Regarding the sections (*padesu*): just as the arising of consciousness (*cittuppāda*) is to be divided, and the others are likewise divided according to their suitability by way of the three groups (*rāsittaya*) and distributed—that is, assigned to their respective portions—in the same way.
"There too" means even in the fourth section. "To be distributed" refers to those things that are not to be described [as such] (*navattabbabhāva*).
"Due to its absence" means due to the absence of that fourth section. "In the same way" means by way of being indescribable (*navattabbabhāvena*).
In the *Uppannattika* (Triplet on the Arisen), the past unwholesome states already mentioned here were not explicitly stated;
yet, even though they lack the status of being "to be expected" (*apekkhitabbabhāva*), they are nevertheless called such because they do not transcend that essential nature (*tassabhāva*).

Thus, in order to avoid the fault of falling into the position of being "inexpressible" (*navattabbatā*), he first shows an example of this by saying, "Or else, just as with those that are with resistance," and so forth. And in this context, their essential nature is...
The state of being abandoned through vision is distinguished by the absence of faultiness. With the words "And this being so," etc., he shows the advantage gained in this position.
Regarding "of those to be abandoned by cultivation," there is both a figurative and a literal sense of being abandoned by cultivation;
therein, because the former lack a primary nature [of being kamma], and because the latter are non-resultant, they possess the condition of asynchronous kamma.

The intended meaning is that they have not been stated. Just as there is no state of asynchronous kamma-conditionality for those things to be abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā*), so too, with respect to those things to be abandoned by vision (*dassana*), there is no acquisition of such conditions;
demonstrating this, he says, "And it has not been stated...," and then states the reason for that: "For those which... proceed. Therein, they are not...
Since those defilements that are to be abandoned by seeing arise only after [the path of] seeing, they belong exclusively to the category of what is to be abandoned by seeing;
thus, there is no way for them to be abandoned by cultivation.
How, then, could it be said—on account of them—that those things to be abandoned by seeing are related to those to be abandoned by cultivation by way of some condition?

This is the meaning. Alternatively, those [defilements] which are not to be abandoned by seeing in the mental continuum of an ordinary person (puthujjana) are not, in the ultimate sense, to be abandoned by cultivation (bhāvanā).
However, as for those [defilements] in the mental continuum of one in training (sekkha), there are no [defilements] existing as their conditions that are to be abandoned by seeing.
Thus, it is also said that a factor to be abandoned by seeing is not stated to be a condition for a factor to be abandoned by cultivation by way of any kind of condition.

This is how it should be understood. Anticipating the objection: "If the defilements to be abandoned by vision are on the side of vision because their conditions are to be abandoned by vision, then restlessness-accompanied [defilement], which has those same conditions, would also have to be abandoned by vision;
how then can its abandonment by exclusive cultivation be stated?", he says: "Of that which has conditions to be abandoned by vision," and so forth.
"Therefore" means: because, in the mental continuums of those with lust and those free from lust...

Just as the state of being subject to ripening or not subject to ripening for an action depends on the deficiency of its concomitants, so too—in the mental continuums of worldlings and trainees—the state of being with or without ripening for agitation-accompanied [consciousness] is established according to the method already stated; therefore [it is said]. "Of that" means of the agitation-accompanied [consciousness].
"Of exactly that kind" means of that which has a single nature by virtue of being accompanied by agitation.
