And herein, as for what was stated in the *Amataggapatha*—namely, "there is also that which is to be abandoned by development, such as [the consciousness] associated with restlessness" (*uddhacca-sahagata*)—that is not a valid reason.

Why? Because that [restlessness-associated state] is exclusively to be abandoned by development. As it is said: "Which states are to be abandoned by development? A consciousness-arising associated with restlessness. For if [it were otherwise], the state associated with restlessness...

If there were no [states] to be abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanāya pahātabba*), then just as in the section on past objects it was stated, "Invariably, there are none with future objects," and then further analyzed by saying, "Ten thought-arising moments from the fruition of sense-sphere wholesome [states]," and so forth—so too here it would have been stated:
"Which states are to be abandoned by cultivation? Invariably, those to be abandoned by cultivation..."

Having said, "It does not exist," one would have to state such things as: "A thought-arising accompanied by restlessness may be abandoned by cultivation, or it may be neither 'to be abandoned by seeing' nor 'to be abandoned by cultivation,'" yet this was not stated.
Furthermore, the logical justification provided by the one who intends to establish that point—beginning with the words, "If they were to say..."—is also invalid.
Why? Because it is precisely the state of being abandoned by vision that is intended for lust, views, doubt, and restlessness, which have objects to be abandoned by vision.

Furthermore, as for the non-inclusion of restlessness in the exposition of the predominance condition—stated in order to show that "restlessness arises" refers to a mental state accompanied by restlessness—that too is not a valid reason, since there is evidence of a different reading that leaves the matter incomplete.

For instance, in the analysis (*vibhaṅga*) of the statement, "A past state is a condition for a present state; a future state is a condition for a present state by way of object-condition (*ārammaṇapaccaya*)," the inclusion of knowledge of others' minds (*cetopariyañāṇa*) was made;
however, in the analysis of the statement, "A present state is a condition for a present state," although the inclusion of knowledge of others' minds is applicable, it was not made.
Furthermore, the state of being an assistant must be examined with respect to the giving of results by those [defilements] to be abandoned by insight and by cultivation.

Is it that, like ignorance and so forth, they become the cooperative causes for those to be abandoned by cultivation by means of producing the capacity to cause disturbance at the very moment of the arising of giving and so forth through insight; or rather, like defilement [is to] karma?
Regarding the phrase "when there is the giving of rebirth-linking": what is the point here?

If the first method is followed, it follows that the state of being a functional (kiriyabhāva) phenomenon—which is to be abandoned by cultivation—would apply to the continuum of a trainee such as a stream-enterer;

for it has been established that [such a phenomenon] lacks the nature of producing a result due to the absence of an auxiliary cause, just like giving and so forth in a continuum where craving and ignorance have been exhausted. If, on the other hand, the second method is followed, then even that which is considered to be abandoned by cultivation...
It falls under the category of what is to be abandoned by vision (*dassanena pahātabba*), because when rebirth-linking occurs, one cannot escape the nature of going to the states of misery (*apāya*).

Whatever else needs to be said here has already been stated below; therefore, the determination of the meaning here should be understood according to the method already explained, in a way that is not in conflict with the Canon (*pāḷi*) and the Commentary (*aṭṭhakathā*).

"Sāti" refers to the volition of restlessness (*uddhacca-cetanā*). "In the state of being a condition for consciousness" means in the state of being a condition for the complete resultant consciousness (*sampuṇṇa-vipāka-viññāṇa*). "Showing the reason" refers to the following reason:

although the volition of restlessness should be excluded from the context of producing a full fruit because it is absent therein, it must nevertheless be included within the state of being an arisen condition (*paccayuppanna-bhāva*) for ignorance (*avijjā*). This is the reason [for its inclusion].
"Showing all" means showing all twenty. Therefore he said, "It should be stated as twenty-one.

"That" refers to the reason why, by the inclusion of the formations (saṅkhāra), the volition of direct knowledge (abhiññā-cetanā) is not included. "Of the other [volition] also" means of the volition of restlessness (uddhacca-cetanā) as well.
What then is that [reason]? It is simply the absence of being a condition for consciousness. "Because there is no distinction" means by way of the bodily and verbal formations.
“Because there is no differentiation. *Saṃyoga* means joining (*saṃyojana*) by way of connecting with another word; thus, the meaning is “inclusion. He says, “by the perception of pleasure...

he shows,” with the intention that “grasping through the perception of pleasure” means relishing. Furthermore, in the phrase “by the perception of pleasure,” this is an instrumental expression used in the sense of the instrument (*karaṇatthe*).
For perversion (*vipallāsa*) is indeed the perception of pleasure in what is suffering. As for that which is in the Commentary...
It was said, “by ignorance (*aññāṇena*); this is the instrumental case used in the sense of a cause (*hetu*), because it demonstrates that ignorance is the cause of perversion and gratification.

Regarding the statement, “a chariot with white trappings (*setaparikkhāro*)” and so forth, since the word *parikkhāra* can also mean “retinue,” it was said, “in the retinue of craving (*taṇhāya parivāre*”).

And by the phrase “in the retinue of craving,” the state of being a cooperative cause (*sahakārikāraṇa*) for the formative forces (*saṅkhārā*) through the fulfillment of craving’s function is indicated.

This was said with intentional meaning (*sandhāya*). Showing that the sense of "requisite" (*parikkhāra*) is like the sense of "ornament" (*bhūsana*), as it is similar to the sense of "conditioning" (*saṅkhāra*), he said, "in what is conditioned and adorned.
It "conditions" (*parikkharoti*) in such a way that they become capable of yielding fruit; thus it conditions.

"For the sake of the deathless" (*amaraṇattha*) means for the sake of the deathless (*amatattha*), that is to say, for the sake of Nibbāna. "Difficult practices" (*dukkarakiriyā*) refers to ascetic practices such as the fivefold heat-exertion (*pañcātapatappanādi*).
“Austerity for the sake of divine status” means austerity for the purpose of attaining divine status. “He kills, thus he is Mara”: here, the sense of cause is internalized.
Even that which is inauspicious is expressed by way of a euphemism for the auspicious, as it is said, “like the word ‘seen’ used for ‘not seen,’” such as when “non-calamity” is called “calamity.

Having considered the precipice to be like the suffering of falling, it is said, “the suffering of the precipice of birth and so forth. The fall from the mountain peaks known as Indadudra and Brahmakūṭa is the “fall of the gods” (*maruppapāta*). That which has merit and its fruit as its aim or purpose is “for that purpose” (*tadattha*).

To a young female wanderer. One who dwells without mastery over the taints (*āsava*) and without independence. It is loathsome to the wise because of the oozing of the impurities of the defilements (*kilesa*).
It is suffering due to the fever of passion and the like, and because its maturation is bitter. He undertakes; he performs. The construction is:

"Even for one who is fearful, the abundance of the strands of sensual pleasure in the city of the *pisāca* is a cause for the perversion of perceiving it as happiness. Non-mixture with that which is of a different nature.
Continuity. Change and transformation through aging and death.

Although the word *tāva* is seen in such expressions as “I shall not pass away, O Evil One,” and in phrases like “Come, dear one, take charge of this kingdom for now,” where it serves merely to fill out the meter or to restrict a measure, here it is used with reference to what is yet to be said.

Regarding the phrase "adhippeto" (intended), it is stated: "The particle *tāva* is a connective (*nipāta*) that requires a subsequent statement. By saying "but [it] shows... conditioned by ignorance...
etc.," he explains the lack of contradiction between what precedes and what follows in the commentary (*aṭṭhakathā*).

Regarding the phrase "at the times of relishing lust and so forth," this means at the times of relishing lust and the other [defilements]. In the passage "associated with lust and views... [the following applies].
Let there first be a connection with ignorance associated with lust, because lust has the nature of gratification; but how is it so for that associated with views?
To this he says: "And the views dissociated from that... should be understood. "Of the formations associated with that" means of the formations associated with lust and so forth.
"The object and so forth of ignorance" means the object and the rest of ignorance. By the word "and so forth,"...

It includes the object-predominance condition (*ārammaṇādhipati*), the object-strong-dependence condition (*ārammaṇūpanissaya*), and the natural strong-dependence condition (*pakatūpanissaya*), as well as the proximity condition (*anantara*) and others.

"Having ignorance as its object" (*anavijjārammaṇa*) means not having ignorance as its object—that is, occurring without taking ignorance as its starting point. Regarding the mention of the object-predominance, proximity, and other conditions:

this refers to that which does not have ignorance as its object among those mentioned under the object-predominance and object-strong-dependence conditions, and among those mentioned under the proximity and other conditions.
It should be connected thus: for the first impulsion that has not been mentioned, and for the second and subsequent impulsions that have been mentioned—which both have ignorance as their object.

That ignorance is a condition for volitional formations (saṅkhāra) by way of the proximate condition (*anantara-paccaya*) for those [impulsions] that obtain it as such, by way of the root condition (*hetu-paccaya*) for the conascent [volitional formations], and by way of the decisive support condition (*upanissaya-paccaya*) for those that are not conascent—this meaning is shown by the passage beginning with "whatever... (*yaṃ kiñci*).
It should be understood. "By way of the aspiration for existence through transcendence" means: for one who produces formless-sphere jhānas for the purpose of transcending ignorance;
and for one who, being deluded by ignorance, aspires to the success of formless existence and thereby brings those very jhānas to fruition.
This refers to the method described regarding the volitional formations of merit (*puññābhisaṅkhāra*), following that same method; such is the meaning.
This results in the doctrine of a single cause, such as the theories of primordial nature (*pakati*), the Lord (*issara*), Pajāpati, the Primordial Man (*purisa*), time (*kāla*), and so forth.

For if there were only one cause for the world, then the entire process of existence would have to proceed completely and at all times from that alone, since there would be no other requisite cause to depend upon.
But this is not the case, because we observe that things proceed only successively. This is due to the dependence upon other causes.

Furthermore, the doctrine of a single cause would be refuted because a single thing cannot possess multiple intrinsic natures (sabhāva). Whatever [effects] are produced from that [cause], they must all possess an identical nature;
they cannot be dissimilar, for otherwise its status as a single entity would not exist. He stated this point with the words:
“Of everything... down to attainment. By the method of exhaustion (pārisesa), one [thing] from one [cause].
When these three modes— namely, "one from many," "many from one," and "many from many"— are non-existent and unapprehended by way of the method of elimination (pārisesa-naya),
and when only the fourth mode, "many from many," exists; then that which illustrates a single cause and fruit, such as "with ignorance as condition,
volitional formations arise" and "with contact as condition, feeling arises," is [presented] here by way of the Teacher's skill in teaching.

Alternatively, by way of the inclination (ajjhāsaya) that has been removed, it shows that the explanation of a single cause and fruit is indeed appropriate for the purpose of clarifying the pre-eminent, manifest, and uncommon nature of phenomena;
this is demonstrated by the words beginning with "because" (yasmā).
"According to contact" (yathāphassaṃ) means in accordance with each respective contact, such as eye-contact and so forth, which is to be experienced as pleasant and so on; this is what is stated.
Having stated "to be experienced as pleasant" and so forth, in order to show the meaning of the phrase "by way of the determination of feeling," it was said:

"among those that are alike," and so on. Therein, "among those that are alike" means among those that are undifferentiated. "By way of contact" means by way of contacts such as those to be experienced as pleasant.

"Because of the absence of reversal" means because of the absence of variation; for never, indeed, does [feeling] arise in dependence upon a contact to be experienced as pleasant [and result in something else].

Painful feeling, or pleasant feeling arises dependent on contact to be experienced as painful and so forth. "Of pleasant and so forth, and of eye-contact-born and so forth" refers to feelings that are pleasant and so forth, and those born of eye-contact and so forth.
By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) in the phrase "gross, subtle, and so forth," the inclusion of inferior, superior, and other such qualities is to be understood.
In this context, that [object] depending upon which a certain feeling is called "gross" or "inferior" is not itself [the feeling].
It is said that "because there is no confusion between the gross and the subtle" because, depending on that [object], it may at some time possess subtlety or refinement.

"Of the aforementioned contact" means of contact to be experienced as pleasant, and so forth. Pleasant feeling arises from contact to be experienced as pleasant alone, not from other types of contact.
From contact to be experienced as pleasant, there is only pleasant feeling, not any other feeling. The same applies to the remaining cases.
By means of the restriction of both terms— namely, the determination of feeling according to contact and the determination of contact according to feeling—
the two phrases demonstrate that the fruit is unmixed with other causes and the cause is unmixed with other fruits,
taking this as the "unmixed determination" in the first position. However, in the second position, by [the phrase] "distinguished by the difference of conditions,"...

The meaning shown here—by taking "resolution" (*sanniṭṭhāna*) and "determination" (*vavatthāna*) as such—is that the distinction between causes is determined by the distinction between effects, and the distinction between effects is determined by the distinction between causes.
Furthermore, in the first position, the determination of phenomena is stated in terms of their non-confusion;
in the second, it is the knowledge of things as they have been determined. This is the difference between them.
By the word "etc. (*ādi*) in the phrase "heat, etc.," mental imbalances such as bile, wind, and so forth are also included.

When one humor is disturbed, the others also become agitated. Even though they are present, phlegm (*semha*) is specifically mentioned because the disease is pacified by treating the phlegm; this is the meaning.
Craving (*taṇhā*) is the cause, or rather the specific cause, of the formations (*saṅkhāra*) that were referred to as "existence" (*bhava*); thus he said, "by craving..."

"Because the state of being the cause of volitional formations has been stated. "Of that too" means of craving as well. For craving is the taint of sensuality (*kāmāsava*) and the taint of existence (*bhavāsava*).

Since the taints of sensuality and existence constitute the clinging of sensuality (*kāmupādāna*), and the taint of views constitutes the other clingings, he said: "The taints of sensuality, existence, and views constitute the four kinds of clinging.
And because of the statement, "With clinging as condition, there is existence," they are also clinging; and [because of the statement], "With craving as condition..."
From the statement "clinging" (*upādāna*), it is evident that craving (*taṇhā*) is the cause of volitional formations (*saṅkhāra*).

Showing that the contemplation of gratification (*assādānupassanā*) regarding volitional formations—which are not to be relished and are permeated with manifold dangers—does not occur without ignorance (*avijjā*), he says: "For one who contemplates gratification... [etc.

...is demonstrated. Furthermore, he shows the status of ignorance as the cause of volitional formations through the method of exclusion (*vyatireka*), namely, because for one whose taints are destroyed (*khīṇāsava*), volitional formations do not exist.
He causes [ignorance] to be eliminated. For it is only the wise one whose taints are utterly destroyed.
By this, he shows that ignorance is stated to be unique to fools alone because it is possible for them; for bases, objects, and so forth are common to others as well.
Having considered the objection that ignorance—just like craving, clinging, and so on—is a common cause for meritorious formations and the rest, he says: "meritorious existence," etc.

In this context, by the word "etc. (*ādi*), non-meritorious and imperturbable existence (*apuñña-aneñja-bhava*) are to be understood. "Meritorious existence" (*puñña-bhava*) refers to rebirth-existence (*upapatti-bhava*) caused by meritorious volitional formations (*puñña-abhisaṅkhāra*).

This same method applies to the remaining types. Furthermore, here ignorance (*avijjā*), which possesses its functions, is shown by being divided according to the distinction between its activity, its instrument, and its locus.
For the state of ignorance that serves as the decisive support (*upanissaya*) for meritorious volitional formations is not the same state [that serves as the support] for others.
In this way, it can be understood that there is a decisive support (*upanissaya*) for the others as well.

And here, "concealing the disadvantage of existence" means, in terms of its actual meaning, the state of being a cause for not realizing the specific nature of suffering—which consists of the various forms of existence—of the formative volitions of merit (*puññābhisaṅkhāra*) and so forth.
It is said that "existence" (*ṭhāna*) is intended in the sense of being present; thus, "opposed to existence" means opposed to presence. [The phrase] "not opposed to existence" (*ṭhānāviruddhā*)...

The eye, visible forms, and so forth. By the passage beginning with “For the preceding consciousness,” an example of contradiction regarding location (*ṭhānaviruddha*) has been cited; thus he says, “This would not be absolute.
For by the passage beginning with “The eye, visible forms, and so forth,” examples that do not contradict location are cited hereafter.

Indeed, because it is impossible for the practice of a craft previously learned to coincide with the performance of a craft occurring later, this constitutes a contradiction regarding location; such is the meaning as stated.
The phrase beginning with "And not of crafts, etc. was stated in order to establish [this]. Therein, "that" refers to the basis such as rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*).
"Here" refers to the inclusion of the basis, nature, function, and so forth. By the word "etc.," opposites such as object, plane, and continuity are to be understood;
and these [opposites] occur in the forward order for the change-of-lineage (*gotrabhū*) from the path, and by way of the transformation of gender and so forth during its manifestation.
It should be understood thus: "Because of the contradiction between bending (*namana*) and being affected by form (*rūpana*), the condition is contradictory in its intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*).

This is the construction. In this context, "bending and being affected by form" demonstrates precisely the state of being non-material form (*arūparūpa*). Action (*kamma*) has volition as its intrinsic nature, whereas material form (*rūpa*) has being affected by form as its intrinsic nature;

thus, they are contradictory in their intrinsic nature. Regarding "sweet, sour tastes, etc.": milk has a sweet taste, pacifies bile, and has the intrinsic nature of a sweet result (*vipāka*); curd... [and so forth].
The sour taste increases bile (*pitta*) and has a pungent post-digestive transformation (*vipāka*);
therefore, there is a contradiction in their inherent natures (*sabhāva*). "Curd and so forth" refers to curd and straw. "Of *bhūtiṇaka*" refers to a specific medicinal herb named *bhūtiṇaka*.
"Sheep" (*avī*) means ewes; since they are for the most part red-fleeced, it is said, "red sheep. [This applies] even to the post-digestive transformations (*vipāka*).

Because they are conditions, and because even those that are not themselves results of kamma (avipāka) are states arisen from conditions, the relationship of condition and state arisen from a condition does not depend upon being a result-of-kamma (vipākadhamma) or a result (vipāka).
Thus it was said: "And these are only results. Therefore he said, "Therefore," and so forth. "Of those non-results" means of those things which are not results of that ignorance.
It is not the case that this is not logical; rather, it is indeed logical, because what is intended is merely the state of being arisen from a condition.
"Non-opposed to that" means non-opposed to that ignorance.
"The determination of before and after" refers to the occurrence of the body's process, destinies, births, and so forth, in their respective prior and posterior states.
To show that this [determination] is not made by anyone, is not a contrived fabrication, and is of a fixed, inherent nature, the example cited by the proponents of necessity (niyativādin) is given.
Regarding the first [view], he said: "Like gems that cannot be cut, spun into thread, or broken. Regarding the second alternative, *saṅgati* means spontaneous occurrence or arbitrariness;
with reference to this, it is said: "Proceeding according to whim, ceasing according to whim," and so forth.
*Bhāva* means the established nature of phenomena (*dhamma*); with reference to this, they say: "The sharpness at the tip of a thorn..."
“Who brings about the roundness of the wood-apple fruit, or the various colors and shapes of wild animals and birds? This distinction is established solely by its own inherent nature.

Therefore he said: “All beings, all living things, all creatures, all souls are powerless, devoid of strength, devoid of energy, subject to the transformation of destiny, chance, and inherent nature. By these conceptualizations...
By means of the conceptualizations such as "a being dies," which arise from delusion regarding death and so forth, and which serve as the cause;
"having made the mind unwholesome" means having made the mind unwholesome through the cultivation of improper attention (*ayoniso-manasikāra*).
"The Dhamma of the discourses and so forth" refers to the Dhamma of the scriptures (*pariyatti*), such as the *Sutta* and *Geyya*. For one who understands the Dhamma of the scriptures correctly...

Having fulfilled the dhamma of practice (paṭipattidhamma), one becomes established in the dhamma of realization (paṭivedhadhamma). "That" refers to that knowledge; the meaning is the direct confrontation with Nibbāna (nibbānābhisamaya).
The commentary on the exposition of the section on formations (saṅkhārapadaniddesa) is finished. [Now begins] the commentary on the exposition of the section on consciousness (viññāṇapadaniddesa).
227. "With the aforementioned formations as condition" means with the aforementioned types of formations, such as meritorious formations (*puññābhisaṅkhāra*), as condition.
Since it is the consciousness and so forth ending with feeling that constitute the present round of kamma-result (*vipākavaṭṭa*) which is intended here, he says:
"Only consciousness produced by that very kamma is fit to come into being. And showing that this explanation of the meaning does not accord with the *Dhātukathā* text, [he says]:

He said, “Now, as for the *Dhātukathā*,” and so forth. Therein, the construction is: “In the *Dhātukathā*, by way of its verbal expression, the inclusion of all consciousness, contact, and feeling has been made.
“With limited scope” means with remainder; the intention is that they are only resultant states.
For when only the resultant states among consciousness and the rest are intended, it is as follows:—

“Those phenomena that are dissociated from resultant phenomena—excluding the unconditioned from the perspective of the aggregates—are included within five aggregates, twelve bases, and thirteen elements.
Within how many are they not included? They are not included in any aggregates, not included in any bases, and not included in five elements.”

The inclusion and non-inclusion of those states dissociated from kamma-result have been answered; in the same way, it should be answered here as well. Therefore he said: "It should be answered in the same manner as for 'resultant states'.

"Therefore" means because, in the exposition of the inclusion and non-inclusion of dissociated states, consciousness, contact, and feeling were taken without exception; "therein" refers to the *Dhātukathā*; "by way of the Abhidhamma-bhājaniya" [is the method].
In this analysis of dependent origination (*paṭiccasamuppādavibhaṅga*), it is according to the *Abhidhamma-bhājanīya* method. Therefore, he says:

"With ignorance as condition, volitional formations [arise]," and so forth. By this, he removes the contradiction shown earlier—that the commentary on the meaning was stated according to the *Suttanta-bhājanīya* method.
If the *Dhātukathā* text proceeds by way of the *Abhidhamma-bhājanīya*, then...

Considering the objection: "Why is *bhava* (existence) explained by way of the appropriated aggregates (*upādinnakkhandha*) as 'sensual existence is comprised of five aggregates, eleven bases, and seventeen elements; fine-material existence is comprised of five aggregates, five bases, and eight elements,' and so forth?
he said: "But *bhava*... [is not] by way of the *Abhidhamma-bhājanīya*."
"Is included. And "having done so" means precisely because it was not included according to the *Abhidhamma-bhājaniya*. "Therein" refers to the *Dhātukathā*.

The word "hi" in the phrase "vipākañhetu" has the sense of a reason (*hetu*). Since the thirty-two types of consciousness mentioned above are resultant (*vipāka*), he says "because consciousness is resultant," and so forth, in order to show this meaning: that [resultant consciousness] has volitional formations as its condition (*saṅkhāra-paccaya*).

The statement, "It was said with reference only to those accompanied by joy (*somanassasahagata*)," must be examined, because it is accepted that even after a wholesome or unwholesome javana accompanied by equanimity (*upekkhāsahagata*), there can be a registration consciousness (*tadārammaṇa*) accompanied by joy. For instance, in the *Aṭṭhakathā*, it is stated:
"At the conclusion of any one of the four types of double-rooted wholesome javanas, a rootless consciousness [arises] as the registration."
Having said, "It is established," it was further stated: "But in the case of a desirable object, both investigation (santīraṇa) and registration (tadārammaṇa) are accompanied by joy alone.
For even an undesirable object, when it is wholesome or unwholesome, sometimes does not occur as neutral due to the way it is conditioned;
however, resultant consciousness experiences the flavor of the object solely according to its own intrinsic nature. Therefore he said:

“It is not possible to evade the result. However, because the functional impulsions (*kiriyajavana*) possess a powerful capacity for the mental formation of an object, it is accepted that the subsequent registration consciousnesses (*tadārammaṇa*) conform to those impulsions by way of feeling, according to their respective objects.
As for those who do not accept a registration consciousness immediately following a functional impulsion, there is simply nothing further to be said. That which...
However, it was stated that "the registration (tadārammaṇa) must be determined by the impulsion (javana)," and it was further stated that this was said with reference to wholesome (kusala) states.

Therefore, what was previously mentioned should be investigated accordingly. The word "and" (ca) has the sense of conjunction, meaning "at the conclusion of a three-rooted impulsion and at the conclusion of a two-rooted impulsion.
Some, however, without making such a distinction, say: "Even at the conclusion of a wholesome impulsion, there is rootless registration..."

They say that the phrase "for the most part" (*yebhuyyena*) is stated because [the state] occurs thus. Or, it is stated as "for the most part" because greed arises frequently in beings. The expression "or once" (*sakiṃ vā*) is stated for the sake of euphony;
he says it should be understood as being like [the expression] "two or three nights," in order to show [the range] from eight or ten. This is because of the absence of the word "or" (*vā*).
This was stated because of the absence of the word "vā" (or) in the recitation; however, in terms of meaning, the word "vā" is indeed present there as well.
But since [the status of] three nights and so forth is already established by the inclusion of two nights, there is no need to mention it separately for three nights;

thus, with the intention that the inclusion of "two nights" is not to be applied independently, it was said, "merely for the sake of euphony in the phrasing. [The term used is] simply "tirattaṃ" (three nights).

When this is stated, one might think that even a period of three nights interrupted by staying elsewhere and so forth should be included; however, since "three nights" as distinguished from "two nights" is being spoken of, it indicates a three-night period that is indeed uninterrupted.
Thus he says: "Or, for the purpose of showing an uninterrupted three-night period.

Regarding the phrase "in an object such as powerful form," this refers to a very great object such as form. By the word "intention" (*adhippāya*), [it is implied] even that which lasts for a single moment of consciousness.
The phrase "at some time with respect to that object" alludes to the meaning already stated in the passage beginning with "only once.
Since it has been stated that "in all doors, only two mental turns for the registration [of an object] are mentioned," this point too should be understood after due consideration.
"By way of a corresponding rebirth-linking" means by the function of rebirth-linking appropriate to each respective individual.
“Since the detailed analysis of rebirth-linking (paṭisandhi), beginning with ‘How many rebirth-linkings are there? How many rebirth-linking consciousnesses?
and so forth, will be explained extensively later, he says: ‘Having made the discussion on rebirth-linking a vast subject, he first demonstrates the process of existence (pavatti) itself.

By the word ‘etcetera’ in the phrase ‘the two rootless [consciousnesses] etcetera,’ he includes the great resultant and sublime resultant [consciousnesses]. The statement regarding the restriction and non-restriction of the doors...”
The statement regarding the door being "determined" or "undetermined" means that it is not stated as either a determined door or an undetermined door.

"From non-arising" means from not arising. Although "rebirth-linking" (*paṭisandhi*) was mentioned below in the phrase "by way of a corresponding rebirth-linking," it is specifically the course of existence (*pavatti*) that is referred to here because of the qualification "but in the course of existence.
Those [factors] previously indicated by way of their status as conditionally arisen (*paccayuppanna*)...
"All mundane resultant consciousnesses also admit of such a designation," thus he said: "Therein, 'of that' means of the thirty-two kinds [of consciousness] during the course of existence.

Just as eye-consciousness and ear-consciousness arise in the fine-material realm (rūpabhava) due to the power of the functioning of the eye and ear faculties—even in the absence of the seed known as sense-sphere rebirth-linking consciousness—likewise, for that same reason, the acceptance consciousness and the others also arise there.
Showing this, he said: “Precisely because of the power of the functioning of the faculties,” and so forth. Therein, the connection is:
“It must exist through the distinction of the eye and ear doors (*cakkhu-sota-dvāra-bhedena*), that is, by way of the specific difference between the eye and ear doors.

“Of that” refers to the eye and ear doors. Since the state of being a door depends upon that which possesses the door, he said: “Because it is dependent on the distinction of the cognitive process (*viññāṇa-vīthi*). And “when that exists” means when that distinction of the doors exists.
And when there is a distinction in the sequence (vīthi). "Bhāva" means arising. "It follows the producer by name" is said by applying that designation to what is similar to it.
"Having stated this" means having stated the non-arising of the resultant consciousness (tadārammaṇa) with respect to states belonging to the fine-material and immaterial spheres.

"By development" (bhāvanāya) means by the increase of defilement through unwholesome development; the meaning is "by the concentration of the defiled. For likewise, even in the arising of a consciousness accompanied by greed or hatred...
Concentration (*samādhi*) is defined as "stability, non-distraction, non-diffusion, and non-diffused state of mind," and so forth.

The phrase "for the purpose of showing the state of being a basis" means for the purpose of showing the state of being a locus, that is to say, for the purpose of showing the state of having no object (*anārammaṇabhāva*).
Regarding the words "by what, where," the meaning stated in brief—namely, "by what consciousness, in what existence"—is now explained in detail.
To demonstrate this, the passage beginning with “nineteen” was stated. Therein, the construction is as follows:

at the moment of rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*), the material and immaterial phenomena that arise together with each respective consciousness—namely, each of the two types of rootless consciousnesses and so forth—are nineteen rebirth-linkings.

This is by way of being the cause through such conditions as co-nascence (*sahajāta*) and so on, acting either as a causal factor (*hetu*) or as an instrument (*karaṇa*). “Therein, there” refers to within each respective existence (*bhava*).
The activity whose purpose is recollection is the "activity of recollection. "Some" refers to the Elder Dhammasiri.

Regarding the phrase "in three cognitive-moment series... must occur," the meaning is that it should proceed through three cognitive-moment series subsequent to the appearance of the kamma and so forth.
Therefore he said: "There is a multiple... and a continuous seizing. "Therefore" means because.
Death does not occur through the mere presence of a single impulsion (javana) or its subsequent stages; therefore [the text says]:

"Of the tangible object" (*phoṭṭhabbassa*), meaning of the tangible object that has been abandoned. While the life-continuum (*bhavaṅga*) is occurring, or while a five-door cognitive process is occurring intermittently, it is logical that first there arises an adverting consciousness of the body door (*kāyadvārāvajjana*) upon contact with a tangible object; nevertheless, when something is being reflected upon...

The intention of the view held by some—that because of the mind’s quality of rapid transformation, the arising of body-door adverting occurs only after the process has proceeded for one impulsion (javana) starting from that very [object]—is as follows:

just as when one who is sleeping awakens through contact with a tactile object, it is only the mind-door adverting that turns toward it, not the body-door adverting. [This is said] regarding the five types of sense-consciousness...
For it is said: “He does not wake up. Or rather, this should be understood in this sense: “light manifestation” means manifesting lightly. The object of the mind-door consists of kamma and so forth.
“Lightness” (lahukatā) means the state of manifesting lightly. “Of forms” refers to the material phenomena such as the eye and so forth.
“Even when there is the state of being an object” means even when there is the presence of objects such as the visible-form base (rūpāyatana). Of those whose object...

"‘Exists’ (atthi)”: this refers to those for whom there is an object in the absolute sense. “For the purpose of showing that very thing” means for the purpose of showing that very [object] which possesses an objective referent (sārammaṇa). “By that” means therefore.

The phrase “by way of the plane, the arising of consciousness, and so forth” is stated with reference to kamma; it is indeed obtainable by way of the sign of kamma as well, because that too has six kinds of objects. However, the classification of the sign of destiny consists only of blue and so forth.
"Uninterrupted" means not abandoned by the Path. "And that [kamma, etc. refers to the kamma and so forth.
This is because the continuum of consciousness has been directed toward another existence due to its being conditioned in such a way by the aspiration for existence (*bhavapatthanā*).

For in whichever continuum of consciousness the cultivation of the aspiration for existence remains uninterrupted—just as it is with volition regarding merit and so forth—it is precisely there that a state of consciousness belonging to another existence arises. And that consciousness...
Thus, as it arises, it is as if led away by that [craving]; hence it is said, “led away by the power of unabandoned defilements.
“In all cases” means in both happy and miserable destinies. “By the other” refers to the death-moment inclined toward rebirth in a happy destiny.
To show the scriptural source for the certainty expressed by the word “nicchinanti,” he says, “clinging to the gratification of signs,” and so forth.
For when the unwholesome state that is a decisive support for a miserable rebirth is determined, the wholesome state as a decisive support for a happy rebirth is likewise determined.
The intention [of the author] is that he mentioned an "unpleasant object" because it is from this that a rebirth-linking in a miserable state is shown.
If this is so, why was it said that it is "the cause of lust and so forth"? He says: "For that too... is," meaning that even the unpleasant object is such. However, because it is inferior...
"Object" (ārammaṇa) here refers to the sign of the deed (kamma-nimitta) that has become the object;
therefore, it is said: "or of those [factors] co-arising with the karma that produces unwholesome resultant," and so forth.

For the object, being the sign of the deed, is the object-condition (ārammaṇa-paccaya) for both those factors co-arising with the karma that generates the result, and for the greed and other [defilements] co-arising with the javana-moments that are similar and proximate to that karma.
In order to show that this very [state] is its inferior condition, the passage beginning with “For that” (*tañhi*) was stated.

It is called "undesirable" (*aniṭṭha*) by way of kamma because it is the object of inferior unwholesome kamma; the intention is that it is undesirable by virtue of being an object, even though it is desirable by its own intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*).
By the passage beginning with “And otherwise,” [the text explains] the unwholesome resultant [consciousness] which has the sign of kamma as its object.

This shows that it is not possible. "In the continuity of the object of the proximate karma" means in the stream of objects of the karma performed immediately prior. "Similar to that" means similar to the object of the aforementioned karma.

"That which presents the object for rebirth-linking" means that which makes the object of rebirth-linking appear. This meaning refers to the fact that the javanas occurring near the moment of death produce rebirth-linking.
Thinking, "It might be obtained," he said, "And not by rebirth-linking," and so forth.
"In the same cognitive series as that" means in the same single series as that rebirth-linking. "Not relished" means not touched by craving, which consists of relishing.

"Completed" means fulfilled or sufficient. From the statement, "At the time of death... [they] are undertaken," it follows that this refers to the impulsions (javana) occurring near the aforementioned death-moment.
He says, "And not by those that are weak," and so forth, with reference to the objection that rebirth-linking (paṭisandhi) is established [by the fivefold sense-consciousness].
With the words, "And he will say," and so forth, he makes the very same point even more evident by way of further elaboration.

For, in the commentary on the *Ñāṇavatthu-vibhaṅga*, while explaining the meaning of the passage, "One does not cognize any state by means of the fivefold sense-consciousnesses," he will say: "All of it... [etc.]".

"...are excluded. In this context, by the word "etcetera" (*ādi*) in the phrase "penetration, etc.," there is included the assuming of postures, the performance of bodily and verbal actions, the establishing [of consciousness], and the undertaking, entering, and emerging from wholesome and unwholesome states.

Since the occurrence of rebirth, dream-vision, and so forth is evident only through mind-door consciousness, he sets those aside and says, "the function ending with death. "Accompanied by impulsion" (*sahajavanakāni*) means together with impulsion; the meaning is: together with the five-door impulsions.
Regarding the phrase "therein": in the commentary on the canonical text (*pāḷivaṇṇanā*), it says, "one does not cognize any state (*dhamma*) by means of the five consciousnesses.
As for the expression "one does not cognize any state," here not all states such as visible forms and so forth are included under the term "state";

rather, in order to show the specific states intended, it is said, "states are preceded by the mind," meaning that one does not cognize even a single wholesome or unwholesome state [by means of the five consciousnesses].
Having shown that this was stated in the *Aṭṭhakathā*, he spoke the passage beginning with "of those" while explaining its meaning.

Its meaning is as follows: for those wholesome and unwholesome states, the nature of being resultants—which is established through their occurrence in the discernment [of objects] and which arises from wise attention (*yonisomanasikāra*) or unwise attention (*ayonisomanasikāra*), and by means of which pleasure or pain follows and pursues that [individual's] continuum—that is the nature of being resultants of the fivefold sense-consciousnesses.
"Rejected" means "prohibited. "Just like that" means exactly similar to the discerning of wholesome and unwholesome states.

Anticipating the objection, "If the process-thoughts accompanied by the impulsions (sahajavana) are prohibited from performing the aforementioned function in the five doors, how can death and rebirth occur therein? he says: "Immediately after that object..."

“...panā” and so forth. Since the state of being mind-door-related (*manodvārika*) in the non-figurative sense is preceded by the arising of mind-door adverting consciousness (*manodvārāvajjana*), he says “with this intention” because that [adverting] is absent.
The construction is: “in the remaining material phenomena (*rūpa*), etc., which last for a single moment of consciousness.

They are to be regarded as similar to access concentration (*upacāra*) because they share the same object and because they are the sign of rebirth (*upapatti-nimitta*). “Some” refers to the Elder Dhammasiri.
He speaks with intentional meaning. Regarding the statement "they speak ending with the sublime":
they say that for one who has emerged from a sublime attainment according to conditions, that cognitive process (*vīthi*) arises, and from that, the death-consciousness (*cuticitta*) occurs.

"The eleven types with past objects" refers to the nine deaths in the sense-sphere happy realms, and the two deaths in the formless realms—the base of infinite consciousness and the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.

Thus, there are eleven types of death in the happy destinies with past objects. There are five belonging to the fine-material sphere, and the remaining two belonging to the immaterial sphere—these seven types of death are to be defined as having unspecified objects.
However, death in the miserable destinies is not included here, as it will be discussed later;
for the author will say: "But death in the miserable destinies... [is] not shown."
By the word "and so forth" (*evamādikā*) in the phrase "and so forth," the statement beginning with "or by a pure impulsion-series" (*suddhāya vā javanavīthiyā*) is included.
For it has been said: "Or by a pure [impulsion-series] means by an impulsion-series having as its object the sign of a sublime kamma.
By the word "is known" (*viññāyati*), although the inclusion of even the objects of immaterial-sphere jhāna is intended by the expression "earth-kasiṇa, etc.," [the specific objects are indicated].
However, he shows that the formulation of an alternative option by means of the two doors alone—namely, "or of the eye and ear"—is an indicator of the intended meaning.
And since an indicator is a recourse when there is no other way, one who does not accept the aforementioned indicator as such says, "But even so," and so forth.
"The application of that which is possible in a given case" is what is meant by "application according to possibility."
"By that. This "rebirth-linking" (*paṭisandhi*) refers to the rebirth-linking that occurs immediately after the death-moment of the formless realm.

"In that very place" refers specifically to the first alternative mentioned in the phrase "the sign such as the earth-kasiṇa, etc. The construction is: "there is no lower and lower rebirth-linking. "Therefore" means for that reason.
"From there" means from the death-moment of the fourth formless realm. "In that very place" means in the fourth formless realm itself. [The consciousness] has a past object.
Rebirth-linking [occurs] from that; then, following the fourth immaterial death-moment, there is rebirth-linking in the sense sphere with past and present objects.
"From the others" means from the immaterial death-moments. He says "as applicable" because the second immaterial rebirth-linking has a past object, while the others have an indeterminable object.
And regarding "rebirth-linking in the sense sphere has past and present objects," here too—
The connection is with the words "the others. And in all instances, the phrase "should be applied" (*yojetabbā*) is to be connected.

"Of this particularity" refers to the particularity already stated by the passage beginning with "by that" (*tena*). A separate extraction is made because an additional statement makes another meaning known.
"In one way by way of object" means in one way by way of having a past object. "Two ways" means [having] a past object and...
And because they have present objects, they are of two kinds. Regarding the death-moment in the woeful planes, the phrase "of one kind" should be brought forward and connected by way of its object.
Sensuous-sphere rebirth-linking is of two kinds by way of having past and present objects; fine-material-sphere rebirth-linking is of one kind by way of having an indeterminable object;
and immaterial-sphere rebirth-linking is of two kinds by way of having an indeterminable past object.
He said: "By way of two, one, and two types of [states] belonging to the sense-sphere, the fine-material sphere, and the immaterial sphere.
By the phrase "in the same way," he draws forward the two phrases: "by way of two, one, and two types of [states] belonging to the sense-sphere, the fine-material sphere, and the immaterial sphere.

"Of two kinds" means being of two kinds by way of not being specifiable as having a past object. "Individually" means separately. Regarding the phrase "of two each of the sense-sphere and immaterial-sphere states," this is the construction.
Following an immaterial-sphere death with an indeterminate object, there are two kinds of sense-sphere rebirth-linking with past and present objects;
two kinds of immaterial-sphere rebirth-linking with an indeterminate object and a past object; and likewise, following a death with a past object as well.
By way of these, it is eightfold.
With the verse beginning “Dvidhā,” he shows the same meaning already stated for the sake of easy comprehension by way of summary.

Although the state of being a decisive support condition (*upanissaya-paccaya*) for the results of karma has indeed been grasped by the phrase “because of having performed the karma” and so forth, the state of being a decisive support condition is nevertheless shown separately by the phrase “wholesome and unwholesome karma” and so forth; thus [the text says] “of the sense-sphere... etc. and so on.
He said, "The state of being a condition for various asynchronous kamma has been shown in its various modes.

By the phrase "by the initial mixed consciousness," he means by the rebirth-linking consciousness (paṭisandhiviññāṇa) which is mixed with material form and constitutes the beginning of a single existence.

"Elsewhere" refers to the moisture-born (saṃsedaja) and spontaneously born (opapātika) modes of birth. Thinking that the non-mention [of certain nutriments] was a negation, [the opponent asks]: "Of the nutriments of odour and taste..."

Having said, "Because it has been rejected," he stated, "Even though the eye, ear, base, seven [mental] factors, life, and six [factors] exist," with the intention that these do not exist at all in the fine-material existence (*rūpabhava*).
"In the text" refers to the text of the *Dhammahadayavibhaṅga*. "The five bases" are the eye, ear, mind, visible-object, and mental-phenomena bases.
"The five elements" are those same five elements. For it is said: "At the moment of rebirth in the fine-material element (*rūpadhātu*), which [elements]..."
Which five bases (āyatana) appear? The eye-base, the form-base, the ear-base, the mind-base, and the mental-object-base.
These five bases appear. Which five elements (dhātu) appear?
The eye-element … [and so on] … the mental-object-element. These five elements appear. Together with the sound-base, there are six bases.
Those same [elements]. "The nine elements" refers to the eye, visible form, eye-consciousness, ear, sound, ear-consciousness, mind, mental phenomena, and mind-consciousness elements.
"By way of the inclusion of all" means by way of grasping them without remainder. "Therein" means in the fine-material element (*rūpadhātu*).
By the phrase "and in the *Kathāvatthu*," etc., it is shown that not only in the text of the *Dhammahadayavibhaṅga*, but also in other treatises (*pakaraṇa*), odors and so forth [are mentioned].
"Rejected" is what is being shown. In that context, "as in the case of the nose-base and so forth" is an illustration by way of a similar example.
Just as the nose-base and so forth exist there in the realm of form (*rūpa-bhava*) and are therefore rejected [as non-existent], so too are the odor-base and so forth.
"Is the nose-base present there? is the question of the proponent of the internal position (*sakavādin*). For whatever base is not present there, [that is what is being questioned]...

This is the challenge. Therefore, the opponent—holding the view that the shape-sign (saṇṭhānanimitta) of the three internal bases, such as the nose and so forth, is itself the "base" (āyatana)—admits, saying, “Yes,” in response.

When questioned regarding the external bases, such as the odor-base (gandhāyatana) and so on, since he does not accept the sensitive matter of the nose (ghānappasāda) and the rest therein, he denies their objective domain (gocara).

“It should not be stated thus,” he rejects [the proposition]. By the word “etcetera” (ādi), one should understand the inclusion of questions concerning the coordination of the direct and reverse orders, which proceed according to the following method: “Is there the tongue-base there? Yes. Is there the taste-base there? It should not be stated thus,” and so forth.
“Of those things that are not the tangible-base” means being devoid of the state of being the tangible-base; the meaning is “of those whose intrinsic nature is not tangible.”
Now, having admitted that smell and taste lack the nature of sense bases (*āyatana*), he speaks of the fault [in doing so] by saying, "And if," and so forth.

There is no reason for them not to be mentioned in the Abhidhamma, which teaches the Dhamma according to its true nature; the intention is that they possess the nature of being insentient and devoid of life.
And just as their status as elements (*dhātu*) is absolute, so too is their status as phenomena (*dhamma*); likewise, their status as sense bases (*āyatana*) is also absolute.

Showing that there is no reason at all not to mention the odor and taste bases (*gandhāyatana* and *rasāyatana*) when they exist there in every respect, he says, "And because of their being phenomena (*dhammabhāvo*)," and so forth.

This is because there is no other ultimate reality (*paramattha*). When one speaks of "some nature of a base" (*āyatanasabhāvo*), it refers specifically to the base of mental objects (*dhammāyatana*).
Therefore, if odors and tastes were present in the form realm (*rūpabhava*), [they would have to be included] for the reasons already stated.
Even if they were not spoken of as being the sense-bases of odor and flavor, they might have been described as being the sense-base of mental objects (*dhammāyatana*); yet they are not so described.
Therefore, one must conclude from this that "odor and flavor do not exist at all in the fine-material existence" (*rūpabhava*).

Furthermore, what else [could there be] for those things which are not mentioned as having the nature of odor and flavor in the fine-material realm (*rūpadhātu*), but are mentioned as such in the sense-sphere realm (*kāmadhātu*)? They cannot be anything other than the nature of odor and flavor.
Is their existence in the form element by way of their own intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*), or rather by way of the intrinsic nature of odor and taste?

If the former position is held, they would be included within the base of mental objects (*dhammāyatana*), because there is no such thing as an intrinsic phenomenon that lacks the intrinsic nature of a base.
If, on the other hand, the latter position is held, for that very reason their status as the bases of odor and taste is established. Demonstrating this point, he said, "And if... and so forth.
Therefore, since odors and tastes are not mentioned in the *Dhammahadayavibhaṅga*, and their existence is denied in the *Kathāvatthu*—
for they cannot be smelled or tasted, being as impossible to perceive as earth and other elements that cannot be touched—
and since they are included by the term "element" (*dhātu*) and their status as phenomena (*dhamma*) is absolute, when that [status] exists...

The existence of the sense bases (āyatana) is established; therefore [it is said]. "In that way" (tathā) means by way of the "eye-septet" (cakkhusattaka) and so forth, omitting those phenomena not mentioned in the canonical text (pāḷi).
"In this way" (evaṃ) refers to when the enumeration of material form (rūpa) is carried out by way of the eye-septet and so forth.

"The nature of phenomena" (dhammatā) refers either to the phenomenon as it appears in the canon (pāḷidhamma), or to the characteristic of the material phenomena that arise within the realm of form (rūpabhava). By the phrase "not inverted" (na vilomitā), he indicates the teaching exactly as it was promised.
And here, because beings of the fine-material sphere lack the sense bases of nose and tongue, odors and tastes—though they do exist—do not perform the function of a sense base.
Therefore, without mentioning them, it is stated in the Canon: "Five bases appear," "Six bases [appear]," and so forth.

Likewise, regarding the phrase "three nutriments," because of the absence of edible nutriment, [only] that which is reckoned as the production of the eightfold materiality consisting of nutritive essence is [intended].

Because it does not perform the function of nutriment, and because odors, tastes, and their nutritive essence are entirely absent [therein], the object is not mentioned, nor is the phenomenon possessing that function.

For in whatever existence the subject (the possessor of the function) is absent, in that existence the status of being a sense-base for the object—which is based upon that subject—does not exist in an absolute sense; thus, even though it exists, it is not mentioned.
Just as, in the fine-material existence (*rūpabhava*), the earth, fire, and air elements possess the status of a sense-base (*āyatana*) by way of being the tangible object-base (*phoṭṭhabbāyatana*).

Furthermore, where there is a mention of something in a particular context, its status as a sense-base is stated and seen in the primary sense (*nippariyāya*) due to the presence of the corresponding subject-object (*visayī*), just as in that very same context for the form-base (*rūpāyatana*).
If the status of an object as a sense-base in the primary sense is caused by the presence of the subject, [then it follows...]

How is it that for the non-percipient beings (asaññasatta) two bases (āyatana) become manifest? For the non-percipient beings have no eye-base (cakkhāyatana), and because they lack the eye-base, the visible-object base (rūpāyatana) is not an object for others. This is not a contradiction.

By the same intention for which the odor-base (gandhāyatana) and so forth are not mentioned among those with perception in the form realm (rūpadhātu), by that same [intention] the visible-object base is also [not mentioned].
It should be stated that for those without perception (*asaññīnaṃ*), one base (*āyatana*) is to be spoken of.

For, when those things which possess the status of a base in an absolute sense—considering their respective nature as faculties and objects—are being pointed out, because [the objects] are absent in the form-element (*rūpadhātu*), the odors and so forth of those with perception are not mentioned separately as bases;
this is because they do not overstep the intrinsic nature (*dhammasabhāva*) of phenomena, and because of the mental consciousness (*manoviññāṇa*).
And because they have attained the state of being objects, they are included within the base of mental phenomena (*dhammāyatana*); thus they are spoken of in the Canon as "the five bases.

For it is for this purpose that the general designation "base of mental phenomena" is applied; or alternatively, having treated them as the "backsides" [of the other bases], they are called "the five bases.
And according to the intention by which the base of visible form (*rūpāyatana*) is said to exist for non-percipient beings, [so too is the base of mental phenomena].
In order to demonstrate this method—that even for those possessing perception, there must be a separate apprehension of odors and so forth—it is said:
"For the non-percipient beings (asaññasatta) gods, two bases (āyatana) become manifest.

For even though their own sense-faculties are absent, there is no transcending the essential nature of the visible base (vaṇṇāyatana) of matter; therefore, that is called simply the "base of visible form" (rūpāyatana). By this...

And by including the three [elements] beginning with odor through the method of inclusion (*nayadassana*), this meaning is shown: that there are eight bases for those with perception and five for those without perception.

This must be accepted in this way; otherwise, because it would be impossible to touch them in the fine-material world (*rūpaloka*), even the sound of speech regarding earth and the other elements would not exist.
For the occurrence of sound does not happen without the friction and impact of resistance.
There exists [earth and so forth], and it is not possible to understand that things whose intrinsic nature is tangible could anywhere have a nature that is intangible.

Furthermore, in the absence of the triad of primary elements (bhūta) comprised within the sense-sphere of the tangible (phoṭṭhabbāyatana), there would be no occurrence even of the sense-spheres of visible form (rūpāyatana) and the rest in the form realm (rūpabhava).
Therefore, although earth and the others are capable of being touched, their status as the tangible (phoṭṭhabba) does not exist there due to the absence of the body-faculty (kāyindriya).
Thus it has been stated. And by doing so, the statement that they possess resistance (*sappaṭigha*) within the fine-material sphere (*rūpadhātu*) is justified. For it is said:
"In the case of non-percipient beings, depending on one invisible and resistant great primary (*mahābhūta*), two great primaries [arise]," and so forth.
Here, "resistance" (*paṭigha*) refers to the state of being directed toward the sensitive body-faculty (*kāyappasāda*) by means of the impact upon the primary elements that serve as its support.
And that [contact] does not exist because there is no impact with something whose nature is incapable of being touched.
Is it not the case that in the phrase “two bases,” a figurative base (*pariyāyāyatana*) is intended; why then, having included the odor-base and so forth, is it not stated as “five bases”?
This very point has already been stated: “The teaching proceeds by way of showing the method. Alternatively, in that context...
The mention of the visible-object base (*rūpāyatana*) alone is sometimes intended with reference to its being the object of the sensitive matter (*pasāda*) belonging to other planes;

it is not, however, because of the non-existence of the others, nor even figuratively, because the odor-base (*gandhāyatana*) and so forth lack the essential nature of a base (*āyatana-sabhāva*) for those beings.

For the visible-object base of non-percipient beings is the object of the gods of the Subhakiṇha (Vehapphala) realm who belong to the same plane, as well as of those belonging to higher planes, namely, the Suddhāvāsa (Pure Abode) deities.
It becomes an object for faith, but since odors and tastes do not [do so], it is appropriate that only those [visible forms] are mentioned there.
Furthermore, in the *Kathāvatthu*, the refutation was made with reference to one who asserts the existence of the odor-base (*gandhāyatana*) and so forth in an absolute sense.
Even if this statement does not explicitly clarify the non-existence of the odor-base and so forth there, [it implies it].
"But is it not the case that even the indication of their existence is merely another statement [and thus not authoritative]?
It is not so; for in the *Aṭṭhakathās*, their existence has been established and explained there.

Whatever statement in the *Aṭṭhakathās* does not contradict the *Pāḷi* is authoritative just like the *Pāḷi* itself, because it has come down to the present day through an unblemished succession of teachers. In this regard:
It might be argued: "Only that which does not contradict the canonical text (pāḷi) is authoritative; however, this [statement] contradicts it.

This is not so, because it has been demonstrated that there is no contradiction. The Blessed One’s teaching on the elements (dhātu-desanā) was for the purpose of demonstrating the emptiness of beings in the sense bases (āyatana) such as the eye, and in the consciousnesses supported by them; thus, it refers precisely to those things already spoken of as sense bases.
Since they illuminate the state of being elements (*dhātu*), it is likewise appropriate that the state of being elements is not mentioned for them; therefore,

one should understand that there is no room for suspicion of contradicting the nature of things (*dhammatā*) here, as the enumeration of material phenomena in the Commentary was made by way of the "eye-decade" (*cakkhudasaka*) and so forth,
in such a way as to avoid conflict with the Canon (*pāḷi*).

The first meaning is that the wool existing at the time of the ewe’s birth is "birth-wool. With reference to its being even finer than that, it is said: "They say... [the fetus] is in the womb," and so forth. "Sambhavabheda" means the breaking up of existence, which is to say, the breaking up of the process of occurrence (*pavatti*).

Regarding the phrase "among the material-brahmā beings" (*rūpībrahmesu*), he states, "He distinguishes the material-brahmā beings from those of the apparitional mode of birth (*opapātikayonika*)," thereby showing that the locative case is used in the sense of a locus (*adhikaraṇa*) for the former, and in the sense of a selection (*niddhāraṇa*) for the latter.
Thus, from the general group mentioned as "among those of the apparitional mode of birth," he specifies them as "the material-brahmā beings."
He determines the distinction. "Does not coincide" means it does not harmonize; the sense is that it is contradictory.
Showing the scriptural passage with which it does not coincide, he says, "In the *Dhammahadayavibhaṅga*," and so forth.
"Eleven" refers to the eleven bases, excluding the sound base (*saddāyatana*), for one whose sense bases are complete. "Ten bases for some" refers to those who lack the mind base (*manāyatana*).
For the blind, there are [the eighteen elements] excluding the eye-base (*cakkhāyatana*). For some, there are the other ten bases, meaning for the deaf, excluding the ear-base (*sotāyatana*).
For some, there are nine bases, meaning for those who are both blind and deaf, excluding both the eye and ear bases. For some, there are seven bases;
this is stated with reference to the womb-born (*gabbhaseyyaka*) being, by way of the visible-form, odor, flavor, body-tangible, mind, and mental-object bases.
The statement, “It is not said that eight bases manifest,” is an explanation of the meaning of the passage beginning with, “For it is not stated in the Pāḷi... [etc. ...stated.
For one being reborn who is deficient in the eye, ear, and nose, there would indeed be only eight bases.
And if there were a rebirth without a nose, it would further have to be stated that “for some, ten other bases manifest.”

It might be so. And if that were the case, then just as it was stated once—on account of one who is both blind and deaf—that "for someone the nine bases manifest," so too it would have to be stated on account of one who is blind but not deaf, and on account of one who is deaf but not blind, that "for someone other [nine bases] manifest, and for someone else other [nine bases] manifest. But this is not so.

The phrase "it is said" indicates this meaning: "In that way... [etc. ...and yet it was not so stated. Thus, regarding the questions on the manifestation of the elements (*dhātu-pātubhāva*) and so forth:
"For some, eleven elements manifest; for some, ten elements; for some, another ten elements; for some, nine elements;
for some, seven elements manifest"—this is the question concerning the manifestation of the elements.

It is to be understood. By the word "etc. (ādi), the questions on the faculties and so forth, which proceed according to the method beginning with "for some fourteen faculties become manifest," are included.
And here, just as the phrase "seventy at most" is applied in this context to the two modes of birth—namely, moisture-born and apparitional—it is not so with the phrase "thirty at least";
rather, this [latter] refers specifically to the moisture-born mode of birth.
It should be joined [to the preceding]; for even a portion of what is indicated as a single compound may receive a connection [with another].

Furthermore, it is stated that for a moisture-born (*saṃsedaja*) being who is blind from birth, deaf, and lacking a nose or genitals, thirty material phenomena arise by way of the decads of tongue, body, and physical basis;
this is not said of a spontaneously born (*opapātika*) being—this is the intended meaning (*adhippāya*) here according to the Commentary (*Aṭṭhakathā*). As for those, however...
Some say, "It is stated in the *Mahā-aṭṭhakathā* that 'for one born spontaneously (*opapātika*) who is blind from birth... [etc. ...they arise,'" but this should not be accepted.
For that is a reading resulting from negligence. And having established it thus, the commentary on the *Āyatana-yamaka* states:

"In the sense-sphere realm (*kāmadhātu*), however, there is no spontaneously born being devoid of eyes. If such were to exist, [the text would have said] 'for some eight bases (*āyatana*) become manifest.'"

"He would say [it]," he will say. However, others have said: "For some eleven bases appear, up to 'for some nine bases'—this text was spoken with reference to those of spontaneous birth (*opapātika*).

Therefore, there is established no contradiction between what precedes and what follows in the commentary; and thus this exegesis of the meaning of the aforementioned text is entirely consistent and harmonious."
However, as for what some say: “By the mention of *opapātika* (spontaneously born beings), moisture-born beings (*saṃsedaja*) are also included.

For instance, in the *Dhammahadayavibhaṅga*, in the enumeration beginning with ‘At the moment of rebirth in the sense-sphere realm, eleven bases appear for some,’ only the term *opapātika* is used—as in ‘for spontaneously born *petas*’—and not the term ‘moisture-born.’”
It should be understood that this is stated by way of including only those moisture-born beings who possess complete sense bases among the spontaneously born.
For he will say: "Those of the moisture-born womb, whether possessing complete sense bases or incomplete sense bases, are stated as being included within the spontaneously born";
and, "Or rather, in order to show the entire womb of complete sense bases under the primary category of womb, [he says] 'of the spontaneously born.'"

And so it is said. However, in the *Aṭṭhakathā*, in order to explain two types of birth (*yoni*) by their specific characteristics and to show that, at the very least, existence occurs even by way of moisture-born birth (*saṃsedaja-yoni*), the term "moisture-born and spontaneously born" (*saṃsedajopapātīsu*) was used without including the other [the womb-born] within the category of spontaneous birth.
All of this must be accepted after careful investigation.
"Of death and rebirth-linking" means: of the death that has just passed away, and of the rebirth-linking immediately following it, which is divided into mixed and unmixed types.
"By aggregates, etc. means by way of the aggregates, the object, the destiny, the root-cause, feeling, zest, applied thought, and sustained thought.
For [a consciousness] with a sublime or internal object, there is a sublime or internal object; for one with an un-sublime or external object, there is an un-sublime or external object.

Because such distinctions as the difference or non-difference between death and rebirth-linking occur only in the formless planes (*arūpabhūmi*), it was said, "having shown merely a methodological approach.

By "certain happy destinies" (*ekaccasugati*), the sublime happy destinies excluding the [formless] are intended; thus he said, "of those belonging to the fine-material and immaterial spheres," and so forth.
However, some say that just as [the formless] excludes the sublime, so too it excludes Uttarakuru. By "death from certain happy destinies":

Regarding the phrase "from death in a happy destination": although there is no fixed rule that "this specific rebirth-linking in an unhappy destination will not occur," they say that the teaching has nonetheless entered the stream of the discourse.
Alternatively, it was stated thus with reference to those Bodhisattvas who are destined for enlightenment;
for some such beings do not undergo rebirth-linking in certain unhappy destinations because they are not reborn in places such as Avīci. [This refers to] "death from certain unhappy destinations."
Here too, the meaning should be understood according to this same method.
Furthermore, "rebirth-linking in some happy destination" should be understood as rebirth-linking in the sense-sphere happy destinations. "By himself alone" means by oneself.
The statement, "And thus the specific distinction has been shown in detail," refers to the passage beginning with "having an object that is not sublime or external."

This was said with intentional meaning (*saṃdhāya*). However, the statement, “There is rebirth-linking for [a consciousness] having four aggregates...,” is merely a demonstration of the non-distinction of its specific varieties.
“In each division” means in each individual portion, such as “having a non-lofty external object” and so forth. “Right there, right there” refers to [the following]:
for one having a non-lofty external object, there is one having a lofty external object; for one having a non-lofty internal object...

The connection between death and rebirth (*cuti-paṭisandhi*) should be understood according to each specific classification—such as "having a sublime internal object" and so forth—or by way of one passing away from this or that very state of existence (*bhava*) and being reborn.
Showing that the word *to* here has the sense of the locative case, he said: "from that cause without [it], or there without the cause. Its meaning is: in that previous existence...
A completed state does not exist without causes such as ignorance and volitional formations (*avijjā-saṅkhāra*).

Reaching a state of extreme feebleness is the incapacity to perform its own function. Death by way of the five sense-door consciousnesses is excluded, but not by way of the consciousness immediately following them.
This meaning was already established in the sub-commentary (*aṭṭhakathā*) below, starting with the words "of the five doors."
He said: “For even immediately after the five-door consciousness, death was previously shown. Regarding this, what ought to be said has already been stated above.
The passage beginning with “And in the Yamaka” was spoken to show that the cessation of the eye-base and so forth occurs together with the death-consciousness.
“Because it has reached its culmination” means, by way of its full maturation, it has gone to its end; this is the intended meaning.
Contact and the rest refer to the contact and other factors co-arising with the aforementioned volition.

Through their repeated arising upon an object such as karma as it presents itself, there is a conditioning of the continuum, which serves as the cause for the establishment of rebirth-linking consciousness therein.
This is because the functions of bending and so forth, which are accomplished through the continuum, achieve their purpose in that single instance of rebirth-linking consciousness alone.

Showing this, he says: "It demonstrates... pe ... it demonstrates. "By means of its own power and effort upon the earth" means by the power of the earth acting as a support, and by its own effort acting as the instrument.
"Caused by sound" is said with reference to sound being the primary factor and so forth. Such a place as the interior of a mountain cave and the like [is also included].
It is for that very reason. By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*) in the phrase "other lamps, etc.," one includes things such as oil and wicks.

This is because they do not exist prior to the occurrence of the sound and so forth. For if echoes and the like were to exist prior to the occurrence of the sound and so forth—assuming their prior establishment—they would have to go to the location of the conditions for those sounds and so forth;
however, they do not exist. Thus it is said: "because they do not exist prior to that. The same meaning applies to the object of comparison (*upameyya*) as well.
It should be joined [to the previous]. And just as it does not go to the location of the cause from which it has arisen, so too it does not come from there;
thus he said, "Therefore... not... come. Those sounds and so forth are the conditions for these, hence they are "conditioned by those" (*tappaccayā*).

"By the method stated" means by the very method stated in the simile. Having been present in the location of the cause of the previous existence, the rebirth-linking consciousness (*paṭisandhiviññāṇa*) [arises] from there...
The meaning is that it does not arise on account of that [condition] by going elsewhere to another existence (*bhavantara*).

The first meaning is that what is being produced from a condition arises as a "condition-produced" (*paccayuppanna*) phenomenon without having gone elsewhere, but rather while remaining precisely in the location of the condition.
Having first come together with the condition, it then goes elsewhere to become the locus of the condition-produced phenomenon.

"Does not incur [a fault]" is the second meaning. "According to what is possible" refers to the application of faults regarding absolute identity and difference made in the case of milk and curd, such as:
"Curd would not have arisen from milk; curd would not belong to the owner of the milk.
By this method, [the same applies] to all causes, such as seeds, and to all things produced from those causes, such as sprouts, according to what is possible.
The application of faults should be made according to the cause and according to what arises from the cause.
Since the grasping at eternalism has been refuted by the negation of absolute oneness among phenomena bound to a continuum, it is said:
"It prevents this view that pleasure and pain are self-made. Likewise, by the negation of absolute difference, the grasping at annihilationism is refuted.
He said: “This [teaching] prevents the view that ‘happiness and suffering are made by another; one person acts and another experiences [the result].

By this, the destruction of what was not done and the arrival of what was not done are excluded. Thus, it should be understood that by the very prevention of the view of fortuitous origination (*adhiccasamuppanna*), the refutation of the doctrines of necessity (*niyati*) and intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*) is also accomplished.”

*Therein*: in the continuity of primary and derived matter known as the series beginning with the sprout. *That*: proficiency in knowledge and so forth. *Of another*: than the mastery of knowledge acquired during childhood and so on. *A condition other than the formation*:
