craving and so forth, which are conditions distinct from that formation. *The fruit of handing over and so forth*: the result consisting of handing over and so forth; that which has not borne fruit [yet] but possesses the fruit of handing over and so forth is "aphalitaniyyātanādiphalam";

... [the term] *phala* refers to the performance of the aforementioned action. *By way of a whole*: by way of the aggregate whose constituent parts have not been analyzed. *In all cases*: in the case of the formation of merit and so forth.
In all conditioned phenomena (paccayadhamma), or in the phenomena arisen from conditions (paccayuppannadhamma) at the moment of rebirth-linking (paṭisandhi).
This should be applied according to the influence of powerful karma. For a strong support is indeed a decisive support (upanissaya).

Although it is stated "without distinction," the formation of merit belonging to the sense-sphere (kāmāvacara-puññābhisaṅkhāra) [acts as a condition] for the five [consciousnesses] such as eye-consciousness during the course of existence (pavatta), while the other [formation of demerit] acts as a condition for the first jhāna resultants and so forth, both during the course of existence and at rebirth-linking.
Regarding the phrase "it is a condition": since this meaning is already evident, it was stated without further analysis simply as "it includes all volitional formations of merit.
The expression "the twelvefold division of unwholesome volition" is not a compound word; rather, it is stated by means of euphonic conjunction (*sandhi*).

Furthermore, "in twelve" (*dvādasasu*) is a nominative plural used in the sense of a locative, meaning "among the twelve unwholesome types of volition. Thus, "the division of unwholesome volition" refers to these twelve.
The meaning should be understood as follows: the classification of eleven unwholesome volitions (*akusalacetanā*) and the classification of twelve unwholesome volitions.

This being so, there is nothing further to be investigated here, as it has already been explained in detail below. However, some say that the phrase "the classification of twelve unwholesome volitions" should be connected with the passage beginning "of six in the course of existence" (*channaṃ pavatte*);
according to their opinion, [this refers] to the volition of restlessness (*uddhaccacetanā*).
The purpose for including [this] must indeed be considered, since it has been stated that [the object] is also a condition for rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*).
Regarding the word "of one" (*ekassa*), he says, "the restriction to the conditionality of one alone," because the particle *eva* is indicated here as being elided. "Of withered garlands, etc.
means of withered garlands, soiled clothes, and so forth. How is it that even other bases for those possessed of mental corruption (*manopadosika*) are undesirable?

The intended meaning is that it may or may not exist. However, because of the lack of abundance [of such things] in the commentaries (*aṭṭhakathā*), that point was not addressed there, and instead it was stated:
“Likewise, even in the world of the sense-sphere devas. Some, however, say: “In the world of the devas, what is called ‘undesirable’ exists only by way of conceptualization;
but in its actual nature, whatever arises there is indeed desirable.”
By the phrase “even the twenty-nine types of volition,” he allows that even the volition of restlessness (uddhacca-cetanā) can give rise to occurrence-resultant (pavatti-vipāka);
or rather, he says this according to the intention of the Aṭṭhakathā.
Regarding the thirteen remaining types of rootless resultant consciousness after removing two from the fifteen: there are two each for the eye- and ear-receiving consciousnesses, and three...

"Investigations" refers to the nine [types]. "By way of being a partial condition" means that the aggregate consisting of twenty-nine types of volition is stated by way of being a condition for a part—namely, the twenty-fold classification of volitional formations (*saṅkhāra*) belonging to sense-sphere consciousness.
"That very same [aggregate]" is expressed by the distinction residing in its parts, just as one says, "the prince is adorned."

"Where" refers to the five-aggregate existence (*pañcavokārabhava*). For therein, in the passage beginning with "First, for one situated in a happy destination of the sense-sphere," an extensive exposition of the result of kamma is given regarding both rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*) and the course of existence (*pavatti*). "The plane of the fourth jhāna" refers to the plane of the Vehapphala deities.
Therefore he says, "excluding the non-percipient and the formless. For it is the fourth jhāna itself, when practiced with a specific degree of development, [that leads to that state].
It should be understood that the commentary is stated according to the fourfold method by way of accomplishing the plane of non-perception and the formless plane.
There are eight great resultants, the last among the limited resultants, and five fine-material-sphere resultants; thus, there are fourteen.
"Of seven" refers specifically to the remaining seven limited resultants.

"Bhavādayo" means the realms of existence (bhava), matrices (yoni), destinies (gati), and abodes of beings (sattāvāsa). "Of the three consciousnesses" refers to the three preceding resultant consciousnesses of the formless realm (āruppa-vipāka-viññāṇa). "In the three" refers to the three stations of consciousness (viññāṇaṭṭhiti) beginning with the fifth.

"By the method stated" refers to the method already explained: "But in the sensual realm (kāmabhava), in the miserable states (duggati), the condition for all eight limited resultant consciousnesses exists likewise during the course of existence (pavatta), but not at rebirth-linking (paṭisandhi)," and so forth.
The commentary on the exposition of the term *viññāṇa* is finished.
Commentary on the exposition of the terms *nāma* and *rūpa*. 228.
Although there is a difference in the teaching of the term *rūpa* in the exposition of dependent origination (*paṭiccasamuppāda*) both in the Suttanta and in the Abhidhamma, [the following applies].
However, in the Abhidhamma, there is indeed a difference in its teaching from that of the Suttanta, as seen in such passages as "All matter is not a root-cause" (sabbaṃ rūpaṃ na hetū).

Therefore, he said: "From the Suttanta... there is a difference. Regarding the enumeration, since the limit is grasped through delimitation, the numerical delimitation therein is established by implication;
thus it was said: "But in terms of meaning, it is already stated."
Regarding the phrase "among beings of spontaneous birth" (*opapātika-sattesu*): either all spontaneous beings are mentioned collectively;

or, since by the mention of the "Brahma-body" (*brahmakāyika*) and so forth, only those belonging to the fine-material sphere (*rūpāvacara*) are stated, the inclusion of the term "the rest of the spontaneous beings" (*sesa-opapātikānaṃ*) is indeed purposeful, as it refers to those other than them.
"By the method already stated" means by the method stated for consciousness mixed with form, beginning with: "two or three decads, together with the first [decad], when subtracted," and so forth.

The phrase “ending with the sevenfold [set]” is stated with reference to the portion of the commentary text beginning from “Two are the peaks of the continuity” up to “Seven are the peaks of the continuity.
By saying “with this intention,” he means that he does not allow for the arising of material form three times within each single moment of consciousness;
rather, his own intention is that all material form arises at the very moment of the consciousness’s arising.

“Born of kamma that does not produce matter” (rūpājanakakammaja) should be understood as a mere statement of fact, because the fivefold sense-consciousnesses lack the nature of being co-nascent with matter.
Alternatively, “born of kamma that does not produce matter” is said with reference to the death-consciousness (cuticitta).

However, the rebirth-linking consciousness (paṭisandhicitta) is excluded by the very term “during the course of existence” (pavattiyaṃ). As stated in the *Aṭṭhasālinī-ṭīkā*: “The death-consciousness of all beings does not arouse matter.”

This very meaning has already been stated. It was said, “with reference to the time of the occurrence of the fivefold sense-consciousness,” because during the moment of the fivefold sense-consciousness there is no arising of material phenomena conditioned by it.

Even there, however, there is indeed the arising of material phenomena conditioned by consciousness that is not co-nascent; therefore he said, “and conditioned by co-nascent consciousness. “Life-continuum, etc.
refers to the life-continuum, reception, investigation, and registration [consciousnesses]. “By another” means other than the aforementioned kamma-consciousness.

By another [type of] formative consciousness (*abhisaṅkhāraviññāṇa*). For it is material form alone that arises at the moment of the occurrence of wholesome, unwholesome, or functional consciousness by way of the condition of formative consciousness;
not the mental factor (*nāma*) of the life-continuum (*bhavaṅga*). "By its producer" means by that which produces the life-continuum and so forth.

At the time of the occurrence of resultant consciousness, this occurs by way of resultant mentality and kamma-originated materiality, conditioned by the kamma-consciousness. [This is] by way of the condition of co-nascent consciousness (*sahajātaviññāṇapaccaya*).

However, since the arising of name-and-form (nāmarūpa) must be shown even at the time of the occurrence of other types of consciousness—by way of the designation "resultant" for the resultant [consciousness] itself, and by way of the materiality originated by that consciousness—it is said: “Sahajāta...

should be connected. And the word *rūpa* is to be construed with the phrase “one part of itself,” according to the rule: “Of words having the same form, one part [is used when they have the same case-ending]” (Pāṇini 1.2.64).
With reference to the characteristic of sound (*saddalakkhaṇa*), he says: "A portion of those that are similar in form" (*sarūpānaṃ ekadeso*).

For even among those whose forms consist of a single part, a portion is intended, as in the expression "by those shown and by their opposites. Here, the meaning is: "the shown," "the opposite of the shown," and "both the shown and the opposite of the shown.
By the word "place" (*ṭhāna*), he expresses the meaning of the remainder (*sesa*). For here, "placing together" (*ṭhapana*) by way of similarity of form is what constitutes being a "remainder."
Because the words *yaṃ* and *taṃ* have an inseparable connection, he brings forward the word *tato* even though it was not explicitly stated, and says:

"Therefore, this should be construed as 'this is indeed appropriate' (*yuttameva*). "Non-productive of result" (*vipākājanaka*) means that which does not produce a ripening result (*vipāka*); it refers to karma that yields only a flow-on result (*nissandaphala*).

"Originated from that non-productive-of-result karma" (*vipākājanakakammasamuṭṭhāna*) means that which has such karma as its source. "In the manner already stated" refers to [the classification] by way of the physical basis (*vatthu*) and the body (*kāya*).

According to the method stated in such passages as, "From the perspective of form, there are two continuities (santatisīsa) and three immaterial aggregates," and so forth. "Both" refers to name and form.

Regarding the phrase "at the time of the rebirth-linking (paṭisandhi) conditioned by kamma and its object," the word "etc. (ādi) should be understood here as including the time of comprehension (sammasana) and so on. "That" refers to the volitional consciousness (abhisaṅkhāraviññāṇa).
Although the conditionality of consciousness for form is established by the Sutta through statements such as, "There is form originated by mind," and so forth...

The dependence of mind (nāma) on consciousness (viññāṇa) is established by reasoning, because desirable experiences and so forth—which are based on consciousness—are present when that [consciousness] exists and absent when it does not, just as faith and other qualities exist in relation to objects such as those worthy of trust.
However, showing the meaning already stated in the Commentary, [the text says]: "Mind is to be known from the Sutta... and so forth.

He said: By showing that the teaching on dependent origination (*paṭiccasamuppāda*) is precisely the turning of the wheel of Dhamma (*dhammacakkappavattana*)—insofar as it demonstrates, without error, the process of occurrence and cessation by way of revealing the mere nature of conditions and the phenomena arisen from conditions—he spoke the words beginning with "Because" (*yasmā*).

Furthermore, because the teaching of the truths (*saccadesanā*) itself is the teaching of the mode of conditions (*paccayākāradesanā*) through its revelation of occurrence and cessation, it is the teaching of the truths.
And [it refers to] the setting in motion of the Wheel of Dhamma. As it is said: "Bhikkhus, 'This is suffering'...
[and so on] ...the unsurpassed Wheel of Dhamma was set in motion by me at Bārāṇasī, in the Deer Park at Isipatana," and so forth.

Therefore, in order to show that the phrase "with consciousness as condition, name-and-form" constitutes the setting in motion of the Wheel of Dhamma by way of illustrating its nature as a teaching on the Truths, it is said: "Or rather, by the very statement of the mere nature of name-and-form," and so on.
The commentary on the exposition of the terms for name-and-form is finished.
Commentary on the exposition of the terms for the six sense bases (229):

"According to their occurrence" means in accordance with how they arise. By that [phrase], first, in the case of the four primary elements, [they are related] by way of co-nascence, support, presence, and non-disappearance.
The five bases, beginning with the eye-base, function as conditions [for their respective consciousnesses].

Regarding the physical bases, however, the heart-base serves as the sixth base for rebirth-linking by way of being conascent, a support, mutually related, dissociated, present, and non-disappeared. During the course of existence, since the physical basis arises simultaneously with the immediately preceding consciousness, it acts as its support through its powerful state of persistence.
It is able to exist [as a condition], but not as a co-nascent one;

therefore, it should be understood that its status as a condition for the other bases is stated by way of the relations of pre-nascence, support, dissociation, presence, and non-disappearance, and for the sixth base—consisting of the fivefold consciousness—by way of the faculty-condition, and for the life-faculty by way of the relations of faculty, presence, and non-disappearance. "In exactly one manner" means...

Just as the eye and the other [sense bases] have a fixed conditionality in one specific way because they conform to their respective restricted functions such as seeing for the mind-base (manāyatana), it is not so with the visible-form base (rūpāyatana) and the others;
rather, their conditionality for that [mind-base] occurs through a different mode, namely by way of being the object (ārammaṇa) of form and so on.
Therefore, it is said to be "by way of non-fixity" (aniyamato). Some, however, take the term "by way of fixity" (niyamato) to mean "included within one's own continuity" (sasantatipariyāpanna).
Connecting with this, they explain the meaning as: "exclusively included within one's own continuity.

By means of the analysis "the sixth base and the mind-base are the 'sixth base'," he demonstrates that [the term] is identical in meaning with the other two [terms], both in terms of sound and in terms of meaning, and identical in form.
[It is said to be] "called 'six bases' (saḷāyatana) together with the eye-base and so forth."

Having applied the grammatical rule of *ekasesa* (retention of one from a group) according to the method already stated, the mental base (*manāyatana*) together with the eye-base and the others is called "the six bases" (*saḷāyatana*) in the Canon, as in the passage:
"With name-and-form as condition, the six bases. "As already stated" refers to the manner explained by himself [in the preceding commentary], beginning with: "The sixth base and the mental base.
"In all instances" refers to the cases where there is similarity of sound with the term "name-and-form" and the term "six bases."

Or [regarding] the conformity with the meaning. If, in the *Suttantabhājanīya*, only the resultant sixth base (*vipākachaṭṭhāyatana*) was intended, then why was it said, "But the other," and so forth?
Anticipating the objection that "for there, the 'other' is intended to be non-resultant (*avipāka*"), he says, "But in the method of conditions (*paccayanaye*)," and so forth.
The mode of conditionality should be understood as tenfold by including the conditions of root, nutriment, and faculty among the co-nascent and so forth; then as ninefold by removing one from those;

and then as eightfold by removing another. Thus, in this context, the minimum is to be understood by way of what is common to all, while the maximum is by way of the specific factors such as the roots, as well as by way of the jhānas and so forth.

Since immaterial phenomena serve as conditions for the arising moment of kamma-born materiality at the moment of rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*), he specifies [the context] by saying "in the course of existence" (*pavatte*). By the restriction "only those such as the postnascent dissociated [condition]," he excludes the co-nascent, prenascence, dissociated, and other such conditions.

To show that the inclusion of the term "remaining" (*avasesa*) in the phrase "of the remaining mind-base" refers specifically to a distinct scope according to the context, he says "in the existence consisting of the five aggregates," etc.;
for this reason, the *Aṭṭhakathā* states "the physical basis (*vatthurūpa*)," and so forth. [This applies] as far as possible.
"It should be applied" means that for name-and-form at rebirth-linking, the state of being a condition such as co-nascence, mutuality, support, presence, and non-disappearance—

the state of being a common condition such as co-nascence and so forth— and the state of being a condition such as association, resultant cause, nutriment, and faculty— the state of being a specific condition such as association and so forth—
should be applied to name; whereas for form, the state of being a dissociation condition should be applied.
The commentary on the exposition of the sixfold base is finished.
Commentary on the exposition of contact (230):
"By way of its non-differentiation" means by way of the non-differentiation of that contact; the meaning is, by way of the commonality of the state of being contact.
"It is not fitting for the word [to apply] to one alone" means it is not fitting for the word to apply to only one. "Also for another" means also for one other than the aforementioned.

By the objection that contact cannot possibly arise from a single sense-base (*āyatana*) among all the sense-bases, he shows—by means of that consequence—that there is no possibility of even several [contacts] arising from a single sense-base;
this is for the purpose of making known that "no such natural law exists," as indicated by the phrase "also for another," and so forth.
"By way of illustration" means by way of showing an example. "Because of the occurrence of a single contact" is a reference to the cause. The construction is as follows:
he shows the resolution that the Blessed One said, "Contact has the six sense bases as its condition," because the occurrence of a single contact is indeed possible.
"In the remaining [cases]" refers to the phrases beginning with "one. When the conditionality is ninefold, one [is] the resultant mind-base (*vipākamanāyatana*).
I shall analyze it. And likewise, by way of object-prenascence, presence, and non-disappearance.

To show for which [states] this conditionality exists, he said: "It was said with reference to present [states]," and so forth. Because even those [states] liberated from past and future time can exist as mere objects, he said:
"It was said with reference to the mere object," and so forth. In that context, "that" refers to the sense-sphere of visible form and the rest.
The commentary on the exposition of the section on contact is finished.
Commentary on the exposition of the section on feeling (231):
"By the immediate and so forth" means by way of the conditions of immediacy, contiguity, decisive support, absence, and disappearance. "Decisive support" (upanissaya) [is explained as follows].

Regarding the proximity-object-condition (*anantarūpanissaya*): for the proximity and contiguity conditions are included within the proximity-object-condition precisely by way of their state of being immediate.
Furthermore, the absence and disappearance conditions are included therein because they possess that same nature as the phenomena of the proximity and contiguity conditions.
"Of that" refers to the object-predominance condition (*upanissaya*).

"Of all" means of both resultant and non-resultant [contact]. For mental contact, which is co-nascent with feeling associated with the rebirth-linking, life-continuum, and death consciousnesses, is a condition in eight ways according to the method already stated.

That which is immediate is a condition by way of the immediate condition (*anantara-paccaya*) and so forth; that which is not immediate is a condition solely by way of the decisive support condition (*upanissaya-paccaya*).
This should be understood as a demonstration of their possible occurrence, not as a demonstration of their status as door-objects for the mind-door.
The commentary on the explanation of the section on feeling is finished.
Commentary on the explanation of the section on craving (232):

Just as the vitality and life-force produced by elixirs [are dependent on them], so too should the pleasure caused by that [feeling] and the suffering such as aging which is to be removed from it be connected to the state of having phenomena as their object.

Since beings also accumulate kamma by way of aspiring for the fruits of kamma, the feeling that is the result (vipāka) is a particularly strong decisive support (upanissaya) for craving, whereas other feelings are not so;
thus he said: “The result [is a support] specifically... and the other [feeling] generally.
Here, “the other” means non-resultant feeling. The phrase “spoken of simply as pleasure” refers specifically to equanimity that has a desirable nature.

It is stated [as such], not as having an undesirable nature. Therefore he said, “But equanimity,” and so forth. “Of all” means of any person possessing feeling, whether they are not free from lust or are free from lust.

The restriction “only with feeling as condition” is intended to exclude other restrictions; it should not be understood as having the purpose of excluding other conditions. By this, the denial of other things arising from that condition is also excluded.
The commentary on the exposition of the term *taṇhā* (craving) is finished.
Commentary on the exposition of the term *upādāna* (clinging): 233.
"The former view" refers to the adherence to eternalism (*sassatagāha*) previously settled upon, namely, "the self is eternal."
This has been stated. Therefore he said: “The grasping of a self... should be seen. *Upādiyamānaṃ* means grasping. “The world” or “grasping”:
the meaning is that the grasping which holds “the world is eternal” is a view (*diṭṭhi*). Therefore he said: “consisting of the clinging to views (*diṭṭhupādāna*)”.
“A compendium of phenomena... merely a view”: this is a demonstration of the connection between the words that have been separated [in the text].
In this context, the intention is that, in brief, the four types of clinging consist simply of the intensity of craving and, in brief, mere views.

Regarding "from the summary and detailed exposition of the phenomena" (*dhammasaṅkhepavitthārato*): from the summary and detailed exposition of the phenomena as a whole, one extracts the summary and the detailed exposition of its constituent parts.

The construction is: "the grasping at a self preceded by the grasping at eternalism, and the grasping at a self preceded by the grasping at annihilationism. "Of these" refers to the aforementioned graspings at eternalism and annihilationism;
it is the master [of them] because, as their root, it is that which establishes them. "By the first, etc. means by the statement beginning with "first, the clinging to the doctrine of self.
That craving for existence (*bhavanikanti*) is the passion for existence by which one, with a mind intoxicated, performs the karma that produces existence and is thereby reborn.
Because they persist for a long time in the continuum and arise repeatedly, they occur as soon as one is reborn; thus he said, "Even though...

because it must continue to proceed. Since even the lust for existence (*bhavarāga*) is subject to the path of Arahantship, it indeed possesses the nature of clinging to sense-pleasures (*kāmupādāna*);
therefore he said, "thinking that there is no intensity of craving (*taṇhādaḷhatta*). For even the lust for existence proceeds strongly within its own domain.
Regarding the statement "all craving is clinging to sense-pleasures" (*kāmupādāna*), here too it should be connected by supplying the phrase "its exclusion by the path of arahantship has been stated.
The intended meaning is that [craving] is the source of arising, not the object. "By that" means by way of being the basis (*ālaya*) for the aggregates.

"Object, proximity, natural, and decisive support" refers to the decisive support of the object (*ārammaṇūpanissaya*), the proximity decisive support (*anantarūpanissaya*), and the natural decisive support (*pakatūpanissaya*).
"Of the conditions such as the proximity condition" means of the proximity, contiguity, object, and other such conditions.
The commentary on the exposition of the section on clinging is finished.
Now begins the commentary on the exposition of the section on existence (*bhava*).

234. “*Bhavatī*” is the etymological derivation (*nibbacana*) for *upapatti-bhava* (existence as rebirth). “Of the two” refers to the two types of existence: kamma-existence (*kamma-bhava*) and rebirth-existence (*upapatti-bhava*). “The fruit of production” (*nipphādana-phala*) is the capacity to bring about the arising of a fruit. “Production” (*nipphādana*) means generation.

In the phrase “rooted in the Blessed One” (*bhagavammūlakā*), although it should have been stated as “existence through perception” (*saññāvaṃbhavo*), the word *vaṃ* is indicated as being elided in the sense of “there is” (*atthi*);
thus he says “existence through perception” (*saññābhavo*). Or, “in its meaning” means in the meaning of that word *vaṃ*, that is, in the sense of “there is.”

"Having made the suffix -a" means: just as the word *jhāna-pītisukha* is used by adding the suffix -a to express the sense "that which has joy and bliss," and thus it is said "jhāna is joy and bliss," so too, [one who] has perception is "percipient" (*saññī*), and that very state of being percipient is "perceptual existence" (*saññā-bhava*).

"In one" refers to the aggregate of form alone. "Because it occurs" is said by way of figurative usage (*upacāra*), even though there is no distinction between the agent of occurrence and the locus of occurrence.
It shows [the result] as if it were separate.
"The continuum consisting of kamma" refers either to that which is to be called "kamma" or to the constituent parts of kamma.

Even in the Sutta, the nature of volition (*cetanā*) as kamma has been established in such passages as: "Bhikkhus, I say that volition is kamma. However, in the ultimate sense (*nippariyāyena*), it is volition alone.
Establishing the meaning already stated by means of the Abhidhamma Piṭaka itself, he says, "For it is said," and so forth.

For by this passage from the *Dhātukathā*—which states that the kamma-existence (*kammabhava*) is associated with the aggregates of feeling, perception, and consciousness; with the mind-base (*manāyatana*) and the mind-consciousness-element (*manoviññāṇadhātu*);

and with a portion of the aggregate of volitional formations (*saṅkhārakkhandha*), the mental-object-base (*dhammāyatana*), and the mental-object-element (*dhammadhātu*)—its nature as volition (*cetanā*) is illuminated.

"By way of the differentiation of phenomena" means by way of the classification of phenomena according to their association with volition or non-volition, and according to their being wholesome, unwholesome, or indeterminate.
By the very phrase "repetition," the opponent's apprehension—that the fault of tautology has been admitted—is shown;

thus he says: "If it is argued that this repetition is not appropriate because it lacks a purpose. "By way of being a part of existence" means because it is a portion of kamma-existence (*kammabhava*).
[This refers to] formations (*saṅkhārā*). By this, he shows that it has already been stated: "Formations are a part of those phenomena whose aggregate is called 'existence' (*bhava*);

and a part of an aggregate is indeed distinct in meaning [from the whole]. Furthermore, having kept in mind the very same distinction as previously stated, he says "or by the subsequent [passage]" and so forth, demonstrating the absence of a redundant statement in terms of meaning.

“Included within” means included within the existence of sensual desire (*kāmabhava*) and so forth, such as the existence of perception (*saññābhava*). “The existence of sensual desire and so forth” refers to the existences of sense-sphere, fine-material, and immaterial realms (*kāma-rūpa-arūpabhava*).
“Distinction of clinging” refers to the specific types of clinging, beginning with clinging to sensual desires (*kāmupādāna*).

“By that” means by the clinging to rules and observances (*sīlabbatupādāna*). “To be explained” refers to the passage in the Commentary beginning with, “This is what is called ‘rules and observances’,” and so on.
In the manner that will be explained. "Ancient" refers to the *Brahmaṇḍa*, *Liṅga*, *Khaṇḍa*, *Purāṇa*, and so forth.

The "sacrificial rite involving animal slaughter" (*pasubandhavidhi*) is the procedure for sacrifice connected with the injunction for killing animals, such as: "One desiring prosperity should begin the *Setavadha* sacrifice," and so on.

Because it consists merely in clinging to one's own path of purification, the clinging to rules and observances (*sīlabbatupādāna*) is stated to be the cause for the clinging to a theory of self (*attavādupādāna*).

They exist as path-conditions because they have the nature of wrong departure. However, since the state of being a condition for clinging by way of proximity, contiguity, immediate-proximity, decisive-support, presence, absence, and repetition toward the immediately preceding existence of sensual desire and kamma is already evident, it has not been stated.
The commentary on the explanation of the section on existence is finished.
Commentary on the Exposition of the Terms Birth, Aging, Death, and so forth: 235.

"The arising of rebirth-existence" (*upapattibhavuppatti*) means the arising of the appropriated aggregates (*upādinnakkhandha*) within the rebirth-existence (*upapattibhava*), or by way of the state of rebirth-existence.
It refers to the aggregate that is being born. Birth (*jāti*) is the transformation consisting in manifestation. Rebirth-existence itself is also a condition for birth.
Why? Because the construction is: "If there is no state of rebirth, there is an absence of birth.
By the phrase "being the proximate cause (*padaṭṭhāna*) for the form that is being born," etc., he likewise clarifies its status as a condition for birth.

Even though external conditions such as semen and blood exist, along with specific internal causes residing in the parents, [birth] is nonetheless not fixed; and since it is the distinction of being inferior, superior, and so forth that is intended here, it is said: "Because of the absence of internal... [etc.]..."
The commentary on the exposition of the terms beginning with birth, aging, and death is finished. Commentary on the Discourse on the Wheel of Existence (Bhavacakka): 242.
That which has come together (*itaṃ*) from this [connection] is "conjoined" (*samita*). Therefore, he said "assembled" (*saṅgata*).
Craving for existence (*bhava*) is passion for existence (*bhavarāga*). "Hearing talk of the formless" refers to hearing talk appropriate to that foolish state of acting improperly.
By this, he shows suffering caused by the reproach of others and so forth; by the phrase "the sight of judicial punishment," he shows that which is caused by physical chastisement;
and by the other [phrase], that which is caused by rebirth in the miserable destinies (*duggati*). "They lead" means they make known. Also, by the result...
For a cause is known by its infallible effect, just as rain falling in the upper region is known by the great flood resulting from it as the sign of rain.
Therefore it is said, "awakening.

The word *matta* has the sense of excluding a distinction, as in such expressions as "without applied thought and with sustained thought only" (*avitakkavicāramattā*). When ignorance (*avijjā*) is not yet abandoned, and the causal conditions are obtained...

He said, "by making [the object] present," meaning that it is in the very vicinity of one who has attained the state of an Arhat through rebirth (*uppattiarahatā*). "Vedayati" means he experiences (*vedeti*).
Its synonym is "he undergoes" (*anubhavati*). Alternatively, "vedeti" means he makes or produces knowledge (*veda*);

its synonym is "he knows" (*jānāti*). Furthermore, regarding the term "vediyati," since it is a designation based on the relationship between the object, the agent, and the action, he shows its meaning as well:
He said: “It is known, and it is cognized. The meaning of the word *ca* (and) is that of conjunction;
the sense is that it is devoid of both a creator such as Brahmā and a feeler such as a self. He calls this a compound with the meaning of the word *ca*, namely a *dvanda* compound.
Alternatively, he speaks with reference to the fourfold emptiness: emptiness of permanence and so forth, and emptiness of a self and so forth.

"From the past" means from the past division. The phrase "or feeling," and so forth, was stated to show that the wheel of existence (bhavacakra) is complete even when it ends with feeling. Alternatively, by the inclusion of ignorance (avijjā), craving (taṇhā) and clinging (upādāna) are included; by the inclusion of volitional formations (saṅkhāra), becoming (bhava) is included;

and by the inclusion of consciousness (viññāṇa) and the rest, birth, aging, and death, as well as sorrow and the other [ten] factors, are included. Thus, in this way too, the wheel of existence ends with feeling.

This is indeed appropriate. And regarding the phrase "rooted in craving" (*taṇhāmūlake ca*), it should be connected with the statement that ignorance (*avijjā*) is included by the mention of craving and clinging (*taṇhupādāna*).

Therefore he said: "Of the two... [etc. ...there is. In this context, "of the two" refers to both the preceding and the succeeding [factors], which are free from the fault of being either cause or fruit.
"Forming a distorted adherence" (*viparītābhinivesaṃ karonti*) is stated using a metaphorical designation for the sign (*nimitta*). The construction is: "He demonstrates precisely non-interruption."

The connection of cause and fruit, the connection of fruit and cause, and again the connection of cause and fruit—thus they are preceded by causes and so forth, and preceded by the sequence of cause-fruit-cause. "By way of cause-fruit and cause-fruit" means:
by way of ignorance and so forth as the cause, consciousness and so forth as the fruit; and by way of craving and so forth as the cause, birth and so forth as the fruit.
Since a specific meaning arises through a specific prefix, the meaning of the word "ākirīyanti" is stated as "they are manifested."

“Defilements, karma, and resultants” refers to those beginning with ignorance (avijjā) and ending with feeling (vedanā). “By means of resultants, defilements, and karma” refers to those beginning with consciousness (viññāṇa) and ending with becoming (bhava).
Furthermore, the connection between karma and its resultant is not mentioned here because it follows the method already stated.
And the term “rounds” (vaṭṭāni) is used by taking what is obtained through the analysis of the phrase “three rounds.”

The word "of this" (*imissā*) is stated with reference to that which is immediate and directly evident, because it has been handed down in the *Aṭṭhakathā* as beginning with the words, "Delusion in the previous kamma-existence," and so forth. Since it is demonstrated by way of the *Vibhaṅga-pāḷi*, there is no contradiction between the earlier and later parts of the *Aṭṭhakathā*;
the intention is that the meaning is explained according to the reading. In that context, [it refers] to those associated with volition (*cetanā*) and to volition itself.

And because it must indeed be described both as the state of volitional formations (*saṅkhāra*) and as the state of kamma-existence (*kammabhava*), the passage beginning with “Therein” was stated in order to demonstrate this by way of explaining the intended meaning of the two scriptural passages.
“Of existence” means of rebirth-existence (*upapattibhava*). The connection is that volition associated [with craving] is what is called “existence.
“Grasping” is the grasping of an object by way of longing for it. Therefore he said: “Sensual clinging is so called by way of its function.”

The construction is: "the others [are included] by way of function. Regarding "in the three alternative explanations of the meaning": this refers to the three alternative explanations of the meaning of the volitions of exertion (*āyūhana-cetanā*) stated in the passage beginning, "the prior volitions of one performing that action," and so forth.
But is it not the case that in the third alternative explanation of the meaning, volition is not mentioned at the conclusion of the exertion?
Even if it is not mentioned in its own form, it is nevertheless implied by the word "associated with that" (*taṃ-sampayuttā*).

With reference to this method—that the accumulation (āyūhana) stated as being primary is, by virtue of being stated as secondary, as if it were stated at the end or after [the volition]—it was said: "In all three... at the end.
However, to show those cases where volition is stated at the end of the accumulation in a non-figurative sense, it was said: "In two... [and so on]... is stated."
It has been stated. When the third interpretation of the meaning was stated, the construction is: “He says ‘associated with that’ [referring] to the formations of accumulation (āyūhana-saṅkhāra).

“Being a condition for karma” means being a condition consisting of formations (saṅkhāra-paccaya). By this, he shows that in the phrase “at the time of performing karma,” the word *kamma* includes all formations as well.
Therefore, he said: “not only that which is associated with karma.”

“Kammāneva” means simply actions (kamma). They are similar to action because they possess the nature of being subject to fruition (vipākadhammatā). They are “conducive to that” (tadupakāraka) because they assist that action by way of co-nascence (sahajātakoṭi) and decisive support (upanissayakoṭi). “Are condensed” (saṃkhippanti) means they are gathered together or brought into a collection.
Having first explained the meaning of the word *saṅkhepa* as a locative construction (*adhikaraṇasādhana*)—namely, “that wherein things are condensed”—it is stated again:
The phrase beginning with “it is condensed” (*saṃkhipīyati*) was stated in order to express [the process] by way of the accomplishment of kamma.

In that context as well, “therein too” (*tatthāpi*) refers even to the constituent factors of kamma mentioned as “kamma. “Subject to going” (*gamanadhamma*) means subject to the process of dissolution.
By that, it is said to be “ephemeral” (*ittara*), meaning it has dissolution as its limit. “By that” (*tena*) refers to the word *ittara*, which indicates the nature of being subject to destruction.

"Devoid of essence" (*nissāra*) indicates the absence of any core substance. Thus, by the terms "ephemeral" (*ittara*) and so forth, he demonstrates how the four phrases—"impermanent," "fickle," "ephemeral," and "unstable"—express distinct nuances of meaning. "In its place" (*ṭhānaso*): here, "place" refers to a condition (*paccaya*).
"Also another": stated elsewhere. When there is the mere arising of phenomena (*dhammamatta*), the cycle of existence (*vaṭṭa*) is severed.
The construction is: "satīti" [meaning] "when there is. "Evaṃ" means when the word "ca" (and) is used in the sense of a conjunction in the manner described.

He says, "from the truth as the source" (*saccappabhavato*) and "from the truth" (*saccato*), referring to the position of grammatical coreferentiality (*samānādhikaraṇa-pakkha*). This refers to the Noble Truth without making a distinction, such as that which is expressed by: "for the sake of abandoning which the holy life is lived under the Blessed One."

“By those sorrows and so forth”: by means of ignorance (*avijjā*), which has been established through the method previously stated in such passages as, “Sorrow, lamentation, and despair are not dissociated from ignorance. “Of the self alone”:

this refers to the function of conditioned phenomena (*saṅkhāra*) as they proceed, without regard for anything arisen through conditions. “For even sorrow and the rest”: here the word “for” (*hi*) has the sense of a reason.

Since it is established by the statement, “Sorrow and the rest depend on conditions and are not subject to one’s own power,” because they arise with birth as a condition—etc., up to the full formula—the meaning is that this [statement] serves to prevent the view that “the self grieves,” and so forth.

Furthermore, since there are various destinies that entail manifold evils once there is grasping—just as there are with kingship—and since consciousness is afflicted by them, the phrase "grasped by volitional formations...
[like] kingship" was stated; this is how the meaning here should be understood.
Just as karma and so forth, having been projected as they arise, are taken up as if by the death-proximate mental processes, so too are they taken up by the rebirth-linking consciousness.
They are as if imagined; and since that imagining of his is in fact nothing other than making them an object, it is said: "pari... pe... to.
Or, imagining is called "conceptualizing," as it is said: "because of conceptualizing by means of applied thought (vitakka).
The eye-base and so forth, together with their material constituents, are the specific bases for the sixfold base (saḷāyatana).
In whatever manner birth occurs and in whatever manner aging and death come to be, and how they proceed in successive order—that is the meaning of "arisen and produced with birth as condition.
The states of a person who has come together and has arisen—their aging and dissolution—are spoken of by the designation "aging and death"; and that state of theirs is preceded by birth.
And since these [aggregates] proceed only when combined, the meaning of the arising and occurrence of aging-and-death from birth should be understood in this way.
Aging-and-death does not fail to exist because of birth; it certainly exists, because aging-and-death necessarily occurs for one who is born.

Nor does it exist without birth, because it is absent in one who is unborn. Thus, the conditionality of aging-and-death upon birth is established through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*).
He analyzes [the dependent origination] by means of the passage beginning with “not by way of birth,” and so forth. “Thus” refers to the mode of production of aging-and-death conditioned by birth.

“From cessation, that which is reckoned as cessation” means that from the cessation of the condition, there is what is reckoned as the cessation of that which has arisen through the condition. And in the forward exposition, the construction is “starting from the middle.
A portion of the unwholesome volitional formations is “with lust,” because it is conjoined with and associated with lust; indeed, the entire unwholesome volitional formation is [so described].

Because lust is something to be abandoned; and because an unwholesome state is of the same nature as another unwholesome state, whereas a non-unwholesome state is of a different nature, and each serves as a condition as appropriate, it is therefore said: "because it is not an antidote, it increases lust.

Also, because of the presence of false adherence—namely, the thought "it is this very consciousness that runs on and wanders through saṃsāra"—it is also [a condition] for the activity of wandering in saṃsāra.
The active state of consciousness has been described. This should be applied respectively to "the strength of the adherence to an active state" and "the strength of the adherence to transition.

By the phrases "because of not functioning together" and "because of functioning together," he shows that non-functioning together is analysis (*vinibbhoga*), while functioning together is non-analysis (*avinibbhoga*).

Illumination is the state of being the sign for the realization of intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*). For, by means of the eye and so forth, the five consciousnesses apprehend the intrinsic nature of visible forms and so on. The others [the mental factors] have the sense of touching, conjunction, and meeting.

Regarding "of the six": this refers to all six types of contact. Regarding "grasping" (*ādāna*): since even without the prefix *upa*, "firm holding" is intended, he said, "The meaning of grasping is common to all four types of clinging. Regarding "clinging" (*gahaṇa*):
because it is a concealing of the object through the mode of yearning, it is said, "The meaning of clinging is that of sensual-clinging (*kāmupādāna*)."
The others are clinging to views and so forth. "Therefore" means because of the non-elision (*aluttābhāva*) of the case ending. "By that" refers to the word *khipana* (throwing).

Regarding the phrase "the meaning of destruction," etc., it is stated that *khaya* (destruction) is either the act of wasting away or the state of being exhausted. "Of the two" refers to aging and death;
or rather, because aging also has the function of leading toward death, the meaning of death is shown to apply to aging as well.
They are "guides" (*naya*) because they lead (*nīyanti*) or cause one to go; these are oneness (*ekatta*) and so forth. By what are they led?

They are led by the meanings of ignorance (*avijjā*) and the rest; it is with this meaning that he says "ignorance and so forth. "By that state" means by its own state of ignorance and so forth, without ever relinquishing it.
For there is no such thing as "oneness" existing in the ultimate sense apart from ignorance and the rest. Or, "by that state" means by its own [state].

By way of oneness and so forth. The state of oneness and so forth—consisting in the fact that the phenomena of cause and fruit fall within a single continuity (*ekasantatipatita*) and so on—which is perceived in ignorance (*avijjā*) and the rest, is known by that very intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*), and not by way of being "ignorance" and so forth.

For they are to be led [along], thus they are the "leadings" (*nayā*). Or, the meanings themselves are ignorance and the rest. Even though many phenomena are common, by means of which there is no interruption of the continuum, they are called "one."
They are known and expressed; thus, that [term] deserves to be stated there in the sense of an instrument (*karaṇa*), and the others likewise.
Therefore he said: "And by means of oneness and so forth, the meanings are led [to be understood] as 'one' and so forth. In this context, "led" means they are known and they are made known.
Because of the uninterruptedness of the cessation and arising of preceding and succeeding phenomena, the body of names (*nāmakāya*) exists in a state of continuous connection.
Because the physical body and both [the mental and physical aggregates] are mutually dependent, their difference is difficult to discern;
thus, as if they were unified, there is a continuity of a solid state. This connection, existing through the relation of cause and fruit, is correctly called *santāna* (continuity).
The non-interruption of that [continuity], its proceeding in such a manner, is "oneness" (*ekatta*). Therefore, he said: "Continuity is the non-interruption of the stream."
"Devoid of connection" means devoid of a mutual relationship by way of cause and effect.

"Another being" means another sentient being (*satta*). "One adopts the view of annihilationism" means that, failing to perceive the arising of an effect from its corresponding cause, one sees a lack of connection and diversity—as if between distinct continua—and thus [clings to] those things arisen previously which are devoid of causal status and purposeless.
Because there is an absence of causal necessity regarding the cessation of phenomena, it is not logical for their arising to be absolute;

likewise, one adopts the annihilationist view by entertaining such alternatives as: "Arising through a continuum is not logical," "Arising with similarity is not logical," and "Arising with identical birth, place, transformation, age, form, strength, and shape is not logical," and so forth.
"Why should there not be an arising [of oil from sesame seeds]?"—because, just as there is oil from sesame seeds, so too there is milk from cows;
since there is no difference between them, for what reason should there not be an arising of those [products] from those [sources], and why should their arising occur only from the other [sources]?
Therefore, if one thing were to arise from another, it would follow that everything could arise from everything.

And this is not the case; therefore [the following is said]. Because the proponent of fatalism (niyativādin) does not accept the arising of a fruit from a corresponding cause, but rather accepts the occurrence of phenomena as established by their own intrinsic nature (sabhāva), it is said: "even though a cause is non-existent.

For indeed, things established by their own intrinsic nature—like a gem strung on an unbreakable thread that cannot be pierced—undergo various transformations into states such as body, sense-faculties, and pleasure, without any violation of the natural order.
Bodies come together solely through *niyati* (destiny), from which there arise the destinies, births, and bonds, as well as liberation;
such is the doctrine of *niyati*. Therefore it is said: “By way of necessity... they proceed. The meaning of *niyati* has already been stated.

A sutta that establishes this meaning follows. *Ākulam* means simply confused, or the state of being confused (*ākulabhāvo*). They are "entangled" (*jaṭitā*) in the sense of being interwoven from bottom to top.

The "tangled mass" (*jaṭā*) refers to birth produced by the ongoing defilements, karma, and kamma-vipāka. "Nest" (*nīḍa*) means a bird's nest. "Saṃsāra" here denotes the continuity of existence within the realms of prosperity (*sampattibhava*), because the continuity of miserable rebirths in the woeful states (*apāya*, etc.
has already been described by those preceding terms. The commentary on the Discourse on the Wheel of Existence (*Bhavacakka-kathā*) is finished.
The commentary on the Suttanta-bhājaniya is finished.
2. Commentary on the Abhidhamma-bhājaniya. 243.
"That dependent origination... contained within each single state of consciousness" means, as in the Abhidhamma-bhājaniya, within each individual [state].

Without making it contained or included within the mind. And regarding the phrase "of those not co-nascent," it should be understood as an *ekasesa* (single-remainder) designation for the first term, [meaning] "of those not co-nascent and of those co-nascent.

In the statement "with volitional formations as condition, consciousness," only those related as condition and conditionally arisen that are not co-nascent are shown, because it is specifically the resultant consciousness (*vipākaviññāṇa*) that is intended. "With ignorance as condition, volitional formations..."
In such passages as "with consciousness as condition, name-and-form," there are both those that are not co-nascent and those that are co-nascent.
The ancient reading was "by each method" (*ekekena nayena*); however, nowadays the reading found in many manuscripts is "by each tetrad" (*ekekena catukkena*).
"The sections on the tetrads of methods" (*nayacatukkavāra*) refers to the sections on the tetrads within the methods; [it concerns] each of the nine methods beginning with those rooted in ignorance.

The meaning is that there are four sections distinguished by specific differences such as “the sixth base [arises] with name as condition,” and so forth, belonging to the four tetrads beginning with the tetrad of conditions.
They are “determined” (vavatthitā) because they are not confused by the aforementioned distinctions.
Alternatively, the intention is that they are called “tetrads” because the sixteenfold set of sections possesses the nature of a method (naya).

1. Commentary on the Tetrad of Conditions (Paccaya-catuṣka-vaṇṇanā) The conditions and the conditionally arisen states are stated as factors (aṅga) because they are accompanied by conditions, not merely as conditions themselves.

Therefore, in the statement "contact has the sixth base as its condition" (chaṭṭhāyatana-paccayā phasso), the sixth base does not possess the status of a factor. Hence it is said: "No, because that [the sixth base] is not a factor."
"And having done thus" means because the condition and the conditionally arisen state function as factors together.
"In the three ways" refers to the three modes stated in the Commentary beginning with, "The first is in the sense of being all-inclusive.

"Specific conditions, etc."—here, "name" and the "sixth base" constitute the specific conditions; by the word "etc.," the specific mode of birth, and the distinction between the incompleteness and completeness of the bases are included.

And it is included [here]. For these [six bases] are what differentiate the second section and the others. Regarding "by way of a specific meaning": although elsewhere the condition of the six bases is stated as "with the six bases as condition, contact arises," nevertheless, because it occurs by way of dependence upon the name (nāma) through such relations as co-nascence (sahajāta), it is also a condition for mere name;
thus, the profundity of dependent origination—which is inferred from its variety of diverse methods—is [demonstrated].
This is by way of the specific meaning consisting in the contemplation of vanishing (*vibhāvanā*) and the contemplation of seeing the conditions for names without remainder.
For it is said: "Ānanda, if those modes, those marks, those signs, and those indications by which the designation of the body of names occurs were absent—would then, in the absence of those modes...
indications, the contact of designation be discernible in the body of forms?"

The *Mahānidāna-sutta* teaching proceeds by way of demonstrating that contact has name as its condition. Likewise, when it is said, “‘With name-and-form as condition, contact’—thus it should be stated,” by one who says “with name-and-form as condition,” it is already implied that “with name as condition” has also been stated.

It should be understood that in the fourth set of alternatives, “volitional formation” is mentioned while sorrow and the rest are not; in the first two sets of alternatives, “form” is not mentioned; and in the three sets of alternatives, “the six sense bases” is not mentioned.
"Of all... [etc. ... "as a source of conflict": because it is common to all states of existence (*bhava*) which serve as the locus for the occurrence of all consciousness;

or because it is common to all states of existence which serve as the locus for the occurrence of consciousness. "A common fruit" and "a common condition": because it is to be assisted by conditions such as co-nascence (*sahajāta*), and because it is an assistant.
"Of that consciousness": of that resultant consciousness. "The bringing forth of consciousness" (*viññāṇāharaṇa*): the production of resultant consciousness. "Of this consciousness."
It is said that the word *hi* expresses the sense of "going" (*gati*) because people in the world speak of it as having the meaning of going.

Regarding the term "gone away" (*vigata*), the prefix *vi-* indicates negation; since two negations imply the original state, he says: "By way of not obstructing the state of being gone away, there is indeed going.
As for the phrase "threefold, fourfold, or fivefold," here [the factors] such as perception and attention [function] by way of the conditions of conascence, support, and presence.
In three ways, such as contact and volition; in four ways, by way of those [factors] and the nutriments (*āhāra*) and so forth;

and in five ways, such as feeling and applied thought (*vitakka*), by way of those [factors] and the jhāna factors, faculties (*indriya*), and so forth. Just as with concentration (*samādhi*), so too should energy (*vīriya*) be understood.
For that too is a condition in six ways: as a predominance condition (*adhipati-paccaya*), an faculty condition (*indriya-paccaya*), and a path condition (*magga-paccaya*).

“By way of expression” (*vacanavasena*): by this phrase, he shows that the intention of those [teachers] is that in this tetrad the teaching proceeds by making the co-nascence condition (*sahajāta-paccaya*) the primary focus.
“Meaning” (*attha*) refers to the conditioned phenomenon (*paccayadhamma*). “In some cases” (*katthaci*):

in certain instances, for whatever has arisen from its own conditions, it is not the case that it does not act as a condition for its own [corresponding] factors. The reading is also “by way of meaning” (*atthato*). “With existence as condition” (*bhavapaccayā*)...

It would not be right to say, "birth," and so forth; yet that has been said. Therefore, he shows that it should not be understood as meaning that the first tetrad was stated solely by way of the co-nascent condition (*sahajāta-paccaya*).

Thus he says, "And it is not the case that this was not stated," and so on. Furthermore, the connection for this [passage] should be understood with the words, "it would not be right to say, 'with existence as condition, birth,' and so forth. The phrase "only the statement of conditions" refers to such instances as "with ignorance as condition" (*avijjāpaccayā*), and so on.
And [it refers to] the very statement of the conditions already mentioned. "Of them" means of those teachers. The connection is:
"stated without being formally joined. To the question "But how was it stated?", he says: "It was stated with reference to the general [rule], etc.

Here, by the words "indicating what is co-nascent," etc., he states [the meaning] through direct expression (*vacana*); but by the words "from what is co-nascent," etc., he states it through implication (*atthāpatti*).
For when another [term] is unavailable, it must be established either by its meaning or by its verbal expression; that is, it accomplishes the intended meaning through its meaning.
"In another" means in another Sutta. Having extracted the past period, it is for the purpose of showing the three periods together with the present and the future.
"For the purpose of encompassing that teaching" means for the purpose of encompassing the teaching of the *Mahānidāna*. And that [is] of both teachings...
It is for the purpose of showing the state of mutual convergence. Thus, the teaching spoken by the Omniscient Buddha converges entirely with all other teachings.
"Of this" refers to this third section.
[This is said] because of the gods of the sense-sphere realm’s lack of dependence on others, their birth being undefiled, and their not being smeared by impurity.
And because all Brahmās are likewise born by spontaneous generation (*opapātika*), it should be understood that this mode of birth is predominant.
"By way of showing inclusion" means by way of demonstrating—in other words, by way of an illustration—the inclusion of the moisture-born (*saṃsedaja*) within the spontaneously born mode of birth.

Although the object-condition (*ārammaṇa-paccaya*) is also a cause for the occurrence of contact (*phassa*), nevertheless, [it is distinguished from] the internal [condition], which serves as a co-nascent (*sahajāta*) and other types of conditions.
It is said that [the condition] is not preeminent like that of the sixth base (chaṭṭhāyatana), hence it is stated: "And herein, the object-condition (ārammaṇapaccaya) is not a producer.
"Of some" refers to those in the womb whose sense bases are complete. The statement, "The last...
always arises," indicates that, unlike those in the womb, for those of other modes of birth there is no gradual arising of the sense bases. Likewise...
And it says in the Commentary: "Because it illustrates simultaneous arising.
The commentary on the tetrad of conditions is finished.
2. Commentary on the Tetrad of Causes (*hetu*).
244. "By way of non-existence" means by way of the non-existence of the state [of being].
For that which exists only at the very moment of birth and not thereafter would be a non-disappearance condition for birth, because of the presence of the rule regarding non-disappearance conditions.
However, since existence continues even beyond the moment of birth, it is therefore not its non-disappearance condition. Hence it was said: "Beyond that..."

The meaning is "as becoming" (*bhāvatoti*). It refers to the word *bhava*, or to that which is to be produced as a state of existence (*bhave*). This same method applies here to birth (*jāti*) and the other [factors] as well.

By the passage beginning with "But just as," he demonstrates that the reasons stated—namely, "because of the absence of the non-disappearance condition (*avigatapaccaya*)" and "because of the absence of a fixed rule"—are not valid causes, by showing through the aforementioned method that they do not pervade the case of a dependently arisen phenomenon that does not exist at all times.

And because it shows that the conditioning state (paccayadhamma) possesses the nature of a non-disappearance condition (avigatapaccaya). The passage beginning with "In the aggregate of volitional formations" (*saṅkhārakkhandhe*) is stated by way of purifying the Path.
He himself provides the resolution for that: "That moment exists for this, thus it is 'of that moment' (*taṅkhaṇika*); not of that moment is 'not of that moment' (*ataṅkhaṇika*);
because of its presence, the meaning is 'the presence of what is not otherwise manifest. But as to how they are causes..."
To demonstrate that, he said: “But of the characteristics of the conditioned,” and so forth.
“Evaṃ” means when it is in the manner just stated; thus, the meaning is “when this is so. By the phrase “For...

there is not,” he shows that just as birth and the other [characteristics] lack the status of being conditionally arisen by way of the non-disappearance condition, they likewise lack the status of being conditions. In that regard:
He states the reason: "Because they are phenomena lacking intrinsic nature (asabhāvadhamma).

But how can birth and the other [characteristics], which lack intrinsic nature, be both produced by conditions and themselves conditions? To this he says: "But for those that are being born," and so forth.
"Of that" refers to birth, aging, and death. "The phrase to be stated" refers to the phrase "having set aside."

But what is that? It is the aforementioned name and name-and-form, because aging and death are included within the aggregate of mental formations (saṅkhārakkhandha) and the aggregate of form (rūpakkhandha).

By the statement, "That existence which is the condition for birth," he shows that although birth and the other factors are also included within existence, they were not mentioned [in the phrase] "setting aside" because they are not conditions for birth itself; this is to prevent any suspicion that they might be conditions.

The intention is that they do not possess such [a distinction] for them. For this very reason, he says it is "doubtful" (*sāsaṅka*) when there exists a distinction between what is to be set aside and what is to be grasped.
The commentary on the Tetrad of Causes (*hetu-catukka*) is finished.
4. Commentary on the Tetrad of Mutual Relations (*aññamañña-catukka*).

246. "Of that which has arisen through conditions" means of that which possesses the state of having arisen through conditions. "Existing separately" means not included within [the category of] existence (*bhava*).
Here, only that which has a specific location is taken, because it is intended as the triad of aggregates beginning with feeling (*vedanā*), and because it is so conventionally established.
Having set aside that which has arisen through conditions, only that which serves as the condition is named; thus, there is no lack of the rule regarding the non-disappearance of the condition.

The construction is: "Just as with fuel, there is an absence of a fixed rule for mutual conditionality regarding clinging. By the method stated means by the method stated in the passage beginning with, "But as for the characteristics of the conditioned" (*saṅkhatalakkhaṇānaṃ panā*).
Showing that the meaning intended here is that "mutual condition" (*aññamaññapaccaya*) is like [the relationship of] "mutually conditioned" (*aññamaññapaccaya*), he says: "Mutual condition... etc."

[The author] said: "It may be intended [in this way]. And so they say: "In this context, 'mutuality' (aññamañña) should not be understood according to the sense of mutuality as it appears in the *Paṭṭhāna*.
Regarding the phrase "the accumulation of the eye-base, etc.": these are the eye-bases and so forth that have arisen, heaped up one upon another;
or, the accumulations of the eye-base, etc., are those factors that support the eye-base and so forth.
The commentary on the Mutual Tetrad is finished.
Commentary on the Matrix of Methods Rooted in Formations, etc.: 247.

Although the distinction between the methods has already been understood in general terms, nevertheless, by means of this general reference, the specific distinctions contained within the methods are presented in their own form.
Regarding the phrase "it is shown": although it was stated that "ignorance has name as its condition," the fact that specific types of name serve as conditions for it must also be demonstrated;
therefore, he said, "of specific types of name... [etc.]... have been stated. In response to the objection—"Why was the passage beginning with 'But whatever is name' stated?

For is it not the case that even though birth and so forth are not included by the term 'name,' they are nevertheless included by the term 'existence,' and thus this meaning has already been shown?"—he says:

“‘And by the inclusion of existence (bhava),’ etc. Here too means: even here in the statement, “with existence as condition, ignorance (avijjā). It would not be possible [to say] that “ignorance is conditioned by ignorance.
Therefore means: because what is stated in general is not itself a specific instance; therefore. “It” refers to existence (bhava). “By that” means:
by the inclusion of both phenomena that possess their own intrinsic nature (sabhāva) and those that do not (asabhāva).
Since clinging (*upādāna*) is also a part of existence (*bhava*), it is said: “With clinging as condition... [omitted] ...when not grasped.
With reference to the statement “With existence as condition, birth,” he says: “The word ‘existence’... when being spoken of...

In the case of “With name as condition, ignorance,” because the condition is grasped while setting aside that which has arisen from the condition, the four aggregates are indeed excluded from ignorance.
He says, "The word *nāma* does not denote [everything] without remainder," because they are expressed by the word *nāma*.

And one should not seek a definitive reason here as to why the word *bhava* denotes everything without remainder while the word *nāma* does not; for he says, "Such is the nature of these linguistic expressions (*niruttiyo*).
With this intention, he means that the word *bhava* denotes everything without remainder because its domain consists of the four aggregates of clinging (*upādinnacatukkhandha*).

With this intention: because they are states of transformation such as "being born" and so forth, birth and the other [characteristics] would be said to be bound to the aggregates that are "being born" and so forth, but not conversely—that the aggregates "being born" and so forth are bound to birth and the others. Thus, he stated "But for those that are being born...

and so on, in order to show that the status of birth and the others as conditions for ignorance is not possible within a single moment of consciousness (*ekacittakkhaṇa*). [This applies to] different moments of consciousness (*nānācittakkhaṇa*).

However, since birth and so forth serve as the decisive support condition (*upanissaya-paccaya*) for ignorance, it was specified as "in a single moment of consciousness. "For that very reason" means precisely because of such impossibility.
The commentary on the matrix (*mātikā*) is finished.
The commentary on the exposition of the unwholesome (*akusala-niddesa*).
248–9. That [view] is the clinging to views (*diṭṭhupādāna*). "Of the other" refers to the clinging to sensual pleasures (*kāmupādāna*).

"By the mention of craving" means because it has already been included by the mention of craving in the phrase "with craving as condition. If that is so, why is craving mentioned again when it was already included by the mention of "name"?
He says: "Because, unlike name, it lacks the status of being a specific condition. For in the passage "with name as condition, the sixfold sense-base," etc., [craving is not mentioned].
Since craving for sense-pleasures (*kāmatanha*) is also included within "name" (*nāma*), the conditionality of name toward the sixth base (*chaṭṭhāyatana*) as appropriate has been stated;

thus, there is a specific conditionality therein. However, since clinging (*upādāna*) is also included within "existence" (*bhava*), there is no difference between the statement "with craving as condition, clinging" and the statement "with clinging to sense-pleasures as condition, existence. This is what is meant by [the phrase] "in name... [and so forth].
“Because, like craving, it lacks the status of being a specific condition. Craving is its condition; thus, it is “with craving as condition,” namely, view.
Being the condition for existence means being the cause for both kinds of existence. By both [terms], he clarifies that grasping must indeed be placed within the description of existence.
Since the conditioned and the condition are one and the same, it is said: “With craving as condition, grasping arises.”
The "conditioned state" mentioned here and the "condition" mentioned in the phrase "with clinging as condition, there is becoming" have one and the same meaning;
therefore, the condition is not analyzed separately from the conditioned state.

252. "By way of the supporting, the originating, and the postnascent conditions" means by way of the originating of mind-originated matter that is supported [by the mind], and by way of the postnascent condition.

254. "Of five" means of the five [bases], beginning with the eye-base (*cakkhāyatana*). "Condition by way of co-nascence, etc. refers to the conditions of co-nascence (*sahajāta*), support (*nissaya*), presence (*atthi*), and non-disappearance (*avigata*), and so forth.

It is the materiality reckoned as the physical basis (*vatthu*). "Condition by way of pre-nascence, etc. refers to the conditions of pre-nascence (*purejāta*), support (*nissaya*), dissociation (*vippayutta*), presence (*atthi*), and non-disappearance (*avigata*).

"Condition by way of post-nascence, etc. refers to the conditions of post-nascence (*pacchājāta*), dissociation (*vippayutta*), presence (*atthi*), and non-disappearance (*avigata*). For the sixth [base], it is "co-nascence, etc."
By the word "etc. (ādi), mutual dependence, support, association, presence, non-disappearance, and so forth are included. 264. Regarding "of whom":

this is said with reference to the word "of whom" (yassa) as stated in the phrase "and for whom it exists" (yassa ca hoti). Therefore he says, "it should be construed with 'exists'. 280. Regarding "of that":
this refers to the phrase "of doubt which has become a powerful defilement. Regarding "by that": [this refers to] "in the place of craving."
By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) in the phrase "in the Cittuppādakaṇḍa and so forth," one includes the Suttantabhājanīya and other sections within this *Paṭiccasamuppādavibhaṅga*.
The commentary on the Description of the Unwholesome (*Akusalaniddesa*) is finished. [Now begins] the commentary on the Description of the Wholesome and the Indeterminate (*Kusalābyākataniddesa*).

306. "Active" (*sabyāpārāni*) means possessing effort; the meaning is that they are subject to maturation (*vipākadhammāni*). "Those for whom the basis of ignorance has been discarded" (*parihīnāvijjāṭṭhānā*) refers to those whose state of ignorance has been abandoned.

He speaks as if clarifying the underlying intention (*sandhāya*), for it is stated in the *Aṭṭhakathā*: "And eye-consciousness and the rest do not originate form. The construction is: "Name-and-form is not non-existent.
The commentary on the exposition of the wholesome and the indeterminate is finished.

**Commentary on the Exposition of the Wholesome Rooted in Ignorance (Avijjāmūlakakusalaniddesa), 334.** Regarding "the fruit of the wholesome": because the rebirth-linking consciousness (paṭisandhiviññāṇa) that is the result of the wholesome is included here, its similarity to the seed of a tree with sweet-tasting sap is stated.

Although a construction such as "having formations as its cause" (*saṅkhārahetuka*) and so forth is possible, the tetrad beginning with "not yet vanished" (*avigata*) and the rest are not included, because the construction was shown according to what was actually available.
The commentary on the description of wholesome states rooted in ignorance is finished.
Commentary on the description of resultant states rooted in the wholesome: 343.
The intention is that, like kamma, it is a condition by way of being a result. Kamma is the condition for the resultant.

"It would be pre-eminent" means that for that [state], it is the non-figurative sense (*nippariyāya*); whereas for those associated with it, it may be the figurative sense (*pariyāya*). With this intention, he said:
"They are called 'adequate condition' (*upanissaya-paccaya*) in a figurative sense. [The text continues: "A wholesome state is a condition for an indeterminate state by way of the adequate condition;
an unwholesome state for an indeterminate state; a state subject to result (*vipākadhamma*)..."

However, from the statement, "A state that is neither resultant nor of a nature to produce resultants is a condition for [another such state] by way of decisive support condition" (*upanissaya-paccaya*),
the meaning is seen to be that, in the direct sense (*nippariyāya*), all wholesome and unwholesome states are conditions for a resultant by way of decisive support.
Furthermore, regarding the reference "the wholesome root, the unwholesome root," the word "this" (*esā*) is used in the masculine gender in view of the word "condition" (*paccaya*).
Showing that it has been stated [thus], he said: “‘Esā... ... ‘should be connected.

By the words “attention also,” etc., he shows that for those whose ignorance (*avijjā*) has not yet been abandoned, the wholesome and unwholesome roots are not the decisive support (*upanissaya*) for the activity of ignorance.
In the latter method, only the formations (*saṅkhāra*) and consciousness (*viññāṇa*) that constitute the round of kamma and the round of result [are intended].
The phrase "intended" refers to what was stated: "But as for the functional [kamma]... they go. The construction is: "in many ways by way of those conditions" is the intended meaning.
"Of the divisions beginning with nine" means of those classified as nine, eight, and seven.
"Of the four tetrads" refers to the four tetrads found according to their occurrence in both the preceding and the subsequent methods. "Of the wholesome and unwholesome..."
However, by means of the word "and" (*ca*) in the phrase "and in the resultant," it should be understood that "wholesome and unwholesome" are also included; thus he says, "wholesome...

[etc.]... should be stated. "By way of the single conditionality of the root-term" means by way of the state of being a single condition for the root-term, namely, by way of the decisive-support condition (*upanissaya-paccaya*).
"Of one method alone" refers to that which has ignorance as its root among the wholesome and unwholesome, and that which has the wholesome and unwholesome as its root among the resultants.

Thus, by means of this single method alone. Regarding the phrase "in the classification of the conditions for phenomena" (*dhammapaccayabhede*): he explains the meaning as "the classification according to the state of being a condition, whether of a phenomenon that has become a condition or of that which has arisen from a condition.

Having stated "of ignorance and so forth" (*avijjādīnam*), etc., he further clarifies that very same point in another manner by saying "from each respective arising of consciousness" (*taṃtaṃcittuppādā*), and so on.
The commentary on the Exposition of the Resultant of Wholesome Roots is finished.
The commentary on the Analysis According to the Abhidhamma is finished.
The commentary on the Exposition of Dependent Origination is finished.
7. Analysis of the Foundations of Mindfulness (Satipaṭṭhānavibhaṅga) 1.
The Exposition according to the Discourses (Suttantabhājanīya) Exposition of the Section on the Summary (Uddesavāravaṇṇanā)

355. *Atthuddhāra* (the extraction of meanings) is the extraction of the meanings of words that are expressed by the same term. Since this is not an investigation (*vicāra*) of the meaning of the word itself, it is said:
“Not here... [etc. ...the showing of the meaning. The prefix *pa-* indicates preeminence (*padhāna*), as in such examples as “excellent states” (*paṇītā dhammā*).
It is the state of being unmoistened and unstained. Therefore he said, "the state of having transcended both.
"Leaping forward" in the sense of intensity means an entry characterized by intense leaping forward.
"Of gratification" refers to craving. [The phrase] "as the cause for the distinction of views," which have the basis of the dogmatic adherence that "it is permanent and self."
