The specific mention [of "mind"] is because craving is also a basis for mental states (*citta-dhamma*); likewise, the phrase "by way of distinction" is used because bodily sensations can also serve as a basis for views.
Mindfulness of the mind is said to be "not overly diversified" because it is taught solely by way of the two divisions of those with lust and those free from lust.
Here, "mental objects" (*dhammā*) refers to the aggregates of perception and formations.

The aggregate of formations (*saṅkhārakkhandha*) has many divisions by way of contact (*phassa*) and so forth; thus, the contemplation of phenomena (*dhammānupassanā*) is said to be "of very many divisions.

Alternatively, because it has sixteen divisions by way of the classification of "with lust" (*sarāga*) and so on, the contemplation of mind (*cittānupassanā*) is said to be not of very many divisions.

However, because it has many divisions by way of the hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*) and so forth according to the method handed down in the Sutta, the contemplation of phenomena is said to be of very many divisions.

The phrase “stated in the *Visuddhimagga*” should be supplied and connected [to the context]. Those contemplations belong to them; thus, they are “those who contemplate those,” namely, persons who contemplate the mind and mental phenomena.
Regarding that, the construction “by seeing the nature of foulness” can indeed be applied even in the sense of how things actually exist (*yathāṭhita*). Of the flood of existence...

Feeling [is included] because it is the basis for the relishing of existence (*bhavassāda*). "By way of grasping at permanence" means by way of grasping at permanence as distinguished by the underlying tendency toward a self (*attābhinivesa*).

For it has been said: "of a permanent self. The application of the same method used for the floods (*ogha*) to the yokes (*yoga*) and outflows (*āsava*) is not mentioned separately, as they are not distinct in meaning;
thus, they are not taken up here. "By way of grasping at permanence" means by way of grasping at permanence as distinguished by the underlying tendency toward a self.

By way of grasping at permanence. In the application of the first flood (*ogha*) and the third and fourth fetters (*gantha*), the fact that body, mind, and mental phenomena (*dhamma*) serve as the basis for the other types of clinging (*upādāna*) should be understood according to the method already stated;
thus, the fact that feeling (*vedanā*) is the basis for the clinging to views (*diṭṭhupādāna*) has been shown.

Likewise, the fact that the body and feelings are the basis for desire, hatred, and wrong course is stated by the mention of their being the bases for the flood of sensuality, the flood of ill-will, and the bodily fetter. Therefore he said: "Of those not [explicitly] mentioned..."
"The state of being a basis (vatthubhāva) should be applied according to the method already stated.
Retention (dhāraṇatā) is non-forgetfulness, or simply recollection (anussaraṇa). "In unity" (ekatta) means in a single nature by way of escape and so forth.

Convergence (samāgama) is realization (sacchikiriyā). The nature of the foundations of mindfulness (satipaṭṭhāna) is right mindfulness (sammāsati), mindfulness of deliverance (niyyānasati), and commonality (samānabhāgatā).
“Being of one birth” (*ekajātitā*) means “homogeneity” (*sabhāgatā*). Regarding the phrase “in the former,” it refers to the sense: “meeting in the unity of Nibbāna is convergence in unity.
“Diverse” (*visuṃ*) means by way of having two different meanings. That very going is called “convergence” (*samosaraṇa*), because there is no other meaning for the word *sati* [here].

… It should be construed as “of the state of oneness” (*ekabhāvassa*). When not stated by way of the meaning of the word *sati*, it is said: “The single nature of the foundations of mindfulness” (*eko satipaṭṭhānasabhāvo*).
When it is not stated by the words beginning with "oneness" (*ekatta*), the meaning is that it is stated thus: "The meeting in oneness, which is Nibbāna, is the convergence in oneness.
"Mindfulness (*sati*) is simply the state of bearing in mind" means that the very state of bearing in mind mentioned as "remembering" (*saraṇatā*) is itself mindfulness (*sati*).

"Because there is no other meaning for the word *sati*" means because there is no meaning other than the meanings of the words "remembering," "oneness," and "convergence," which are reckoned as *sati*. "The former... [is the end of the sentence].

Regarding the phrase "the state of convergence": even in the sense of "converging in Nibbāna," that is, in the second meaning already mentioned, the words "refuge" (*saraṇa*), "oneness" (*ekatta*), and "convergence" (*samosaṇa*) together indicate the single nature of the foundations of mindfulness (*satipaṭṭhāna*).

Likewise, even in the sense of "converging in Nibbāna"—that is, in the sense that "the meeting in the oneness of Nibbāna is the convergence in oneness" (*ekattasamosaṇa*)—there are [these] reasons... [and so forth].

"Of the sections on mindfulness of breathing, etc. refers to the sections on mindfulness of breathing, the four postures, clear comprehension, the analysis of the body parts, attention to elements, and the nine cemetery meditations.
Now, since among these some do not succeed as meditation subjects for certain deities, those have been omitted;
and although the teaching here proceeds by way of the analysis of the body parts and attention to elements, that which has come down in other teachings [is also included].
In order to show the complete classification of the contemplation of the body (*kāyānupassanā*), it is said: "having developed the contemplation of the body in fourteen ways.
Therefore, he says: "of those stated in the Mahāsatipaṭṭhāna Sutta. By the word "likewise" (*tathā*), he refers back specifically to that phrase: "of those stated in the Mahāsatipaṭṭhāna Sutta.

"In five ways" refers to [the contemplation] of the hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*), the aggregates of clinging (*upādānakkhandha*), the sense bases (*āyatana*), the factors of enlightenment (*bojjhaṅga*), and the noble truths (*ariyasacca*).
It is fivefold by way of [its] cultivation. "The power of cultivation" is the capacity for grasping the Noble Path.

"By its restriction" means by the restriction of that practice, such as the contemplation of the body (*kāyānupassanā*). When that [practice] is restricted to the state of being a monk, it is indeed said to be restricted to the state of being a monk.
Commentary on the Summary of Contemplation of the Body (*Kāyānupassanā-uddesa-vaṇṇanā*)
"Herein" means in the body (*kāya*). That which has parts is a "whole" (*avayavī*); the meaning is a composite or a collection.
However, the misconception that this whole is a distinct substance separate from its parts is the "adherence to the whole" (*avayavigāha*).

To transcend the conventional designations of "limbs" and "body"—which are applied based upon the specific arrangement of the major and minor limbs such as hands, feet, fingers, and nails—and to instead imagine a distinct substance such as a woman, a man, a chariot, or a jar, [is adherence to the whole].

"Deviation from conventional designation" (*samaññātidhāvana*) means either running beyond the conventional designation as previously stated, or the conceptualization of other referents such as "primordial matter" (*pakati*), "substance" (*dravya*), "life-force" (*jīva*), or "body" (*kāya*).
"Adherence to grasping at a core" (*sārādānābhiniveso*) is the dogmatic adherence consisting in the grasping of a permanent essence and so forth.

"That is not seen" (*na taṃ diṭṭhan*) means that woman, man, and so forth—which are [merely] seen—are not [ultimately real]; or the construction is: "what is seen, namely woman, man, and so forth, does not exist. "As previously stated" refers to what is designated as the aggregate of the primary elements and the derived matter, beginning with hair and so forth.

"Earth beginning with head-hairs" means earth together with its constituent parts (sasambhāra) designated as "head-hairs" and so forth. "By way of prior and posterior state" means by way of continuity (santāna). "Elsewhere" refers to such passages as "the water-body" and so on.

"Internal and external" refers to the body as spoken of within one's own and others' continuums. And here, by "body," material phenomena (rūpadhammā) suitable for comprehension (sammasana) are intended;
thus he says, "of internal and external phenomena. "A conjoined object" (*ghaṭitārammaṇa*) is an object that is joined together or bound into a single unit.
The meaning is "having become a single object. Therefore he said: "There is no state of being an object from two [sides] simultaneously.
"Antoolīyanā" means internal contraction or internal cessation.
"By two" refers to the removal of covetousness and the removal of dejection.

Mindfulness and clear comprehension constitute "mindfulness-and-clear-comprehension"; by means of that, acting as the instrument. Because it is uninterrupted—being unobstructed by contrary states—that universal meditation subject [is maintained].
The commentary on the summary of the contemplation of the body is finished.
Now follows the commentary on the summary of the contemplation of feelings, and so forth.
"Of pleasure and so forth" means of pleasure, pain, and neither-pain-nor-pleasure.
The connection is that [the classification] should be applied by way of the diversity of objects such as visible forms and so on; and the same applies to the remaining cases.

By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) in the phrase "with bases, without bases, and so forth," it includes the divisions of inferior and other types of birth, etc. This indicates the objection that [the classification] cannot be stated separately for each.

The construction [of the sentence] is as follows: "In one" (*ekattha*) means in one among the body and so forth. "By the previous objection" (*purimacodanāya*) refers to the objection that "since it has already been abandoned previously, its abandonment again need not be stated.
"Abandoned" (*pahīna*) means suppressed (*vikkhambhita*). "By the cultivation of the opposite" (*paṭipakkhabhāvanāya*) means by the cultivation of the Path (*maggabhāvanā*).

"In both cases" (*ubhayattha*) means in response to both objections. "Both" (*ubhaya*) refers to the two ways of resolving [the objection]. Since, regarding the first objection, the resolution is that they pertain to different persons;

The avoidance of [the fault of] different moments of consciousness is possible; however, in the case of the second objection, it is only the avoidance of different moments of consciousness that applies.
Therefore it is said: "It should be applied according to what is possible. This was stated with reference to the development of the foundations of mindfulness pertaining to the Path.
"In all cases" means in regard to all [objects], such as the body and so forth.
The commentary on the summary of the contemplation of feelings and so forth is finished.
The commentary on the section of the summary is finished.
The commentary on the detailed exposition of the contemplation of the body.

356. Regarding the phrase "internal, etc.": it should be understood that by the word "etc.," not only the modes of contemplation mentioned here—namely, internal, external, and both internal-and-external contemplation—but also the modes of contemplation mentioned in the Mahāsatipaṭṭhāna Sutta, such as "contemplating the nature of arising" and so forth, are included because they constitute body-contemplation (*kāyānupassanā*).
"Therein" means in this contemplation of the internal and so forth. There are fourteen modes in the Mahāsatipaṭṭhāna Sutta.

These have been mentioned here with reference to the fourteen types and so forth that have already been discussed. Since the internal type and so forth constitute a single category, he says, "by way of indicating a single type.
Regarding the phrase "among outsiders": this refers to certain followers of other sects.
For even among them, body-contemplation belonging to the side of serenity (samatha) can occur by means of mindfulness of breathing and the like. Therefore, he says, "because it occurs in part."
The construction is as follows: "There is the state of being delimited by skin and the state of not being delimited by skin.

Just as in expressions such as "let Dīghabāhu dance," where even in a compound the inclusion of the meaning of the individual members is still obtained despite the presence of another referent, it is said:
"the skin, which constitutes a part of the body, is indeed included. [This refers to] the nails, teeth, sinews, and flesh that are connected to the skin; [of those things] connected to the skin...

Showing that the entire body—which is a collection consisting of the head-hairs and body-hairs whose roots have entered therein, as well as the other [parts] connected to those [roots]—is indeed described as "bounded by skin," he says "connected to those" and so forth. The connection is:
"There are head-hairs; there are body-hairs. In this context, "atthi" (there are) is a single indeclinable word expressing plurality, not a verb.
For in the case of a verb in the active voice (*kiriyāpada*), one would have to say "it exists" (*santīti*); or else, it is stated here using a change of grammatical number (*vacanavipallāsa*).
Alternatively, "learning" (*uggaha*) refers to the mastery of the meditation subject through reciting it aloud and so forth.

For while the mastery of the text of the sections (*koṭṭhāsapāḷi*) consists in making it familiar by recitation, here "learning" refers to bringing to proficiency the retention of the hair and so forth according to their color and other characteristics through mental attention.
The method by which the practitioner becomes skilled in that regard is called the "procedure" (*vidhi*).
The phrase "by the former ones" refers to the connection with each preceding set of five. For, after the "flesh...
kidney" sequence for the kidney pentad in direct order, there is again the "kidney... hair" sequence for the kidney pentad and the skin pentad.
And thus the sequence of recitation (*sajjhāyakrama*) in reverse order has been shown. This is the connection [to the phrase] "this recitation.

"Separately for three or five days" means: five days in direct order, five days in reverse order, and five days in both direct and reverse order; thus, for each of the sets of five, there are three periods of five days.
"Together with the preceding ones for three or five days" refers to the skin-group of five (*tacapañcaka*), and so forth.

Together with the fivefold [recitation] in forward order (*anuloma*), having grouped the five groups beginning with the "urine-group" (*vakkapañcaka*) together, it is stated according to the same method as before.

"By way of showing the beginning and the end" means by way of showing the forward recitation which constitutes the beginning, and the reverse recitation (*paṭiloma*) which constitutes the end of the recitation that includes both forward and reverse orders.
Therefore he said: "The forward... [etc. ...the last. "And this too" refers to what follows after the previous [sections].

The meaning is that this mode of recitation is distinct from the modes of recitation such as the *anuloma* (forward order) applied individually to the pentads and so forth; it refers to the recitation of the pentads and so on all together.

"A row of fingers" is said here because the fingers placed with their tips joined together in a single line across two hands are intended by the term *hatthasaṅkhalikā*. This is the characteristic of the foul (*asubha*).
The repulsiveness of the hair and so forth; the characteristic of the elements (dhātu) such as rigidity and so forth;

"one's own portion" (sakoṭṭhāsa) means one's own division or a similar division; that which exists therein is "belonging to one's own portion" (sakoṭṭhāsika), namely the meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna).

"Having abandoned the contemplation of the body" means not applying attention to the contemplation of it either as foul or by way of the elements. It means not proceeding to the "final beat" (pariyantatāla) and the "initial beat" (āditāla) as was done previously.

“Higher mind” (*adhicitta*) means a mind that is superior due to its association with specific qualities such as concentration (*samādhāna*). Therefore, it is called “the mind of serenity and insight” (*samathavipassanācitta*).
“Mindfulness of the mind” (*manasikāra-citta*) refers to a mind that is exclusively directed toward the sign of concentration (*samādhinimitta*).
Here, “dispersal” (*pabhañjana*) is the mind’s scattered engagement with various objects by way of distraction; because this is absent through concentration, there is no dispersal.

And it has the nature of a wind. "The state of being a witness" means direct manifestation. By the word "etc. in the phrase "due to prior causes, etc.," it includes such things as application to appropriate attention.
"Proceeding evenly" means free from laxity and agitation. "By proceeding in that manner" refers to the practice of the sign of middling serenity.

And therein, by means of the leaping forward [into concentration] that accomplishes the aforementioned balanced progression, one "satisfies with wisdom" (paññāya toseti). This refers to the wisdom of development (bhāvanā-paññā) which is the basis for these four factors:
the non-overstepping of the states arisen therein, the single flavor (ekarasa) of the faculties, the driving force of the corresponding effort (viriya), and repeated practice (āsevana);
by means of this, one satisfies the higher mind (adhicitta), making it joyful. This is achieved precisely through the accomplishment of the aforementioned distinctions.

For by means of that superior wisdom, that mind is said to be "gladdened. And because one who thus gladdens it is said to "purify" the mind through wisdom by completely cleansing all hindrances, it is therefore stated: "and he inspires him.
"Lacking relish" means devoid of the flavor of development due to not obtaining further distinction between what precedes and what follows. "He gladdens" means...
Through cultivation, one rightly brightens and gladdens the mind. "Encourages" means one rightly incites it toward that [object].
"Abode" (āsaya) is the place of occurrence.
"Determinedness" (vavatthitatta) is the state of being unmixed.
*Anto* means within the internal parts. *Sukhumaṃ* (subtle) is said with reference to subtle sinews and so forth.
*Tālapaṭṭikā* is a small box made from the fibers of palm leaves.
The word *matta* is used in counting to indicate that it is slightly less than [the full number]. Excluding teeth and bones, by three...

There are three bone-hundreds less [one]; therefore, it is said “only three hundred. As for what is stated in the *Visuddhimagga* as “a collection of more than three hundred bones,” that was stated by including the teeth-bones as well, according to the method of comprehensive inclusion.
One should not say, “the ankle-bones and so forth are not mentioned,” because it has been stated that “there are two ankle-bones in each foot”; however, one may say “the hip-bone and so forth.”
"By that bone" means by the thigh-bone.
"By the marumba-powder" means by the powder of *marumba* (a type of gravel).

"By the well-concentrated mind acting as the cause" means by way of being free from the agitation caused by various objects. "By the absence of the fluctuation toward various objects" means by way of the state of having no diverse objects [of focus].

"Vipphandanaṃ" means the agitation toward various objects; by the absence of that. Of the meditative consciousness that has not yet transcended joy and pleasure, or of the person possessing that state.
"Paṭikkūladhātuvaṇṇavisesaṃ" means the specific characteristic of the repulsive, the specific element, and the specific color-kasina.

Regarding the five sets beginning with the "fivefold group of the kidneys" (vakkapañcaka), by reciting them individually and together with those preceding them, five full months are obtained by way of six sets of five days each;
however, for the "fivefold group of the skin" (tacapañcaka), it is only three or five days individually. Thus he said, "even when less than half a month [has passed].
"Going to another month" means going to the seventh or subsequent month of the recitation.
[The text] speaks of "binding" and "tying.

By means of the passage beginning with "blue, yellow," etc., the determination of blue and so forth in the saṅghāṭi (robe) is said to be "derived from the great elements" because it depends upon them;
thus [the author] says: "The great element... [and so on] ...the foul odor," etc. Derived matter is delimited by the great elements.

The construction [of the compound] is as follows: *tassa* means "of that derived form" (*upādārūpa*). *Tato* means "from the great primary elements" (*mahābhūta*). Regarding the state of shadow being conditioned by sunlight:

"sunlight is its condition" means that sunlight is the condition for it; "the state of sunlight being the producer of shadow" refers to the relationship between shadow and sunlight where sunlight is the producer of shadow.
By this, he shows the relationship between that which is to be produced and the producer, namely, their mutual delimitation. And the sense bases (*āyatana*) are the doors.
And the twelve bases (*āyatana*), as well as the doors which constitute a portion of them.
"The state of being with conditions" means because they possess conditions.
"In the manner already stated" refers to [the passage beginning]: "Having thus properly grasped these seven kinds of skill in learning," and so forth.
"Or by the method stated in such passages as: 'But by one who, having developed this meditation subject, desires to reach Arahantship...
"In general, however, it should be understood in this way by way of what is common to all," they say; and they also say, "From here onwards. "By way of color, etc.
means by way of color, repulsiveness, and emptiness. "Appearance" means the appearance of the meditation subject.
"Uggaha" (learning) is what is spoken of here. "Therein" means it is connected to one of the following: the fourfold or fivefold jhānas, the first jhāna, or insight (vipassanā). By what means?

Precisely by the attention (manasikāra) directed toward the meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna). Therefore, it should be understood that "uggaha" itself is the connection; thus, it is called "uggahasandhi. "Uṭṭhānaka" means that which arises.

"Sātirekāni cha ambaṇāni kumbhaṃ" means more than six ambuṇa-measures of a jar. "Tato" means from the functions of washing the face, eating, and consuming food. "Nivattati" means it turns back by way of the absolute cessation (accanta-nivatti) through the attainment of Arahatship.
"Kamma alone" means the kamma of attention itself. "Object" refers to the object of preliminary development (*pubbabhāga-bhāvanā*).
"In that way" means like a monkey in a forest.
"One" means one portion.
“Free from the apprehension of a being” is said because it was taught without even touching upon the designation of a being.

“With ego-conceit shattered” refers to the mode of having abandoned conceit regarding the basis for the notion of “I,” which persists as long as there is a continuity of the personal stream (saṃsāra). “Therein” means in another’s body.
357. At the beginning, “cultivation” is the undertaking, which is the production of mental attention (manasikāra).
362. "Gone" means departed.
The commentary on the exposition of the contemplation of the body is finished.
Now begins the commentary on the exposition of the contemplation of feelings.

"Of one who is clearly comprehending" (sampajānassa) means of one who knows correctly by way of its various modes; the meaning is: of one who knows feeling without error together with its basis, its object, and its specific modes such as being accompanied by pleasure or being carnal.
He said "by way of mere conventional expression" because development in the preliminary stage proceeds precisely according to conventional usage.
The phrase "I feel" is stated as a reference to a self, as in "I feel"; yet even one who has fully understood feeling [does not conceive it thus].
Or, when a pleasant feeling has arisen, one knows and expresses in worldly convention, “I am experiencing a pleasant feeling,” and the other [the worldling] does so all the more.
Therefore he said, “stated merely by way of conventional expression.

“Both” refers to energy and concentration. “Having joined them together” means having made them equal in their function, neither deficient nor excessive. Path-wisdom, which proceeds by way of destroying delusion regarding the meaning, the phenomena, and so forth, is precisely the supramundane analytical knowledge (*paṭisambhidā*).
In all three ways, beginning with the aspect of color. "Of the apprehension" means of the apprehension of the immaterial (arūpa).
By stating, "The basis is called the body born of karma," he shows what is excluded by saying, "the six bases, such as the eye, are not [the basis].

This is a demonstration of how the mental body (nāmakāya) exists in dependence upon the material body (rūpakāya), just as one of two bundles of reeds standing by mutual support exists in dependence on the other.
This is the demonstration of the specific nature of the condition of dependence (*nissayapaccaya*).
"Of those" means of those for whom contact and consciousness are manifest; "of others" means of others than those, for whom contact and consciousness are not manifest.
Because the occurrence of pleasant and painful feelings is clearly evident, it is said: "of all those who are to be trained."

"Feeling is manifest. Having melted it again and again means: having melted very pure butter, once it has become cool, one places it into extremely cold water, crushes it while it remains solid, kneads it together, melts it again—having done this in this manner a hundred times.

"In that case too" means: where only the immaterial meditation subject (*arūpa-kammaṭṭhāna*) is shown... [etc. ...in that case too. The construction is: "In those suttas in which the material meditation subject (*rūpa-kammaṭṭhāna*) is included therein.
The commentary on the exposition of the contemplation of feelings (*vedanānupassanā-niddesa-vaṇṇanā*) is finished.
The commentary on the exposition of the contemplation of mind (*cittānupassanā-niddesa-vaṇṇanā*).

365. The connection is: "For those associated with defilements, there is no purity. "By the others as well" means by those not associated [with the mind] other than the defilement associated with itself.
"A separate mention" means mentioning it separately from other unwholesome states. "The apprehension of distinction" means the apprehension of its distinctiveness;
the sense is that it shows a unique state of delusion (*samoha*), which is why both of these are called "the mind of utter confusion" (*momūha-citta*).
The commentary on the exposition of the contemplation of mind is finished.

Part One: Commentary on the Chapter on the Hindrances (nīvaraṇa).
367. *Yuganaddhatā* (yoke-farness) is the simultaneous occurrence [of two factors] like oxen harnessed to a single yoke.

"By way of grasping" means by way of grasping even an unattractive object as "beautiful. The construction is: "and it is called the 'sign' (*nimitta*) and the 'sign of the beautiful' (*subhanimitta*).
This is because, as a rule, sentient beings wish only for their own welfare and happiness.
It is said: "Of the welfare and happiness desired. And improper attention (*ayoniso-manasikāra*) is indeed not a means for the happiness distinguished by welfare;
or rather, it is that which is not a means for the welfare and happiness intended and desired. For those blinded by ignorance proceed even toward such [a goal].
"To be accomplished" means to be produced by improper attention, namely, sensual desire (*kāmacchanda*).

"Conducive to that" means being conducive to the improper attention (*ayoniso-manasikāra*) and proper attention (*yoniso-manasikāra*) that respectively occur toward the beautiful as "beautiful" and toward the foul as "foul.

The fact that the adherence to permanence and so forth regarding forms and the like, as well as perceptions of permanence and so forth, have the aforementioned types of attention as their proximate cause (*upanissaya*), constitutes their conduciveness to that.
The connection is: "He generates the perception of repulsiveness in nutriment. "Of its transformation" refers to the transformation of the food.
“Of that which has its outflow, etc.”: “Its support” means the stomach, or the body itself. “He” refers to one who knows the proper measure in eating.
He says “by way of the Abhidhamma method” because, according to the Suttanta method, sensual lust is called the “hindrance of sensual desire. For in the Abhidhamma it is said:
“Dependent on a state that is a hindrance, a state that is a hindrance arises, not by way of the pre-nascence condition.”

From the statement in the *Vibhaṅga*, “In the formless realm, dependent on the hindrance of sensual desire, the hindrance of sloth-and-torpor, the hindrance of restlessness, and the hindrance of ignorance arise,” it is understood that attachment to existence (*bhavarāga*) is also called the hindrance of sensual desire.
Therefore, he said: “All greed whatsoever is the hindrance of sensual desire.”
"In breaking the boundary" (*sīmābhede*) means when the boundary consisting of oneself and so forth has been broken;

the meaning is that the development of loving-kindness (*mettābhāvanā*) is of a single form throughout all [objects] beginning with oneself. "Devoid of designations such as 'monastery'" (*vihārādiuddesarahitaṃ*) means devoid of the delimitation of locations such as monasteries. "Of the loving-kindness already acquired.

"Twenty-eightfold": it is sevenfold by way of [the objects] beginning with women, and each of these is twenty-eightfold by way of being joined with [the qualities] beginning with "free from enmity" (*avera*).

Regarding the phrase "by way of association with beings and so forth, women and so forth, and enemies and so forth": here, by way of association with beings and so forth and enemies and so forth, there are twenty;
and by way of association with women and so forth and enemies and so forth, there are twenty-eight. Thus, for one direction, there are forty-eight. Likewise for the remaining directions;
having included them all together, he says, "divided into four hundred and eighty."

The construction is: "and there is no grieving over what has been done or left undone. From such statements as, "He has heard much—suttas, geyyas," and so forth, it should be understood that "having heard much" refers to the ninefold teaching (*navanga-sāsana*), not merely to the Vinaya alone;
thus it was said, "without regard for seniority," and not "and having heard much."

"Doubt stands here" means it persists among those previously arisen states of doubt—which have many divisions according to their occurrence such as "Did I exist in the past? and so forth—among these [states] it is said to be "stationed.
"Even with eight bases" means not only with sixteen bases, nor even only with the three-jewel bases, but indeed even with eight bases;
for in one who has fallen into uncertainty regarding the Three Jewels, doubt arises concerning the training and so forth. In that regard:
And because one who has attained freedom from doubt lacks that [doubt], it should be understood that the remaining types of doubt are rooted in doubt regarding the Triple Gem.
"Entering" means leaping into the object by way of believing, "It is exactly so.
The commentary on the section on the hindrances is finished.
Kha. Explanation of the Section on the Factors of Enlightenment (Bojjhaṅgapabba):
"By that" means by the apprehension based on the meaning.
Weakness is the state of being dull due to the influence of conditions.

They say that even though the village was hidden by mountain regions and forest thickets, it was not far away; because one had to travel by encircling the mountain, the dwelling possessed the characteristics of the forest (arañña). Therefore, he heard it with his physical ear alone.
"Satisfaction" (pasāda) is spoken of as a synonym for affection (sineha) because it is the cause of attainment.
"Sharpening" (tejana) is the act of bringing about the state of sharpness in the faculties. "Delighting" (tosana) means gladdening.
The commentary on the Chapter on the Factors of Enlightenment is finished.
[It was stated] by way of serenity and insight for the first foundation of mindfulness, and by way of pure insight for the others.
The intention is that, otherwise, how could right mindfulness of the path have the body as its object, given that it is described according to its mode of arrival?
Regarding the four types of persons mentioned, such as those who dwell contemplating the body and so forth, he therefore said: "For it is not possible... to speak of one [person]...

This is because of the consequence of the simultaneous occurrence of multiple mindfulnesses; that is, because through a single arising of consciousness there would follow the occurrence of multiple mindfulnesses, and with that [single] mindfulness, the awareness of multiple [objects].
"Distinguished by their own specific functions" means distinguished by the particularity of their respective functions.
"By a distinction of phenomena" means by a specific phenomenon distinguished by a distinction of its object.

"One phenomenon does not perform the function of another phenomenon" means that for a single phenomenon, there is no such thing as performing the function of a different phenomenon, because of the absence of such a thing.

"By a distinction of phenomena" means by the differentiation of phenomena. "Its distinction" means that there is no distinction of that function. Therefore—because here there is no [distinction] of a phenomenon...
A distinction of functions is intended by way of analysis, and a distinction of phenomena is intended by way of the distinction of functions; therefore, it was said:
“In one way,” and so forth.

2. Commentary on the Exposition of the Abhidhamma (Abhidhammabhājanīya) 374.
“Contemplating the body in the body”: this is a qualification of the foundations of mindfulness (satipaṭṭhāna) by way of reference to a person (puggalādhiṭṭhāna).
And that is established by the tradition of the source, for otherwise it would be impossible; thus he said, “having taught... by way of the source. This means without mentioning a specific person.

“Contemplating the body in the body”: this is stated without referring to a person (*puggala*). Likewise, because there is no naming [of a subject], no qualification regarding the origin [of the contemplation] is made.
In these two methods—the method of contemplation (*anupassanā-naya*) and the pure method (*suddhika-naya*)—the commentary on the *Abhidhamma-bhājaniya* is concluded.
The commentary on the Analysis of the Foundations of Mindfulness (Satipaṭṭhānavibhaṅga) is finished.
8. The Analysis of the Right Exertions (Sammappadhānavibhaṅga).
1. Commentary on the Suttanta Exposition (Suttantabhājanīya).

390. The word *kāraṇa* (cause/reason) signifies "reasoning" (*yutti*), as in such passages as "all this he says is without reason. Therefore, "having reason as their primary focus" means having reasoning as their primary focus;

or alternatively, the meaning here should be understood as "having as their primary focus that which is appropriate for the activity of not producing unarisen evil, and so forth. "The non-arising, etc., of unarisen evil, etc. refers to the non-production and so on of unarisen evil states and the like.

391. “It is not another state (na añño dhammo): Just as craving and so forth—which possess the nature of yearning, desire, adherence, and exertion—have the designation ‘zeal’ (chanda) yet are not called ‘another state’ because the factor of zeal defined as the desire-to-act is absent from them;
however, the zeal for the Dhamma (*dhammacchanda*) is not ‘another state’ because it possesses that same nature. Therefore he said: ‘The zeal for the Dhamma is zeal for its own-nature (*sabhāva*).’”
"In the *Aṭṭhakathā*" means in the ancient commentary (*porāṇa-aṭṭhakathā*). "Because it leads to the occurrence of the cycle of existence" means because it gives rise to the suffering of *saṃsāra*.
"They are not able" refers to the statement: "Having fallen away from peaceful attainments, they are unable to steady themselves while living the holy life (*brahmacariya*).

In this context, it should be construed as "of the two kinds. "Only those that have arisen before" means that only those [defilements] which have previously arisen manifest by way of their active manifestation (*samudācāra*) and so forth.

“In all circumstances” means in circumstances such as those of a regular monk (*pakatatta*) and so forth. For, in the state of being a regular monk, none of those [prohibitions] are to be practiced at all;
yet, in other states, only those specific ones pertaining to that particular state are to be practiced. Regarding the phrase “‘It should be spoken,’ etc.,” the word “etc. includes:
“One should not dwell in a non-residence where there is no roof-covering; nor should one dwell in a residence or a non-residence where there is no roof-covering.”
"One should dwell [with them]; one should not sit on the same seat; when they are seated on a low seat, one should not sit on a high seat;
when they are seated on the ground, one should not sit on a seat; one should not walk back and forth on the same walking path;
when they are walking on a low walking path, one should not walk on a high walking path; when they are walking on the ground, one should not walk on a walking path."
These he includes. "Of them" refers to those who are senior to one on probation (*pārivāsika*) and so forth. "Having grouped together" means having combined them.
"Making each one" means making even the nine [offenses] into single units. "Salutation, rising to greet, joining of palms, and respectful service should not be accepted;
nor should the offering of a seat, the offering of a bed, water for washing the feet, a footstool, or a foot-scraper."
"Accepting a bowl and robes is not to be consented to"—all this is one [category] by way of the commonality of non-consent. "Ten" refers to:
"Not by failure in virtue, not by failure in conduct, not by failure in view, not by failure in livelihood;
monks are not to be split by monks; the banner of householders is not to be borne; the banner of sectarians is not to be borne... [and so forth].
“Titthiyas are to be associated with, bhikkhus are to be associated with, one should train in the training of a bhikkhu”—thus ten [factors] have been mentioned.

Regarding the phrase “and action,” it is stated in the nominative case; however, in the expression “of action whose ripening has not yet matured,” it should be construed by transforming it into the genitive case as “of action.
This is to be connected with the statement: “that which is past, departed, and arisen.”
“Here” means in this *Sammohavinodanī*. When he says, “When the occasion has been thus prepared, the result...
is said to have arisen,” he is speaking specifically of the result (*vipāka*). “Therein” refers to the *Aṭṭhasālinī*.

He says, “The latent tendencies (*anusaya*) are those lusts for sense-pleasures and so forth that have been eradicated by the Path and have become firmly rooted,” because they are to be abandoned by the Path.
The object is like a milk-tree that has been struck. How so? By way of grasping its sign (*nimittaggāha*).

He explains this very point with the words beginning "attained" (*adhigata*). Therein, because the object is grasped by way of grasping its sign, that object is indeed said to be "attained" from the standpoint of being a place of arising for the cause of the arising of defilements at every moment it is recollected.
He said, "It has been attained by way of grasping the sign," the intention being that the object is one in which defilements have become manifest.
Because it is the cause for the arising of defilements, the defilement ready to arise is called "the object containing the defilements within.

And this is said by applying the term [defilement] to the object of grasping, while it actually applies to the grasper, just as the term [support] is applied to the supported while it actually applies to the support.

Having approached [the matter] by way of figurative usage (*upacara*), it was said: "The beds are making a shout. Now, abandoning figurative usage and showing the meaning according to the direct method (*nippariyāya*), he said:
"Grasping the sign... [etc. ...are similar. "Should be explained in detail" means it should be explained in detail by such passages as: "Just as if there were a milk-tree... and so forth.

"In three ways" means in three ways by way of the past and so on. "Brought forward" is by way of a simile. By the word "also" (*pi*) in the phrase "also for the purpose of showing non-abandonment,"...

The phrase “also for the purpose of showing that it is not to be stated in three ways” summarizes what has already been said. Thus, the defilements abandoned by the path are to be understood as follows:
even though they were capable of arising when the path had not yet arisen, they are entirely and completely non-existent once the path has arisen.
The commentary on the *Suttantabhājanīya* is concluded.
3. Commentary on the Section of Questions (Pañhapucchakavaṇṇanā) 427.

Regarding the development of the path where energy is predominant, it cannot be said whether the right exertions (sammappadhāna) have the path as their dominant factor or do not have the path as their dominant factor.
In this regard, for the first [exertion], there is an absence of another form of energy; for the other, there is the predominance of the other [factors].
And the absence of energy that has not yet become the path-factor is the reason for its being "inexpressible"; he stated this point with the words "having the path as their dominant" and so forth.
"Then" refers to the time of cultivating the path in which energy is predominant.
The commentary on the Section of Questions is finished.
The commentary on the Analysis of the Right Strivings (Sammappadhāna-vibhaṅga) is finished.
9. The Analysis of the Bases of Psychic Power (Iddhipāda-vibhaṅga).
1. Commentary on the Suttanta Exposition (Suttantabhājanīya).

431. The first meaning is that of the agent (kattū): “It succeeds (*ijjhati*), thus it is success (*iddhi*”). The second is the meaning of the instrument (karaṇa): “By means of this they succeed,” thus [it is success].
Success is said to be that which is to be attained, in the sense that “they attain (*pajjanti*) and reach (*pāpuṇanti*) success.

This is because it is impossible for the word *iddhi*, when analyzed as an agent-noun (*kattusādhana*), to have grammatical coreferentiality (*samānādhikaraṇatā*) with the word *pāda* when analyzed as an instrument-noun (*karaṇasādhana*), and because of the nature of the meaning of that which succeeds.
Because it must be attained by means of the foot as an instrument (*karaṇa*), the grammatical construction of the words as "the foot is indeed psychic power" (*iddhi eva pādo*) is not possible;

thus he stated this point: "And... [it cannot] be said. The construction is: "Psychic power (*iddhi*) is that which is to be accomplished through the meaning of the foot as the instrument for the act of succeeding (*ijjhanakiriyā*)," and it is to be attained. "Of the two instruments" refers to the instruments for the acts of succeeding and attaining.
This is the meaning of *iddhipāda*. It is not possible for there to be a lack of grammatical coreferentiality (*asamānādhikaraṇatā*), because two negations establish the original state.

Therefore—meaning, because the first sense [of the compound] does not admit of a coordinate compound (*samānādhikaraṇasamāsa*) and the second sense does not admit of a genitive compound (*sāmivacanasamāsa*) for the words *iddhipāda*—therefore, the construction is to be understood according to the previously stated first sense by way of a coordinate compound alone.

It is appropriate [to analyze it] as a *pāda* because it has the nature of a portion (*koṭṭhāsa*) that is being produced. According to the second sense, the analysis is appropriate through the other type of compound (*itarasamāsa*), because the *pāda* has the nature of a means (*upāya*) and an instrument (*karaṇa*) for success (*ijjhana*).
"Some" refers to the Elder Dhammasiri. "For the two kinds of purpose" means for the purpose of production (*nibbatti*) and for the purpose of growth (*vuddhi*).
“Separately” means apart from this [definition]: “the foot itself is the basis of success, thus it is the ‘basis of success’ (iddhipāda).

“By way of compound-construction” means by way of such a compound-construction as: “the foot of success is the ‘basis of success’ (iddhipāda). “As appropriate” means whichever [term] is appropriate in the sense of the agent or the instrument.
“Of the prior stages to attainment” means, respectively, the state of being the agent, the success, and the instrument, which are the prior stages to the specific realization (*visesādhigama*).
The construction is: "spoken with intentional meaning" (*sandhāya vutto*). Because it is stated in the *Uttaracūḷabhājanīya* that "desire itself is the basis of psychic power consisting of desire;

likewise, consciousness, energy, and investigation themselves are the bases of psychic power consisting of investigation," he says: "by means of the bases of psychic power such as desire, etc., which are mentioned in the *Uttaracūḷabhājanīya*," and so forth.

Regarding the bases of psychic power consisting of desire, mind, and investigation, the inclusion of the "volitional formations of striving" (*padhāna-saṅkhāra*) is appropriate because it has not been mentioned previously;

however, with reference to the objection as to how this applies to the base of psychic power consisting of energy (*vīriya-iddhipāda*), he says, "In the exposition of the base of psychic power consisting of energy," and so forth.

If there are only two factors of possession (*samannāgama-aṅga*), one might ask what the purpose of desire and the others is; therefore, he says, "They are qualifiers of concentration. It is not stated here [in the definition of the base of psychic power] because they are not qualifiers of that [concentration].

Although it has been stated that energy (vīriya) is mentioned twice for the purpose of showing its possession as a specific qualification of concentration (samādhi), this is already established by the expression "endowed with energy and concentration" (*vīriya-samādhi-samannāgata*) alone.

Since this is already established, one might occasionally suspect that the repetition is intended to illuminate the presence of a different kind of energy; therefore, [the text] is provided to dispel that suspicion.
He said, “And energy,” and so forth. “Distinguished by zeal and the rest” means distinguished by the specific predominance-condition (adhipatipaccaya) status of zeal and the others.
For it is for this very reason that the bases of psychic power (iddhipāda) are taught specifically through the gateway of zeal and the rest. And thus it has been said:
“If a bhikkhu, making zeal his predominant influence, attains concentration,” and so on. “By way of their respective requisites” refers to that...
The meaning is: by way of being the support for that desire and concentration; that is, by way of being a specific condition (*paccaya-visesatā*). In the sense of a means (*upāya*)... [etc.
...it is stated that the state of being a means for attainment is indeed nothing other than the state of being a support (*nissaya-bhāva*).

With the words “By that very [fact],” etc., he clarifies through the scripture itself that desire and the others are the bases of psychic power (*iddhipāda*) as previously described. Therein, “by that very [fact]” means precisely by way of desire and the others having the status of being a means.
Because the development of the bases of psychic power (*iddhipāda*) is intended [here]. "Precisely for the purpose of showing the basis of psychic power as a means" means:

having made desire (*chanda*) and the others the primary, chief, and precursors, the concentration produced thereby shows that desire and the others are the means for attaining psychic power; this is the demonstration of the basis of psychic power as a means.
It is precisely for that purpose that, in various places in the Canon, it is stated: "For one who has become thus, the aggregate of feeling... [and so on] ...the aggregate of consciousness."

The demonstration of the bases of psychic power (*iddhipāda*) has been made with reference specifically to the aggregates of feeling and so forth as distinguished by zeal and the other [factors], because that is what is intended.

This must be accepted in this way; otherwise, if the status of being a base of psychic power were understood solely in terms of the aggregates associated with psychic power, there would not be fourfoldness due to the absence of any distinguishing cause—this is the intention.
433. *Tosanaṃ* means pleasing the Teacher or [pleasing] the training. *Thāmabhāvato* means from the state of being firm.
Regarding the statement, "One born of a noble lineage becomes a leader of men," it is said that this is because the mind is preeminent and resembles a distinguished birth.
Because the *manta* (incantation) has investigative wisdom as its cause, its similarity to *vīmaṃsā* (investigation) is easily understood; therefore, it is not separately mentioned.
“Chandādikā” means the volition-concentration-exertion-formation, the energy-concentration-exertion-formation, and the mind-concentration-exertion-formation—these three sets of three factors.

Without making a distinction, that is, without dividing them, they are grouped together by way of their commonality as bases of psychic power (*iddhi*) and their commonality as bases of success (*iddhipāda*).
Therefore he said, “having combined them. Alternatively, “division” (*bhedana*) means separation or mixing; thus he said [this].

“Having mixed them together”: for instance, it is stated that “the remaining four associated aggregates are indeed the bases of psychic power (iddhipāda),” thus speaking even without mixing psychic power (*iddhi*) with the bases of psychic power (*iddhipāda*). “Specifically” means by way of distinction, because they are unique due to their unmixed state among the four bases of psychic power;
for desire and the others are unique to each respective base of psychic power. “Without distinction” means without differentiation.
The meaning is: "by way of being common to the four bases of psychic power (*iddhipāda*).

By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*) in the phrase "the basis of psychic power of desire, the basis of psychic power of concentration, etc.," the formative factors of striving (*padhānasaṅkhāra*), as well as energy, mind, and investigation, are included.
The term "basis" (*pāda*) refers to the four aggregates associated with those [factors]. This is shown by the passage beginning, "They enter into the basis of psychic power of desire," and so forth.

Without specifying entry only into the superior [states], he says "in four": namely, desire (*chanda*), concentration (*samādhi*), the volitional formations of striving (*padhāna-saṅkhāra*), and the aggregates associated therewith;
thus it is "in four. Since concentration is intended here as being either rooted in desire or predominant in desire, he says:
"For one who possesses desire, what concentration would not succeed? "Thus" (*iti*) means in this way, by this manner, regarding that gateway to the development of concentration.
The aggregates developed through application to the cultivation of concentration are "developed by concentration.

By the words beginning with "For those who," he explains in detail what was stated briefly as "there is nothing new. "Of the three" refers to the desire-concentration and the volitional formations of striving.
"This" refers to the statement beginning with "For these three. "Of the former" refers to the statement beginning with "Desire is concentration. "By way of being the cause" means...
By way of being the means of accomplishment (*sādhanabhāva*). "By that" refers to the statement beginning with, "For these three factors...

Since the three factors, starting with desire (*chanda*), function as a mutual support for one another and as a support for their associated states, therefore the status of "basis of psychic power" (*iddhipāda*) is also attributed to them.

Furthermore, since that state of being a support is inseparable from association (*sampayoga*), he says, "because they are included therein," meaning because they are included among the associated states.

The meaning [is as follows]. Since the associated aggregates do not possess the state of *iddhi* by way of their own intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*) in the same manner as desire (*chanda*) and the others, he said:

"There is a figurative expression (*pariyāya*) for the state of *iddhi*. By this it is stated: "The remaining associated [factors]... [are] not by way of their own intrinsic nature. "Of one part" refers to desire and the others.
Or, it refers to all four aggregates, or to the four beginning with desire. Furthermore: "The associated..."
He spoke thus with reference to the passage beginning with "pana. By this, he indicates that the four aggregates and a portion of them constitute supernormal power (*iddhi*).
He said, "having made it 'not previously stated,'" because it is different from what was stated previously in terms of the sequence of the words.

As for the application according to the respective order: in what sense is "attainment" (*paṭilābha*) *iddhi*, and in what sense is the "foot" (*pāda*) the "prior part" (*pubbabhāga*)? If "foot" is in the sense of a foundation (*patiṭṭhāna*), then it is specifically the "foot of the support-superpower" (*nissaya-iddhipāda*).
It might be said that it is not the "basis of psychic power consisting in means" (*upāyiddhipāda*); therefore, he says, "And the means," and so forth.
"In all instances" refers to both the *Suttanta-bhājaniya* and the *Abhidhamma-bhājaniya*. Thus he says, "In the *Suttanta-bhājaniya*," and so forth.

"By way of being a qualification of concentration" refers to [the definition of] concentration as "concentration dominated by desire, caused by desire, or preponderant in desire" (*chandasamādhi*), and so on.
[The phrase] "by way of being a qualification. There is also the reading "by way of cultivating concentration" (*samādhisevanavasena*).
In that context, "by way of cultivating concentration" means by way of the cultivation of concentration after making it the dominant influence (*adhipati*) when zeal (*chanda*) is predominant.

"Of those who have become means" means of those for whom the cultivation of concentration has become a means [thinking], "If concentration succeeds for one possessed of zeal, it will succeed for me as well."
The commentary on the Suttanta-bhājaniya is finished.
2. Commentary on the Abhidhamma-bhājaniya: 444.
There are one hundred and eight sections with predominance [of the factors]; in each of these, the four bases of psychic power (iddhipāda) do not occur individually.
He said: “Because of the absence of the bases with their respective predominants when they are complete. Therein, he states the reason: “For there are no predominants of predominants.

For if there were predominants, then by way of the divisions of the bases of success (iddhipāda) with their respective predominants, there would be three hundred and thirty-two methods, and including the pure ones, four thousand eight hundred; however, that is not the case.
This is the intended meaning (*adhippāya*). To show how many methods (*naya*) are obtainable here, it is said: "In each one, however... and so forth.
There are eight hundred pure methods and likewise eight hundred with a governing principle (*sādhipatika*); thus, by way of the four paths, there are sixteen hundred methods.
The commentary on the *Abhidhammabhājanīya* is concluded.
3. Commentary on the Section of Questions:
Because they function by way of being mutually pre-eminent, the four predominances do not regard one another with respect.
Therefore it was said: "The four bases of psychic power (iddhipāda) do not have the Path as their predominance. For this reason he said: "But [they are] the predominances of one another..."
"They do not become [dominants]"—this refers to the meaning: "The dominants do not become dominants for one another.
"Of the dominants" means of those capable of being dominants. "They do not act as dominants" means they do not proceed by making [the other] a dominant or by honoring it as a dominant.
"In the coexistence of dominants" means in the simultaneous occurrence through the performance of the function of a dominant.

The statement, “Because of the absence of a path that has non-deliberation as its dominant factor,” was said by way of attributing a fault—namely, that “phenomena capable of being dominant factors would function solely as dominant factors”—and not according to how they are actually attained. For when there is a prior formation (pubbābhisaṅkhāra), dominant phenomena function as dominant factors, and not otherwise;
thus, the qualification is made with reference to the absence of such a [prior] state even when [the factors] are co-existent.
It cannot be said that "it should not be done. Regarding the state of acting as mutual predominance:

this refers to their occurrence by making one another the predominant factor. The statement regarding "having investigation as the predominant factor" is a statement concerning the state of having investigation as the predominant factor.
The intention is that it cannot be said that all [mental factors] have a predominant factor, because they all possess a predominant factor. Co-existence has been rejected.
Thus, because it is stated that there is no single-sided certainty regarding the state of having a dominant influence (*adhipatibhāva*).
The commentary on the *Pañhapucchaka* is finished.
The commentary on the *Iddhipādavibhaṅga* is finished.
10. Analysis of the Factors of Enlightenment (Bojjhaṅgavibhaṅga) 1.
The Exposition According to the Discourses (Suttantabhājanīya) Commentary on the First Method (Paṭhamanayavaṇṇanā)
466. "Establishment" (*patiṭṭhāna*) here means remaining within this cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*); its root is the defilements (*kilesa*). Thus it is said: "establishment by way of defilement.
Furthermore, the engagement in activity for the sake of that establishment is called "kamma"; thus it is said: "accumulation by way of volitional formation" (*abhisaṅkhāra*).
Since, among the defilements, craving and views are specifically the leaders of the cycle of existence for those whose temperament is dominated by craving and views, [they are singled out].
Furthermore, it is only karma accompanied by defilements that serves as a basis for rebirth, not karma alone; therefore it is said: “By means of craving and views... [etc. ...the accumulation.

Likewise, because craving consists in a relish for existence (*bhava*), and because view—which takes the form of delighting in non-existence (*vibhava*)—consists in the formation of non-existence, it is said:
“Establishment by way of craving, and accumulation by way of view. Even among views, that which functions inwardly...

Because one remains specifically in *saṃsāra* due to the view of existence (*bhava-diṭṭhi*), it is called "slouching" (*olīyanā*); thus he said, "establishment in the view of eternalism (*sassata-diṭṭhi*).
Even the view of non-existence (*vibhava-diṭṭhi*), though it functions by turning outward, does not transcend the formative activity of existence;

thus it was stated, "the exertion (*āyūhanā*) of the view of annihilation (*uccheda-diṭṭhi*). "Lapse into despondency" (*layāpatti*) is the failure to bring to completion an undertaking that has already been begun.
Because it has the nature of internal contraction, he said: "establishment by way of sluggishness.
Because the offense of agitation is a lack of means and the offense of exertion is a lack of non-contraction, it is stated: "exertion by way of restlessness.
Likewise, because devotion to sensual pleasure belongs to the side of indolence, and devotion to self-mortification belongs to the side of restlessness, [it is so called] by way of both.
“Establishment” and “accumulation” have been explained; the remainder should be understood according to the method already stated.

“Herein” means in this *Sammohavinodanī*. Regarding the phrase “of those not mentioned,” the construction is: establishment and accumulation are to be understood by way of such expressions as “establishment by way of defilement.
“In states proceeding evenly” means in associated states that proceed evenly, being free from sluggishness (*līna*) and restlessness (*uddhacca*). “Reflects upon” means...

He compares, reckons, and weighs what is appropriate. Therefore it is said: "He examines by way of arising. "Its mode" refers to the mode of reflective contemplation and the mode of examining by way of arising.
And "having done so" means precisely because the enlightenment factor of equanimity has the nature of reflective contemplation.
"The state of being the successive cause" means the state of being the cause for each subsequent [factor]. For the preceding...
It is the specific condition for each subsequent one. 467.

Mindfulness (*sati*) is indeed powerful because of its capacity to grasp the true nature (*sabhāva*) of the body and so forth without error. The meaning of "wisdom (*paññā*) is grasped by mindfulness and circumspection" is as follows.
"With a mind such as this" means with a mind dependent upon gain, honor, and fame. "By way of long-established conduct and so forth."

By way of the phrase "having been done long ago" (*cirakata-vattādi*), the construction is as follows: even with the word "said" (*vutto*), it should be joined thus: "Having performed [it], he said... [the bodily intimation]... the constituent part.

The phrase "of others" (*pare*) does not refer to those immediately following. It should be applied to all [factors] thus: "All factors of enlightenment (*bojjhaṅga*) certainly become specific conditions for all [others].
"Desires" (*kāma*) means that which one desires; "carnal bait" (*āmisa*) means that which one touches by way of relishing; thus, "carnal bait" is desire itself as bait.

Defilement-desire (*kilesakāma*). As for object-desire (*vatthukāma*), it is called "flesh" (*āmisa*) because it is something to be touched. The same applies to the remaining two types of desire. Among these, "the world" (*loka*) refers to the cycle of existence (*vaṭṭa*); it is so called because specific pleasures or specific rebirths are found therein. Greed that proceeds by way of the gratification of sensual desires is "the flesh of sensual desire" (*kāmāmisa*).
Greed that proceeds by way of the aspiration for a specific state of existence is "the flesh of the world" (*lokāmisa*). For what purpose does so-called "non-existence" (*vibhava*) exist?
"Who would long for that? refers to greed, which is characterized by attachment to the round of existence (*vaṭṭa*);

they call this "the bait of the round. "Its object" means the object of that craving, namely form and so forth. "Worldly conditions" refers to gain and the rest. All remaining types of craving mentioned are passion (*rāga*) that generates the cycle of rebirth (*saṃsāra*).
The commentary on the first method is concluded.

Commentary on the Second Method (Dutiyanayavaṇṇanā) 468–9. "All beings" (sabbe sattā): this refers to all beings in every state of existence—whether in the realms of sense-desire existence (*kāmabhava*) and so forth, in the realms of perception existence (*saññībhava*) and so forth, or in the realms of one-constituent existence (*ekavokārabhava*) and so forth.
"Sustained by nutriment" (*āhāraṭṭhitikā*): those whose persistence is through nutriment; that is, those whose persistence is through conditions (*paccaya*). By whatever condition...
They remain; that one single phenomenon is to be directly known by means of direct knowledge—known as "subsistence through nutriment"—which is termed full understanding through knowledge.
"Two elements" refers to the conditioned and unconditioned elements. "Three elements" refers to the sense-sphere element, the fine-material element, and the immaterial element.
"Five bases of liberation": "In this case, bhikkhus, the Teacher teaches the Dhamma to a bhikkhu, or another..."
The causes for liberation are those mentioned in such passages as “or one who stands in the position of a teacher.

“Incomparables” (anuttariyāni) refers to the six incomparables, beginning with the incomparable vision. “Bases for being without the ten” (niddasavatthūni) refers to those reasons by which one becomes “without the ten” (niddasa); this is merely a conventional designation.
For instance, a monk who has exhausted the taints (khīṇāsava), having been ten years [ordained], attains final nibbāna; then, after another ten years...
It does not exist. And it is not only one who has ten years [of standing] that does not exist; even one with nine years...

down to one with a single moment [of standing], does not exist at all because of the absence of further rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*). However, this was stated by way of a specific occasion (*aṭṭhuppatti*).
Those [qualities], moreover, are indeed mentioned in the Sutta as follows: "Here, bhikkhu, one has intense desire for the undertaking of the training," and so forth. "For a person of right view..."
“Wrong view is worn away,” and so forth—these are the ten bases for wearing away (*nijjaravatthu*). “The aggregates, etc. refers to the aggregates, sense-bases, elements, and so on.
“Bonding” (*vinandhana*) indicates that craving is called “desire” (*vāna*) in the sense of being a bond for existence and so forth.
“Going” (*gamana*) refers to the occurrence [of consciousness] toward an object by way of relishing it; therefore it is said, “in regard to forms that are dear and pleasant.”
It should be understood as "accompanied by insight" because it originates from intimation (*viññatti*).
However, because it was stated specifically as "bodily energy that has not yet reached the Path," it is thereby indicated that supramundane energy also exists in a figurative sense as "bodily.

As for why the factor of enlightenment of rapture (*pītisambojjhaṅga*) is not mentioned in the fine-material sphere (*rūpāvacara*), he said: "In the fine-material sphere... [it is] rejected. Just as...

Joy accompanied by insight is, in a figurative sense, called the "joy enlightenment factor" (*pītisambojjhaṅga*); thus, joy belonging to the fine-material sphere (*rūpāvacara*) could also be said to be conducive to penetration (*nibbedhabhāgiya*).
Although it is obtainable in this way, it is not so stated because it is mentioned only in relation to what is not [ordinarily] obtained.

The qualification "without applied thought and sustained thought" (*avitakkavicārā*) is for the purpose of showing that this joy is peaceful and sublime. "Becoming enlightenment factors" means becoming enlightenment factors in a figurative sense.

"Joy without applied thought and sustained thought... [and so on]. It was not mentioned because that [joy] possesses applied and sustained thought; for there is no joy belonging to the sense-sphere (kāmāvacara) that is without applied and sustained thought.
The meaning is that it is mentioned here by way of a figurative expression (pariyāya).

Because they accord with the penetration of the Path, mindfulness and the other factors are called "factors of enlightenment" (bojjhaṅga) even in the foundational jhānas, just as they are in insight (vipassanā); thus he said, "Because they partake of penetration (nibbedhabhāgiya), they should not be rejected."

Having thus stated the intention of those who extract the enlightenment factors (*bojjhaṅga*) from the kasiṇa-jhānas and so forth, he says, "But those who do not extract them," etc., in order to state the intention of those who do not extract them.

For they extract the enlightenment factors at the moment of insight (*vipassanā*), because their functions are produced in close proximity [to that moment], but not at the moment of jhāna, because of the absence of such factors then. Therefore he said: "Just as with the function of insight... etc."
“They do not extract [the defilements],” he said. Because the formless attainments are the outflow of the kasiṇas, he said, “They are dependent upon them.
The commentary on the second method is finished.
Commentary on the third method.

“Relinquishing (*vossajjana*) is abandoning (*pahāna*), relinquishment (*vossagga*); or relinquishing is the state of having let go, which is the entry into a state free from apprehension. Thus it is said: “The word ‘relinquishment’...
the twofold nature has been stated. At the moment of insight (*vipassanā*), it occurs by way of partial eradication (*tadaṅga*) and leaning toward that [Nibbāna];
at the moment of the Path (*magga*), it occurs by way of total eradication (*samuccheda*) and making that [Nibbāna] its object (*tadārammaṇa*).
The commentary on the third method is finished.
The commentary on the Suttanta-bhājaniya is finished.
2. Commentary on the Abhidhamma-bhājaniya.
472. Equanimity (*upekkhā*) is the intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*) of the enlightenment factor of equanimity (*upekkhā-sambojjhaṅga*).

And this, unlike the enlightenment factors of concentration and energy which are occupied with the deficiency or excess of associated states, functions as a state of neutrality (*majjhattākāra*) regarding their lack of deficiency or excess.

He expressed this meaning by saying, "by way of equanimating," and so forth. In that context, "equanimating" (*ikkhana*) by way of "approaching" (*upapatti*) refers to reflective discernment (*paṭisaṅkhāna*).
The commentary on the Exposition of the Abhidhamma is finished.
The commentary on the Exposition of the Factors of Enlightenment is finished. 11.
The Exposition of the Factors of the Path.
2. Commentary on the Exposition of the Abhidhamma (Abhidhammabhājanīyavaṇṇanā) 490.
Regarding the term "Abhidhamma," it refers to the *Dhammasaṅgaṇī*. For that is a teaching of the Abhidhamma as it has been produced;

it is not, like the teaching in the *Vibhaṅga*, a mixture of the Suttanta method. He does not apply the prefix "Ariya" [to it], because its status as noble (*ariya*) is established even without that prefix.
Therefore, it is said in the *Aṭṭhakathā*: “Just as,” and so forth.

(493) The phrase “by means of worldly time” is stated for the purpose of showing that through the power of prior-stage cultivation (*pubbabhāga-bhāvanā*), there is the accomplishment of an exceeding task.
“Of these” refers to right view and the rest. [This is] by way of discerning the disadvantages and advantages in both non-abandonment and abandonment.
Because they are specific conditions (*visesa-paccaya*), right view and the others are said to cause one to abandon wrong speech and so forth.
It is said that "abstinence is the performance of right speech and so on," meaning the turning away from wrong speech and so forth is the activity of right speech and so on.
This is not by way of being an instigator like right view and the others, nor by way of being an agent like the person possessing them. [This applies] even at the moment of the supramundane path.
Not only in the mundane moment, but also in the supramundane moment.

"It ripens as the substrate of the aggregates" is said with reference to that which bestows rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*). In that context, "it ripens" refers to that which bestows the fruition of the course of existence (*pavatti-vipāka*).

"Each one" means having asked about each individual factor, beginning with "In this regard, what is right view? and so forth. "Of each respective one" [refers to the specific factor under discussion].
It refers to each individual factor alone, not to the collection of factors as a whole. "But having asked together" means having asked, "In that regard, what is the five-factored path?
[The phrase] "because of the presentation of the answer as a single unit" means that although the answer was given individually in such passages as, "In that regard, what is right view?
It is wisdom," it was nonetheless presented as a single unit in response to the question, "In that regard, what is the five-factored path?"
Because it functions as a detailed exposition (*paṭiniddesa*) by way of answering the questions already posed, there is no separate question-and-answer section.

However, with reference to the objection—"Why is a separate question-and-answer section given here only for the section on the five factors (*pañcaṅgika-vāra*), and not for the section on the eight factors (*aṭṭhaṅgika-vāra*)?"—he says "Therein," and so forth. "By way of each single heading" means by way of right view and the other factors.
Therefore it was said: “Bhikkhus, I will teach you noble right view together with its proximate cause and its equipment,” and so forth.
[The factors] are accomplished through prior purification. For it has been said: “But previously, his bodily action, verbal action, and livelihood were already quite purified.
Therefore, the intention is that there is no cultivation by way of right speech and so on [as a primary means]. Thus he said:
“Not by means of the preliminary stage of the path.
The commentary on the *Abhidhammabhājanīya* is finished.
The commentary on the *Maggaṅgavibhaṅga* is finished.
12. Analysis of Jhāna (Jhānavibhaṅga) 1.
The Exposition According to the Discourses (Suttantabhājanīya) Commentary on the Matrix (Mātikāvaṇṇanā)

508. Regarding "restraint by the Pātimokkha, etc.": by the word "etc.," it includes such factors as guarding the doors of the sense faculties, moderation in eating, mindfulness and clear comprehension, and devotion to wakefulness. "Recollections of foulness" refers to the jhānas of foulness and the jhānas of recollection.
Mindfulness is also the state of being a recluse when there is success in the preliminary duties that constitute the qualities of a recluse.
He said, "It is indeed established," meaning that he "shows... empty," and so forth; for when the cause is established, the fruit is also necessarily established.
The passage beginning with "In the training rules" was stated in order to show the nature of the training rules, the manner in which they are to be practiced, and their brief classification.
Therein, "by way of the sets of names, etc. means by way of the sets of names (*nāmakāya*), sets of phrases (*padakāya*), and sets of phonemes (*byañjanakāya*) as they have been stated. By this—
This shows that the nature of the training rules (*sikkhāpada*) is their being a formal declaration (*paññatti*) that serves as the means for attaining the training (*sikkhā*).

Among these, the manner of training consists precisely in not transgressing the Teacher’s injunction; thus he said: "In the words... [etc.]... in those [rules]. Regarding the "sections of training" (*sikkhā-koṭṭhāsa*), this refers to the portions of the training in higher virtue (*adhisīla-sikkhā*) according to the divisions already mentioned.
Among these, the very act of undertaking (*samādāna*) is the manner of training; thus it was said: "By way of fulfilling..."
"In those things that ought to be trained in. Being "a portion of the training precepts" means being a constituent part of the aggregate of training precepts.
For it is the training of the bhikkhus that is intended here, because of the statement "here, the bhikkhus. Thus he will say later:
"But the remaining training is mentioned for the purpose of showing the meaning of the word 'training' by way of an extraction of its sense."
The commentary on the *mātikā* is finished.
Commentary on the Exposition (Niddesa). 509.

“Because it has been seen” means because it has been realized by means of self-awakened knowledge (*sayambhūñāṇa*). The same method applies to patience (*khanti*) and the other qualities as well. By means of self-awakened knowledge...

For the Blessed One’s acceptance, approval, and so forth, occur solely by way of personal realization (*sacchikaraṇa*), and not, as with others, by way of hearsay, mental forms, discursive thought, and the like.

The meaning of "unmistaken" (*aviparīta*) should be understood in the sense of being exclusively conducive to liberation (*ekantaniyyāna*). "One who is training" (*sikkhiyamāno*) means one who is practicing according to the training (*sikkhā*).

"The training rules to be trained in" (*sikkhitabbāni sikkhāpadāni*) refers to the textual recitation of the training rules (*sikkhāpada-pāḷi*). "The three aggregates" (*khandhattaya*) refers to the three aggregates beginning with virtue (*sīla*).
Because of the statement, “Of all evil... [the Buddha’s word] the teaching of the Buddhas,” he said, “the three trainings, which constitute the giving of instruction.

“As a condition for right view” means because it is the absolute cause of the right view of the path. And here, “right view” refers to both the right view of the ownership of kamma and the right view of the courses of kamma.
“By way of the metaphor of the fruit and its cause” means by way of the metaphor of the fruit.
Because it has right view as its condition, and because it is preceded by right view through the metaphorical application of the cause to the effect.

"By wholesome states that constitute a part of itself" refers to the state of right view. Alternatively, seeing is called "view" (diṭṭhi) in the sense of the discerning and understanding of wholesome wisdom and consciousness.
By this, he shows that the designation of the whole is applied metaphorically to its constituent part. It is so called because it is an activity of training.
He spoke of the three trainings as being the very essence of the teaching. “By means of the Dhamma” means by that which is not devoid of the Dhamma.
“By way of an even nature” means by an even intrinsic nature;

the sense is “by what is even. (510) “In the sense of non-otherness” means by its own meaning, free from other meanings such as censure. “Wearing torn cloth” means wearing robes cut into five pieces and so forth, according to the standard appropriate for a bhikkhu.
It is stated by way of the method of "breaking" (bheda). Therefore, it is meant that one is a *bhikkhu* because of the abandoning of defilements (*kilesa*) and the breaking of defilements.
"By way of qualities" means by way of qualities such as the states of training (*sekkhadhamma*). By this, the word *bhikkhu* is shown according to its essential meaning (*bhāvattha*).
"These two" refers to what is stated later by way of showing the inclusion [of types], beginning with "And here," namely, "the trainee" (*sekkha*), and so forth.
There are two statements. "By this" means by the demonstration of the meaning of the phrases, “a trainee bhikkhu... because of having broken away from evil things.
