This does not accord [with the former statement], because it illustrates both the trainee and the non-trainee, as well as the worldling and the non-trainee. "That very thing" refers to the first two [statements].

It is a demonstration of the non-figurative sense for the noble ones, because it illustrates that only among the non-trainees do the defilements of a trainee exist in a broken state. "It is said" is a statement of admission.
The meaning is "spoken as truth. However, it is not intended here [in this context], because it is shown by way of extracting the meaning.
"The word of the Blessed One" refers to the formal act (*kammavācā*) of full ordination (*upasampadā*). "In accordance with that" means suitable for that;
the sense is "as previously stated. The perfections of the assembly, the subject matter, and the boundary are manifested by the phrase "by a united and unshakable Saṅgha."

For the word "fitting" (*ṭhānāraha*), he states only this much as its meaning: "not deficient... [and so on]... not left unsaid. 511. Regarding the phrase "by way of the state of non-transgression and abstention":

taking it that abstention is the undertaking of non-transgression, it is said that even for volitional virtue (*cetanāsīla*), "abstention" is used as a synonym, because once the virtue of restraint (*vārittasīla*) has been reached, abstention itself is primary. "The city architect, a teacher of the science of sites (*vatthuvijjā*)."
This is the illustration of the city-builder intended here. For the science of building (vaḍḍhakīvijjā) is twofold: the science of sites (vatthuvijjā) and the science of palaces (pāsādavijjā).
"To be licked" means to be tasted. "To be spat upon" means to be dropped.
"By way of the restraint of the faculties as nutriment" means by way of having the restraint of the faculties as its cause. The Pātimokkha virtue is the virtue of the training rules (sikkhāpada).
It is not grasped by means of natural virtue (*pakatisīla*) and so forth; therefore, he said: "By the inclusion of bodily non-transgression and so on, a virtue other than the *pātimokkha* is grasped.
However, one cannot say that this [virtue] is not included within the virtue of the *pātimokkha*, because there is no bodily or vocal restraint apart from it.
Demonstrating this, he said: "This was stated with this underlying intention (*adhippāya*)."
In this context, the meaning of the word *pātimokkha* should be understood as follows:

because of the powerful nature of the defilements, because evil deeds are easy to perform, and because meritorious deeds are difficult to perform, the worldling (*puthujjana*) has the habit of falling frequently into the states of misery;
thus he is a *pātī*. Alternatively, due to impermanence, he is tossed by the force of karma through various existences like a potter’s wheel, owing to his lack of stability.

It is called *pāti* because it has the nature of falling (*pātana*) due to its wandering; or, by way of death, it is called *pāti* because it has the nature of causing the personal existence (*attabhāva*) to fall here and there among the various classes of beings.

This refers to the continuity of beings (*sattasantāna*), or simply to the mind itself. Because it releases (*mokkheti*) that which falls (*pātinaṃ*) from the suffering of *saṃsāra*, it is called *pātimokkha*.
For through the liberation of the mind, a being is also said to be "liberated. Indeed, it is said: "Through the purification of the mind..."
“...is being purified,” and “the mind is liberated from the taints through non-clinging.

Alternatively, one who falls, goes, or proceeds in saṃsāra by means of causes such as ignorance is a *pātī*. For it is said: “Of beings hindered by ignorance, fettered by craving, wandering and transmigrating. From the three defilements, such as craving, of that falling being (*pātī*):

It is called *pātimokkha* because liberation (*mokkha*) is attained by means of it. Its formation as a compound should be understood in the same way as in such terms as *kaṇṭhekāḷo* (“one with a black throat”).

Alternatively, it is called *pāti* because it causes one to fall (*pāteti*) or cast down into suffering; that is, the mind. For it has been said: “The world is led by the mind; by the mind it is drawn along.
Since liberation is attained by this [discipline] for that which falls—the mind—it is called *pātimokkha*. Or else, one falls into the suffering of the states of misery (*apāya*) by means of it.
Or, *pātī* means the suffering of *saṃsāra*; it refers to the defilements such as craving (*taṇhā*). For it is said: "Craving gives birth to a person;
a person has craving as his companion," and so forth. Liberation from that is *pātimokkha*.
Alternatively, *pātīni* means those into which one falls; they are the six internal and external sense bases (*āyatana*). For it is said: "In the six..."
“The world has arisen; it forms intimacy with the six. Therefore, because liberation (mokkha) falls away from what is comprised by the six internal and external sense bases, it is the *pātimokkha*.
Alternatively, that which possesses falling away (*pāta*) or ruin (*vinipāta*) is *pāti*, namely, *saṃsāra*; liberation from that is the *pātimokkha*.
Alternatively, the Blessed One is called the "Lord" (*pati*) because he is the sovereign of the entire world and the master of the Dhamma; that by which one is liberated is "liberation" (*mokkho*);
it is the "Prātimokkha" because it is prescribed by that Lord as liberation (*pati-mokkho*).
Or else, because it is the root of all virtues, it is the "Lord" (*pati*) in the sense of being supreme, and it is "liberation" (*mokkho*) in the sense already explained; thus it is the *Pātimokkha*.
The *patimokkha*—the very act of releasing—is the *pātimokkha*. For it has been said in detail: "‘Pātimokkha’: this is the mouth (*mukha*), this is the foremost (*pamukha*)";

or else, *pa-* is a particle in the sense of ‘in various ways’ (*pakāra*), and *ati-* is a particle in the sense of ‘exceedingly’ (*accanta*). Therefore, it is called so because it releases [one] exceedingly in various ways.

The Pātimokkha. For this virtue is called *pātimokkha* because it absolutely liberates (*mokkheti*) or causes liberation (*moceti*) by its own means through the method of substitution (*tadaṅga-vasena*), and when accompanied by concentration and wisdom, through the methods of suppression (*vikkhambhana-vasena*) and eradication (*samuccheda-vasena*).

Alternatively, it is *patimokkho* in the sense that there is liberation (*mokkho*) for each individual (*pati pati*); the meaning is that there is liberation from each respective fault of transgression. Thus, *patimokkho* itself is *pātimokkha*.
Liberation (*mokkha*) is *nibbāna*; that which has become its counterpart is the *pātimokkha*.
For the restraint of virtue (*sīla-saṃvara*) conducive to penetration is like the rising of the dawn for the sun;
it is a *pātimokkha* because, being its counterpart, it extinguishes the defilements accordingly. *Pātimokkha* is simply *patimokkha*.
Alternatively, it is "facing toward liberation" (*mokkhābhimukha*) because it pertains to liberation; thus, it is *patimokkha*. And *pātimokkha* is simply *patimokkha*.
This, too, is merely a brief indication of the meaning of the word *pātimokkha*.
However, in its entirety, only the Blessed One, the Conqueror’s *pātimokkha*, could describe the *pātimokkha* that is free from fault.
513. "Garubhaṇḍavissajjana" means that which has the function of disposing of valuable goods;
it refers to stable property such as land and so forth. "Deficiency is not permitted" refers to the requirement for compensation (phātikamma).
"An excess value is permitted, or a value equal to that [of the original]" means that the aforementioned work—such as the removal of earth from a lotus pond—is considered a stable act.
“He maintains or nourishes others’ children.

This means it was said with reference to what is done for householders, not for the Saṅgha or a group (gaṇa). Regarding “piṇḍapaṭipiṇḍa,” this is a compound where the latter member of the first word is elided;

having applied the elision of the latter member in both parts, the explanation is given as “for the sake of alms,” and so forth. “Improper investigation” is practice that does not accord with reality.
514. They are called *gāva* because they move about in their respective domains; thus, the sense-faculties such as the eye are meant.
"Shaking" (*vidhunana*) means striking or clearing away; this is the meaning. 515.
Just as the word *karaṇīya* has the sense of "that which is to be done," so too it has the sense of "that which is to be scattered. Therefore, he says: "they are to be dispersed" (*vikkhipitabbāni*).
The meaning is "to be destroyed. Alternatively, *saṃyamanīyāni* means "things to be restrained";
restraint (*saṃyama*) is the mental resolution or determination of oneself, thinking, "I shall not do so again. Thus, "things to be restrained" means things to be guarded (*saṃvara*).
Since the Teacher intended that restraint and guarding depend solely upon the mind, he said, "they lead to non-offense."

The Elder Antevāsika, however, maintains that since even the teaching itself does not occur without the arising of consciousness and attention, he declares the purity of the teaching to be the escape.
In passages such as, “Even if he is adorned... he is a bhikkhu,” here too, it is one endowed with specific qualities who is intended by the term “bhikkhu.
Thus it has been said: “‘Bhikkhu’ is used here because it demonstrates the state of being a bhikkhu through practice. To whatever extent—
It is possible for a single person to undertake [the training] without exception; with reference to this, it is said:

"By that undertaking through which all the trainings are undertaken. This is just as, for the sake of the perfection of full ordination (*upasampadā*), there is the undertaking of the training of one who is fully ordained without exception.
"That" refers to the undertaking. "In many" means in various individual undertakings. Just as by the training that has been undertaken... by the whole—

The non-transgression of everything is the manner in which one should train. This being so, when there is a transgression, there is confession for that which leads to confession, and restoration for that which leads to restoration;
the means for this consists of performing the duties of one on probation and so forth.
Thus it is said: "By the manner of non-transgression... [and so on]...". That training rule which was transgressed through negligence is no longer being trained in; thus it is "left behind" (sesita).
He said, "It is called so by way of transgression of the remainder.

(519) "Cultivation for the purification of the mind" means that the cultivation of concentration and insight which purifies the mind and suppresses obstructive states is "cultivation for the purification of the mind. "Well-grasping" means grasping [the state of] sleep.
"This" refers to the non-occurrence of functional consciousnesses (*kiriyamayacitta*), which is known as "crossing over the life-continuum" (*abbokiṇṇabhavaṅgottaraṇa*).
This is called "the boat. There is nothing prior to this crossing over of the life-continuum, nor anything subsequent to the occurrence of these functional consciousnesses.
This bodily fatigue and lethargy (*thinamiddha*) are the conditions for this discourse.

522. Regarding "the foundations of mindfulness and so forth": the meaning is that the foundations of mindfulness, the right efforts, and the bases of psychic power, as well as certain path-factors, do not occur simultaneously;

therefore, they are not mentioned in the Pāḷi. One might think that these [other factors] should not be included because they do not occur together on a single object, but why then are the faculties and powers not included? To this he says: "occurrence... [etc.]"
"...exist. Thus, with reference to the objection that the faculties (*indriya*) and powers (*bala*) are not included among the factors of enlightenment (*bojjhaṅga*), he says:
"Because of the statement: 'Joy... [and so on]. 523.
"In every respect" means in all parts, in all [actions] such as advancing and so forth; or, from every side, in those very [actions] such as advancing and so forth.
"In every respect" means from all aspects, including the possible and the impossible. "Samma" means correctly (*aviparīta*) and fundamentally (*yoniso*).
"Samam" means without unevenness; the meaning is that one acts free from the unevenness of lust and other defilements toward desirable objects and the like.
"Bhikkhācāra" is that wherein alms-food (*bhikkhā*) is sought; it is the place for wandering for alms, which is itself the range (*gocara*) for alms. For alms...
Alternatively, the foot itself is the "range" (*gocara*) because it is the domain of clear comprehension (*sampajañña*); [the phrase] "in that range of walking for alms" refers to this.
Furthermore, by way of the qualification "divided into the distinctions of advancing and so forth," it is said: "but in advancing and so forth.

"In what is reckoned as the meditation subject" (*kammaṭṭhāna-saṅkhāte*) means in the object (*ārammaṇa*) reckoned as the locus where the practice of yoga (*yogakamma*)—that is, meditation—occurs; or else, it refers to the work of meditation itself for the yogi.
Or, it is in the sense of being the object of clear comprehension—known as the meditation subject—by virtue of its being the cause of a particular kind of happiness, within its proper range.

"In going forward and so forth" means in both going forward and returning, as well as in putting on the robes and so on. "Non-confusion" is the knowing of things as they truly are, [realizing] that their occurrence takes place solely through the expansion of the air-element and the mental activity, and not otherwise.

"Making the meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna) his primary concern" means that even at times when he must perform duties such as putting on his robes and attending to the body, he makes the attention to the meditation subject his primary concern.
"Therefore" means: because you have become so eager and are entreating me most earnestly; because you say that the obstacles to life are difficult to discern;
and because your faculties have reached maturity—for these reasons. "Tiha" is a mere particle. "Te" means by you. "Evaṃ" means thus.

Now he states the manner in which it should be spoken. "It should be trained in" means that training must be undertaken by way of all three trainings, beginning with the training in higher virtue (*adhisīla-sikkhā*). Showing how it should be trained in, he said: "In the seen, there will be only the seen," and so forth.
In this context, "the mere seen in what is seen" means the mere seen by way of eye-consciousness in the sense-sphere of visible form (*rūpāyatana*).
For just as eye-consciousness sees in a visible form only the mere form, and not its intrinsic nature as permanent and so forth, so too one should train oneself with the thought:
"By the other five door-consciousnesses as well, there shall be for me here only the mere seen. Alternatively, "the seen in what is seen" means:
Eye-consciousness (*cakkhuviññāṇa*) means the discerning of form as form. "Matter" (*mattā*) means measure. "Seen-matter" (*diṭṭhamatta*) means that for this [consciousness] there is only the seen;
the meaning is: "My mind shall consist only of eye-consciousness. This is what is meant:

just as eye-consciousness does not become lustful, does not become hateful, and does not become deluded toward a form that has come into its range, so too, by being free from lust and the other [defilements], it remains thus.
"Let my impulsion consist of eye-consciousness alone; I will establish it by the measure of eye-consciousness alone.
Alternatively, "the seen" refers to the visible form seen by eye-consciousness.
"In the seen" refers to the triad of consciousnesses—namely, receiving, investigating, and determining—which arise right there. Just as one does not become lustful or hateful toward that.

It does not become deluded; thus, the meaning here should be understood as follows: "When a visible form has come into range, I shall arouse the impulsion (javana) with that same measure consisting of the reception (sampaṭicchana) and so forth; I will not allow it to arise by way of passion and so on, exceeding that measure.

This same method applies to what is heard and what is sensed. And "the sensed" (muta) refers to the sense-bases of odors, tastes, and tangibles together with the consciousnesses that take them as objects.

It should be understood thus. Regarding the phrase "in what is cognized, only the cognized": here, "cognized" (*viññāta*) refers to the object cognized by the mind-door adverting consciousness (*manodvārāvajjana*);
"in that which is cognized" means in that object. "Only the cognized" (*viññātamatta*) refers to the measure of the adverting consciousness. One should think:

"Just as the adverting consciousness does not become lustful, does not become hateful, and does not become deluded, so shall I establish the mind at the very measure of the adverting consciousness, not allowing it to arise through lust and the like."
This is the meaning here: "In this way, Bāhiya, you should train"—that is to say, Bāhiya, you should train by means of this practice through the successive application of the three trainings.

Thus, because Bāhiya took delight in brevity, the Blessed One [taught] the object of insight—which is distinguished by the sixfold division of objects together with the six groups of consciousness—by means of the seen and so forth.
Having divided it into four sections, he demonstrates therein the full understanding consisting of knowledge and scrutiny (*ñāṇatīraṇapariññā*). How so?

For here, the visible-form base (*rūpāyatana*) is called "seen" in the sense of being what is seen; eye-consciousness, together with the consciousnesses belonging to that door, is [called "seeing"] in the sense of the act of seeing.
Yet both of these, as they proceed according to their respective conditions, are merely phenomena (*dhammamatta*).

In this there is no agent or instigator whatsoever. Since it is impermanent in the sense of non-existence after having been, suffering in the sense of being oppressed by arising and passing away, and non-self in the sense of lack of mastery, how could there be any occasion for a wise person’s attachment and so forth?
This is the intended meaning here. The same method applies to the ear and the other [senses] as well.

Now, in order to show the full understanding of abandoning (*pahānapariññā*) together with its fruit for one who is established in the full understandings of knowing and scrutinizing (*ñātatīraṇapariññā*), the passage beginning with “But when, Bāhiya...
is commenced. Therein, *yataḥ* means “when” or “because. *Te* means “your. *Tataḥ* means “then” or “therefore.
*Tenā* means “by that”—namely, by that view and so forth, or by passion and so forth bound up with view and so forth. This is what is said:

It is so, Bāhiya: at whatever time or by whatever means you practice according to the method I have taught regarding what is seen and so forth, through the realization of their true nature as it is, there will be for you only the mere appearance of what is seen and so forth;

and at that time, or by that means, you will not exist together with the passion and other defilements bound to those things seen and so forth—neither as one who is lustful, nor as one who is hateful, nor as one who is deluded.
"Or you will not exist because you have abandoned passion and the other [defilements]; or you will not be bound together with that view and so forth. Therefore, Bāhiya, "you will not be there":
when, or because, you will not be impassioned by that passion, nor corrupted by hatred, nor deluded by delusion; then, or for that reason, you will not exist there in those views and so forth.
When you see, hear, sense, or cognize that [object], you shall not be attached to it, nor established in it through craving, conceit, or views, thinking, "This is mine; this I am; this is my self.
To this extent, having brought the full comprehension of abandonment to its culmination, the stage of one whose taints are destroyed is shown.
Then, Bāhiya, neither here, nor beyond, nor in between the two—when you, Bāhiya, [are thus].
By means of that passion and so forth, you will not be bound to those [objects] such as what is seen;

then you will exist neither in this world, nor in the next world, nor in both. "This indeed is the end of suffering" means that this is the end, the limit, and the state of finality for the suffering of the defilements and for the suffering of the round of existence (*saṃsāra*); this is precisely the meaning here. As for those who...
Taking the phrase "between both," some assert what is called an intermediate existence (*antarābhava*); their view is incorrect.
What should be said regarding that matter will be clarified later in the discussion on the intermediate existence.
"Of these" refers to the carrying forward and the carrying across.

By the words “In that case” (*tattha hi*) and so forth, he shows that in the cognitive process of the fivefold sense consciousness (*pañcaviññāṇa-vīthi*), due to the prior occurrence of improper attention (*ayonisomanasikāra*), there is merely the arising of greed and so forth toward a desirable object through improper advertence (*āvajjana*) and so on;
however, there is no grasping of conceptual distinctions such as “woman” or “man,” for that occurs only at the mind-door (*manodvāra*). Regarding the word “of that” (*tassa*): “a woman,”...
"Person": [this refers to] lust and so forth. "Life-continuum, etc. means the life-continuum, adverting, seeing, receiving, investigating, determining, and the five-door impulsion.
"By way of being unprecedented and limited" means by way of their states of being unprecedented and limited.
"Carries across" means it carries [the object] beyond the door of the mouth. "Producer of the discernment of each respective [object]" means of that respective...

It is the producer of both the search and so forth as its object, and of the cognition [of that object]. For by whatever application the search and so forth are accomplished, that [application] is said to produce the cognition of that object as well.
"Right practice" means practice regarding phenomena that is non-erroneous, which is to say, awakening to things as they truly are (*yathābhūta*).
"Even in going" means even during the application of going. "Bringing forward" (*atiharaṇa*) is the act of directing the body, as it stands, toward the desired location.

Going is the arising in another location. "To be explained" refers to the distinction that will be stated: "In going forward and returning... [etc. ...it is described in terms of traveling on a journey;
in 'going, standing, and sitting,' it is described here in terms of the minor postures such as shifting about while staying in one place.
"Occurring" refers to material and immaterial phenomena occurring during walking meditation and so forth. "For one who comprehends them" means for one who comprehends them as impermanent and so on.

The javana that produces bodily action and so forth is described as "consisting of bodily action, etc. by way of a metaphorical designation (*phalūpacāra*) for the fruit. However, it is described as such by way of a metaphorical designation for the cause (*kāraṇūpacāra*) because it originates from action.

526. "Of the cultivation of the meditation subject" means of the development of the meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhānabhāvanā*). "The path of practice" means the way in which the activity suitable for development proceeds.
537. "In the body, etc. refers to the body, feelings, mind, and mental objects. "By way of thorough engagement" means by way of the contemplation of foulness and so forth.
"Of the onward-flow": right mindfulness itself has the nature of leading out (*niyyāna*). "Establishment" shows mindfulness by way of its function.

And here, the meaning should be understood as follows: that which has been grasped (*pariggahitā*) is so called because this [mindfulness] has arisen with such a grasp; thus, "having made that mindfulness—which is the state of leading out—the object of grasp."
542–3. *Pakuppanaṃ* here means the state of undergoing transformation or change.
550. *Tappaṭipakkhasaññā* means perception that is the opposite of sloth and torpor (*thinamiddha*).

In terms of its meaning, it is a perception associated with wholesome thought (*kusalavitakka*) that functions in the mode of dispelling sloth and torpor by way of "overcoming through substitution" (*tadaṅga*) and so forth; or it is a mental state (*cittuppāda*) that has become such.
It should be understood that this is stated by way of the term "perception" (*saññā*).

553. *Sārambhaṃ* means possessing exertion; the sense is "together with exertion. *Nirāvaraṇābhogā* refers to a perception of mental application (*samannāhāra-saññā*) that is free from obstruction due to the disappearance of the darkness of sloth and torpor (*thinamiddha*). *Vivaṭā* means uncovered or unobscured. 564.
*Tattha tattha* refers to passages such as, "By this restraint of the Pātimokkha, he is endowed," and so forth.

588. Just as when something has been turned upside down by someone, it is not known by one who possesses ordinary knowledge as being "this or that," so too, that which is unknown in every respect is like something turned upside down;
thus he said, "The state of being turned upside down is the state of being unknown in every way.

"The absence of delimitation without remainder" means the absence of being able to delimit [the object] completely due to its being difficult to discern, or else the absence of a delimiting agent. Only by way of a single part...
For it is known as profound.
"They explain" means they speak clearly from the beginning. "They teach" means they speak by way of pointing out, or they cause [others] to awaken.
"They establish" means they cause others to understand; the meaning is that they make it fully manifest. "They set forth" means by various modes, without confusion.
They establish. "They reveal" means they make it disclosed. "They analyze" means they make it analyzed.
"They clarify" means they make what was not clear—that which is deep—clear and manifest. And here, by the six phrases beginning with "they point out," the phrases of meaning (atthapada) are shown;
whereas by the two phrases "they declare" and "they teach," the phrases of phrasing (byañjanapada) are shown.
Thus he demonstrates the praising [of the Dhamma] by means of this sublime praise, which is perfect in meaning, phrasing, and words.
As for what ought to be said regarding these meanings, phrasings, and words, that has already been stated in detail in the *Nettippakaraṇa-aṭṭhakathā*;
therefore, it should be understood according to the method explained therein.
602. This very point should be applied here, because it illustrates the means for attaining the distinction of planes by way of transcending the lower planes.
"In all instances" refers to all expressions concerning transcendence, such as "through the transcendence of perceptions of form" and "having transcended the base of infinite space."

610. "That very consciousness pervades that space": the meaning is that one attends to the first immaterial-sphere consciousness—which stands having pervaded and suffused that very space cleared of the kasiṇa by means of the mental attention "infinite"—as "infinite consciousness.
In the second interpretation, however, since a general description applies to a particular, by the word "pervaded" it is consciousness itself [that is meant].
"Stated" means "clearly cognized"; this refers to the consciousness of the first immaterial attainment (*āruppa*). For that is the consciousness which pervades space.

In the phrase "by consciousness," the instrumental case is used in the sense of an instrument; and since that refers to the consciousness of the second immaterial attainment, he says: "He attends by means of the consciousness of the base of infinite consciousness (*viññāṇañcāyatana*).
"By that" means by the consciousness of the first immaterial attainment. "The mode apprehended" refers to it by way of its infinite pervasion.
"Having grasped the aspect": he attends to it by means of the preparatory attention for the second immaterial attainment. "Thus":

while he is attending precisely to that aspect which was grasped by the consciousness of the first immaterial attainment through its quality of infinite pervasion in the space cleared of the kasiṇa—in that very manner.
"That consciousness": that consciousness of the second immaterial attainment. "It pervades infinitely."
“It pervades as ‘infinite’”; therefore, the second meaning alone is appropriate. With the words beginning “For that which...”, he makes the aforementioned point clear.
“Accompanied by that mode of pervasion” means accompanied by the mode of pervasion in that space. “Consciousness” refers to the consciousness of the first immaterial attainment (āruppa).

615. "Previously" refers to the time of the preliminary work for the second immaterial attainment. That which was attended to as "infinite consciousness" is precisely that same consciousness of the first immaterial attainment;
it is that very same [consciousness] which one causes to cease. For these attainments are to be obtained by means of transcending the object.
The commentary on the Exposition is finished.
The commentary on the Suttanta-bhājaniya is finished.
2. Commentary on the Abhidhamma-bhājaniya: 623.

In the fourfold method, it is precisely the second jhāna that does not appear as gross to some, while it does appear as gross to others, because of their presence or absence of applied thought (vitakka).
"By means of these [factors], having divided them into two ways, it was taught"—thus the fivefold method is extracted from the fourfold method; therefore he said:
"Because of the extraction of just the four... and because of the seeing.
The commentary on the *Abhidhammabhājanīya* is finished.
3. Commentary on the Section of Questions (Pañhapucchakavaṇṇanā) 640.
"In three" means in the first three [categories]. For that was stated according to the fourfold method (*catukkanaya*). "Thus divided into sections" means they are said to be immeasurable.
Therefore he said: "The intention is that they are indeed supramundane (*lokuttara*). ... [omission] ... of the fourth [meditations], the space delimited...

Because it serves as the basis for insight into the round of existence (*vaṭṭa-vipassanā-pādakattā*), it is said that they are "included in the fourth [jhāna] which has everything as its basis" (*sabbatthapādaka*).

This discussion refers to the discourse on limited objects and so forth. It is stated that "the lower noble one cannot penetrate the supramundane consciousnesses of the higher noble one," hence the words "and...
cannot. There is also a reading: "from twelve functional [consciousnesses]. It speaks together with them by virtue of the commonality of being the fourth supramundane fruit.

This is the intended meaning (*adhippāya*). Here, because the word "all" (*sabba*) denotes a partial "all," it should be understood that even though a single part is impossible [in this context], it serves as the basis for the "all" everywhere;

thus he said, "In all places... should be seen. By the word "etc. in the phrase "the fourth [jhāna] of the limited space-kasiṇa, etc.," the fourth [jhāna] of mindfulness of breathing (*ānāpāna*) and others are included. "By way of being indeterminable" means by way of having an indeterminable object (*navattabbārammaṇatāya*).
And it should be stated that "Nibbāna" is also included, because even though it has that as its object, it is still an external object.
The phrase "even that which belongs to one's own continuum" should be connected with both the word *rūpa* (form) and the word *kamma* (action):

"Just as the divine eye reveals form—even that belonging to one's own continuum which is not manifest—so too [the knowledge of past lives] reveals action—even that belonging to one's own continuum which is not manifest. Regarding what is manifest...

However, since there is no purpose for the knowledge of direct higher power (*abhiññā-ñāṇa*) regarding matter belonging to one's own continuum or regarding kamma, it is stated as being "not manifest" (*apākaṭa*), thus making this distinction.
The commentary on the *Pañhapucchaka* is finished.
The commentary on the *Jhānavibhaṅga* is finished.
13. Analysis of the Illimitables (Appamaññāvibhaṅga) 1.
Explanation of the Suttanta-Section (Suttantabhājanīyavaṇṇanā) 642.

Regarding "purification by direction and place": this refers to purification by direction such as "one direction," and so forth; and purification by place such as the monastery, village, town, city, district, kingdom, and so forth.
“By the delimitation of beings (*sattodhi*)”: by means of the delimitation of beings occurring in such ways as “all women,” “all men,” “the noble ones,” or “the non-noble ones.
“Of this”: of this word, or of its referent. “That which follows along” (*anuvattaka*):
that which functions by way of a governing topic (*adhikāra*). “Both of those”: both the word *tathā* and the word *iti*. For when it is said, “Thus the second,” [it refers to both].

The word *tathā* (thus) illuminates this meaning: “Just as he dwells having pervaded one direction, such as the eastern one, with a mind imbued with loving-kindness (*mettā*), so too does he dwell having pervaded a second direction with a mind imbued with loving-kindness.
This same method applies to the remaining two [directions] as well. Since this particle *iti* is used in the sense of manner, it is equivalent to saying “in this way” (*evam*).

Therefore, this explains the meaning: “Just as one dwells pervading one direction, a second, a third, and a fourth direction with a mind imbued with loving-kindness (mettā), so too one dwells pervading upwards, downwards, and across with a mind imbued with loving-kindness.
For that reason it is said: “Loving-kindness... [and so on]... that dyad. *Tassa* means of that dyad. *Pharaṇantarādiṭṭhānaṃ* means the locus of the intermediate pervasion, etc.
A different pervasion than the [initial] pervasion is "another pervasion" (*pharaṇantara*); that which has this as its beginning is "that which begins with another pervasion" (*pharaṇantarādi*).

This "another pervasion" refers to the state of vastness (*vipulatā*) in the development of loving-kindness (*mettābhāvanā*). By the word "beginning," the state of being proficient in other stages and so forth is included;

the specific excellence of the development of loving-kindness, described by the words "with the vast" (*vipulena*) and so forth, is the locus, the very ground, of that which begins with another pervasion.

The non-occurrence and lack of opportunity for that pair, which consists of the aforementioned mere misapprehension—this being the case, the meaning is that for this reason, that pair was not mentioned.

(643) "Of lust" means of sensual lust (*kāmarāga*). "Of affection" means of affection such as affection for one's children. "By failure" means by the failure or destruction of the cultivation of loving-kindness (*mettābhāvanā*), which is characterized by lust and affection. "Because of its non-arising" means because it does not arise due to the power of moral shame (*hiri*) and dread of blame (*ottappa*).
645. *Adhimuñcitvā* means having properly released the mind of meditation upon the object.
Since this fixing (*adhimuccana*) occurs here specifically by way of suffusion (*pharaṇa*), it is said, "having fully extended [it].
Furthermore, since that fixing in the development of loving-kindness occurs precisely by way of not gliding over the object, it is said, "by one who is powerful..."
And it is said: “or having resolved through resolution.

(648) “By all these terms” means by every single limit, including the distinctions of direction, place, and so forth. “By all modes of pervasion of directions, places, and limits” means by the ways of pervading the directions, places, and persons that constitute all such limits.
(650) “By way of suppression” means by way of temporary restraint (*vikkhambhana*).
The commentary on the Suttantabhājanīya is finished.
3. Commentary on the Section of Questions (Pañhapucchaka): 699.
Of the wholesome and other phenomena already mentioned, those [phenomena] spoken of here in this Analysis of the Illimitables (Appamaññāvibhaṅga) are the illimitables.

And since these, by their very nature, are merely mundane (*lokiya*)—and not supramundane (*lokuttara*) like the aggregates (*khandha*) and so forth explained in the *Khandhavibhaṅga* and other texts—the commentary states "In this case, however," and so on, in order to demonstrate definitively that all the immeasurables (*appamaññā*) are exclusively mundane.
Showing this point, he said: "In this case, however... [etc] ...occurs."
The commentary on the "Examination of Questions" is finished.
The commentary on the "Analysis of the Illimitables" is finished. 14.
Analysis of the Training Precepts (Sikkhāpada-vibhaṅga).
1. Commentary on the Abhidhamma-Bhājaniya 703.
Regarding the wholesome states comprised by the trainings (sikkhā), the five factors of virtue (sīlaṅga) may serve as either a support (nissaya) or a decisive support (upanissaya).
Demonstrating both of these, he says: "By way of association, by way of decisive support, and by way of providing an occasion."
704. Because the restriction "only as paths of action" (kamma-pathā eva) has been made, it is stated "in those not common to all.

For it is not possible to make a restriction by way of categories common to the faculties and so forth. They are only categorized as paths of action, not categorized as meditative absorptions (jhāna) and so forth.
It is said that they are presented as paths of action because they serve as the means for the occurrence of an unhappy rebirth (duggati) and the suffering that arises therein.
The intention is as follows: [the condition] of that drinking of liquor is its being a contributing factor for all [unwholesome states]. Its similarity is with sexual misconduct.

The phrase "by way of having formations apprehended in the mode of a 'being' as their object" means that the objects are formations apprehended in the mode of a "being"—as in "I am stealing a being," "I am committing misconduct toward a being," and so forth—but not by way of having the designation "being" (sattapaññatti) as their object; this is the intended meaning.
He explains that same meaning with the words, “The five training rules,” and so forth.
“For this or that” means for whichever purpose of ruin [is intended].
Either one shoots an arrow or the like oneself, digs a pitfall or the like, recites such a spell, employs supernormal power born of kamma, or causes another to do all of that.
Regarding the statement "he causes [it] to be made," it is said: "The *nissaggiya*... [etc. ...only two are taken.

Although in the section on the factors (*koṭṭhāsa*) abstention (*virati*) does not appear by its own specific form but is merely mentioned as being "included" (*yevāpanaka*), nevertheless, when analyzed, it partakes precisely of the nature of the Path;
thus it is said: "But the virtue of abstention belongs to the category of the Path. As for "the remaining virtues":
Of those whose virtue has not been transgressed. 712.

"Incapable states" refers to killing living beings and so forth. Just as killing living beings and the like are called "enmity" (*vera*) because they are causes of enmity, so too are other unwholesome states;
thus it is said: "because they share that same nature, they are become enmity. The arising of the abstinences... [is not] possible.
The construction is: "There will not be [any] for those in training (sekkhā).

By the phrase beginning with "And those originating from the unwholesome," it is likewise clarified that for those in training there is indeed the presence of abstinence in both ways. Its meaning is as follows:

those bodily actions and so forth originating from the unwholesome are, for those in training, precisely "enmities" (verāni) such as bodily misconduct; by means of those enmities, for those in training...

Abstentions indeed arise. "Yato" means because, even in the absence of the literal enmity that must be abandoned—namely, killing living beings and so forth—abstention occurs for those in training (sekkhā) due to the mere presence of enmity such as bodily misconduct.

"Naphalabhūtassāpi" means that just as the fruit might possess the state of being seven- or eightfold because it is a reflection of the Path, so too does that which has not yet become the fruit [possess this quality].
The intention is that the eightfold nature [of the path] arises from the occurrence of abstinence starting from the once-returning path; otherwise, it would consist of only five factors.
The commentary on the *Abhidhammabhājanīya* is finished.
2. Commentary on the Section of Questions (Pañhapucchakavaṇṇanā) 714.
"In accordance with what ought to be abstained from" means by way of abstaining from each respective thing that ought to be abstained from, such as the taking of life and so forth.
The commentary on the Section of Questions is concluded.
The commentary on the Analysis of the Training Rules (Sikkhāpadavibhaṅgavaṇṇanā) is finished.
15. Analysis of the Analytical Knowledges (Paṭisambhidāvibhaṅga).
1. The Exposition According to the Discourses (Suttantabhājanīya).
1. Explanation of the Section on Compendium (Saṅgahavāravaṇṇanā) 718.
“The same method applies” is an extended application (atidesa) made to the factors such as the Dhamma; he says “having shown them in brief” because their presentation is intended to be concise.

“Their objects” (tabbisayā) refers to the objects of those [faculties], namely, the objects of the analytical knowledge of language (niruttipaññā) and the analytical knowledge of ingenuity (paṭibhānapaññā); that is, those things which have become the objects of the analytical knowledge of language and ingenuity.
Meaning (*attha*). "By way of the distinctions of the conditionally arisen, etc. means by way of the distinctions of the conditionally arisen, Nibbāna, the spoken meaning, and so forth.
Suffering, its cause, its fruit, birth, and so on, as well as aging and death, are the phenomena beginning with suffering.

In the sections on the Truths, Causes, Phenomena, and Modes of Conditionality, the cause that produces a fruit is presented by way of synonyms such as the origin of suffering; in the sections on the Truths and Modes of Conditionality, it is the Noble Path.

The phrase "and likewise the states" is stated to show that five factors are to be understood solely on the basis of those very things mentioned in the Canon—namely, what is spoken of in the section on the Discourses (Pariyattivāra) and as wholesome or unwholesome in the Abhidhamma-Bhājaniya. "Of the producing cause, etc.

refers to the producing, the bringing-about, and the making-known causes. "The former" has the sense of proceeding; "therein" refers to the path; and "the latter" should be understood as having the sense of reaching.
"Unmistaken terminology" (*aviparīta-nirutti*) refers to the correct linguistic expression established by the Buddha and others as denoting this or that specific meaning.

Since his own position is that "designation" (*paññatti*) is sound accompanied by modification through intonation (*viññatti*), he says, "some explain it," having qualified it as "not consisting of speech" in order to show that from the ultimate standpoint (*paramattha*) it is so. "This being the case" means: in the case of such terminology...
"When there is the state of being a designation (paññatti-bhāva). If it is argued that 'a designation must be expressed,' one might perhaps say, 'Let it be;
what fault is there in its being expressible? Anticipating this objection, he says: "And because of the expression... there is nothing to be uttered.
Of those meanings and phenomena (attha-dhamma). "Not an expression" means non-expression, having the nature of non-expression. "Of such a kind."
"Of such a kind" means having the form of indicating specific, fixed genders.

"From another" means in the subsequent part, namely, immediately at the mind-door. They say that the analytical knowledge of language (*niruttipaṭisambhidā*) proceeds with respect to the names and expressions grasped according to the apprehension of sounds.
If this is so, why does the Pāḷi [state] "the analytical knowledge of language"?
Since it is stated that [this knowledge] has the present as its object, he says: "It was said with reference to *nirutti*...
etc. "Knowing subsequently" means knowing the name and *nirutti* at a time subsequent to the grasping of the sound.

Thus, when it is understood that the analytical knowledge of language (*niruttipaṭisambhidā*) is the knowledge that proceeds by taking the name and *nirutti* as its object after the grasping of the sound—thus, in the case where *nirutti* is on the side of the designation of names (*nāmapaññatti*)—...

Having shown the contradiction with the Pāḷi and the Aṭṭhakathā, he said, “But as...,” etc., demonstrating the absence [of such a contradiction] on the side of the word-meaning. Regarding the phrase “that which clarifies each respective sound”:

just as the divine ear-knowledge (*dibbasotañāṇa*), which serves as the condition for determining the various distinctions of sounds, makes each respective sound manifest by taking that very sound as its object, so too...

The knowledge of the analytical insight of language (niruttipatisambhidāñāṇa) takes as its object only the sounds of language which serve as the condition for determining the distinctions of language;
it is said to have a present object because it makes those [sounds] manifest.

Furthermore, when making the sound manifest, it necessarily makes manifest the designation (paññatti) bound up with that sound, whereby the discernment of the distinction between what possesses intrinsic nature and what lacks it is accomplished.

For otherwise, if there were only the apprehension of the mere sound, there would be no comprehension of the specific distinction; thus the ancients maintain that it also clarifies the formal definition (paññatti).
"That which clarifies it" means that which clarifies the etymological word (*niruttisadda*). There is no contradiction with the Canon;
for although it is stated in the *Abhidhammabhājaniya* that "by whatever language the designation of those phenomena occurs," even so—
The statement is made with reference solely to the awakening of phenomena by means of the word "language" (*niruttisadda*), and not to a conceptual designation (*paññatti*) separate from that;
thus, when it is said, "the analytical knowledge of language has the word as its object," there is no contradiction with the Canon—this is the meaning.
Because of the phrase "of one who is reviewing," [it follows that] after grasping the sound, there is a reviewing of the conceptual designation grasped subsequently.
"If one were to suspect that [something] must come to be," he says "having made that sound, which is the natural expression, the object" and so forth,
in order to eliminate that suspicion. "Only while clarifying the natural expression" means that because confusion regarding the domain of the natural expression has already been dispelled,
it clarifies it precisely by way of establishing the meaning, just like the knowledge of direct higher knowledge (*abhiññā-ñāṇa*).
It occurs. Therefore he said: "It arises precisely while breaking through and penetrating the etymological analysis (nirutti).

And here, "penetrating the analysis" means knowing the divisions of etymology without exception. The same applies to the remaining [categories]. "Sanskrit names and so forth" refers to nouns, verbs, and so on, as expressed according to the Sanskrit system.

A particle-word (*nipātapada*) does not express a meaning in the same way that noun-words and so forth do; rather, it clarifies and illuminates it, and thus the particle-word is called "expression" (*byañjana*).

Because enlightenment-knowledge (*bodhi-ñāṇa*) is the essence (*maṇḍa*) here, it is called the "seat of enlightenment" (*bodhimaṇḍa*), which is the site of Great Enlightenment. Therefore he said, "at the place of the first full awakening. "In another manner" means by way of learning and so forth.
"They become otherwise" means that as they undergo partial changes in each successive pair of human generations, they take on different forms over time.

"They perish" means that due to the disappearance of the people who speak those respective languages, they are no longer known; or [they perish] through the difficulty of humans in grasping them and so forth.

Although it may undergo transformation in some places and at some times—such as in the Brahma-worlds and so forth—it does not transform everywhere, at all times, and in every way, because it remains established according to its own intrinsic nature.
Therefore he said: “Even at the destruction of an eon, it simply persists. This refers to the knowledge of the analytical insight into language (*niruttipaṭisambhidāñāṇa*).

Knowledge regarding the meaning and so forth is the analytical insight into meaning (*atthapaṭisambhidā*) and the others. It exists in three ways: by way of meaning, phenomena, and language; and by way of meaning, phenomena, language, and ingenuity (*paṭibhāna*).
Or [it applies] to all four. It is "possessing the meaning" (sātthaka) because it possesses the meaning together with the meaning, dhamma, and so forth, by which it is to be manifested by itself.
It is "all-pervading" (sabbatthaka) because this knowledge possesses as its object the entire range of meanings, including dhamma and so forth.
It is "thrown into" (khitta) every object, such as meaning and so forth; that is, established and made to proceed by its own conditions. It is "clear" (visada) for the attainment of Arahantship.

[They are so called] because opposing states have been entirely destroyed. "Of the five" refers to realization (adhigama), study (pariyatti), listening (savana), interrogation (paripucchā), and prior practice (pubbayoga).
"According to what is appropriate" means that whatever is suitable for the clarity of a particular individual should be applied accordingly.
Since a discourse that proceeds by way of interrogation is called "interrogation," he said: "By interrogation... it is called interrogation."
"By those" means by the paths. "Acquisition" (paṭilābha) is the cutting off of delusion regarding the objects such as the meaning (attha) through the attainment of prior application;

since that is indeed the function of the path, he said, "That is supramundane. The differentiation (pabheda)—the discerning, the manifesting, and the defining—of the meaning and so forth occurs, as appropriate, by way of limited wholesome and great functional consciousnesses; thus it is said, "The differentiation is sense-sphere."

The intention is this: just as previous practice (*pubbayoga*) is a powerful condition for realization because it serves as its natural cause (*sabhāvahetu*), it is not so for the various categories [of the Dhamma], since those are not its natural causes and it is only a remote condition (*paramparapaccaya*) for them.

This same principle applies to the fact that study (*pariyatti*) and the rest are powerful conditions for the categories, while for realization, their absence follows the very same logic. In this context, the locative case in *tattha* (therein) expresses the sense of a "sign" (*nimitta*).
The meaning is: "when those [activities]—the study, listening, and interrogation—have become the signs.
"That which has been stated" refers to the matter that has been stated by the commentary's words beginning with "But among these... "Showing that" means showing it after having determined it.
Having said "from the attainment of previous practice," the statement "both" implies that even previous practice is accompanied by attainment.
This is for the purpose of showing that it is not merely [the previous condition], but rather a powerful condition for the specific classification. Therefore, it is stated in the *Aṭṭhakathā*:
“Both together. When it is said, “Both are causes of purification,” the fact that prior application (*pubbayoga*) is also a cause of purification is indeed implied;
thus he says: “Both are causes of purification... so it is stated.”
The commentary on the Section on the Modes of Comprehension (Saṅgahavāra) is finished.
2. Commentary on the Section on Truths (Saccavāra), etc.
719. "In all three times" means in the three times, beginning with the past. "Phenomena that are causes and fruits" refers to those phenomena which have become the fruits of causes.

The meaning is "produced by conditions. And as for the phrase "the causal phenomena of those": the construction is that the phenomena which serve as the causes for those results produced by conditions are called "phenomena" (*dhammā*). "According to the persons to be trained" means according to the inclinations of the individuals who are to be trained in such a way.

The passage beginning with "arisen, fully arisen, emerged, fully emerged, present," and so forth, was not stated [in the previous section]. "Arisen, fully arisen, emerged, fully emerged, present," etc., [is what follows].
It was not stated [there] because it includes only that which is strictly present. "Their producers" means those that bring about their existence as objective entities (*atthabhāva*).
"Dhammas" means those spoken of as having the nature of phenomena (*dhammabhāva*).
The commentary on the section on the Truths (*Saccavāra*) is concluded.
The commentary on the Suttantabhājanīya is finished.
2. Commentary on the Abhidhammabhājanīya: 725.

Having spoken in terms of generality, because it was not stated in terms of distinction, [the phrase] "their result" (*tesaṃ vipāke*) refers to the generality of being the result of wholesome states and so forth as previously mentioned.

The meaning is: because it was not stated with the distinctions of being "with cause" (*sahetuka*) or "without cause" (*ahetuka*), and because it was not stated by way of its specific form (*sarūpa*). "Because they are non-resultant" means because they have the nature of not producing a result (*avipākadhamma*). "If this were so" means:

if, although the state of being a phenomenon (*dhammabhāva*) is obtained through their status as conditions, that state of being a phenomenon is not mentioned for functional states (*kiriyā*) due to their non-resultant nature—this being the case.
Even though they possess the status of being "arisen from conditions," [they are not mentioned] because of their non-resultant state.
Even the state of being an "existent" (atthabhāva) cannot be predicated [of them]. Therefore he said: "They are not results, and thus the state of being an existent cannot be predicated.

And as for the phrase "if it is so": if the state of being an existent is stated for functional states (kiriyā) because they are produced by conditions, the meaning is that this is neither prohibited nor desired.
If this is so, why was it not stated? To this he replied: "But of the result," and so forth. "Of those" refers to the wholesome and unwholesome [states].

And [it applies] to resultant (vipāka) and functional (kiriyā) phenomena. Although the state of being an object (atthabhāva) and the state of being a phenomenon (dhammabhāva)—which are obtained according to the method already stated—are not explicitly mentioned by the phrase "the state of being an object and a phenomenon," he nevertheless expresses the very nature of being a resultant phenomenon through the three terms:

"the state of being a condition," "a specific capacity," and "that which is to be produced. For that [nature] is the state of being a condition because it serves as the cause for resultants, and it is the capacity to produce them.
It is a particular power; because it is as if pregnant with those [powers], it is called "the state of having that which is to be accomplished.
Seeing that, the analytical knowledge of phenomena (*dhamma-paṭisambhidā*) also becomes dependent upon that which is to be accomplished, even though it is itself a particular power that accomplishes.

"By connection with that" means by connection with that which is to be accomplished. When the analytical knowledge of phenomena is spoken of, the analytical knowledge of meaning (*attha-paṭisambhidā*) is also thereby stated.

He says, "not by a designation such as 'a being' (satta)," because a designation for a phenomenon that possesses an intrinsic nature (sabhāva) is a "designation of intrinsic nature" (sabhāvapaññatti). Or, he says, "or by an unerring designation," because a designation of intrinsic nature is stated to be either the intrinsic nature itself or the linguistic expression (nirutti) [for it]. 746.

Having combined the plane of conventional usage (vohārabhūmi) and the plane of realization (adhigamabhūmi) into one, he says, "the plane consisting of the sense-sphere (kāmāvacara) and the supramundane (lokuttara) is the 'plane' (bhūmi). Alternatively, the arising of consciousness (cittuppāda) is the "plane" because it is the state of occurrence.
The commentary on the *Abhidhammabhājanīya* is finished.

3. Commentary on the Section of Questions (Pañhapucchakavaṇṇanā) 747. "Because it has all-knowledge as its object" means because it has the analytical knowledge of the analytical knowledges (paṭisambhidā-paṭisambhidā-ñāṇa) as its object. As for the statement, "In the *Suttantabhājanīya*, however...
[etc. ...it may be," this contradicts the *Abhidhammabhājanīya*, or else it is a teaching that leaves something remaining.
Thinking of the objection, "Does it not follow [that the Abhidhamma is incomplete]?", he says, "In the *Abhidhammabhājaniya*," and so forth.

"Exposition without remainder" means an exposition that leaves nothing out. By this, he shows that the burden of the *Abhidhammabhājaniya* here is the teaching of the meanings comprised within the arising of consciousness without leaving anything out, rather than all knowable phenomena (*sabbaññeyyadhamma*). "By way of words for the objects as they have been shown" refers to the objects according to the manner in which they were demonstrated.

The meaning is: by way of explaining, by way of the status of the phenomena (*dhammattha*), and by way of explaining knowledge through the expression of the linguistic definition of those respective mental arisings (*dhammaniruttābhilāpa*).
The intention is that it does not deny the state of having other objects, because its nature is not restricted to that alone.

It is not an exhaustive explanation, because objects not included within the category of mental arisings have not been mentioned. This is likewise true for the scope of the analytical knowledge of perspicuity (*paṭibhānapaṭisambhidā*).

It does not state this exhaustively; rather, in the *Suttantabhājanīya*, by means of a general statement, it establishes that the analytical knowledge of ready wit (*paṭibhāna-paṭisambhidā*) has all-knowledge as its object.
The same is true for the textual passage consisting of questions and answers beginning with "Three analytical knowledges" (*tisso paṭisambhidā*).

Here, "three" refers to the analytical knowledges of meaning (*attha*), phenomena (*dhamma*), and ready wit (*paṭibhāna*); for the analytical knowledge of language (*nirutti-paṭisambhidā*) is stated to have only limited objects (*parittārammaṇā*).
"Even if it were so, there would be no state of having a sublime object (mahaggatārammaṇatā) for that"—this is the connection.

By the statement, "For the Path is not something arisen through conditions," he clarifies how this establishes the meaning of the claim that "the analytical knowledge of meaning (atthapaṭisambhidā) does not have the Path as its object.
Is it not the case that for that [analytical knowledge], namely the analytical knowledge of eloquence (paṭibhānapaṭisambhidā), a state of having a sublime object is not possible?
The intention is: "for one who recollects this method. "Both" refers to these two texts: "The analytical knowledge of meaning (atthapaṭisambhidā) does not have the Path as its object;
the other three analytical knowledges may have limited objects, may have exalted objects, or may have immeasurable objects.
Through the means of showing the basis for the stronger of these two [texts] and the way to follow the intention of the other, [the meaning is established].
In order to show that these [four analytical knowledges] do not contradict one another, he said, "But as for the wholesome and unwholesome," and so forth.

By the statement, "Therein, the analytical knowledge of phenomena (dhamma-paṭisambhidā) is in the primary sense," he indicates that the analytical knowledge of meaning (attha-paṭisambhidā) therein is only figurative.
Likewise, the passage beginning with "of the resultant and the functional" is an illustration of a dissimilar example for the intended meaning. By both of these [statements],...

The statement, “the analytical knowledge of meaning (atthapaṭisambhidā) does not have the Path as its object,” demonstrates that it conforms to the method of the Suttas, because the non-figurative (nippariyāya) sense is intended therein.
The passage beginning with “But what kind of knowledge... provides an explanation for the scriptural passage starting with “the three analytical knowledges.
“Paṭibhāna” is the illumination or manifestation of the intended meaning; therefore, he said, “because of the making known of the knowable.”

Thus, by demonstrating the powerful nature of the passage "the three analytical knowledges" (*tisro pratisaṃvidah*), it should be understood that the intended meaning of the other [passage] has been traced.
"In the non-figurative sense" (*nippariyāya*) means devoid of figurative expression, proceeding directly and in its own true form. Regarding the phrase "in the non-figurative... proceeding":

in this teaching, knowledge whose object is an absolute meaning is the analytical knowledge of meaning (*attha-paṭisambhidā*), while knowledge whose object is knowledge itself is the analytical knowledge of discernment (*paṭibhāna-paṭisambhidā*). This is how they are to be understood.
"So eva" (just so) refers only to the sound of another's utterance. Its "conformity" (anuvattamānatā) should be understood by way of such statements as:
"The analytical knowledge of language (niruttipaṭisambhidā), taking only the present sound as its object, knows upon hearing the sound:
'This is a natural linguistic expression; this is not a natural linguistic expression. etc.
The commentary on the Section of Questions is finished.
The commentary on the Analysis of the Analytical Knowledges is finished. 16.
The Analysis of Knowledge (Ñāṇavibhaṅga).
1. Commentary on the Singlefold Summary (Ekakamātikāvaṇṇanā) 751.

The sense of "space" (okāsaṭṭha) should be understood as the state of being a supporting condition (nissayapaccayatā) for associated states, and as the locus of occurrence (pavattiṭṭhāna) for the object.
By the word "and so forth" (ādi) in the phrase "not-root, etc.," all the singlefold bases of knowledge beginning with "rootless" (ahetuka) are included.

"One is not-cause" means that by way of being not-cause, the fivefold consciousness is called "not-cause"; this refers to their state of being not-cause. For it is because they are of one kind through their absolute state of being causeless that they are said to be of a single mode.

"And another" refers to those that are causeless and so forth. "Endowed with the commonality of non-falsity" means endowed with that very same state of equality—namely, the state of being causeless and so forth—exactly as it is.
"Object of knowledge" refers to the object of knowledge, such as the aforementioned fivefold consciousness and the rest.

“Analysis of the bases” (*vatthuvibhāvanā*) is the wisdom that analyzes and clarifies the bases of knowledge—such as the fivefold sense-consciousness—by means of the specific distinctions already mentioned.

“Of the pair at the end” refers to this pair: “wisdom that makes the meaning known” and “wisdom whose meaning has been made known. When he says, “without depending on the pair-matrix,” he means that it is stated without relying on the pair-matrix as recited in the *Dhammasaṅgaṇī*.
When he says, “thus, in accordance with the triads,” he means that it is stated here as well without relying on the triad-matrix beginning with “wisdom consisting of reflection” (*cintāmayā paññā*).

"It should be understood. Although the word *jāpa* occurs in the sense of "eloquent speech" and "mental recitation," he says "because verbal roots have multiple meanings," etc., showing that it should also be understood in the sense of "producing.

This is because wholesome wisdom (*kusalapaññā*) produces the meaning designated as the result (*vipāka*), and functional wisdom (*kiriyapaññā*)—consisting of the preliminary stages (*parikamma*) and so forth—produces the meaning designated as the fruit to be brought about by itself.
Because it is said that [wisdom] "makes its object known," he says: "Wisdom that has reached its cause makes its object known.

Since resultant wisdom (*vipākapaññā*) and functional wisdom (*kiriyapaññā*) make their respective objects—namely, the result and so forth—known and produce them by way of such conditions as co-nascence (*sahajātā*), he says:

"That whose object is made known—that is, produced—is 'one whose object is made known' (*jāpitatthā*). Even though co-nascent factors possess the state of being conditions, resultant and functional wisdom do not...
Because wholesome states receive the conventional designation of being the cause of their results in a direct sense, it is said that “it resembles the wisdom of a cause.
Because wisdom has the sense of making manifest, it illuminates its associated states just as it does its object; thus it is said that “it consists in the illumination of the result.
For this reason, it is made manifest by the terms “light,” “radiance,” and “splendor.”
10. Explanation of the Tenfold Schedule (Dasakamātikāvaṇṇanā) 760.
“The knowledge that ‘with birth as condition, there is aging-and-death’; the knowledge that ‘in the absence of birth, there is no aging-and-death.
Regarding the past time as well, the knowledge that ‘with birth as condition, there was aging-and-death’; the knowledge that ‘in the absence of birth, there was no aging-and-death.’”
There is the knowledge: "In the future time as well, with birth as condition, there is aging-and-death"; there is the knowledge: "In the absence of birth, there is no aging-and-death.
There is also the knowledge that this very knowledge of the stability of phenomena is itself subject to destruction, subject to vanishing, subject to fading away, and subject to cessation.
[The same applies to] "with existence as condition" ... "with ignorance as condition, volitional formations arise" ... up to "... subject to cessation."

Thus there are seventy-seven kinds of knowledge that have been mentioned: the forty-four kinds of knowledge mentioned thus, “Knowledge of aging-and-death, knowledge of the origin of aging-and-death, knowledge of the cessation of aging-and-death, knowledge of the way leading to the cessation of aging-and-death;
knowledge of birth … [and so on] … knowledge of volitional formations … [and so on] … knowledge of the way leading to the cessation of volitional formations”;
and those beginning with knowledge consisting in what is heard and ending with unobstructed knowledge.
There are seventy-three knowledges (ñāṇa) recorded in the *Paṭisambhidāmagga*. Therefore he said: “But the seventy-three... [etc.
...not in the *Saṃyutta*. Alternatively, the word “in the *Saṃyutta*” should be connected with the phrase “seventy-seven knowledges,” and not with “the seventy-three.
[The term] “elsewhere” refers to the *Nikkhepakaṇḍa* and so forth. Just as, due to the absence of right penetration, there are false knowledges (*micchāñāṇa*) and so on within a heap of chaff.

Like a pillar that has been driven deep into the ground, it is unshakable; it is not like a cognition that wavers toward its object and thus fails to bring about the realization of things as they truly are (yathābhūta).
Therefore, he said: "It is itself unshakable through the penetration of reality as it is" (yāthāvapaṭivedhato sayañca akampiyaṃ). Support (upatthambhana) means the act of strengthening.
Applying this to the person, he said: "And it makes the person... [etc. ...strong. Or else, the meaning of "unshakability" refers to being unshakable by discordant states (visabhāgadhamma).
The sense of providing support among the qualities of the assembly should be understood.
"They go towards" (*abhimukhaṃ gacchanti*) is an explanatory gloss for the word "they approach" (*upagacchanti*). And here, "approaching" refers specifically to the profession of omniscience;
thus it is said, "by way of professing. Or, regarding the phrase "the eight assemblies approach," here too—
"Omniscience" should be construed with "by way of professing. The connection is: "endowed with the knowledge of unshakability demonstrated in the eight assemblies.

"The occurrence of the attainment of the fruit" refers to the manifestation of the excellence of such factors as dwelling in a suitable locality and right aspiration for oneself—the fruits resulting from causes such as relying upon true persons (*sappurisa*).
By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), the remainder of the Sutta is included. In that context, [the question is] regarding reliance upon true persons and so forth: why?

Regarding this, with reference to the objection that—since the purpose of the goal (*atthakicca*) is the same here—the arising of the knowledge of teaching (*desanāñāṇa*), like the knowledge of penetration (*paṭivedhañāṇa*), is not stated to continue up to the path of Arahatship, he says: "Because it is the culmination of penetration," and so forth.

"Because it is the culmination of penetration" means because it is the final limit of penetration. "By that" means by the knowledge of the path of Arahatship, which constitutes the culmination of penetration.

For by the attainment of that [knowledge], the Blessed One—having perfected all the qualities of omniscience and possessing infinite eloquence—became capable of teaching the Dhamma through the incomparable grace of a Buddha.
By the phrase "even though it has been acquired," he demonstrates that the knowledge of teaching cannot be fully equal to the penetration [of realization] in every respect;
and by this, he shows that the purpose here is accomplished by the mere act of penetration alone.
This is what he shows. Therefore he said, “of the knowledge of teaching,” and so forth.

“A state conducive to decline” means the cause for the condition of being conducive to decline. “States such as perception accompanied by sensual desire” refers to perception, attention, and so on, which have the strands of sensual pleasure as their object.
“From the previously performed volitional formations” means [from those formed] regarding the moon or the sun...

"Or, having gone this far, I shall emerge"—by such [thoughts], one refers to the preliminary mental formations (*cittābhisaṅkhāra*) and the preparatory work (*parikamma*) occurring prior to the attainment.
"By the grasping of its absence" means by the grasping of the absence of the obscuration of defilements (*kilesāvaraṇa*). "Stability" means existence.
"By its opposite" means by wrong view (*micchādiṭṭhi*) such as "there is no giving. "Absence of standing" means non-occurrence or non-existence.
"Upari" (above) means immediately following this discourse on the sequence of powers.

"For the purpose of showing the absence of the obstruction of kamma-result, etc."—by the word "etc.," the showing of the absence of the obstruction of karma is included. "The other" refers to the showing that [the obstruction] is not a basis for attainment.
"Of those elements accompanied by that" refers to the intrinsic natures (sabhāva) accompanied by lust and so forth. And their diversity is established by the specific difference in their conditions.

[These] are to be understood through distinctions such as their specific states (*avatthā*). "Of the causes of temperament" (*cariyāhetūnaṃ*) means of those phenomena that have become the causes for temperaments such as lust (*rāga*), etc.
1. Commentary on the Singlefold Exposition (Ekakaniddesavaṇṇanā) 761.

"This distinction" refers to the fact that, although the two methods are similar in their illumination of those [factors] being non-causes and so forth, one [method] possesses the quality of negating their being causes and so forth.
The distinction is this: for the other [type of nutriment], there is inclusion within a different heap (*rāsantarāsaṅgaho*).

"By a single birth" means by a single existence (*bhavo*) delimited by taking up and laying down [the aggregates]. "By being included therein" means by being included within that particular destiny (*gatiantogadhatāya*). "In each respective place" means in those various existences of death and rebirth within the respective destinies.

"Thus" means by way of having a different door and object. Regarding the statement "of milk and so forth... dissimilarity": just as milk, by becoming curds, [is transformed]... [the rest of the sentence follows].

The meaning is this: curd undergoes a change into a different characteristic state by way of becoming buttermilk (*takkabhāva*), but for the five types of sensory consciousness, there is no such attainment of a different intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*) other than their status as causes and so forth.
(763) "Even in greatness" means even in plurality;
for this word *mahā* expresses multiplicity, as in such terms as "the great multitude" (*mahājana*).

Because it is intended as a collection of forms (rūpa-saṅghāṭa) [rather than a single form]. Otherwise, what would be the "greatness" or "subtlety" of a phenomenon that possesses an intrinsic nature (sabhāva-dhamma)?
Because it was stated by referring to the eye-consciousness (cakkhu-viññāṇa), he said: "In the sensitivity of the eye (cakkhu-pasāda), which is my basis.
"The place of sovereignty" means the place where sovereignty functions. For indeed, when developed elsewhere, it manifests only there.
It remains; and other consciousnesses proceed there according to the very method provided by it, even the knowledge of the divine eye, since that does not arise for one who is blind. 764.
"Even though they are distinct" means even though they are not mutually confused. "The rule of sequence" is the state of having a fixed order. "By that" refers to the expression "uninterrupted."
766. The state of turning toward is the function of adverting (*āvajjana*).
"Of these" refers to visible forms and so forth. For there is a coming together of these visible forms and so forth with the five types of consciousness.

They are to be "fallen upon" (*abhinipatitabbāni*), that is, to be taken as objects (*ālambitabbāni*), and to be cognized (*vijānitabbāni*); this is the meaning. Therefore he said: "They are to be individually cognized by way of making them objects."

The connection [of the sentence] is: "the discerning of that which is to be discerned," namely, wholesome and unwholesome volition and those factors associated with it, as stated in the passage beginning, "Mind is the forerunner... [or] unwholesome.

For this genitive case is used here in the sense of the object (kamma). By "the dhamma that is the co-nascent forerunner" means by contact and so forth, which are co-nascent with seeing and the other [mental activities], acting as the forerunner.
By means of adverting and so forth. "Another function" refers to functions such as receiving, which are distinct from functions such as seeing.
"By way of being non-resultant" means by that reason, or together with it. "Other" refers to the state of matter and so forth.

"Those that produce speech and action" are the wholesome and unwholesome mental states that arise by way of originating intimation; these alone constitute the members of the body and the members of speech.
“Proceeding without having been disturbed” means occurring as something similar [to the object]. “Discerning by way of precedence” means discerning through the state of being a precursor;
it is the grasping [of the object] by way of preceding the mind-door impulsion (*manodvārika-javana*). Regarding the phrase “therein,” it refers to the five sense doors.
Having stated, “It is not prohibited,” he says, “Because bodily action... is permitted,” in order to show that this non-prohibition is obtained by implication (*sāmatthiya*).

It has been said. The word “likewise” (tathā) should be understood as serving to conclude that, just as there is no undertaking of bodily or verbal actions, so too there is no undertaking of wholesome and other states.
If one does not pass away from existence, how is it that death at the five sense-doors is spoken of? He says: “Not at the five doors...
because of its being doorless. Regarding that text: “merely reaching the range” (āpāthamattaṃ).

It is merely the coming into the range [of the senses] and merely the state of being an object-condition (*ārammaṇapaccaya*). "Another" refers to specific phenomena (*dhammavisesa*) such as "form is blue" and so forth;

therefore he said, "the individual essence of phenomena" (*dhammasabhāva*). "And it does not grasp 'form'" means that even though it has form as its object, it does not grasp it as "this is called form.
Thus some have said: "One endowed with eye-consciousness cognizes blue, but not..."

"Blue" refers to the designation of the mode of the object of form (rūpārammaṇa) and the mode of the appropriation of form (rūpādāna), such as the aspect of blue-form and so forth. This is a designation born from that (tajjāpaññatti), just like impermanence and so on.

It is particularly [emphasized] because it possesses both initial application (vitakka) and sustained application (vicāra). "Other than that" means other than the object of sound (saddārammaṇa); it is the object of the designation of name (nāmapaññatti).
The intention is that otherwise, the prohibition of simultaneous arising would not be possible.

"In the mind-door too" means not only in the second "Futile" section concerning the five doors, but also in the mind-door. "Adverting [should be seen] two or three times... [and so on], because such [repetition] is impossible in the arising of adverting, which lasts for only a single conscious moment (*ekacittakkhaṇika*).
"Of that" refers to the wisdom that discerns the object as it truly is.
The commentary to the Singlefold Exposition is finished.
2. Commentary on the Exposition of Pairs (Dukaniddesa) 767.

"In the locative cases" (*adhikaraṇesu*) means: in the meanings of the words. "Taking [the meaning] other than its own intrinsic nature" (*aññatra sabhāvaṃ gahetvā*) is a demonstration of the manner in which the word *attha* functions therein;
by this, he shows that the word *attha* has the sense of "intrinsic nature" (*sabhāvattha*). Thus, through the function of the locative case, it undergoes a change of gender.
"For gender and number conform to the meaning," so say those learned in grammar.
