The commentary on the Exposition of Pairs is finished.
3. Commentary on the Exposition of Threes.
768. *Paripācitesu* means "in those that have been accomplished. Regarding the phrase *vihitesu*, since the sense of past time—as in the case of milk and so forth—is not intended here, he says:
"It is merely a specification of the object. Since wisdom is spoken of by way of a metaphorical designation for its cause as "work" (*kamma*) or "craft" (*sippa*), he says:
"Or rather, it should be understood as wisdom itself... and so on.

Wholesome (kusala) kamma is "its own" (saka) because it brings about its own exclusive benefit and happiness. Because it is the opposite of that, the other—unwholesome (akusala) kamma—is "not its own" (nosaka).
Since "conformity with the truths" (saccānulomana) is said to be conformity with the penetration of the truths, he says, "by way of being a condition for the penetration thereof.
Alternatively, it possesses the quality of conforming to the truths because it conforms to the truth of the Path, and likewise because it conforms to the ultimate truth (paramattha-sacca).
Therefore, it is said in the *Aṭṭhakathā*: “Of the truth of the path,” and so forth. Wisdom is mentioned because the function of wisdom regarding the objects of wisdom has been shown.

The description of the planes is given by the passage beginning with “In those established through yoga”; the description of the specific form is given by the passage “Kamma-ownership is in conformity with the truths”;
and the description of the modes is given by the passage “Form is impermanent,” and so forth—thus they are as previously stated...pe...

These are the explanations. They should be connected with the terms "acceptance" (*khanti*) and so forth, according to the passage beginning: "Acceptance regarding the spheres of action established by yoga, acceptance regarding the ownership of one's actions, and acceptance that 'form is impermanent.
"Beholding" (*olokana*) means making manifest through direct experience. By stating "the phenomena accept beholding," it expresses the capacity of wisdom (*paññā*) to behold them.

769. “Muñcati” means he abandons. It is said that it is appropriate to say “let go...,” because [the root] signifies the undertaking of an action, the state of being endowed with it, the locus, and the establishment [of the act].
770. With reference to the five precepts and the ten precepts, which constitute a portion of the cycle of kamma, their inclusion within the stability of phenomena (dhammaṭṭhiti) has been stated.
Even though there is hearing [of the Dhamma], as in: “Here, monks, a noble disciple abstains from the destruction of life,” and so forth.

Even though there is hearing from a Tathāgata, that which is spoken regarding the higher virtue (*adhisīla*) of monks and others is not exclusive to the Buddhas (*buddhāveṇika*), just like the proclamation of higher virtue.

"Produced by higher wisdom" (*adhipaññānibbatte*) refers to those other states of the path and fruit (*maggaphala-dhamma*) apart from higher wisdom itself. "Having that as their basis" (*tadadhiṭṭhānesu*) refers to the states of insight (*vipassanā-dhamma*) which are the bases for that higher wisdom. 771.
"The production of an unfavorable rebirth" (*apāyuppādana*) means the production of non-prosperity. "In that very place" (*tasmiṃyeva ṭhāne*) means at that very moment.
The commentary on the Exposition of Threes is finished.
4. Commentary on the Exposition of Fours: 793.

*Paritassana* means fear or anxiety; it is the agitation of the mind. Thus, for the phrase "he does not tremble" (*na paritassati*), the meaning is stated as "he does not long for [existence] and he does not fear."
796. In the context of the Noble Truths, the word *dhamma* is used as in such expressions as "the seen *dhamma*" (*diṭṭhadhammo*).
The Noble Path and its fruit are *dhamma* because they sustain those who practice according to the instruction, preventing them from falling into the states of misery.
In that context, "wisdom" (*paññā*) refers to the wisdom that has that Noble Path and its fruit as its support. Therefore he said, "concomitant with that. It makes the unknown known, as it were.

"Leading" (*naya*) means making known (*ñāpeti*). It is inference (*anumāna*); its "leading" is its occurrence or operation. To dispel the suspicion that this is merely the production of a distinct, separate knowledge, he says:

"Not another... [there is] no difference. For "leading" is the inference of the modes of occurrence of the paths and so forth in the three times as attained by others, according to one's own attainment.
Indeed, it is with reference to the very mode of inferring that [this is said].
It is stated that "it is simply a specific mode of the operation of knowledge. And the reason for this is that the eye of guidance operates through direct perception regarding the truths.
By the word "likewise" (*tathā*), he concludes the following point:

just as it is appropriate to say "by means of this Dhamma" in reference to knowledge other than the knowledge of the path, so too does the meaning fit here—"by means of this Dhamma, which is knowledge"—even when expressed in a different manner.
"Tenā" means: therefore, because it is known by means of knowledge (*ñāṇa*), and because it leads [to liberation] through its associated factors (*sampayoga*).

"By way of being the object of knowledge" means by way of being the objective domain (*visaya*) of penetrative knowledge (*paṭivedha-ñāṇa*). "By what is known" refers either to the Dhamma of the Four Noble Truths as it has been penetrated, or to the Dhamma of the Path and Fruition which stands having been known through association with knowledge.
"In every way" (*sabbena sabbaṃ*) means in every manner, that is, entirely without remainder;

for all that is comprised within the three periods of time—the conditioned phenomena of the three planes—is thoroughly comprehended. "By way of method" (*nayanato*) means by way of grasping the method.
Alternatively, the word *kāraṇa* (reason/method) expresses a corresponding meaning, as in such phrases as "he states the reason" (*kāraṇaṃ vadati*).
Because it proceeds even after having thoroughly mastered *anvaya-ñāṇa* (subsequent knowledge), its comprehension of the object is distinguished; thus it is said: "Knowledge of the Dhamma... [etc.

...due to the absence [of that]. "By way of the commonality of knowing the mere manifestation of the object" means by way of the mere commonality of comprehension, which consists in the illumination of the object, even though there is no grasping through direct penetration (*abhisamaya*).
"Designated as 'knowledge'" means those things conventionally expressed as "knowledge."

Regarding those expressions used for "gained knowledge": "by way of conventional designation" (*sammutivasena*) means that it does not proceed directly toward the object like the knowledge of the Dhamma (*dhammañāṇa*) and so forth, but proceeds by way of a conceptual description (*paññatti*).

"The remainder" refers specifically to conventional knowledge (*sammutiñāṇa*). "Dissimilar to the other three knowledges" means being devoid of the triad of knowledges beginning with the knowledge of the Dhamma.
797. *Kāmabhavadhamme* means in the phenomena (dhamma) comprised within sensual existence (*kāmabhava*).
798. *Sā* refers to the wisdom of the first jhāna. *Vītarāgabhāvanāvatthassa* means of one who is described as "he becomes free from lust.
*Taṃ* refers to the sixth direct knowledge (*abhiññā*). For path-knowledge, by way of its function, penetrates even the truth of the path itself. *Itarā* refers to the wisdom of the lower paths.
"Because it is its decisive support" means that it is called "penetrating" because it serves as the decisive support (*upanissaya*) for that sixth direct knowledge or for that penetration.

"Accordingly" means according to the respective [defilements] such as the taints of views (*diṭṭhāsava*). "In the destruction of the taints" is used by way of figurative designation (*kāraṇūpacāra*) for the discourse on the destruction of the taints.
"Because of producing that" means because of producing that fruit known as the destruction of the taints.
And this is stated because it is said in the Sutta: “The knowledge of the destruction of the taints is the sixth direct knowledge.
(801) Or, “making manifest by means of distinguished knowledge” means making it clear and evident through the mode of attainment.

(802) “Not brought to mastery” means it has merely been acquired without having attained the fivefold mastery. Regarding “by way of pointing out the path as the object of wisdom,” he says this because wisdom accompanied by the path as its object is connected with the path as its object.
The commentary on the Exposition of the Tetads is finished.
5. Commentary on the Exposition of the Pentads 804.

That same wisdom is analyzed by means of the passage beginning, “Wisdom in two jhānas is through the pervasion of rapture,” and so forth. There are also the terms *abhisandana*, *parisandana*, and *paripūraṇa*.
Just as with sprinkling, the specific functions of the pervading joy and the pleasure associated with it are intended;
thus he said, "it drenches... [etc. ...should be understood. By the method beginning with "it drenches" refers to the manner in which it is presented in the Sutta.
And here, "pervasion" (pharaṇa) should be seen as the suffusion of the body by sublime material forms produced by that joy and pleasure. Regarding the object:

In the objects of the triplets and couplets of jhānas spoken of by way of the pervasion of rapture (*pīti*) and the pervasion of bliss (*sukha*). "By those" means by the pervasion of rapture and the pervasion of bliss.

"By way of concentration" (*samādhimukhena*) means having made concentration the entrance (*mukha*) or the primary factor; the meaning is "by way of the head of concentration," or by an exposition where concentration is the primary factor.
Other defilements are views, conceit, and so forth. "Without much effort" (*appayogena*) [is said] as in the case of the jhānas, liberations, and so on.

"Without the application of preparatory effort for producing [the attainment]" means that the course of comprehension (*sammasanacāra*) has the same purpose as the advertence (*āvajjanā*) for the attainment of fruition (*phalasamāpatti*).
"Because it has been established" means because it has been set in motion. "By way of abundance of mindfulness" means by way of the frequent arising of mindfulness.
The construction is: "He shows the mindfulness of time by means of delimiting mindfulness."
The commentary on the Exposition of the Pentads is finished.
6. Commentary on the Exposition of the Hexads. 805.
“The state of purity” means the existence of purity. “Because it is a part of the knowledge of the divine eye”—this refers to that [knowledge].

This was stated by way of an explanatory supplement (*paribhaṇḍa*). For in the Pāḷi, having begun with “He directs and inclines his mind toward the knowledge of the passing away and rebirth of beings,” it is said:
“With the divine eye, purified...,” and so forth.

This refers to the knowledge of the divine eye (*dibbacakkhu-ñāṇa*), which is capable of seeing both the divine form-sphere (*rūpāyatana*)—which is distinguished by its being hidden, remote, and so on—and other [ordinary] forms.
He said, "And by one who has reached the crown," and so forth, because a *sikkhāpatti* (a training-offense) consists in seeing beings passing away and being reborn.
The commentary on the Exposition of the Six is finished.
7. Commentary on the Exposition of the Seven.

806. The sixfold reviewing knowledge (*paccavekkhaṇañāṇa*) is the knowledge that occurs by way of reviewing the factors of dependent origination, as stated in such passages as: "The knowledge that 'with birth as condition, there is aging-and-death,'" and so forth.

"Having taken together" means having taken them collectively, having taken them as a unity through their commonality as objects of insight (*vipassanā*). "As stated in brief" refers to what was said previously.
The connection is as follows: "the knowledge of the stability of phenomena (dhammaṭṭhitiñāṇa) shown as if stated in six ways" refers to what was spoken thus in brief;
"the seeing in the manner beginning with ‘subject to destruction’" is the link.

"Of the knowledge of occurrence" means of the knowledge occurring in the form "with birth as condition, aging-and-death," or of the knowledge regarding the occurrence of the cycle of existence (saṃsāravaṭṭa). Insight that has knowledge as its object is "knowledge-insight" (ñāṇavipassanā).

"Insight" (vipassanā) here refers to the knowledge of the stability of phenomena (dhammaṭṭhitiñāṇa), because it demonstrates, by way of analysis, the relationship between conditions and the phenomena arisen from conditions, such as "with birth as condition, aging-and-death comes to be.
The subsequent realization of those same phenomena as subject to destruction and so forth is "counter-insight" (paṭivipassanā).
Therefore, he said: "It is merely the seeing of insight and counter-insight."
Having thus shown the meaning of the text according to the intention of the *Aṭṭhakathā*, he now says, "But in the text...

and so forth, in order to show it according to his own intention. "In all cases" (*sabbattha*) means in the three periods of time, for the purpose of specifying the particularity of the conditionally arisen based on the particularity of the conditions.

"By the term 'knowledge'" (*ñāṇavacanena*) means by the inclusion of knowledge [in such passages] as "with birth as condition, aging-and-death. "Of the factors" (*aṅgānaṃ*) refers to the seventy-seven [factors].
“Of the factors. By the word *iti*: by the word *iti* used here in the phrase “subject to cessation. “Having made manifest”: having illuminated the mode of occurrence of knowledge.
By this, he shows that the knowledge mentioned at the conclusion is indeed distinct from the knowledge of the stability of phenomena (*dhammaṭṭhitiñāṇa*).
Therefore, he says: “Insight-knowledge is the seventh knowledge. And showing that this alone is the appropriate meaning in this context:
He says, “Indeed not,” and so forth. In that context, the phrase “that too is knowledge” does not constitute a valid connection;
the meaning is that such a connection is not appropriate because it fails to clarify its status as a distinct factor. Therefore it was said: “That knowledge... [etc. ...because it is not intended.
For what is stated separately does not become something different merely by being spoken together. “Subject to destruction... [etc.]”
By the phrase “and,” he points out the fault in the former position through its accumulation.
The commentary on the exposition of the septad is finished.
8. Commentary on the Exposition of the Octad.

808. "Adverse states" (paccanīkadhamma) refers to adverse states such as the hindrances (nīvaraṇa), etc. "Suffering" (dukkha) refers to the suffering that arises when there is no attainment [of jhāna].
The commentary on the Exposition of the Octads is finished.
10. The Exposition of the Decads.
Commentary on the Exposition of the First Power (Paṭhamabalaniddesavaṇṇanā) 809.

"Not a possibility" (*aṭṭhāna*) means a non-possibility (*anaṭṭhāna*). He says, "A non-existent possibility is a 'non-possibility' (*aṭṭhāna*)," because this letter *a* has the sense of non-apprehension.

Alternatively, it has the sense of non-existence; it does not have the sense of being the opposite of something else, etc. Therefore, he says, "Or, a place that does not exist is a 'non-possibility' (*aṭṭhāna*)."
What, then, is the distinction between these two meanings? The first speaks of the state of being unapprehendable through causes and conditions;
the second speaks of total non-existence—this is the distinction between them.

Regarding craving, clinging, and so forth, their status as causes for approaching [objects] as pleasant is particularly predominant in the perversion of view, because it causes that [view] to proceed strongly even toward what is not pleasant. Thus he said: "The perversion of view alone... [etc.]"
"...is intended. Why was it stated with the qualification "by way of the view of self" (*attadiṭṭhivasena*), given that a noble disciple (*ariyasāvaka*) has no views at all?
It is true that he has none; however, it was stated—"by way of the view of self" means "it refers to the primary view"—in order to show that all views are dependent upon the view of self.
[This applies] to the object corresponding to its division. By way of the division...
“By way of the progression beginning with ‘dhamma in what is non-dhamma’ and so forth.

“That very same” means: that very continuity of the life-faculty (jīvitindriya) belonging to the life-constituent (bhavaṅga) which exists in that individual existence (attabhāva) when the gender has not changed.

For it is by depending on that [continuity] that there is the conventional designation of a single birth; and here there is no objection based on the life-faculty of the aggregate of states (bhāvakalāpa).

It should be understood as referring to something other than that, because that [other] is what is intended there. For that [other] receives the designation of a "continuum" (pabandha) due to its uninterrupted occurrence therein;
or alternatively, the other [case] may also be included by virtue of the commonality of "maintaining an existence.
Thus, the objection is entirely out of place. It should be applied by way of an enemy: "In the place where an enemy is lying down with the intention, 'I shall kill my enemy'..."
It should be applied by way of such passages as: “one who is human killing a mother or a father who is human while they are lying down,” and so forth.
“In all cases” means in all four alternatives. “The prior intentional mind” refers to the preliminary intention for death.
It is “immeasurable” because there is no accomplishment of the objective through it. Regarding the statement, “that [kamma] is given only to a worldling (puthujjana),” here, just as...
Even if one has attained Arahatship, a gift given during the time of being an ordinary person (puthujjana) remains simply a "gift to an ordinary person.

Likewise, when a blow is struck with the intention of killing during the time of being an ordinary person, why is it that if the victim dies from that very blow after having attained Arahatship, it constitutes the "killing of an Arahat" and not the "killing of an ordinary person"?
Because of the occurrence of a distinction. For just as in the case of a gift...

It occurs merely by the relinquishing of the object to be given; it is not in this way a killing. For that [act of] killing occurs only when there is the fulfillment of these five factors—the living being, the perception of it as a living being, the volition to kill, the means employed, and death by that means—and not when they are incomplete.
Therefore, the killing of one who has attained Arahantship is indeed "killing an Arahant," whereas the killing of an ordinary person (puthujjana) is not.

However, because the continuum (santāna) with reference to which there is the desire to kill—thinking "I shall kill this one"—is indeed non-distinct [from the continuum of the victim], despite the difference in continua due to the states of being an ordinary person (puthujjana) and an one whose taints are destroyed (khīṇāsava) respectively, and due to the moments of the preparatory effort and the moment of death; and because when the purpose is accomplished, it is the state of having destroyed taints [that is reached];
therefore, it is certain that it is precisely the killing of an Arahant. But how, in this case, does the volition of killing (vadhakacetanā) [arise]?
He said, "It may have a present object," in the passage: "The murderous mind... even though its object is present, continues to proceed.
Therein, "by way of severing the continuity" means that one performs such an application by which the continuity is severed.
By this, he establishes that when the continuity is severed, there is then "deserving"—that is, the aforementioned killing of an Arahant.
It is not so; unlike the murderous mind, whose function is established in dependence on another time, the volition of relinquishment (*cāgacetanā*) is not like that.
By the words "For it... and so forth, he clarifies precisely how the volition of relinquishment has its function established without depending on another time.

"Making it the property of another" means making it the possession of another person worthy of offerings (*dakkhiṇeyya*), having released it from oneself. "Of that" refers to the object to be relinquished.

“Of the object”: of whichever ordinary person (*puthujjana*). “That gift belongs to him alone” means that even if [the recipient] has attained *arahantship* and has used it, [the merit] belongs to that very donor.
Regarding the phrase “at the destruction of an eon,” since this was stated in reference to “when an eon is reconstituted,” it is said with respect to the destruction of a great eon (*mahākappa*).
He said, "It does not agree with the *Kappaṭṭhakathā*," because here the "aeon" (*āyukappa*) is intended.
And in this context, the "life-span aeon" should be understood as the maximum lifespan of beings born in Avīci, measured by an intermediate aeon (*antarakappa*).
It is with reference to this that it was stated: "Having divided one aeon into eighty parts, [this duration is] merely one part of that time. This, then, is the "one..."
If the meaning is "if one *mahākappa*," then it follows that one *asaṅkhyeyyakappa* is measured by twenty intermediate *kappas*.
Alternatively, if the meaning is "one *asaṅkhyeyyakappa*," this must be examined as it contradicts the statement "sixty-four intermediate *kappas*" in every respect.
However, as for this [passage] in the *Kappaṭṭhakathā*:
It accords with the *aṭṭhakathā*; to show this, he said: “But ‘only at the destruction of the eon,’ etc.

Alternatively, one who is of natural character (*pakatatto*) and not one who has committed a defeat (*apārājika*). One who shares the same communion (*samānasaṃvāsaka*)—by virtue of having received the formal acts (*kamma*)—is one who does not live apart from the community (*anānāsaṃvāsaka*); such is the meaning to be understood here. The construction is:
“having denied the existence of a fixed person (*niyata-puggala*). In that context, “having denied” means: “the person... [The sentence continues: “...is not found. [End of fragment.]

Having thus denied [the existence of a fixed person] by saying, "But there is no such thing as a 'fixed person,'" he states the reason for this: "Because [a fixed person] does not exist by way of intrinsic nature (sabhāva), like the phenomena fixed in falsehood or fixed in truth.
For this so-called "fixed person" is a mere designation (paññatti-matta) based upon phenomena fixed in falsehood or fixed in truth.
"In the manner asked" refers to the mode of questioning beginning with, "Does the prior cause fix [the destiny]? and so forth.

The cause of determination (*niyāmakahetu*). "By which" means by that knowledge of insight (*vipassanā-ñāṇa*) belonging to the three higher paths. "The distinction between the determined and the undetermined" refers to the determined distinction of stream-enterers (*sotāpanna*) and so forth, and the undetermined distinction of those who have "seven births at most" (*sattakkhattuparama*) and so forth.

For it is said that the state of being determined for a stream-enterer is such that one alone is called "seven-births-at-most," another "one who goes from family to family" (*kolaṅkola*), and another "one-seeded" (*ekabījī*); thus he spoke [of this].
“And the stream-enterer is fixed. Here, the word *ca* (and) has the sense of exclusion (*byatireka*). “Prior to that” means prior to the path of stream-entry.

The statement “there is no function of a prior cause” was said with the intention of keeping in mind the fault that will be mentioned later, because it was stated that the stream-enterer’s state of being fixed [occurs] due to that.
When the higher paths possess supporting conditions (*upanissaya*), the first path must also possess supporting conditions.
Anticipating the objection that [the result] is already established, he says, "If indeed," and so forth. And that is its fixed nature. "Of this" means of the stream-entry path (*sotāpattimagga*).

"Exhausted by that very [path]" means exhausted by the stream-entry path itself; for the cessation of the fruit occurs through the cessation of its cause. "Than that" means than the state of being one who is reborn seven times at most, etc.
"That" refers to the state of being one who is reborn seven times at most, etc. "From the occurrence" means from the continuity of the resultant [consciousness].
“Ten” means by way of the stream-entry path (*sotāpatti-magga*). “In emerging” (*vuṭṭhāne*) means when there is emerging. Since there is no fruit without a cause, he said: “Sakkāya... must exist.

By the phrase “from the perspective of the cause for the designation,” he clarifies the determinative nature of the cause for the designation, because designations such as “one-seeder” (*ekabījī*) and so forth are not literal (etymological) names. Therefore, he said: “It was said with reference to insight... and so forth.
By the word "etc. (*ādi*), such passages as "I am the one, the perfectly enlightened one; I have become cool, I am extinguished" are included. And here, [the passage] beginning with:
"When asked, 'Is there anyone now, O Bhante, whether a recluse or a brahmin, who is equal to the Blessed One in perfect enlightenment?
I would say, 'No,'" and so forth, is also included. In this context, [it is said]: "There is no one equal to me; I am the one, the perfectly enlightened one."
It should be understood that by these words, the arising of another Buddha in another world-system is precluded, just as it is in this world-system.
For while [a Buddha] exists, it is impossible to say, "There is no one equal to me," and so forth.
As for what they say—that this was stated with reference to a specific world-system—that too is not the case, because there is no such qualification, given the power of the Buddhas.

And [it is said] because of the manifestation of the state of being incapable [of such power]. Here, the description of the field of authority (*āṇā-khetta*) is for the purpose of showing the nature of things (*dhammatā*);
for the Blessed One is able to exercise his command wherever he wishes.

And the phrase "in one world-system" is stated for the purpose of indicating the world-system that constitutes a Buddha-field (*buddha-khetta*). In this regard, the meaning is as follows: [that which constitutes] a Buddha-field...
This world-system is one. In it, at one time, only one perfectly enlightened Buddha arises. Therefore he said: "The Buddha-field...
[etc. ...the intention. "Therefore" means:
because the Pātimokkha depends upon full ordination (upasampadā), and full ordination depends upon going forth (pabbajjā), therefore [it is so]. Regarding the Pātimokkha:
When those [two], namely ordination (*pabbajjā*) and full admission (*upasampadā*), have been accomplished, then after that, it is said to be "ruined.

This means that after the final penetration (*pacchimapaṭivedha*), the teaching of penetration (*paṭivedhasāsana*) is ruined; and after the final breach of morality (*pacchimasīlabheda*), the teaching of practice (*paṭipattisāsana*) is ruined.
However, showing both together by treating them as one through their commonality as "the Teaching" (*sāsana*), he says: "After the final... having combined them into one."
"Lamentation and compassion" means the state of being pitied through lamentation, the act of pitying.

It is impossible to maintain the specific nature of phenomena (dhammasabhāvavisesa), since even when making the great earth tremble by taking the ocean as its limit during the investigation of the perfections (pāramīpavicaya) and so forth,
and on the day of the full enlightenment (abhisambodhi), [the earth shook] except for the eastern and northern directions.
At the foot of the Bodhi tree, the ground was unable to support the Great Being;
rather, the interior of the world-system (cakkavāḷa) turned over like a ship overloaded with an excessive burden when a heavy load is placed on one side.

To show that where it should have been said "samuppādikā," the vowel *a* has been changed to *ā*, and one instance of the consonant *p* has been elided, he says: "It rises up evenly, thus it is 'sāmupādikā'."
Or, it is called *samupādā* because it takes up [the object] evenly (*samaṃ upādiyatīti*); *sāmupādikā* is simply *samupādā*, meaning "that which takes up evenly" (*samupāhinī*).
"By way of the moment of continuity" (*santatikhaṇavasena*) should be construed as: by way of continuity, there is the possession of accumulation (*āyūhanasamaṅgitā*);

and by way of the moment of volition, through the grasping of what precedes and follows, there is the possession of volition (*cetanāsamaṅgitā*). When one [object] has appeared, by way of condition, [there is the grasping] of another...
Attendance and turning over.
The commentary on the exposition of the first power is finished.
The commentary on the exposition of the second power.
810. The construction is: "He does not know how to enjoy wealth; he destroys it.
The intended meaning is that life is subject to rapid change.
The intention is that he did not give [the gift] because it had arisen through the speech of another who was instigating him.
"By right application" means by right practice.
The commentary on the exposition of the second power is finished.
[Now begins] the commentary on the exposition of the fifth power.
813. "The individual essence of the elements" (dhātusabhāva) refers to the individual essence of the elements reckoned as the primary elements (bhūta), etc.

This is by way of their homogeneity (sabhāga) with respect to the fruit they produce. "By delimiting the element of inclination" means by knowing the individual essence of inclination after having delimited it as either "inferior" or "exalted," just as one knows the rain from an upper cloud by means of a great flood of water acting as a sign of rain.
The commentary on the exposition of the fifth power is finished.
Commentary on the exposition of the sixth power:
The verbal meaning arises through the compound ending alone, as that is how the word is established by grammatical rule. "Of those" refers to the successive ones, both the clear and the obscure.

Of the faculties beginning with faith. And "having done so" means precisely because the diversity of inclinations is distinguished from the knowledge of the higher and lower faculties (indriya-paropariyatta) by way of underlying disposition and so forth, and because the knowledge of the higher and lower faculties is distinguished from the diversity of inclinations by way of their distinct intrinsic natures. 815.
Having asked, "But what are those noble abodes (ariyāvāsa)?", he shows them by means of the sutta itself, citing the canonical text beginning with, "Here, monks... and so forth.

Having brought them forward and concluded with the words "thus it was said," he spoke the passage beginning with "In these" in order to show their attainment once again through the very attainment of the path.
Therein, "the others" refers to the six factors consisting of being endowed with the six limbs, the single protection, the practice, and so forth.

Regarding the phrase "in the underlying tendencies toward objects and toward the continuity [of existence]," this refers to the two types of underlying tendencies: the underlying tendency toward objects (*ārammaṇānusayana*) and the underlying tendency toward the continuity [of existence] (*santānānusayana*).

Just as lust that has not been eradicated by the Path—being worthy of arising when its conditions are met—is said to "underlie" (anuseti) the continuum in the sense of being firmly established, so too does it underlie a desirable object; thus should its underlying tendency toward the object be understood.
To show that this underlying tendency becomes manifest through its actual arising, the commentary states, "Just as if," and so forth.
It is said: by the phrase “habituated and thoroughly habituated,” it clarifies the long-term cultivation of lust toward a desirable object.
Furthermore, because it remains as if enveloping that which has been thus long-cultivated, it is said:
“it shows the state of being latent (anusayita) by way of its standing as if completely wrapped around. For it is indeed like one submerged in water.

It has been stated: “All phenomena belonging to the three planes are ‘sensual pleasures’ (kāmā) in the sense of being desirable,” and so forth; by means of such scriptural passages, it should be understood that even craving for existence (bhavarāga) possesses the quality of being a sensual object (vatthukāmatā).
“By way of lust” (rāgavasena) means by way of being colored by passion toward an object. 818.
The distinction of faculties refers to the knowledge of the higher and lower degrees of the faculties of those to be trained.
819. "One seeks the abandoner for the sake of the cessation of that which is afflicted by what is to be abandoned" means that first there is the object to be abandoned, and afterwards the abandoner;

this sequence of abandoning what is to be abandoned is expressed by the phrase "the sequence of abandoning. "Of which" (yassa) refers to that which is to be abandoned. "That" (taṃ) refers to what is to be abandoned.
"Is stated first" (paṭhamaṃ vuccati) means it is stated first among the investigations into abandoning. After that, [the abandoner].
That which is not to be abandoned, as in the case of the triad of vision (*dassanattika*) and so forth.
"That" refers to the life-continuum (*bhavaṅga*). "Of that" refers to the supramundane (*lokuttara*). "The basis" is said with reference to the life-continuum of one in their final existence.
The commentary on the exposition of the sixth power is concluded.
Commentary on the Exposition of the Seventh Power (Sattamabalaniddesa):
828. “He conceives ‘I have attained’” is the meaning.

The construction is: either concentration, or the meditation subject that has become its object, is the “casket of the mind. “To set down” means to cause the attainment-consciousness to proceed for the duration of time previously delimited.

"By that" means by perception and attention. "Having that as its nature" means having the nature of not lapsing into the second jhāna and so forth, such as the realm of sensual desire. "Skilled purification" is the purity of the jhāna established through its state of proficiency, which is the opposite of its adversaries.
The commentary on the description of the seventh power is finished.
The commentary on the description of the tenth power.
831. “Wisdom itself is liberation” (*paññāva vimutti*): the construction is that wisdom itself, having become liberated from lust and the other defilements, is liberation.

The meaning is: “The result of one kind of karma is indeed another kind of result,” because knowing the result of one kind of karma is the function of the second power, whereas knowing the karma itself is the function of the third power.
“Similarity to the powers” means similarity to some of the powers. But why, in this context, [is it said] regarding the functions of the powers and knowledge?
In response to the objection that the knowledge of the powers of jhāna and so forth was mentioned when [the powers] were being described, he says, "Even though," and so on.
"Included therein" means included within that seventh power-knowledge whose nature is the reviewing of jhāna and so forth. "In this way" means just like the knowledge of jhāna and so forth.

He says "to project and to transform" with reference to the manner previously stated by himself. Furthermore, there is also the function of certain types of knowledge, such as the abandoning of the origin [of suffering].
How could the knowledge of omniscience (*sabbaññutaññāṇa*) perform functions such as absorption (*appanā*) and the various meditative attainments (*jhāna*), which are not its province?

Rather, these are to be known by the powers of knowledge (*balañāṇa*). Furthermore, although it knows even beyond those, because it does not perform certain specific functions of the powers, it is shown that "the powers of knowledge are one thing, and the knowledge of omniscience is another," with the words beginning: "But it does not perform all their functions."
This is stated in the *Aṭṭhakathā*. Therein, it is said, "Having become that jhāna, let it enter," and so forth, by way of showing an illustration:
just as omniscient knowledge (*sabbaññutaññāṇa*) does not perform some of its functions because they are weak, so too [jhāna] does not perform some of its functions because they are weak.
To show this, it was stated: "Alternatively... should be seen."
The commentary on the Exposition of the Ten Powers is finished.
The commentary on the Exposition of Knowledge is finished.
17. The Exposition of Minor Matters (Khuddakavatthuvibhaṅga).
1. Commentary on the Singlefold Exposition (Ekakaniddesavaṇṇanā) 843–4.
"Dependent upon existence" (*atthipaccaya*) means the meaning of "dependent upon" (*paṭicca*) is "existence" (*atthitā*).

Even though [other types of conditions] such as co-nascence (*sahajāta*) and pre-existence (*purejāta*) exist, when something exists and another thing arises because of it, that [former] is made the condition for the latter; thus, in whatever manner it may be, the mere state of existence is here the meaning of "dependent upon."
This is the meaning. However, in order to make that sense of "dependent" (paṭicca) more evident by way of contrast, he said "just as" and so forth.

Therein, it is said "dependent" (paṭicca) because of the state of being a condition such as a support; thus, the eye and so forth, which function as conditions by way of being supports and other such conditions, are called "dependent.
"Of one faction" means: among the eighteen factions, we [belong] to such-and-such a faction.
"We were born, not like others who are unknown"—thus they explain the meaning here.
"Placing in front" means making someone the leader. A "hoard of wealth" is a collection of riches set aside by being buried. "Fame" (yaso) means lordship.
Furthermore, that [fame] becomes manifest among those over whom it prevails through the acts of appointing and commanding; thus it is called "the pride of appointment."
And it is said: "the intoxication of carrying out commands. 845.
"By way of the basis" means by way of the cause for the occurrence of birth and so forth. 846.
"The absence of a foundation" means the absence of a firm footing in wholesome kamma; and that, because of wholesome action...

It is not possible; therefore, he said, "it is impossible to perform what is wholesome. The construction is that this is the first among the synonyms for the state designated as negligence (*pamāda*).
By the word "etc. (*ādi*), the inclusion of such [states] as "the relaxation of the mind in verbal misconduct, mental misconduct, flattery, and disparagement" should be understood.
The passage beginning with "negligence is the act of neglecting" and so forth is an elucidation of that same meaning.
The connection is as follows: the phrasing that elucidates its synonyms, beginning with “the relinquishing of the mind, the non-arising of relinquishing,” is also limitless.
By the statement “it shows the four aggregates,” he says that the four unwholesome aggregates which occur in the mode of the relinquishing of mindfulness constitute negligence (*pamāda*).
847. A specific kind of pride consisting in the exaltation of the mind, which serves as the cause for an unshakeable state of conduct.

848. "Superiority" (*uttariya*) means the state of being superior (*uttara-bhāva*); by means of an instrument (*karaṇa*), it is "superiority by means of an instrument" (*karaṇa-uttariya*); through exertion, it is "superior action" (*uttari-kiriyā*) compared to the action of another. 849.
"According to the rules of etymology" (*neruttika-vidhānena*) means by the transformation of the vowels *i* and *a* into the letter *r*.

“Self-interest” (*attahita*) is explained as “self” (*atta*) by eliding the latter member of the compound, just as one says “form-existence is form” (*rūpabhavo rūpaṃ*) or “Bhīmasena is Bhīma. Alternatively, the etymological derivation of the word should be understood according to the method of *nirukti*, where the meaning of “that which has been taken up” (*ādinnō*) or “that which has been reached” (*patto*) is “self” (*atta*).
“Of one who is marked” (*mudditassa*) means of one who is branded.
850. “Even while the great multitude knows” refers to the conditions for clinging and so forth, such as fuel, water, robes, and other causes for fulfillment.
851. It is called a *gaṇṭhikā* because it itself forms a knot (*gaṇṭhi-karaṇa*). It has become a "knot" because its words are appropriate and because it pierces the knots of others. 852.
Because of its state of being indivisible within, because of being well-practiced, and because of being thoroughly cultivated. 853.
By virtue of having been developed over a long period, there is "moistening" (*temana*), which means making [the mind] wet; the meaning is that it flows out due to greed.
This being so, he says “and they criticize” (*khīyanti*) and so forth, in order to explain how it is that they criticize.

(854) Regarding “adornment with robes, etc. (*cīvaramaṇḍanādīnam*): this refers to these three—adornment with robes, adornment with bowls, and adornment with lodgings. Now, in order to show how these function as qualifiers, “by means of a robe,” and so forth, is stated.

(855) “Dissimilar” (*asabhāga*) means either devoid of similarity or the opposite of similarity; it is the state of being repulsive toward those things that are not agreeable. Therefore, he says: “arrogance and stubbornness, or opposition.”
856. *Saṅkampanā* (wavering) is instability or lack of attention due to longing and dissatisfaction; it is the yearning for this or that object. 857.
*Kāyassa* means of the mental body (*nāmakāya*). For when that is not agitated, the physical body (*rūpakāya*) is also not agitated. 860.
*Rāgādīnaṃ* means of lust, delusion, shamelessness, lack of moral dread, doubt, and so forth.
861. The connection is: "In order to show the threefold basis for hypocrisy (*kuhanā*). Regarding the phrase "therein" (*tattha*), it refers to the *Mahāniddesa*.

He says, "by means of this canonical text which serves as a support," because the teaching in the *Mahāniddesa* proceeds by relying on the method of exposition found here in the *Khuddakavibhaṅga*, beginning with: "Therein, what is hypocrisy? It belongs to one who is dependent upon gain, honor, and fame."
"Antarahitāni" means those that cut through while being inwardly deficient.
"Kohañña" is the display of a self-restrained appearance with the intention of gaining esteem, for the sake of gain, honor, and praise; thus he said:

"Koraja is the suppression of useless fluctuations of body and speech due to evil desire. One who is full of spiritual urgency (saṃvega) and conscientiousness [observes] what precedes and what follows...
Even when reflecting upon his own actions, he remains suspicious; thus, showing himself as if he were such a person, he is called "excessively suspicious.
864. "Censure by way of praise" means casting out or discarding someone from the basis of their praise, as in: "Oh, what a generous master!—though he is no giver at all."
865. *Gavesanakammaṃ* (the act of seeking) is the activity of seeking something great in exchange for a small gain.

866. *Pokkharaṃ* is said to mean "beautiful. Since the beautiful state of color is the perfection of color (*vaṇṇapāripūrī*), he says: "Or, the perfection of color is the beauty of color (*vaṇṇapokkharatā*).
879. Regarding the explanations of conceit such as "better": "In this context, what is the conceit of one who is better, thinking 'I am better'? and so forth.
Regarding the nine explanations of conceit (*māna*) that have been pointed out: the phrase "a person who is superior, etc.

is stated there because the nine types of persons, beginning with the superior, are touched upon in that Pāḷi text. However, here, since the persons are being touched upon, the "person who is superior" might also need to be included.
For this very reason, he said: "even in the state of conceit as being superior. In the phrase "even in the state of conceit as being superior," the particle *pi* (even/also) is inclusive.

Because the person who does not honor [others] has already been treated in the *Aseyyamānaniddesa* (the Exposition on the One Who Does Not Honor). "Of anyone whatsoever" means of any person whatsoever among those such as those who sleep and so forth. 880.
"Of the former conceit" refers to the conceit of similarity that occurred previously, or to inferior conceit; however, the text was transmitted specifically by way of the conceit of similarity. 881.
Because of the statement, "The jackal is among the beasts, but the crow is among the birds," he said: "Among the species of birds, the crow is the base one."
882. *Virāga* is *arahatta* (Arahatship). 883.

*Mānasampayuttachanda* is the desire associated with craving (*taṇhāchanda*). Alternatively, it is the desire for agency associated with conceit (*mānasampayuttakattukamyatāchanda*), which follows the nature of conceit and proceeds by way of grasping at superiority and so forth;

thus it is called *mānachanda*. 884. *Tattha* means "in that" [state] to be accomplished through delay. *Yuttaṃ* means suitable or appropriate. *Muttaṃ* means released or relaxed. *Siliṭṭhaṃ* means smooth or coherent, or else that which clarifies two meanings.
"Anuddayasseva" means "as if feeling loving-kindness (mettā) or as if feeling compassion (anukampā). He says "of one who rejoices together, etc.
because it refers to the affection based on worldly life that occurs under the guise of loving-kindness and so forth; this is the meaning. Therefore he says, "such lust. The meaning is appropriate:
in this way, the meaning of the Pāli word "tattha" is also appropriate. For that thought is accompanied by concern for others, having concern for others as its cause.

890. Because the world for the most part esteems the fulfillment of the strands of sensual pleasure, it is said: "One aspires to the strands of sensual pleasure solely for the sake of not being despised.
The commentary on the Exposition of Single Terms is finished.
2. Commentary on the Exposition of Pairs.

891. "It binds" (*bandhati*) means it binds and constrains the mode of being angry. For resentment (*upanāha*) is like something that binds the mind to the basis of the grievance (*āghātavatthu*); for even if it has proceeded otherwise, as long as the resentment is not known [to have ceased], it remains dependent upon the basis of the grievance.
892. "Having cut with the teeth" means having removed one part and taken another part, as if cutting with the teeth;

this is the intended meaning. 894. "Having committed an offense" (*accayaṃ katvā*) means having transgressed. "In concealment" (*paṭicchādanē*) means in the concealing of the offense committed by oneself.

“Cutting off” (vocchindana) means severing by way of not admitting the act of transgression. “Concealment by cutting off” (vocchindanachādanā) means the hiding [of the fault] through that very cutting off.
He said, “He who does not speak rightly is a rogue (saṭha),” because in the world the word *saṭha* is conventionally established in the sense of speaking improperly.
To show that a rogue resembles a yakṣa or a boar, he said, “Neither its belly nor its back can be discerned,” or rather, it should be regarded as being like a magical illusion (*indajāla*).

One who, although his underlying disposition (*ajjhāsaya*) is entirely corrupted, deceives the world by presenting himself as if he were accomplished through mere outward conduct of body and speech, and thus proclaims himself to be one thing while being quite another—of him it is said:

"Therefore, this deceit (*sāṭheyya*) should be regarded as a form of deception even more powerful than trickery (*māyā*). For trickery is simply the concealment of existing faults. "By that very [fact]"...
It is precisely because there is no deception by those who possess greater strength. For in the *Daḷhakaraṇīya*, it is stated that "it is being fully equipped.
By the word "even" (*pi*) in the phrase "even in its absence," he shows: "How much more so when it is present!

For even though the function of the fetters such as lust for form (*rūparāga*), which is assisted by the adherence to a self (*attābhinivesa*) and so forth as appropriate for worldlings (*puthujjana*) and certain trainees (*sekkha*), [is not performed by the Noble Ones].
It accomplishes [its purpose]; however, for some, even without those [means], because no defilement whatsoever has been suppressed, sensual existence (kāmabhava) is not liberated in any way.
Thus, it is called "internal" (*ajjhatta*) as a specific condition for internal grasping;

and due to the absence of that [grasping], it proceeds in the form and formless existences (*rūpārūpabhava*), which are designated as "external" (*bahiddhā*), performing exclusively the function of fettering (*saṃyojana*).

For this very reason, it is called "external fetter" (*bahiddhāsaṃyojana*) because it arises from the cause of the state of external fetters for beings belonging to the fine-material and immaterial realms.
He stated this point when he said: "The fettering of personality-view and so forth... is what is called 'fettering'.
The commentary on the Exposition of Pairs is finished.
3. Commentary on the Exposition of Triads 909.

Just as through ignorance (*avijjā*) and craving for existence (*bhavataṇhā*), so too through hatred (*dosa*)—which has envy (*issā*), stinginess (*macchariya*), and dejection (*domanassa*) as its companions—there occurs the formative activity of existence (*bhavābhisaṅkharaṇa*). Therefore, it is said: "The unwholesome roots themselves are the roots of the round (*vaṭṭamūla*). For this reason, he said: "By three... [etc. ...it is explained. 919.

Because the resultant states of the fine-material and immaterial spheres possess a state of being peaceful and sublime, they are most excellent; therefore, attachment to existence (*bhavarāga*) is stated to be predominant therein.
920. *Mānena ṭhapanā* means establishing oneself through conceit (*māna*) by way of [considering oneself] superior and so forth. "Establishing" (*ṭhapanā*) also means burning or uplifting.
921. *Tamsampayuttā* means associated with hatred (*dosa*). 922.
*Tesaṃ vaṇṇabhedaṃ* means the distinction in the complexion of those living beings, or having heard them speaking in such a manner.
"Pervasive" (*byāpī*) means pervading the entire world, or pervading the entire body. "Spherical" (*parimaṇḍala*) means being spherical in size, even down to the measure of an atom (*paramāṇu*).
By the word "etc. (*ādi*), it includes [sizes] such as the measure of a thumb or the measure of a youth.

(923) "Born of seasonal change" (*utuvipariṇāmaja*) means produced by the shifting of seasons such as cold and so forth. "Resulting from an effort" (*opakkamika*) means produced by one's own or another's corresponding exertion.
That born from uneven postures (*visama-parihāra-ja*) arises from the body’s maintenance in an uneven position through such means as sitting for a long time or standing for a long time.
That born from a derangement of the humors (*sannipāta-ja*) arises from the convergence of the three humors (*doṣa*), each assuming an uneven state starting from the time of their accumulation.

That originated by karma (*kamma-samuṭṭhāna*) arises from karma alone, independent of changes in the seasons and so forth. As for those originated by bile, phlegm, and wind (*pitta-semha-vāta-samuṭṭhānā*), [they arise] from bile and the others...

They are stated as such by way of predominance. For the three types of defilement (*doṣa*) are the proximate cause for every disease, since there is no occurrence [of disease] without the provocation of the defilements.
Karma is the primary cause, because it arises only when that [provocation] has been provided with scope; the other, however, should be regarded as its cooperative cause.
Those who maintain the doctrine of past-action causality (*pubbekatahetuvāda*) reject this, [claiming] that even the fruit to be experienced in the next life...

He uses the word *kira* (it is said) to indicate his lack of approval for the position that [kamma] has its cause in what was previously done (*pubbekatahetuka*), because that kamma belongs to the past;
thus he says, "and they reject [the idea of] what is to be experienced upon rebirth (*upapajjavedanīya*).
(924) "By way of being a cause of burning" means by way of being the cause for the burning of the ten kinds of fires, such as lust, and for the burning of the fires of hell.
926. *Puthunimittasabhāvesūti*: in the individual natures (*sabhāva*) of various causes such as the defilements (*kilesa*).
931. *Addanaṃ addā maddavo*: because verbal roots have multiple meanings, it is said that "lack of softness" (*anaddā*) is the opposite of that; thus he says, "or lack of softness is *anaddā*. 936.
Because it has improper attention (*ayoniso-manasikāra*) as its cause, the function of advertence (*āvajjanā*) should be understood as being conducive to the unwholesome (*akusala*).
The commentary on the Exposition of Threes is finished.
4. Commentary on the Exposition of Fours: 939.
"By the word ‘thus’" means by the word ‘thus’ in the sense of illustration; this is the intended meaning. Existence itself, when increased, is [called] *abhivuddha*.
Non-existence (*abhava*) is, for example, as in the case of "the qualities of one beyond training" (*asekkhā dhammā*).
In the second alternative, it should be understood that by the terms *bhava* and *abhava*, success and failure, or increase and decrease, are expressed.
"Improper course" (*agati*) means an unsuitable course, that is to say, an unbecoming action.
“Agitation through anger” … [and so on] … “or women as a danger from waves and the like”—this is the construction. Regarding the mention of the five strands of sensual pleasure and women:
this refers both to the mention of the five strands of sensual pleasure and to the mention of women.

Although the view that “pleasure and pain are self-made” exists among other proponents of views as well, it is called the “Timbaruka view” because Timbaruka, holding such a view, approached the Blessed One and questioned him.
Thus it was said. Therefore he said: “Because the *timbaruka*... has arrived.
The commentary on the Exposition of the Tetads is finished.
5. Commentary on the Exposition of the Pentads.
940. The intention is that [the term] "coming" refers to the grasping of rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*).
941. "From accumulation" means from increase. "In another way" means that it is apprehended in a manner other than through acquisition or conjecture;

showing this, he said, "by means of faith, inclination, and so forth. For faith arises from hearsay (*anussava*), whereas inclination can arise even from the knowledge of remembering past births (*jātissara-ñāṇa*).
[The word] "etc. (*ādi*) includes patience (*khanti*) and the other [virtues]. 942.

Those whose root is impatience (*akkhanti*) are called "rooted in impatience" (*akkhantimūlaka*). Faults such as misconduct (*dukkaṭa*), wrong speech (*dubbhāsita*), and so forth, are such types of misconduct of body, speech, and mind. 943.

The lack of tranquility (*avūpasama*) characterized as agitation (*udaggatā*) is not what is meant by restlessness (*uddhacca*); rather, it refers to the state of being diffused (*savipphārikatā*) which belongs specifically to joy (*pīti*).

He speaks of that which is not the true nature [of things]. "Becoming a cause for non-quiescence" means becoming a cause for distraction. "The mode of occurrence of joy" refers to the manner in which joy manifests.
The commentary on the exposition of the pentad is finished.
6. Commentary on the Exposition of the Hexad.
944. "Ten" refers specifically to anger and the rest, because they are the roots of dispute.
945. "Constant application to the wholesome" (*kusalānuyoga-sātacca*) means persistence in the practice of what is wholesome.

"Socializing with a group" (*gaṇasaṅgaṇikā*) is the gathering together (*saṅgaṇi*) or meeting (*saṅgati*) with a group (*gaṇa*), that is, with a collection of seven people. "Of anything," such as food, clothing, and so forth.
946. *Upatthapetīti*: having approached the object (*ārammaṇa*), one reflects upon it. 948.
*Adhiccasamuppanniko*: one who holds the doctrine that "the self and the world have arisen fortuitously.
The commentary on the exposition of the six [factors] is finished.
8. Commentary on the Exposition of the Eightfold [Factors] 952.
"By way of sinking" means by way of not exerting oneself in the task that ought to be done.
958. They say: "These are the views of non-perception; they speak by means of these."
The commentary on the Exposition of the Octad is finished.
9. Commentary on the Exposition of the Nonad (Navakaniddesa) 960–963.
"Of the tenth" refers to the non-place killer (aṭṭhānaghāta).

"Inward" (ajjhatta) is intended here as "inward in terms of the range of experience" (gocarajjhatta); this is the meaning of the statement in the verse. "Having concluded" (niṭṭhapetvā) means having adhered to [the view]. 964.

Since other factors such as contact (phassa) and so forth are conditioned by their respective conditions, in order to show the specific manner in which conceit (māna) functions with particular intensity, it is said:
"I am," and "I am. "Of self" (attanoti) refers to that which is imagined through the various speculative views (diṭṭhigata).
Just as [the movement] of conceit occurs by way of its intensification, so too the occurrence of craving occurs by way of "mine-ness," and that of views occurs by way of "permanence" and so forth;
yet, although they are alike in not apprehending the future time, it was said: "They will be... and so on.

However, since [the state of] "I am" belongs only to that which is currently occurring, the state of being "shaken" and so forth is described only with reference to conceit, which is common to all the terms.
This has been stated in the commentary (*aṭṭhakathā*).
The explanation of the exposition on the groups of nine is finished.
10. Explanation of the Exposition on the Groups of Ten.
970. *Saṅkappana* (conceiving) is a synonym for the term "skillfulness" (*kusalatā*) that was mentioned. Regarding that reflection on means: its falsity is its state of being blameworthy.
Delusion in that mode is the delusion present in a mental state that occurs in the manner already described. Also, regarding that aforementioned reflection, and also regarding the evil committed:
the perception associated with overestimation occurs by way of seeing another person as being of ordinary nature, and so forth.
The occurring consciousness associated with views should be understood as being grasped as "liberation," like a fruit.
The commentary on the Exposition of the Decads is finished.
The commentary on the Exposition of the Wanderings of Craving begins.

973. "Without making a distinction" means without comparison—that is, without making this division between comparing what is equal and what is unequal. That which is expressed by the terms "thus," "in this way," and "otherwise" [is the distinction].

"Of the distinction" refers to that very distinction as previously stated: "thus," "in this way," and "otherwise. By the word "view" (*diṭṭhi*), craving (*taṇhā*), which is inseparable from that view, is indicated when the view is grasped.
"By the four heads and twelve roots" means by the four heads and the twelve [roots].
And [the phrase] "together with those rooted in views" is to be construed as: "and craving itself is shown.

If the grasping at views and conceit were also intended here—since it is stated in the *Aṭṭhakathā* that "[they are included] because of the grasping at the mass by way of craving, conceit, and views"—then how can there be the expression "craving-proceedings"?
To this he says: "In views and conceit," and so forth. "Because they are rooted in that" means because they are rooted in craving.
"974. It is not cast away (*anavakārī*); having made it thus not cast away, he says 'having made it not cast away' while clarifying that term by means of another word.
Dispersion (*vikkhepana*) is division according to parts. 'Without separating it from the self' means without making it distinct from that self which is imagined by those who hold wrong views."
976. The construction is: craving that proceeds by approaching the forms and so forth belonging to the external world is called "clinging" (*upādāna*).

Regarding the statement, "for a certain person, within a single existence, there may be the non-occurrence of some type of craving's wandering (*taṇhā-vicarita*), while for another there is its occurrence," he says: "It was stated for the purpose of showing the occurrence of such [craving] in someone.
The commentary on the exposition of the wanderings of craving is concluded.
The commentary on the Analysis of the Minor Subjects is finished. 18.
The Analysis of the Heart of the Dhamma.
1. Commentary on the Section on the Compendium of All.

978. Regarding the passage beginning with “Dhātusambhava... pe... saṅgahitattā,” the application [of the meaning] should be understood through analysis as follows: “because the aggregates (khandha) and so forth—which are distinguished by their arising within the realms such as the sense-sphere realm (kāmadhātu)—are included without remainder. The same applies to the remaining cases, starting with “distinguished by the various categories of what is included (pariyāpanna),” and so on.
In that context, by the phrase “because they are included without remainder,” this is designated as the “all-inclusive section” (sabbasaṅgāhikavāra), as it conforms to its actual meaning.

He shows [this] by means of the term "convention" (*samaññā*). And because here there is a complete inclusion of the twelve sections, such as the aggregates (*khandha*) and so forth, it should be understood that the second section and those following are included herein.
For it is appropriate to say that the investigation of their arising and so forth—pertaining precisely to those aggregates and the rest—is the section showing their occurrence and non-occurrence;
this is the construction [of the sentence]. Furthermore, the demonstration of non-occurrence here is established through logical implication (*atthāpatti*).
It should be understood that there is no textual passage (pāḷi) such as "How many aggregates do not appear" regarding that [matter].
979. "In accordance with the question" means according to the intention with which the question was asked. Unerring explanation (*avitatha-vyākaraṇa*) is unique (*āveṇika*) to the Buddhas alone;
for others, it is merely arbitrary and like the syllables of what has been heard. Therefore, he said: "Because it was made after understanding the speech of the Omniscient One."
The commentary on the section on the comprehensive inclusion is finished.
2. Commentary on the Section on Arising and Non-arising: 991.

Having stated "in the sensual existence" (*kāmabhava*) by way of the plane, he says again "and of those born in the sensual element" (*kāmadhātusambhūtānañca*) in order to speak by way of the continuity of sentient beings.
To show that specific meaning of what was stated, he said: "By means of psychic power... [the] purpose. Why was it said, "It should not be so stated"?

Even though the visible-object base (*rūpāyatana*) is beyond the range of non-percipient beings because they lack eyes, and because it is extremely subtle, and because it is not the domain of those belonging to lower planes, it is nevertheless the domain of the eye-base (*cakkhāyatana*) of those belonging to the same plane—the Vehapphala gods—and of those belonging to higher planes—the Suddhāvāsa deities.
It can be said that "it becomes a resort" means it simply performs its function as a sense base (*āyatana*) and so forth.
Whatever remains to be stated here in detail has already been explained below.
The phrases beginning with "having made the Avīci hell the lower limit and including the Paranimmitavasavatti devas above" refer to the spheres such as the sense-sphere realm (*kāmāvacara*).
And those groups of beings are called "elements" (*dhātu*), because they are the constituent parts and the support of the aggregate, just as a heap of beans is called "beans.
It is the arising of beings (*satta*) therein that is "the arising of beings" (*sattuppatti*);

in the sense of being what arises, beings themselves are the arising—thus should the designation "arising of beings" be understood for both the world of space and the world of beings. Arising by way of the state of a being...
The intention is that they do not exist merely as formations (*saṅkhāra*) like the non-clung-to aggregates (*anupādinnakkhandhā*). As to what they are, he says:
"By way of the abodes of beings... [etc. ...the clung-to aggregates. "Of those included in this or that" means of beings included in this or that abode of beings, or of formations themselves.
"By way of having a similar basis" means of the aggregates that occur in a similar manner.
By way of being a foundation. For, in the majority of cases, phenomena in that abode of beings proceed in a uniform manner.
The commentary on the section concerning arising and non-arising is finished.
3. Commentary on the Section Concerning the Included and the Unincluded.

999. Therein, "elsewhere" (*aññattha*) means in that [present] existence (*bhave*) and in another [future] existence, as well as in [other] locations (*okāse*). They are called "included" (*pariyāpanna*) because they have been delimited and grasped by the craving for sense-pleasures (*kāmataṇhā*), etc., which acts as a delimiting factor; thus, they are "included" in this or that existence, being contained within this or that [realm].
The commentary on the section concerning the included and the non-included is finished. 6.
The Section on Productive Kamma and the Duration of Life (*Uppādakakamma-āyuppamāṇavāra*)
1. Explanation of Productive Kamma (Uppādakakammavaṇṇanā) 1021.
"By way of the three elements, the beings, and the deities" means by way of the deities reborn within the three realms, such as the sense-sphere realm (*kāmāvacara*).
The explanation of productive kamma is finished.
2. Commentary on the Life Span 1026.
It shines and glows like a well-polished golden mirror; thus it is *subha* (splendid). That which is strewn (*kiṇṇā*) or covered (*vikiṇṇā*) by that bodily radiance (*subha*) is *subhakiṇṇā*.
1027. "Various acts of attention" refers to the attention directed toward the limited earth-kasiṇa and so forth. "Even at the moment of absorption" means...
By the word *pi*, the preceding stage is included. *Chandana* is the seeking of an object; it is the desire characterized by the wish to act (*kattukamyatā-chanda*).

*Paṇidhāna* is the fixing of the mind; it is aspiration (*paṇidhi*), which is the distinguishing of the object through the fading of perception (*saññā-virāga*) and so forth, and is simply the making of that [object] the focal point for the development (*bhāvanā*) proceeding in such a manner.

"Vipula" means great. Since even the state of peace (santabhāva) is great by virtue of its majesty, it is said: "Vipulā phalā means having results such as vast peace, happiness, long life, beauty, and so forth. 1028.
That which is the lifespan of the gods of the Four Great Kings is one day and night in the Sañjīva hell;
thirty nights of that duration make a month; twelve months of that duration make a year; and five [years] of that year...
The lifespan in the Sañjīva hell is one hundred years. That which is the lifespan of the Tāvatiṃsa gods is a single day and night in the Kālasutta hell...
[and so on] ...by that reckoning of years, the lifespan in the Kālasutta hell is one thousand years.
That which is the lifespan of the Yāma gods is a single day and night in the Saṅghāta hell... [and so on] ...by that reckoning of years, [the lifespan there] is two thousand years.
The lifespan in the Saṅghāta hell is as follows: that which is the lifespan of the Tusita devas is one day and night in the Roruva hell...
[and so on] ...by that reckoning, the lifespan in the Roruva hell is four thousand years. That which is the lifespan of the Nimmānarati devas is one day and night in the Mahāroruva hell...
[and so on] ...by that reckoning, the lifespan in the Mahāroruva hell is eight thousand years.
The measure of lifespan: That which is the measure of the lifespan of the Paranimmitavasavatti devas is one night and day in the Tāpana hell...
[and so on] ...by that year, the measure of lifespan in the Tāpana hell is sixteen thousand years. In the Mahātāpana hell, it is half an intermediate aeon (antarakappa).
They say that in the Avīci hell, the measure of lifespan is one full intermediate aeon. It is like the death of devas occurring according to their own inclination.
It should be understood that because death may occur even in the interim due to such power of merit, it is said that "kamma alone is the measure.
And by taking this view, the determination of the lifespan limits for the *abbuda* and other stages becomes more logical.

What is "jhāna"? Among the eight jhānas, which jhāna is it? "Summits of existence" (*bhavasīsāni*) means the peaks of existence; [here it refers to] the summit of existence for worldlings (*puthujjana*).

The "noble state" (*ariyabhava*) refers to the "summit of all states," which is a designation for the *vehapphala* heaven and others. The phrase "of some beings" refers to the worldling (*puthujjana*);
"of some five" refers to the stream-enterer (*sotāpanna*) and the once-returner (*sakadāgāmin*); and "of some three" is stated with reference to the non-returner (*anāgāmin*).

Therefore, one should understand that such a person, having passed away from the Brahmakāyika and other heavens, is reborn in the formless realm (*arūpa*). [This applies] to those among the nine Brahma-worlds...

With the intention that the reading in the Aṭṭhakathā is “for noble disciples who have been reborn [there], there is only rebirth in that very place, not rebirth in a lower place,” the passage beginning with “But as for what...

was stated. However, if the reading were “there is rebirth in that place and rebirth in a higher place, but not rebirth in a lower place,” then there would be no purpose for the statement beginning with “only rebirth in a lower place is excluded. [This concerns] rebirth in the formless realm (arūpadhātu).

And the connection is that [rebirth] is not excluded. Rebirth in the formless realm (arūpadhātu) is not excluded because the restriction—that "one attains final nibbāna while still standing at the very top"—is not intended [to apply there].
"Elsewhere" means in the sense-sphere world (kāmaloka).
"There" means in the fine-material world (rūpaloka). This is the commentary: "In the plane of the first jhāna..."

The commentary proceeds thus: “...is reborn... [and so on] ...attains final Nibbāna. “For that very reason” means because it is one who has already been reborn in the fine-material sphere (*rūpadhātu*) who is intended, not one who is merely destined for rebirth there; it is for this specific cause.

“Of him” refers to the noble disciple (*ariyasāvaka*) who has been reborn in the fine-material sphere as previously described. By means of that lust for form (*rūparāga*) through which he was reborn there in the fine-material existence, by means of that [lust], [he is liberated] through the immaterial jhāna (*arūpajjhāna*).
When the dangers of views and so forth have been properly suppressed, he says, "Again...
it will surely not be," showing that just as there will be no longing for future existence in the realms of sense-desire and form, so too there will be none in the formless realm.
In this context, "reborn" means having arisen in the fine-material element (*rūpadhātu*). "Having developed the noble path" means having accomplished the lower noble paths.
"By way of seeing the danger in the state of rebirth" means by way of seeing the danger in that very same fine-material existence (*rūpabhava*), even though one has been reborn there.

"One whose desire for existence has not turned back" means one who has not relinquished the aspiration for higher existence in the formless realm (*arūpabhava*), and is therefore worthy of being reborn in the formless element (*arūpadhātu*).
"By way of such a person" means by way of such a noble disciple (*ariyasāvaka*). "For some five, for some... [and so forth].
“Three underlying tendencies underlie”: thus this Yamaka-pāḷi proceeds.
The commentary on the measure of the lifespan is finished. 7.
Commentary on the Section on What is to be Directly Known, etc. (Abhiññeyyādivāra)

1030. “Matter has the characteristic of being molested; feeling has the characteristic of experiencing,” and so forth—this refers to the discernment of general characteristics. “Contact has the characteristic of touching; pleasure has the characteristic of gratification,” and so forth—this refers to the discernment of specific characteristics.
Regarding such statements as “the four aggregates may be wholesome,” whatever needs to be said here has already been stated in the *Khandhavibhaṅga* and other texts;
therefore, the intention is that it should be understood according to the method explained therein. As for the rest that has not been stated here:
"That is indeed easy to understand.
The commentary on the section beginning with "to be directly known" is finished.
The commentary on the *Dhammahadayavibhaṅga* is finished.
Thus ends the sub-commentary on the *Vibhaṅga*, titled the *Līnatthavaṇṇanā*,
within the commentary (*Ṭīkā*) known as the *Sammohavinodanī*.
